column12: Variant of Ah, from Chinese 阿 (ā), used in front of the last character of someone’s given name to express familiarity or friendliness (traditionally used in rural or southern Chinese dialects). It is also a Hokkien honorific prefix to rank seniority for kinship terms.
Sundanese diminutive of masculine names containing the sound ab (or other similar sounds), such as Abdullah or Abdurrohman.
Means "name of the angel" in Arabic. It is rarely used in India.
Estonian form and Finnish variant of Abel.
Means "glow, luster, brilliance" in Hindi. See Abha.
Alternate transcription of Arabic/Urdu عابد (see Abid).
Means "fleeting, transient, passing by" or "interpreting" in Arabic.
Uralic short form of Abram 1 or Abraham.
From Persian آبرو (ābru) meaning "honour, reputation, face".
Diminutive of Agathe, as well as names that begin with agi meaning "sword".
Diminutive of names beginning with agi meaning "sword".
Short form of Adriaan and Adrianus.
Urdu, Somali, and Estonian form of Adam.
Alternate transcription of Hindi आदर्श (see Adarsh).
Old Swedish variant of Odde or Adde.
Of uncertain origin and meaning. Theories include a derivation from Estonian aade "idea, thought" (compare the Finnish masculine name Aate).
Variant of Adel, a short form of names starting with the Germanic name element adal "noble".
Derived from Sanskrit आदेश (ādeśa) meaning "order, mandate, injunction".
Alternate transcription of Tamil ஆதவன் (see Adhavan).
Tamil and Malayalam form of Sanskrit Ardra (the name of a nakshatra in Indian astronomy).
Means "original power" or "first creator" in Sanskrit.
Alternate transcription of Adil as well as the Urdu form.
Derived from Sanskrit आदिश् (aadiś) meaning "design, intention, aim".
Derived from the Sanskrit word "Aaditya" meaning "Sun."
Estonian short form of Adam or Adolf.
Originally a vernacular form of Aadolf and Aadam, now used as a given name in its own right.
Alternate transcription of Arabic عافية (see Aafiya), as well as the Urdu form.
Alternate transcription of Arabic عافية (see Aafiya).
Frisian feminine form of Ave, with the diminutive suffix ke included.
Diminutive of names beginning with Alf meaning "elf".
Variant of Affo recorded in the 19th and 20th centuries in East Frisia.
Variant of Affo with the diminutive suffix -ko recorded in the 19th century in East Frisia.
Alternate transcription of Arabic عفرا (see Afra 2) chiefly used in North Africa.
Variant transcription of Afreen used by Muslims in India.
Derived from the Persian آفرین (âfarin) meaning "bravo!, well done!".
Feminine form of Aage, or perhaps a variant spelling of Ågot.

Form of Åke found in church records from the 15th century. Note that there were no standardized spelling of names in Sweden at this time; someone called Aaghe in one document could be called Aakæ in another, for example.
Short form of Agatha. In some cases there might also be a connection to Age 1.
Means "order, command" in Hindi and Nepali, ultimately from Sanskrit आज्ञा (ājñā).
Sundanese diminutive of names containing the sound ah (or other similar sounds), such as Aminah or Solahuddin.
A variant of the Arabic name Aahil, meaning "great king" or "emperor."
Possibly from Sanskrit आह्लाद (aahlaad) meaning "exultancy, hilarity, rejoicing".
Archaic Frisian short form of names that contain the element agjō or adal.
Diminutive of names beginning with Agi or Adal.
Derived from the Arabic word عَائِلَة (ʿāʾila) meaning "family".
Derived from Urdu آئینہ (ā'īnā) or Hindi आईना (āīnā) both meaning "mirror", ultimately from Persian آئینه (â’ine).
Alternate transcription of Arabic عائشة (see Aisha).
Alternate transcription of Urdu عائزہ (see Aiza).
From Greenlandic -aaja, an affix used for and by children used as a name.
From a childish pronunciation of the Greenlandic word angaju "older sibling of the same sex" (see Angaju).
Means "dear older sibling" in Greenlandic, from a combination of Aaju and the diminutive suffix nnguaq "sweet, dear, little".

Form of Åke found in church records from the 15th century. Note that there were no standardized spelling of names in Sweden at this time; someone called Aakæ in one document could be called Aaka in another, for example.
Means "desire, wish" in Sanskrit. (See feminine form Akanksha)
Alternate transcription of Hindi आकाङ्क्षा or आकांक्षा (see Akanksha).
Alternate transcription of Hindi or Marathi आकाश (see Akash).
Possibly a dialect form of Âkasik.
Finnish diminutive of many names with the ak sound, both masculine and feminine ones.
Alternate transcription of Arabic عاكف or Urdu عاکف (see Akif).
Finnish diminutive of Aron or Abraham
A'akuluujjusi is the great creator mother among the Inuit people.
A variant of Alayah, likely influenced by the spelling of Aaliyah.

A knight from whom Caradoc, one of Arthur’s knights, rescued a maiden named Guignier. After their duel, Aalardin and Caradoc became friends, and Aalardin accompanied Caradoc to Arthur’s court.When Guignier (whom he once loved), wife of Caradoc Briefbras, lost her breast to a serpent when aiding her husband, Aalardin supplied a magic shield boss which provided a golden breast.He married Arthur’s grand-niece Guigenor. His father was named Guiniacalc.
Variant of Alderich recorded in the 18th century in East Frisia.
Estonian form of Alla and Estonian diminutive of Rosalia.
Dutch short form of Adolf and West Frisian short form of Alef and Alof, which are both Frisian variants of Adolf.
Variant of Elijah perhaps influenced by Aaliyah.According to the USA Social Security Administration, 11 boys and 15 girls were recorded with the name Aalijah in 2017.

East Greenlandic name of uncertain meaning, perhaps partly derived from the Greenlandic suffix -lik meaning "equipped with" (which indicates that the first element is amuletic or a form of helper spirit).
A variant of Aaliyah likely influenced by Lily.
Short form of Aaliparti, a Greenlandic form of Albert.
Means "nice character, good disposition" in Mongolian, from ааль (aali) meaning "disposition, conduct" and сайхан (saikhan) meaning "nice, beautiful, handsome".
Variant of Alivia, likely influence by names like Aaliyah.
Means "water nymph", from Finnish aalto, meaning "wave", combined with feminine suffix -tar.
Perhaps a Bengalized form of Alcyone (the brightest star in the Pleiades, in Western astronomy).
Variant of Alrich recorded in the 19th century in East Frisia.
Means "wave" in Finnish. More commonly used as a surname.
Variant of Aliana, possibly influenced by the spelling of Aaliyah.
Variant of Alicia (probably influenced by the name Aaliyah).
Sundanese diminutive of names containing the sound am (or other similar sounds), such as Amir 1, Purnama, Aminah or Amilia.
This is the Hawaiian name for Grapsus tenuicrustatus, a rock crab with yellow back. The 'A'ama crab is strong and swift thus another meaning of this name is "a swift, strong warrior" in Hawaiian.
Derived from Greenlandic aama "glow, glowing coal" (cf. Aamaq) combined with the diminutive suffix nnguaq meaning "sweet, dear, little".
According to Diu Crône, a knight whose nickname was “the other Gawain,” due to his uncanny physical similarity to Sir Gawain.
Means "oh Allah, accept our prayer" in Arabic. This is a cognate of the English word amen.
Alternate transcription of Arabic/Urdu عامر (see Aamir 1).
Means "worker" in Arabic. It may also mean "one who hopes", making it related to Amal 1.
Means "bait, lure, something that tempts" in Sanskrit.
Alternate transcription of Arabic آمنة or Urdu آمنہ (see Amna).
Possibly a variant of Aanor influenced by Latin amor "love".
Derived from the Ojibwe word aanakwad meaning "cloud" and ikwe meaning "woman".
Derived from the Ojibwe word aanakwad meaning "cloud" and inini meaning "man".
Derived from the Ojibwe word aanakwad meaning "cloud" and meskwa meaning "red".
Variant of Aanarsi; a Greenlandic form of Anders.
Said to be a Greenlandic form of Hansina or Hansigne; compare Hansiina. Also compare the masculine name Aanasi (a Greenlandic form of Anders).
Possibly a variant of the Sanskrit Anaya or as a modern English name, a variant of Anaya.
Alternate transcription of Hindi आंचल (see Anchal).
Form of Åne, a variant of either Ånund, Ånje 2, or Áni.
Variant transcription of Devanagari अंग (see Anga).
From Äänisjärvi, the Finnish name for Lake Onega, a lake in East Karelia Russia.
Variant of Anjan. A known bearer is Aanjjan Srivastav (1976-), an Indian actor.
Means "she was brought down inside" in Bandial.

Variant of Azenor. Folk etymology likes to associate this name with Éléonore due to confusing the variant Aenor with the possibly Germanic name Aenor borne by the mother of Eleanor of Aquitaine (see Eleanor for further information).
A shortened version of Adamardis or Adenordis.
This theophoric name means "the mercy of God is abundant", coming from the Yoruba words àánu ("mercy"), Ọlọ́run ("God"), and pọ̀ ("abundant, plentiful").
Steward of the castle Amonstus and the vassal of Lady Fortune. He hosted Gawain during the knight's visit to the country.
Alternate transcription of Arabic عواطف (see Awatif) chiefly used in Morocco.
Means "the beautifully red one" in Greenlandic, originally a byname.
Alternate transcription of Arabic and Urdu عاقب (see Aqib).
Sundanese diminutive of names containing the sound ar (or other similar sounds), such as Lazuardi or Aryani.
Means "one who adorns, beautifier" in Arabic.
Alternate transcription of Hindi आराधना (see Aradhana).
Variant of Aradhya. This name was used by Indian actress Aishwarya Rai for her daughter born 2011.
Variant of Aara, though it may also be used as a feminine form of Aaron.
Alternate transcription of Persian آرش (see Arash).
Derived from Estonian aare "treasure" and cognate of Finnish Aarre.
Variant of Aria 1, the spelling is influenced by that of Aaron.
Variant of Ariana influenced by Aaron.
Variant of Eric influenced by Aaron.
Variant of Erica influenced by the spelling of Aaron.
Variant of Ariel. This is the name of an angel found inscribed on an Ophitic amulet, alongside the name of the god Ialdabaoth.
Alternate transcription of Arabic/Urdu عارف (see Arif).
Means "first ray of sun" in Hindi.

The name Aarit has its origins in Sanskrit and is primarily used in Indian cultures. It carries meanings associated with nobility and virtue, often interpreted as "one who seeks the right path" or "honorable."
Variant of Aria 1, the spelling is probably influenced by Aaliyah.
Feminine form of Ariaen, a medieval variant of Adriaan.

From Sanskrit अर्ण (árṇa) meaning "wave, flood, stream" (which is related to अर्णव (arṇava) "ocean", the source of the masculine name Arnav). This is said to be an epithet of the Hindu goddess Lakshmi, who emerged from the Ocean of Milk (Kshira Sagara) during the churning, leading some to consider her a 'daughter of the ocean'.
Combination of Aaron and Leigh, modeled on the name Ashley.
Modern Greek variant and Lithuanian form of Aaron.
Either an elaborted form of Aarona or a feminization of Aaron.
Possibly from Ho-Chunk Ahuru’ąwįga meaning "raise wing".
Means "words of the Rishis" or "ancient" in Sanskrit. Rishis were Vedic poets who composed hymns and invoked deities with poetry.
Derived from Sanskrit आर्षेय (arśeya) meaning "of sacred descent" or "respectable, venerable".
Means "belonging to the Sun" in Odia.
Sundanese diminutive of feminine names containing the sound as (or other similar sounds), such as Asiyah, Astuti or Hasanah.
Commonly derived from Estonian aas "meadow", this name might have originally been a variant of Aase.
Alternate transcription of Hindi/Marathi/Nepali आशिष (see Ashish).
Means "someone who gives shelter" in Sanskrit.
Means "blessed and victorious" or "little mare" in Hindi.
Alternate transcription of Arabic/Urdu آصف (see Asif).
Alternate transcription of Arabic آصفة or Urdu آصفہ (see Asifa).
Alternate transcription of Arabic آسيا or آسية or Urdu آسیہ (see Asiya).
Alternate transcription of Arabic أسماء (see Asma) chiefly used in North Africa.
Variant of Åsta. A notable bearer is Aasta Hansteen (1824-1908), Norwegian painter, writer and early feminist.
Variant spelling of Åste predominantly used in the Telemark region of Norway.
Urdu or possibly Arabic form of Asya
Means "thought" or "ideology" in Finnish. It is also used as a short form of Aatami and Aadolf.
Said to be a Tamil name meaning "star", "prayer", "light", "lightning" or "quick".

Aathreya comes from Sanskrit and refers to the descendant of the sage Atri, a significant figure in Hindu tradition and one of the Saptarishi (seven great sages). The name is associated with wisdom, intelligence, and a rich cultural heritage, often used as a name or surname in South India and other Indian communities.
Alternate transcription of Arabic or Urdu عاطف (see Atif).
From Hindi आतिश (ātiś) meaning "fire, flame", of Persian origin.
Sanskrit for one with knowledge of self

column3: ああと(Japanese Hiragana)|亜々人, 吾々斗, 亜吾都, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 亜 (a) meaning "second, Asia", 々 used to duplicate 亜 combined with 人 (to) meaning "person", 斗 (to), which refers to a Chinese constellation or 都 (to) meaning "metropolis, capital, all, everything". Other kanji combinations are possible.This is the Japanese form of Arto or Art.

Means "calf" or more specifically, "young bull" in Basque. In Basque mythology, Aatxe is either the androgynous deity Mari 3 embodied as a young cow or bull, or a lesser shapeshifting spirit that takes the form of a bull and occasionally a human; the latter emerges at night, especially in stormy weather, from his cave dwelling in the Basque mountains.
Manx form of Eve via Old Irish Eua.
From Sanskrit आवेश (avesa) meaning “frenzy, excitement, impulse”.
Originally s short form of Avraham, now used as a given name in its own right.
Alternate transcription of Hindi आव्या (see Avya).
Means "rode the enemy's horse" in Siksika.
Means "intelligence; happiness" in Hindi and Arabic.
A Hindu name meaning “long life”. It is a variant of Aayush and Aayushi.
Alternate transcription of Hindi आयुष (see Ayush).
Alternate transcription of Hindi आयुषी (see Ayushi).
Meaning uncertain, perhaps a derivative of the Arabic verb زين (zayyana) "to adorn, to decorate". This name was used by Indian cricketer Gautam Gambhir for his daughter born 2014.
Meaning, "goes across the sky woman" or "the hanging cloud."
Means "born on Thursday" in Fante, a dialect of Akan.
The name of a god from Guaraní mythology credited with creating the moon.
Senegalese form of the Arabic name Abu Bakr.
Ababuo means a child that keeps coming back. This name is mainly used in Ghana
Found in the Arvisurák (Arvisuras), an eclectic system of myths and a book summarising the beliefs contained in them, written down by Zoltán Paál. Not supported by scholars.

Variant of Abacucco. It concides with the Italian word for abacus, a calculating tool that was in use in the ancient Near East, Europe, China, and Russia, centuries before the adoption of the written Hindu–Arabic numeral system.
From Spanish abad "abbot", after saint Anthony the Great (known in Spanish as san Antonio Abad, "saint Anthony the Abbot"). This name is often given as the compound name Antonio Abad.

Derived from Portuguese abadia "abbey", this name is usually used in reference to the title of the Virgin Mary Nossa Senhora da Abadia "Our Lady of the Abbey". The title itself goes back to a Marian apparition near the Abadia do Bouro in Braga, Portugal. Nossa Senhora da Abadia is the patron saint of Uberaba.
Means "a person from the sea" in Ijaw.
Means "mighty father". This was a Phoenician name for the highest deity. It was borne by a legendary Coptic saint who was martyred with his sister Irais (or Iraja, Herais, Rhais).
Perso-Arabic-origin multi-part name consisting of the elements Abad and ḥaqq.

Latinized form of Greek Ἀβαῖος (Abaios) meaning "of Abai", an epithet of the Greek god Apollo, given because the ancient town of Ἄβαι (Abai) (see Abae) in Phocis was the site of an oracle of the god and of a temple dedicated to him.
Means "they are not dead" or "undead" in Zulu.
The meaning of Abagbe is we begged to have this one to lift up
Derived from the Biblical Hebrew name, potentially meaning "father of Gor."

Etymology unknown, possibly derived from a prefixed form of the Old Persian name Bagadata. Other sources claim it may mean "fortunate", from the Avestan word gabata "fortunate one" or Sanskrit baga "fortune", or (less likely) "father of the wine press" from Hebrew אָב (ʾav) meaning "father" and גת (gat) meaning "winepress" or "wine vat". In the Book of Esther, this is the name of one of the seven eunuchs of the court of King Ahasuerus of Persia.

Possibly from the Manchu abdaha ("leaf"). This was the personal name of Nurhaci's fourth primary consort, who was given the posthumous name Empress Xiaoliewu. The usage of this name to refer to Hong Taiji is apparently now considered to have been mistaken on the part of Western scholars, he is never recorded in contemporary sources as bearing this name.
The meaning is uncertain and unknown.
Means 'east' or dawn' and comes from the Gilbertese language (the language of Kiribati)
Meaning unknown. In demonology, Abalam is a king of Jinnestan and one of the assistants of Paimon. This demon was featured in the 2010 film 'The Last Exorcism'.
Abam’s meaning is “second child after twins”
Arabized form of Apamoun, as apa- typically becomes aba- in Arabic, since Arabic doesn't have the phoneme /p/.

From Middle Persian ābān meaning "waters" (plural of āb), from Avestan āpas. In modern Persian it refers to "the eighth solar month of the Persian calendar (October-November)". In Persian mythology, this is also the name of the Angel of October.

Means "daughter of the waters" (or possibly "daughter of Aban", the name of a yazata or angel in Zoroastrianism), from Middle Persian ābān meaning "waters" (plural of āb) combined with دخت (doxt) meaning "daughter". By some accounts, this was the name of a wife of Darius III, the last Achaemenid emperor.
Arabized form of Apanoub, as apa- typically becomes aba- in Arabic, since Arabic doesn't have the phoneme /p/.
This was the name of a brother of Shilu. The meaning is uncertain.
Means "one who has birthed or fathered relatives", derived from Shona kubara "to bear offspring, to bud" and hama "relatives". This is the Shona equivalent of Abraham.

Derived from Greek ἀβάρβαρος (abarbaros), ἀβόρβορος (aborboros) meaning "without filth", itself from α (a), a negative prefix, and βόρβορος (borboros) meaning "mud, mire, filth". This was the name of two naiads (nymphs) in Greek mythology.
This name is mentioned in the Vita Lebuini antiqua as belonging to a widow in Frisia, who hosted Saint Lebuinus and his companion Marchelmus.
Meaning unknown. In Greek mythology Abaris was a sage, healer and priest of Apollo who came to the Athenians as envoy from the Hyperboreans when famine was affecting Greece.
Meaning unknown, though it may be a feminine form of Abraham.
Alternate transcription of Arabic عباس (see Abbas), as well as the Indonesian and Malay form.
Bosnian female form of Abbas. It is also the name of the 80th sura of the Qur'an.

Latinized form of Abaskantos. However, it is also possible that in some cases, this name is derived from the Latin adjective abascantus meaning "unenvied".This name was also used as a Roman cognomen; sometimes by (former) slaves, but not always.
Alternate transcription of Pashto اباسين (see Abasin).
Means "it is God that loves" or "God's love" in Ibibio and Efik.

Derived from the Greek adjective ἀβάσκαντος (abaskantos) meaning "protected against enchantments, free from harm", which consists of the Greek negative prefix ἀ (a) and the Greek verb βασκαίνω (baskaino) meaning "to bewitch, to cast an evil spell upon".
Combination of the honorific title Abba "father" and skhyron "the strong". This was the name of a 3rd century Coptic martyr.
Borne by the American sculptor, social activist and suffragist Abastenia St. Leger Eberle (1878-1942), who was the daughter of Canadian parents.
Son of Galehaut in La Tavola Ritonda. He ruled the castle Ferelois, where he held a tournament during the Grail Quest. His counterpart in French romance is Galehodin.
Of uncertain meaning. This was the name of a prince of the Qing dynasty who held the title Prince Raoyu of the Second Rank.

Means literally, "father of the Uthre" in Mandaean, which translates roughly to "father of the angels," derived from aba "father" combined with uthra ('utria) "angel". In the Mandaean Gnostic cosmology, Abatur is "the third of four emanations from the supreme, unknowable deity", and the father of Ptahil, the Mandaean demiurge.
Means "little father" in Hebrew. The rabbi Nachmani (see Nachman) (c. 280 – c. 339) was known as Abaye, to differentiate him from his grandfather with the same name.
Means "you are the Nile" in Amharic.
Derived from Aramaic אבא (’abā’) meaning "father", which is ultimately derived from Proto-Semitic ʾab meaning "father".
Borne by Abbad ibn Bishr, a companion of the Prophet Muhammad.
Means "servant of Abbas", from the given name Abbas and Qulu meaning "servant, slave".
Alternate transcription of Arabic عباس (see Abbas).

From Latin abbatissa meaning "abbess". While this was more usually found as a title, there are a handful of English occurrences of it used as a given name. Also compare the Old English masculine name Abbud.
Variant of Abbe with the diminutive suffix -cke recorded in the 16th and 17th centuries in East Frisia.
Diminutive of Abraham, Albin and Albert.
Variant of Abbe recorded in the 16th century in East Frisia.
Variant of Abbe recorded in the 16th century for men and in the 17th century for women in East Frisia.The suffix -en can either be of patronymic nature or an old hypocorostic name suffix.
Variant of Abbes influenced by French orthography.
Variant of Abbe recorded in the 17th century in East Frisia.
Obscure variant of Abigail based on the words abbey and gale.
Abbia is a slightly longer form of Abia, which is a form of Abijah.
Variant of Abbe recorded from the 16th to 19th centuries in East Frisia
Combination of Abbie and Jean 1. Used the FX tv show 'Archer' for Lana's daughter-- the character is named after show creator Adam Reed's own grandmother.
Variant of Abbe recorded in the 19th century in East Frisia.
Name of the actress Abbilyse Caudle. It is likely a combination of the names Abby and Elise.

Variant of Abbe recorded in the 16th century in East Frisia.The suffix -ing was originally used for patronymic names, Abbing was probably the son of Abbe, but later it became a general diminutive suffix.
Means "knight; strong, mighty" in Hebrew. It is also a variant transcription of Abir.

Either from Proto-Germanic *abô meaning "husband, man", or a diminutive of Alberich and other names beginning with Old High German alb "elf", as well as a Frisian diminutive of Old High German names beginning with the element adal "noble" and a second element beginning with b (compare Abe 2). This was borne by the 10th-century French saint Abbo of Fleury.
French and Dutch variant of Abbo.
Uzbek and Tajik form of Abbas.
From the given name Abbos combined with the Turkic military title beg meaning "chieftain, master"
Transferred use of the surname Abbott.
Derived from Arabic word "abd", and meaning "servant of God". One notable bearer is Abboud Al-Abboud from the TV show Block 13.
Derived from Old English abbud meaning "abbot".
Variant of Abbe recorded in the 15th century in East Frisia.
Variant of Abigail. This name was given to 63 girls in the year 2007.
Rare variant of Abilene using the popular suffix -lyn. Also an combination of Abby and Lynn.
From the first five letters of the English alphabet. This name is chiefly used in Texas.
Variant of Abbe with the diminutive suffix -cke recorded from the 16th to 18th centuries for men and in the 18th century for women in East Frisia.
Spanish traditional transcription of the name Abdullah.
Means "servant of the giver" from Arabic عبد ال (ʿabd al) meaning "servant of the" combined with Aati "giver, bestower".
Means "servant of the just" in Arabic.
Means "servant of the highest" from عبد (ʿabd) meaning "servant" combined with عليّ (ʿalīy) meaning "lofty, sublime".
Means "servant of the all-knowking" from عبد (ʿabd) meaning "servant" combined with عليم (ʻalīm) meaning "learned, expert, scholar".
Means "servant of the mighty" from Arabic عبد (ʿabd) meaning "servant" combined with عظيم (ʿaẓīm) meaning "magnificent, great, powerful".
Alternate transcription of Arabic عبد العزيز (see Abd al-Aziz). Abdalaziz Alhamza (1991-) is a Syrian journalist, human rights defender activist and IT trainer.
Means "servant of the everlasting" from Arabic عبد (ʿabd) meaning "servant" combined with باقي (baqi) meaning "eternal, everlasting".
Means "slave of the wise" in Arabic, from عبد (ʿabd) meaning "servant, slave" and البصير (al-basir) meaning "the wise"
Means "servant of the expander" from Arabic عبد ال (ʿabd al) meaning "servant of the" combined with باسط (basit) meaning "expander, extender".
Means "servant of the all-forgiving" from Arabic عبد (ʿabd) meaning "servant" combined with غفار (ghaffār) meaning "much-forgiving, inclined to forgive".
Means "servant of the ever-forgiving" from Arabic عبد ال (ʿabd al) meaning "servant of the" and غفور (ghafur) meaning "forgiving, merciful".
Alternate transcription of Arabic عبد الحفيظ (see Abd al-Hafiz) chiefly used in North Africa.
Means "servant of the preserver" from Arabic عبد (ʿabd) meaning "servant" combined with حفيظ (ḥāfiẓ) or حافظ (ḥāfiẓ) both meaning "preserver, guardian, keeper".
Means "servant of the patient" from Arabic عبد (ʿabd) meaning "servant" combined with حليم (ḥalīm) meaning "patient, tolerant, mild".
Means "servant of the almighty" from Arabic عبد (ʿabd) meaning "servant" combined with جبار (jabbār) meaning "almighty, powerful".
Means "servant of the exalted one" from Arabic عبد (ʿabd) meaning "servant" combined with جليل (jalīl) meaning "great, important, exalted".
Means "servant of the beautiful one" from Arabic عبد (ʿabd) meaning "servant" combined with جميل (jamīl) meaning "beautiful".
Abd al-Jawad means "servant of the merciful".
Means "servant of the creator" from Arabic عبد (ʿabd) meaning "servant" combined with خالق (khāliq) meaning "creator, maker".
Alternate transcription of Arabic عبد الله (see Abd Allah).
Means "servant of the beneficent" from Arabic عبد ال (ʿabd al) meaning "servant of the" combined with منان (mannan) meaning "beneficent, benevolent, generous".
Means "servant of the messiah" from عبد (ʿabd) meaning "servant" combined with مسيح (masīḥ) meaning "anointed, messiah". This name is primarily used by Arabic-speaking Christians.

Means "servant of the Messiah", from Arabic عبد ال (ʿabd al) and المسح (masih) "messiah, Christ". It was borne by a ninth-century martyr who was executed for reverting to Christianity after having converted to Islam. It is typically used by Christian Arabs.
Means "servant of the dishonorer" from Arabic عبد (ʿabd) meaning "servant" combined with مذلّ (mudhill) meaning "giver of dishonor" or "humiliator," one of the 99 Names of Allah.

Means "servant of the believer" from Arabic from Arabic عبد (ʿabd) meaning "servant" and مُؤْمِن (muʔmin) meaning "mu'min, believer". This was the name of a prominent member of the Almohad movement who was the founder and first caliph of the Almohad Caliphate.

Uncertain etymology, probably a hellenised form of a Phoenician name. Alternatively, could mean "the man with the whip", from Hesychian Greek ἄβδης (abdes) meaning "whip, scourge". In Greek mythology, Abderos was considered a divine hero as a son of the god Hermes, or in some accounts of Poseidon or Thromius. He is most notably known for his tragic role in Heracles' eighth labour, where he was eaten by the Mares of Diomedes.

column12: Means "begged to be born" in Yoruba, from bẹ̀ "beg, pray" and bí "to give birth, be born". Compare Abeni.
Variant of Abbe with the diminutive suffix -co.The suffix -co is in earlier times a masculine latinisation of the diminutive suffix -ke, later it became used as a diminutive suffix on it's own.
Bengali form of Abida. Compare the masculine form Abed.
Possibly means "she/he sees in the distance" in Ojibwe, from Ojibwe waabi "she/he has vision, sees" and debaabam "see at a distance". It also means "seen at dawn; dawn" in Chippewa.
Means "Where do I stay?" in Alur language. It is given to someone who is born to a parent or parents who are disliked by, or in conflict with, their familymembers or community.
Persian and Albanian form of Abidin.
Means "The one who came with the masquerade" in Yoruba.
Means "born on Wednesday" in Fante, a dialect of Akan.
From the Arabic عَبِير‎ (ʕabīr) meaning "scent, perfume".
Means "the one who pouts" in Bandial.
Possibly from Spanish abeja (meaning "bee"), ending in a similar fashion to Abundio.
Means "one begged to care for" in Yoruba.
Languedocian, Provençal, Gascon, Franco-Provençal and Haitian Creole form and Walloon variant of Abel.

Obsolete Low German short form of both Apollonia and Alberta. There is, however, another theory which derives this name from Old Saxon aval "strength; force; fortitude". This name was also occasionally used in southern Sweden and got accepted by Icelandic authorities in the early 2000s.
Polish and Guernésiais form of Abélard.
Italian and Spanish feminine form of Abelardo and Niçard feminine form of Abelart.
North Frisian variant of Apollonia recorded on the island of Föhr.
Form of Abel with the nominative suffix, used in Georgian when the name is written stand-alone.
French and Hungarian form of Abelia.
Feminine form of Abel. Abelia is also a type of flowering shrub in the honeysuckle family, named after British surgeon and naturalist Clarke Abel (1780-1826).
Spanish elaboration of Abelia, Niçard diminutive Abelìa as well as a German feminine form of Abel and a German elaboration of Abela.
Coined by Sabino Arana Goiri and Koldo Elizalde as a Basque equivalent of Avelina 2 and Aveline.
Variant of Abbe recorded in the 19th century in East Frisia.
Variant of Apollo used in Crete.
German diminutive of Abela and Abelina.
Variant of Abbe recorded in the 17th century for men and women in East Frisia.
East Frisian variant and Milanese Lombard form of Abel.

The object of Tor's first quest in Le Morte d'Arthur by Mallory. Abelleus stole a white brachet from Arthur's hall; Tor tracked him down and retrieved it. Having promised Abelleus's head to the hound's owner, Tor reluctantly decapitated him.

Some scholars have postulated that Abellio is the same name as Apollo, who in Crete and elsewhere was called Abelios (Greek Αβέλιος), and by the Italians and some Dorians Apello, and that the deity is the same as the Gallic Apollo mentioned by Caesar, and also the same as the Belis or Belenus mentioned by Tertullian and Herodian.Other scholars have taken the reverse position that Abellio might have been a similar solar deity of Celtic origin in Crete and the Pyrenees, but the Cretan Abellio may however not be the same god as the Celtic one, but rather a different manifestation, or dialectal form, of the Greek god Apollo or his name.
Hebrew name meaning meadow on the waters.It was an ancient city located in Upper Galilee, northern Israel (thought to be the modern-day site of Abil-el-Ḳamḥ).

Abenámar is the main character of El romance de Abenámar anonimously written and set in 1431. Abenámar is either King Yusuf IV (Abenalmao) himself or one of his courtiers. The poem is a dialogue between Abenámar and King John II of Castille, who wishes for complete possession of Granada (that occurs only in 1492).
Probably from アベ (abe) meaning "fire" and ナンカ (nanka), combined from ナン (nan) meaning "face" and カ (ka) meaning "top."

Of Guanche origin, possibly from *abănăšar(a) meaning "great tear" or "great separation". This was the name of the wife of Tenesor, the last guanarteme or king of Gáldar on the island of Gran Canaria, during the European conquest of the Canary Islands in the late 15th century. She was also the mother of Guayarmina.

Abeona is the ancient Roman goddess of outward journeys, departures, and safe travels. She is best known for protecting children taking their first steps, as well as watching over individuals as they leave their homes or comfort zones for the first time.

Possibly means "she stays at home" in Ojibwe, from Ojibwe abi "s/he is at home, sits in a certain place" and ishkwii "s/he stays behind" or nazhikewabi/anzhikewabi "s/he lives alone, is home alone, sits alone".
Means "I'm better" or "I'm good" in Alur language.
Variant of Abraham recorded in the 17th century in East Frisia.
Possibly a form of Abraham, as it supposedly means "he who has many children" in Romani. It is the name of a character in the television show 'Peaky Blinders'.
From Guanche *aberəwwi-keyyă, meaning "dented skull". Alternatively, it may mean "swarthy".
Italian and Spanish form of Abercius (see Aberkios).
Transferred use of the surname Abercrombie.
Means "mouth of the Don (river)" in Scottish Gaelic. This is the name of the name of a city in northern Scotland, as well as several other cities worldwide named after the Scottish city.
Means "from the mouth of the river" in Welsh.

Variant of Aberford, a village in West Yorkshire, meaning "Eadburg's ford" in Old English. This was the name of schoolmaster Albus Dumbledore's more eccentric brother in J. K. Rowling's 'Harry Potter' books, released between 1997 and 2007.
Variant of Abraham recorded in the 16th century in East Frisia, possibly a misspelling.

Uncertain etymology, possibly derived from Latin aberceo meaning "to keep away, ward off". This name was borne by a 2nd-century saint of Phrygia in Asia Minor, a bishop and wonderworker of Hieropolis who is the subject (and probable author) of an early Christian inscription.
Transferred use of the surname Abernathy.

Coined in the 19th century by Sabino Arana Goiri who based it on Basque aberri "fatherland; homeland" (ultimately derived from Basque aba "father" and herri "country; village; people, nation"). The name was in use until 1939. After the Spanish Civil War, however, women answering to Aberria were forced to change their name due to its "conflict-laden meaning".
Means "sacrificial" in Welsh, from aberth "sacrifice". This was the name of an evil druid in the movie 'Arthur and Merlin' (2015).

column3: 愛鈴(Japanese Kanji)|あべる(Japanese Hiragana)|アベル(Japanese Katakana)
column12: Transliterated form of Abel (for boys), in use among the Japanese in recent years.For girls, it can also be written into kanji as 愛鈴 with 愛 (ai, ito.shii, kana.shii, me.deru, o.shimu, mana, a) meaning "love, affection" and 鈴 (rei, rin, suzu, beru), read like the English word bell, which is what that kanji means.It is very rarely used.
Means "the one who respects elders" in Yoruba, derived from a meaning "one person", bẹrù meaning "fear, be afraid" and àgbà meaning "elder".

Aberycusgentylis Balthropp, baptized 25 January 1648 in Iver, Buckinghamshire, England, was named in honour of the Italian-born Oxford professor and jurist Alberico Gentili (1552-1608) via the Latinized form of his name: Albericus Gentilis.

Georgian form of Abessalom, which is the hellenized form of the Hebrew name 'Avshalom (see Absalom).In Georgian literature, Abesalom is the name of a central character from the medieval Georgian folk epic Eteriani. He also features in the opera that was based on the tale, namely Abesalom da Eteri (1919) by Zacharia Paliashvili (1871-1933).
Means "one who has complete possession or control" in Bengali.
Transferred use of the surname Abeson.

Coined by Sabino Arana Goiri who based the name on Basque abes "to sing" and the suffix -ti. According to R. M. Azkue, by 1927 abesti had acquired the meaning "song" and has been in everyday use as a synonym for the older kanta ever since.

From Classical Syriac ܐܒܓܪܐ (abgara) meaning "lame". This was the name of 10 rulers of the ancient kingdom of Osroene, including Abgar V Ukkama, said to be one of the first Christian kings, having been converted by Thaddeus of Edessa, one of the seventy disciples.A notable modern bearer of the name is Assyrian-Swedish professional footballer Abgar Barsom (b. 1977).
Derived from Sanskrit आभरण (ābharaṇa) meaning "ornament, decoration".

The name Abhayankari is of Sanskrit origin, and is used mostly in Hindi speaking countries but also in a few other countries and languages of the world.Sanskrit is regarded as the ancient language in Hinduism, where it was used as a means of communication and dialogue by the Hindu Celestial Gods, and then by the Indo-Aryans. Sanskrit is also widely used in Jainism, Buddhism, and Sikhism.

In Buddhism, Arhat Abheda (also known as Abhedya or Subinda) is one of the Sixteen Great Arhats, legendary disciples of the Buddha tasked with protecting the Dharma until the arrival of the future Buddha, Maitreya. He is revered in Mahayana and Vajrayana traditions as an eternal custodian of the teachings.

Abhijnaraja is a highly revered figure in Tibetan Buddhism, best known as the "King of Clear Knowing" or "King of Supreme Knowledge". He is one of the Eight Medicine Buddhas who make up the healing mandala. His name derives from the Sanskrit term abhijna, which means "higher knowledge," "direct perception," or "supernormal knowledge"

From Sanskrit अभिनन्दन (abhinandana) meaning "greeting, welcoming, praising, applauding" and नाथ (nātha) meaning "master, lord". In Jain tradition this is the name of the fourth of the 24 tirthankaras (enlightened spiritual teachers).
From Sanskrit अभिनव (abhinava) "young, fresh" and गुप्त (gupta) "protected". This was the name of a Kashmirian philosopher, mystic and aesthetician who lived during 950 to 1016 CE.
Meaning: “expression in an act”Also: an art of expression in Indian classical dances
Means "acted (as in a play)" in Hindi.
cow-herd, The name of destiny, The mighty one
Abhisarika is an Indian name meaning "optimistic," "brave," and "creative".
Alternate transcription of Thai อภิสิทธิ์ (see Aphisit). A notable bearer is former Thai prime minister Abhisit Vejjajiva (1964-).
From Old Irish ablach "having apple trees".

In the Cthulhu mythos, Abholos (aka Devourer in the Mist) is a great grey, festering glob of endless malevolence.According to one account he is a product of Ghisguth and Zstylzhemghi mating , which gave birth to Tsathoggua. This made Abholos more of a self-willed placenta that had taken form in-and-of-itself, rather than a brother or cousin of the others.According to another account, Abholos is a spawn of Cthulhu, born from his bile and tears.

From the English word abhor "to regard with horror or detestation". It is the name of the executioner in William Shakespeare's 'Measure for Measure' (written in 1603 or 1604; first published in 1623).
Means "father of strength". In the Bible, this was one of David's thirty warriors.

Means "my father has gathered" in Hebrew, derived from אָב (ʾav) meaning "father" and the verb אסף (asap) meaning "to gather, to collect" (compare Asaph). This name is mentioned in the Old Testament as belonging to a son of Korah son of Izhar (the cousin of Moses and Aaron).
Georgian and Romanian form of Abiathar.
Abiatha, Hathes, and Mamlacha were virgins and martyrs of the Beth-Garma province of Syria.
Has its origins in the Moroccan language and means "first child born after the grandmother has died."
Italian and Spanish form of Abibus.

Latinized form of Ἄβιβος (Abibos) or (Habibos), which is also found written as Ἄββιβος (Abbibos) or (Habbibos). It is a hellenization of the Hebrew name Aviv, and not of the Arabic name Habib, which most people would think at first glance.Notable bearers of this name include the Syrian saints Abibus of Samosata (died in 297 AD) and Abibus of Edessa (died in 322 AD).
Means "my father is might" or "father of strength" in Hebrew.
Variant of Abbe recorded in the 17th century in East Frisia.

Interpreted as meaning "my father took knowledge", "the father knows" or "father of knowledge", derived from Hebrew אָב (ʾav) meaning "father" combined with י (i), the letter yod (which probably turns אָב (ʾav) into a possessive form, meaning either "my father" or "father of", depending on the context) and the verb ידע (yada') meaning "to know" (as well as "to have intimate relations"). This name is mentioned in the Old Testament as belonging to a grandson of Abraham and Keturah through their son Midian. He had four brothers: Ephah, Epher, Hanoch and Eldaah.
Alternate transcription of Arabic عابدة (see Abida), as well as the usual Malay and Indonesian form.
Form of Abida used in Dagestan.
Directly taken from Turkish abide meaning "monument".
From Arabic عابدين (ʿābidīn), the plural of عابد (ʿābid) meaning "worshipper, adorer". It is sometimes used as a shortened form of Zayn al-Abidin.
From the name of a town in the Basque region of Spain.

Means "my father is help" in Hebrew, derived from אָב (ʾav) "father" and עֵזֶר (ʿezer) "help". It belonged to three men in the Old Testament—the second son of Hammoleketh, a warrior in King David's army, and the prince of the tribe of Dan.
Dutch form of Abigail and French variant of Abigaïl.
Variant of Abigail. Masculine usage is mostly restricted to Latin America and the Philippines (though it is still more often used as a feminine name in that part of the world).
Esperanto and Romanian form of Abigail.
Form of Abigail used in some versions of Greek Bible.
Variant of Abigail. This name was given to 35 girls born in the United States in the year 2010.
Italian form of Abigail, used for a character in Verdi's opera 'Nabucco' (1842).
Variant of Abigail used in the Norwegian translation of the Bible.
Variant of Abigail. In some Bible translations Abigal is mentioned as the daughter of Nacha and the mother of Amasa.

In Christian demonology, this was an upper demon ("great duke") of hell. Allegedly Abigor (also known as Eligor and Eligos) was the demon of war, in command of 60 legions, portrayed riding a winged or skeletal steed. He made deals with princes, selling them the secrets of military victory in exchange for their souls.
Form of Abiel used in the Latin Old Testament.
Means "the father is glory" or "father of glory". It is the name of two characters in the Bible.

From Hebrew אֲבִיָּם (ʼĂḇīyyām) meaning "my father is Yam" or "my father is the sea" (or "father of the sea"), derived from אָב (ʾav) "father" and ים (yam) meaning "sea" (which was also used to mean "west" (i.e. seaward) as well as "the future", as 'east' corresponds to 'past'); alternatively the last element could be the name of Yam, a Semitic god of the sea. This name was borne by the second king of Judah (who was also known as Abijah).
Means "born to treasure" or "born to be pampered" in Yoruba, from bí "to give birth, be born" and kẹ́ "to cherish, care for".
An Arthurian knight who was unsuccessful in the Perilous Passage (Passage Perilleux) adventure.
One of four brothers who aided their uncle, Duke Calles, in a revolt led by Calles’ sons.
The name of a character (played by actress Geraldine Chaplin) in the 2011 movie There Be Dragons, a period drama set during the Spanish Civil War of the 1930s.
From the given name Abyl combined with the title khan meaning "king, ruler"
Possibly a combination of Abyl and Mansur. This was the birth name of Kazakh ruler Ablai Khan (1711-1781), see Abylay.
Abilyx was a Roman nobleman from Hispania who appeared in The Histories of Polybius.
Form of Abimael used in the Latin Old Testament.
Armenian form of Abimelech. Rarely used nowadays.
Means "I was born for the lord".
Means "my father is king", deriving in part from the Phoenician element 𐤌𐤋𐤊 mlk ("king"). Name borne by a prince of Tyre known from his correspondance with Akenhaten, recorded in the Amarna letters.

Means "my father is generous" in Hebrew, derived from the noun אָב (ʾav) meaning "father" and the verb נָדַב (nadav) "to give willingly" (by implication "to be noble"; also compare Nadab). This was the name of three Old Testament people, including one of King Saul's sons, one of Jesse's sons (thus a brother of King David), and a Levite who housed the Ark of the Covenant for 20 years.

From the Hebrew abi "my father" and nadi "present with you," meaning "my father is present with you." In The Book of Mormon, Abinadi is a prophet who preaches to a wicked king and his corrupt priests that God will come down and be with man, among other messages. For refusing to deny that message, the king has him burned at the stake. One of the corrupt priests, Alma, heeds his teachings and eventually becomes a prophet himself.
Son of Chemish, Nephite historian, and Nephite warrior.
The name comes from the Guru Granth Sahib Ji and it means to be imperishable or lasting forever.

Means "my father is pleasantness" or "father of delight", derived from the Hebrew roots אָב (ʾav) meaning "father" and נָעַם (naʿam) meaning "to be pleasant". In the Old Testament this name belonged to the father of the famous general Barak.
An invented name, possibly inspired by the sounds of names such as Abraão or Noah.
Variant diminutive form of Albinos (Ἀλβῖνος) primarily used in Italy. (Archaic)

Means "born during a journey" or "born into the arts" in Yoruba, from bí "to give birth, be born" and sí "to, on" combined with either ọ̀nà "way, road, journey" or ọ̀nà "art, artistry, craftsmanship". Traditionally given to a child born while travelling, or during a transitional period in their parents’ lives.
Derived from the Germanic name element agi "awe, terror", or egg "edge, sharpness (of a weapon)", or ana, an emphasizing prefix, or anu "ancestor" with Björn.
Greek form of Abihu, as it first appeared in the Septuagint.

Means "strong, mighty" in Hebrew (compare Adir), derived from the root of אבר (ʿabar) "to strive upward, mount, soar, fly" (allegedly the name also means "aroma"; cf. the feminine אבירית (Avirit) "air, atmosphere, spirit").
Means "my hero" or "my strength" in Hebrew.
Greek form of Abiram, as it first appeared in the Septuagint.
Likely a combination of Abby and Rose.
Short form of names beginning with Ab, such as Abdonas, Abromas and Abelis.
Variant of Abishai. This was borne by Abisha Woodward (1752-1809), an early American lighthouse builder.

Means "my father is peace" or "father of peace", derived from Hebrew אָב (ʾav) "father" and שָׁלוֹם (shalom) "peace". (Also compare Absalom, which lacks the letter י (i) "my" suffixed to the first element.) This name belongs to the father-in-law of King Rehoboam and maternal grandfather of King Abijam in the Old Testament.
Meaning uncertain, perhaps "father of salvation" or "father of wealth". It is the name of a High priest of Israel mentioned in the Biblical books 1 Chronicles and Ezra.
Greek form of Abishur, as it first appeared in the Septuagint.
Form of Abishur used in the Latin Old Testament.
Variant of Abbe with the diminutive suffix -je recorded in the 18th century in East Frisia.
Danish and Norwegian form of Ábiǫrn, common in 17th century Norway.
A name given to females born on Tuesdays.
Probably derived from Greek ἀβλαβής (ablabes) meaning "without harm, undamaged, unhurt".
Alternate transcription of Arabic عبلة (see Abla).
Likely a variant of Ablat. Ablajan Awut Ayup is a well known singer in Xinjiang.

Meaning uncertain. It looks like this is a compound name, of which the first element is probably either 'Abla or Ablay. The second element might possibly be the Persian noun یار (yar) meaning "friend, companion" as well as "assistant, helper" (see Elyar).This name is archaic in Uzbekistan today, but its modern forms Oblayor and Obloyor are still used there, albeit rarely.
Crimean Tatar form of Abd al-Aziz.
Either a variant of Abel, or from the English word able, "having the power, skill, means, or opportunity to do something", ultimately from Latin habere "to hold".
Uncertain etymology. In Greek mythology, Ablerus was a Trojan soldier killed by Antilochus, son of Nestor, with his lance during the Trojan War.
From the English phrase a blessing, a combination of the indefinite article a with Blessing (see Blessyn)
Possibly a form of Abd al-Aziz.
Finnish adoption and elaboration of Abluna.
An invented name, comprised of Ab (such as in Abigail) and Lyn.
Means "precious stone", deriving from the Akkadian word aban nisiqtu ("a choice stone, a precious stone, a gem").
Transferred use of the surname Abney.
Diminutive of names beginning with Abn, such as Abner.

The name of an obscure Gaulish goddess, thought to be connected to Celtic abona "river" (source of Avon). The second element may be derived from either Proto-Indo-European nogʷo-, meaning "naked, nude" or "tree", or the verbal root *nebh- "burst out, be damp".

Abnody (Russian: Абно́дий) is an old and rare Russian male first name. The patronymics derived from this first name are "Абно́диевич" (Abnodiyevich), "Абно́дьевич" (Abnodyevich; both masculine); and "Абно́диевна" (Abnodiyevna), "Абнодьевна" (Abnodyevna; both feminine).

The usage of this name started in honour of the 8th-century saint Abo of Tiflis, who was of Arab origin and martyred for having converted from Islam to Christianity.His original name was Abu, though some Georgian sources claim that it may have been Habib instead, since its short form is Habo, which is very similar to Abo.
From Arabic Abu-Nazr, possibly meaning "father of the herald" or "father of the commitment".
Alternate transcription of Arabic أبو بكر (see Abu Bakr).
Means "one who walks in the company of hunters" in Yoruba.
From the English word abominable "horrible, odious." This name is borne by a man whose surname is Snowman.

Abonsam is the name of a malevolent spirit from the Gold Coast region of West Africa and Ghana. When accidents, disease, etc. afflict an area and local shamans have determined that Abonsam is to blame, the spirit is driven into the sea in a ritual that begins with four weeks of total silence, followed by removing all furniture from the homes involved. The interior of the homes are then beaten with sticks, and loud noises are created by shouting and gun fire.
Form of Abu Bakr used by South Indian Muslims.
Alternate transcription of Dhivehi އަބޫބަކުރ (see Aboobakuru).
Dhivehi form of Abu Bakr. This was the name of a 15th-century sultan of the Maldives.
From the Arabic word عَبَدَ (abada) meaning "worship"
Alternate transcription of Persian ابوذر (see Abouzar).

From a Guanche name for the star Canopus, which was derived from Guanche *ăbōra "seed (of a plant)", literally "coarse-grained sorghum" (sorghum being a tall cereal grass). This was the name of the supreme god of the heavens in the mythology of the Guanche (Berber) people native to La Palma, one of the Canary Islands.
Form of Abu Bakr used in Western Africa.
Alternate transcription of Arabic أبو بكر (see Abu Bakr), chiefly used in Northern Africa.
Variant transcription of Abudi. When used in the Jewish culture, is transferred use of the surname Aboudi.
Unknown origin, possibly from the Latin word abra meaning "maid". A known bearer was Saint Abra of Poitiers, a Gallo-Roman nun of the 4th century.
Form of Abraam with the Georgian nominative suffix -ი (-i). It is only used in Georgian when the name is written stand-alone.
Variant of Abram 1 recorded in the 18th century in East Frisia.
Judeo-Arabic variant of Abraham and Ibrahim.
Scottish Gaelic form of Abraham used in the Bible.
Variant or feminine form of Abram 1 and Abramo.
Form of Abram 2 with the nominative suffix, used in Georgian when the name is written stand-alone.
Dutch variant of Abrahamina as well as an Italian diminutive of Abrama, since the name contains the Italian feminine diminutive suffix -ina.
Medieval Polish feminine form of Abraham.
Medieval Italian diminutive of Abramo, as -uccio is an Italian masculine diminutive suffix.
Breton and Gallo form of Abraham and Older Franco-Provençal form of Abram 2 found in the Swiss canton of Fribourg.

From a word thought to have originated with the Gnostics or the Egyptians, found on many amulets during the last years of the Roman Empire. Abraxas was used by the Basilideans, a Gnostic sect of the 2nd century, to refer to the Supreme Being or god whom they worshipped; they believed it to be a name of power because it contained the seven Greek letters which, computed numerically, equal the number 365 (the number of days in the year). However, older mythologists placed Abraxas among the Egyptian gods, while some demonologists cite him as a demon with the head of a king and serpents forming his feet. He has been represented on amulets with a whip in his hand. The mystic word abracadabra is supposedly derived from his name (itself perhaps derived from Aramaic avra kedabra "what was said, occurred" or "I will create as I speak"). Many stones and gems were cut with his capricious symbolic markings, such as a human body having a fowl's or lion's head, and snakes as limbs, which were worn by the Basilideans as amulets. Gnostic symbols were later adopted by many societies devoted to magic and alchemy, therefore it is likely that most "abraxas-stones" made in the Middle Ages that contained kabbalistic symbols were talismans.
Variant of Abraxas. An angel mentioned in the Gnostic tradition that appears later on Jewish amulets and in Medieval Jewish angelologies.
Possibly a variant of Abraxas. This was used by American author Sarah J. Maas for a character (a wyvern) in her Throne of Glass series of high fantasy novels (2014-2018).
Variation of Abraham, feminine. Used in USA in rare cases. Said like Abraham, without the ham.
Possibly derived from Greek ἁβρός (habros) meaning "delicate, graceful, refined" or "splendid". This was the name of a Macedonian soldier who died defending Alexander the Great.
Possibly an elaboration of Bree, using a as both a prefix and a suffix.
A North Caucasian term used for a lonely warrior living a partisan lifestyle outside power and law and fighting for a just cause. Means "bandit" in Russian.
Masculine exclusive portuguese spelling of Apreline
Variant of Aubriana or a combination of the prefix a and Briana.
Means "apricot-plum" in French. This is the name of a character in Madame d'Aulnoy's fairy tale "The Imp Prince" (1697). Abricotine is a fairy who is the beloved of the protagonist, Léandre.
Strictly the feminine form of Abriel and a variant of Aubriella.
Variant of Aubriella or a combination of the prefix a and Briella.
Combination of the prefix a and Brielle, or a variant of Aubrielle.
Meaning: "Power of Planets"History: Only person I know with this name(and I've done reasearch) was my grandad amd he was obsessed with planets.
A knight who joined the Round Table after Perceval visited his castle, slew his ferocious lions, defeated him in combat, and sent him to Arthur's court.

Latinized form of the given name Aβρόκoμας (Abrokomas) or (Habrokomas), which is either the hellenized form of an unknown Persian given name, or a genuine Greek given name. In case of the latter, the name is probably derived from Greek ἁβροκόμης (habrokomēs) meaning "with delicate hair" as well as "with luxuriant foliage". The word is ultimately derived from Greek ἁβρός (habros) "graceful, delicate, pretty" (or "refined") combined with Greek κόμη (komē) "hair (of the head)". A known bearer of this name was Abrocomas, a Persian satrap from the 4th century BC.
A Karelian form of Abraham and Abram 1.
A feminine version of Abronius. Named after the Abronia gens.
Spanish and Italian form of Abronius.
Roman family name of uncertain or unknown origin.This name was borne by a 1st century BC poet.
Combination of the given name Abror and Persian جان (jān), meaning "soul, life".

Meaning unknown, traditionally connected to the Greek word ἁβρός (habros) meaning "delicate" but more likely a loanword, possibly borrowed from Akkadian. Abrotonon was the name of the Thracian mother of Themistocles, of a Thracian hetaera in the writings of Plutarch, and a plant mentioned by Pliny the Elder.

Probably derived from the Persian noun آبروی (aberuy) meaning "reputation, standing" as well as "honour, prestige". A more literal meaning would be "the face of honour", since the word consists of the Persian noun آب (ab) meaning "honour, reputation, standing" combined with the Persian noun روی (roy) meaning "face" as well as "copper, brass, bronze". Also compare modern Bashkir абруй (abruy) meaning "reputation, standing, prestige".This was the name of a 6th-century tyrannical amir (ruler) of Bukhara (located in what is now Uzbekistan), who may have been of Hephthalite origin. He was also known under the name Abarzi, which is possibly etymologically related to Middle Persian or Pahlavi abar meaning "higher, superior".
Polish, French, Gascon, Haitian Creole, Danish, Faroese and Norwegian form of Absalom.
Variant of Absalom, possibly influenced by its French form Absolon. A known bearer of this name was Absolom M. West (1818-1894), an American Confederate general and state politician.
French and Hungarian form of Absalom.
From the English word abstinence, referring to the act of abstaining from sin. This name was used by the Puritans.
Uncertain etymology. This was the name of a Colchian prince in Greek Mythology, son of Aeëtes, and Medea's brother. It was also the name of one of the earliest recorded veterinary surgeons.
Either a short version of Athalbert or a short version of Abbe with adding of the name element têt meaning "glad".
The name of a character in the 11th-century Persian epic 'Shahnameh', the father of Fereydoun.
Combination of Abu and Abbas. This was another name for Ali, who had a son named Abbas.
Combination of Abu and Qasim. This was another name for Muhammad, who had a son named Qasim.
Malay and Bengali form of Abu Bakr.

Derived from Arabic أَبُو (ʾabū) meaning "father (of)" combined with بكير (bakir) possibly meaning "learner, student" or بَكَرَ (bakara) meaning "to get up early" (figuratively meaning "early ripened" or "quickly learned").
Alternate transcription of Arabic أبو بكر (see Abu Bakr) used outside of the Islamic world.

Means "father of Dharr" in Arabic. Abu Dharr al-Ghifari was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad and one of the first people to convert to Islam. His name was a tekonym referring to his daughter, Dharr.
Means "devoted worshiper of God" in Arabic, ultimately from Arabic عَبَدَ (ʿabada) meaning "to worship, to venerate".
A feminine version of Abudius. Named after the Abudia gens.

Combination of Abu and حنيفة (Ḥanīfa) of disputed meaning, possibly from a dialectal word meaning "inkpot" or from the feminine name Hanifa. This was the name of an 8th-century Muslim scholar and jurist and the namesake of the Hanafi school of thought in Sunni Islam.
Alternate transcription of Arabic أبو حنيفة (see Abu Hanifa), as well as a Malay and Indonesian variant.
Malay and Bengali form of Abu al-Hasan.
Means, "water of life" or "the blessed water."
In Dinka mythology (south Sudan), the first woman. She is the patron goddess of women and gardens. Her emblem is a little snake. She is the mother of Deng (Danka).
Somali and Ingush form of Abu Bakr.
From Arabic أَبُو (ʾabū) meaning "father" and حَاجّ (ḥājj) meaning "pilgrim (to Mecca)".

The first element is derived from Arabic abun "father" (see also Abu). The second element is possibly derived from the imperial rank Khan that was first used among certain Turkic peoples; khan is a contraction of khagan which means "ruler, sovereign".
Means "she entrusts to raise (her child)" in Bandial.

Means "father of the" in Arabic, derived from Arabic أبو (abu) meaning "father of" (see Abu) combined with Arabic ال (al) meaning "the". Also compare names like Abul-Fazl.Notable bearers of this name include the Indian scholar Abul Kalam Azad (1888-1958) and the Pakistani philosopher Abul A'la Maududi (1903-1979).
Alternate transcription of Arabic أبو الخير (see Abu al-Khayr).
Derived from Arabic أَبُو (ʾabū) meaning "father" combined with مُسْلِم (muslim) meaning "Muslim, follower of Islam".
From the English word, ultimately from Latin abundantia "fullness, plenty". This name was used in the 17th century by Puritans, referring to the abundance of God's blessings.
Spanish form of Abundantia. This is also the Spanish word for "abundance".

Feminine form of Abundantius. She was the Roman personification of abundance, prosperity and good fortune, portrayed as distributing grain and money from a cornucopia. (The mythological character has survived in French folklore as Lady Hobunde.) The name was also borne by an Italian saint martyred during the persecutions of emperor Diocletian.
Derived from Latin abundans "overflowing, abundant". This was the name of several Christian saints.
Basque, Catalan and Georgian form of Abundius.

Means "father of Quhafa" in Arabic. The name Quhafa is of unknown meaning. Abu Quhafa was the father of the first Rashidun caliph, Abu Bakr (Abd Allah). His name was in fact a kunya (a nickname) using Abu, his real name is Uthman ibn Amir 1 ibn Amr.
One of the royal gates of Dagbong Kingdom denoting "Corrupted name of Abdulai"
In reference to 1 Corinthians 9:18, "What is my reward then? Verily that, when I preach the gospel, I may make the gospel of Christ without charge, that I abuse not my right in the gospel."
Means, 'little boy' often used to denote the youngest child of a family.
Derived from Arabic أَبُو (ʾabū) meaning "father of" combined with the title سُلْطَان (sulṭān) meaning "Sultan, king, ruler".
Derived from Arabic أَبُو (ʾabū) meaning "father of" combined with the name Supyan.
From Arabic أبو (ʾabū) meaning "father" and زَادَ (zāda) "to add, to increase".
Alternate transcription of Arabic أبو ذر (see Abu Dharr).
Refers to a person with fair skin from the Arabic word abyad.
From the Somali word Abyee which translates to "to complete or to perfect"
Kazakh form of Abul. This name is also frequently used as a short form of Abylay.

Combination of Abyl with the Kazakh noun ай (ay) meaning "moon". As such, the meaning of this name is basically "father of the moon".This name is usually given in honour of the Kazakh ruler Abylay Han (1711-1781), who is known in English as Ablai Khan.
From the Kazakh personal name Abylay meaning "father of the moon" combined with the Turkic title khan (Mongolian: kaan) meaning "ruler, leader".

From the name of the former name of the Ethiopian Empire or the ancient African region Abyssinia, which is derived from a Latinized form of Arabic الْحَبَشَة (al-ḥabaša) "Abyssinia", from حَبَش (ḥabaš) "Abyssinian", possibly derived from Egyptian ḫbzwt "beard".
From the Bashkir абыз (abyz) meaning "educated" and feminine name element бикә (bikä).
Appears to be a corrupted form of the Greek ἄβυσσος ábyssos "abyss", the Greek itself was borrowed from Akkadian Apsu or Sumerian Abzu.
Means "seeds, spice, seedsman, one who sows" in Arabic.
Derived from Arabic أَب‎ (ab) meaning "father" and Persian جان‎ (jan) meaning "soul".
Means "wonderful coquetry", ultimately from Arabic عجب ('ajab) meaning "wonder, amazement" and Persian ناز (nāz) meaning "delight, comfort, coquetry, affectation".

This was a word for the narcissus flower used in Crete. It is said to mean "unwalled" in Greek, possibly from the Greek negative prefix α (a) with an element related to ἀκή (ake) "point, edge". In Greek mythology this name was borne by a Cretan princess, the daughter of Minos, who was loved by the god Apollo and bore him sons: Miletus, Amphithemis and Garamas. This character was called Ἀκάλλη (Akalle) by Apollodorus, a name likely derived from Greek ἀκαλλής (akalles) meaning "without charms".
French form of Akakios via Acacius.
Medieval Judeo-Spanish form of Isaac attested in Navarre.
Means "reed shield" in Nahuatl, from acatl "reed, cane" and chimalli "shield".
Spanish and Italian form of Akakios.

From Greek ἄκακος (akakos) meaning "harmless, guileless, innocent", ultimately derived from ἀ (a), a negative prefix, combined with κάκη (kake) meaning "evil" (see Akakios). In Greek mythology, Acacus, a son of Lycaon, founded the city of Acacesium and raised the infant Hermes there.

Latinized form of Greek Ἀκάδημος (Akademos), of uncertain etymology. The first element is probably the same as in ἑκάεργος (hekaergos), which means "far-working, striking from afar" or "free-working". This was the name of a legendary Athenian hero, and a site sacred to Athena in Athens was supposedly named after him. This site was later used by Plato as the grounds for a gymnasium and school, and the English word academy ultimately derives from it. This gave rise to the folk etymology of "silent district", drawing from ἀκή (ake) "silence" and δῆμος (demos) "district, country; the people".

From the name of a colony in New France in North America, derived from Arcadia and coinciding with Mi'kmaq suffix -akadie, meaning "place of abundance". This is also the name of a National Park in Maine.
From the name of the Açaí palm; derived from Old Tupi asa'y or ybasa'y, meaning "fruit that expels water".
Means "immovable, steady; constant; unceasing", from Sanskrit a "without" and cala "moving".
This was the name of the wife of King Tros in some accounts of Greek mythology, making her the queen of Troy.
Form of Acacallis found in the Bibliotheca, a compendium of Greek myths.
Means "a handful of reed arrows". Name borne by several rulers of Tenochtitlan.
Derived from Arabic Ākhir an-nahr, meaning "end of the river". This is the traditional name of the star Theta Eridani in the constellation Eridanus.

Latinized form of Akamas. This was the name of several characters in Greek mythology, one of whom was the son of Theseus and Phaedra. According to Virgil, he took part in the Trojan War and was one of the men who hid inside the Trojan horse and was thus smuggled into the city.
Means "reed arrow" in Nahuatl, from acatl "reed" and mitl "arrow, dart".
Means "groan". This is the name of the Mayan God of wine and celebration.
Acanorex was a Taíno cacique (chief) on Hispaniola, a Caribbean island.
French form of both Acantha and Acanthus.

Latinized form of Greek Ἀκανθίς (Akanthis), which was the name of a type of finch, known as thistle finch in English, literally meaning "prickly" from Greek ἄκανθα (akantha) "thorn, prickle, thistle" (compare Acantha, Acanthus). In Greek mythology this was the name of a sister of Anthus; after her brother was eaten by a horse, she and her family members were all transformed by Zeus into birds, with Acanthis becoming the thistle finch. This was also used by the 1st-century BC Roman poet Propertius for an old witch in one his poems.

Latinized form of Greek Άκανθος (Akanthos), which is derived from Greek ακανθος (akanthos), the name of a plant with large spiny leaves. The plant ultimately derives its name from Greek ακη (ake) "thorn, point" and Greek ἄνθος (anthos) "flower, blossom". Also see Acantha. This was the name of several characters in Greek mythology, including a son of Autonous and Hippodamia who was named after the acanthus bush, a plant common in his infertile homeland. Acanthus was also the name of multiple ancient Greek cities. Finally, in real life, this name was borne by Acanthus of Sparta, a sportsman who participated in the Olympic Games of 720 BC.

Italian and Spanish form of Acharius. The 7th-century Frankish saint Acharius, bishop of Noyon-Tournai, is known as Acario in Italian and Spanish. This was used by Gigio Artemio Giancarli for a character in his play La Zingana (1545). It was also used by Lope de Rueda for one of the main characters in his play Medora (1567).

Variant of Acharius. Saint Acarius (died 14 March 642) was bishop of Doornik and Noyon, which today are located on either side of the Franco-Belgian border. He was especially attentive to the poor and afflicted, whose needs he enjoyed relieving and calming their suffering.

Latinized form of Greek Ἀκαρνάν (Akarnan), which is derived from Greek ἀκαρνάν (akarnan), which is said to mean "laurel", but can also refer to a kind of thistle. In Greek mythology, Acarnan was the son of Alcmaeon. After his father's death he fled to South-Epirus, which was also known as Acarnia, derived from his name.
Means "stream, river, running water" in Turkish.

Latinized form of Greek Ἀκάστη (Akaste), probably a feminine form of Akastos (see Acastus). This name is borne by two characters in Greek mythology. One was an Oceanid nymph and companion of Persephone, the other was the nurse of the daughters of king Adrastus of Argos.

Latinized form of Greek Ἄκαστος (Akastos), which is possibly derived from Ancient Greek ἄκαστος (akastos) meaning "maple tree (Acer monspessulanum)". Alternatively, it could derive from κέκασμαι (kekasmai) meaning "to excel, to shine" combined with the intensifier prefix ἀ- (a-) (compare Castor). In Greek mythology, Acastus was the king of Iolcus, the oldest son of Pelias. He was one of the Argonauts.
Acat was a deity in Maya mythology associated with the process of tattooing.
Means "reed, cane" in Nahuatl. This is the thirteenth day-sign of the tonalpohualli.
Derived from Gaulish acaunon or acauno- "stone".
From acaxochitl "reed flower", the name of an aquatic plant with red or white flowers.
Variant of Acaime or else of Akaymo.
Italian form of Akakios and variant of Acacio.

In Roman legend this was another name of Larentia, the foster mother of the twins Romulus and Remus, and wife of the shepherd Faustulus. In her honour the Romans celebrated in December a feast called Larentalia or Accalia. This name also occurs in Virgil's Aeneid, belonging to a companion of Camilla.

According to questionable sources, such as baby name books and websites, this was another name for Acca, the human foster-mother of Romulus and Remus in Roman legend, also known as Acca Larentia (see Acca). It coincides with the Latin word Accalia referring to a Roman festival celebrating Acca Larentia, meaning literally "things pertaining to Acca".A known bearer of this name is Accalia Hipwood, an English radio personality in Dubai.
Form of Rebecca used by Malayalam-speaking Syriac Christians in the Indian state of Kerala.
Referring to being accepted into the Kingdom of God.
Roman nomen perhaps meaning "a call, summons" or "of Acca". A notable bearer was the tragic poet Lucius Accius.
Derived from Gaulish *acu- "swift, quick, fast". Acco was a chief of the Senones in Gaul, who induced his countrymen to revolt against Julius Caesar in 53 BC.

Of uncertain origin, perhaps a derivative of the Gaulish name Acco (itself from Gaulish *acu- meaning "fast, swift, quick"). Sir Accolon, also spelled Accalon, is a character in Arthurian legends, possibly first appearing in the Post-Vulgate Suite du Merlin (c.1230-40). He is a knight from Gaul and the paramour of Morgan le Fay, who uses him as an unwitting participant in a plot against her half-brother Arthur; sensing the deception, Arthur defeats Accolon in battle. Thomas Malory included the tale in his 15th-century compilation of Arthurian legends Le Morte d'Arthur. Sir Accolon also appears in subsequent modern Arthurian works.
Italian accorsa from Latin accursia "aided, helped".The hypocoristic Corsa was more common than the full form.
Italian name derived from Accorso and short form of Bonaccurso.
Likely a combination of Ace 1 and Alejandro.
The name of the Philippine singer Acel Bisa-Van Ommen. It was probably created from her full given name Maria Cecilia.
A king in Arthur's service in Floriant et Florete. He joined Arthur's campaign against Maragoz, an enemy
Feminine elaboration of Ace 1 using the popular name suffix lyn, possibly inspired by Aislynn or the medieval name Aceline.

From the word acennan meaning "to beget, bring forth, produce" in Old English. The word acennan is of Old English origin but the name Acennan is modern. Acennan is a character in Warrior of Woden by Matthew Harffy.
Saint Aceolus of Amiens worked as a sub-deacon who was studying for the priesthood when he was arrested and murdered as part of the persecutions of Emperor Diocletian in 303 near Amiens, France.
Latinized form of Akepsimas. Saint Acepsimas was a 4th-century bishop of Hnaita in western Persia who was martyred in 376.
Derived from Aceró, which is the name of a territorial demarcation in the island of La Palma, meaning "strong place". This name was borne by the wife of the Guanche mencey (leader) Tanausú.

From Ancient Greek ἄκεσις (akesis) "healing, cure". This was apparently the name of a famous Ancient Greek physician, known exclusively through the proverb Ἀκεσίας ἰάσατο (Akesias iasato) meaning "Acesias cured him", referring to an ailment that has been made worse through treatment.
From Ancient Greek ἄκεσις (akesis) "healing, cure". This was an epithet of Apollo in Ellis, as well as the name of a bishop who live during the reign of Constantine.

From the Greek Ἀκεσώ (Akeso), derived from ἄκεσις (akesis) meaning "healing, curing". She was the Greek goddess of healing (wounds) and curing (illness); unlike her sister Panakeia (Panacea), Aceso personified the process of a curing rather than the cure itself.

Latinized form of Akestes. In Greek mythology, this was the name of a hero of Trojan origin, who founded Segesta on Sicily. In a trial of skill, Acestes shot his arrow with such force that it caught fire. He helped Aeneas when the latter arrived on Sicily after his wanderings.

Latinized form of Akestor. Bearers of this name include two sculptors and a tragic poet.In Greek mythology, this was an epithet of the god Apollo. It was also the name of a character, who was slain by Achilles during the Trojan War.
Latinized form of Akestorides. A notable bearer of this name was Acestorides of Corinth, who became tyrant of Syracuse in the 4th century BC.
Combination of Ace 1 and the popular name suffix ton.

Variant of Acfrid. This name was borne by four noblemen from West Francia in the 8th and 9th centuries: Acfred I of Carcassonne; Acfred, Duke of Aquitaine; Acfred, Count of Toulouse; and Acfred II of Carcassonne.
Derived from Proto-Germanic *agjō meaning "blade" combined with Old High German fridu or Old Saxon frithu meaning "peace".
The name of a Deiran princess who later married king Æðelfrið of Bernicia.
Polish form of Akakios via Acacius.
Polish form of Akakios via Acacius.
A knight who wounded Tristan during a joust in the Prose Tristan.

Latinized form of Achaimenides. In Greek mythology, Achaemenides was one of the companions of Odysseus who remained on Sicily with the Cyclopes. When Aeneas arrived on the island, he took Achaemenides with him.

Latinized form of Achaios. In Greek mythology, this was the name of the son of Xuthus, who the Achaean people regarded as their (mythical) ancestor. Other bearers of this name include Greek tragic poet Achaeus of Eretria (5th century BC) and the son of king Seleucus I Nicator (3rd century BC).
Derived from Uzbek acha meaning "mother, grandmother" and gul meaning "flower, rose".

Of uncertain etymology, possibly derived from Greek ἄχος (achos) meaning "grief, pain, distress" (also see Achaios, Achilles). This was an Attic and Boeotian epithet of the goddess Demeter, possibly used in reference to her grief for the loss of her daughter Persephone.It was also the name of an ancient region of Greece (better known by its latinized form Achaea) which was possibly named in honour of Demeter, or pre-Greek in origin. In the New Testament, Achaia and Macedonia are frequently mentioned together to indicate all Greece, being the two provinces into which the Romans divided Greece when it fell under their dominion.
Polish form of Achaikos via Achaicus.
Means "son of Achaimenes" in Greek, derived from the hellenized Persian name Achaimenes combined with the Attic and Ionic Greek patronymic suffix ἴδης (ides).

The meaning of this name is a little uncertain; it may have been derived from Greek ἄχος (achos) meaning "grief, pain, woe" (also see Achilles). It is also interesting to note that there is the Greek word achaia, which was an epithet of the Greek goddess Demeter. The etymology of this epithet is similarly uncertain, but sources speculate that it is also derived from achos. Given that the male name Achaios (better known by its latinized form Achaeus) was first the name of two characters from Greek mythology before it became borne by real living men, it seems unlikely that both characters were named in honour of the goddess Demeter, so at least in their case a direct derivation from achos would be more likely than a direct derivation from achaia. Where living men were concerned, however, they could have been named in honour of the two characters of Greek mythology or directly after the goddess Demeter. It is also possible that they were named after the ancient region Achaia (better known by its latinized form Achaea), but this region was probably named in honour of Demeter. As such, in all cases and scenarios, everything can eventually be traced back to Greek achos, assuming that is the correct root.
French form of Achaikos via Achaicus.
Scottish given name meaning 'Friend of a horse'.
Derived from Sanskrit achala "constant; unceasing" and "the earth".
Variant transcription of Ahlai.This transcription is used in The Compete Jewish Bible, Hebrew Names Version, and Orthodox Jewish Bible.

Achall, daughter of Cairbre Nia Fer, king of Tara, and his wife Fedelm Noíchrothach, is a minor character from the Ulster Cycle of Irish mythology. After her brother Erc was killed by Conall Cernach, she died of grief on a hill near Tara, which was named Achall after her.
One of the names of the god Acoran, along with Achuhuran, Achahucanac, Achguayaxerax, Achoron, Abora, Orahan and Eraoranhan.
Chechen and Ingush form of Atsamaz.
Form of Susanna used by Malayalam-speaking Syriac Christians in the Indian state of Kerala.
Means "female child in the first pair of twins" in Dinka.

Means "water dweller", from Nahuatl atl "water" and chane "homeowner, resident, inhabitant". This was a creature from Aztec mythology said to bring water from the ground, depicted as a snake, a lizard, or occasionally a beautiful woman.Alternately, it may be derived from the negative prefix a- and chantli "home, residence", meaning "homeless".
Alternate transcription of Thai อัจฉรา (see Atchara).
Alternate transcription of Thai อัจฉราพร (see Atcharaphon).
Alternate transcription of Thai อัจฉรีย์ (see Atchari).
Latinized form of a Germanic name which was derived from Proto-Germanic *agjō "blade" and Old High German heri "host, army". This was the name of a 7th-century saint, also known as Acarius.

column3: อัจฉริยา, อัจฉริยะ(Thai)
column12: Alternate transcription of Thai อัจฉริยา or อัจฉริยะ (see Atchariya).
Derived from the Uzbek word acha meaning "mother, grandmother" and sanam meaning "idol, beautiful woman".
Perhaps derived from the name of a river in Sicily, Italy, or from the name of the type of rock often found there. This is the name of two separate characters in Roman and Greek mythology.
German form of Achatius.The name resembles the German word Achat "agate (a gemstone)".
Greek form of Ahaz used in the New Testament.
Means "gnawing" and is, by extension, used as the word for "mouse."
The name used by some Mormon groups for the Brother of Jared, despite Joseph Smith's official statement saying that his name was Mahonri.

Arthur's sister and Perceval's mother in the Middle English Sir Perceval of Galles.Her husband, also named Perceval, was slain by the Red Knight, leading Acheflour to raise Perceval ignorant of war and knighthood so that he might avoid the same fate. Eventually, Perceval left for Arthur's court. Acheflour went insane when she mistakenly thought Perceval had been killed. At the end of the romance, however-and in contrast to other Perceval romances in which his mother dies-Perceval and Acheflour are joyously reunited and Acheflour regains her sanity.Her name is probably a corruption of Blancheflour.
