Variant of Acheflour, which is probably a corruption of Blancheflour (see Blanchefleur) meaning "white flower" in Old French. In the Middle English romance 'Sir Perceval of Galles', Acheflour was the sister of King Arthur and mother of Perceval.
Feminine form of Acheloios. In Greek myth this was the name of a minor moon goddess as well as a general name for water nymphs and an epithet of the Sirens (as the daughters of Achelous).
This has been explained as a Greek name meaning "Achaean, of Achaea" (also compare Achaeus). It is borne by three women living in Denmark, as of January 1, 2023.
Italian form of Achaios via Achaeus.
Middle French form of a Germanic name that was Latinized as Acharius.
Derived from Arabic ākhir an-nahr, meaning "the end of the river". This is the name of the brightest star in the constellation Eridanus.

Derived from Greek ἄχεα ῥέων (áchea rhéōn) meaning "the stream of woe". Also compare Greek αχος (achos) meaning "pain". Some consider the aforementioned meaning to be folk etymology, saying that instead the name might be derived from Greek acherousai meaning "marsh-like water". In Greek mythology, the Acheron was a branch of the underworld river of Styx, which newly dead souls needed to cross in order to get into Hades.
This is one of Acoran's names and it means "behold the Spirit that sustains the firmament".

Dutch form of Achilles via its French form Achille.Known bearers of this name include the Flemish politician and prime minister Achiel Van Acker (1898-1975), the Flemish painter Achiel Van Sassenbrouck (1886-1979) and the Flemish cyclist Achiel Buysse (1918-1984).
From the English word meaning "a person who successfully reaches goals."
Hebrew form of Ahiezer. A known bearer of this name is Achiezer 'Achi' Brandt (1938-), an Israeli mathematician.
Derived from the diminutive form of աչ (ačʿ), a poetic term meaning "eye".
Means "take the things of the world easy" in Igbo.

Achila II (died circa 714) was the Visigothic king of Hispania from 710 or 711 until his death. The kingdom he ruled was restricted to the northeast of the old Hispanic kingdom on account of the Arabo-Berber invasions.
Derived from Proto-Germanic agio "blade" and Old High German hiltja "battle".

Bishop and theologian who lived in an era of dispute in the Church. Achillas was the bishop of Alexandria, Egypt, one of the most powerful cities in the world at the time. Succeeding as bishop a man named St. Peter the Martyr, Achillas ordained Arius, who was to begin the influential heresy of Arianism. When Achillas recognized the untruths in Arius' preaching, he took steps to defend the faith and was attacked by Arius and another heretical group called the Meletians. Achillas remained firm in the faith. A council held in Alexandria condemned Arius and forced him to flee to Palestine. Achillas, however, did not live to see this condemnation.
Feminine form of Achille. It is also the botanical name of the genus of flowering plants (Yarrow).

Italian form of Achilleus.This is the name of an early Christian saint and of an usurper of the Roman Empire (Aurelius Achilleus). The Ancient Greek hero from the Troian war is named Achille in Italian.
Occitan and Franco-Provençal form of Achille.

My maternal grandfather gave it as a name that represents unknown happeness and indistinguishable, he was trying to find a name that is different from others and well-defined the felling he had when he saw me saved from death due to a tumer, growing with me and sucking all the water in her. He told me later, the felling was for both my mother and me
Achindra name is 8 characters long and commonly given to both Boys and Girls. Achindra is originated from Sanskrit language and means "Flawless, Uninterrupted, Perfect, Without Faults."

From Sanskrit अचिन्त्य (acintya) meaning "unthinkable, inconceivable, incomprehensible", derived from the negative prefix अ (a) combined with चिन्त्य (cintya) meaning "considered, thought over, conceived, comprehended".
Meaning "one who remains" or "one who is still here".
Means "my brother is exalted" in Hebrew.
In Astronomy it is a name of a star, otherwise known as η Cassiopeiae
A unisex name meaning "one who still remains there".
Etymology unknown, perhaps related to ἄχος (akhos) meaning "distress, grief" and ρόη (rhoe) meaning "flow, stream, river".
Taken from the title of the Virgin Mary Maria Santissima Achiropita, this name is typically and predominantly found in the province of Cosenza, in the Calabria region in Southern Italy.
Combination of the names Achi and Shalom, meaning "my brother is a peace" or "my brother will bring peace" in Hebrew.
Means "benevolent hero" in Mongolian, from ачит (achit) meaning "gracious, benevolent" and баатар (baatar) meaning "hero".

Means "my brother is foolish" or "brother of foolishness" in Hebrew, derived from Hebrew ach "brother" and aph'el "to act foolishly". In the bible, this was the name of one of King David's most trusted advisors.
From Mongolian ачит (achit) meaning "gracious, benevolent" and сайхан (saikhan) meaning "nice, beautiful, handsome".
Means "benevolent fate" in Mongolian, from ачит (achit) meaning "gracious, benevolent" and заяа (zayaa) meaning "future, destiny, fate".
Means "clear water, luminous water", from Quechua yaku meaning "water".
Indonesian form of Ahmad as well as the usual form used by South African Muslims.
This is one of Chaxiraxi's names and it means "behold his mother, the Spirit that sustains the universe".
Borne by a Guanche man from Tenerife who was sold at the slave market in Valencia.
Alternate transcription of Arabic أشرف (see Ashraf) chiefly used in North Africa.
Greek form of Hathach, as it first appeared in the Septuagint.
Alternate transcription of Arabic أشرف (see Ashraf) chiefly used in North Africa.

Variant of Achsah used in some versions of the Old Testament, including the Vulgate and the Douay-Rheims Bibles. It was borne by American spiritualist Achsa W. Sprague (1827-1862), a popular trance medium lecturer in the 1850s.
The Irish heroine who bore Cormac, the king.
Transferred use of the surname Achton that means "without land".
From Guanche *at-u wayyu, meaning "here is the spirit". This name was an epithet of Acoran.
From Guanche *at-u hu əkanak , meaning "here is the one in the rain". This name was an epithet of Acoran.
From Guanche *at-u hu raɣan, meaning "he who is in the brilliance". This name was an epithet of Acoran.
Of uncertain etymology. Name borne by a deity associated with the goddess Turan.
Alternate transcriprion of Arabic أشواق (see Ashwaq), chiefly used in Northern Africa.
Means "the blue bottle flower" in Spanish.
Variant of Aizivella via the variant Azivelle.
Derived from Greek ἀκίς (akis) meaning "pointed object; barb, arrow". This was the name of the wife of Scamander, whom he named the well of Boeotia after.
Italian and Portuguese form of Acilius.
Means "wit, sharp" in Ancient Latin from the word aciēs itself derived from the Ancient Greek word ἀκή (ake) with the same meaning.
Derived from Old Persian aç- meaning "fire".
Latinized form of Akindynos. St. Acyndinus was a Persian Christian and ordained priest. He was arrested and slain for the faith during the reign of King Shapur II.

From Sanskrit अचिन्त्य (acintya) meaning "unthinkable, inconceivable, incomprehensible". This is the name of the supreme deity in Balinese Hinduism, also known as Sang Hyang Widhi Wasa ("the Divine Order") and Sang Hyang Tunggal ("the Divine Oneness") in Balinese.

Latinized form of Ἄκις (Akis), from the name of the Jaci or Aci river on the east coast of Sicily, now destroyed by lava flow from Mount Etna. In Greek mythology, Acis was the lover of the Nereid Galatea, who turned him into a river after he was killed by the jealous cyclops Polyphemus.

Possibly from Latin asciculus meaning "adze, stone hammer", itself a diminutive of ascia ("axe"). This is the name of a Hispano-Roman saint of the 3rd century BC in Cordoba (Spain) who was martyred in the Diocletianic Persecution along with his sister Victoria. He is the patron saint of the Spanish city of Cordoba.
Transferred use of the surname Ackerman.
Transferred use of the surname Ackley.
Variant of Aclulf or Agilulf, using an extended form of the first element (Old French agil "blade", and then retaining the -d from its use in other compound names such as Agledeus and Agledrudis).
Derived from Proto-Germanic *agio "blade" and Old High German heri "host, army".
Variant of Agilhard. Also see Egilhard and Achard.
Derived from Old French agil, a lengthened form of Proto-Germanic *agjō meaning "blade", and Old High German hilt meaning "battle".
Derived from Proto-Germanic *agio "blade" and Old High German man "man".
Derived from Old French agil, a lengthened form of Proto-Germanic *agjō meaning "blade", combined with Proto-Germanic *þrūþiz "strength" or Proto-Germanic *trut "maiden".
Derived from Old French agil, a lengthened form of Proto-Germanic *agjō meaning "blade", combined with Old Saxon wald or Old High German walt meaning "power, authority".
Meaning unknown. In some religious traditions, this is the name of the first human female born, a daughter of Adam and Eve.
Proto-Germanic agio "blade" lengthened to Old French agil + Proto-Germanic linþaz "gentle, sweet, mild".

Means "who in heaven’s name made him/her?", derived from Nahuatl ac "who? which one?", mach "certainly, totally", used here as an intensifier to the question, and quichiuh "to make something, to do something".
Maranao and Maguindanao form of Ahmad.
Means "water snake" in Nahuatl, from atl "water" and coatl "snake, serpent".

Latinized form of Greek Ἀκοίτης (Akoites) meaning "bedfellow, husband". This was the name of several characters in Greek mythology, including the helmsman of a ship that landed on the island of Naxos, where some of the sailors found a beautiful sleeping boy and brought him on board with them. The sleeping youth was the god Bacchus in disguise; Acoetes alone recognized the god and resisted against their plan to abduct him. When Bacchus awoke he eventually revealed himself and turned the sailors into dolphins, but Acoetes was spared and made a priest of Bacchus on Naxos.
Possibly derived from Nahuatl acolli "shoulder" and huehue "elder, old man".

Derived from Nahuatl acolli "shoulder" and miztli "mountain lion, wildcat". This was the name of an Aztec god of the underworld, also known as Acolnahuacatl. It was also the name of two rulers of Tlatelolco.
Means "inhabitant of Acolnehuac", itself meaning "near the river bend".
Possibly a variant of Akontios. In Greek mythology, this was the name of an Ethiopian chief who sided with Perseus in his fight against Phineus, and was turned to stone by Medusa’s head.
From the Hitchiti word oconee meaning "water eyes of the hills", which lent itself to the name of a wildflower found in the Appalachians Mountains, Acony Bell.
Borne by a Guanche ambassador from Tamarán (modern-day Gran Canaria). It is now used as a feminine name.
Accented form of Acoran, used in modern times.

From Guanche aqqoran, derived from *āhɣuran "God", literally "the Celestial", from *ahɣur "firmament, vault of heaven, sky". This was the name of the supreme god in the mythology of the Guanches indigenous to Gran Canaria, one of the Canary Islands.

Knight of the Round Table, brother of Danubre the Brave, and kinsman of Lancelot. During the Grail Quest, he was slain by Arpian of the Narrow Mountain, who hated Lancelot's family for their prowess. His death was swiftly avenged by Danubre. He may be the same character as Acantan the Agile.
One of the noble warriors that the knight Alexander brought to Britain from Constantinople. He fought for Arthur in the battle against the traitor Angres of Windsor.
In Romani lore, the acorn was an ancient fertility and phallic symbol.
A Knight of the Round Table who participated in the Grail Quest
Meaning uncertain, possibly derived from a place name.
Meaning uncertain. Second element may derive from Nahuatl tlehuacqui "something toasted".

This name was brought to some public attention by the American actress Acquanetta (1921-2004), born Mildred Davenport. Though she claimed her stage name meant "laughing water" or "deep water" in Arapaho, it appears to be an invented name, possibly an elaboration of Italian acqua "water" using Netta 1.
Cousin of Arthur's Sir Hervi of Rivel.

In Eilhart von Oberge's Tristrant, an evil little dwarf whose astrological powers won him a place in Mark's court. He divined the affair between Tristan and Isolde, and conspired to expose it to Mark. Acquitain appears in Beroul as Frocin, and in Gottfried von Strassburg as Melot from Aquitaine.

Acrab is a name of a star in constellation Scorpius, also known as Beta Scorpii. Beta Scorpii bore the traditional names Acrab, Akrab or Elacrab, all deriving from the Arabic name (Arabic: العقرب‎) al-'Aqrab "the Scorpion"

From Spanish acracia, which stands for the doctrine that advocates the suppression of all authority, ultimately from the Ancient Greek words ἀκράτεια (akráteia, "no power") or ᾰ̓κρᾱσῐ́ᾱ (akrāsíā, "intemperance"). This name was used during the Second Spanish Republic by Anarchist parents who were eager to reject traditional religious names.

Latinized form of Greek Ἀκραία (Akraia), an epithet of numerous goddesses whose temples were situated on hills or mountains, including Athena and Hera, which meant "of the heights" or "dwelling on the heights". It is derived from Greek ἄκρος (akros) "highest, upper".

Etymology unknown, although it may be related to ακραίος (akraios) meaning "extreme", or "marginal, at the edge". In Greek mythology, Acraepheus was a son of Apollo and the eponymous founder of the ancient town Acraephia.

Latinized form of Greek Ἀκρατοπότης (Akratopotês) meaning "drinker of unmixed wine", derived from ἄκρατος (akratos) "unmixed, undiluted, pure", a word used of liquids and effectively meaning "wine without water", and πότης (potês) "drinker". In Greek mythology he was a divine companion of Dionysus, and also called Acratus.

Potentially transferred use of the surname Acre or from Old English æcer (denoting the amount of land a yoke of oxen could plow in a day), of Germanic origin; related to Dutch akker and German Acker ‘field’, from an Indo-European root shared by Sanskrit ajra ‘field’, Latin ager, and Greek agros.
Middle English vernacular form of Zacharias.

Latinized form of Greek Ἀκρίσιος (Akrisios), which is possibly derived from Greek ἀκρίς (akris) meaning "locust". In Greek mythology, Acrisius was a king of Argos who enclosed his daughter Danaë in an impenetrable bronze tower (or a deep underground cave). He did this in order to keep her childless, because of a prophecy that he would be killed by her son.
Abbreviation of "Alpha Crucis", a star in the constellation Crux.
Alternate transcription of Achsah used in various modern versions of the Bible.

Latinized form of Greek Ἀκταῖος (Aktaios), probably derived from Ancient Greek ἀκταῖος (aktaios) meaning "from the coast, of the shore", from ἀκτή (akte) "headland, foreland, promontory, cape; coast, shore" (compare Actaeon). However, it could also have been derived from Greek ἄγω (agō) meaning "to lead". For the latter etymology, just compare the Greek word ἄκτωρ (aktōr) meaning "leader", which is related to Latin actor "doer". In Greek mythology, Actaeus was the name of the first king of Attica.
Derived from Old High German ahta meaning "attention, reflection" combined with Old Saxon hard or Old High German hart meaning "strong, hard".
Catalan and Portuguese form of Actaeus.
Transferred use of the surname Acton. A known bearer of the name was British barrister and politician Acton Smee Ayrton (1816-1886).
Latinized form of Greek Aktorion, which is a diminutive form of Aktor (see Actor).

From Acts of the Apostles, the title of the fifth book of the New Testament. A man named Acts-Apostles Pegden (1795-1865), nicknamed 'Actsy', had four older brothers named Matthew, Mark, Luke and John.
Old High German ahta "attention, reflexion" + Old High German wini "friend".
Means "stirring stick" in Nahuatl, usually for stirring cacao. This was also the name of a flowering plant, sometimes used medicinally.
Means "hawk" or "crane hawk" in Nahuatl, ultimately derived from atl "water" and cuauhtli "eagle".
The traditional name of a star in the constellation Cancer. It's also known as the Alpha Cancri, α Cancri.
A Saxon knight defeated by Arthur's Sir Hervi.
The Aztec goddess of the ocean, running water, and rivers, closely associated with Chalchiuhtlicue of whom she is another appearance. She is invoked by Aztec women in labor.
Meaning uncertain. The first element might be atl "water" or the negative prefix a-, and the second might derive from cuetla "break" or cuetlauh "to wither".

Latinized form of Greek Ἀκουσίλαος (Akousilaos), derived from ἀκούω (akouo) meaning "to hear, to listen to" and λαός (laos) meaning "people". This was borne by a 6th-century BC Greek logographer, who also wrote genealogies according to the Suda.
Roman cognomen which was derived from Acutius.

Roman nomen gentile which was derived from Latin acutus meaning "sharpened, pointed". It is ultimately derived from the Latin verb acuō "to sharpen, to make pointed". This name was borne by a Roman plebeian tribune from the 5th century BC.
From the Old English elements ac "oak" and wulf "wolf".
Means "inhabitant of Acxotlan", a merchant district, itself derived from acxoyatl "laurel branches; fir branches".
German, Croatian, Galician, Slovene, Hungarian, Polish, Kashubian and Spanish form of Adah.
Combination of Ada 1 and the popular name suffix bel.
Meaning uncertain. This name may possibly be a combination of the name Ada 1 with any feminine name ending in -cia, such as Acacia, Alicia, Felicia and Patricia.
Means "Adad has saved", possibly deriving from the Old Akkadian element gamalum ("to save"). Name borne by a prominent priestess of the moon god Sin.

Means "adornment of god, god is eternal, god's ornament", from עָדָה (ʿaḏa) "to adorn, to pass by" combined with אֵל (ʾel) "god".According to the Social Security Administration, at least 325 boys had this name between 2002 and 2021.A famous bearer of this name is Adael Alexander Amador (2003-).
Medieval Dutch form of Adam via its latinized form Adamus, as is indicated by the pronunciation of both names.
From the Italian adagio meaning "slowly, at ease", a word to indicate a musical composition should be played slowly.
The Venezuelan Carib personification of the Sun.
Either a variant of Adalia, or a combination of the prefix a with Dahlia.
This is the name of Adai Khan, a khagan of the Northern Yuan dynasty who ruled from 1425 to 1438.
Hebrew variant and Spanish form of Adaiah.
Probably a combination of the elements ad- (like in Ademar) and -ir (like in Alair and Edir).
Variant of Adara influenced by Adair.
Meaning "one who has loved the Lord"

From Japanese 仇 (ada) meaning "enemy, foe" and 吉 (kichi) meaning "good luck". This is the name of a geisha character in the 1832-1833 novel Shunshoku Umegoyomi by Japanese novelist Tamenaga Shunsui (1790-1844). The novel tells the tale of two geisha who yearn for the same man. The name spilled over to real life use in Japan in the late 1890s.
Idoma name meaning "father of the house", "head of family", or "head of the home". This name is usually given to the firstborn male or female child in Idoma households.
From Turkish ad "name" and al- "receive". Means "May your name be spread, may you achieve fame" in Turkish.
Of uncertain origin and meaning. Theories include a variant of Adela and a short form of names containing the element adal-.
Occitan and Gascon form of Adelais.

Germanic name, in which the first element is adal "noble". The second element may be derived from either Old Saxon wald, Old High German walt meaning "power, authority" (making it a variant of Adalwald) or Old Saxon and Old Frisian ald, Old High German alt meaning "old".
Variant of Adalher. 8th-century Saint Adalar was one of the companions of Saint Boniface.
Means "justice" in Azerbaijani, of Arabic origin.
Derived from Old High German adal "noble" and Old High German bald "bold, brave."
Containing name elements adal and bearn the name was recorded in the 9th and 11th centuries in East Frisia.
Combination of German adal "noble" and bero "bear".
German, Polish and Hungarian feminine form of Adalbert and Sicilian feminine form of Adalbertu.
Sicilian and Medieval Corsican form of Adalbert.
Form of Aðalbjörg used by Icelanders living abroad in countries that don't use the letter ð.
Old High German name derived from the elements adal "noble" and boto "bid, offer".
Means "noble sword", derived from Old High German adal "noble" combined with Old Norse brand "sword".

The first element of this Germanic name is derived from Old High German adal "noble." The second element is derived from Gothic bairgan (bergan in Old High German) "to keep, to save, to preserve", or from Old High German burg "fortress."
From Old Frankish ad, perhaps a reduction of Old High German adal "noble" and Old High German walt "power, authority".
Means "noble day", derived from Old High German adal "noble" combined with daga "day."
Elaboration of Ada 1 using the popular name suffix lee, possibly inspired by Adalynn. Also compare Adley and Adélie.
Possibly a combination of Ada 1 and Leia.
Old High German short form of Adalheidis (compare Adelais).
Variant of Adalhelm. This name was borne by a count of Troyes from the 9th century AD.
Old High German adal "noble" + Old Saxon lēkian, Old High German leihhen, leichen "to dance, sport, play".
Means "noble peace", derived from Old High German adal "noble" combined with Old High German fridu "peace".
The first element of this Germanic name is derived from Old High German adal "noble" and ger "spear". This was the name of a 10th-century saint who was the third archbishop of Bremen.
Derived from Old High German adal "noble" and Gaut "Geat".
Variant of Adalgar. It is also a cognate of Old English Æðelgar.
Derived from Old High German adal "noble" combined with Gothic gairns "eager, desiring."
Means "noble sacrifice", derived from Old High German adal "noble" combined with Gothic gild "sacrifice."

The first element of this Germanic name comes from Old High German adal "noble." The meaning and origin of the second element is rather uncertain: we know that it comes from gis (the original form was possibly gîs), but we don't exactly know where gis itself comes from. But there are a few possibilities. It might come from Gallo-Celtic gaiso "spear" (see Gaiseric) or it might be a short form of gisel, which means "hostage" or "pledge" (see Giselle).
Feminine form of Adalgiso. Adalgisa is a character in Vincenzo Bellini's opera Norma (1831).
Derived from Old High German adal "noble" combined with gisel "hostage" or "pledge."
Italian, Portuguese and Spanish form of Adalgis.
Derived from Old High German adal "noble" combined with Gothic guths "god" or Gothic gôds "good."
Romansh form of Adalgod. This was the name of Saint Adalgott II of Disentis (died 1165), a 12th-century monk and bishop. His feast day is celebrated on 3 October.
Means "noble mask", derived from Old High German adal "noble" combined with Old Norse grîma "mask."

Derived from the Old German elements adal meaning "noble" and heim meaning "home".It is quite possible that this name existed; it simply has not been attested with absolute certainty, as the actual name of the men in question could just as easily be Adalhelm instead. In other words: so far, the name has proven to be very difficult to separate from Adalhelm.
Means "noble protection", derived from Old High German adal "noble" combined with Old High German helm "helmet, protection".
Means "noble army", derived from Old High German adal "noble" combined with Old High German heri "army."
Means "noble battle", derived from Old High German adal "noble" combined with Old Norse hildr "battle."
Anglicized form of Adalindis.The name came to prominence with Adalind Schade, a main character on the television show "Grim" (2011-2017).
Derived from the Germanic elements adal "noble" and lind "linden tree, lime; shield (made of lime wood); gentle, soft".
Possibly a (rhotacized) variant of Adalida, a cognate of Adelaide.
Combination of the names Ada 1 and Livia 1

column5: Rainbow Serpent Of The Nothern Territories Of Australia
column12: Aboriginal / Indigenous Name Of The Nothern Territory’s Of Australia Meaning Rainbow Serpent Spirit
Possibly a combination of the element adal and the name Aaliyah.
Means "noble land", derived from Old High German adal "noble" combined with land "land."
Means "noble man", derived from Old High German adal "noble" combined with man "man."
Means "noble and famous", derived from Old High German adal "noble" combined with Old High German mâri "famous." Also, see Elmer.

Used by Zacharias Topelius, a Finnish fairy tale writer, in his story 'Adalmiinan helmi' ('Adalmiina's pearl' in English, 'Adalminas pärla' in Swedish), which was published during the late 1800s.Constructed of adal, meaning "noble" and mina, a common suffix in female names.
Means "noble protection", derived from Old High German adal "noble" combined with Old High German mund "protection."
Means "noble mind", derived from Old High German adal "noble" combined with Gothic môds (mut in New High German) "mind, spirit."
Variant of Adalwald. Adaloald was the name of a 7th-century king of the Lombards.
French form of Adalwolf via the Latinized form Adalolphus.
Variant of Adalar via the form Adolar.
Combination of Ada 1 and common suffix -lore.
Means "noble counsel", derived from Old High German adal "noble" combined with Old High German rât "counsel."
Means "noble raven", derived from Old High German adal "noble" combined with hraban or hramn "raven."

Means "noble power", derived from Old High German adal "noble" combined with rîcja "powerful, strong, mighty." The second element is also closely related to Celtic rîg or rix and Gothic reiks, which all mean "king, ruler."
Derived from Old High German adal "noble" and runa "secret lore, rune". This was used for a character in a minor German opera, De Kaisertochter (The Emperor's Daughter; 1885) by Willem de Haan.
Means "noble path", derived from Old High German adal "noble" and Gothic sinths "way, path."
Variant of Adalsind. Saint Adalsinda is a Catholic saint especially venerated in Douai, France.
Latinized form of Adalsinda. This was the name of two saints.
Means "noble strength", derived from Old High German adal "noble" combined with Gothic svinths (swind in Old High German) "strength."
Combination of Ada 1 and Luna. This was also the Roman name of the River Lune in Cumbria and Lancashire, England.
Derived from Old High German adal "noble" combined with Gothic valdan "to reign."
Means "noble guard", derived from Old High German adal "noble" combined with Old High German wart "guard."
Means "noble warrior", derived from Old High German adal "noble" combined with Old High German wîg "warrior."
Means "noble wolf", derived from Old High German adal "noble" combined with Gothic vulfs "wolf." See also Adolf.
Jèrriais and older Walloon form of Adam.
Form of Adam used in parts of western Africa.
Alternate transcription of Greek Αδαμαντία (see Adamantia).
A Hobbit character in JRR Tolkien's works. The name is likely based on the word "adamant".

Apparently derived from Greek ἀδάμαντος (adamantos) meaning "unbreakable, inflexible" (compare Adamantia). The 1st-century BC Roman writer Hyginus called the nymph Amaltheia by this name in his Fabulae (139).
Possibly a corruption of Adamanteia, a name used by Hyginus in reference to Amalthea.
From the English word meaning "made of adamant, incapable of being broken, like a diamond".
Feminine derivative of Adamantios. This was the name of a Thracian saint, also known as Adamantia, who was martyred during the persecutions of the Roman emperor Diocletian in the early 4th century.

Latinized form of Adamantios. This was borne by the 3rd-century Christian theologian Origenes Adamantius, who acquired the nickname because of his "character of steel", evidenced by severe ascetic practices (allegedly including self-castration based on a literal reading of Matthew 19:12 - "There are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven").

Variant of Adamaris.A noted bearer is Puerto Rican actress Adamari López (b.1971). Known for her roles in several Puerto Rican and Mexican telenovelas, she is currently a host on the Telemundo morning show 'Un Nuevo Día'.
Variant of Adamaris, or a combination of Ada 1 and Marie.
Either a combination of Ada 1 and Maris 2, or a combination of the prefix a with Damaris, or from Latin adamō meaning "I love truly, earnestly, deeply or greatly; covet".

Derived from Greek ἀδάμαστος (adamastos) meaning "untamed" or "untameable" (also see Adamastos). The giant Adamastor is a personification of the Cape of Good Hope in the 16th-century Portuguese poet Luís de Camões' epic work Os Lusíadas (The Lusiads). The character is also mentioned in Victor Hugo's novel Les Misérables (1862) and some works of Alexander Dumas, including Le Comte de Monte Cristo (1844).

Means "untamed, inflexible" in Ancient Greek, composed of the negative prefix ἀ (a) and δαμάζω (damazo) meaning "to tame". This was an epithet of Hades. In Greek mythology Adamastus of Ithaca was the father of Achaemenides, Odysseus' companion.
Variant of Adamaris or a combination of Ada 1 and May.
A British king mentioned in Arthour and Merlin among those who could not be counted on to help against the invading heathens.
Male given name of italian origin.
Variant of Adam recorded in the 17th century in East Frisia.
Meaning uncertain. A known bearer of this name is the Bosnian politician Adamir Jerković (b. 1958).
Combination of Ada 1 and the popular suffix -mira.
Transferred use of the surname Adamos.
Transferred use of the surname Adams.
Transferred use of the surname Adamson.
Medieval Italian diminutive of Adamo, as -uccio is an Italian masculine diminutive suffix.
Meaning uncertain. Also compare names like Astamur and Asțamyr.
Latinized form of Adam, used primarily as a baptismal name or as an official name on birth certificates. In western Europe, this name was especially common in the medieval period.
Meaning uncertain. Also compare names like Astamur and Asțamyr.
Allegedly a feminine form of Adán.
From Arabic `adana meaning "to settle down (in a place or a country)".
Means "she saved" or "she rescued" or "she has rescued them" in Amharic.
Means "elfman, half-elf" in Sindarin, from the elements adan "man" and edhel "elf".
Combination of the name prefix a and the name Dante. It might also be influenced by Adonis.
Variant of Adanna used in the United States.
Means first Daughter of The Family.

Variant of Adara ("noble, exalted, praised"). Adar features in the Jewish calendar as the name of the twelfth month of the biblical year and the sixth month of the civil year, when Purim is celebrated ('thus girls born during this period often bear the name Adara').
Possibly an elaboration of the names Adara or Daria.
Combination of the popular phonetic prefix a and Darius.
Belarusian and Russian form of Odarka.
From the name of a magical bird in Filipino folklore.
Georgian form of Adurnarseh, probably via its hellenized form Adarnases. This name was borne by a medieval king of Abkhazia and by several princes of Iberia and Tao-Klarjeti (also in medieval times).
Means "model, ideal, example" in Hindi, ultimately from Sanskrit आदर्श (ādarśa) meaning "mirror, reflected image".
From the name of a mountain in the Basque region of France. The name of the mountain itself is derived from Basque adar "branch; horn" and the quantifying suffix -tza.
A combination of the name prefix A- and Daryll. This was the middle name of Toriano (Tito) Jackson.
Means "free man, not a slave" in Sanskrit.
Meaning unknown. It was borne by a Guanche man from Tenerife who was sold at the slave market in Valencia.
Combination of the prefix a and an elaborated form of Dasha.
From the Latin phrase ad astra "to the stars". It may have been inspired by the similar name Adrasta (see Adrasteia).
Latinized form of Adastreia, which is a variant of Adrasteia.
Means "gift" in ancient Hebrew. This was the name of the wife of Japheth in the Book of Jubilees.
In Mandaeism, Adathan is an uthra who stands with Yadathan at the Gate of Life in the World of Light, praising and worshipping Hayyi Rabbi.
Derived from Basque adats "long locks; mane".
Archaic French name of unkown origin and meaning. It seems to have been a local name only found in the Bourgogne-Franche-Comté region.
Derived from Latin adauctus meaning "augmented, increased". This was the name of a Christian martyr and saint from the 4th century AD.
Croatian and Polish form of Adauctus.
Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Adauctus. A bearer of this name was Adauto Puñales (1935-2009), a former Uruguayan politician.

From Charco Aday ("Aday Pond"), a place in the island of Gran Canaria, Canary Islands. It may ultimately come from a Spanish surname or from a Guanche name. In any case, it was reclaimed as a Guanche name and has been used in modern times.
Means either "disciplined by God", "miracle of God" or "sorrow of God" in Hebrew; in any case, the second element is אֵל (ʾel) "God". In the Bible, this was the name of the third son of Ishmael.
Derived from Old High German ōt "wealth, riches" and berg "mountain, hill".

Of debated origin and meaning.Some scholars argue that this might be a place name rather than a personal name, and if so, that it would most likely be a contraction/abbreviation of A(l)d(e)beri, which might correspond to modern-day Albury, Oxfordshire.Others point out that it does appear in a list of persons in the Domesday Book and that it is a "feasible mistake" to read the abbreviation "Adb't" as Adbrei. If that were the case, "Adb't" would have been short for Ad(el)bert(us) and the name thus a cognate of Old English Æþelbeorht or Eadbeorht.
Derived from Proto-Celtic ad- "very" and Gaulish *bugio- meaning "blue".
Alternate transcription of Thai อัจฉรา (see Atchara).
Alternate transcription of Thai อัจฉราพร (see Atcharaphon).

column3: อัจฉริยา, อัจฉริยะ(Thai)
column12: Alternate transcription of Thai อัจฉริยา or อัจฉริยะ (see Atchariya).
Variant of Adeline using the popular suffix lyn.
Variant of Adeline using the popular suffix lynn.

Variant of Adam. Possibly influcenced by the TV show "The Addams Family" in which the surname of the family is Addams. According to U.S. Social Security Administration, 33 boys were recorded wtih the name Addam in 1984.A notable bearer is a Xenoblades character called Addam Origo.
Perceval's great-grandfather in Wolfram's Parzvial. Descended from fairies, he was the son of Lazaliez and the father of Gandin. An active warrior, Addanz died in combat
Derived from the given name Adda, a short form of names containing the element aðal "nobility" (see Ada 1), and the Old Norse element borg "fortress, fortification, citadel".
Diminutive of Anders and names starting with ad-, like Adrian, Adam and Adolf.
Variant of Addo recorded in the 17th and 18th centuries in East Frisia.
Variant of Adalhard recorded in the 19th century in East Frisia.
Variant of Adeline using the popular name suffix lyn.
Variant of Addo recorded in the 18th century in East Frisia.

minor Greek goddess and personification of gluttony and abundant satiety. Derived from words meaning "surfeit" or "to eat one's fill," she had a sanctuary in ancient Sicily where she was uniquely worshipped alongside Demeter, goddess of grain.minor Greek goddess and personification of gluttony and abundant satiety. Derived from words meaning "surfeit" or "to eat one's fill," she had a sanctuary in ancient Sicily where she was uniquely worshipped alongside Demeter, goddess of grain.
Likely an invented name combining the popular sounds ad found in names such as Adelyn and Addison, and the popular suffix essa. The name might take inspiration from names like Odessa.
Combination of Addi and Bell inspired by other -bell names.
A combination of Addie and Belle.
Variant of Addo recorded in the 17th and 18th centuries in East Frisia.
Variant of Addo recorded in the 17th century in East Frisia.
A combination of Addie and the popular name suffix lee, or otherwise a variant of Adalee, Adelie or Addilyn.
Elaboration of Addy 1, or variant of Addilyn or Addison with the suffix leigh. This was likely influenced by popular names like Everleigh.
Variant of Addison possibly influenced by English sun.
Comes from Yawanese word meaning "Alpha, Leader,
Variant of Addo recorded in the 19th century in East Frisia.
Cognate of Adea as well as an elaboration of Ade and Ada 1.
Means "the crown is complete" in Yoruba.
Means "the crown suits the king" in Yoruba.
Means "The crown has added to my joy" in Yoruba.
Means "my crown mixed with blessing" in Yoruba.
Means "the crown has become two" in Yoruba.

Means "the crown has become small" or "one has arrived small" in Yoruba, from either adé "crown" or dé "to arrive, come" combined with di "become, change into" and ẹ̀wẹ́ "small, thin". Alternatively, it could mean "the crown is shattered", from adé and di combined with awẹ́ "fragment".
Means "royalty becomes generational" in Yoruba, from adé "crown" combined with di "become, change into" and ìran "generation, lineage".
Means "the crown has become good fortune" in Yoruba, from adé "crown, royalty" combined with di "become, change into" and ire "luck, good fortune, goodness".
Means "the crown is now honey" in Yoruba.
Alternate transcription of Arabic أديبة or Urdu ادیبہ (see Adiba).
Alternate transcription of Arabic عادلة (see Adila), as well as the Urdu form.
Means "the crown has given me to cherish" in Yoruba.
Means "the crown did not forget me” in Yoruba.
Means "the crown did not insult me” in Yoruba.
Means "the crown has elevated our honour" in Yoruba.
Means "one who has crowned your care" in Yoruba, from adé "crown" and ìkẹ́ "fondness, care, cherishing".

Latinized form of Greek Ἀδείμαντος (Adeimantos) meaning "fearless, dauntless", ultimately derived from ἀ (a), a negative prefix, and the verb δειμαίνω (deimaino) meaning "to be frightened". This was borne by a brother of Plato. This was also the name of a Corinthian admiral at the Battle of Salamis in 480 BC.
Name of Nigerian origin, meaning "giver (father) of good things" or "giver (father) of wealth".
Means "royalty does not perish" in Yoruba, from adé "crown, royalty" combined with jù "does not, cannot be" and gbé "carry, lift; take by force, overpower".
Means "the crown does not allow honour to perish" in Yoruba.

Adekagagwaa is the name of the Iroquois Spirit of Summer. According to myth, Adekagagwaa oversees other weather gods, including Gǎ-oh (wind), Hé-no (thunder), and Gohone (winter), and departs for southern skies during winter, leaving behind a "sleep spirit."
Means "the crown is now my turn" from Yoruba adé meaning "crown", kàn meaning "to touch, to concern" and mi meaning "me, my".
Means "the crown does not fall" in Yoruba.
Means "the crown rejects suffering" from Yoruba adé meaning "crown", kọ̀ meaning "to refuse, to reject" and ìyà meaning "punishment, suffering".
Means "the crown does not perish" in Yoruba.

Means "an eternity with God" in Hebrew, from עַד (ʿaḏ) "an eternity" and אֵל (ʾēl) "God, the supreme deity, esp. the supreme God of Israel".See also El'ad, which uses the same elements but in reverse order (cf. Nathanael and Elnathan for another Hebrew example of this phenomenon).This name is also used as a Yiddish form of ʿĂḏînāh, a modern feminization of Adina 1 (see 'Adinah). Many also see this name as a Hebrew equivalent of the Germanic name Adela, despite the two names being etymologically unrelated.
Provençal, Languedocian and Franco-Provençal form of Adela.
Alternate transcription of Arabic عادلة (see Adila).
Sardinian and Piedmontese form of Adelaide.
Means "the crown opens the womb" in Yoruba.
Sardinian form of Adelasia. Adelàsia Cocco Floris (born 1885, died 1983) was a 20th century Sardinian doctor. Born in Sardinia, she became one of the first female doctors in Italy.

Medieval Italian variant of Adelaide.Adelasia of Torres (1207-1259) was the Judge of Logudoro from 1236 and Judge of Gallura from 1238, while Adelasia del Vasto (c. 1075 – 16 April 1118) was the third wife of Roger I of Sicily and mother of Roger II of Sicily, as well as Queen consort of Jerusalem due to her later marriage to Baldwin I of Jerusalem, as his third wife.Adelasia ed Aleramo (1806) is an opera composed by Johann Simon Mayr.

Franco-Provençal and Ukrainian form of Adelaide. It is also used to refer to many people or things called Adelaide in Ukrainian, such as Mary Adelaide of Cambridge or city in Australia. Rarely used today (in Ukraine) outside of heavily Christian communities in refrence to St. Adelaide.
Containing name elements Adel und Berg.

Italian form of Adelgis. Adelchi was an associate king of the Lombards from August 759, reigning with his father, Desiderius, until their deposition in June 774. He is also remembered today as the hero of the play Adelchi (1822) by Alessandro Manzoni.
Belarusian diminutive of Adelaida as well as a Polish diminutive of Adelajda and other feminine names that contain the Germanic element adal meaning "noble".

Variant of Adel or alternatively derived from the Hebrew phrase אש דת למו (esh dat lamo) meaning "fiery law unto them", used in reference to the Torah. The spelling has been influenced by the unrelated name Adele.
Possibly an American variant of Adelaide.
Variant of Adaleigh, or sometimes Adalae depending on the pronunciation.

Medieval name recorded in Domesday Book (1086), probably from the continental Germanic name Adalhelm. (The Old English cognate Æðelhelm or Æthelhelm had become reduced to Æthelm by circa 940, making it a less likely source.)

Italian, Spanish and (Brazilian) Portuguese form of Adelhelm via Adelelmus.A known bearer of this name was the English-Italian musician and entomologist Enrico Brunetti (1862-1927), who had Adelelmo as a middle name.

Variant of Adelhelmus, which is the latinized form of Adelhelm. Also compare Adalhelmus. This name was borne by two saints, namely Adelelmus of Burgos (died around 1100 AD) and Adelelmus of Flanders (died in 1152 AD).
Accented form of Adelen, borne by Spanish-Norwegian singer Adelén (b. 1996).
Italian and Spanish form of Adelphia.
Feminine form of Adelfo via the variant Adelfio.
Italian and Spanish form of Adelphus.
Dutch and German variant of Adelfrid.
Dutch and French form of Adelgund.
Polonisation of Adelheid. Last year this name was borne by 11 women in Poland.
Latvian form and Banat Swabian variant of Adelheid.
Hungarian and Portuguese form of Adelia. Also compare Amélia versus Amelia.A known bearer of this name is the Brazilian writer and poetess Adélia Prado (b. 1935).
Variant of Adelicia. In France, this name was revived in the 1990s.
Anglicized form of Adélie and medieval English short form of Adelicia.
Dutch form of Adelais, or a combination of Adelheid and Lies.
Lithuanian, Latvian and Slovene form of Adelia.
Scandinavian feminine variant of Adelina, Romanian, Languedocian, Niçard and Gascon masculine form of Adelina and Walloon and medieval French masculine form of Adeline.
Diminutive of Adela, Adelaida, Adelina, and other names starting with Adel-.

Portuguese form of Adelio.Known bearers of this name include the Portuguese former soccer player Adélio Guilherme Pacheco (b. 1920), the Timor Lestean soccer player Adélio Maria Costa (b. 1987) and the Brazilian painter and sculptor Adélio Sarro (b. 1950).

Italian and Spanish masculinization of Adelia.Known bearers of this name include the Italian former soccer player Adelio Moro (b. 1951), the Paraguayan former soccer player Adelio Salinas (b. 1968) and the Argentine television and radio host Adelio Suárez (1940-2007).
Invented name, likely based on Adela and the popular suffix -ir (see Ademir, Edir, Lucelir, etc.).
From the Old Germanic name Adalheidis (See Adelaide). It means "noble", "noble kind", "nobility", etc.
Variant of Adeliza, recorded in the 17th and 18th centuries.
Russian and Ukrainian form of Adelia.
Medieval English and Old Swedish form of Adelais. The second wife of Henry I of England bore this name.
Czech and Kashubian diminutive of Adéla as well as a Kashubian diminutive of Adélajda.
Combination of Old High German elements adal "noble" and man meaning "man".
Italian and Portuguese adoption of Adelmar.
Derived from Old High German adal "noble", or a short form of names beginning with this element. Also compare the feminine equivalent Adela.

Dithematic name made of Old High German adal meaning "noble" combined with laug meaning "vowed, promised, bound in oath" or "bath" or "flame". St. Adeloga of Kitzingen, also known as Hadeloga and Adela, is a German saint.
The name origin came from Nigeria with the name meaning: "The crown brings honour"
A knight who fought on the side of King Urien and the King of North Wales during a tournament at the city of Levegnic.
Means "the crown has honour" or "the crown has respect" in Yoruba.
Meaning unknown. This is the name of a character in the play 'Poenulus of Plautus'.

Derived from Greek ἀδελφός (adelphós) "brother" (literally "from the same womb", from the copulative prefix a- "together with" and delphys "womb"). Adelphus was a bishop of Metz, France, who is now venerated as a saint in the Catholic Church.
Derived from the Germanic elements adal "noble" and þruþ "strength".
The name belonged to Vicente Adeltú, a charruan tribe leader who lived in Buenos Aires. He was used by the Viceroy Avilés to convince other tribe leaders to be reduced and christianized.

The name of a number of persons mentioned in Rauf de Boun’s Petit Brut.The first two were kings before Arthur’s time. The third was a son of Arthur, his brothers were Morgan the Black and Patrick the Red.
Created with the element adel meaning "noble."
Diminutive of Adela, Adelajda, Adelina, Adelinda, or other names beginning with Adel-.
Variant of Adelia using the popular Latin American name suffix ly, as in Marely; or perhaps inspired by French Adélie.
Russian, Ukrainian and Belarusian form of Adela.
Means "the crown brought goodness" in Yoruba.
Romansh form of Adam, traditionally found in central Grisons, and Gallo variant of Adan.
Malay and Indonesian form of Adnan.
Means "the crown has fame" in Yoruba.
Apparently a rhyming variant of Ademir.
Means "the crown has a lineage" in Yoruba.
Bulgarian, Croatian, Macedonian, Polish, Romanian, Russian, Serbian, Slovak and Ukrainian form of Adeodatus.
Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Adeodatus.
The Roman goddess who guides the child back home, after it has left the parental house for the first time and monitored its coming and going in learning to walk.
Means "royalty does not fade" in Yoruba, derived from adé meaning "crown, royalty", (k)ò meaning "does not" and tí meaning "fade, be blemished".
From Yoruba adé oyè, which literally means "the crown of chieftancy", and is understood to mean "the crown given to me to celebrate my acquired chieftaincy title".
Means "the crown pacifies" or "the crown calms" in Yoruba.
Means "gluttony" in Ancient Greek. This was the name of a goddess said to be worshipped alongside Demeter in ancient Sicily, likely a deity of agricultural bounty.
Likely a variant of Ada 1 based on the Appalachian pronunciation of the name.

Aderet comes from Ezekiel 17:8, meaning "glorious" in the phrase לְגֶ֥פֶן אַדָּֽרֶת (legefen ’addaret) "a glorious vine", a symbol of reborn Israel.= the Biblical Hebrew אַדֶּ֣רֶת (addereth) meant "mantle, cloak, cape" also (figuratively) "amplitude, splendor, glory, magnificence"
The first part, Aderi, means "crown" or "royalty," the second part, Nola, means "wealth" or "riches." The name is interpreted as "crowned with wealth" or "royalty with riches".
Meaning "a crown walks into wealth" or "royalty walks into wealth", from the Yoruba words adé (crown), rìn (to walk), sí (into) and ọlá (honor, wealth).
Variant of Adelrich recorded in the 16th and 17th centuries in East Frisia.
Variant of Adalhard recorded in the 17th century in East Frisia.
Derived from Sanskrit आदेश (ādeśa) meaning "order, mandate".
Means "the crown has opened the way" or "the one who arrives and opens the way" in Yoruba, usually given to the firstborn child in a family.
Means "the crown has woken up" from Yoruba adé meaning "crown" and sọjí meaning "to arise, to awake".
Means "the crown honored us" in Yoruba.
Combination of the prefix a with Destin.
Variant of Adesuwa.A famous bearer is Nigerian Nollywood actress Adesua Etomi.
Means "in the midst of prosperity" in Edo.
Means "the crown has come to me" in Yoruba.
Means "the crown is gentle" in Yoruba.
Borne by a notable Guanche ambassador from Gran Canaria.
Derived from the name of a menceycato (kingdom) located in Tenerife, meaning "mountainous massif". It is called Adeje in modern days.
Perhaps in part from Yoruba adé meaning "crown". This name was used by the American singer Kehlani for her daughter born 2019.
Means "the crown suits the child" in Yoruba, from adé "crown, royalty" combined with yẹ "suitable, worthy" and ọmọ "child".
Means "honour befits the crown" in Yoruba.
Means "the crown surrounds me" in Yoruba.

Means "the mother of locality" or "place mother", from Georgian ადგილი (adgili) meaning "place" and დედა (deda) meaning "mother". In Georgian mythology, Adgilis Deda is the goddess of fertility and livestock portrayed as a beautiful woman with silver jewelry. She became associated with the Biblical figure Mary after Christianity was introduced to Georgia.
Possibly means "defender, protector, brave", from Abkhaz аӷәӷәа (aghwghwa) meaning "strong".

Means "sacrifice" in Arabic. It is most often used to refer to the Islamic holiday Eid al-Adha, during which an animal sacrifice is made. In Indonesia, for example, it is sometimes used as a name for a child born on or around Eid al-Adha.
Derived from Arabic al-ðafīrah, meaning "braid, curl". This is the traditional name of the star Zeta Leonis in the constellation Leo.
Variant of Adam recorded in the 16th century in East Frisia.
From the name of the Islamic call to prayer, derived from the Arabic word أَذَّنَ (adhdhana) meaning "to call, to announce".

Adheena is a modern and graceful name inspired by Athena, the Greek goddess of wisdom, courage, and strategy, symbolizing intelligence and strength. It also subtly echoes the Sanskrit word Adhīna, meaning obedient or guided, blending qualities of wisdom with humility and discipline. Together, Adheena represents a person who leads with both insight and grace, balancing inner strength with respectful guidance.
Name of a Numidian prince meaning "Baal is great".
Derived from Tagalog and Cebuano adhika meaning "zeal, ambition, honorable objective".
Derived from Arabic الذيل (að-ðayl) meaning "the train (of a garment)". This is the traditional name of several stars in the constellation Andromeda.
The literal translation of the name in Tamil is "the shaker"

column5: uh-dEE-sah-yin(the "dh" sound is difficult to explain in english, my apologies)
column12: The name is of Tamilian origin, it means one who is filled with wisdom.
Indonesian and South Indian form of Aditya.
A name for the Hindu Lord Vishnu, Adhrit means " the one who supports everyone but does not need to support himself " it is also of Sanskrit origin.
Icelandic form of Adi 1, or short form of names beginning with Ad.
Means "queen" in Igede and "(valuable) gift" in Swahili, from Hausa adia "gift".
Means "first daughter of a second son" in Ibibio.
Possibly a variant of Diana or an elaboration of Adi. In Latin American cultures, this may have come from an alternative name for the Adzaneni language. The name has been in use since the late 1890s.

Possibly derived from Greek ἀδίαντον (adianton) meaning "maidenhair" (a plant, species Adiantum capillus-veneris) or ἀδίαντος (adiantos) meaning "unwetted, not bathed in sweat", from the negative prefix ἀ (a) and the verb διαίνω (diaino) "to wet, to moisten". In Greek mythology Adiante was one of the 50 daughters of Danaus (the Danaids).
Name of the lover of the owner of a gold ring discovered in Thiaucourt.
Alternate transcription of Arabic أديبة (see Adiba), as well as a Malay variant.
From Thai อดิ (adi) meaning "great, excellent" and ชัย (chai) meaning "victory".
Pet form of Ade 2. Also compare Addick, which is a pet form of the related name Adde.A notable bearer of this name is the Dutch retired soccer player Adick Koot (b. 1963).
After the clothing brand Adidas, itself an acronym of its founder's name Adi 3 Dassler.
From Sanskrit आदि (ādi) meaning "first, prime" combined with देव (deva) meaning "god". This is an epithet of several Hindu gods, most commonly Vishnu and Shiva.
Name of the mother of Aia on the Larzac Tablet.
Means "ornament of God" or possibly "God passes by". This is the name of several characters in the Bible.
Gaulish name, composed of Proto-Celtic ad- "to" and yantu "zeal, jealousy" with māros "great".
Name of an Italian river that runs through the regions of Trentino-Alto-Adige-Südtirol and Veneto.
Means "pillar of the house" in Isoko.
From Azerbaijani ad meaning "name" and gözəl meaning "beautiful".
Means "bound upright" in Yoruba, figuratively "well-planned and successful".
Form of Adiel used in the Latin Old Testament.
Means "injustice, iniquity" in Greek, derived from ἀ (a), a negative prefix, and δίκη (dike) "justice". Adikia is the goddess and personification of injustice and wrongdoing in Greek mythology.
Alternate transcription of Arabic عادلة (see Adila), as well as the Malay and Indonesian form.
From Mongolian адил (adil) meaning "like, akin, similar" and баяр (bayar) meaning "celebration, joy".
From Kazakh әділ (adil) meaning "fair, just" combined with the Turkish military title beg meaning "chieftain, master".
Means "dissimilar, unlike, not the same" in Mongolian, from адил (adil) meaning "like, akin, similar" and биш (bish) meaning "not, isn’t" or "other, different".
From Mongolian адил (adil) meaning "like, akin, similar" and чимэг (chimeg) meaning "ornament, decoration".
Perhaps a variant of Adelina or an elaboration of Adila. This name appears in the 1986 song Adilene by Los Yonic's (or Los Yonics), a Mexican Grupero band.

From Arabic عَادِل (ʿādil) meaning "just, fair" (see Adil) combined with the Turkic title giray denoting a khan of Crimea. A notable bearer was Adil Khan Giray, the khan of the Crimean Khanate from 1666-1671.
Combination of Adi 1 and Li 2 means "my jewel" or "my ornament" in Hebrew.

Variant of Adélia, which is the Hungarian and Portuguese form of Adelia.A known bearer of this name is the Portuguese poetess Adília Lopes (b. 1960), although it should be noted that in her case, the name is a pseudonym: her real name is Maria José da Silva Viana Fidalgo de Oliveira.
Variant of Adèle (compare Adélie). Sainte Adèle d'Orp-le-Grand (also known as Adilie) is particularly venerated in Wallonia.

Variant of Adélio, which is the Portuguese form of Adelio. This name is not to be confused with Atílio.Known bearers of this name include the beatified Brazilian teenager Adílio Daronch (1908-1924) and the Brazilian former soccer player Adílio de Oliveira Gonçalves (b. 1956).
Uyghur elaboration of Adil using the suffix جان (jan) meaning "dear, darling" (of Persian origin).
From Kazakh әділ (adil) meaning "fair, just" combined with the Turkic title khan meaning "ruler, leader".
This name is probably a short form of Adilmara. But in other words, you could also say that this name is a (Brazilian) variant form of Adelma.
Younger version of Aðils. From the Proto-Norse Aþagīslaz. Aþa, short for aþala, meaning "noble", "foremost". And gīslaz meaning "arrow shaft".
From Arabic عادل ('adil) meaning "just, fair, equitable" and Persian شاه (shah) meaning "king, shah".
From Mongolian адил (adil) meaning "like, akin, similar" and цэцэг (tsetseg) meaning "flower".
is derived from adi עדי combined with יה Ya (Yahweh) meaning "Jewel of Yahweh"
Crimean Tatar feminine form of Adil.
Derived from Kazakh әділ (adil) meaning "fair, just" and жан (zhan) meaning "soul".
Means "the primal mother", from adi "primeval, first" and mata "mother".
Uncle of Hector des Mares (Ector de Maris).
Combination of adin (עֲדִין) (see Adina 3) and El means “God is gentle” in Hebrew.
From Sanskrit आदि (ādi) meaning "first, prime" and नाथ (nātha) meaning "master, lord".

Means "original lord, the first lord, the primordial master" or "the Supreme Lord, lord of lords" in Sanskrit, composed of आदि (ādi) "primeval, first" and नाथ (nātha) "master, lord". This is another name of the Hindu god Shiva. It was also the name or title of an ancient saint who founded a religious order.
Derived from Persian آدینه (âdine) meaning "Friday" combined with Kyrgyz ай (ay) meaning "moon".

From an honorific term of address for a younger sibling, derived from Indonesian adik meaning "younger sibling" combined with the respectful suffix -anda. As a Dutch name its use is likely influenced by the story "Saïdjah and Adinda" in the 1860 novel Max Havelaar by Dutch author Eduard Douwes Dekker (1820-1887), also known as Multatuli.
Variant of Adina 2. As a Norwegian name, also possibly a feminine form of Adrian.
Diminutive of Adela, Adelaida, Adolfo, and other names containing ad.
Means "bundled up and stood erect" in Yoruba, referring to someone who stands strong and tall.

The Spirit of Safe and Speedy Returns. She is indigenous to the Roman region but predates the Romans. (In other words, they found her there.) She often works in conjunction with her sister, Abeona, Spirit of Departures. Together they provide for the safety of travelers in general, but especially of children away from home for the first time.
Means "jewel of light" in Hebrew, from a combination of Adi 1 and Or.
From a noble title meaning "duke, regent", ultimately from Sanskrit अधिपति (adhipati).
Combination of the name Adi 1 and Paz 2 means "golden jewel" in Hebrew.
From Thai อดิ (adi) meaning "more, great, excellent" and พงษ์ (phong) meaning "lineage, family".
Alternate transcription of Thai อดิพงษ์ (see Adiphong).
From Indonesian adi meaning "first" and putra meaning "son" (both of Sanskrit origin).
Apparently means "magnificence of God" in Hebrew. This is the name of a fallen angel in Jewish mysticism.
Combination of Adir, meaning "strong, mighty", and Ram 1, meanings "exalted" in Hebrew.
Coined by Sabino Arana as a Basque form of Adrian.
Coined by Sabino Arana Goiri as a Basque equivalent of Spanish Adriana and French Adrienne.
Means "benediction, blessing" or "extraordinary, exceptional, superior" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit अतिरेक (atireka).
Means "God is mighty" in Hebrew, a combination of Adir and El.
The place name Mérida spelled backwards. The Mexican rhythmic gymnast Adirem Tejeda (2002-) was born in the state of Yucatán, the capital city of which is Mérida.
From Thai อดิ (adi) meaning "great, excellent" and ศักดิ์ (sak) meaning "prestige, power, honour".
Comes from Persian, meaning "fire" or "of fire". In Sanskrit, it means "supreme leader".
From Guanche *adis-uda, meaning "satisfied belly" (stopped giving birth). This was recorded as the name of a 30-year-old Guanche woman who was sold at the slave market in Valencia in 1494.
Variant of Addison, though it is also possible that this name is a variant of Edison in some cases.
Alternate transcription of Thai อดิศร (see Adison).
Alternate transcription of Thai อดิเทพ (see Adithep).
From Thai อดิ (adi) meaning "great, excellent" and เทพ (thep) meaning "god, deity".
South Indian and Indonesian form of Aditya.
Possible transferred use of the surname Adityanath. Possibly after the famous yogi with the chosen surname of Adityanath.
Means "of Aditi", referring to the offspring of the Hindu goddess.

Means "protection of Aditya" from the name of the Hindu god Aditya combined with Sanskrit वर्मन् (varman) meaning "protection, shelter". This was the name of a 7th-century king of the Chalukya dynasty of southern India.
Indonesian form of Adityavarman. It was borne by a 14th-century king who founded the Pagaruyung (Malayapura) kingdom in western Sumatra.

From the Latin adiutus meaning "help", in this case referring to divine assistance in a Christian context.It was the name of one of the first martyrs of the Franciscan order, killed in Marrakesh in 1220.
Meaning "one who is beloved or desired", a longer form of the name can be Adiwanashe, deriving from the verb kudiwa.
Derived from Arabic عَادِيّ (ʿādiyy) meaning "normal, regular, ordinary".
Derived from Baoulé jɔlɛ "Tuesday", referring to the day of the week on which the child was born and hence to be understood as "born on Tuesday".
Means "helper" in Latin. Adjutor is the patron saint of swimmers, boaters, and drowning victims, as well as of Vernon, France.
Means "fair, just" in Arabic, from the root عدل (ʿadala) meaning "to act justly".
Alternate transcription of Arabic عدلان (see Adlan) chiefly used in North Africa.
Variant of Adlene influenced by French orthography.
Alternate transcription of Arabic عدلان (see Adlan) chiefly used in North Africa.
Means "my justice, my righteousness" from Arabic عدل (ʿadl) meaning "justice, fairness, righteousness".
Alternate transcription of Arabic عدلي (see Adli), as well as a Malay and Indonesian variant.
Means "his horizon" from Amharic አድማስ (admas) meaning "horizon".
Means "a cloud of death" or "a mortal vapor" according to Hitchcock's Dictionary of Biblical Names. One of the seven princes of Persia in the book of Esther.
Feminine form of Admetos. This name belonged to two characters in Greek mythology: the daughter of King Eurystheus (for whom Herakles stole the girdle of Hippolyta), and one of the Oceanids.
Italian, Portuguese and Spanish form of Admetus.
Combination of Admir and the suffix -ilson, present in names like Wilson and Nilson.

One of Jesus' ancestors in Luke 3:33 of the New Testament.This name only occurs in some versions of the Greek New Testament, such as the Nestle-Aland (NA) Greek New Testament and the United Bible Societies' (UBS) Greek New Testament. In other versions of the Greek New Testament, Jesus' ancestor is called Aram 3 instead.

Feminine form of Admir. A known bearer of this name was the Bosniak woman Admira Ismić (1968-1993), who was killed by snipers when she and her Serbian boyfriend Boško Brkić (1968-1993) were trying to cross a bridge in Sarajevo. An international documentary was made about them, which was titled Romeo and Juliet in Sarajevo and released in 1994.
From the English word admiral meaning "a commander of a fleet or naval squadron, or a naval officer of very high rank".
Transferred use of the surname Admire, or directly from the English word admire.

it belongs to a tana תנא (tana, a rabbinical sage whose views were recorded in the Mishnah) דיין (dayan) (a judge in religious court)his name means "red one" referring to one with a red face or complexion, in modern Hebrew due to a mistranslation of the bible into foreign languages and modern Hebrew it became a synonym of the word "redhead" a derivative of אדום meaning "red"

One of the family of Pahath-moab, who returned with Ezra and married a foreign wife. ( Ezra 10:30 ) (B.C. 459.) A priest, descendant of Harim in the days of Joiakim, the son of Jeshua. ( Nehemiah 12:15 ) (B.C. 500.)
Alternate transcription of Arabic عدنان (see Adnan).
Variant transcription of Adnah 2, used in The Complete Jewish Bible and the Hebrew Names Version of the Bible.
Means "rest of God" in Hebrew. This is the name of the angel who rules over the zodiac sign Sagittarius.
Variant transcription of Adnah 1. This transcription is used in The Complete Jewish Bible.

The name comes from the Hebrew noun עדן ('eden), meaning "luxury", "delight", or "pleasure".In the Bible, Adnah is one of the commanders of a King Jehoshaphat's army. He is only mentioned once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 17:14.
Alternate transcription of Arabic عدنان (see Adnan) chiefly used in North Africa.
Alternate transcription of Arabic عدنان (see Adnan) chiefly used in Tunisia.
Alternate transcription of Arabic عدنان (see Adnan) chiefly used in North Africa.
Transferred use of the surname Adney, as well as a diminutive of Ariadne.
Meaning unknown, perhaps a contracted form of Adonis. It was the name of American rapper Jay-Z's father, about whom he wrote a song.
This name represents a sacred ancestral being in the form of a gecko lizard. Adnoartina is associated with the formation of Uluru, the iconic sandstone landmark in the Northern Territory.
Vernacular form of Aadam and Aadolf.
From the surname Adobe meaning "mudbrick" in Spanish.
Occitan and Walloon form of Adolphe.
One of Arthur’s knights in La Tavola Ritonda. He fought in the Leverzep tournament.

A dithematic Germanic name with prototheme adal "noble" and deuterotheme arô "eagle" or hari "army".In modern German literature and popular culture it is used as a villain name, e.g., in 'Hui Buh das Schlossgespenst' or Adolar von Scheußlich (meaning 'Sir Adolar Ugly') in the TV Commedy Show 'Klimbim'.
Means "justice" in Uzbek and Tajik, ultimately from Arabic عَدَلَ ('adala) meaning "to act justly".
From the given name Adolat and xon meaning "king, ruler".
Means "father of the house" in Idoma.
Icelandic and Kashubian form of Adolf.
Louisiana Creole variant and Gallo and Walloon form of Adolphe.
Czech diminutive of Adolf, as it contains the Czech diminutive suffix -ek.
Dutch, German and Afrikaans variant and Walloon form of Adolphine.
Greek form of Adolf, mainly used to render the name of foreigners in Greek.
Corsican and Sicilian form of Adolph.
Derived from Ancient Greek ἄδολος (adolos) meaning "guileless, honest, genuine", literally "without fraud", from the negative prefix ἀ (a) and δόλος (dolos) "deceit, trick".
Variant of Adolfina, influenced by the French Adolphine.
A dithematic name formed from the Germanic name elements adal "noble" and walt "to rule".

Akan/Ghanaian Origin: In the Akan language, Adom means "grace," making Adoma a popular name representing favor.Igbo/Nigerian Origin: The name can translate to "praise God" or "God is good," reflecting deep religious values.Notable Individuals: It is used as a friendly and welcoming given name, such as the creative Ghanaian-American filmmaker and artist Adoma Owusu.
Old Irish diminutive of Adam. Saint Adomnán was the ninth abbot of Iona Abbey, considered one of the most significant churchmen and intellectuals of the seventh century.
Spanish form of Adon. It coincides with the Hebrew epithet for God אדון (Adón) meaning "lord".
Means "my lord is God" in Hebrew. This was the name of an angel mentioned in the Testament of Solomon.
Acadian and Creole form of Donatille.
Means "second of the twins" in Luo.
Variant of Adonijah, said to be the Cushite wife of Moses per the Book of Jasher (an unknown book mentioned twice in the Hebrew Bible).
Spanish form of 'Adoniyah (see Adonijah) via its hellenized form Adonias.
Greek form of 'Adoniyah (see Adonijah), as it first appeared in the Septuagint.
Polish form of 'Adoniyah (see Adonijah) via its hellenized form Adonias.
Form of Adonikam used in the Latin Old Testament.
Russian and Ukrainian form of 'Adoniyah (see Adonijah) via its hellenized form Adonias.

Means "my lord is righteousness" in Hebrew, from אָדוֹן (ʾaḏon) meaning "lord, master" and צֶדֶק (zédek) meaning "righteousness". In the Old Testament, this is the name of the king of Jerusalem at the time of the Israelite invasion of Canaan.
Possibly a feminine form of Adonis, influenced by Donna.
Short form of Dominador, Adorable, and other names containing ador.
This name can be a derivation of the Latin adjective adorabilis meaning "adorable, worthy of adoration" as well as be a combination of the names Adora and Bella.
From the English word meaning "befitting to be adored; cute or loveable".
Variant of Adorée, or perhaps an elaboration of Adore using the phonetic element ray.
Adoras of the Island of the Door is a Knight of the Round Table found in Prose Tristan
Derived from Romanian adorata, the feminine form of the adjective adorat, "adored".
Italian form of the feminine given name Adoración.
Late Middle English via Old French from Latin adorare ‘to worship’, from ad- ‘to’ + orare ‘speak, pray’.
Means "adored" in French. It is not commonly used as a name in France itself. Bearer Adorée Villany (born 1891) was a French dancer and dance theorist.

Derived from the greek "doron", meaning "gift", so the meaning is "gifts giver".

Visigothic name possibly derived from the Germanic elements auds "wealth" and sinþs "path". This was the name of an 8th-century queen of Asturias, Spain. It was also borne by the maternal grandmother of the 10th-century Galician saint Rosendo (as well as a sister of his).
Hellenized form of Old Persian Āδušya, meaning "the pleasant one".
Not a native Samoan name, as previously cited, but a modern invented name of unknown meaning.
Burmese form of Ardra, used as the name of the sixth lunar mansion of the Burmese zodiac.
Feminine form of Adraboran, a Breton variant ("Bretonnisation") of the name of the star Aldebaran.

Combination of the prefix a and the English word dragon, a legendary serpentine or reptilian creature. Child prodigy Adragon De Mello was given the name because he was born in the Chinese year of the dragon.
Two characters in JRR Tolkien's works. Likely from the fictional Adûnaic language, although its meaning is uncertain.

Latin form of אַדְרַמֶּלֶךְ (Adar-malik) meaning "king of fire" in Hebrew. This was the name of a Babylonian deity to whom infants were burnt in sacrifice (II Kings xvii, 31). He is possibly the sun god worshipped at Sippar (Sepharvaim). In 'Paradise Lost', Milton refers to Adramelech as an "idol of the Assyrians".

Means "gift of Adranos" in Greek, derived from the name of the Sicel fire god Adranos combined with the Greek noun δῶρον (doron) meaning "gift".This was the name of a Greek tyrant of Syracuse in Sicily, who lived in the 3rd century BC.
The name of a fire deity worshipped by the Sicels of ancient Sicily, especially in the town of Adranus (modern Adrano). He is said to have been driven out of Mount Etna by Hephaestus.
Variant of Adrián via the form Adriano.
Russian, Ukrainian and Azerbaijani form of Adrasteia.
One of the Latinized forms of Adrasteia
Galician, Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Adrastus (see Adrastos).

Latinized form of Adrastos. Traditionally translated as "nonparticipant" or "uncooperative." The king of Argos. He married his daughters to Tydeus and Polynices, both chased out of Thebes. To return his sons-in-law to their homeland, he mounted an expedition, known as the Seven Against Thebes. On this expedition, all the leaders except Adrastus fell. Adrastus died later from grief over the death of his son Aegealeus and was venerated as a half-god in various Greek cities, among which Sicyon.
Combination of the prefix a- with Dream.
A name with unknown etymology with historical usage in medieval Europe.

Variant form of Adrastia, which is one of the various latinized forms of Adrasteia. In Greek mythology, this was the name of a war figure and goddess of revenge and balance, who often battled in war. She was a daughter of Ares and Aphrodite. This was also the name of a nymph who fed an infant Zeus goat's milk.
Diminutive of Adrian and South African variant of Adri, or a variant of names Audrey and Ardrey/Airdrie.
An elaboration of the feminine name Adrey.
Diminutive of Adrian, Adriana, and other names beginning with Adri.
Possibly a blend of Adriana and Ariadna.

Medieval Dutch form of Adriaan. A well-known bearer of this name was Adriaen van der Donck (c. 1618–1655), a pivotal figure in the establishment of the middle colonies of colonial America, and the ultimate significance of Manhattan as a place of commerce.
Hungarian and Slovak form of Adriana.
African american elaborated form of Adrian.
Variant of Adrianne reflecting the Brazilian Portuguese pronunciation of the French variant of Adrianna.
Sicilian, Sardinian and Corsican form of Hadrianus (see Hadrian).
Older Portuguese form of Adrian, used often before the 20th century. This is the Portuguese name of Saint Adrian of Nikomedia, a popular saint in the medieval period after whom many places are named.
An anagram of Dirac, the surname of Nobel Prize-winning physicist Paul Dirac. This is the name of a character in the series 'Doctor Who', a companion of the fourth and fifth doctors.
Combination of Adriel and the suffix -son.
Dutch form of Adrien. As a feminine name, it may be a variant of Adriënne.
Feminization of Adrian (via the French form Adrien) by way of adding the French diminutive suffix -ette.
Means "daughter of the mountain". This is an epithet of Parvati.
Means "small mountain" in Sanskrit. According to the Mahabharata, Adrika is an apsara (a female spirit of clouds and waters) who was the mother of Matsya and Satyavati.
From Sanskrit आदृत (ādṛta) meaning "honoured, respected, worshipped".
The name of an antagonist in the Red Rising series of science fiction novels by American author Pierce Brown.
Bulgarian and Russian variant of Adrian.
Bulgarian, Russian, and Ukrainian variant of Adriana.

The God of the Lugbara, who dwell in the area between Zaire and Uganda. Adroa had two aspects: good and evil. He was looked on as the creator of heaven and Earth, and was said to appear to a person who was about to die. Adroa was represented as tall and white, with only half a body --- one eye, one ear, one arm, one leg. His children are the Adroanzi.

Derived from a Germanic name that was apparently composed of the elements odal or uodal "heritage, fatherland" and wald "rule". This name was borne by several Brazilian politicians, such as Adroaldo Mesquita da Costa (1894-1985) and Adroaldo Peixoto Garani (b. 1950).
Bulgarian, Russian and Brazilian Portuguese variant of Adrian. A famous bearer of this name is Brazilian footballer Adryan Oliveira Tavares.
In Brazil and France, this name is considered a variant of Adrian and Adryan.In Rare English, this name is considered a variant of Adrianne and Adrienne.
Alternate transcription of Thai อัษฎา (see Atsada).
Alternate transcription of Thai อัษฎาวุธ (see Atsadawut).
Alternate transcription of Thai อัษฎาวุธ (see Atsadawut).
Means "child of the warrior star" in Atlantean, the fictional language used in Marion Zimmer Bradley's novel, 'The Fall of Atlantis'.
Danish and Icelandic form of Asher.

Form of Azzo. Adso da Melk is a fictional Medieval character in Umberto Eco masterpiece 'Il nome della rosa' (1980). That character is loosely based on a real person: the monk Adso de Montier-en-Der (910/915 – 992). In Italy this name is no longer used and known just for the character and as a Medieval name.
Transferred use of the surname Adson.
Meaning unknown, possibly British adsiltia "she who is gazed at". This was the name of a river goddess worshipped by the Continental Celts. It may be an older form of Esyllt.
Variant of Addo or a name on it's own containing name elments adal and bern recorded in the 16th century in East Frisia.

Italian form of ዓድዋ also spelled Adwa or Aduwa. This is an Ethiopian town whose name means "village of Awa (people)" in Tigrinya.Adua catched the attention of the Italians because of The Battle of Adwa, a battle of the First Italo-Ethiopian War. Led by Emperor Menelik II, Ethiopian forces defeated an invading Italian force on 1 March 1896. Adua became a given name during the Fascism (1925-45) when Adua was a symbol of a dreamed revenge that became real in 1935-36.
Borne by a 10-year-old Guanche boy sold at the slave market in Valencia in 1497.
Means "one we struggled to birth" in Yoruba, from dù "to fight, struggle" and bí "to birth, be born". Sometimes given to children named Ige as a nickname.
Means "one (people) struggle(d) to care for" in Yoruba.
Alternate transcription of Thai อดุลย์ (see Adun).
Diminutive of Ada 1, Adelajda, Adrianna, or other names beginning with Ad-.
Medieval English variant of Adolph and Medieval Polish variant of Adolf.
Diminutive of Ada 1, Adelajda, Adrianna, or other names beginning with -AD.
Latinized form of Oddulf and variant of Adolphus.
Means "incomparable, matchless" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit अतुल्य (atulya).
From the name of a town in the Basque Country. The origin is unclear, although it may com from Old Basque adun ("new wheat").
Diminutive of Adrianna, Adriana and Ada 1.
Means "sweet to have" in Yoruba, from dùn "sweet, pleasant" and ní "obtain, have, possess".Adunni is the main character in the novel: 'The Girl with the Louding Voice' (2020) by Abi Daré.
To endure, to suffer something difficult with patience, dignity, and grace.

Derived from Middle Persian ādur (also ātur) meaning "fire" combined with the name Narseh. As such, the meaning of the name as a whole is roughly "the word of a fiery man" or "the fiery word of a man".
Russian diminutive of various given names including Adam, Adavkt, Adrian and other names starting with the syllable ad.
Diminutive of Ada 1, Adelajda, Adrianna, or other names beginning with Ad-.
This name is borne by Adut Akech Bior ( born 25 December 1999), a South Sudanese-Australian model.
From Scythian *Artavatauxma meaning "offspring of a righteous man".
Means "herdsman, ostler; good with horses" in Mongolian, ultimately derived from адуу (aduu) meaning "horse".
Means "horse herder, horse wrangler" in Mongolian.
Derived from Sanskrit अद्वैध (advaidha) meaning "united, unified" (literally "not divided into two parts, not disunited").
Means "not dual" in Sanskrit. One of its forms advaita is a branch of Hinduism called advaita vedanta.
Derived from Sanskrit अद्वैती (advaitī) meaning "oneness, single, unique" (literally "one without a second, without duality").
Old English, from Latin adventus ‘arrival’, from advenire, from ad- ‘to’ + venire ‘come’.
Derived from Sanskrit अद्वैत (ádvaita) meaning "unrivalled, unique".
There are two siddhantas (schools of thoughts) dwait and adwait. Dwait specifies duality in the universe whereas adwait specifies unity ie all is one there is no difference.

Welsh name, in which the second element is gwen meaning "white, fair, blessed". It was borne by a Cornish saint, considered to be "the Cornish Saint Dwynwen" as a patron of sweethearts. The village of Advent near Camelford is named after her.

Derived from Guanche *aḍəhuni meaning "strong man" or "proud man". It was borne by the mencey (leader) of Abona, Tenerife, at the time of the conquest carried out by the Crown of Castille. He was christened as Gaspar Hernández and became the servant of Spanish conqueror Alonso Fernández de Lugo.
likely a combination of the elements עד ('ad) "eternity" and יהו (yahu) referring to the Israelite god. Put together the name means "Yahweh is everlasting"
From beginning to end; Lord Shiva
Probably derived from Ancient Greek ἥδυμος (hedymos) meaning "sweet, pleasant". This was another name for Phaethon in Greek mythology, and a Minoan epithet for the morning star and evening star.

The adze is a vampiric being in Ewe folklore. It takes the form of a firefly and will transform into human form upon capture.A notable user of this name is Adze Ramanga, from the BBC children's show Young Dracula 2006-2014
Likely a Judeo-Catalan feminine form of Asher.
Tausug form of Azman as well as a Malay variant.
