あづさ(Japanese Hiragana)|アヅサ(Japanese Katakana)

column12: Uncertain etymology. In Greek mythology, she was a huntress turned into an island by the gods to escape the river god Phasis.
Latinized form of Aiakes. This name was borne by two rulers of the Greek island of Samos, the earliest of which lived in the 6th century BC.
Latinized form of Aiakides. This was the name of a king of Epirus, who lived in the 4th century BC.

Latinized form of Aiantides. Bearers of this name include the Greek tyrant Aeantides of Lampsacus (6th century BC) and the Greek tragic poet Aeantides of Alexandria (3rd century BC).In Greek mythology, Aeantides was the name of a son of Ajax.
Short form of Adalbert, used in the 16th century.
Variant of Abbe recorded in the 16th century in East Frisia.
From Sino-Korean 愛 (ae) meaning "love, affection" and 차. Means "loving daughter"

Latinized form of Greek Αἰχμαγόρας (Aichmagoras), from the elements αἰχμή (aichme) meaning "point of a spear" and ἀγορά (agora) meaning "assembly, marketplace". In Greek mythology, he was the son of Herakles and Phialo.
Older form of Aodhagán, from áed "fire" and the double diminutive -acán.
The name Aedalkha means time of power
Anglicized form of Áedán as well as a Manx cognate of this name via Manx Ae.
From the Irish áed "fire". This name was borne by a king of Ireland.
Welsh form of Áedán and diminutive of Aedd. In Welsh Legend, Aeddan was the son of Caw, a Pictish overlord. He was an enemy of King Arthur.

Derived from Ancient Greek αἰδέσιμος (aidesimos) meaning "venerable; causing respect, awe, reverence". This was the name of a philosopher of the Neoplatonic school who lived in Alexandria in the 5th century CE.

Martyr and brother of St. Apphian. Aedesius, a Christian of some note in Caesarea, now part of modern Israel, witnessed the persecution of Christians, the result of Emperor Diocletian's policies. He publicly rebuked the local Roman officials who were placing Christian virgins in brothels as part of the persecutions. Arrested, Aedesius was tortured and then drowned.
Feminine form of Aedius, a Roman family name.

An Irish name meaning "little flame". It is derived from the name of the Celtic sun god "AED", with "ÍN" the diminutive for "little". It is a feminine version Aidan.It is commonly spelled with the anglicized form "Aideen".
Name for a major character in the Throne of Glass Series by American author Sarah J. Maas. The name is meant to resemble Aiden and Aodhán.

Derived from Greek ἀηδών (aēdōn) "songstress" or from Greek ἀηδονίς (aēdonis) "nightingale". Also compare Greek ἀοιδή (aoidē) meaning "song". This was the name of a legendary queen of Thebes who plotted to kill her rival Niobe's son, but killed her own son accidentally. In grief, she was transformed by the gods into the first nightingale, a bird that still haunts the night with its mournful cry. Similarly, in the Homeric legend Aëdon was the wife of Zethus and mother of Itylus, whom she slew by mistake; Zeus transformed her into a nightingale, which nightly laments its murdered child.
Italian, Russian and Ukrainian form of Aëdon.
Latinized form of the Greek Αιδως (Aidos) which meant "modesty, decency". In Greek mythology, Aedos was a goddess or daimona of modesty, reverence and respect and a companion of the goddess Nemesis.
Derived from ǣdre "stream, river; vein, artery" or "quickly, instantly".
Reconstructed old Celtic form of Aimend.
Possibly a Latinized form of Aodh.Some dictionaries dating back to the 1800s have Aedus listed as an Irish saint.

Latinized form of Greek Αἰήτης (Aiêtês), possibly derived from Greek αἴητος (aiêtos) "terrible, mighty". In Greek mythology Aeëtes was a king of Colchis in Asia Minor (modern Georgia) and the father of Medea. He was also the brother of Circe and Pasiphae. During his reign, Phrixus brought the Golden Fleece to Colchis; it was Aeëtes who owned the fleece which Jason and the Argonauts sought in their quest, and eventually acquired.
Meaning unknown. This was the name of the Ossetian protector of wild animals, deer, boars, and mountain goats.

Latinized form of Greek Αἴγη (Aige), derived from αἴξ (aix) "she-goat" or ἄϊξ (aix) "gale of wind". In Greek mythology, Aega or Aex nursed the infant Zeus in Crete, along with her sister Helice, after Rhea gave Cronus a stone to swallow instead of the newborn Zeus. She was afterwards changed by the god into the constellation Capella, the rise of which brings storms and tempests.
Means "stormy one", "goatish", or "Aegean" in Greek. Aegaeon is the god of the storms of the Aegean Sea in Greek mythology.

Back-formation from the Aegean Sea, given by the 1911 edition of the Encyclopædia Britannica as the name of an Amazon queen and a possible eponym of the Aegean Sea. It almost certainly derived this name from that of Egee, a legendary Amazon queen from Libya who led an army against Troy. In some accounts, her fleet sank in a storm on the return journey.
Diminutive of names beginning with Ægen, such as Ægenbald and Ægenwulf.
Derived from the Old English elements āgan, "to own, possess" and beald "bold, brave".
Derived from the Old English elements āgan "to own, possess" and wulf "wolf".

Latinized form of Greek Αἰγιάλη (Aigiale), derived from Greek αἰγιαλός (aigialos) meaning "beach, shore" (also see the masculine form Aigialos). In Greek mythology Aegiale was the daughter of Adrastus and Amphithea. She married Diomedes but was unfaithful to him during his absence.

Latinized form of Greek Αἰγιαλεύς (Aigialeus), which is derived from Greek αἰγιαλός (aigialos) meaning "beach, sea-shore". Also compare Greek αἴξ (aix) meaning "a tall wave". In Greek mythology, this is the name of a son of the river god Inachus, as well as the name of a son of king Adrastus of Argos.

The first element Ægi- may be related to Old Icelandic Ægir, "the sea" or "the god of the sea", found in compounds as ægisandr "sea-sand" or the Icelandic place-name Ægisiða. Alternately, it may be related to Old Icelandic ægja, "to frighten, make terrible", found in compounds such as ægilikr, "terrible, awful". The second element -leif, -læif or -lof is a feminine name element derived from Primitive Scandinavian *-laibó a formation from the stem in OW.Norse leif "inheritance, legacy", but as an element in personal names "one who comes after, heir" and thus to -læifR/-lafR.

Anglicized form of Old Norse Ægir. This is the name of one of Saturn’s moons, as well as an exoplanet (also known as Epsilon Eridani b) orbiting the star Epsilon Eridani, both named for the figure in Norse mythology.

From the mythological device called the Aegis. In the Iliad, the Aegis is a device worn by Greek gods Athena and Zeus, resembling an animal skin or a shield and sometimes bearing the head of a Gorgon.

Latinized form of Greek Αἰγληίς (Aigleis), a derivative of αἴγλη (aigle) meaning "radiance, splendour, light of the sun or moon" (compare Aegle). In Greek mythology this name belonged to one of the Hyacinthides, the four daughters of Hyacinthus the Lacedaemonian, who was said to have moved to Athens and, in compliance with an oracle, to have caused his daughters to be sacrificed by the Athenians on the tomb of the Cyclops Geraestus for the purpose of delivering the city from famine and the plague, under which it was suffering during the war with Minos.
Sindarin form of Aikanáro. In the works of J. R. R. Tolkien, Aegnor is an Elf, the brother of Finrod, Galadriel, Angrod and Orodreth. He fell in love with the mortal woman Andreth.
Meaning "goat-horned".An epithet of Pan descriptive of his figure with the horns of a goat.

Derived from the Germanic element agjō "edge of a sword" and the Greek word αγώνας (agónas) "struggle". This is the name of multiple characters in George R. R. Martin's 'A Song of Ice and Fire' series, as well as the TV show based on the books 'Game of Thrones'.

column12: From Sino-Korean 愛 (ae) meaning "love, affection" combined with 花 (hwa) meaning "flower". Other Hanja combinations are possible.
Combination of Old Norse einn "one, alone" and leifr "descendent" or ǣvi "life" and leifr "descendent", as well as a variant of Øylæifr.
Alternate transcription of Burmese အိမ် (see Eain).
Alternate transcription of Burmese အိန္ဒြာ (see Eaindra).

Ancient Scandinavian name with the combination of einn "one, alone" and Old Norse ríða meaning "to ride", a combination of einn "one, alone" and Old Norse reiða meaning "to swing (a sword)" or a variant form of Einráði.
Alternate transcription of Burmese အိမ့် (see Eaint).
Derived from Old Norse eistr "Estonians" and maðr "man".
From Sino-Korean 愛情 (aejeong) meaning "love, affection". Other hanja combinations can also form this name.

column12: From Sino-Korean 愛 (ae) meaning "love, affection" and 智 (ji) meaning "wisdom, intellect" or 地 (ji) meaning "earth, soil, ground". Other hanja character combinations are possible.

Means "one, single" or "unique, exceptional" in Khmer.
