column3: 亜依子, 亜衣子, 安衣子(Japanese Kanji)|アエ子, アヱ子(Kanji/Katakana)|あえこ(Japanese Hiragana)|アエコ(Japanese Katakana)
column12: This name can be used as 亜依子, 亜衣子 or 安衣子 with 亜 (a, tsu.gu) meaning "Asia, come after, rank next", 安 (an, yasu, yasu.i, yasu.maru, yasu.raka, a) meaning "cheap, contented, low, peaceful, quiet, relax, rested", 依 (i, e, yo.ru) meaning "consequently, depend on, due to, reliant, therefore" and 衣 (i, e, kinu, -gi, koromo) meaning "clothes, dressing, garment."This name can also be used as アエ子 with アエ (the 2 katakana characters that combine 'Ae') with 子. Alternatively, the 'エ' can be replace by the outdated katakana character 'we'/'ヱ' (pronounced the same as 'エ').This name is very rarely given to girls, if given at all. Also, girls whose name is written as one of the kanji combinations seen above may most likely be called Aiko.
Derived from Breton ael "angel", this is considered the Breton form of Angelus.
Feminine form of Ael and cognate of Angela.
Possibly a transcription of عِلان meaning "announcement, proclamation" in Arabic.
Means "fine sky, delicate" in Hawaiian from 'ae meaning "fine, smooth, soft" and lani meaning "sky, heaven".
Variant of Ealdgyð found in Domesday Book.
Variant of either Aldric or Eldric/Eldrick. See also Elric, Æðelric/Æthelric.
Variant of Ale 2 recorded in the 17th century for men and in the 15th and 17th centuries for women in East Frisia.
Father of Escol, a follower of king Arthur.
Younger form of Old English Ælfgifu created with the Germanic elements ael meaning "hall, temple" and ewa meaning "ever." Compare Aelfeva.
Variant of Aela. The name coincides with Breton aelez "angels".
Derived from the Old English elements ælf meaning "elf" and beorht meaning "bright".
Derived from Old English ælf "elf" and ġeard "yard, enclosure" (from gardaz). Cognate to Old Norse Álfgerðr, a feminine name in contrast.

Old English cognate of Algautr, derived from the elements ælf meaning "elf" and Geat referring to a member of a North Germanic tribe from present-day Götaland in southern Sweden (note, the legendary hero Beowulf was a Geat).
Composed of the Old English elements ælf "elf" and helm "helmet, protection".
Derived from the Old English elements ælf "elf" and here "army", making it a cognate of Alfher.
Derived from Old English ælf "elf" and perhaps hun "bear cub".
Derived from the Old English elements ælf meaning "elf" and mære "famous".
Derived from the Old English elements ælf "elf" and run "secret, mystery". It is a cognate of the Old Norse name Alfrún.
Derived from the Old English elements ælf "elf" and waru "guard, protection; care, watch" (compare weard and wær).
Derived from the Old English elements ælf "elf" and weald "leader, ruler".
Derived from Welsh ael meaning "(eye)brow" and haearn "iron". This was the name of a 7th-century saint.
English form of Aelianus. A bearer of this name was Claudius Aelianus - often called Aelian in English - a Roman author and philosopher from the 3rd century AD.
Possibly inspired by Aylin. It is the name of a character in the 'Throne of Glass' series by Sarah J. Maas.
Possibly derived from Old English æl- "all, complete". It was borne by several Anglo-Saxon kings, including the legendary first king of the South Saxons.
Sparse records tell of a King Ida of Bernicia and a King Ælli or Ælle of Deira in the middle of the 6th century.
Combination of Anglo-Saxon elements ael meaning "hall, temple" and lic with the contested meaning of "like" or "body."
Derived from the name Ælli, Ælla or Alla combined with the suffix ing.
Derived from Greek ἄελλα (aella) meaning "whirlwind, tempest, gust of wind". This was the name of a "storm-swift" harpy in Greek mythology. It was also the name of one of Actaeon’s dogs.
Variant of Aellopous. This was the form used by Homer (in his Iliad, as an epithet of the goddess Iris).

Means "swift as a whirlwind", literally "whirlwood-footed", from Greek ἄελλα (aella) meaning "a stormy wind, whirlwind" and πούς (pous) "foot". This was an epithet of the Greek goddess Iris, the swift messenger of the gods. According to later sources this name belonged to one of the Harpies. (Compare also Aello, Aella.)
Variant of Adelold, possibly a form of Adalwald or Æthelwold.

Variant of Elphaba. In the novel 'Wicked: The Life and Times of the Wicked Witch of the West' (1995), this was the name of a legendary saint, Elphaba's namesake, who disappeared behind a waterfall for hundreds of years to read a book.
Variant of Æthelric or Ælfric; see also Elric.
Archaic Dutch form of Aaltje, a diminutive of Adelheid.
Obsolescent variant of Aaltje primarily used in the 1600s and briefly between the 1930s and the 1960s.
Derived from Welsh ael "brow" and gwen "white; fair; blessed". This name has been used from the early 20th century onwards.
Likely an elaboration of Aël modelled after Maëlys.
Alternate spelling of Aemilia. Some versions of Shakespeare's Comedy of Errors spell Aemelia this way.
From Sino-Korean 愛 (ae) meaning "love" combined with 美 (mi) meaning "beautiful". Other hanja combinations can form this name as well.
English form of Aemilianus. This name was borne by a Roman Emperor from the 3rd century AD.

Created by author George R. R. Martin for a character in his series "A Song of Ice and Fire". It is possibly derived from Emma. In the series, Aemma Arryn is the mother of Rhaenyra Targaryen, a claimant to the throne of Westeros.
Possibly derived from Amon. This is the name of a character in George R. R. Martin's 'A Song of Ice and Fire' series, as well as the TV show based on the books 'Game of Thrones'.

Created by author George R. R. Martin for a character in his series "A Song of Ice and Fire" and the television series "House of the Dragon". Prince Aemond is a member of House Targaryen. He is the second son of King Viserys I Targaryen by his second wife, Queen Alicent Hightower, and the younger brother of King Aegon II Targaryen.

Variant of Aemilia used by Edmund Spenser for a character in his epic poem The Faerie Queene (1590). Aemylia is one of the maidens featured in Book IV, which deals with friendship. She falls in love with Amyas, a squire 'of low degree', and they attempt to elope but are captured.
From 愛(ae) meaning "love" combined with 娜(na) meaning "beautiful, elegant" or 奈(na) meaning "apple tree". Other hanja combinations can also form this name.
Created by author George R. R. Martin for a character in his series "A Song of Ice and Fire". In the series, Aenar Targaryen is an ancestor of the Targaryen monarchs in Westeros.

Possibly intended to be a feminine form of Aeneas, or possibly taken from the Latin word aēneus meaning "made of copper, made of bronze; brazen" (feminine aēnea), a derivative of aes "copper, bronze". This was used by the author Dan Simmons in his 'Hyperion' series of science fiction novels, where it belongs to a character who first appears in 1996.
Perhaps a feminine form of Aeneas
Latinized form of Ainesidemos. Known bearers of this name include the ancient Greek philosopher Aenesidemus (1st century BC) and a tyrant of Leontini (5th century BC).

Latin form of the Greek Αἰνήτη (Ainete), derived from Greek αἰνητός (ainetos) meaning "praiseworthy, deserving praise", from αἰνέω (aineo) "to praise". In Greek mythology Aenete was the wife of Aeneas, the legendary founder of the ancient Thracian city of Aenus.
From Sino-Korean 櫻 (aeng) meaning "cherry, cherry blossom".

column3: 앵하(Korean Hangul)|櫻霞, 櫻夏(Korean Hanja)
column12: From Sino-Korean 櫻 (aeng) meaning "cherry, cherry blossom" combined with 霞 (ha) meaning "mist, haze, rosy clouds" or 夏 (ha) meaning "summer". This name can be formed using other hanja combinations as well.
From Sino-Korean 櫻 (aeng) meaning "cherry, cherry blossom" combined with 花 (hwa) meaning "flower, bloom, anger".
Derived from Old Norse enni "forehead" and brattr "steep".
Means "attacking/charging hawk", from the Cheyenne aénohe 'hawk' and -a'eotse 'attack/charge'.

From a place name mentioned briefly in the New Testament, which may be the Greek form of Hebrew ay-yin "spring, natural fountain". The Gospel of John (3:23) identifies it as a place near Salem where John the Baptist performed baptisms.It is occasionally, if rarely so, used as a given name.
Breton form of the french name Éléonore.
Created by author George R. R. Martin for a character in his series "A Song of Ice and Fire". In the series, Aenys Targaryen is the second Targaryen monarch in Westeros.
A person mentioned in Bede. The form there is Æodbaldum, which is the accusative.Possibly a form of Eadbald.
Latinized form of Greek Αἰολία (Aiolia), itself derived from αἰόλος (aiolos) meaning "moving, swift" (see Aiolos).

Used by animator Peter Chung for his character Æon Flux, from the name of a type of spirit being in Gnosticism, an emanation from the Godhead, ultimately from a Proto-Indo-European base meaning "vital force, life, long life, eternity".In Greek mythology this was an alternative name of the god Chronos.
Latinized form of Aion. Aion became a symbol during the Roman Empire and as such coins with his imagery were issued.
Possibly a variant of Ione, borne by British singer-songwriter Aeone Victoria Watson (1959-).

A Kamuy (god or spirit) in Ainu mythology. Described as a man encircled by smoke and flame, under which he wears a coat of bark, he is said to have taught humans domestic skills, earning him the moniker Aynurakkur ("father of humanity").
Variant of Asep. It can also be used as a diminutive of masculine names containing the sound aep (or other similar sounds), such as Saepuloh.

The name "aequa" originates from Latin, where it is a feminine form of the adjective meaning "equal" or "even." It is derived from the Latin word "aequus," which conveys a sense of balance or sameness in quantitative or qualitative terms.

Means "equity, equality, fairness" in Latin. During the Roman Empire, Aequitas as a divine personification was part of the religious propaganda of the emperor, under the name Aequitas Augusti, which also appeared on coins. She is depicted on coins holding a cornucopiae and a balance scale (libra), which was more often a symbol of "honest measure" to the Romans than of justice.
From Sino-Korean 愛 "love" and 羅 "net for catching birds". A famous bearer is South Korean actress Shin Ae-ra (1969-).

Of unclear origin. It has been connected with Latin aes, aeris "copper, bronze, money, wealth" as well as era "mistress" and the name of the Greek goddess Hera.This was the name of a goddess of Celtic origin, associated with Proserpina and the Roman underworld god Dis Pater. She may originally have been an earth goddess, associated with such attributes of fertility as the cornucopia and apple baskets; she may have also been associated with Silvanus and the Rhine Valley.

Aerandir is a Sindarin word for 'Sea Wanderer'.Aerandir's kindred and birthdate are unspecified, but it is assumed that he lived in Arvernien, in the Havens of Sirion.When Eärendil was resolved to sail to Aman to plead for Valar's help, Aerandir went with him, as did Falathar and Erellont. When they reached the shores of the Blessed Realm, he and the others remained aboard while Eärendil sought the Valar. After Eärendil's embassy was complete, Eönwë, herald of Manwë, came to Aerandir and the others and set them upon another ship. Manwë then sent a great wind to blow them east back to Middle-earth.His fate afterwards is unknown.
Aere means "storm" in Marshallese and is also used for naming typhoons in the West Pacific basin.
Form of Aericura occurring in Roman mythology.
Allegedly directly taken from Welsh aeres "heiress". Seems restricted to the Carmarthen district, in South Wales.

Welsh form of Aerten, the name of a Brythonic goddess of fate. Aerten is derived from Proto-Celtic *agro- "carnage, slaughter" (cf. Agrona) and *tan-nu "to broaden, to spread" or *ten-n-d-o- "to break, to cut". She had a shrine at Glyndyfrdwy on the River Dee in North Wales, and according to legend presided over the outcome of wars. Cymric legend tells of her being invoked during the struggles between the native Cymry (Welsh) and the Anglo-Saxon invaders and, according to local legend, three human sacrifices had to be drowned in the Dee near her shrine to ensure success in any battles to come.In former times Aerfen has been equated with the classical Fates (as all Celtic deities had to have a Roman counterpart). In truth, however, it's probably more accurate to equate her with the Irish Morrigan, herself a deity of battle fates.
Means "idleness" in Ancient Greek, derived from the negative prefix α (a) and ἔργον (ergon) "work". This was the name of the Greek personification of sloth and idleness.
Old Welsh form of Agricola, meaning "farmer"
From Sino-Korean 愛 (ae) meaning "love" and 利 (ri) meaning "gains, advantage, profit, merit". Other hanja combinations are possible. A famous bearer is South Korean actress Jung Ae-ri (1960-).

column3: あえり(Japanese Hiragana)|亜永利, 亜絵里, 亜江里, 亜枝利, 阿永里, 阿英里, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 亜 (a) meaning "second, Asia", 永 (e) meaning "eternity, lengthy, long" combined with 利 (ri) meaning "profit, benefit". Other kanji combinations are possible.
Variant of Ariel. The spelling is apparently influenced by the English adjective aerial meaning "pertaining to the air; ethereal" (ultimately from Greek ἀήρ (aer) "air").
Variant of Ariana, influenced by Greek aer "air".
Variant of Arianna influenced by the Greek aer meaning "air"
Variant of Erica. Alternatively, one of the seven Hesperides (nymphs of the evening) from Greek mythology according to Hyginus' Fabulae.

The origins of this name are uncertain; probably a Latinized form of a Celtic name, although some Latin roots have been suggested (including aes, genitive aeris, "brass, copper, bronze, money, wealth"; and era, genitive erae, "mistress of a house"). This was the name of a Romano-Celtic chthonic underworld goddess, described by archaeologist Miranda Aldhouse-Green as a Gaulish Hecuba.
Diminutive of names beginning with Aer, coinciding with the English word aerie, "a bird of prey's nest".
Variant of Arielyn, a combination of the name Ariel with the popular name suffix lyn.
Combination of Ancient Scandinavian ǫrn "eagle" and gunnr "battle, fight".

Old Norse name with several possible meanings. The first element can be derived from Old Norse ǫrn or ari, both meaning "eagle". It's also identical to Old Swedish ærin (Old Norse arinn) "hotbed, hearth".The second name element could be derived from Old Norse -ví, from Ancient Germanic *-wīhō, referring to female fighters or priests. Another possible meaning is that it's derived from Old Norse vé (Old Swedish vī) "sanctuary".
Variant of Aerith, due to translation confusion. It may also be considered a variant of Eris.
From a near-anagram of the English word earth. This is the name of a character in the 1997 videogame 'Final Fantasy VII'.
This was the real name of American sprinter Mae Faggs (1932-2000).
Variant of Arnulf recorded in the 15th century in East Frisia.
Old Norse combination of ǫrn "eagle" and gautr "goth".

Perhaps derived from the Greek verb ἀείρω (aeiro), αἴρω (airo) "to lift up, to raise". In Greek mythology, Aero (also called Haero, Aerope and Maerope) was a princess of the island of Chios, a daughter of Oenopion and Helice. She was beloved by Orion, who was, in consequence, blinded by her father.

Feminine form of Greek Ἀέροπος (Aeropos) (see Aeropus). In Greek myth Aerope was a daughter of King Catreus of Crete, granddaughter of Minos and wife of Atreus (to whom she was married after the death of his son and her first husband Pleisthenes). Her sons, Agamemnon and Menelaus, were generally believed to be Atreus' sons. However, Aerope was faithless to Atreus, being seduced by his brother Thyestes. She gave Thyestes the golden lamb (or the fleece) which made him king of Mycenae.
Derived from Greek ἀὴρ (aer) meaning "air, wind" and ὄψ (ops) meaning "eye". This was the name of two kings of Macedon.
Derived from agro-, "carnage", and tan-nu, "to broaden" or "to spread", or ten-n-do-, "to break" or "to cut".
Combination of Aeru and the suffix -na, indicating a personal name.
Variant of Aaryn or Eryn. Aeryn is one of the female aliens on the show Farscape.
Old Norse, Icelandic and Faroese variant of Ása.

Latinized form of Greek Αιςακος (Aisakos), probably meaning "branch of myrtle". In Greek mythology he was a Trojan prince (son of Priam by Alexirhoe) who loved the naiad Asterope, but, fleeing his advances, she stepped on a venomous adder and died. In grief, Aesacus hurled himself into the sea, but was changed into a bird by Tethys (the Titan who personified the sea).
Latinized form of the Greek Aisara. Aesara of Lucania was a Pythagorean philosopher who wrote a work called On Human Nature, of which scholars today only have a one-page fragment.

The first element of this name is Old English æsc "ash tree". The second element may be Old English ferhð "soul, spirit, mind, life" (compare Unferð) or a variant form of Old English friþ "peace" (in which case this is a variant of the attested Old English name Æscfrith). This name occurs in the Old English poem 'The Battle of Maldon'.
Probably derived from Old English æsc "ash tree" and friþ "peace".

Derived from the Old English elements æsc "ash tree" and here "army". This name occurs in the 8th-century epic poem 'Beowulf' belonging to King Hroðgar's most trusted adviser; Æschere is killed by Grendel's mother in her attack on Heorot after Grendel's death.
Derived from Ancient Greek αἰσχρός (aischros) meaning "shameful, dishonouring, ugly" combined with the patronymic suffix ίων (ion).

Probably originally a byname from Old English æscmann "sailor, pirate", i.e. one who sailed in an ash-wood boat, from the elements æsc "ash tree", sometimes referring to a kind of light ship, and mann "person, man".
Derived from the Old English elements æsc "ash tree, spear" and mund "protection".
Derived from the Old English elements æsc "ash tree; spear (made of ash wood)" and wig "war, battle". This name was borne by a 10th-century bishop of Dorchester.
Derived from the Old English elements æsc "ash tree" and wine "friend".
Derived from the Old English elements æsc "ash tree" (poetically "spear" or "boat") and wulf "wolf".

From the Aesepus river, of uncertain etymology. This was the name of a god personifying the river in Greek mythology, as well as of one of his grandsons, who died in the Trojan War alongside his twin brother Pedasus.
Gujarati for something or other. I don't know, I didn't do any research
From Sino-Korean 愛 (ae) meaning "love, affection" and 沈 (sim) meaning "sink, submerge, addicted to". Other hanja combinations are possible.
Icelandic masculine form of Æsa. This is the name of a character in Norse mythology.
Alternate transcription of Korean Hangul 애숙 (see Ae-suk).

One who provides direct connections to others to benefit everyone and consistently seeks new information to provide to those connected. Relative to the English word "Learned" and African name "Sekou" (SAY~KOO)
Possibly derived from the Latin word aestas, meaning "summer".
From Sino-Korean 愛 (ae) meaning "love, affection", and 淑 (suk) meaning "good, pure, virtuous, charming". Other Hanja combinations are possible.
This name derives from the a palm tree called the Aeta Palma (Mauritia Flexuosa), discovered in British Guiana and named by a the botanist William Davis Lamb who then used the name for his daughter.
Aeternitas was a Roman goddess and the personification of eternity.
Latinized form of Aithalides. In Greek mythology, Aethalides was the herald of the Argonauts.
Latinized form of Aithalion. In Greek mythology, Aethalion was a sailor who was turned into a fish by Dionysus.
Latinized form of Aithalos. In Greek mythology, Aethalus is a man whose son was killed by Aeneas during the Trojan War.
Form of Ethan used in the Latin Old Testament.
Variant of Ethel. This name was borne by Aethel Tollemache (c. 1875-1955), a British suffragette and pacifist activist.
Derived from Old English æðele "noble" and beald "bold, brave". Æthelbald was King of Wessex from 855 or 858 until his death in 860.
Means "noble fortress", derived from the Old English elements æðele "noble" and burg "fortress."
Means "noble spear", from Old English æðele "noble" and gar "spear". It is a cognate of Adalgar.

Derived from the Old English elements æðele meaning "noble" and Geat referring to a member of the North Germanic tribe from present-day Götaland in southern Sweden (note, the legendary hero Beowulf was a Geat).
Means "noble gift", from the Old English elements æðele "noble" and giefu "gift".
Derived from the Old English elements æðele "noble" and guð "war". It is a cognate of Germanic Adalgund. This was the name of an Anglo-Saxon saint (Æthelgyth of Coldingham).
Old English form of Alice and Adelaide, derived from the Old English elements æðele "noble" and hād "nature, character" (from haiduz). Cognate to German Adelheid.
Derived from the Old English elements æðele "noble" and helm "helmet, protection" (making it a cognate of Adalhelm). By the mid-10th century, this name had become reduced to Æthelm (see Athelm).
Derived from the Old English elements æðele "noble" and here "army".
Derived from the Old English elements æðele "noble" and hild "battle". It is a cognate of Adalhild.
Derived from the Old English elements æðele "noble" and mōd "mind, spirit" (from mōdaz). This was the name of a King of Hwicce.
Variant of Æthelsige recorded in Domesday Book.
Variant of Æðelsige, an Old English name derived from the elements æðele "noble" and sige "victory".

Derived from the Old English elements æðele "noble" and swiþ "strong". Æthelswith was the daughter of King Æthelwulf of Wessex, and wife of King Burgred of Mercia. This name is cognate to the Germanic Adalsind.
Variant of Æthelweald. Also compare Æthelwold. A known bearer of this name was Æthelwald Moll, an 8th-century king of Northumbria.
Derived from the elements æðele "noble" and wealh "foreigner, Celt" meaning "noble foreigner, noble Celt". This was the name of the first Christian king of Sussex Æthelwealh of Sussex.
Derived from the Old English elements æðele "noble" and wig "war, battle".
Variant of Æþelwine (see Æthelwine), which itself is a variant of Æðelwine.
Variant of Æthelweald. Also compare Æthelwald. A known bearer of this name was Æthelwold of East Anglia, a 7th-century king of East Anglia.
Derived from the Old English elements æðele "noble, famous" and wynn "joy, rapture, pleasure".
Likely a variant or corruption of Æthelnoð. This was the name of the horse of Lady Godiva who rode down the streets of Coventry, England in the nude.

Latinized form of Aitherios.This name was borne by multiple saints, the earliest of which were the 4th-century saints Aetherius of Chersonesus (in Crimea) and Aetherius of Nicomedia (now İzmit in Turkey).
Latinized form of Aithion. In Greek mythology, Aethion was an Ethiopian chief who was killed by Perseus.

A hound needed by Culhwch, as one of his tasks, to hunt the boar Twrch Trwyth. Other tasks required that Culhwch find certain people to manage Aethlem. Arthur obtained the dog for his kinsman. After the hunt, Aethlem could not be found and was never seen again.
Means "winning the prize, running for the prize" in Greek.
Latinized form of Aithon. This is the name of several characters in Greek mythology, one of them being the father of Hypermestra.

Derived from Ancient Greek αἴθρα (aithra) meaning "clear sky, fair weather" or "air", cognate to Aether. This was the name of several characters in Greek mythology, including the mother of Theseus, who was a handmaiden of Helen in Troy, and an Oceanid who is sometimes called the wife of Atlas.
Derived from Ancient Greek ἀετός (aetos) meaning "eagle". In Greek mythology, Aetion was one of the defenders of Thebes against the Seven.
Variant of Ate 3 with the diminutive suffix -je recorded in the 17th century for men and in the 16th and 18th centuries for women in East Frisia.
Variant of Ate 3 with the diminutive suffix -ke.
Variant of Ate 3 with the diminutive suffix -ko.

Latinized form of Greek Αἴτνη (Aitne), possibly derived from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eydʰ- meaning "fire" or "to ignite, burn" via archaic Sicilian *aið-na "the fiery one", making it a cognate of Ancient Greek αἴθω (aitho) "to burn, blaze, kindle". Alternatively, it could derive from Phoenician attuna meaning "furnace, oven, chimney". In Greek mythology, this was the name of the nymph of Mount Etna, a volcano in Sicily under which the god Hephaestus was said to have his forge.
Latinized form of Greek Αἰτναῖος (Aitnaios) meaning "of Mount Etna", a volcano in Sicily (see also Aetna). This was an epithet of several Greek gods associated with Mount Etna, including Zeus.
Uncertain etymology. This was the name of several characters in Greek mythology, including a king of Elis and eponymous founder of Aetolia in Greek mythology, a son of Endymion.
Derived from the Old English element æðele "noble". This name is used as a diminutive of any feminine Anglo-Saxon name beginning with Æthel, or as a monothetic name on its own.
From Old Basque aetz meaning "from Aezkoa Valley", in the north of Navarre.

column3: 아은(Korean Hangul)|娥恩, 娥銀, 雅恩, 我恩, etc.(Korean Hanja)
column12: Combination of an a hanja, like 娥 meaning "pretty, lovely, beautiful," 雅 meaning "clean, pure" or 我 meaning "I, me," and an eun hanja, such as 恩 meaning "favour, grace" or 銀 meaning "silver."

Modern Icelandic form of Ævarr or Ǣvarr, an Old Norse name in which the first element derived from ǣvi meaning "eternity, time, life" (compare Aiva, from the Gothic cognate); the second element may have been herr "army" or geirr "spear".
From Sino-Korean 愛 (ae) meaning "love, affection" combined with 原 (won) meaning "source, origin, beginning". Other hanja combinations can also form this name.

Latinized form of Greek Αιξ (Aix) meaning "goat". In Greek mythology Aex or Aega was a goat nymph who nursed the infant Zeus in Crete, and he afterwards changed her into the constellation Capella. She may be identical with Aix Amaltheia (see Amalthea). It was also borne by the Gorgon Aex, a primordial monster whose skin Zeus crafted into the aegis shield.
Short version of the name Ainard recorded in the 15th century in East Frisia.
Short version of the name Ainard.
Short version of the name Ainard recorded in the 16th century in East Frisia.
Short version of Ainard recorded in the 17th century in East Frisia.
Short version of the name Ainard.
Means "the first child of the second husband" in Ewe.
Means "I am on guard, alert" in Kasem.

Derived from Welsh y fagddu meaning "utter darkness". In Welsh legends this was originally a nickname belonging to the Arthurian warrior Morfran, who was so ugly and hairy that when he fought at the battle of Camlann, none of the other warriors struck him because they thought he was a devil; later legends transferred the character's ugliness and nickname to a brother, Afagddu.
Derived from Persian آفاق (afagh) meaning "horizons, world". Alternately, it may be a form of Athanasius via Russian Афанасий (Afanasiy).

Probably derived from Middle Welsh afall "apple". This may be cognate with Abelio or Abellio, the name of a Gaulish god, which is thought to come from Proto-Celtic *aballo- "apple" (also the source of the mythical place name Avalon). According to a medieval Welsh triad, Afallach was the father of the goddess Modron. The 12th-century chronicler William of Malmesbury called him Avalloc and said he lived in Avalon along with his daughters.
The name of a river in South Wales, usually Anglicized as Avon or Avan, presumably derived from Celtic *abon- "river" (making it a cognate of Afon). It was also borne by a 6th-century Welsh saint.

According to Welsh tradition, Afaon fab Taliesin was the son of the bard Taliesin and a member of King Arthur's retinue. He appears both in the Welsh Triads and in the medieval Arthurian tale Breuddwyd Rhonabwy.
From Arabic آفاق ('afaq) meaning "horizons, the world", the plural form of أفق ('ufuq) meaning "horizon". According to some, this was the name of poet Nizami Ganjavi's first wife.
Meaning "one who is happy or joyous".
Italian and Spanish form of Aphareus.
Catalan and Portuguese form of Aphareus.
Bulgarian, Russian and Ukrainian form of Aphareus.
Means "misfortune, mischief; beautiful woman, beauty" in Azerbaijani, ultimately from Arabic آفة ('āfa).
Arabic alternate transcription of Afzal as well as the Indonesian form.
Alternate transcription of Arabic أفضل (see Afzal), as well as the Indonesian and Malay form.
Alternate transcription of Arabic عفيف (see Afif), as well as the Dhivehi form.
This name is possibly a combination of the names Afik and Ofek
Variant of Affo with the diminutive suffix -ke recorded in the 16th century for men and in the 16th to 18th centuries for women in East Frisia.
Unnaccented form of Afërdita. This name is more common than accented form.
Possibly a varient transcription of Afeworq.
Means "mouth of gold" from Amharic አፍ (ʾäf) "mouth" and ወርቅ (wark) "gold".
Short version of the name Alfwin.
Variant of Affe with the diminutive suffix -ke.
Meaning uncertain, possibly of Old English origin. It may be related to Avery or Aphra. Affery Flintwinch is a character in Charles Dickens' novel 'Little Dorrit' (1855-7).
Diminutive of Alfreda or a variant of Effie.
A duke from the Middle-East or Africa who became the vassal of Feirefiz, Perceval’s half-brother.
Variant of Affe with the diminutive suffix -ke.
Short version of the name Alfwin.
Likely a form of Afua. This name is chiefly used in Ivory Coast.
Derived from Baoulé fue "Saturday", referring to the day of the week on which the child was born and hence to be understood as "born on Saturday".
Of uncertain origin and meaning. Theories include a Manx form of Affraic.
Italian saint, also known as St Dafrosa. Married to St Flavian.
Diminutive of names starting with the af- sound, including Aphra, Aphrodite and Evert.
Means "venomous snake" in Azerbaijani, ultimately from Arabic أفعى ('af'an). It could also possibly be short form of Əflatun.
Means "grandfather" in Old Norse. In the Rígsþula, Afi and his wife Amma are one of the three couples the god Rígr visits.
Derived from Turkish afif meaning "chaste" or "uncorrupted".
Russian and Ukrainian form of Athenaios.
Variant of Affe recorded in the 16th century in East Frisia.The suffix -ing was originally used for patronymic names but later it became a general diminutive suffix.
Russian and Ukrainian form of Athenodoros.
Variant of Affo recorded in the 20th century in East Frisia.
Malay and Azerbaijani form of Rafiq.
Means "sun" in Ottoman Turkish, ultimately from Persian آفتاب (āftāb).
Alternate transcription of Urdu عافیہ (see Aafia).
From the Arabic عافية (âfiye(t)) meaning “health, well-being”.
Old Danish and Old Swedish younger form of Afkarr.
Old Norse byname, from Old Norse afkárr meaning "strange", "prodigious".
Alternate transcription of Arabic أفنان (see Afnan) chiefly used in North Africa.
Means "she/he gets buried around" in Bandial. This is considered a death prevention name.
Hypocoristic of Afonso. Not generally used as a given name in its own right.
Means "Afghan, person from Afghanistan". Also possibly derived from Persian افغان (afghān), meaning "lamentation, cry".
Means "joys, mirths, celebrations" in Arabic, the plural of فرح (farah) meaning "happiness, joy".
Name of one of the angel
Possible Arabic feminine variant of Ephraim.
Feminine form of Afranius. A bearer of this name was the ancient Roman woman Gaia Afrania, wife of the senator Licinius Buccio.
Portuguese form of Afranius. Bearers of this name include Brazilian medic, writer and politician Afrânio Peixoto (1876-1947) and Brazilian literary critic Afrânio Coutinho (1911-2000).
Italian and Spanish form of Afranius.
Roman nomen gentile of uncertain origin. A bearer of this name was the ancient Roman poet Lucius Afranius (1st century BC).
Afrelia was a late 6th century saint, and princess of Powys. It has been suggested that she may be identical to the little-known Saint Arilda of Gloucester.
French form of Africanus. It coincides with the modern French adjective africain "African" and the noun Africain "(man) from Africa".
From Persian آفریده (âfaride) meaning "created; creature, (particularly) human being".

Russian form of Africanus. A known bearer was the 19th-century Russian philosopher Afrikan Spir (1837-1890), who was of German-Greek descent, and whose father reportedly chose the name from an old Greek calendar of saints.
Modern Greek spelling of Aphrikanos, which is the ancient Greek form of Africanus.
meaning "Bravo, Well done, motivational, Fascinator"born to make something good for people

Old Norse name with uncertain meaning. The first element Á- is possibly from either Old Norse áss "god", or *az "fear, terror, point, edge", or from *anu "ancestor". The second element is fríðr "beautiful, beloved". The name Áfríðr appears on runestone U 1011 in Uppland, Sweden where it says that she carved the runes together with Vígmundr. This makes Áfríðr one of the very few known female runemasters.
Derived from Arabic أفضل ('afdhal) meaning "best, highest, most outstanding".
Means "African" in Italian. A known bearer was artist Afro Basaldella (1912-1976).
Italian and Spanish form of Aphrodisius (see Aphrodisios).
Turkish version of the name Aphrodite.
Alternate transcription of Persian افروز (see Afrouz).

Meaning uncertain; it might possibly be related to Albanian afër meaning "close, nearby".Alternatively, the name might be the Albanian form of Aurora, in which case it was likely derived from its Russian form Avrora.
Albanian form of Aphrodite (via Greek Afroditi).
Alternate transcription of Urdu افروز (see Afroz).
Means "That which illuminates; bringer of light" in Arabic.
Alternate transcription of Persian افروز (see Afrouz).
Means "born during happy times" in Ewe.
Polish and Ukrainian form of Africanus.
Bengali, Urdu and Dari Persian form of Afsaneh.
Alternate transcription of Persian افسانه (see Afsaneh).
Derived from Persian افسانه (afsâne) meaning "tale, story" (see Afsaneh).
Urdu form of Afshin, also used as a feminine name.
From the Middle Persian name Pišīn which was derived from a title used by Sogdian rulers; its ultimate origin and meaning are unknown.
From Persian آفتاب (aftab) meaning "sun" or "sunlight, sunshine".
Means "sun of the religion" in Arabic.
Azerbaijani and Kyrgyz form of Avtandil. A known bearer of this name is the retired Azerbaijani soccer player Aftandil Hacıyev (b. 1981).

Transferred use of the surname Afton. It is also the name of a river in Scotland, and it coincides with the Swedish noun afton meaning "evening".This name enjoyed a brief revival in the early 1980s, thanks to the character of Afton Cooper from the popular American television series Dallas (1978-1991).
Afu means "hot" in Tongan; āfu means "waterfall, perspire" in Samoan.
Means "does one see God?" in Igbo.

column3: 感, 洸, etc.(Japanese Kanji)|あふる(Japanese Hiragana)|アフル(Japanese Katakana)
column12: From 溢る (afuru), modern afureru, meaning "to flood, overflow, brim over," written as 感, from kan meaning "feeling, emotion, sensation," and 洸, from 洸洸 (kōkō) meaning "surge (of water), valiant, brave."This name is extremely rare.
Combination of Azerbaijani ağa meaning "lord, master" and Əli.
From the Turkish title ağa meaning "lord, master" and Azerbaijani bala meaning "child".
Italian form of Agabius and variant of Agapio.
Latinized form of Agapios and variant of Agapius.
Portuguese and Spanish form of Agabus.
Derived from Guanche *ag ăsănsĭhe or *ag ăsănsĭhu, meaning "son of hospitality".
Variant of Agatha (compare medieval French Agace).
Italian and Piedmontese form of Agacles.
Russian variant transliteration of Agafya and Moldovan form of this name.
Latvian and Lithuanian form of Agatha.
From Ottoman Turkish آغا (agha) meaning "lord" and geldi meaning "came, arrived"
Combination of Azerbaijani ağa meaning "lord, master" and the given name Hadi.
From the Turkic title ağa meaning "lord, master" combined with the name Həsən.
From the Turkic title ağa meaning "lord, master" combined with the name Hüseyn.
From Turkish آغا (ağa), meaning "lord, master," and Persian جان (jân), meaning "soul, life-force."
Combination of Azerbaijani ağa meaning "lord, master" and the given name Kazım.
From Azerbaijani ağa meaning "lord, master" and kişi meaning "man".
Means "very famous, glorious, highly renowned", derived from Greek ἄγαν (agan) meaning "very, much" and κλέος (kleos) meaning "glory".
Means "very glorious, famous", derived from Greek (agan) meaning "very, much" and κλυτός (klytos) meaning "famous, noble".
Means "lords, masters" in Azerbaijani, from the plural form of ağa.
Means "iris (flower)" in Greek, specifically referring to the Greek iris (Iris attica).
Derived from Greek ἄγαλμα (agalma) meaning "honour, glory, pride, delight" or "a statue, a bust".

A king in Arthur's service in La Tavola Ritonda. Agalone served as steward of Britain, along with a fellow king named Allielle, while Arthur was away in Gaul. He thus occupies the role assigned to CARADOC SHORTARM in the Prose Tristan.
A vassal of Lord Golagros in the Scots poem of Golagros.During the war between Golagros and Arthur, Agalus was captured by Arthur’s knights.
Means "my master is (Imam) Ali", from Azerbaijani ağa meaning "lord, master", the Turkic possessive suffix -m, and the name Əli. Also see Ağamalı.

Means "my master is Ali", from Azerbaijani ağa meaning "lord, master", first person possesive suffix -m, and the name Ali 1. Alternatively this name may come from Azerbaijani ağa and mal meaning "property" (accusative malı).
Serbian, Russian, Spanish and Basque form of Agamede.

Means "very cunning", derived from Greek ἄγαν (agan) meaning "very much" and μήδεα (medea) meaning "plans, counsel, cunning". This was the name of two women in Greek mythology. One was, according to Homer, a Greek physician acquainted with the healing powers of all the plants that grow upon the earth, and the other was a princess of Lesbos as the daughter of King Macar.

Possibly derived from Ancient Greek ἄγαν (agan) meaning "very much" and μήδεα (medea) meaning "plans, counsel, cunning". In Greek mythology, this was the name of a famous architect who worked alongside his brother (or in some accounts his son or step-son) Trophonius to build the temple of Apollo in Delphi, as well as the treasury of the king Hyrieus, in which they constructed a hidden back door they could use to steal through.
Derived from Greek ἄγαν (agan) meaning "very, much" and μήστωρ (mestor) meaning "counsellor, advisor".
Chamorro word for blood used as a name for baby girls
Variant of Agnes.The name is not uncommon among Mennonites.
Derived from Guanche *azgan-ey, meaning "one-armed". This name was applied to the Guanche leader Mayantigo after having lost his arm during a battle.
From Ilocano and Maranao agani meaning "harvest".
Derived from Greek ἀγανός (aganos) meaning "mild, gentle, kind" and ἵππος (hippos) meaning "horse".

Possibly derived from Greek ἀγανός (aganos) meaning "mild, gentle" and ἵππος (hippos) meaning "horse". This was the name of various figures in Greek mythology. The most well known Aganippe was the name of both a fountain and the naiad associated with it. The well was created by the hooves of Pegasus and was associated with the Muses as a source of poetic inspiration. The nymph Aganippe is called a daughter of the river-god Termessus.
Means "the one with the stiff face" in Yoruba, a clipping of Aganjusola.

Means "the one with the stiff face makes honor" in Yoruba. According to Yoruba tradition, this is the name of a warrior king deified after his death, said to fight by shooting fire. He is associated with wilderness, the desert, and volcanoes. This is also a rare given name.

A knight who, with his brother Agion, joined their cousin Harpin in his siege of the Castle of Three Maidens. Sir Hector of the Fens and the King with the Hundred Knights arrived to defend the castle, and Agano and Agion were killed.
A knight in the service of King Mordrain, ruler of the Arabain kingdom of Sarras. When Mordrain left his land to seek Joseph of Arimathea in Britain, he bequeathed his kingdom to Aganor.
Benedictine abbot of St. Gabriel's in Campania, Italy.

Derived from the Greek noun ἀγάπη (agape) meaning "love, affection, esteem" (see Agape) combined with the Greek noun ἀνήρ (aner) meaning "man".In Greek mythology, this is the name of a king of Arcadia. He was one of the Achaean leaders in the Trojan War.
French and Niçard form of Agapetos.
Possibly derived from Greek ἄγαν (agan) meaning "very, much" and φαντός (phantos) meaning "visible" (see phanes).
Romanian & Slavic (Russian Агапия) form of the ancient Greek name Agapi means - "love".
Italian and Spanish form of Agapios.

Martyr in the reign of Emperor Aurelian. Buried in Palestrina, in Italy, Agapitus is traditionally identified as a fifteen-year old caught in the persecutions of the Christians in Antioch. He was brought before the governor when he announced his faith. The young man was tortured and beheaded. The tale is perhaps apocryphal, and Agapitus' cult was limited in 1969 to local status. A similar tale has been told about saints named Porphyrius and Venantius.
Means "one who is loved", from Greek ἀγαπάω (agapao) meaning "to love, be fond of, show affection for" (see agape).
Probably derived from Greek ἀγάπη (agape) meaning "love" and the Epic form of πόλεμος (polemos) meaning "war". This was the name of a son of Aegyptus in Greek mythology.

Meaning unknown. This is the name of a demon who appears in several works on demonology, including the 17th-century grimoire The Lesser Key of Solomon (author unknown), the Pseudomonarchia Daemonum (1563) by Dutch physician Johann Weyer and the Dictionnaire Infernal (1818) by French occultist Jacques Collin de Plancy.
Probably derived from Greek ἄγαν (agan) meaning "very, much" and ἄριστος (aristos) meaning "best".

column3: あがさ(Japanese Hiragana)|アガサ(Japanese Katakana)|開夏彩, 明雅砂, 有伽沙, 阿笠, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 亜 (a) meaning "second, Asia", 芽 (ga) meaning "bud, sprout, shoot" combined with 沙 (sa) meaning "sand". Other kanji combinations are possible.Usage of this name is most likely influenced by the name Agatha.
Combination of Azerbaijani ağa meaning "lord, master" and Səlim.
Possibly derived from Greek ἀγαστός (agastos) meaning "admirable" ἀνδρός (andros) meaning "of a man". Alternatively, a variant form of Agesandros.
Possibly means "shrieker". This was the name of an early Semitic goddess of war who was merged into Ishtar in her identity as fearless warrior of the sky.
Derived from Greek ἀγαστός (agastos) meaning "admirable" and δᾶμος (damos) meaning "the people", a Doric Greek variant of δῆμος (demos).
Derived from Greek ἀγαστός (agastos) meaning "admirable" and an uncertain second element, possibly γράτις (gratis) meaning "grass, green fodder".
Derived from Greek ἀγαστός (agastos) meaning "admirable" and κλέος (kleos) meaning "glory".
Derived from Greek ἀγαστός (agastos) meaning "admirable" and κράτος (kratos) meaning "power, strength".
Probably derived from Greek ἀγαστός (agastos) meaning "admirable" and λαός (laos) meaning "people, folk". Compare Agesilaos.
Possibly derived from Greek ἀγαστός (agastos) meaning "admirable" and either μένος (menos) meaning "mind, strength, courage" or μένω (meno) meaning "to stay, wait, remain".
Derived from Greek ἀγαστός (agastos) meaning "admirable" and ἵππος (hippos) meaning "horse".
Derived from Greek ἀγαστός (agastos) meaning "admirable" and σθένος (sthenos) meaning "vigour, strength".
Possibly derived from Greek ἀγαστός (agastos) meaning "admirable" and στρατός (stratos) meaning "army". Also compare Agesistratos.

Means "very strong", derived from Greek ἄγαν (agan) meaning "very, much" and σθένος (sthenos) meaning "vigour, strength". This was the name of a king of Elis from Greek mythology, and of one of the Gigantes slain during the Gigantomachy.
Derived from Greek ἄγαν (agan) meaning "very, much" and στρέφω (strepho) meaning "to turn, to twist". This was the name of a Trojan soldier in the Iliad.

From Sanskrit अगस्ति (agasti) of uncertain meaning. This is the Sanskrit name for the star Canopus, which may have been derived from the root अञ्ज् (añj) meaning "to shine, to make clear". Another theory has proposed the meaning "mover of mountains", from Sanskrit अग (aga) meaning "mountain" combined with अस्ति (asti) meaning "one who surpasses, pervader, thrower". This is the name of a great sage who appears in several Hindu texts, including the Puranas, Ramayana and Mahabharata.
Catalan, Sardinian, Piedmontese and Sicilian form of Agatha. The name coincides with Catalan àgata "agate".
Variant of the feminine name Agatha recorded in the 19th century in East Frisia.
Possibly derived from Greek ἀγαθός (agathos) meaning "good" and ἀγητός (agetos) meaning "admirable, wonderful".
Derived from Greek ἀγαθός (agathos) meaning "good" and ἄναξ (anax) meaning "lord, king, master".
Derived from Ancient Greek ἀγαθός (agathos) meaning "good" combined with ἀνδρός (andros) meaning "of a man" (compare Agathanor).
Means "good man", derived from the Greek adjective ἀγαθός (agathos) meaning "good" combined with the Greek noun ἀνήρ (aner) meaning "man".

Means "son of Agatharchos" in Greek, derived from the name Agatharchos combined with the patronymic suffix ἴδης (ides).A notable bearer of this name was the Greek historian and geographer Agatharchides of Cnidus (2nd century BC).

The first element of this name is derived from Greek ἀγαθός (agathos) meaning "good". The second element is either derived from Greek ἀρχός (archos) "master" or from Greek ἀρχή (arche) "origin, source".
Alternate transcription of Greek Ἀγάθαρχος (see Agatharchos).

Probably means "of good days, one who brings lucky days", derived from Ancient Greek ἀγαθός (agathos) meaning "good, noble, fortunate" combined with ἡμέρα (hemera) meaning "day". Compare the word ἀγαθήμερος (agathemeros) meaning "of good days, of lucky days". Alternatively, the second element could derive from ἥμερος (hemeros) meaning "civilized, gentle".
Means "good day" in Ancient Greek, a masculine form of Agathemeris.
Derived from Greek ἀγαθός (agathos) meaning "good" and στρατός (stratos) meaning "army".
Means "good fortune", from Greek ἀγαθός (agathos) meaning "good" and τύχη (tyche) meaning "fortune, chance, fate".
Derived from Greek ἀγαθός (agathos) meaning "good" (see Agathon). It was borne by a 6th-century Greek historian and poet, who chronicled the reign of Byzantine emperor Justinian I.
Variant transliteration of Αγαθή (see Agathi and Agathy).
Diminutive of Agathe, as it contains the French feminine diminutive suffix -ine.
Derived from Greek ἀγαθός (agathos) meaning "good" and ἵππος (hippos) meaning "horse". This was the name of a lover of Apollo.
Latinized form of Agathon. This name was borne by a 7th-century pope.

Derived from the Greek adjective ἀγαθός (agathos) meaning "good" combined with the Greek verb βούλομαι (boulomai) meaning "to will, to wish, to prefer". Also compare the Greek noun βουλή (boule) meaning "will, determination" as well as "counsel, advice" and the Greek verb βουλεύω (bouleuo) meaning "to take counsel, to deliberate".
Latinized form of Agathoboulos. This was the name of a Cynic philosopher from the 2nd century AD.
Latinized form of Agathokleia. This was the name of the favourite mistress of the Egyptian Greek pharaoh Ptolemy IV Philopator (3rd century BC).
Variant latinization of Agathokleia, because its proper (and most common) latinized form is Agathoclea.
Variant latinization of Agathokleia, because its proper (and most common) latinized form is Agathoclea.This was the name of a Roman saint from Hispania, who died around 230 AD.

Latinized form of Greek Ἀγαθοδαίμων (Agathodaimon) meaning "noble spirit", from ἀγαθὸς (agathos) "good, noble" and δαίμων (daimon) "spirit".In Greek mythology he was the daemon, or presiding spirit, of the vineyards and grain fields, and a personal companion spirit, ensuring good luck, health, and wisdom. In Ptolemaic Egypt he was associated with the Egyptian god of fate Shai. He was depicted as a serpent or as a young man holding a cornucopia and a bowl in one hand and a poppy and an ear of grain in the other. The agathodaemon was later adapted into a general daemon of Fortuna, particularly of the continued abundance of a family's good food and drink. Pausanias conjectured that the name was a mere epithet of Zeus.
Derived from Greek ἀγαθός (agathos) meaning "good" and δίκη (dike) meaning "justice, custom, order".
Ancient Greek name meaning "good gift" with the elements ἀγαθὸς (agathos) "good" and δῶρον (doron) "gift". In turn, the name means “gifted person, good gift, donor of goods.”
Latinized form of Agathodoros. Agathodorus was an early Christian martyr in Pergamon, Asia Minor.
Feminine form of Agathokles. This name was borne by an Indo-Greek queen from the 2nd century BC.
Derived from Greek ἀγαθός (agathos) meaning "good" and an uncertain second element; possibly μένος (menos) meaning "mind, strength, courage" or μένω (meno) meaning "to stay, wait, remain".
Derived from Greek ἀγαθὸς (agathos) meaning "good" and μόρος (moros) meaning "fate, destiny; doom".
Latin variant of Agathonice, which is the latinized form of the Greek given name Agathonike. This name was borne by Agathonica of Pergamus, a martyr and saint from the 3rd century AD.

Latinized form of Agathonike. This name was borne by an early Christian saint from Thyatira, who was either martyred with her brother Papylus and a companion named Carpus, or committed suicide after Carpus and Papylus were tortured and sacrificed by pagans.
Latinized form of Agathonikos. This name was borne by saint Agathonicus of Nicomedia (3rd century AD).

Feminine form of Agathonikos. This name was borne by an early Christian saint from Thyatira, who was either martyred with her brother Papylus and a companion named Carpus, or committed suicide after Carpus and Papylus were tortured and sacrificed by pagans.
Derived from the Greek adjective ἀγαθός (agathos) meaning "good" combined with the Greek noun νίκη (nike) meaning "victory".
Means "of good name, of honourable name", derived from Greek ἀγαθός (agathos) meaning "good" and ὄνυμα (onyma) meaning "name".
Derived from Greek ἀγαθός (agathos) meaning "good" and φανής (phanes) meaning "appearing, seeming".
Derived from Greek ἀγαθός (agathos) meaning "good" and φέρω (phero) meaning "to bring, to carry, to bear".
Derived from Greek ἀγαθός (agathos) meaning "good" and φωνή (phone) meaning "voice".
Means "bearing good tidings, bringing good news" in Greek, derived from ἀγαθός (agathos) meaning "good" and φέρω (phero) meaning "to bring, to carry, to bear".
Derived from Greek ἀγαθός (agathos) meaning "good" and πόλις (polis) meaning "city".
Derived from Greek ἀγαθός (agathos) meaning "good" and πούς (pous) meaning "foot".
Derived from Greek ἀγαθός (agathos) meaning "good" and στρατός (stratos) meaning "army".
Derived from Greek ἀγαθός (agathos) meaning "good" and ξένος (xenos) meaning "foreigner, guest, stranger".
Portuguese form of Agathios via Agathius.
Spanish and Italian form of Agathoclia. This is the name of a patron saint of Mequinenza, Aragón, Spain.
Romanian and Serbian form of Agathodoros.
Italian Spanish and Portuguese form of Agathodorus via Agathodoros.
Polish and Swedish form of Agathon.
Polish and Serbian form of Agathonikos.
Vernacular form of Agathe and Agätt.

Medieval Italian diminutive of Agata, as -uccia is an Italian feminine diminutive suffix.A known bearer of this name was Agata "Agatuccia" de Pesce (also Pesci), the mistress of king Martin I of Sicily (1374-1409).
From the Turkic titles ağa meaning "lord, master" and khan meaning "ruler, leader".
From Azeri ağa "lord, master" and yar "friend, helper".
Means "elderly warrior" or "most senior of the brave ones" in Yoruba, from àgbà "elder, adult" and akin "bravery, valour; a brave person, warrior".
Means "carried and cared for" in Yoruba, from gbé "to carry, hold, lift" and kẹ́ "to care for, pamper, cherish".
Means "he/she has fallen" in Jagham and Kenyang, spoken in Nigeria and Cameroon. It derives from the Jagham root gbɔ̌ meaning "to fall" maybe referred to God's blessings falling from above.

The geographer Pausanias (7.17.10–12) records the following story about Agdistis, which he says the people of Pessinus told. Zeus, while asleep, spilled some of his semen on the earth, which in time gave rise to a deity (δαίμων) with both male and female sexual organs called Agdistis. Now the other gods, afraid of Agdistis, cut off the male genitalia, and from this grew an almond tree.
Means "hole in the ice for fishing" in Greenlandic.

Agee was the father of Shammah, who was one of David's mighty men (II Samuel 23:11). Based on interpretations of I Chronicles 11:34 and II Samuel 23:32-33 Agee was either the grandfather of Jonathan or his brother.

column3: 揚羽, 亜夏羽, 亜華羽, 愛華羽(Japanese Kanji)|あげは(Japanese Hiragana)|アゲハ(Japanese Katakana)
column12: This name can be used as 揚羽, 亜夏羽, 亜華羽 or 愛華羽 with 揚 (you, a.garu, -a.ge, a.geru) meaning "fry in deep fat, hoist," 亜 (a, tsu.gu) meaning "Asia, come after, rank next," 愛 (ai, ito.shii, o.shimu, kana.shii, mana, me.deru, a) meaning "affection, favourite, love," 夏 (ka, ga, ge, natsu) meaning "summer," 華 (ka, ke, hana) meaning "flower, gay, gorgeous, luster, ostentatious, petal, shine, showy, splendour" and 羽 (u, ha, hane, wa) meaning "feathers."As a word, Ageha (揚羽) refers to a type of butterfly known as the swallowtail, abbreviated from agehachō (揚羽蝶), derived from a combination of 上げ (age), the imperfective and continuative form of the verb 上げる (ageru) meaning "to raise," and 羽 (ha).Fictional bearers include Ageha (揚羽) from the shōjo manga Basara, Ageha (アゲハ) from the 1996 film Swallowtail and Ageha Yoshina (夜科 アゲハ) from the manga series Psyren.This name is rarely given to girls, if given at all.
Derived from the Latin agellus meaning "little farm; little field".
This is the name of an Empress and Queen of Italy, the wife of Guy III of Spoleto, who reigned from 891 to 894.

In Yoruba mythology, Agemo is a chameleon who is the messenger of the gods. He is the main deity of the Ijebu people, as he is believed to protect children and safeguard the future of Ijebu people through his blessing.

Agena is the traditional name of a star in the constellation Centaurus, also known as Hadar or the Beta Centauri. It is believed to be derived from Latin genua, meaning "knees", referring to the star's position on the left knee of the centaur depicted in the constellation Centaurus.

Agenaric was an Alemannic prince in the 4th century. Agenaric was the son of petty king Mederic and the nephew of another petty king, Chnodomarius. In 357, together with his uncle, Agenaric commanded the Alemannic army at the Battle of Strasbourg, in which the Alemanni were defeated by Julian.
Possibly a medieval diminutive of names beginning with the Old French element agin, a lengthened form of Proto-Germanic *agjō "blade" (e.g. Agenulf; see Aginulf).
Derived from Old French agin, and thus ultimately from Proto-Germanic *agio "blade", and Old High German hiltja "battle".
Goddess who endowed a child with the capacity to lead an active (actus) life. Her name is presumably derived from the Latin verb ago, agere, egi, actum, "to do, drive, go."
Means "son of Agenor" in Greek, derived from the name Agenor combined with the patronymic suffix ἴδης (ides).
Perhaps a variant of Aginulf. Also see Einulf.
Spanish and Italian form of Haggai and variant of Hageo and Aggeo.

Derived from the nickname of Basque writer Balentin Aurre-Apraiz (Valentín Aurre Apraiz in Spanish), who was also known as Agerrekoa. His nickname was likely derived from the name of the farmstead where he grew up, Mendieta-Agerre.
Derived from Basque agerkunde "appearance, apparition; revelation; Epiphany", Agerkunde is the Basque equivalent of Spanish Epifanía and French Épiphanie (compare also English Epiphany).
Derived from Basque agertu "to reveal; to appear", this name is a fairly recent coinage (most likely by Sabino Arana) intended as a variant of Agerkunde.
Latinized form of Agesandros. This was an epithet of the Greek god Hades, as well as the name of the Greek sculptor Agesander of Rhodes.
Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Agesander.

The first element of this name is either derived from Greek ἆγειν (agein) meaning "to carry, to fetch" or from Greek ἄγω (ago) "to guide, to lead" (also see Agis). The second element is derived from Greek ἀνδρός (andros) meaning "of a man".
Italian and Spanish form of Agesilaus.

The first element of this name is either derived from Greek ἆγειν (agein) meaning "to carry, to fetch" or from Greek ἄγω (ago) "to guide, to lead" (also see Agis). The second element is derived from Greek λαός (laos) meaning "(the) people".
Portuguese and Catalan form of Agesilaus.
Latinized form of Agesilaos. This was an epithet of the Greek god Hades, as well as the name of two kings of Sparta.
Bulgarian and Russian form of Agesilaos (see Agesilaus).

The first element of this name is either derived from Greek ἆγειν (agein) meaning "to carry, to fetch" or from Greek ἄγω (ago) "to guide, to lead" (also see Agis). The second element is derived from Greek πόλις (pólis) meaning "city, city state". This name was borne by three Agiad kings of Sparta.
Derived from Greek ἄγω (ago) meaning "to lead" and stray (stratos) meaning "army". Alternatively, could be a Doric Greek form of Hegesistratos.

Means "host-leading, one who leads the army" in Ancient Greek, derived from ἄγω (ago) meaning "to lead, guide" and στρατός (stratos) meaning "army". This was the name of a Trojan warrior killed by Ajax the Great in Greek mythology. It was also an epithet of the goddess Athena.
Portuguese and Catalan form of Haggai.
Derived from Greek ἄγγελος (angelos) meaning "messenger" and ἵππος (hippos) meaning "horse".
Possibly a Sami form of Aggi.

column5: EG-gi(Danish, Old Danish)|AG-gi(Norwegian, Swedish, Old Swedish)|/ˈacː.ɪ/(Icelandic)
column12: Diminutive of Ágúst, Angelica and other names containing Ag.
Variant of Haggith which means Means "festive" in Hebrew.

A variant of Agravain. The second and probably the most unpleasant son of King Lot and Queen Margawse of Orkney (sometimes Anna), nicknamed aux dures mains (‘of the hard hands’). Brother of Gawain, Gaheris and Gareth, and Mordred. He married Laurel, the niece of Lionors and Lynette. He is a nephew of King Arthur.
Derived from Persian aga ("master") and Turkish bey (title given to provincial governors and senior officers).
Means "war is in the house" in Igbo.
Derived from Persian aga ("master") and jan ("dear").
Aghan is the name of a human being in J.R.R. Tolkien's "Lord of the Rings" book series.
Derived from Persian aga ("master") and Armenian pap ("grandfather").
From Ottoman Turkish آغا (ağa) meaning "agha (an honorific for high officials)".
Means "from the field of the old tree" in Irish.
Georgian form of Akbugha (also found spelled as Ağbuğa in Turkish). This name was borne by two princes of Meskheti, namely Aghbugha I Jaqeli (1356-1395) and Aghbugha II Jaqeli (1407-1451).
According to one online source, this is a rare Armenian name meaning "white rose" from Proto-Turkic *ak "white" and Persian گل (gol) "rose", 'now especially used in villages.'
Of uncertain origin and meaning. This was the name of two Irish saints.
Derived from the Armenian elements աղու (aghu) "suave" and վեհ (veh) "sublime".
Means "Caucasian Albanian" in Armenian. Caucasian Albania was an ancient country in the Caucasus, not connected to the modern state in the Balkans.
Means "she sings praises" in Bette Obudu.
Derived from the Germanic element agil (which is an extended form of ag - see Agmund and also Egil) combined with Old High German bald "bold, brave."
Derived from the Germanic element agil (which is an extended form of ag - see Agmund and also Egil) combined with Proto-Germanic beran or bernu "bear" (bero and bern in Old High German).
Derived from the Germanic element agil (which is an extended form of ag - see Agmund and also Egil) combined with Old High German beraht "bright".
Derived from the Germanic element agil (which is an extended form of ag - see Agmund and also Egil) combined with Old Norse brand "sword."
Derived from the Germanic element agil (which is an extended form of ag - see Agmund and also Egil) combined with Old High German fridu "peace."
Derived from the Germanic element agil (which is an extended form of ag - see Agmund and also Egil) combined with Gothic hardus (hart in Old High German) "brave, hardy."
Derived from the Germanic element agil (which is an extended form of ag - see Agmund and also Egil) combined with Old High German mund "protection."
Italian and Portuguese form of Agilulf.
Spanish form of Agilulf and Italian and Portuguese variant of Agilolfo.
Latinized form of Agilulf. Agilulfus of Cologne was an 8th-century saint.
Derived from the Germanic element agil (which is an extended form of ag - see Agmund and also Egil) combined with Old High German wart "guard."
Derived from Basque hagin "yew (tree)" and the suffix -aga. It is also the name of a town in the Basque region of Spain, which is occasionally the inspiration behind this name.

Taken from the name of an ancient monastery near Ihabar (in the general area of Navarre). This monastery doesn't exist anymore, however it is known that García Sánchez III of Navarre made a donation to it in 1025.
Derived from the Germanic element agin (which is an extended form of ag - see Agmund) combined with Old High German bald "bold, brave."
Derived from the Germanic element agin (which is an extended form of ag - see Agmund) combined with Old High German beraht "bright."
Derived from the Germanic element agin (which is an extended form of ag - see Agmund) combined with Old High German fridu "peace."
Derived from the Germanic element agin (which is an extended form of ag - see Agmund) combined with Gothic hardus (hart in Old High German) "brave, hardy."

Derived from the Germanic element agin (which is an extended form of ag - see Agmund and compare Egino) combined with rîcja "powerful, strong, mighty." The second element is also closely related to Celtic rîg or rix and Gothic reiks, which all mean "king, ruler."
Derived from the Germanic element agin (which is an extended form of ag - see Agmund) combined with þruþ "strength."
From the Germanic elements agin "edge of a sword" (which is an extended form of ag - see Agmund) and wulf "wolf".
Means "ease" in Italian.It is used as diminutive of many names ending with -agio.

A knight who, with his brother Agano, joined their cousin Harpin in his siege of the Castle of Three Maidens. Sir Hector of the Fens and the King with a Hundred Knights arrived to defend the castle, and Agion and Agano were killed.
From the name of a town in the Basque region of Spain.

Derived from the Greek verb ἄγω (ago) meaning "to lead, to guide" as well as "to bring, to carry". It is closely related to the Greek verb ἡγέομαι (hegeomai) meaning "to go before, to lead (the way)" as well as "to guide". This name was borne by several kings of Sparta.
Of uncertain origin and meaning. Theories include a variant of Agate.
Cognate of Aglaia. According to Orthodox Christian ecclesiastical traditions, Aglaida is venerated as a Virgin-Martyr alongside Saint Drosis.
Hungarian and Slovak form of Aglaia.
Derived from the Greek adjective ἀγλαός (aglaos) meaning "splendid, shining, bright" (see Aglaos) combined with the Greek noun ἀνήρ (aner) meaning "man".

Derived from the Greek adjective ἀγλαόδωρος (aglaodoros) meaning "bestowing splendid gifts", which consists of the Greek adjective ἀγλαός (aglaos) meaning "splendid, shining, bright" (see Aglaos) combined with the Greek noun δῶρον (doron) meaning "gift".This was also an epithet of Demeter, the Greek goddess of the harvest, agriculture, sacred law and the cycle of life and death.

Derived from the Greek adjective ἀγλαόκαρπος (aglaokarpos) meaning "bearing beautiful fruit", which consists of the Greek adjective ἀγλαός (aglaos) meaning "splendid, shining, bright" (see Aglaos) combined with the Greek noun καρπός (karpos) meaning "fruit" (see Carpus).This was an epithet of Demeter, the Greek goddess of the harvest, agriculture, sacred law and the cycle of life and death.
Derived from the Greek adjective ἀγλαός (aglaos) meaning "splendid, shining, bright" (see Aglaos) combined with the Greek noun μάχη (mache) meaning "battle".
Latinized form of Aglaonike. This name was borne by a Greek astronomer from the 1st or 2nd century BC.
Derived from the Greek adjective ἀγλαός (aglaos) meaning "splendid, shining, bright" (see Aglaos) combined with the Greek noun νίκη (nike) meaning "victory".

Derived from the Greek adjective ἀγλαός (aglaos) meaning "splendid, shining, bright" (see Aglaos) combined with the Greek noun νόος (noos) meaning "mind".In Greek mythology, Aglaonoe is the name of one of the Sirens.

Derived from the Greek adjective ἀγλαός (aglaos) meaning "splendid, shining, bright" (see Aglaos) combined with either the Greek noun ὄψ (ops) meaning "voice" or the Greek noun ὤψ (ops) meaning "eye, face, countenance".In Greek mythology, Aglaope is the name of one of the Sirens.
Derived from the Greek adjective ἀγλαός (aglaos) meaning "splendid, shining, bright" (see Aglaos) combined with Greek φανής (phanes) meaning "appearing" (see Theophanes).

Derived from the Greek adjective ἀγλαός (aglaos) meaning "splendid, shining, bright" (see Aglaos) combined with the Greek adjective φαντός (phantos) meaning "visible", which is ultimately derived from the Greek verb φαντάζω (phantazo) meaning "to make visible".

Derived from the Greek adjective ἀγλαόφημος (aglaophemos) meaning "of splendid fame", which consists of the Greek adjective ἀγλαός (aglaos) meaning "splendid, shining, bright" (see Aglaos) combined with the Greek noun φήμη (pheme) meaning "prophetic saying" as well as "rumour" and "(good) report, repute, fame".In Greek mythology, Aglaopheme is the name of one of the Sirens.

Derived from Greek ἀγλαός (aglaos) meaning "splendid, shining, bright" (see Aglaos) and φωνή (phone) meaning "voice" as well as "sound, tone".This was the name of an ancient Greek painter, who is thought to have lived around the late 6th or early 5th century BC.

Derived from Ancient Greek ἀγλαόφωνος (aglaophonos) meaning "with a splendid voice", which consists of ἀγλαός (aglaos) meaning "splendid, shining, bright" (see Aglaos) combined with φωνή (phone) meaning "voice" as well as "sound, tone".In Greek mythology, Aglaophonos is the name of one of the Sirens.
Latinized form of Aglaophonos. In Greek mythology, Aglaophonus is the name of one of the Sirens.
Derived from the Greek adjective ἀγλαός (aglaos) meaning "splendid, shining, bright". Also compare the related name Aglaia.
Derived from the Greek adjective ἀγλαός (aglaos) meaning "splendid, shining, bright" (see Aglaos) combined with the Greek noun σθένος (sthenos) meaning "vigour, strength".
Derived from the Greek adjective ἀγλαός (aglaos) meaning "splendid, shining, bright" (see Aglaos) combined with the Greek noun στρατός (stratos) meaning "army".

Derived from the Greek adjective ἀγλαότιμος (aglaotimos) meaning "splendidly honoured", which consists of the Greek adjective ἀγλαός (aglaos) meaning "splendid, shining, bright" (see Aglaos) combined with the Greek verb τιμάω (timao) meaning "to honour, to esteem, to revere".This was also an epithet of Demeter, the Greek goddess of the harvest, agriculture, sacred law and the cycle of life and death.
Variant of Aglaurus used by Sir John Suckling for the title character in his 1637 play Aglaura, set in Persia.

Derived from Ancient Greek ἄγλαυρος (aglauros), a variant of ἀγλαός (aglaos) meaning "bright, shining, splendid". The name is also written as Ἄγραυλος (Agraulos), in which case it could be from ἄγραυλος (agraulos) meaning "rural, rustic, of the fields". In Greek mythology, Aglauros was the eldest daughter of the Athenian king Cecrops, and appears in various legends.
Latinized form of Aglaos. This name was borne by a Roman governor of Crete from the 3rd century AD.In Greek mythology, Aglaus is one of the sons of king Thyestes of Olympia, whom he had with a Naiad.

The maiden daughter of King Nascor.The devil tricked her brother, Nabor, into raping her by a spring, but Aglinda prayed, and Nabor fell dead.In memory of Aglinda's plight, the spring was called the Spring of the Virgin, and it was enchanted to paralyze visiting non-virgin knights. Erec became one of its victims.

The maiden daughter of King Nascor. The devil tricked her brother, Nabor, into raping her by a spring, but she prayed, and Nabor fell dead. In memory of her plight, the spring was called the Spring of the Virgin, and it was enchanted to paralyze visiting non- virgin knights. Erec became one of its victims
Derived from the English-speaking words "a glistening," meaning shining or glittering.
In Inuit mythology, Agloolik is a spirit that lives underneath the ice and gives aid to fishermen and hunters.
Aglovale de Galis is the eldest legitimate son of King Pellinore of Galis (Wales), introduced in the Vulgate Lancelot.

Form of Agmundr. The first element of this name is derived from ag, an uncertain element for which a few possible origins exist. The accepted explanation is that it comes from Proto-Germanic *agjo, which means "sharp, pointed." Because of that, it also means "edge", as in the sharp cutting side of a sword - which is why the meaning of the element has ultimately come to be "sword". See also Anglo-Saxon ecg (in e.g. Egbert) or Old High German ekka (New High German ecke, which means "corner"). Other possibilities for the meaning and origin of ag include: Gothic agan "to fear, to be afraid", Old Norse agi "unrest, agitation", Gothic ahjan "to believe" and Old Norse aka "to do, to act." The second element of this Germanic name is derived from Old High German mund "protection."
Short form of Agneta and Agnes, but can also be a feminine form of Agnar.
Scandinavian variant of Agna. In the case of the Latvian usage, this name might also be a variant of Lithuanian Agna.
From the Nordic name elements ag meaning "edge of sword, blade" and nelli.
Italian form of Agnellus, the name coincides with Italian agnello "lamb"-

Derived from Latin agnus "lamb" and the diminutive suffix -ellus. Agnellus of Naples (535 - 596) was a Basilian monk and later Augustinian friar. He is venerated as a saint by the Catholic Church, with a feast day on 14 December, the date of his death.
Spanish and Portuguese form of Agnello.
Medieval Aragonese and Kashubian form of Agnes.
Kashubian variant of Agnés and Cremish Lombard form of Agnes.
Elaboration of Agnes using the suffix -ine.
Diminutive of Agnesa, not used as a given name in its own right.
Diminutive of Agnes, recorded in Switzerland between the 14th and 15th centuries.
Walloon and Gallo form of Agnès.
Silesian form of Agnes via Polish Agnieszka.
East Prussian German, North Frisian and East Frisian variant of Agnes via the variant Agnete. As a North Frisian name, Agnet was recorded on the island of Föhr.

From Latin Agnetis, which is the genitive of the third declension of Agnes, the latinized form of the Greek name Hagne.In the Netherlands, this has been used as a Latin form of Agnes (thus basically making it a latinization of a latinization) since at least late medieval times.
Means "fiery, belonging to Agni 1" in Sanskrit. In Hindu mythology Agneya (also known as Agneyi) is the daughter of the fire god Agni.
Variant of Agnes which is now sometimes considered a variant of Agna.

Means "friend of fire" from Sanskrit अग्नि (agni) meaning "fire" and मित्र (mitra) meaning "friend". This was the name of a ruler of the Shunga Empire, which existed in the 2nd century BCE in north-central India. He was featured as one of the titular characters in the play Mālavikāgnimitram by 5th-century author Kalidasa, in which he falls in love with his chief queen's handmaiden Malavika.
Old Swedish variant and Luxembourgish form of Agnes.
Variant of Agnes, recorded in Silesia in the 14th century.

Derived from Ancient Greek ἁγνός (hagnos) meaning "pure, chaste, holy" and δίκη (dike) meaning "justice". According to legend, this was the name of the first woman to legally practice medicine in Ancient Greece (4th century BC), having disguised herself as a man to study in Egypt, then to work in Athens. Agnodike was so successful that rival doctors accused her of seducing her female patients; when she revealed herself to be a woman during trial, they attempted to charge her for illegally practicing medicine. Her patients, many of them wives of important Athenians, defended her, and so she was allowed to continue working. She was most likely not an actual historical figure, as the earliest account of her existence is found in Fabulae, a Latin handbook of mythology authored in approximately the 2nd century AD.
Derived from Ancient Greek ἁγνός (hagnos) meaning "pure, chaste, holy" and κριτής (krites) meaning "judge, critic".
Variant of Angiolo. This name was borne by Agnolo di Tura, an Italian chronicler from the 14th century AD.
The name of the daughter of a French count Stephen of Penthièvre.
Derived from Ancient Greek ἁγνός (hagnos) meaning "pure, chaste, holy" and στρατός (stratos) meaning "army".
Etymology unknown, mother of Iñupiaq writer Joan Naviyuk Kane.
Variant of the feminine name Agnes recorded in the 19th and 20th centuries in East Frisia.
Combination of the name element agn taken from names like Agnes or Agnar, and the name element ny "new".

Agobard of Lyon (c. 779–840) was a Spanish-born priest and archbishop of Lyon, during the Carolingian Renaissance. The author of multiple treatises, ranging in subject matter from the iconoclast controversy to Spanish Adoptionism to critiques of the Carolingian royal family, Agobard is best known for his critiques of Jewish religious practices and political power in the Frankish-Carolingian realm. He was succeeded by Amulo of Lyons.
Older spelling of Agung influenced by Dutch orthography.
Older spelling of Agus influenced by Dutch orthography.

Latinized form of a Frankish name derived from the elements aggju meaning "blade" and friþu meaning "peace". This was the name of an 8th-century French saint, also known as Aifroy, who served as a Benedictine monk and abbot. He was the brother of Saint Leutfridus.
Derived from Albanian agon "to become morning, dawn".
Name of a Guanche warrior in the Canarian island of La Gomera. It was revived in the 1980's.
One of the rarer virtue names introduced by the Puritans, referring to Jesus' agony in the garden of Gethsemane.
Meaning unknown. It was borne by a 8-year-old Guanche girl sold at the slave market in Valencia in 1495.

The first element of this name is either derived from Greek ἀγορεύω (agoreuo) "to orate, to speak publicly" or from Greek ἀγορά (agora), which can mean "assembly" as well as "market". The second element is derived from Greek κριτης (krites) meaning "judge, critic."
Derived from Greek αγόρι (agori) meaning "boy, lad" and combined with the feminine suffix -ω (-o).
Basque form of Augustin. This name was borne by Basque writer and politician Agosti Xaho.
Cremish and Bergamesque Lombard form of Agostino.
Aragonese and Galician form of Augustinus.
Milanese Lombard, Venetian and Ligurian form of Agostino as well as a medieval Spanish variant of Agustín.
Corsican variant of Agustinu and Sardinian form of Agostino.
Means "thick-billed Murre", which is a type of bird.

Archaic spelling of Appaaq using the old Kleinschmidt orthography. Appaaq is a West Greenlandic name meaning "chick of a thick-billed murre", the thick-billed murre being a bird (species Uria lomvia).
From Sanskrit अग्रजा (agrajā) meaning "older sister, first-born".

Georgian form of Agrippina, possibly via its Russian form Agrafena.This is the standard Georgian form of the Roman name. The form Agripina (აგრიფინა), which is closer to the original, is also used in Georgia, but it has always been much rarer.
The name of a nephew of King Arthur in Arthurian tales.

a Variant of Agravain The second and probably the most unpleasant son of King Lot and Queen Margawse of Orkney (sometimes Anna), nicknamed aux dures mains (‘of the hard hands’). Brother of Gawain, Gaheris and Gareth, and Mordred. He married Laurel, the niece of Lionors and Lynette. He is a nephew of King Arthur.
Italian and Spanish form of Agreus.

Derived from Latin agrestis meaning "rural, rustic, wild, brutish", from ager "field, farm". This is the name of an ancient pagan king of Camelot in the Old French Arthurian romance 'Estoire del Saint Graal' ("History of the Holy Grail", 1220-35). In a time long before Arthur, God punishes Agrestes for massacring the Christians in Camelot (converted by Josephus, son of Joseph of Arimathea and guardian of the Holy Grail) with madness and death; the king commits suicide by diving into a fire after eating his hands and slaughtering his family.

Derived from Ancient Greek αγρεύς (agreus) meaning "hunter". In Greek mythology, Agreus was the name of one of the Panes, three spirits or aspects of the god Pan. It was also an epithet of the rustic deity Aristaeus, as well as of Apollo, Poseidon, and Bacchus.

A variant of Agravain. The second and probably the most unpleasant son of King Lot and Queen Margawse of Orkney (sometimes Anna), nicknamed aux dures mains (‘of the hard hands’). Brother of Gawain, Gaheris and Gareth, and Mordred. He married Laurel, the niece of Lionors and Lynette. He is a nephew of King Arthur.

Means "farmer; grower" in Latin from ager; agri meaning "field, land" combined with the verb colere meaning "to cultivate; to grow".Currently it is an Italian feminine adjective meaning "agricultural; farming; rural".

Means "wild, savage, harsh; living in the fields" in Ancient Greek. This was the name of several figures in Greek mythology, including one of the Giants (or Gigantes) killed in the Gigantomachy, a half-bear son of Polyphonte, a centaur, a suitor of Penelope, and a Calydonian prince.
Armenian and Old Armenian form of Agrippa.
Feminine version of Agrippa. Meaning "breech birth". Babies who survived these births were considered to have a lucky life.
Latinized form of Agrios. This is the name of several characters in Greek mythology, including a son of the Calydonian king Parthaon, brother of Oeneus.

This was an epithet of the Greek goddess Artemis, under which title she was regarded as the patron goddess of hunters. Conceivably related to Greek ἄγρᾱ (agra) "hunt, catch" and the name of the Brythonic war goddess Agrona, from old Celtic agro "battle, carnage".
Old Norse and Icelandic form of Agatha.
Old Norse byname meaning "a person from Agder".
Means "being touched" in Greenlandic, derived from the Greenlandic attorpaa "to touch him/her/it".
