Alternate transcription of Arabic علاء الدين (see Ala ad-Din), chifely used in Morocco.
Means "daughter" in Medieval Basque. It was documented from the 12th century onwards.
The first element of this name is derived from Gothic alls "all" or from Gothic alhs (alah in Old High German) "temple." The second element is derived from Old High German bald "bold, brave."

From the name of the American state (see Alabama). It was borne by a short-lived daughter of the novelist William Faulkner (11 January 1931-20 January 1931), who was named after his great-aunt Alabama 'Bama' McLean (1874-1968). This was used by Zelda Fitzgerald for the main character in her semi-autobiographical novel Save Me the Waltz (1932). It was also used for one of the main characters in the movie True Romance (1993), played by actress Patricia Arquette. The name may also be given in reference to the popular Southern rock and bluegrass band Alabama, which was formed in Fort Payne, Alabama, in 1969.The American drummer and television personality Travis Barker used this name for his daughter in 2005. It was also used by actress Drea de Matteo and musician Shooter Jennings for their daughter born 2007.

Means "horse victory", from the Carian ala "horse" and banda "victory". In Greek mythology he was a Carian hero, son of Euippos and the naiad Callirrhoe, and the eponymous founder of Alabanda in Caria, Anatolia (modern day Turkey). He was apparently given the name Alabandus after winning a horse race, and his original name is unknown. He is sometimes also known as Hipponicus, which has the same meaning in Ancient Greek.
The first element of this name is derived from Gothic alls "all" or from Gothic alhs (alah in Old High German) "temple." The second element is derived from Old High German beraht "bright."
Means "born of the white cloth, born of purity" in Yoruba, from àlà "white cloth, purity" and bí "to give birth, be born".
Derived from Kurdish ala "flag" and can "life".

From the French surname Alacoque. Its popularity as a name, especially among Catholics, is likely due to Saint Margaret Mary Alacoque, V.H.M., a French Roman Catholic nun and mystic, who promoted devotion to the Sacred Heart of Jesus in its modern form.
"a fence" from Filipino dialect Ilocano.Can be a short form of Aladin.
Hungarian form of either Aldric or Aldemar.
Means "royalty has accepted shade" in Yoruba.
Means "nothing is superior to royalty" in Ijaw.
Means "royalty has found the right path" in Yoruba.
Means "the king has prestige" in Yoruba.
Derived from Arabic al-’uz̧fur, meaning "the talons of the swooping eagle". This is the traditional name of the star Eta Lyrae in the constellation Lyra.
Alternate transcription of Arabic علاء الدين (see Ala al-Din), as well as the Maguindanao, Indonesian and Bosnian form.
Aladine is Priscilla's lover who appears in Book 6, Cantos 2–3. He is wounded by the wicked knight but survives.
Italian and Spanish form of Aladdin.
From Arabic عَلَاء (ʿalāʾ) meaning "exalted, lofty, excellent" (related to Ali 1 and Aali).
Variant transcription or form of Ala ad-Din.
Alternate transcription of Arabic علاء الدين (see Ala ad-Din) chiefly used in North Africa.
Alternate transcription of Arabic علاء الدين (see Ala ad-Din), chifely used in Morocco.
Meaning unknown. This is the name of a general of the Narts in the Ossetian Nart epic.
Means "queen, woman of substance" in Ijaw.
Perhaps an Anglicized variant of Elettra.

Of uncertain meaning, possibly a corruption of Alethea (compare Alethaire). In the United States, this name was first found in 1768; in the United Kingdom, there were several uses throughout the 1800s (and most likely before that as well). While the background of the American bearers of this name is unknown, almost all British bearers were born to traveling Romani families.
The first element of this name is derived from Gothic alls "all" or from Gothic alhs (alah in Old High German) "temple." The second element is derived from Old High German fridu "peace."
From Tamil அழகு (aḻaku) meaning "beauty" and அப்பா (appa) meaning "father" or "lord."

The first element of this name is derived from Gothic alls "all" or from Gothic alhs (alah in Old High German) "temple." The second element is derived from gardan "to hedge in, to enclose, to fence in" or from Gothic gards "house, garden, (court)yard."

The first element of this name is derived from Gothic alls "all" or from Gothic alhs (alah in Old High German) "temple." The second element is derived from Gothic gasts (gast in Old High German) "guest, stranger."The name is reconstructed from the historic place name Alagastesheim (766), preserved in the current place names Gau-Algesheim and Waldalgesheim (Germany).
From Mongolian алаг (alag) meaning "multicoloured, dappled, patchy, piebald" and баатар (baatar) meaning "hero".
From Mongolian алаг (alag) meaning "multicoloured, dappled, patchy, piebald" and чимэг (chimeg) meaning "ornament, decoration".
The first element of this name is derived from Gothic alls "all" or from Gothic alhs (alah in Old High German) "temple." The second element is derived from Gothic gairns "eager, desiring."

Contracted form of Adelagia. The Genoese noblewoman Alàgia dei Fieschi, who Dante praises in his 'Purgatorio' (c.1318), was a niece of Pope Adrian V and the wife of Dante's friend Moroello III Malaspina.

The first element of this Germanic name comes from Gothic alls "all" or from Gothic alhs (alah in Old High German) "temple." The meaning and origin of the second element is rather uncertain: we know that it comes from gis (the original form was possibly gîs), but we don't exactly know where gis itself comes from. But there are a few possibilities. It might come from Gallo-Celtic gaiso "spear" (see Gaiseric) or it might be a short form of gisel, which means "hostage" or "pledge" (see Giselle). Alagis was the name of a 7th-century king of the Lombards.
The first element of this name is derived from Gothic alls "all" or from Gothic alhs (alah in Old High German) "temple." The second element is derived from gisel "hostage" or "pledge."
The first element of this name is derived from Gothic alls "all" or from Gothic alhs (alah in Old High German) "temple." The second element is derived from Old High German gund "war."
The first element of this name is derived from Gothic alls "all" or from Gothic alhs (alah in Old High German) "temple." The second element is derived from Old Norse hildr "battle."
The name of a 7th-century Lombard king.
The name of the Chumash goddess of the moon who also governs over purification, health and menstruation.
Possibly an invented name based on Adelaide or Anaíde.

Derived from the surname of the noble family Alaimo, which emigrated from the kingdom of Aragon to the kingdom of Sicily in the 12th century. Theirs is a patronymic surname, and there are two possibilities for its etymology. The first is that it consists of the Spanish article al combined with the Germanic name Aimo or Haimo. The second possibility is that it is derived from a shortened form of Adalheim, such as Alhaim or Alheim. Whichever possibility applies, the surname is primarily Germanic either way.
Variant of Alaina. 39 girls in the USA were named Alainah in 2011.
Medieval French feminine form of Alain.
Probably a combination of the elements al- (like in Alaíde) and -ir (like in Ademir, Edir and Lucelir).
From the name of a mountain range in Navarre, Spain.
Taken from the name of a Marian church in the greater Álava area.

'The Haunting Of Alaizabel Cray' (2004) is a Gothic steampunk horror/alternate history novel by Chris Wooding about a young man and an amnesiac girl fighting a cult in an alternate Victorian era London.
Combination of अलाक (alaka) meaning "forelock" and नन्द (nanda) meaning "joy". This is the name of a river in the north of India.
Combination of Əli and Əkbər, used in honor of Ali al-Akbar, son of Husayn ibn Ali.
Means "survived to be cherished" in Yoruba, from là "to survive" and kẹ́ "to care for, cherish".
Presumably a variant of the Scottish name Alickina, a feminine form of Alick or Alec (which possibly developed from Ailigean, a diminutive of Ailig, itself a Gaelic rendering of English Alick).
From Karachay-Balkar ала (ala) meaning "light" and кёз (köz) meaning "eye".
Alternative transcription of Belarusian Аляксандр (see Aliaksandr).
Alternative transcription of Belarusian Аляксандра (see Aliaksandra).
Ancient Hittite form of Alexandros (see Alexander). This was the name of a Wilusan king who signed a treaty with the Hittite kings Muwatalli II and Mursuli II.

The name of the older sister of Lakshmi and the Hindu goddess of misfortune. She is sometimes viewed, according to one source, as another avatar of a form of the goddess Kali. It is derived from a, a negative participle, and the name Lakshmi, meaning "one who is not the goddess Lakshmi".
Means "may I see his path", deriving from the Akkadian element alaktu ("the route,the journey (of gods, of people)").
Possibly from the Kurdish al meaning "banner, flag".

Means "the exalted". Laqab of Ala 1. This was the personal name of Abu Sa'd al-'Ala' ibn Sahl (c. 940–1000), a Muslim mathematician, physicist and optics engineer. Ibn Sahl is credited with first discovering the law of refraction, and used it to create anaclastic lenses.

Derived from Greek ἀλαλή (alalē) meaning "war-cry, battle-cry". This onomatopoeic name belonged to the female personification of the war-cry in Greek mythology. She was an attendant of the war god Ares, whose war-cry was her name: Alale alala.

Probably means "the Protectress, the Defender" from the Greek verb ἀλαλκεῖν (alalkein) "to ward, to keep off". This was an epithet of the goddess Athena as guardian of Boeotia. It is connected with the name of Ἀλαλκομεναί (Alalkomenai), a city in Boeotia; also compare Alalcomenes.

Means "guardian", derived from Ancient Greek ἄλαλκον (alalkon) meaning "to ward, keep off; to defend, succour, protect", a variant of (or related to) ἀλέξω (alexo) "to defend, help" (compare Alexamenos). Alalcomenes was an autochthon in Greek mythology, and the eponymous founder of the ancient town Alalcomenae. In some accounts, he raised or tutored the goddess Athena.

Derived from the Georgian adjective ალალი (alali) meaning "honest, truthful, upright". It ultimately comes from Arabic حلال (halal) meaning "allowed, permitted" as well as "lawful, legal, legitimate".

"The All-Knowing One", "The Knowledgable One"God, Allah, KnowledgeMost commonly known as one of the 99 names given to Allah in Islam. When used in the context of God, it means the all-knowing one. When used to name a human, it means the knowledgable one.
Possibly a variant of Ellamae or Alma 1.
Means "mark of the religion" from Arabic علم ('alam) meaning "sign, mark, flag, banner" and دين (dīn) meaning "religion, faith".
The first element of this name is derived from Gothic alls "all" or from Gothic alhs (alah in Old High German) "temple." The second element is derived from man "man."
Medieval Basque and Gascon feminine form of Alaman.
The first element of this name is derived from Gothic alls "all" or from Gothic alhs (alah in Old High German) "temple." The second element is derived from Old High German mâri "famous."

From Persian عالمگیر‎ (alamgir) meaning "conqueror of the world", derived from Arabic عالم (ʿālam) meaning "world, universe" combined with Persian گیر (gīr) meaning "catch, seize, conquer". This was another name of the 17th-century Mughal emperor Aurangzeb.
Most likely a corruption of Wilhelmina.
A duke in the service of Feirefiz, Perceval's half·brother.
From the Tagalog word alam (ultimately from Arabic عَالَم‎ ālam) meaning "knowledge, learning, wisdom, understanding".
From Indonesian alam meaning "universe, world", ultimately from Arabic عالم (ʿālam), and Persian شاه (shāh) meaning "king".
The first element of this name is derived from Gothic alls "all" or from Gothic alhs (alah in Old High German) "temple." The second element is derived from Old High German mund "protection."

The first element of this name is derived from Gothic alls "all" or from Gothic alhs (alah in Old High German) "temple." The second element is derived from Gothic môds (mut in New High German) "mind, spirit."
Derived from Arabic عالم (ʿālam) meaning "world, universe" combined with Persian زیب (zib) meaning "embellishment, ornament, beauty".

column3: 阿兰, 阿岚, etc.(Chinese)|Алан(Ossetian)|阿懶(Chinese)

column12: From alana meaning "awakening, rise" in Hawaiian, or from ʻālana meaning "offering" in Hawaiian.
Late medieval Gallicized Breton feminine form of Alan 1 by way of combining it with the French feminine diminutive suffix -ette.

As a Brazilian Portuguese name, the origin and meaning are unknown. As an English name, it is likely a feminine form of Alan 1.It may also be given as a personal name in reference to the medieval kingdom of Alania, whose territory spanned the North Caucasus. In the case of the kingdom, Alania derives from the Old Iranian stem Aryāna-, a derivative form of the Indo-Iranian stem arya-. It is cognate with the name of Iran (Ērān), which stems from the Old Persian Aryānām, "of the Aryans."
Possibly a variant of Alani or a diminutive of a Alannah.
Means "the strong-willed", from Anoud prefixed with the Arabic definite article.
Transferred use of the surname Alans.
Derived from Old Lithuanian alėti "to stream merrily; to run (referring to water)". Alanta is also the name of a river in Lithuania.
An elongation of Proto-Germanic *allaz 'all; every; whole' + Old High German deo 'servant'.
Diminutive of Alapaʻinuiakauaua, a king of Hawaiʻi island in ancient Hawaii.
From ala pa'i nui a ka uaua meaning "great revenge path of the hard-headed". Alapa'i was the king of Hawai'i Island in 16th century Hawai'i.

Used by Refik Halit Karay for one of the main characters in his 1950-51 serialized novel 2000 Yılın Sevgilisi (Sweetheart of the Year 2000). Karay based the name on that of Alara Castle, a medieval fortress near Alanya in southern Turkey.However, it is sometimes claimed to be a Turkish rendering of Elere or Elire, the name of a character in some Siberian tales, or to be the name of a beautiful water fairy in Turkic mythology, who is said to live in the lakes and rivers of the Caspian basin and to grant wishes for those she deems worthy; she is also able to repair broken hearts and make them capable of love again.
The first element of this name is derived from Gothic alls "all" or from Gothic alhs (alah in Old High German) "temple." The second element is derived from Old High German rât "counsel."
Germanic name, in which the second element is hramn meaning "raven". The first element may be ala "all" (compare Alaric) or a form of Gothic alhs "temple" (Old High German alah).
From the play The Tragedy of Titus Andronicus (late 16th century) by William Shakespeare. Alarbus is the son of Tamora.

A knight from whom Caradoc, one of Arthur's knights, rescued a maiden named Guignier. After their duel, Alardin and Caradoc became friends, and Alardin accompanied Caradoc to Arthur's court. He had some knowledge of magic and later, when Guignier lost her breast to a serpent, Alardin provided a magical shield which replaced the lost flesh with gold. Alardin married Guigenor, Arthur's grand.niece. His father was named GuiniacalcAlso, a knight encountered by Gawain during the latter's quest to retrieve a white hart stolen from Arthur's hall. Alardin refused to allow Gawain to cross a river without a battle, and Gawain slew him in the subsequent duel.
Medieval Latin form of Adalhard via its contracted variant Alard.
Meaning unknown. This is the Ossetian lord of smallpox who had to be placated.

column5: al-la-rees(Afrikaans, Australian English, New Zealand English)|al-la-ree-kuh(Afrikaans, Australian English, New Zealand English)

column12: Czech and German form of Alaric.
Galician, Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Alaric.
The first element of this name is derived from Gothic alls "all" or from Gothic alhs (alah in Old High German) "temple." The second element is derived from Anglo-Saxon ridan "to ride."
Most likely a transferred use of the Québecois surname Alarie which is derived from the Visigothic personal name Alaric.
Variant form of Alaric.Name day in the Finland Swedish calendar: May 24th
Russian and Ukrainian form of Alaric.

A knight who cuckolded Sir Claristant by riding off with his amie. Claristant caught up with them and engaged Alaris in combat. Alaris was assisted by Claristant's treacherous maiden. Claristant would have been killed, but Kay and Gaswain intervened and saved him.
Combination of Əli and Azerbaijani əsgər meaning "soldier" or Asghar meaning "smallest, youngest" (referring to Ali al-Asghar, son of Husayn).
Medieval Italian contracted form of Adelasia which became the regular Piedmontese form of Adelaide.
Gothic name derived from the elements alhs "temple" (Old High German alah) and sinþs "way, path".

From the name of the American state of Alaska, which is ultimately derived from Aleut alaxsxaq "mainland". A famous bearer of the name was Alaska P. Davidson (1868-1934), an American law enforcement officer known for being the first female special agent in the FBI.

The first element of this name is derived from Gothic alls "all" or from Gothic alhs (alah in Old High German) "temple." The second element is derived from Gothic svinths (swind in Old High German) "strength."
Means "king's love" or "love of royalty" in Ijaw.
Form of Galadriel in the fictional Telerin language, meaning "maiden crowned with a garland of radiance".
This is the traditional name of a star in the constellation Lyra - Mu Lyrae. Its traditional name Alathfar comes from the Arabic الأظفار al-ʼaẓfār, meaning "the talons (of the swooping eagle)".

An epithet of Mars found on an altar at South Shields in England, and on a votive plaque found in Hertfordshire in England. There is disagreement of its meaning, with some academics interpreting it as "hunstman" and others as "cherisher". This was the name of a sorcerer in the BBC series, Merlin.

The Alatyr in Russian legends and folklore is a sacred stone, the "father to all stones", the navel of the earth, containing sacred letters and endowed with healing properties. The awareness of the existence of such a stone exists in various parts of the Slavdom. It is often mentioned in stories and referred to in love spells as "a mighty force that has no end."
From Basque alatz, an uncommon word meaning "miracle". It is the masculine form of Alazne.
Alternate transcription of Arabic علاء الدين (see Ala ad-Din), as well as the Bengali and Indonesian form.
Alternate transcription of Arabic علاء الدين (see Ala ad-Din), as well as the Indonesian, Malay and Ingush form.

Alauina (also spelled Alauna or Alavina) is a mother-goddess from ancient Celtic (Gaulish) mythology. Worshipped primarily in the Rhineland region of modern-day Germany (such as in Pantenburg), she is typically depicted as a nurturer, often represented in figurines holding children or carrying baskets of fruit.Linguists translate her name as "the Nourisher". It shares linguistic roots with Old Irish and Old Norse words meaning "to nourish" or "to feed".Her cult survived into the Roman era, with inscriptions and altars erected by Roman citizens and worshippers who honored her as a provider of abundance and fertility.
Means "light of the early dawn" or "sunset glow" in Hawaiian, literally "flaming road" from Hawaiian ala "path, road" and ula "flame".
Likely a modern variant of Alana. Alauna, as a toponym, has Romano-Celtic origins meaning "nourishing river".
Also a Gaulish god of healing and prophecy, who was venerated in the areas of Mannheim (Germany) and Salzburg (Austria).
Elaborated form of Laura or a variant of Elora.

The first element of this Gothic name is derived from Gothic alls "all" or from Gothic alhs (alah in Old High German) "temple." The etymology of the second element is uncertain; it may be derived from Gothic qvivs "alive, living". It could also have been derived from Gothic weihan "to battle, to combat" (which is ultimately derived from Proto-Germanic wigwó or wihwó "battle"), which would then make this name a cognate or a variant of Alawig. Last but not least, it could also have been derived from Latin vivus "alive, living", thus making Alaviv name a hybrid Gothic-Latin name. Since this spelling of the name could possibly have been influenced by Latin, the original Gothic form of Alaviv may have been Alaweihs or Alaweigs or Alaweiws, but this is uncertain.
Italian and Spanish form of Alavivus.
Latinized form of Alaviv. Alavivus was a leader of the Thervingi (a Gothic tribe), who lived in the 4th century AD.
Derived from Welsh alaw "melody, tune; lily, water lily".
The first element of this name is derived from Gothic alls "all" or from Gothic alhs (alah in Old High German) "temple." The second element is derived from Old High German wart "guard."
Derived from the Arabic ʿAlāʾ ad-Dīn, meaning ”servant of Allah, nobility of faith, nobility of religion, nobility of the faith”. It is one of a large class of names ending with ad-Din.

Derived from Old Norse element ala ("entire; all") combined with one of several possible elements: vīðr ("wide, far, extensive"), viðr ("forest, wood, tree") or veðja ("engage, stake, wager").This is possibly the by-name of a god in Norse mythology.
The first element of this name is derived from Gothic alls "all" or from Gothic alhs (alah in Old High German) "temple." The second element is derived from Old High German wîg "warrior."
The first element of this name is derived from Gothic alls "all" or from Gothic alhs (alah in Old High German) "temple." The second element is derived from Old High German wini "friend."
Derived from Old Norse elements ala "entire, all" and vinr "friend".

The first element of this name is derived from Gothic alls "all" or from Gothic alhs (alah in Old High German) "temple." The second element is derived from Old High German wîsan "to rule, to lead" (or wîso "leader" or wîs "wise").
Derived from Welsh alaw meaning "melody, harmony" (see Alaw). This was the name of an early bard, said to be one of the three founders of druidism.
Alawo means "white, green" in Yoruba.When combined with "ewe", it means "splendid, ok, good, nice".
Most likely a combination of the names Allison and Asia 1 (or Aja). May be related to Elijah.
Most likely a combination of the prefix a- and the prefix Layla.According to the USA Social Security Administration, 117 girls were recorded with the name Alayla in 2017.
Variant of Elaine or feminine form of Alan 1. This is the name of a minor character in George R. R. Martin's 'A Song of Ice and Fire'.
Likely an invented name using the same sounds found in names such as Alicia (or Alysia, Alesia), Alayah, Asia and Malaysia.
Of uncertain origin, possibly a variant of Elizabeth.
Meaning "I have given birth to royalty" in Ijaw.
Derived from Romanian alb "white; (figuratively) clean, pure, immaculate".
Derived from Romanian albă, the feminine form of the adjective alb "white; (figuratively) clean, pure, immaculate".
Romanian form of Snow White, from Romanian albă ca zăpada "white woman of snow".
Combination of Alba 1 and Chiara. Use of this name is most likely influenced by the song 'Albachiara' by Vasco Rossi.
The name given in La Tavola Ritonda to the Queen of Orkney. As Gawain's mother and Arthur's half·sister, she is therefore the counterpart of Anna or Morgues.
Action oriented, pioneer, natural leader, independent, strong willed, positive, energetic, enterprising, enthusiastic, brave and innovative.
This is the official name of the star Pi Saggitarii. Albaldah was the traditional name of a star system. It comes from the Arabic بلدة bálda "the town".
This is the traditional name of the star Epsilon Aquarii. It comes from Arabic البالع (albāli‘), meaning "the swallower".

From the name of the country in the Balkans, as well as various other places, perhaps ultimately from a pre-Indo-European word *alb meaning "hill" or from the Indo-European root *alb "white" (see Albus).It can also be used as an elaboration of Alba (the Scottish Gaelic name for Scotland) or a feminine form of Alban.
Latinized form of Snow White, from Latin alba ("white") and nix ("snow").
Corsican and Sicilian form of Albanus.
Transferred use of the name of the city of Albany.
Means "the free, the exempt, the innocent" in Arabic, ultimately from the root برئ (bariʾa) meaning "to be free, to be innocent". This was the name of two companions of the Prophet Muhammad.
Alternate transcription of Arabic البراء (see Al-Bara).

column3: Албасты(Russian, Uzbek Cyrillic)|Алвасти(Altai, Tajik, Tatar, Kazakh, Kyrgyz)
column12: A spirit in Caucasian mythology who is seen as being a personification of guilt, associated with punishing crimes which have gone unpunished.
East Prussian German variant of Alba, as well as a short form of Albine.
Transferred use of the surname Albee
Derived from Old High German alb (which comes from Old Norse âlfr) "elf" combined with Old High German gund "war."
Meaning unknown. Perhaps a transcription variation of Alpelindis, itself a variation of the Germanic female name Alflind, from alf meaning "elf, spirit" and lind meaning "soft, tender".
Derived from Old High German alb (which comes from Old Norse âlfr) "elf" combined with Old High German rât "counsel."
Either a masculine form of Adalburg or a variant of Albert.
Derived from the Old German names Alberga and Albergia which ultimately derive from the name Ethelburga.
French form of Alberich. A known bearer of this name was the French composer Albéric Magnard (1865-1914).
Possibly a feminine variation of Albero.
Short form of Adalbero or Adelbero, derived from Old High German adal meaning "noble" combined with Old High German and Old Saxon bero meaning "bear", making it a variant of Adalbern.
Jèrriais, Languedocian, Gascon and Cremish Lombard form of Albert.
Gascon form of Alberte 2 and Jèrriais and Cremish Lombard feminine form of Albèrt.
Italian form of Albertanus. Albertano da Brescia was an author of Latin social treatises and sermons.
Possibly derived from Albertus. Albertanus of Brescia (born Albertano da Brescia) was an author of Latin social treatises and sermons.
Latinized form of a diminutive of Albertus. Used by a saint.
Galician and older Greek form of Albert.
Transferred use of the surname Albertson.
Corsican, Sardinian and Sicilian form of Albert.
Medieval Italian diminutive of Alberta, as -uccia is an Italian feminine diminutive suffix.
Medieval Italian diminutive of Alberto, as -uccio is an Italian masculine diminutive suffix.

A dwarf king in Der Pleier's Garel. Albewin's people were terrorized by the giant Purdan. Arthur's Sir Garel saved them by slaying the giant, which the grateful Albewin rewarded by helping Garel kill a demon named Vulganus. Garel appointed Albewin the steward of Anferre.

Taken from the name of a grotto in the Aralar Range in the Basque Mountains where a dolmen was discovered in 1915, as well as from the name of a suburb of Bilbao where Sabino Arana Goiri was born. Goiri was a writer, creator of the Basque flag, founder of the Basque Nationalist Party (PNV) and is generally considered "the father of Basque nationalism".
Feminine form of Albiero, itself a variant of Alberico.
Generally the Dutch form of Albinus, but in some instances it can be derived from Albuin as well. A bearer of this name was the Flemish painter Albijn Van den Abeele (1835-1918).

Means "the lady", derived from the Arabic definite article ال (al) combined with Turkic bika meaning "lady, mistress, woman" (a feminine form of the Turkish military title beg meaning "chieftain, master").
Tatar and Bashkir form of Albina.
Originally a diminutive of Albina, now used as a given name in its own right.
Coined by Sabino Arana and Koldo Elizalde as a Basque equivalent of Spanish Albina and French Albine.

Medieval French diminutive of Albin (as -et is a French masculine diminutive suffix). This given name is no longer in use in France, but it still survives there as a patronymic surname. Also compare Aubinet.
Feminine form of Albinius and Albin. It was introduced to Britain in the 17th century, and was frequently used by members of the aristocratic Cecil family.
Roman cognomen which was derived from Albinius. A bearer of this name was Lucius Sestius Quirinalis Albinianus, a Roman proquaestor and suffect consul from the 1st century BC.
Roman nomen gentile which was derived from Albinus. This was the name of several ancient Romans, some of which lived as early as the 4th century BC.
Diminutive of Albína, not used as a given name in its own right.
Hellenized form of Albinus. This name was borne by a Greek Platonist philosopher from the 2nd century AD.

Roman family name of Etruscan origin. This was borne by an obscure Plebeian family only known from inscriptions. They are most remembered by a single member, Publius Albinovanus, who is still fairly obscure.
Corsican and Sicilian form of Albin.

From the alternative name for Great Britain, now used poetically. It is thought to derive from Proto-Celtic *Albiu "upper world, high mountain", which is itself possibly derived from Proto-Indo-European *albʰós "white". It is hypothesized that the Romans took it as connected with albus "white", in reference to the white cliffs of Dover.Famous bearers of the name include American governor Albion Parris (1788-1857) and American sociologist Albion Woodbury Small (1854-1926).

Albiorica is an ancient Celtic/Gaulish goddess associated with the deep earth, healing waters, and the underworld. She is the female counterpart to the Celtic "King of the World" god, Albiorix (frequently associated with the Roman war god Mars).he name is derived from the Proto-Celtic elements albijo-, meaning "world" or "earth", and likely shares linguistic roots with the ancient name for Great Britain, Albion. Her name signifies "Worldly One" or "Ruler of the Earth."As a chthonic deity (meaning she is tied to the powers of the deep earth and water rather than the bright sun), she was worshiped alongside Albiorix at healing springs and subterranean water sources. She is known from Gallo-Roman inscriptions, notably documented in the dative form Albiorice on altars found in southeastern France (such as the Vaucluse region).
A name given on an inscription at Avignon to a Celtic war god, who may have been Tīwaz (see Tyr) or Teutates (Latinized form of Toutatis). Said to mean "king of the world".

This is the name of the star Beta Cygni.The origin of this name according to Wikipedia:The system's traditional name Albireo is a result of misunderstanding and mistranslation. It is thought that it originated in the Greek name ornis for the constellation of Cygnus, which became urnis in Arabic. When translated into Latin, this name was thought to refer to the Greek name Erysimon for the plant called Hedge Mustard (Sisymbrium officinale, which in Latin is ireo), and so was described in Latin in the Arabo-Latin Almagest of 1515 as 'Eurisim: et est volans; et jam vocatur gallina. et dicitur eurisim quasi redolens ut lilium ab ireo' ('Eurisim: and it is the flyer, and now it is called the hen, and it is called Eurisim, as if redolent like the lily from the 'ireo''), via a confusion between ireo and the scented flower Iris florentina. This was variously miscopied, until 'ab ireo' was treated as a miscopy of an Arabic term and changed into al-bireo.
Queen of the Wild Mountain. A malevolent knight named Kurian declared war on her, intending to steal her land. She was saved by Arthur's Sir Tandareis, who defeated Kurian in combat.
Albofledis was a Frankish noblewoman, the daughter of the Frankish king Childeric I, and the Thuringian noblewoman Basina.
Italian and Spanish form of Alboin.
Possibly derived from an Old High German cognate of Old English Ælfweald and Old Norse Alfvaldr, in which the first element is Old High German alb "elf".

Variant of Alban. A notable namesake is American attorney, scientist and inventor Albon Man (1826-1905) who experimented with early forms of photography and in the development of the incandescent light bulb, an invention later famously perfected by Thomas Alva Edison (1847 -1931).
From alborada meaning "dawn", which in turn comes from Latin albus meaning "white".
Feminization of both Albericus and, in early medieval times, of Alfred.
Medieval German feminine form of Alberich.

Albruna, Aurinia or Albrinia are some of the forms of the name of a probable Germanic seeress who would have lived in the late 1st century BC or in the early 1st century AD. She was mentioned by Tacitus in Germania, after the seeress Veleda, and he implied that the two were venerated because of true divine inspiration by the Germanic peoples, in contrast to Roman women who were fabricated into goddesses. It has also been suggested that she was the frightening giant woman who addressed the Roman general Drusus in his own language and made him turn back at the Elbe, only to die shortly after, but this may also be an invention to explain why a consul of Rome would have turned back. In addition, there is so little evidence for her that not every scholar agrees that she was a seeress, or that she should be included in a discussion on them. She may also have been a minor goddess, a matron.Her name has been discussed since the 19th century based on various different forms in the manuscripts where her name appears, and several theories have been put forward, of which Albruna used to be the most accepted one. The emendation Albruna has been explained with definitions such as 'having secret knowledge of elvish spirits', 'confidante of elves' and the 'one gifted with the divine, magical powers of the elves'. However, in 2002, the interpretation Albruna was seriously questioned by a Swedish scholar, who called it a "phantom name" (spöknamn), and since then more scholars have begun to doubt that the form was correct, and may be more in favour of the forms Aurinia and Albrinia. Other suggestions are that it has been derived from a Germanic word *auraz meaning 'water', 'sand' and 'luster', or that it may be a hybrid word containing the Latin word aureum for gold, but they have not become generally accepted. Moreover, it is pointed out that the emendation Albruna is noteworthy in its possible meanings, and that it is similar to the name of another early Germanic priestess.

Combination of Old High German alb "elf; supernatural being" (ultimately from Proto-Germanic *albh- "to shine; gleam") and run "secret lore" (ultimately from Proto-Germanic *rûno- "secret; magic; murmur; session").

She may also have been a minor goddess, a matron.

From the Old German elements alb "elf" and swind "strong". Albsuinda (or Alpsuinda) was the only child of Alboin, King of the Lombards in Pannonia (reigned c. 560-572), and his first wife Chlothsind, daughter of the Merovingian king of the Franks Chlothar (reigned 511-561).
This is the name of two stars in the constellation Aquarius: Mu Aquarii and Nu Aquarii. The name comes from an Arabic term al-bulaʽān (ألبولعان) meaning "the two swallowers".

Of uncertain origin. This is a commemorative name paying homage to the Battle of Albulena (1457) fought between Albanian forces led by Skanderbeg and an Ottoman army under Isak bey Evrenoz and Skanderbeg's nephew, Hamza Kastrioti. This battle, won by Skanderbeg, is now considered a symbol of Albania's freedom. Notable bearer is Albulena Haxhiu (1987-), current leader of Kosovo since 4th April 2026.

Possibly derived from Latin albus meaning "white". In Roman mythology Albunea was a nymph who dwelt at a sulfuric spring or fountain near the town of Tibur (modern Tivoli). This was also the name of the Tiburtine Sibyl, a sibyl (i.e. oracle or prophetess) worshiped in a grove at Tibur.
Derived from Old High German alb (which comes from Old Norse âlfr) "elf" combined with Old High German wini "friend".
Derived from Guanche *alby, meaning "colossus, giant". Alternatively, it might be a corruption of Mahy.
Diminutive of Alena 1, not used as a given name in its own right.
Derived from Greek ἀλκή (alke) meaning "strength, prowess" and μένος (menos) meaning "mind, strength, courage, force".
Latinized form of Alkandros. This name was borne by different figures in Greek mythology.
French form of Alkandros via Alcander.
Italian form of Alkandros via Alcander.
Latinized form of Alkanor. This name was borne by two characters from Greek mythology.
Given in honour of the 16th-century Spanish saint and mystic Peter of Alcántara (1499-1562). The place name Alcántara is itself from Arabic القنطرة (al-Qanṭarah) meaning "the bridge".

Latinized form of Greek Ἀλκαθόη (Alkathoê), which is derived from Greek αλκη (alke) "strength" and θοός (thoos) "swift, nimble". In Greek myth Alcathoe (or Alcithoe) was one of the Minyades, the three daughters of King Minyas of Orchomenus in Boeotia, Greece.
Derived from Greek ἀλκή (alke) meaning "strength, prowess, force" and θοός (thoos) meaning "quick, swift". This was the name of several characters in Greek mythology.
Latinized form of Alkenor. This name was borne by one of the Argives that fought in the Battle of the 300 Champions, which took place around 546 BC.
Italian, Galician and Spanish form of Alcaeus.
French and Italian masculine and feminine form of Alcestis.

Catalan, Portuguese, Romanian and Sicilian form of Alcaeus. Known bearers of this name include Brazilian writer and journalist Alceu Amoroso Lima (1893-1983) and Brazilian soccer player Alceu Rodrigues Simoni Filho (b. 1984).

From the English noun alchemy referring to "the causing of any sort of mysterious sudden transmutation" or "the ancient search for a universal panacea, and of the philosopher's stone, that eventually developed into chemistry", which ultimately comes from Greek χυμεία (chymeia) "art of alloying metals, alchemy" via Arabic al-kimiya (the source also of Persian Kimiya).
The giant, pagan king of Sarras in Arthur's time. He withstood an attack by King Richard of Jerusalem, but he was later baptized.
Form of Ealhhere found in the Phillimore translation of Domesday Book.

This is the name of the star Alpha Corvi in the Corvus constellation. It bore the traditional names Al Chiba (Arabic ألخبا al-xibā meaning "tent") and Al Minliar, al Ghurab (Arabic منقار الغراب al-manxar al-ghurab) or Minkar al Ghurab.
Means "rosy-cheeked," and is a very popular name for girls in Uzbekistan.
Old Irish form of Aergol used among Irish speakers in the early middle ages in the Kingdom of Dyfed.
French, Italian and Romanian form of Alcibiades.
Catalan, Portuguese, and Spanish form of Alcibiades.

Latinized form of Greek Αλκιβίη (Alkibie) which was derived from ἀλκή (alke) meaning "defense, defensive strength, valour" and βία (bia) "bodily strength, force, act of violence" (compare Alcibiades). In Greek mythology, this was the name of an Amazon who fought with Penthesilea at Troy.
Perhaps a feminine derivative of Alcide used by Marin le Roy de Gomberville for a princess in his 1636 novel 'Polexandre', which was later adapted by Jean-Baptiste Lully into a ballet (1658).

Latinized form of Ἀλκιδίκη (Alkidike), which is derived from Greek αλκη (alke) "strength, prowess" combined with δικη (dike) meaning "justice, judgement" as well as "custom, usage". In Greek mythology, Alcidice was the mother of Tyro.

Derived from Ancient Greek ἀλκή (alke) meaning "strength, prowess" and μήδεα (medea) meaning "plans, counsel, cunning". Alternatively, it could be a feminine form of Alcimedon, the second element instead being μέδω (medo) meaning "to protect, rule over". This was the name of the mother of the hero Jason in Greek mythology.
Latinized form of Alkimos. This name was borne by a Greek rhetorician, who flourished around 300 BC. It was also the name of several characters from Greek mythology.
This was the name of a Qing dynasty Minister of Justice.
Spanish and Portuguese form of Alkínoös (see Alcinous).
Spanish and Catalan form of Alcyone.
Italian and Spanish form of Alcyoneus.
Catalan and Portuguese form of Alcyoneus.
Latinized form of Alkiphron. This name was borne by an ancient Greek sophist.
Latinized form of Alkippos and Masculine form of Alcippe.
Derived from αλκη (alke) meaning "strength" and θοός (thoos) meaning "swift, nimble".
Latinized form of Alkmaion. This occurs in Greek mythology belonging to the son of Amphiaraus and Eriphyle.
Latinized form of Doric Greek Alkman. This was the name of an Ancient Greek choral lyric poet from Sparta. He is the earliest representative of the Alexandrian canon of the Nine Lyric Poets.
Latinized form of Alkmenor. In Greek mythology, this is the name of one of the sons of king Aegyptus of Egypt.
Medieval English and Middle English form of Ealhmund.
Alcor is a binary star system in the constellation of Ursa Major. Alcor was originally Arabic سها‎ Suhā/Sohā, meaning either the "forgotten" or "neglected" one.
Transferred use of the surname Alcott.
A name recorded in Domesday Book, perhaps a medieval form of an Old English name composed of the elements æðele "noble" and cuþ "known, familiar".

Old French name of Germanic origin, derived from Old Germanic alhs "temple" and wini "friend" (compare Alawin and Ealhwine). Alcuin was an 8th-century Anglo-Saxon scholar and theologian. He was also a teacher at the court of Charlemagne.
King of Iceland, who subjugated himself to Arthur in return for Arthur's promise to make his son, Esscol, a knight. Alcus married the daughter of the King of Russia.

Latinized form of Greek Ἀλκυονεύς (Alkyoneus), which is the masculine form of Alkyone (see Alcyone). This name was borne by four characters in Greek mythology, one of them being a Thracian Giant. In real life, Alcyoneus (also called Halcyoneus) was a son of Antigonus Gonatas, king of Macedonia (3rd century BC).
From the name of a town in the Basque region of Spain.
From the name of the Aldan River that flows through Yakutia.
Possibly a combination of Alda 1 and Bella. Aldabella was the name of the wife of Orlando and the sister of Oliver. She is also known as Aude and Alda 1.
Means "all-father", derived from Old Norse elements ala ("entire, all") and faðir ("father"). This is a by-name for Odin in Norse mythology.
From the town of Aldán in Galicia. It is named after the medieval owner of those lands, whose name comes from the Germanic root aldiz ("age, time") or aldaz ("old").

From Mongolian алдар (aldar) meaning "fame, glory" and жаргал (jargal) meaning "happiness, blessing"

Short form of Aldonas and of given names (often of foreign origin) that end in -aldas, such as Donaldas and Geraldas.It should be noted that at least one Lithuanian source states that this name is derived from the old Lithuanian noun aldas meaning "echo, sound" (compare Aidas), which is etymologically related to Aldonas.
Possibly the Kyrgyz form of Aldiyar.
Georgian form of the Alanic name Alda. A known bearer of this name was the Georgian artist Alde Kakabadze (1932-2016).

Derived from Arabic الدبران (al-Dabarān) meaning "follower" (from دبر (dábar) "to turn one's back"). This is the name of the brightest star in the constellation Taurus, presumably so named because it appears to follow the Pleiades rightward across the night sky. The apocryphal Book of Enoch describes Aldebaran as a fallen angel, who attempted to seduce an Assyrian queen in the form of a bull.
Latin form of Aldebrand. A famous bearer of the name was Saint Aldebrandus, who was born in the city of Sorrivoli, Italy and died in Fossombrone, Presaro e Ubrino, Italy.
Variant of Aldemir, replaced by the suffix -cir, taken from names ending with that pattern, e.g. Moacir.

It is most likely a metathesis of Adalgisel, although it is also possible that it is a name on its own. In that case, the name is derived from Gothic alds (alt in Old High German) "old" and gisel "hostage" or "pledge." Aldegisel I was a 7th-century ruler of Frisia.
Dutch and French form of Aldegund.
Derived from Gothic alds (alt in Old High German) "old" combined with Old High German mâri "famous". The name might also be a metathesis of Adalmar.
Variant of Aldenira influenced by Nora 1.

This is the name of the star Alpha Cephei in the constellation Cepheus. It bore the traditional name Alderamin, a contraction of the Arabic phrase الذراع اليمين al-dhirā‘ al-yamīn, meaning "the right arm".
Derived from Aldred, which is ultimately derived from Æthelred. Also compare Eldred.
Ancient Germanic variant of Aldric and Niçard form of Aldéric.
Transferred use of the surname Alderman or directly from the English word.
From the name of the territory of Alderney, in the channel islands.
Recorded in Switzerland in the 15th century.
From the Old English name Ealdgifu.
Derived from the Icelandic elements alda "heavy swelling wave, a roller" and either ey "island" or ey "good fortune".
Means "old peace", derived from Gothic alds (alt in Old High German) "old" combined with Old High German fridu "peace." The name might also be a metathesis of Adalfrid.
From Old English Ealdfrið, from Germanic Aldfrid.
Means "old mask", derived from Gothic alds (alt in Old High German) "old" combined with Old Norse grîma "mask." The name might also be a metathesis of Adalgrim.
This is the name of the star Gamma Gruis in the constellation Grus. The name Aldhanab comes from Al Dhanab, from the Arabic الذنب al-dhanab meaning "the tail (of the Southern Fish)".

Means "old helmet", derived from the Germanic elements ald "old" and helm "helmet, protection". However, it should be noted that there are also various cases where this name is a variant form of Adalhelm, due to metathesis.This name was borne by an Anglo-Saxon saint from the 8th century AD. His original name was actually Ealdhelm, but it was often variantly written as Aldhelm.
This is the traditional name of the star Zeta Draconis in the Draco constellation. Zeta Draconis has the old Arabic name الذئب al-dhiʼb "the wolf", given in its feminine form Al Dhiʼbah (ذئبة)
Form of Ealdhild found in the Phillimore translation of Domesday Book.
Meaning uncertain, possibly of Arabic origin.
Either a short form of Geraldine or a variant of Alden
Old Norse name, derived from *alu "protection, fortune" and dís "goddess", or possibly a variant of Alfdís.
Diminutive of names ending in -alda, such as Rómùalda.
Means "old man", derived from Gothic alds (alt in Old High German) "old" combined with man "man." The name might also be a metathesis of Adalman.
Diminutive of Reynaldo, Geraldo and other names ending in aldo.

Derived from the Lithuanian name Aldonis, which consists of two elements. The first element is either derived from the old Lithuanian verb aldėti meaning "to echo, to (re)sound" (see Aidas) or from the related old Lithuanian verb aldoti meaning "to shout, to scream" as well as "to make noise". The second element of the name consists of the masculine patronymic suffix -onis.With that said, it should be noted that the name Aldonas is also frequently encountered as a masculine form of Aldona, which is a feminine name of uncertain meaning and origin that is used in both Lithuania and Poland. One of the available possibilities for the etymology of that name is a derivation from the same root as Aldonas, however.
Either a truncated form of Caledonia or, more likely, an elaboration of Aldona.
Medieval Basque name of unknown meaning. It was recorded in 1175.
Younger form of Alfþórr and Hallþórr.

Perhaps derived from the Old English aldor, a form of ealdor meaning "elder, parent, head of family, chief, lord; author, source; age, old age" with the name suffix -nia to feminize the name.It might also be a variant of Aldonia.
A form of Ealdræd recorded in Domesday Book, which was written in Medieval Latin. It is also the form of the name used in the Phillimore translation of Domesday Book.
Variant of Aldrich, possibly incorporating Rick.
Transferred use of the surname Aldridge.
Possibly a variant of Aldric, used rarely in South America and the Philippines.

A King of Brittany two generations before Arthur. When the Archbishop Guethelin, Aldroen's kinsman, came to Brittany to beg for Aldroen's help in driving the Picts and Huns from Britain, Aldroen sent his brother Constantine, Arthur's grandfather, to accomplish the task and assume the throne of the island.

English and French form of Aldwin. Alduin was a king of the Lombards in the 6th century AD.In the popular video game series 'The Elder Scrolls', Alduin, or the World-Eater, as he is known to the residents of Skyrim, is an immensely powerful dragon. He is depicted as a malevolent force who destroys the world periodically, and the Nords (people of Skyrim) believe that his reappearance heralds the end of time. He is the self-proclaimed First-Born of Akatosh and aspect of Akatosh. His name can be separated into al du in in the Dragon language, which means "Destroyer Devour Master".
Means "old wolf", derived from Gothic alds (alt in Old High German) "old" combined with Gothic vulfs "wolf." The name might also be a metathesis of Adalwulf (see Adolf).
This is the name of the star Epsilon Delphini in the constellation Delphinus.
Latinized form (strictly feminine) of Aldus. It was recorded in Yorkshire in 1219.
Means "old guard", derived from Gothic alds (alt in Old High German) "old" combined with Old High German wart "guard." The name might also be a metathesis of Adalward.
Derived from Old English ealdwif "old woman".
Form of Ealdwig found in the Phillimore translation of Domesday Book.
Modern form of Ealdwine and/or Æðelwine. A known bearer of this name is Aldwyn Sappleton (b. 1981), a Jamaican track and field athlete.
From Tuvan алдын (aldyn) meaning "golden" and ай (ay) meaning "moon".
Means "golden girl" from Tuvan алдын (aldyn) meaning "gold, golden" and кыс (kys) meaning "girl, daughter".
Means "golden boy" from Tuvan алдын (aldyn) meaning "gold, golden" and оол (ool) meaning "boy, son".
Probably a short form of various Old Norse names, for example Áleifr and Alríkr. Oldest known usage of the name is from a runic inscription from the 9th century.
Means "the sweet voice of the heavens", from the Hawaiian 'ale'a, meaning "sweet voiced" and lani, meaning "heaven, sky, royal, majesty".

Alecrim is a woody, perennial herb with fragrant, evergreen, needle-like leaves and white, pink, purple, or blue flowers, native to the Mediterranean region.It is a member of the mint family Lamiaceae, which includes many other herbs. The plant is also sometimes called anthos, from the ancient Greek word ἄνθος, meaning "flower".
Possibly a modern combination of the male name Alec and the female name Electra.
Doric form of Electryone, instead deriving from Ancient Greek ἀλέκτωρ (alektor) meaning "rooster, cock", likely referencing her possible role as a goddess of the morning and waking from sleep.

Means "rooster, cock, chicken" in Ancient Greek. In Greek mythology, this was the name of a soldier who failed to alert Ares of Helios’s approach while guarding his door, causing the god’s affair with Aphrodite to be discovered. In anger, Ares transformed the youth into a rooster, which thereafter always announced the rising sun.

A hermit priest encountered by Perceval in a forest, beating a giant cross with a rod. Perceval refrained from punishing this blasphemy only because Alecys looked like a priest. He later discovered that Alecys hated the cross because Christ had died on one, just as one would hate a weapon which had killed one's relative.
Possibly a variant of Aludra or a diminutive of Alexandra
Variant of Alea or Allie, or a combination of a- and the name suffix -lee.
Alternate transcription of Arabic أليف (see Alif), as well as the Urdu form.
Arabic alternate transcription of Alim as well as the Urdu form.
The name of a character in the Van Helsing franchise.

Variant of Alevtyna created due to Russian pronunciation of v before consonant having f sound.

The first element of this name is derived from either the Epic Greek verb ἀλέγω (alego) meaning "to have a care, to mind, to heed" or the adjective ἀλεγεινός (alegeinos), which is the Epic Greek form of ἀλγεινός (algeinos) meaning "painful, grievous". The second element of this name is derived from the Greek noun ἀνήρ (aner) meaning "man".In Greek mythology, Alegenor is the father of the Boeotian warriors Clonius and Promachus, who both fought and died in the Trojan War.
From the name of a town in the Basque region of Spain.
Angela (English) or Ángela (Spanish) spelled backwards (compare Spanish Legna).
A Spanish name. Means happy, exitment,etc. Often used as a nickname.
Derived from Spanish and Galician alegría "joy, happiness", taken from the Spanish title of the Virgin Mary Nuestra Señora de la Alegría, meaning "Our Lady of Joy".
Combination of a and Leidy, standing for the English phrase "a lady".
Combination of a and Leidys in the same fashion as Aleidy.
Variant of Ali 2 with the spelling influenced by that of Leigh.
It’s not a common name but it’s Daniela backwards (like Airam for María) it exists
Variant of Elaine used in the 13th-century French 'Perceval de Didot'.
Old Norse form of the Old French name Alain.
Possibly from lei'ō meaning "to act wild" or Hawaiian form of Alejo.
Variant of Alister. According to Aleister Crowley (1875-1947), born Edward Alexander Crowley, this is "the Gaelic form of Alexander".
From Spanish alejandrita, referring to the alexandrite, a form of chrysoberyl.
Means "the one who trivialises things" in Bandial.
Means "black-and-white cow" in Dinka.A famous bearer is Sudanese-British model Alek Wek.
Means "older sister (of a boy)" in Greenlandic.
Originally a Low German diminutive of names containing the element adal, particularly Adelheid, now used as a given name in its own right.
Means "beautiful, precious older sister of a boy" in Greenlandic, from a combination of Aleĸa and the suffix -tsiaq "beautiful, precious".
Originally a diminutive of names containing the element adal, particularly Adelheid, now used as a given name in its own right.
Samoan form of Alexander or Alexis.
Shortened form of Aleksandar, a South Slavic name.
Polish, Slovene, Bulgarian and Latvian short form of Aleksandra as well as a Polish feminine form of Aleksy.
Serbian, Latvian and Lithuanian form of Alexandria.
Variant of Aleksander inspired by Alexandros.
Croatian and Serbian form of Alexian.
Possibly a Esperanto form of Alexis.

Finnish and Latvian form of Alexis. This name was borne by Finnish author Aleksis Kivi (originally Alexis Stenvall) who wrote the first significant novel in the Finnish language, 'Seitsemän veljestä' ('Seven Brothers') in 1870.

Bulgarian and Russian form of Alexios (see Alexius). At least in Russia, the difference between this form and the more common Aleksey is possibly that Aleksiy comes directly from Alexios, while Aleksey comes directly from Alexis. Either that, or Aleksiy is an older Russian form of Aleksey. A known bearer of this name is the late 15th patriarch of Moscow (1929-2008), who spelled his name as Алексий (Aleksiy) rather than Алексей (Aleksey).
Feminine form of Aleksiy. Or, in other words, this is the Bulgarian and Russian form of Alexia.
Macedonian form of Alexios as well as short form of Aleksandar.
Means "rooster, cock" in Ancient Greek. It also coincides with two identical words meaning "husband, consort" and "unwedded" respectively. This was the name of several men in Greek mythology.

Derived from Old French alemande, the feminine form of the adjective alemant "German". This name might originally have been given to someone of German ancestry or to someone whose ancestors came from the town of Allemagne in Normandy (present-day Fleury-sur-Orne).

Possibly from Old French alemandine, the name of a gem of a deep red colour (and the source of English almandine); this word was a corruption of Latin alabandicus "Alabandic (stone)", the name applied by Pliny the Elder to a variety of carbuncle worked at the city of Alabanda in Asia Minor (see Alabandus). Alternatively, it may be connected to Alamanda. This was the name of a queen in the 13th-century Arthurian romance 'Floriant et Florete'.

Alemania is an alternate Latin name for Germany (and the Spanish name of the country).The name is not used in Germany itself and will probably be questioned by the registrar because some popular football clubs bear this name, e.g. Alemannia Aachen.
Strictly feminine form of Alem (Frisian), where the Frisian diminutive suffix -ke has been added to the name.
Roman birth deity that feeds the embryo or generally nourished growth in utero.

Perhaps related to Greek ἀλήμων (ălēmon) "a wanderer, rover". In Roman mythology, Alemona or Alemonia was a minor, tutelary goddess of the fetus, the entity responsible for feeding the unborn child (i.e., nourishing growth in utero).
From Ottoman Turkish alem meaning "world, universe" combined with şah meaning "shah, king".
From the Galician adverb alén meaning "beyond", ultimately from Latin illinc "from there". It gives its name to various hamlets in Ourense and Pontevedra, as well as to a common Galician surname.
Originally a diminutive of Alenka, now used as a given name in its own right.
Variant of Aline via the form Alene.
Italian and Spanish form of Aleus.
Variant of Alef. In the case of Natalie Portman's son, it refers to the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet.
Alternate transcription of Armenian Ալեքսանդր (see Aleksandr).
Alternate transcription of Georgian ალექსი (see Aleksi).

Possibly a variant of Ilaria or Valeria.It could also be given because of the town of Aléria in the Haute-Corse department of France on the island of Corsica. While many baby name sites and books list this name as being Latin for 'eagle', that is Aquila. The source of this mistaken etymology may be due to the Avalerion, sometimes called an Alerion, a mythological bird compared to an eagle, and seen in medieval heraldry (coats of arms). Aleria, however, is the Latin and Corsican form of the original Ancient Greek name for the town, Alaliē (Ἀλαλίη). This could possibly have been derived from the Ancient Greek lalia (λαλιά) 'talking, talk, chat; form of speech, dialect', from laleō (λαλέω) meaning 'talk, chatter, chirp, make sound'.
Low German and Dutch form of Athalhart.
Sami and Asturian form of Alex.
Basque name coined by Sabino Arana Goiri and Koldo Elizalde as an equivalent to Alexandra and Alejandra.
Romansh form of Alexis, traditionally found in the Engadine valley.
Cremish Lombard form of Alexis and Alexius.
Variant of Alekisanita probably influenced by the spelling of Senitula.
Probably a form of Elisabeth, recorded in Switzerland in the early 1300s.
Possibly means "she plays all the time" in Coos or Iroquois.
The name Marisela spelled backwards. It was brought to limited public attention in 2013 by Alesiram Meza, a contestant of American TV series 'La Voz Kids'.
Slovene diminutive of Aleša and Czech feminine form of Aleš.
Form of Alexander primarily used in Brazil.
Brazilian variant of Alexandre based on Italian Alessandro.
Sardinian form of Alexander and Sicilian variant of Alissandru.
Piedmontese and Milanese Lombard form of Alexis and Alexius.
Means "wanderer, vagabond, rover" in Ancient Greek. This was the name of several figures in Greek mythology, including the youngest son of Clytemnestra, who was killed by his half-brother Orestes.
Corruption of Alethea. This name arose among Catholics in Kentucky in the 1700-1800s.

Derived from Greek ἀλήθεια (aletheia) meaning "truth". (Compare English Alethea.) According to some Greek myths she was the personification of truth, a daughter of Zeus and one of the nurses to Apollo.

From the genus name of a bell-shaped flower also known as colic root, blazing star, unicorn root, or stargrass. Its roots have medicinal properties and are used to aid digestive and muscle problems. Its name derives from Greek ἀλετρίς (aletris) meaning "corn grinder, female slave who grinds corn" (a derivative of ἀλέω (aleo) "to grind, to pound") because of the mealy texture of the flowers.

Latinized form of Greek Ἀλεός (Aleos), which is derived from Greek ἀλέομαι (aleomai) meaning "to avoid, to divert". Also compare Greek ἀλεείνω (aleeinō) meaning "to avoid, to shun". In Greek mythology, Aleus was the son of Apheidas and the grandson of Arcas, and went on to become king of the Arcadian city Tegea in the Peloponnesus.
Short form of Alejandra or Alexandra.
An invented name that combines Alexa and Beth, most likely inspired by Elizabeth.

The first element of this name is derived from the Greek verb ἀλέξω (alexo) meaning "to defend" as well as "to help". The second element is derived from either the Greek verb ἀγορεύω (agoreuo) meaning "to orate, to speak publicly" or the Greek noun ἀγορά (agora), which can mean "assembly" as well as "market, marketplace".

Modern Greek diminutive of Alexios and Alexis, as it contains the modern Greek diminutive suffix -άκης (-akis). This name is typically only used informally, meaning: it does not appear on birth certificates.

Derived from Greek ἀλεξάμενος (alexamenos), which is the participle of the Greek verb ἀλέξω (alexo) meaning "to defend" as well as "to help". Also compare Aleximenes.This name appears in a famous graffito of the early Christian era, which mocks the Christian beliefs of a Roman soldier called "Alexamenos the Faithful".

Latinized form of Alexamenos. This name was borne by an Aetolian general from the 2nd century BC as well as by Alexamenus of Teos, a Greek writer of Socratic dialogues who lived in the 4th century BC.
Variant of Alexandria. According to the USA Social Security Administration, 49 girls were recorded with the name Alexanderia in 1993.
Elaboration of Alexandra. Also a modern combination of Alexandra and Ella 1.
Combination of Alexandra with the suffix -etta.
Combination of Alexandra with the suffix -ette.

Means "son of Alexandros" in Greek, derived from the name Alexandros combined with the patronymic suffix ἴδης (ides).A known bearer of this name was the ancient Greek historian Alexandrides of Delphi.
Either a diminutive of Alexandros (see Alexander) or a patronymic meaning "son of Alexandros" that was turned into a given name; compare Alexandrides for this.
From the name of a chrysoberyl that displays a colour change depending on the light source, named after the Russian tsar Alexander II of Russia (1818-1881).
Louisiana Spanish form of Alejandro, as well as a variant of Spanish Alejandro and Portuguese Alexandre.
Variant of Alexandria. According to the USA Social Security Administration, 20 girls were recorded with the name Alexandrya in 2005.

Derived from the Greek verb ἀλέξω (alexo) meaning "to defend" as well as "to help" combined with the Greek noun ἀνήρ (aner) meaning "man".In Greek mythology, Alexanor is a grandson of the god Asclepius.

Derived from the Greek verb ἀλέξω (alexo) meaning "to defend" as well as "to help" combined with either the Greek noun ἀρχός (archos) meaning "master, leader" or the Greek noun ἀρχή (arche) meaning "origin, source".
Latinized form of Alexarchos. Notable bearers of this name include the Greek general Alexarchus of Corinth (5th century BC) and the Greek scholar Alexarchus of Macedon (4th century BC).

Greek name, possibly originally a short form of Alexandros or another name beginning with the element ἀλέξω (alexo) "to defend, help". This was used by William Shakespeare for a character in his play 'Antony and Cleopatra' (1606).

Romanian short form of Alexandru, as well as the archaic spelling of Greenlandic Alexi 4 (according to the old Kleinschmidt orthography used to write Greenlandic until 1973, when orthographic reforms were introduced).
French transcription of Russian Алексей (see Aleksey).
Variant of Alexiana. As a modern Greek name, it is a combination of Alexia and Anna.
Spanish and Portuguese form of Alexian.

Derived from Ancient Greek ἀλεξιάρης (alexiares), the masculine form of ἀλεξιάρη (alexiare) meaning "she that guards from death and ruin". It consists of ἀλέξω (alexo) meaning "to defend, to help" combined with ἀρή (are) meaning "bane, ruin". Also compare the name of the Greek war god Ares, which is thought to be etymologically related.In Greek mythology, this was the name of one of the divine sons of the Greek hero Herakles and the goddess Hebe, to whom he was wed following his apotheosis. Alexiares and his brother Anicetus may have been considered gatekeepers of Olympus, alongside their father.

Derived from the Greek verb ἀλέξω (alexo) meaning "to defend" as well as "to help" combined with either the Greek noun βία (bia) meaning "bodily strength, force" or the Greek noun βίος (bios) meaning "life".This name was borne by an Olympic victor from 312 BC.
Latinized form of Alexibios. This name was borne by an Olympic victor from 312 BC.

Derived from Greek ἀλέξω (alexo) meaning "to defend, to help" and βουλή (boule) meaning "counsel, advice" as well as "will, determination".Also compare the Greek verbs βουλεύω (bouleuo) meaning "to take counsel, to deliberate" and βούλομαι (boulomai) meaning "to will, to wish, to prefer".

Latinized form of Alexikakos.This was an epithet of the Greek hero Herakles. It was also applied to several Greek gods, such as Zeus, Hermes and Apollo. The latter was worshipped in Athens as Apollo Alexicacus, because as the god of (among others) disease and medicine, he had been credited with stopping the disastrous Plague of Athens (5th century BC).
Latinized form of Alexikles. This was the name of an Athenian general from the 5th century BC.
Latinized form of Alexikrates. This was the name of a Pythagorean philosopher, who lived around the turn of the 1st century AD.
Derived from Greek ἀλέξω (alexo) meaning "to defend, to help" and δᾶμος (damos), the Doric Greek form of (demos) "the people".Also compare the name Alexidemos, which is closely related.

Derived from Greek ἀλέξω (alexo) meaning "to defend, to help" and δήϊος (deios) meaning "hostile, destructive" as well as "unhappy, wretched", which is related to δηϊόω (deioo) meaning "to slay, to cut down" (see Deianeira).
Derived from the Greek verb ἀλέξω (alexo) meaning "to defend" as well as "to help" combined with the Greek noun δῆμος (demos) meaning "the people".
Derived from Greek ἀλέξω (alexo) meaning "to defend, to help" and δίκη (dike) meaning "justice, judgement" as well as "custom, usage".
Combination of the name Alexis with El or Elle.

Derived from the Greek adjective ἀλεξίκακος (alexikakos) meaning "keeping off ill, averting evil", which consists of ἀλέξω (alexo) meaning "to defend, to help" and κάκη (kake) meaning "wickedness, vice".This was an epithet of several Greek deities, such as Apollo, Hermes and Zeus.
Derived from the Greek verb ἀλέξω (alexo) meaning "to defend" as well as "to help" combined with the Greek noun κλέος (kleos) meaning "glory".
Derived from the Greek verb ἀλέξω (alexo) meaning "to defend" as well as "to help" combined with the Greek noun κράτος (kratos) meaning "power".
Derived from the Greek verb ἀλέξω (alexo) meaning "to defend" as well as "to help" combined with the Greek noun λαός (laos) meaning "(the) people".
Derived from Greek ἀλέξω (alexo) meaning "to defend, to help" and λαός (laos) meaning "the people" (see Leos).

Derived from Greek ἀλέξω (alexo) meaning "to defend, to help" and λόχος (lochos) meaning "ambush", a word that later came to signify a tactical sub unit of the ancient Greek army. The word is ultimately derived from the Greek verb λοχάω (lochao) meaning "to lie in wait for, to waylay" as well as "to snare".
Derived from the Greek verb ἀλέξω (alexo) meaning "to defend" as well as "to help" combined with the Greek noun μάχη (mache) meaning "battle".
Derived from the Greek verb ἀλέξω (alexo) meaning "to defend" as well as "to help" combined with the Greek verb μήδομαι (medomai) meaning "to think, to plan, to plot".

Derived from Greek ἀλέξω (alexo) meaning "to defend, to help" and either μένω (meno) meaning "to stay, to remain" as well as "to last, to withstand" or μένος (menos) meaning "mind, strength, courage, force".Also compare the name Alexamenos, which is similar in appearance and also partially related.
French form of Alexinus. The name seems to have all but disappeared after 1960.
Latinized form of Alexinikos. This name was borne by an Olympic victor from 268 BC.
Derived from the Greek verb ἀλέξω (alexo) meaning "to defend" as well as "to help" combined with the Greek noun νίκη (nike) meaning "victory".This name was borne by an Olympic victor from 268 BC.
Derived from Greek ἀλέξω (alexo) meaning "to defend, to help" and νόμος (nomos) meaning "usage, custom, law, ordinance" (see Eunomia).
Latinized form of Alexinomos. In Greek mythology, this is the name of the father of the warriors Alcidamas and Melaneus, who were both slain by Neoptolemus during the Trojan War.
Hellenized form of Alexinus, which is a Latin diminutive of Greek masculine names that start with Alex-.This was the name of a Greek philosopher from Elis, who lived from circa 339 BC to 265 BC.
Derived from Greek ἀλέξω (alexo) meaning "to defend, to help" and νοῦς (nous), which is a contraction of νόος (noos) meaning "mind".

Latin diminutive of Greek masculine names that start with Alex- (such as Alexis and Alexius), since it contains the Latin masculine diminutive suffix -inus.A notable bearer of this name was the Greek philosopher Alexinus of Elis, who lived from circa 339 BC to 265 BC. He was known as Alexinos in his native Greece.
Brazilian Portuguese variant of Aleixo and older Lombard form of Alessi.
Derived from Ancient Greek ἀλέξω (alexo) and the patronymic suffix ίων (ion).
Derived from the Greek verb ἀλέξω (alexo) meaning "to defend" as well as "to help" combined with the Greek noun ἵππος (hippos) meaning "horse".
Latinized form of Alexippos. This was the name of an ancient Greek physician from the 4th century BC.In Greek mythology, Alexippus was an Ethiopian who fought in the Trojan War.
Variant transcription of Alexirhoe, which in turn is a variant spelling of Alexirrhoe.

Derived from Ancient Greek ἀλέξω (alexo) meaning "to defend, help" combined with ῥοή (rhoe) meaning "river, stream, flow". Also compare the Greek noun ῥόος (rhoos) meaning "stream, flow of water, current" as well as the name Alexirrhoia, which are both closely related.In Greek mythology, Alexirrhoe is one of the many wives of king Priam of Troy.

Derived from Greek ἀλέξω (alexo) meaning "to defend, to help" and ῥοία (rhoia) meaning "flow, flux", which is related to ῥοή (rhoe) meaning "river, stream".In Greek mythology, this is sometimes an alternative name for the two characters whose name is Alexirrhoe.
Languedocian and Gascon form of Alexis.
Derived from Greek ἀλέξω (alexo) meaning "to defend, to help" and στρατός (stratos) meaning "army".
Derived from Greek ἀλέξω (alexo) meaning "to defend, to help" and τέλος (telos) meaning "purpose, aim, goal" as well as "completion, accomplishment, fulfillment" (see Aristotle).
Derived from the Greek verb ἀλέξω (alexo) meaning "to defend" as well as "to help" combined with the Greek verb τιμάω (timao) meaning "to honour, to esteem, to revere".
Most likely a variant of Alexis.
Galician variant of Aleixo and Louisiana Spanish form of Alexis.
Derived from Ancient Greek ἀλέξω (alexo) meaning "to defend, to help".
Transferred use of the surname Alexson.
Variant of Alexis. Alexxis was given to 14 girls in 2017 per the SSA.
Alexzade is an Polynesian unisex name used primarily in Fiji and Samoa. It has no specific meaning, but can be inferred as spiritual.
Variant of Alexandre. Also compare Alexzander.
Bulgarian, Russian and Ukrainian form of Aleus.
Variant of Aleit. It was recorded in Silesia in the 14th century.

Older form of Aleidis. Aleydis of Schaerbeek, also known as Alice of Schaerbeek, (c. 1220–1250) was a Cistercian laysister who is venerated as the patron saint of the blind and paralyzed. Her feast day is 15 June.
A Phoenician god of springs and vegetation.

A type of flowering plant. A notable fictional bearer of this name is Alfalfa Switzer from the series of early short films "The Little Rascals" also known as "Our Gang". There was a movie adaptation in 1994. His original actor, Carl Dean Switzer, also commonly went by the name Alfalfa Switzer.
The name of a fictive native American girl in the song 'The Blue Juniata' by Marion Dix Sullivan (1844).
Dutch and Frisian form of Alfhard.

Has several possible etymologies. Maybe derived from Old Norse alfr ("elf, supernatural being") and ǫrn ("eagle"); alf and arinn ("fire, immolation place"), a word meaning "far, long" and far ("to travel"), or ala ("entire, all") and a word meaning "deserted".In Norse mythology this is the name of a giant.
Combination of the name elements alfr "elf" and fastr "firm".
Combination of the Old Norse elements alfr "elf" and bjǫrn "bear".
Combination of the Old Norse elements alfr "elf" and dís "goddess".
Croatian and Serbian form of Alphaeus.
Italian and Polish form of Alphesiboea.
Bulgarian and Russian form of the biblical name Alphaeus, as well as of the Greek name Alpheus.
Combination of Old Norse alfr "elf" and finnr "finn, lapp".
Anglo-Scandinavian form of Alfgeirr, or a medieval form of Ælfgar.
Variant of Ælfgeat found in the Phillimore translation of Domesday Book.
Derived from Old Norse alfr "elf" combined with Old Norse geirr "spear".
An Ancient Scandinavian with the combination of alfr "elf" and garðr "enclosure, protection".
Anglo-Scandinavian name, derived from the Old Norse elements alfr meaning "elf" and gríma meaning "mask, helmet".
Derived from Old Norse alfr "elf" and heiðr "bright, clear, cloudless; honour".
Diminutive of Alfred, Alfonso, and other names that begin with alf.
Possibly derived from Arabic ألف (ʾalf) meaning "thousand" or أليف (ʾalīf) meaning "close, friendly, familiar, intimate".
Combination of the name Alfian combined with Persian شاه (shāh) meaning "king".
Meaning unknown. This name was borne by the mother of the first Roman empress Livia.
Probably an Old Norse and Icelandic form of Old English Ælfgifu. Alternatively, could derive from the Old Norse elements alfr "elf" and fífa "cottongrass; arrow (poetic)".
Diminutive form of Alfons or Alfréd.
This is the traditional name of the star Beta Cephei in the constellation Cepheus. The name is derived from the Arabic الفرقة al-firqah "the flock" (of sheep).
Norwegianized form of Ælfgifu. Ælfgifu (Alfiva) of Northampton was the regent of Norway from 1030 to 1035.
Old Norse variant form of Alfketill.
Derived from Old Norse alfr "elf" combined with Old Norse kettil "kettle, cauldron" (see also Kettil).
Old Danish and Anglo-Scandinavian form of Alfkæll.
Derived from Old Norse alfr "elf" and laug possibly meaning "vowed, promised, bound in oath".
Old Norse name derived from elements alf "elf" and móðr "wrath; courage."
Derived from the Germanic name elements alf "elf" and ny "new".
Walloon form and English borrowing of Alphonse.
Dutch feminine form of Alfons and Walloon feminine form of Alfonse.
Diminutive of Alfonso. Alfonsino d'Este was an Italian nobleman and the heir apparent to municipality Montecchio Emilia.
Maltese, Corsican, Sardinian and Sicilian form of Alfons.
Transferred use of the surname Alford.
Name borne by Alfradis von der Borch, a 14th century nun and abbess who came from Westphalian nobility.
In the case of American actress Alfre Woodard (1952-) her godmother claimed she saw a vision of Alfre's name written out in gold letters.
Occitan and Walloon form of Alfred.
variant of Alfreda, a genus of flowering plants in the daisy family
Combination of Alfred and Frederick. Its usage was inspired in 1985 by American former basketball player Alfredrick Hughes (1962-), who took part in the NBA draft of the same year.
Medieval Italian diminutive of Alfredo, as -uccio is an Italian masculine diminutive suffix.
Variant of Alfreda based on the spelling of Freida.
Female form of Alfreð with -sína suffix.
Old Norse friðr "beautiful" combined with either alfr "elf", allr "all, entire, whole", or aðal "noble".
Short form of Adalfried and variant of Alfred.
Variant of Alfríkr or combination of alf "elf" and freginn "experienced". This is the name of one of the four dwarfs who made Freyja's necklace Brísingamen in Norse mythology.
Derived from the Old Norse elements alfr "elf" and rós "rose".
Derived from Old Norse elements alfr "elf" and rún "secret".
Norwegian and Swedish form of Alfrún.
Derived from the Old Norse elements alfr "elf" and sól "sun".
Derived from Old Norse alfr "elf" and þórr "thunder".
Derived from Old Norse alfr "elf" combined with Old Norse valdr "ruler".

Supposedly native name of Yefanda, wife of Ryurik in Kyivan Rus. Origin of name is unknown. Possibly mistranscription of Alfhild. First part of name definitely derives from alf "elf". Second part could derive from vind "victor", though this is unlikely due to rarity of this name and fact that it is only used in masculine names (such as Øyvind). Her name could possibly come from combination of her parents names.

The first element of this name is derived from Lithuanian al meaning "everything, every last one". The second element is either derived from the Lithuanian verb gaudyti meaning "to take" as well as "to catch, to hunt" or from the Lithuanian adjective gaudus meaning "sonorous, resonant, ringing, loud, echoing".
Variant of Algautr. Algaut was a legendary Geatish king of Västergötland, now a part of Sweden. He was murdered by his son-in-law, the semi-legendary Swedish king Ingjald illråde.
Short form of names beginning with the element Al-, like Algirdė. This name is also considered a feminine form of Algis.

From either of the Old English names Ælfgeard or Æthelgeard. The former name was composed of the Old English elements ælf "elf" and geard "protector"; the latter was derived from æðele "noble" and geard.
Possibly a variant of Old English Ælfgeat or Old Norse Algautr.
Sami combination of alge (unknown Sami element) and Beaivi.

The first element of this name is derived from Lithuanian al meaning "everything, every last one". The second element is either derived from the old Lithuanian verb gedauti meaning "to ask" or from the (more) modern Lithuanian verb gedėti meaning "to mourn, to grieve" as well as "to miss" and "to long, to yearn, to pine (for)".
This is the traditional name of the star Gamma Pegasi in the constellation Pegasus. The name Algenib comes from the Arabic al-janb, meaning “the side.”
Belarusian early medieval name, carried by the famous Grand Duke Algerd, died in 1377.Meaning possibly derived from old Germanic name Aldagar, where "adal" means "nobility" и "gar" means "spear".
A knight who served the Duke of Lorraine in a battle against Gawain during the Roman War. His brother, Earl Antele, fought by his side
From the name of the African country.
Possibly derived from the name of the Spanish town Algeciras. which is from the Arabic الجزيرة (al-jazira) meaning "the island".
Feminine form of Algis, itself the French form of Adalgis.
Derived from Arabic Al-Jabhah, meaning "the forehead". This is the traditional name of the star Gamma Leonis in the constellation Leo.
Derived from alei vienas "everyone" and ginti "to defend; to protect".
Means "to defend everything", derived from Lithuanian al meaning "everything, every last one" combined with Lithuanian ginti meaning "to defend, to protect".
Possibly derived from the feminine suffix маа (maa) combined with an uncertain first element.
Feminine short form of names beginning with the element Al-, this is a derivation of Algė. It can also be considered a feminine form of Algis.

Possibly from Arabic سيف) الجبّار) ((sayf) al-jabbār) meaning "(sword of) the powerful one" or "(sword of) the giant". This is a name of Eta Orionis, a star in the constellation Orion, also called Ensis.
