The first element of this name is derived from Lithuanian alga meaning "salary, wage, pay" as well as "reward". The second element is derived from the Lithuanian verb minėti meaning "to celebrate" as well as "to remember, to commemorate".
Name of a star in the constellation Perseus. Derived from Arabic, meaning "Head of the Ghoul", direct translation in English is "Demon Star"
This is the name of the star Delta Corvi in the constellation Corvus. It bore the traditional name Algorab derived from Arabic الغراب al-ghuraab, meaning "the crow".
Borne by a 26-year-old Guanche man sold at the slave market in Valencia in 1494.

A rare Hispanic variant of the Greek name Argyris or Argyrios, meaning "silver." This specific form is a phonetic adaptation popularized in the late 20th century via Spanish translations of the works of the organizational theorist Chris Argyris (notably his 1978 book Organizational Learning: A Theory of Action Perspective). The spelling reflects a transliteration designed to preserve the hard 'g' sound and distinct vowels for Spanish speakers.
The first element of this name is derived from Lithuanian alga meaning "salary, wage, pay" as well as "reward". The second element is derived from Baltic vil meaning "hope" (see Viltautas).
Diminutive of Algernon, used in the play The Importance of Being Earnest by Oscar Wilde.
Means "tenacious, capable, person with great erudition".
Combination of Alhaji meaning "the pilgrim" with Ahmad meaning "most commendable, most praiseworthy".
From the Arabic phrase الحمد لله (al-hamdu li-llahi) meaning "praise be to Allah".

According to the catalogue of stars in the Technical Memorandum 33-507 - A Reduced Star Catalog Containing 537 Named Stars, Al-Haud were the title for seven stars : f as Alhaud I, τ as Alhaud II, e as Alhaud III, h as Alhaud IV, this star (θ) as Alhaud V, υ as Alhaud VI and φ as Alhaud VII .
Archaic short form of Adelheid, in use between the 1400s and 1800s.
Means "wallflower" in Spanish, a word of Arabic origin.
Derived from Arabic الهنعه (al-Han'āh) "sign (on the neck of a camel)", this is the name of the third-brightest star in the constellation of Gemini.
Low German short form of Adelheid.
Phonetic variant of Ulrich and Ulrik.
Means "the beautiful". Laqab of Husayn. This was the personal name of Avicenna, a famous physician in the medieval Islamic world.
Possible variation of the Arabic Aliyah 1 or Alya 1.
Alternate transcription of Arabic علياء (see Alya 1) chiefly used in Egypt, as well as a Malay form of the name.
Combination of Ali 1 and Akbar. It is sometimes transcribed into Latin characters with a dash or a space.

column3: 阿理安, 阿立安, 阿黎安, 阿力安, 阿丽安, 阿梨安, 阿莉安, 阿李安, 阿里安, etc.(Chinese)
column12: Chinese form of Arian or Aryan or a combination of the names Ah, Li 1 and An 1.
Variant of Eliane.It is the name of one of the main characters in Tamora Pierce's books 'Trickster's Choice' and 'Trickster's Queen'.

In the Netherlands, this given name is usually a combination of the names Alie (which is usually a short form of Alida) and Anne 1.In English-speaking countries, this name is usually a combination of given names starting with Ali- (such as Alice and Alison 1) with Anne 1.
From Old Germanic aljaz "other, else; foreign" and rīks "ruler, king".
Variant of Elias. It coincides with the English alias meaning "a false name used to conceal one's identity; an assumed name".
Combination of the names Ali 1 and Asaf 2.
From the name Ali 1 combined with Arabic أصحاب (ashab) meaning "companions, friends, owners, possessors", the plural of صاحب (sahib).
French form of Adalhelm. Previously a name that had gone out of fashion after the Middle Ages, but it has enjoyed a modest revival in France since the late '80s (which reached its peak in 1996).
A squire present at the tournament of Lancien, held by King Mark.
The first of the given names of the musician known as Akon (1973-).

column3: علی بخش(Shahmukhi, Urdu)|علي بخش(Sindhi-Arabic)|الی بکش(Balochi)|ਅਲੀ ਬਖ਼ਸ਼(Gurmukhi)|अली बख़्श(Hindi)

column12: Combination of Əli and Azerbaijani bala meaning "child".

One of Perceval's eleven paternal uncles in Perlesvaus. He was the twelfth son of Gais the Large and the brother of Alain. Aliban reigned as lord of the Waste City until slain by the Red Giant. Alain avenged his death
A Saxon knight defeated by Lancelot at a fountain
Combination of Əli and Azerbaijani bəy meaning "gentleman, mister; lord, master".
Combination of Ali 1 and the Turkish military title beg meaning "chieftain, master".
A strong knight who served King Claudas of Gaul, fighting in Claudas’ war against Arthur. His brothers were Brumand (Brumant), Canart, and Cadant.
From Old Germanic aljaz "other, else; foreign" and berhtaz "bright". Alternately, the first element could derive from allaz "all; whole, entire". Could also be a variant of Albertus.
From the given name Ali 1 combined with a form of the Turkish military title beg meaning "chieftain, master" (see Alibek).

A valorous knight who brashly challenged a young Lancelot at the Queen's Ford, where Alibon's father served as vavasor. Lancelot defeated him and sent him to Arthur's court. Alibon later participated in a quest to find Merlin.
Gascon and Languedocian form of Alix.
Combination of Alice and Beth, modeled on Elizabeth.
Variant of Alison influenced by Alice.

Created by author George R. R. Martin for a character in his series of fantasy novels A Song of Ice and Fire and the television adaptation House of the Dragon (2022-). In the series, Alicent Hightower is the daughter of Otto Hightower, the Hand of the King, and the second wife of King Viserys I Targaryen. It might be inspired by medieval names such as Alison, Millicent and Elisenda.
Variant of Alison 1, influenced by Alice.

Alichino is one of the devils in the Inferno of Dante Alighieri's Divine Comedy. Alichino is a member of the Malebranche, whose mission is to guard Bolgia Five in the Eighth Circle, the Malebolge. Alichino's name is commonly regarded as a garbled version of the Italian word for harlequin, Arlecchino, perhaps for his flying attempt to catch Ciampolo of Navarre in his escape.His only significant contribution to the plot is when he persuades the other devils to leave Ciampolo of Navarre alone. Ciampolo is supposed to summon other sinners from the lake of boiling pitch (that don't dare to appear when the devils are near), on request by Dante (who wants to speak with them). But Ciampolo doesn't call at his friends. Instead, he fools the devils and escapes back to the lake, and Alichino tries in vain to catch him. This causes a fight between Alichino and Calcabrina, which causes them to fall into the lake. The other devils put the blame on Virgil and Dante, though and hunt them vexed.
Late medieval English variant of Alicia and Brazilian variant of Alícia.
Diminutive of Alica, not used as a given name in its own right.
Variant of Alison 1, likely influenced by the spelling of Alice.
Means "gift of Ali" from the given name Ali 1 combined with Persian داد (dād) meaning "gift".
Dutch and Flemish form of Alidor. A known bearer of this name was the Belgian politician Alidoor De Keyser (1920-2012).

An old and obscure French given name of unknown meaning, which may possibly ultimately be of Occitan origin (compare Aliénor) or even Basque origin. It seems that it was mostly used in the 19th century, not just in France but also in (the French-speaking part of) Belgium and the Canadian province Quebec. The name appears to never have been very common, but it continued to be in use in the 20th century and has also seen use in the 21st century so far. One should consider the name as being extremely rare in this day and age.
Armenian form of Alix. This name was borne by the 13th-century noblewoman known in English as Alice of Armenia, the eldest daughter of Ruben III, Prince of Armenia.

Diminutive of names beginning with Al, most typically Alida.Known bearers of this name include the Dutch gymnast Alie van den Bos (1902-2003), the Dutch former breaststroke swimmer Alie te Riet (b. 1953) and the Dutch former speed skater Alie Boorsma (b. 1959).
Diminutive form of Alie, seeing as the name contains the Dutch diminutive suffix -ke.
In the Septuagint, this name is used instead of Eliel in chapter 11 of 1 Chronicles.

Dutch phonetical spelling of the French name Aline. The name also occurs as a short form of the related name Alina, in which case it is used strictly informally (i.e. not as an official name on birth certificates).In medieval times, Alien also occurred as a variant spelling (or even a misspelling) of the unisex name Aljen, as the letter 'j' was regularly written as an 'i' in medieval records. Examples of other such names are Antien and Jantien.

Means "stranger" in Latin. This was the false identity of Celia in Shakespeare's play 'As You Like It' (1599) when she goes into hiding in the forest of Arden, presumably a pun on the word alias. It was also used by author Ken Follett for a character in his historical novel 'The Pillars of the Earth' (1989).
French and Dutch form of Aliena.
Medieval Latin form of Eleanor, recorded in France.
An invented name, likely inspired by names like Alianna and names ending in ani/oni/onni.
Variant of Alice or possibly Elise (See also Alesia).

Dutch form of Aliette. However, it should be noted that in the Netherlands, there may also be cases where this name is a combination of the Dutch feminine given name Alie with the French diminutive suffix -ette. In other words: in some cases, it could be an attempted gallicization of Alie.
French variant of Éliette. This name is borne by Aliette de Bodard (1982-), a science-fiction and fantasy writer.
Angliziced variant of Aliou, chiefly used in the Gambia, Sierra Leone and Liberia.
Means "close, friendly, familiar, intimate" in Arabic, from the root ألف (ʾalifa) meaning "to be familiar with".
Alternate transcription of Arabic أليفة (see Alifa), as well as the Malay and Indonesian form.
Variant of Alafare. It was borne by a victim of the American Hatfield–McCoy feud: Alifair McCoy (1858-1888), daughter of feud patriarch Randolph "Ole Ran'l" McCoy.
Malay and Indonesian variant of Alifa.
Malay and Indonesian variant of Alifa.
From the word English word alight.
Short form of Fiordiligi as well as Tuscan form of Aloisio.
In Inuit mythology, Alignak is a lunar deity and god of weather, water, tides, eclipses and earthquakes.
Means "mountain crystal, quartz" in Greenlandic, referring to a type of rock used as raw material for stone tools in traditional Greenlandic society.
A knight who served Lord Parsamant, a ravisher. Perceval defeated Aligres when he conquered Parsamant
Tausug and Indonesian form of Ali 1.
This was the personal name of Consort Zhao of the Pucha clan, a consort of the fourth emperor of the Jin dynasty Digunai. The meaning of her name is uncertain at this time.
From ali'i meaning "chief, king" and kai meaning "sea", so the meaning is "king of the sea".
Means "brave king" or "warrior king," from aliʻi meaning "chief, officer, ruler, monarch, peer, headman, king, commander" and koa meaning "soldier, warrior, fighter."
Said to mean both "distant chief" and "high chief" in Hawaiian.
Means "firm chief" from alii "chief" and mau "firm, hold".
Finnish form and Estonian variant of Alina.
Elaboration of Alja via the variant Alija.
Combination of the given name Ali 1 and Persian جان (jân) meaning "soul, being, spirit".
Archaic spelling of Aalik, using the old Kleinschmidt orthography.
Combination of Ali 1 meaning 'high, supreme' and the word akbar meaning 'greatest, biggest'.
Variant of Allat. The Arabian mother goddess.
A variant or alternative for Alissia and Alicia.
From Mongolian алим (alim) meaning "apple" and the feminine suffix маа (maa).
Form of Alima used in western Africa.
Of Ethiopian origin, meaning "in honour of God". It is primarily used as a surname, but can also be used as a given name too.
Combination of Alim and the Ottoman Turkish title بك (beg) meaning "ruler, chief, lord".
Derived from Arabic Alim and Turkish Can.
Means "knowledgeable, learned" from Arabic عَلِمَ (ʿalima) meaning "to know, to have knowledge, to be informed" (see Alim).
Derived from Arabic عالمين ('alimin) meaning "knowers", the plural of عالم ('alim) meaning "scholar, knowledgable person".
Combination of the Islamic name Alim, meaning "scholar", and the Kazakh and Persian word jan, meaning "soul" or "dear".
From Arabic عليم meaning "learned, expert, scholar" and the tital khan meaning "king, ruler"
Derived from Arabic عليم (alim) meaning "learned, expert, scholar" combined with Kazakh/Kyrgyz жан (zhan) meaning "soul".
Dutch, Afrikaans, Finnish, Swedish and Hungarian contracted form of Adelinda and Gascon contracted form of Aidelina.
Best known as the Atayal name of Taiwanese actress Jane Huang.
Meaning uncertain. This was the name of a 17th-century Manchu nobleman.
Originally a diminutive of Alina, now occasionally used as a given name in its own right. It is also Russian and Ukrainian diminutive of Alina.
Masculine form of Alina and Aline.
Medieval Latin form of Eleanor, recorded in late 15th-century Wales.
English variant of Eleanora and Sardinian variant of Elianora.

Means "fire, flame" in Nyari, spoken in Victoria state and New South Wales state, south-eastern Australia.Alinta was the name of one of the main characters in the 1981 SBS television mini-series 'Women of the Sun' which portrayed the lives of four Indigenous women in Australian society from 1820 to 1980.
Contracted form of Alianora or variant of Eliora.

Georgian form of Alyosha as well as an alternate transcription of the name.A known Georgian bearer of this name was Aleksandre "Aliosha" Svanidze (1886-1941), an Old Bolshevik who was the brother-in-law of Joseph Stalin (1878-1953).
Derived from Arabic alyat, meaing "fat tail of a sheep". This is the traditional name of the star Epsilon Ursae Majoris in the constellation Ursa Major.
Form of Ali 1 used in parts of western Africa.
Form of Ali 1 used in parts of French-influenced western Africa.
Fijian and Tongan form of Albert.
Italian and Spanish form of Alypius.
Russian and Ukrainian form of Alypios via Alypius.
Means "servant of (Imam) Ali". This name is a combination of Əli and Qulu meaning "servant, slave".
Variant of Aliria and feminine form of Aliro.
named after an important character in shia islam, Ali Al-Ridha
Short form of names beginning with Al-, such as Alanas, Aleksandras, and Aloyzas.
Demoiselle Alisande a la Carteloise is a medieval character in Mark Twain's 1889 novel A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court. She is nicknamed "Sandy" in the novel.
Medieval variant of Alexander occurring in Shakespeare and Malory. The herb Smyrnium olusatrum is also known commonly as "alisanders".
Possibly a variant of Alison 1 probably influenced by the name Anne 1 (or possibly Lisanne, Alisander/Alexane) or else a blend of Alice and Anne 1.

A local god in Gaul who is mentioned in inscriptions in central France. Attempts have been made to identify him as a mountain-ash god or a god of rowan trees. The ancient Gaulish city of Alesia, now called Alise-Sainte-Reine, may well be connected with him.

Scots form and medieval English variant of Alexander. 'King Alisaunder' or 'Kyng Alisaunder', dating from the end of the 13th century or the early 14th century, is a Middle English romance or romantic epic telling the story of Alexander the Great's career from his youth, through his successful campaigns against the Persian king Darius and other adversaries, his discovery of the wonders of the East, and his untimely death.
It is a feminine forename of Philippines origin that is used globally(I found this informatiom on the only source u could find on my name)
Local French form of Alice recorded up to the 1700s in the French Bourgogne-Franche-Comté region and the Canton of Châtenois in the Vosges département of eastern France and in the region of Lorraine.
Most likely a variant of Alise 1.

Modern Urdu name of uncertain meaning, which became popular in Pakistan in the 1980s. It might be formed from Arabic عليّ (ʿalīy) "high, exalted" and shobh allegedly meaning "appearance, likeness". Alternatively it may be derived from Elisheba (compare Syriac ܐܠܝܫܒܥ (Elişbah)), the name of Aaron's wife in the Old Testament and of John the Baptist's mother in the New Testament, but traditionally Elizabeth was Ilshaba or Ilshabet in Urdu.
From "alisier", meaning "whitebeam tree" in French. This name has been authorised in France since 1966, alongside its feminine form, Alise.
Latvian borrowing of Alison or Allison.
Variant of Alison. This is the name of the Wife of Bath in Geoffrey Chaucer's 'The Canterbury Tales'.
English variant and Piedmontese form of Alice and Gallo form of Alice and Alix.
Old Swedish Latinized form of Alice.
Occitan and Guernésiais form of Alexander.
Hungarian form of Alissa. German origin, meaning "noble".
A knight who participated in the Grail Quest. His companion was named Gloans the Red.
From the name of a river in Lithuania, it is occasionally used as a given name
Means "sandbank next to a river where horses can roll" in Ancient Greek. In Greek mythology, Alistra was a lover of Poseidon who bore him Ogygus.
Archaic spelling of Aaliit, a Greenlandic form of Alice.
Variant of Alethea. This is the name of a character in William Wycherley's Restoration comedy 'The Country Wife' (1675).
Variant of Alethea or of Alicia (Spanish pronunciation with English spelling)
Meaning uncertain, possibly an elaboration of Itzel using the phonetic prefix Al- (from a name such as Alicia or Alizé).
Means “I brought olives”, from Bengali অলিভ (aliv) meaning “olive”, and এনি (eni) meaning “I brought”.
Combination of Alivia and Livie or Olivie
Variant of Alexander. The USA Social Security Administration has recorded 18 baby boys with the name Alixander in 2005.
Variant of Alexane influenced by Alix.
Recorded in 15th-century French-speaking Switzerland. It might be a Latinization of Alix.
Circassian and Balkar form of Ali 1.
Name of a sorcerer and antagonist in "The Princess and the Frog" by Robin McKinley.
Combination of Əli and Persian یار (yar) meaning "friend, companion".

Modern Urdu name, popularly claimed to mean "daughter of Ali 1" (compare the Persian surname Alizadeh which means "descendant of Ali", as well as the second element in Mirza), though it may actually be a borrowing from the Hebrew name Aliza.

From alizarin crimson, the English name of a shade of red. The color is named after a red dye originally obtained from the root of the madder plant, ultimately from Arabic al-usara meaning "the juice". This was used for a male character in the romance novel 'Pandora' by Jilly Cooper.
Composed by "ali", meaning "noble" and "zay", meaning "daughter of", so the meaning is "daughter of nobility".
Alternate transcription of Urdu علیزے (see Alizeh).
Basque and Aragonese form of Alice.
Assimilated Siraya deity that is worshipped by former plains people in southern Taiwan.
Form of Jawhara prefixed with the Arabic difinitive article.
Alternate transcription of Arabic الجوهرة (see Al-jawhara).

Medieval Navarran Jewish name, derived from Andalusian Arabic الجوهر‎ (al-jawhar) meaning "the jewel", from Arabic جَوْهَر‎ (jawhar) "jewel, gem, pearl", from Persian گوهر‎ (gowhar). This name was used by Jewish women in the medieval kingdom of Navarre, occurring in 14th- and 15th-century documents written by Jews in Hebrew or Ladino.
Can be seen as a variant of Aljon, or a combination of Alan and John. It merges meanings of "noble," "bright," or "handsome" with "God is gracious".
German transcription of Russian Алёша (see Alyosha).
Derived from the Greek element αλκη (alke) meaning "strength, force". A famous bearer is Croatian singer Alka Vuica (1961-).

From Arabic الْقَائِد (al-qāʼid) meaning "the leader", taken from قائد بنات نعش (qā'id bināt naʿsh) "leader of the daughters of the bier". This is the traditional name of the star Eta Ursae Majoris in the constellation Ursa Major. The 'daughters of the bier', i.e. the mourning maidens, are the three stars of the handle of the Big Dipper, Alkaid, Mizar and Alioth; while the four stars of the bowl, Megrez, Phecda, Merak and Dubhe, are the funeral bier.

From Greek καλαῦροψ (kalaurops) meaning "shepherd's staff" prefixed with the Arabic definite article. This is the traditional name of Mu1 Boötis, a binary star in the northern constellation of Boötes.
Full form of Kamal 1 which means “Perfectionist.”

Derived from Greek αλκη (alke) meaning "strength" combined with ανδρος (andros) meaning "of a man". This was the name of several figures in Greek mythology, including a Molossian prince whose entire family was turned into birds by Zeus to save them from a fire, Alkandros becoming a wren, and a Lycian soldier in the Trojan war.
Derived from the Greek noun ἀλκή (alke) meaning "strength" combined with the Greek noun ἀνήρ (aner) meaning "man".

Meaning unknown (but from Pitjantjatjara language).A known bearer of this name was Alkawari Dawson (c. 1930-2010), an Australian Aboriginal painter who was also the first wife of fellow artist Nyakul Dawson (c. 1935-2007).
Diminutive of names that contained the name element adal, most notably Adelheid.
Croatian and Serbian form of Alcaeus.

Younger form of Old English Hǣlcelde. Saint Alkelda (died on 28 March c. 800) was ostensibly an Anglo-Saxon princess who was strangled by pagan Viking women during Danish raids in about 800 at Middleham in Yorkshire, England. She is the patron of the church at Giggleswick and also of that of Middleham.
This is the name of a star Alpha Crateris in the constellation Crater. It bore the traditional name Alkes, from the Arabic الكاس alkās or الكأس alka's meaning "the cup".

A name inspired by Alcestis, though it probably had more influence from the Greek version Greek Ἄλκηστις (Alkestis), meaning "defense, defensive strength, valour". It was chosen by Adelinde Weiss, wife of the astronomer Edmund Weiss, for the name of an asteroid discovered by C.H.F. Peters.
Bulgarian, Russian and Ukrainian form of Alcaeus.
Probably from Mongolian алхаа (alkhaa) meaning "step" and баатар (baatar) meaning "hero".

From Arabic الخنساء (al-Khansā), which is said to mean "the snub-nosed" or "the gazelle". This was the nickname of a 7th-century Arab poet who was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad. Her birth name was Tumāḍir bint ‛Amr.This name appears to be very rare; as an Arabic feminine name, the form Khansa (without the definite article al-) is given more frequently.
Derived from Mongolian алх (alkh) meaning "hammer" and баатар (baatar) meaning "hero".
Diminutive of Angeliki. This name was borne by Angeliki „Alki“ Zei (December 15, 1925 – February 27, 2020), a Greek novelist and children's writer.

Derived from the Greek adjective ἀλκίμαχος (alkimachos) meaning "fighting bravely", which consists of the Greek noun ἀλκή (alke) meaning "strength" combined with the Greek noun μάχη (mache) meaning "battle".
Derived from Greek ἀλκή (alke) meaning "strength, prowess" and μέδων (medon) meaning "ruler" (see Medon).
Derived from the Greek adjective ἄλκιμος (alkimos) meaning "stout, strong, brave", which is ultimately derived from the Greek noun ἀλκή (alke) meaning "strength".
Russian and Serbian form of Alcyone.
Russian and Ukrainian form of Alcyoneus.
Means "stout-hearted, courageous, generous" in Ancient Greek, derived from ἀλκή (alke) meaning "strength, prowess" and φρήν (phren) meaning "mind, heart, emotions".
Derived from Ancient Greek ἀλκή (alke) meaning "strength, prowess" and ἵππος (hippos) meaning "horse". Masculine form of Alkippe.
The star Xi Cephei in the constellation Cepheus bore the traditional names Kurhah, Alkirdah or Alkurhah. It derives from al-qírada (ألقردة) meaning "the Ape".

Derived from Ancient Greek ἀλκή (alke) meaning "strength, prowess". As a modern name, it’s often a short form of names containing the element. In Greek mythology, this was an epithet of the goddess Athena.

Means "keeper of sacred places". Derived from Lithuanized ancient Prussian "alkas" (a sacred woods, sacred hill, a place of worship) and Lithuanian "menanti" (the one, who remembers), which, in turn, came from "minėti" (to remember, to talk about).

The first element of this name is derived from either the Greek adjective ἀλκμαῖος (alkmaios) meaning "young" or the Greek name Alkmene (see Alcmene). The second element is derived from the Greek noun ἀνήρ (aner) meaning "man". As such, this name is either a dithematic name that means "young man", or a rare trithematic name with a meaning along the lines of "man born under a strong moon".
Modern English form of Ealhmund via Alcmund.
Means "start, beginning, inception, incipience" in Finnish. The name may also be a variant form of Algot.

The star Xi Cephei in the constellation Cepheus bore the traditional names Kurhah, Alkirdah or Alkurhah.I'm uncertain about the meaning of this name, but it is derived from Al Ḳurḥaḥ (القرحة al-qurhah)
It is urdu name meaning "God saven"
Combination of the Kazakh word Allah, meaning "God" (derived from Arabic) and the Kazakh word bay, meaning "powerful, rich".
Kazakh word for "God-given" or "brought by God". Combination of the Kazakh word Allah, meaning "God" (ultimately derived from Arabic Allah, meaning "God" as well).

column3: ਅੱਲਾ ਦਿੱਤਾ(Gurmukhi)|اللہ دتا(Shahmukhi)|اللہ دتہ(Balochi, Urdu)|अल्लाह दित्ता(Hindi)|الله دته(Pashto)
column12: Punjabi translation of Persian الله بخش (Allah Bakhsh), meaning “God-given.” Used primarily by Muslims.
Means "slave of Allah", from Arabic الله (Allah) combined with Azerbaijani qul meaning "slave".
Indigenized hybrid theophoric name, meaning “kept by God.”
Means "thankfulness of Allah" from şükür meaning "thankfulness, gratitude" combined with Allah
Means "given by God", from Arabic الله (Allah) and Azerbaijani verən "giver", the participle of vermək "to give".
Means "friend of Allah" from Arabic الله (Allah) combined with Persian یار (yar) meaning "friend, companion".
Possibly a Danish form of Adelaide or Alaine.
Possibly deriving in part from the Hurrian element allai=ni ("lady, mistress"). Name borne by a Hittite ritual practitioner, likely of Hurrian origin, known from several texts that bear her name.
Russian form of Allah, rarely used as a given name by Muslim communities in Russia.

Etymology uncertain, possibly deriving from the Hurrian element alla=i, meaning "lady, queen". Another possible element is the Hurrian alu-, meaning "to speak". Name borne by a Hurrian goddess that was often worshipped alongside Ḫepat, who was considered to be her mother.
Anglicized form of Alasdair. This name was used on a character in Sir Walter Scott's 'Rob Roy' (1818).
Means "the Goddess" from Arabic al-Lat. She was an ancient mother and fertility goddess of the pre-Islamic Arabs.
This was the name of the Mesopotamian goddess of copulation, equal to the Sumero-Babylonian goddess Ereshkigal; perhaps her name was a Semitic form of Ereshkigal. Allatu was the wife of Nergal.
The goddess of the underworld in early Iranian mythology. She is believed to be of Mesopotamian origin (Ellat).
Swedish diminutive of names starting with Al-, like Alexander and Albin.

Roman name meaning "selected, chosen" in Latin. This was the name of a Roman-Britannic usurper-emperor in Britain and northern Gaul from 293 to 296 who assassinated Carausius, a Menapian officer in the Roman navy.
Dutch variant of Aldegonda (see Aldegund), now more popular than its parent name. Compare Hillegonda/Hildegonda.
Judeo-Italian name derived from Italian allegrezza, a poetic term for "joy; happiness".
Transferred from the surname "Allegro", a masculine form of "Allegra".
Variant of Ally 1 with the spelling influenced by that of Leigh.
From the Marian title Virgen de Allende, who's a patron saint of Ezcaray (La Rioja). The name seems to derive from allende "beyond, on the other side."
The German word for All Saints' Day given to a child who was born or baptized on this day.

Means "all kinds of fur" in German. This is the name of the title character of a fairy tale collected by the Brothers Grimm. Allerleirauh is a princess who flees from her father, who wants to marry her, and brings three dresses and a coat with all kinds of furs with her. She ends up living as a servant in another kingdom.
Transferred use of the surname Allers.
Variant of Alexa. Allexa was given to 5 girls in 2014.
Variant of Alexia that was given to 7 girls in 2007.
Variant of Alexis. Allexis was given to 5 girls in 2014.
Variant of Alexis that was given to 7 girls in 2006.
Medieval Latvian short form of Adelheide.
Meaning unknown. It may be derived from Latin allium meaning "garlic."
Variant of Alicia (See also Allice and Allison).
Diminutive of Alexander, Allan, and other names beginning with Al-.
From Old Germanic aljaz "other, else; foreign" and friþuz "peace". Alternately, the first element might derive from aljaną "zeal, vigour, courage".
Either a variant of Aliena or of Aliana.
This is the name of the main character in Swedish children’s book Allikin (1986) by Runo Lindskog.
Form of Ælling found in the Phillimore edition of Domesday Book.
Meaning unknown, perhaps from a Seneca word meaning "hat". A noted bearer was Queen Alliquippa, a leader of the Seneca tribe of American Indians during the early part of the 18th century.
Allirea is a name meaning “quartz” in one of the Aboriginal Australian languages.
Scandinavian and Romani variant of Alice.
Scots phonetic variant of Gaelic Ealasaid found in the early 16th century.
From the name Willa spelled backwards. It is used in Robert Beatty’s novel 'Willa of the Wood'.
Means "good person" or "good thing" in Quechua.

Allogenes (from Greek Allogenēs, meaning “stranger” or “of another race/kind”) is a revelatory figure in Sethian Gnostic literature, most prominently the protagonist of the text Allogenes from the Nag Hammadi library. He is portrayed as a spiritual seeker who receives visionary instruction from higher divine beings, especially concerning the nature of the ultimate, unknowable God and the structure of the transcendent realms. In related texts such as Zostrianos, the name also appears as a title or designation for an enlightened figure who has become “other” to the material world through gnosis. Allogenes thus represents the ideal Gnostic initiate; through revelation and contemplation, he transcends the cosmos and returns to the divine source.

This is apparently either a variant of Alora or Allura or else an American combination of Alice and Lora.It coincides with the Italian word allora "then; thus; so". Note that this name is not used in Italy.
Transferred use of the surname Alloula.

Manx name of uncertain origin, used until the 17th century. Kneen (1937) suggests Old Norse alfr "elf"; Gill (1963) points to the Manx surname Callow, which derives from MacCalo, an Anglicized form of either of the Gaelic surnames Mac Calbach "son of Calbhach" (the Gaelic name Calbhach meaning "bold") or Mac Caolaidhe "son of Caoladhe" (the Gaelic name Caoladhe being a derivative of caol "slender, comely").
Presumably from the English phrase all's well.
From Welsh allt “wooded hillside” and‎ gwen “white, blessed”. This name may be given in reference to the village in Wales.
Means "hole in the ice for fishing" in Greenlandic.
Derived from Basque atx "rock" and luze "long". This is the name of a mountain in Biscay.
Recorded in the 1400s in both Latvia and Swedish Estonia.
Apparently based on the English word allure. This was the name of a princess in the 1980s anime television show 'Voltron'.
From the name of a 1996 Chanel perfume, derived from the English word allure (which also has French roots) meaning "fascination, charm, appeal".
Variant of Alvaldr. In Norse mythology this is the name of Þjazi's father.
Derived from Manx aaley "fairer" and aalin "fair, handsome, beautiful, splendid". It is also considered a cognate of Ailie.
Variant of Alina, possibly influenced by Allyn.

Possibly of Germanic origin. This was the name of a 4th-century Gallo-Roman saint praised by Gregory of Tours. Also known as Illidius, he was a bishop of Clermont in Auvergne, France, which he worked to establish as a center of religious teaching and devotion. According to tradition he died after returning from Trier, where he cured a daughter of Magnus Maximus of demonic possession.
Variant of Alice influenced by Alyssa.
Rare variant of Elizabeth influenced by Ally 1.
Derived from Old Norse "álmr," which translates to "elm tree." "Alm" is also the Swedish word for "elm tree."The name may also be a reference to alms as items given in charity.

column3: ألماس(Arabic, Acehnese Jawi, Wadaad Arabic, Urdu)

column12: This is the name of the star Epsilon Aurigae in the Auriga constellation. The name comes from Arabic Al Maʽaz meaning "the billy goat".
Combination of Bashkir алма (alma) meaning "apple" and бикә (bikä), which is a name element.
Derived from the Arabic العناق (al-‘anāq), "the caracal" (desert lynx). This is the traditional name of the star Gamma Andromedae in the constellation Andromeda.
Means "apple blossom" from Kazakh and Kyrgyz алма (alma) meaning "apple" and гүл (gul) meaning "flower".
Derived from Arabic الماهرة (al-māhira) meaning "the skilful, the adept".
Variant of Alma 1. This is the name of the titular character in French poet Francis Jammes' novel Almaïde d'Etremont ou l'histoire d'une jeune fille passionnée (1900).
Derived from aliai vienas "everyone; every last one" and either manyti "to think; to suppose" or sumanus "quick-witted; astute".

From the word for the deep red garnet, which was derived from a corruption of Latin alabandicus "of Alabanda", as described by Pliny the Elder. Alabanda is an ancient Carian city known for its garnet gemstones. The city itself was derived from the given name Alabandus.
Form of Mansur prefixed with the Arabic definite article.
From Arabic al-Manṣūr meaning "the Victorious". Almanzor was a powerful military leader and statesman in Ummayad Al-Andalus who acted as the favourite of caliph Hisham II.
A moon-god and tutelary god of the South Arabian kingdom of Saba.
Contraction of Athalmar and its variants, such as Adelmar.In Scandinavia, this name is a younger form of Almarr. It can also be a masculinization of Alma 1 over there.
A character mentioned in JRR Tolkien's works. The name is derived from the fictional Quenya language, possibly from the Quenya word almare meaning "blessedness".

A fictional character created by J.R.R. Tolkien. Almáriel was young woman of Númenor. Almáriel was a peer of Herendil, who was mocked by him with the nicknames Eärendel or Terendul. In fact, despite his royal blood, Herendil's peer accused him of being a "half-Noldo".Almáriel means "blessed woman" in Quenya.
Old Norse name from the combination of the name elements ALM "elm" and HER "army." It is the Nordic form of the Old High German name Athalmar and a variant form of Álmgeirr.
From Kazakh and Kyrgyz алмас (almas) meaning "diamond" (of Persian origin) and the Turkish military title beg meaning "chieftain, master".
From Bashkir алма (alma) meaning "apple" and сейә (seyä) meaning "cherry".

Meaning unknown. It might possibly be a combination of Alma 1 with any feminine name that ends in -tine, such as Christine and Martine.A notable bearer of this name is the Dutch theologian, preacher and writer Almatine Leene (b. 1984).

Transferred use of the Spanish surname Almeda.In the English-speaking world, Almeda is as much a borrowing of the Spanish name as it used to be the traditional "translated" form of a Welsh saint's name. Which saint exactly would have been Anglicized as Almeda is debated by modern-day academics: the most popular theory opts for Eluned or Eiliwedd (via its old Latinization Almedha).
Former Latinization of Welsh Eluned and Eiliwedd.
Elaboration of Almeda.This is also the name of towns in both Pennsylvania and Louisiana.
Derived from Arabic al "the" and medina "city".
The name Almendra comes from Latin and refers to the same fruit of the "almond" tree in Spanish. It is an unusual name but that makes it very special and peculiar

Variant of Almera and Elmira 1. This is the name of the main character in the 1697 theatre play 'The Mourning Bride', by William Congreve. The play takes place in Spain, so her name was likely chosen for its similarity with the Spanish city of Almería.
The name of a character in Jean-Pierre Camus' l'Iphigene (1625).
Old Norse name, combination of ALM "elm" and GEIR "spear."
Diminutive of names with Alm- such as Alma 1 or Almar.
Used in "The Lord of the Rings" by Tolkien. It means "blessed maiden".
From the English word almighty meaning "unlimited in might, all-powerful".

Almıla is the original, ancient Turkic form of the name, preserved in historical records as the authentic precursor to the later, modernized variant Almila. The name is a compound of the ancient Turkic root Alma (the primary Turkic word for "apple") and the attributive suffix -lı, creating the meaning "She who is like the apple" or "The Apple-Bearer." This formation follows the classical Turkic morphological rule where the suffix -lı denotes possession or inherent quality, comparable to the naming process seen in place names like Elmalı (the place of apples/apple-bearing land).The etymological trajectory of this root is foundational across the Turkic world: the original Turkic Alma evolved into the Turkish Elma, the Uzbek Olma, and the Chuvash Ulma. Following the consistent Turkic suffixation pattern, these result in the descriptive forms Almıla (Turkic), Elmalı (Turkish), Olmali (Uzbek), and Ulmală (Chuvash). Almıla stands as the refined, anthroponymic evolution of these linguistic roots, symbolizing pristine beauty, health, and vitality.While certain Eurocentric or external etymological theories (most notably popularized by contemporary loanword dictionaries and alternative hypotheses) erroneously attempt to link the Turkic Alma to the Ancient Greek mēlon (mālon) or Latin mālum via a vague Bronze Age "wanderwort" or an Indo-Iranian borrowing (as occasionally debated in speculative 20th-century papers), modern comparative Turkology has thoroughly dismantled this claim. Phonetic, geographical, and historical realities prove that Alma is a purely native, autonomous Turkic creation. It is structurally derived from the primordial Turkic root al, meaning "scarlet," "vermilion," or "bright crimson" (the exact color of the wild steppe apple) combined with the nominalizing/descriptive suffix -ma. This reveals the word's primary semantic origin as "the crimson fruit," a descriptive naming pattern native to nomadic observation. Because this term exists with unyielding phonetic stability across every single isolated branch of the Turkic language family (from Siberian Yakut and Chuvash to Oghuz, Karluk, and Kipchak) long before any historical contact with the Aegean or Mediterranean lexical worlds, the Greek/Latin mēlon/mālum hypothesis is structurally and chronologically impossible.
Derived from Turkish al "red" and elma "apple".
Derived from Arabic الْأَمِين (al-ʾamīn) meaning "the trustworthy".

Possibly a diminutive form of Alma 1 or a variant form of Elmina. This name was borne by the English aristocrat Almina, Countess of Carnarvon (1876-1969) - she was the wife of George Herbert, Earl of Carnarvon (1866-1923), who was involved in the discovery and excavation of the tomb of the Egyptian pharaoh Tutankhamun.

The first element of this name is derived from Lithuanian al meaning "everything, every last one". The second element is derived from the Lithuanian verb minėti meaning "to celebrate" as well as "to remember, to commemorate".

The first element of this name is derived from Lithuanian al meaning "everything, every last one". The second element is derived from the Lithuanian noun mintis meaning "thought", which is related to the Lithuanian verb minti meaning "to remember, to recall".
Walloon form of Almire used exclusively as a feminine name.
Possibly related to Elmira 2 or Almira 2.
The name of a character in Georg Friedrich Händel's opera 'Rinaldo' (1711).
In Kahlil Gibran's book The Prophet (1923), Almitra is a female prophet or seeress.
Italian form of Almos via its latinized form Almus.
Old Norse younger form of Almóðr.
Variant of Amon used in the 19th century.

Of debated origin and meaning. Theories include a variant of Alemande, a contraction of Alemandina and a derivation from Middle English almond, almaund and Old French almande "almond" (seeing as almonds were considered "things of value", naming a daughter after them would fit the naming conventions of the time). This name was recorded in England's Jewish and Judeo-Anglo-Norman communities between the 11th and 13th centuries.
Possibly the Portuguese form of Almoratel.
Old Norse variant form of Álfmóðr.
Combination of Old Norse álmr "elm tree" (see almr) and steinn "stone".
This name was borne by Almucs de Castelnòu (c. 1140 – bef. 1184), a trobairitz from a town near Avignon in Provence.
Possibly a feminine form of Almund, or an altered form of Almut.

Derived from Arabic منتصر (muntasir) meaning "victor". This is part of the title المنتصر بالله (al-Muntasir bi-llah) meaning "He who triumphs in God", which was the regional title of Abu Ja'far Muhammad, an Abbasid Caliph in Baghdad.

Latinized form of Greek Ἄλμος (Almos), of uncertain etymology. Possibly derived from Ancient Greek ἄλμα (alma) meaning "grove", which in turn is apparently related to ἄλσος (alsos) meaning "sacred grove, hallowed place". Another possibility might be that the name is derived from ἅλμα (halma) meaning "spring, leap, jump", or perhaps ἅλμη (halmē) meaning "sea water, brine" (see hals). In Greek mythology, Almus was a son of Sisyphus and the Pleiad Merope.
Means "seeker of aid" in Arabic, derived from the verb استعان (istaʿāna) meaning "to seek help". This is the name of two Abbasid caliphs.
Means "the reliant" in Arabic, derived from توكّل (tawakkala) meaning "to rely (on God)". This is the name of four Abbasid caliphs.
Derived from Old Norse elements álmr "elm tree" and veig "power, strength".
Variant of Almira 1, perhaps influenced by Myra.

Either derived from Lithuanian alnė or alnis, dialectal words for elnė "deer" and elnias "roebuck", or a direct adoption of the name of the river Alna (referred to by its Polish name Łyna in English), whose name is derived from Old Prussian. The Old Prussian name Alna itself is said to be derived from the Proto-Germanic element el-l or ol- "to flow; to run (referring to water)".

Means "the bright (one)" in Arabic, from نَيِّر (nayyir) meaning "luminous, bright" (related to نور (nūr) "light") prefixed with the Arabic definite article. This is the name of Alpha Gruis, the brightest star in the constellation Grus. Its full Arabic name is al-nayyir min dhanab al-ḥūt (al-janūbiyy) meaning "the bright one from the (southern) fish's tail" (see Aldhanab).
Derived from Arabic an-niżām, meaning "string of pearls". This is a star in the constellation Orion.
Directly taken from Latvian alnis "elk, moose".
Derived from Arabic an-niṭāq, meaning "the girdle". This is the name of a star in Orion.

Sigma Scorpii and Tau Scorpii together bore the traditional name Al Niyat (or Alniyat) derived from the Arabic النياط al-niyāţ "the arteries" and referring to their position flanking the star Antares, the scorpion's heart, with Sigma Scorpii just to the north.

Livonian name of uncertain origin and meaning, mentioned in the Chronicle of Henry of Livonia. In modern-day Estonia, this name is used as a short form of Aleksander and associated with Estonian alustus “beginning".
Etymology unknown. This was the name of a 10th-century princess regnant of Capua.
Basque name coined by Sabino Arana Goiri and Koldo Elizalde as an equivalent to Alodia.

Aloe is a genus containing over 500 species of flowering succulent plants. The most widely known species is Aloe vera, or "true aloe". It is called this because it is cultivated as the standard source for assorted pharmaceutical purposes.
French version of Aloe, The name is often used in fiction for the joke "Aloé Véra". Also a other version of Aloés

Probably derived from Greek ἀλοάω (aloaō), which can mean "to thresh, to tread" as well as "to crush, to smash". In Greek mythology, Aloeus was the son of Poseidon and Canace, and husband to Iphimedeia. The Aloadae, two giants, were named after him.

Medieval Dutch and German variant of Adolf as well as the West Frisian form of the name. Also compare Aalf (its medieval form is Aelf) and Alef.A known bearer of this name was Alof de Wignacourt (1547-1622), a French nobleman of Flemish descent who was the 54th Grand Master of the Order of St. John of Jerusalem.
From alofi meaning "to sit in a circle", and sula meaning "to praise one's riches" in Samoan.
Short form of Kealoha and other Hawaiian names containing aloha meaning "love" or otherwise derived directly from the word.
Alohalani is derived from Hawaiian elements Aloha meaning "love" and Lani meaning "heaven" or "royalty". Which, means "beautiful love" or "heavenly love".
Means "heavenly brightness" from Hawaiian alohi "shine" and lani "heaven, sky". In Hawaiian myth this was the name of a heavenly land.
Transferred use of the name of Monte Aloia, a summit in the mountains of Galicia, Spain.
Coined by Sabino Arana Goiri and Koldo Elizalde as a Basque equivalent of Luisa and Aloisia (via Aloisa).
Upper Sorbian and Lower Sorbian form of Aloysius.
Polish and Kashubian feminine form of Alojzy as well as a Kashubian and Slovene feminine form of Alojz.
From Sanskrit आलोक (āloka) meaning "light, lustre, splendour, illumination".
Name of a river in India which flows from the Himalayan range.
A Mayan god of the sky, and one of the seven gods who created the world and the humans.

A pseudo-Hawaiian name invented by LeRoy Clemens and John B. Hymer for the title character of their 1925 Broadway play Aloma of the South Seas, which was twice adapted to film, in 1926 and again in 1941. This name briefly jumped in popularity in the United States after the premiere of the 1941 film.
Alternate transcription of Bengali আলমগীর (see Alamgir).
Taken from the name of a massif on the Basque Mountains range.According to Basque folklore, there is a refuge of Mari 3, one of the key characters in Basque mythology, on the Aloña massif.
An invented name which has been used consistently in America since the 1960s, possibly influenced by Yolanda, Alondra and Alejandra.
Alternate transcription of Thai อลงกต (see Alongkot).
Means "ornament, decoration" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit अलङ्करण (alaṅkaraṇa).
Alternate transcription of Thai อลงกรณ์ (see Alongkon).
Means "to decorate, to adorn, to embellish" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit अलङ्कृत (alaṅkṛta).
Basque feminine form of Alfontso recorded between the 15th and 16th centuries.

Borne by the first wife of the Apache chief Geronimo (1829-1909), daughter of Noposo, from the Nedni-Chiricahua band of Apache. She and her three children with Geronimo were killed by Mexican raiders.
Alor of Quimper was a Breton saint in the 5th century AD and bishop of Quimper in Brittany, France. He is the patron saint of aleviners, foals and horses, and was also invoked to attract rain.
Alora meaning 'God is my light' in Hebrew and "-iana" meaning 'golden' or 'belonging to'(-ia)
Variant transcription of Alyosha, most common in Poland.
Possibly an elaborated form of Lotte, influenced by Alette or French alouette meaning "lark (songbird)" (see Alouette). This was first documented in Norway in 1780.
Derived from Breton al louarn "the fox".

Derived from French alouette "lark, skylark". Alouette is a popular Quebecois children's song, commonly thought to be about plucking the feathers from a lark. Although it is in French, it is well known among speakers of other languages as many US Marines and other Allied soldiers learned the song while serving in France during World War I and took it home with them, passing it on to their children and grandchildren.This is a nickname used for Cosette as a young girl in Victor Hugo's novel Les Misérables (1862). As a given name, however, it is not used in France itself.
Derived from Arabic علي الأوسط ('ali al-awsat) meaning "Ali the middle".
Aloy is the protagonist in the 2017 video game Horizon Zero Dawn and its upcoming sequel Horizon Forbidden West.
German variant and Silesian German form of Alois, and Dutch short form of Aloysius.
Silesian German feminine form of Aloys and Alois (compare Aloysia).
Creole form and Québécois variant of Aloysia.

The name Alpagut is a venerable title and proper name of Old Turkic origin, a compound formed from Alp (meaning "heroic, brave, noble, strong, champion, victor, powerful, legendary") and the archaic suffix +ağut. According to the Dīwān Lughāt al-Turk by Mahmud al-Kashgari, an Alpagut is depicted as a "solitary, invincible warrior who fights alone without seeking aid, a paragon of individual martial prowess and sovereign spirit." It carries a profound weight of historical autonomy and battlefield excellence, symbolizing one who stands as an unbreakable sentinel of the people.
French form of Alpaidis. This name belonged to the mother of Charles Martel, the 8th-century Frankish military and political leader.

Derived from Alp ("Brave," "Hero," "Warrior") and the ancient Turkic intensifier suffix -amış (signifying "supreme likeness," "magnitude," or "becoming the ultimate archetype"). Rather than a mere title, this linguistic fusion elevates the root to mean "The Ultimate Warrior," "The Giant Hero," or "The Hyper-Alp." Alpamysh is the legendary protagonist of the Epic of Alpamysh, representing the archetype of the nomadic savior. The name conveys immense physical strength, profound chivalry, and an unyielding commitment to justice. It is the definitive name for an individual destined to lead and protect.
The Etruscan goddess of love and the underworld. She belongs to the Lasas and is usually portrayed naked.

From the name of a Bengali folk art form consisting of coloured motifs painted on floors and walls using rice flour paint. The word is ultimately derived from Sanskrit आलिम्पन (alimpana) meaning "whitening, painting".
The Etruscan goddess of the underworld, associated with rebirth, revenge, and triumph out of suffering.
Means "Brave moon" in Turkish. Alp meaning "Brave" and Ay meaning "Moon".

It is composed of the three words alp "brave" or "hero", er "soldier" or "male" and tunga "tiger". A mythical hero who was mentioned in Turkic mythology and the Epic of Alp Er Tunga. The name is sometimes mentioned as the khan of Scythia. See Alper.
Alphabeta Swithinbank (-1849) died in Hunslet, Yorkshire.Her name was a combination of the two first Greek letters, alpha (Α, α) and beta (Β, β).
Name of a 12th century French woman, venerated by the Catholic Church as a Blessed.
Derived from Arabic الفرد (al-fard) "the solitary one". Alphard is the brightest star in the constellation Hydra, with no other bright stars near it.

Derived from the name of a suburb in the American city of Atlanta, which itself is derived from Alfarata, the name of a fictional Native American girl in the popular 19th-century parlor song "The Blue Juniata". Also compare Alpharita.

This name is best known for being the name of the Cuban-Jamaican singer Rita Marley (b. 1946), who was born as Alpharita Constantia Anderson. She is the widow of the Jamaican reggae singer Bob Marley (1945-1981). Given that she was born in the Spanish-speaking country of Cuba, her name is most likely a variant spelling or form of Alvarita.However, since both of her parents clearly originated from an English-speaking country (it is unclear which one - it could be Jamaica, but it could just as easily be the United States) and were thus native English speakers, it is possible that they had actually somehow been inspired by the American song "The Blue Juniata" when they named their daughter. The song features a fictional Native American girl named Alfarata, you see. Alternatively, they could have been inspired by Alpharetta, which is the name of a suburb in the American city of Atlanta. The suburb derives its name from the Native American girl in the aforementioned song "The Blue Juniata".
Means "the broken", taken from Arabic نير الفكّة (nayyir al-fakka) meaning "the bright (star) of the broken (ring of stars)". This is the traditional name of the star Alpha Coronae Borealis.
Norman form of Alphege and French and Norman variant of Elphège.

Epithet of the Greek goddess Artemis which was derived from the name of the river god Alpheios, who loved her. Artemis Alpheiaia was worshipped at Letrini in Elis and on the island of Ortygia near Syracuse; she also shared an altar with Alpheios at Olympia. Under this name she was associated with the wearing of masks, largely due to the legend that Artemis and her nymphs escaped the pursuit of Alpheios by covering their faces.

Derived either from Greek ἀλφή (alphê) meaning "produce, gain, profit" or from Greek ἀλφός (alphos) which meant "whiteness" as well as "white leprosy", a cognate of Albus. In Greek mythology he was a river deity, the personification of the Alpheios, the longest river in the Peloponnese. The son of Oceanus and Tethys, he fell madly in love with the Nereid Arethusa and pursued her under the sea to Sicily. There she pleaded to Artemis who changed her into a fountain. The river Alpheios then worked its way underground to mingle with the waters of Arethusa.

The first element of this name is not entirely certain, as there are two possible etymologies for it. The first is that it is derived from the Greek noun ἀλφή (alphe) meaning "produce, gain, profit", which is etymologically related to the Greek verb ἀλφάνω (alphano) meaning "to bring in, to yield, to fetch (a price)".The other possibility is that it is derived from the Greek noun ἀλφός (alphos), which was a rare word that originally meant "white, whiteness" (cognate to Latin Albus) but later came to refer to leprosy or a similar type of skin disease that is characterized by the formation of dull white lesions on the skin. There were other words more commonly used for the colour of white in ancient Greece, namely the noun λευκόν (leukon) and the adjective λευκός (leukos). The same goes for leprosy: this was usually known as λεύκη (leuke). Each of these three words is cognate to Latin Lux.The second element of this name is derived from the Greek noun ἀνήρ (aner) meaning "man". As such, the meaning of the name as a whole is either "a man's gain" or "white man" (as in, a white-haired man, i.e. an old and wise man). The meaning of "leprous man, leper" is highly improbable (at least for a given name), due to the heavy stigma that surrounded leprosy at the time.In Greek mythology, Alphenor is the name of one of the Niobids.
Derived from Arabic surrat al-faras ("the navel of the mare"). This is a traditional name of the star Alpha Andromedae in the constellation Andromeda.

Latinized form of Greek Ἀλφεσίβοια (Alphesiboia) meaning "much-courted" (literally "earning cattle, bringing in oxen", from ἀλφάνω (alphano) meaning "to bring in, yield, earn" and βοῦς (bous) meaning "bullock, bull, ox"). This was an epithet of maidens whose parents received many oxen or cattle as gifts from their suitors. In Greek mythology this was the name of several characters, including a daughter of Phegeus who married Alcmaeon.
Variant of Alphaeus and Latinized form of Alpheios.

Contracted form of Adelphia, which itself is a short form of Philadelphia. However, in some cases, this name is a feminine form of the English masculine name Alfie. A recent example of this is the 18th child born to the Radford family, who were featured in a Channel 4 documentary. Her full name is Hallie Alphia Beau: she was named after her deceased brother Alfie.
Diminutive of Alphard and Alphonso. In some cases, it is also a variant of Alfie.
Perhaps a feminine form of Alphaeus or Alphonse.
Feminine form of Alphonsus (see Alfonso). Saint Alphonsa (1910-1946) adopted this as a monastic name in honour of Saint Alphonsus Liguori (1696-1787).
Feminine form of Adalfuns, and Alphonsus.
Original Greek form of Alphonsus (see Alfonso).
Meaning unknown. This is the name of a character in the popular RPG game 'Undertale'.
Possible 7th century Pictish princess. Etymology unknown.
Late Middle English from Latin Alpinus, from Alpes ‘Alps.’

The name Alpkan originates from Old Turkic roots. It is a compound of Alp and Kan. Alp means "hero" or "brave warrior" and was commonly used in names of ancient Turkic warriors and rulers, such as Alp Er Tunga. Kan means "ruler" or "sovereign," related to the historical title "Khan." The combination reflects the ideal of a heroic and noble leader in Turkic culture. The name itself is rarely attested in medieval sources and is more commonly used in modern Turkey as a revival of traditional Turkic naming elements.
Alternate transcription of Bengali আলপনা (see Alpana).

Alqama is an Arabic name for boys that refers to a fruit of a plant known al-ḥanẓal (known as bitter apple and desert gourd in English, scientific name Citrullus colocynthis). It is also used to mean “bitterness”.
Nephew of Count Agrippe the Tall. He assisted his uncle in a war against King Hoel of Brittany, and was slain by Tristan during the siege of Alinge.

Gamma Cephei is a binary star system in the constellation Cepheus. The system bore a traditional name variously spelled as Errai, Er Rai or Alrai, deriving from the Arabic الراعي (ar-rā‘ī), meaning "the shepherd".
Variant of Alruna, also coinciding with the German word for "mandrake". This is the name of the title character in the novel 'Alraune' (1911) by Hanns Heinz Ewers.

Razi (Persian: رازی‎) or al-Razi (Arabic: الرازی‎) is a name that was historically used to indicate a person coming from Ray, Iran.A person described as being superior to everyone in every stat possible. Straight up BEAST. Smarter, stronger, faster, even better looking than anyone or anything.
Form of Rim prefixed with the Arabic definite article.

This is the name of a binary star system Alpha Piscium in the constellation Pisces. The system bore the traditional name Alrescha (alternatively Al Rescha, Alrischa, Alrisha) derived from the Arabic الرشآء al-rishā’ "the cord" and less commonly Kaitain and Okda, the latter from the Arabic عقدة ʽuqdah "knot".
Combination of elements al meaning "noble" and ric "power, ruler."
Variant of Ahlrich or Alarich recorded from the 15th to 20th centuries for men and in the 17th century for women in East Frisia.
Modern Swedish form of Old Norse Alríkr.
Possibly a variant of Alarik, Adalrik or Alfríkr. Alternatively, it may be derived from the Old Norse elements ǫl "ale" and rikr "mighty, distinguished".
Icelandic and Faroese form of Alrun.
Younger form of Adelrun and Albrun.

Germanic name, in which the second element was derived from Old High German runa or Old Norse rún meaning "secret lore, rune" (Proto-Germanic *rūnō). Modern-day scholars consider it a younger form of the Old High German name Ailrun, in which the first element is agi "terror" (which quite often became ail- in names). At the same time, it is also a contracted form of Adelruna (or Adelrun, Adelrune), in which the first element is adal "noble". Lastly, those same academics also consider it a younger form of the Old Norse name Alfrún, in which the first element is alfr "elf".The Old Norse cognate Ǫlrún occurs in the Eddic poem the Völundarkviða, belonging to a Valkyrie who marries the archer Egil. This form of the name was borne by an 11th-century Bavarian recluse, Alruna of Cham, a patron saint of pregnancy. Also see Aurinia. It coincides with the name of the mandrake plant, being alruna in Swedish, alrune in Danish and Norwegian and Alraune in German.
East Prussian German short form of Aldone.
Medieval English variant of Isabel via the variant Assabell.

This is the name of the star Sigma Draco is in the constellation Draco. It bore the traditional name Alsafi, derived from the Arabic Athāfi, itself erroneously transcribed from the Arabic plural Athāfiyy, meaning "the cooking tripods". This refers to the tripods used by nomads for open-air cooking.
This is the name of the star 31 Lyncis. It bore the traditional names Alsciaukat, from Arabic الشوكة (aš-šawkat) meaning "the thorn" and Mabsuthat.
Derived from Arabic al-safīnah meaning "the ship". Alsephina, also known as Delta Velorum, is a triple star system that is a part of the constellation Vela.
A son of Maelgwn (Maelgwyn), one of Arthur’s chieftains in Welsh legend. He rode a horse named Grey.
Derived from alashoe, the name of a kind of duck.
From Bashkir алсын (alsïn) meaning "falcon" and feminine name element бикә (bikä).
Anglicized form of Allsún, recorded in late medieval Ireland on women born into English and Anglo-Norman families.
Medieval form of any of the Old English names Æðelstan, Ælfstan, Ealdstan or Ealhstan.
Transferred use of the surname Alston.
Derived from the Germanic name elements allr "all, everybody, entire" and svartr "black". This is the name of a giant in Norse Mythology.
Means "all-swift; very fast" in Old Norse. In Norse mythology this is the name of one of the horses that pulls the Sun.
Derived from Old Norse ala "entire, all" and svinnr "fast, clever". In Norse mythology this is the name of both a jotunn and one of Sól's horses.
Taken from the Spanish title of the Virgin Mary Nuestra Señora de Altabás meaning "Our Lady of Altabás". Altabás is the Spanish form of Adelbald and is used as a surname as well.
Derived from Italian alta, the feminine form of the adjective alto, meaning "high; deep; big; towering; elevated" and, when used in a poetic context, "grand; sublime; noble" and donna "woman; lady".
Means "kinder, nicer, lovelier" in Arabic, the elative of لطيف (laṭīf) meaning "gentle".
