column12: The name of a character in the classic 1956 science fiction film, Forbidden Planet. Altaira Morbius was the daughter of the scientist and space voyager Dr. Edward Morbius. The name Altaira is derived from Altair, the brightest star in the constellation of the Eagle (Aquila).

Derived from Italian alta, the feminine form of the adjective alto, meaning "high; deep; big; towering; elevated" and, when used in a poetic context, "grand; sublime; noble" and luna "moon".A known bearer of this name was Altaluna della Scala, daughter of Mastino II della Scala, a 14th-cenutry lord of Verona, sister of Viridis and wife of Louis V, Duke of Bavaria.Whether Altalune, the name Uma Thurman gave her daughter born in 2012, is a medieval variant of this name, is still debated.
Possibly a variant of Altaluna. This is one of the middle names of the daughter of Uma Thurman and Arpad Busson.
Meaning unknown, possibly an altered form of Arthémise.

This name is either a variant form of Aldemaro or derived from the Spanish locational surname Altamira, which takes its name from a place called Altamiros or Altamira. Both mean "high view" in Spanish, as they consist of the words alta meaning "high" and mira meaning "view, sight". Also compare the names Altagracia and Altaluna.A known bearer of this name is the Brazilian musician and composer Altamiro Carrilho (1924-2012). In literature, Altamiro is the name of the protagonist of the Spanish comic strip series Altamiro de la Cueva, which was first published in 1965.
Means "golden hero" in Mongolian, from алтан (altan) meaning "golden" and баатар (baatar) meaning "hero".
Means "golden pillar" in Mongolian, from алтан (altan) meaning "golden" and багана (bagana) meaning "pillar, column"
From Mongolian алтан (altan) meaning "golden" and баяр (bayar) meaning "celebration, joy".
Means "gold jewelry" in Mongolian, from алтан (altan) meaning "golden" and чимэг (chimeg) meaning "ornament".
Means "golden stone" in Mongolian, from алтан (altan) meaning "golden" and чулуун (chuluun) meaning "stone".
Means "golden flame" in Mongolian, from алтан (altan) meaning "golden" and дөл (döl) meaning "flame".
Means "golden forehead" in Mongolian, from алтан (altan) meaning "golden" and дух (dukh) meaning "forehead, brow".
Means "golden helmet" in Mongolian, from алтан (altan) meaning "golden" and дуулга (duulga) meaning "helmet".
Means "golden rose", from Mongolian алтан (altan) meaning "golden" and Tajik гул (gul) meaning "flower, rose", ultimately from Persian گل (gol).
Means "golden blessing" in Mongolian, from алтан (altan) meaning "golden" and хишиг (khishig) meaning "blessing, favour".
Means "golden son, golden boy" in Mongolian, from алтан (altan) meaning "golden" and хүү (khüü) meaning "boy, son; child".
Means "golden armour" in Mongolian, from алтан (altan) meaning "golden" and хуяг (khuyag) meaning "armour".
Means "golden autumn" in Mongolian, from алтан (altan) meaning "golden" and намар (namar) meaning "autumn".
Means "golden sun" in Mongolian, from алтан (altan) meaning "golden" and нар (nar) meaning "sun".
Means "golden leaf" in Mongolian, from алтан (altan) meaning "golden" and навч (navch) meaning "leaf".
From Mongolian алтан (altan) meaning "golden" and пүрэв (pürev) meaning "Thursday" or "Jupiter".
From Mongolian алтан (altan) meaning "golden" and саргай (sargai) meaning "rose, lily".
From Mongolian алтан (altan) meaning "golden" and солонго (solongo) meaning "rainbow".
From Mongolian алтан (altan) meaning "golden" and соёмбо (soyombo), referring to a traditional symbol of Mongolia.
Means "golden axe" in Mongolian, from алтан (altan) meaning "golden" and сүх (sükh) meaning "axe".
Means "golden pearl" in Mongolian, from алтан (altan) meaning "golden" and сувд (suvd) meaning "pearl".
Means "golden peacock, golden peafowl" in Mongolian, from алтан (altan) meaning "golden" and тогос (togos) meaning "peacock, peafowl"
Means "golden light beam" in Mongolian, from алтан (altan) meaning "golden" and цацрал (tsatsral) meaning "radiation, light beam".
Means "golden splendour" or "golden embers" in Mongolian, from алтан (altan) meaning "golden" and цог (tsog) meaning "embers, glowing coals" or "splendour, glory".
Means "golden flag" in Mongolian, from алтан (altan) meaning "golden" and туг (tug) meaning "flag, banner, tuft".
Means "golden key" in Mongolian, from алтан (altan) meaning "golden" and түлхүүр (tülkhüür) meaning "key".
From Mongolian алтан (altan) meaning "golden" and тунгалаг (tungalag) meaning "serenity, clarity" or "clear, unclouded, transparent".
Means "golden ray" in Mongolian, from алтан (altan) meaning "golden" and туяа (tuyaa) meaning "ray, beam (of light)".
From Mongolian алтан (altan) meaning "golden" and заяа (zayaa) meaning "future, fate, destiny".
From Mongolian алтан (altan) meaning "golden" and жаргал (jargal) meaning "happiness, blessing".
Means "tulip" in Mongolian, ultimately from алтан (altan) meaning "golden" and зул (zul) meaning "light, lamp, torch".

Likely derived from Italian alta, the feminine form of the adjective alto, meaning "high; deep; big; towering; elevated" and, when used in a poetic context, "grand; sublime; noble" and pasqua "Easter".
Meaning uncertain, possibly derived from Spanish altar, meaning "altar".
Form of Tariq prefixed with the Arabic definite article.
Possibly from the Aymara alt’at chuymanïña meaning "modesty, humility".
Derived from Lithuanian al meaning "everything, every last one" combined with Baltic tauta meaning "people, nation" (see Vytautas).

Derived from Old High German alt, Old Saxon, Old Frisian ald meaning "old" together with Old High German beraht, Old Saxon berht meaning "bright" from Proto-Germanic *berhtaz.Some forms of this name are impossible to distinguish from forms of Albert.

Feminine form of Altbert.It is impossible to distinguish some forms of this name, in which the first element is from Old High German alt "old" (or Old Saxon and Old Frisian ald), from forms of Alberta, in which the first element derives from Old High German adal "noble".
Created from the German name elements alt "old, ancient" and burg "protected place, castle".
Meaning uncertain, possibly derived from a place name.
Medieval Latinized form of an uncertain name, perhaps a misspelling of Ælfheah or *Ealdheah.
From the Germanic name Althar meaning "old army", derived from the elements ald "old" and heri "army".

A Lelegian king who resided at Pedasus, which was situated in or near the Troad. According to Homer's Iliad Altes was the father of Laothoe, one of the many wives (or concubines) of King Priam. In other accounts, Altes is also said to be the father of the Argonaut Ancaeus of Samos; perhaps because this Ancaeus was also of Lelegian stock.
A dithematic Germanic name formed from the name elements alt "old" and fridu "peace".
The son of Catreus and brother to Apemosyne, Aeropa, and Clymene.
Transferred use of the surname Altham. A locational name from the parish and village of Altham on the river Henburn in North East Lancashire.
French borrowing of Althea. This is also the French name for the marshmallow plant (species Althaea officinalis).
Possibly a blend of Althea and Theda.This is the name a character in the "Harry Potter" series written by J.K. Rowling.
An invented name. Possibly a combination of Althea and Athene.
Derived from Old Norse ala "all, entire" and þjófr "thief". This is the name of a dwarf in Norse mythology.
One of Acoran's names, used in the islands of Lanzarote and Fuerteventura.
Likely a variant of Alighiero. Altichiero da Zevio was an Italian painter, inspired by Italian painter Giotto di Bondone.
Diminutive of Althea and other names beginning with Alt-.
From Altildis, a Latinized form of a Germanic name derived from the elements alt meaning "old" and hilt meaning "battle", making it a cognate of Old English Ealdhild.

Variant transcription of Altinai.A famous bearer is Princess Altinaï Petrović-Njegoš (1977-), the only daughter of Nicholas, Prince of Montenegro, head of the house of House of Petrović-Njegoš and his wife, Francine Navarro.
From the Kazakh алтын (altın) meaning "gold" and ‎ бай (bay) meaning "bey".
From the Bashkir aлтын (altin) meaning "gold" and feminine name element бикә (bikä).
Derived from Tatar altın meaning "gold" and çäç meaning "hair".
From the Karachay-Balkar алтын (altın) meaning "gold, golden" and Persian جان (jan) meaning "soul".
From the Hausa word Lī̀tìnîn "Monday". This name is traditionally given to girls born on Monday.
Derived from Guanche *allətin, meaning "moles, birth marks".
The sky father of the Aranda tribes of Central Australia, Altjira is looked on as the god of the Alchera, the dream time.
Means "gold" in Kalmyk, ultimately from Proto-Turkic *altun.

Directly taken from Latin altus meaning "to raise, to make high, to elevate". As a musical term it refers to the contrapuntal part higher than the tenor and its associated vocal range.Alto of Altomünster was an Irish or Scottish saint who lived in Germany.

Altonathan is a contemporary English name, meticulously crafted to bridge the gap between industrial heritage and spiritual significance. Founded on 31 January 2026 in the East Midlands, United Kingdom, it represents a modern evolution of British nomenclature.The Etymology and Origin of this name is a portmanteau—a linguistic blend of two established English names:Alton: Derived from Old English (alt meaning "old" or "source," and tun meaning "settlement/town").Nathan: Derived from the Hebrew Nātān, meaning "he gave" or "gift."By weaving these two lineages together, Altonathan acts as a bridge between the Old English landscape and Hebrew theological tradition.Traditionally Meaning: "God’s Place" or "God’s Town".While "Alton" provides the physical foundation of a town or place, "Nathan" brings the divine connection. In this new context, the name symbolizes a sanctuary or a community established under divine providence. It suggests a person who is a "pillar" or a "foundation" for others.However, unlike traditional names like Jonathan, Altonathan follows the rhythmic cadence of words like Automation or Alternation.Phonetic Spelling: AL-ten-ATH-anIPA Notation: /ˌæl.tən.ˈæθ.ən/Rhythm: It features a secondary stress on the first syllable and a primary stress on the third (ATH), creating a sophisticated, rolling flow.The name is contemporary-rooted in the East Midlands, UK. This region—known for its blend of industrial history (Leicester, Nottingham, Derby) and rolling countryside—mirrors the name's structure and what ultimately inspired the creation of such name:The "Alton" prefix reflects the stony, grounded history of English settlements.The "Nathan" suffix adds a melodic, modern brightness.Usages and Potential NicknamesBecause of its four-syllable structure, Altonathan offers several versatile short forms:Alt: For a modern, tech-focused feel.Nate: For a classic, friendly touch.Athan: Drawing from the stressed syllable, sounding like the Greek Athanasios (immortal).
Possibly an altered form of Antonio influenced by Al, Alto or Alton.
Most likely a variant of Altonio.
Archaic spelling of Altoora (using the old Kleinschmidt orthography, used to write Greenlandic until 1973).
This was the Xianbei name of Murong Chui, the founder of the Later Yan dynasty of China. Perhaps from Proto-Turkic altūn meaning "gold".
Possibly a corrupted form of Arturo.
From Turkmen alty meaning "six" combined with the name Myrat.
Derived from Kazakh алтын (altyn) meaning "gold" combined with бай (bay) meaning "rich, wealthy".
Derived from алтын (altyn) meaning "golden" and бикэ (bike) meaning "princess".
From Kazakh алтын (altyn) meaning "gold" combined with гүл (gul) meaning "flower".
Means "golden hair" from Kazakh алтын (altyn) meaning "gold" combined with шаш (shash) meaning "hair".
The great spirit of the Arawak of Guyana.

The name Dracula spelled backwards. Though regularly featured in (animated) films, notably 'Son of Dracula' (1943), it is perhaps best known in more recent times from Kouta Hirano's 'Hellsing' manga and the 'Castlevania' video games.

This name is best known for being the name of the eponymous hero of the epic poem Aluda Ketelauri (1888) written by the Georgian poet and writer Vazha-Pshavela (1861-1915).It is unclear to me whether the author had invented the name or not, but either way, the meaning of the name is uncertain. Some sources believe that it is of either Ossetian or Scythian origin and means "brewer of beer" or is otherwise etymologically related to beer. Compare modern Georgian ლუდი (ludi) meaning "beer" and its dialectal variant ალუდი (aludi). Other sources find this etymology doubtful and state that the name should be seen as a derivation of the Arabic name Aladdin.
Possibly a feminine form of Albar.
Derived from Mapudungun alwe (also used as am), referring to (the spirit/soul of) a dead person.
Probably a Norman name derived from Adalwolf (see Adolf).

Means "horn of the red deer" or "seed of the red deer" in Sumerian, deriving from the elements 𒀉 a ("arm, wing, horn") and 𒇻𒅆 lulim ("red deer stag"). This was the name of the legendary first king of Sumer, who is thought today to be a mythological figure. There is evidence it was never used as an ordinary given name in the Early Dynastic period of Sumer.
On the Caroline Islands the god of knowledge and navigation. He is the son of Palulop.

Possibly from the (medieval) Hebrew word אֲלוּמָה (aluma) meaning "strong, brave" (which, in modern Hebrew, sounds like the word אֲלֻמָּה (alma) "sheaf"). It is sometimes associated with the word עלמה (alma) "a young girl, a damsel".
Rare Ukrainian name with only 3 bearers, all in Shyryayivskyy Rayon (Odessa Oblast). Possibly linguistic spelling variation of Alona due to Ukrainian language phenomenon ukannya.
Mapuche name, it means "woman with heart of light", or it might mean "joy".
Name used by the Suludnon people of Panay for Laon, the sky goddess in Visayan mythology. Means the "the ancient one," from Visayan 'laon' meaning "ancient" or "old" and 'sina' meaning "foreigner."
Means "born on overcast morning" in Luo.
Direct adoption of the name of the river Aluona whose name is derived from alėti "to flow; to run (referring to water); to trickle; to drip".
Variant of Allura influenced by Alora.

This is a Manx name, said to be a cognate of Alfred via its latinized form Aluredus, a variant of Alvredus.In some cases, it may be derived from an Old English name composed of the elements ealu "ale" and ræd "counsel".

Alush is a surviving personal name in the Edisto language of South Carolina. This was the name of a captain or chief of the Edisto Nation encountered by Robert Sandford in 1666.The etymological meaning of this personal name has been lost to time, as the Edisto language, related to other Cusaboan languages, is largely unattested.Superficial comparisons can be drawn between the name "Alush" and the town or province name "Aluete," alternatively rendered as "Aluste," as encountered by Pedro de Ibarra during an expedition of the South Carolina low country in the 17th century. However, the exact etymological meaning of this name is also unknown due to the extinction of all related languages.
Diminutive of Alicja, Alina, Aldona, Aleksandra or other names beginning with Al-.

Tsar of Bulgaria for short time in 1041. One night, during dinner, Alusian took advantage of Peter II's inebriation, and cut off his nose and blinded him with a kitchen knife in 1041. Since Alusian was of the blood of Samuel, he was quickly proclaimed emperor in Peter II's place by his troops.
Means "be prosperous" or "grow up" in Tshivenda.
Light or star in Ancient Mayan of Mexico
The ancient Arabian goddess of might, protection and love. Her name is derived from al-‘Azīz meaning "the mighty".
Variant of Elva 2 influenced by the Swedish word älva "elf, fairy".

The first element of this name is derived from Lithuanian al meaning "everything, every last one". The second element is derived from the old Lithuanian verb vaidyti meaning "to visit, to appear", which is related to the modern Lithuanian verb vaidentis meaning "to haunt" as well as "to appear, to see". Also compare modern Lithuanian vaiduoklis meaning "ghost, apparition" and vaidytis meaning "to quarrel, to wrangle".
Variant of Alvaldr. In Norse mythology this is the name of Þjazi's father. This is also the name of one of Saturn's moons.
Derived from Old Norse ala "all, entire" and valdr "ruler, mighty one".
Possible corruption of Alvina, oddly seems to be exclusively a masculine.
Means "multicolored, variegated" in Azerbaijani, ultimately from Arabic ألوان ('alwān) (compare Elvan).

Derived from the Hebrew verb עָלָה ('alah) meaning "to ascend, to rise". Also compare the related name Alvah. In the Old Testament (Genesis 36:23), Alvan is the eldest son of Shobal and a descendant of Seir the Horite; in 1 Chronicles 1:40, he is called Alian.
From the name of a mountain range in western Iran, possibly derived from Avestan aurvañt meaning "quick, swift, steed, horse".
One of Ulysses Everett McGill’s many daughters in the movie O Brother Where Art Thou?
Modern form of Alfhard and Norwegian variant of Alvar.
Transferred use of the surname Alvarez.
Spanish diminutive of Álvaro. A known bearer of this name is the Spanish retired soccer player Álvaro Rodríguez Ros (b. 1936), who is commonly known as Alvarito.
Contracted form of Alviine and cognate of Alva 1.
Variant of Ǫlvér, or possibly derived from allr "all, entire" and vér "fighter" or aluh "temple" and vér.
Old Norse variant of Alfr as well as the Old Swedish form of AlvéR.
Occitan cognate of Elvira. Sainte Alvère (Senta Alvèra in Occitan) was a martyr from the Dordogne region in France.
Derived from the Germanic elements alf "elf" and ræd "counsel" (compare Alfred).
Apparently a feminized form of Alfred via the Latin Alvredus. 'Used from time to time in the 19th century, and has been noted in the 20th century as Alvedine.'
Name of a 3rd century Italian soldier, martyr and saint.
Meaning unknown. Perhaps an altered form of Laverna. It could also maybe have been taken from Alvera or Alvena, drawing inspiration from Verna.
Derived from the Manor of Alverton on the west side of Penzance in Cornwall. The first person with this name is likely to be Edward Alverne Bolitho born 1842.
Modern Greek spelling of Albertos, which is an older Greek form of Albert.
Transferred use of the surname Alves.
Possibly an elaboration of Alva 2 using the suffix -etta.
Transferred use of the surname Alvey.
Possible variant of the second sense of Alva 2 stemming from Alvah.

Old French name derived from the continental Germanic name Adelwidis, which was composed of Old High German adal meaning "noble, well-bred" and wit meaning "wide". Alternatively the second element could be derived from Old Saxon widu, wido or Old High German witu meaning "wood".It is often difficult to distinguish forms of this name from forms of Alice and Eloise.
Finnish and Estonian form of Alvina and Finnish variant of Alfiina.
Estonian form of Alwine and variant of Alviina.
Derived from Lithuanian al meaning "everything, every last one" combined with Baltic vil meaning "hope" (see Viltautas).
Lithuanian form of the Germanic name Alwin (and in some cases also of the English name Alvin). Also compare Elvinas.
Feminine form of Alf 1 or Alvin.
Portuguese form of Alvin or Albin.
Medieval form of Old English Æthelwacer or Ælfwacer.
Means "the newborn", derived from Arabic ولد (walada) meaning "to bear a child, to give birth". This is the name of two Umayyad Caliphs.
Variant of Alwaru, itself a variant of Ælfwaru or Æthelwaru.
Variant of Alvice. This spelling occurs in Domesday Book.
Adoption of the name of a Welsh river in Clwyd. The origin and meaning of this river's name are uncertain; current theories, however, include a derivation from Proto-Celtic *al(aun)o- "nourishing".

Of uncertain origin and meaning. Current theories include an adoption of the Welsh name (which is unlikely as the Breton name seems to be older than the Welsh name in question), a younger form of Breton Alc'houen and a variant of Anglo-Norman Alfwena.
From Arabic علوي ('alawiyy) meaning "of Ali 1", referring to descendants or followers of Ali ibn Abi Talib.
Variant of Ælfweald. This spelling is used in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle to refer to Ælfwald I, king of the Northumbrians from 778 or 779 to 788.
A scholar and suitor in 'Honoria and Mammon', a Caroline era stage play by James Shirley.
Combination of elements al "noble" and wulf "wolf."
Late Old English variant of Ælfwynn and Æthelwynn.
Alternate transcription of Arabic علياء (see Alya 1).
Arabic form of Elisha 1, used in the Quran.

column12: Hellenized form of Lydian 𐤥𐤠𐤩𐤥𐤤𐤯𐤤𐤮 (Walwateś), derived from 𐤥𐤠𐤩𐤥𐤤 (walwe) meaning "lion" and the abstract suffix -𐤠𐤯𐤠 (-ata).
Variant of Alison 1, possibly influenced by Alice or Alicyn.
Variant of Aleida and Alida (depending on the pronunciation used). A known bearer of this name is the Dutch racing cyclist Alyda Norbruis (b. 1989).
Invented name, maybe based on Alyssa or Alethea
Ukrainian spelling of Russian pronunciation of Oleg.
Ossetian and Abkhaz form of Alexander.
Alyla, pronounced 'AH-LIE-LAH' means sophisticated, unique and mysterious.
One of Arthur's knights who fought in the war against Mordred.
Variant of Alina. As a Russian name, it is mostly used by Russian speaking Ukrainians who want to spell their name the same in Russian and Ukrainian Cyrillic.

Variant of Aline. It appears in Thomas Malory's 15th-century compilation of Arthurian legends Le Morte d'Arthur, where it belongs to a daughter of Pellinore who commits suicide after her lover is killed.
Possibly a feminine form of Hélion.
French form of Alypius or Alypus.
Feminine form of Alypios. This name was borne by a 5th-century Roman noblewoman, the daughter of Western Roman Emperor Anthemius.
Latinized form of Alypios. A known bearer of this name was Alypius the Stylite, an ascetic saint from the 7th century AD.
Means "without pain, not causing grief" in Ancient Greek, derived from the negative prefix ἄ- (a) combined with λύπη (lype) meaning "grief, pain, sorrow".
Latinized form of Alypos. This was the name of a sculptor from ancient Greece.
Variant of Elizabeth, influenced by Alyssa.
Variant of Alexandra, probably influenced by the name Alysa.
Variant of Alison 1 or a combination of Alys and Anne 1.
Variation of Alison with the popular feminine diminutive suffix -ette
Variant of Elizabeth influenced by Alyssa and Beth, or a combination of both.
Variant of Allison influenced by Alyssa.
Variant of Alison influenced by Alyssa. It caught on as a masculine name in Brazil.

From the flowering plant native to the Mediterranean. The name alyssum actually comes from the Greek word 'lyssa', meaning “rage” or “madness” and the 'a', meaning “against” giving it its meaning today, “without madness”, since it was believed to cure madness.
A variant of Ailith. Rhymes with Aerith and Aelyth.
Means "to be able to" or "will not suffer, does not lose" in Mongolian.
The name of a 12-year-old Guanche boy sold at the slave market in Valencia in 1497.
Belarusian form of Elizabeth, Belarusian cognate of Alžběta.
Possibly derived from Arabic النِسَاء‎ (an-nisāʾ) meaning "the woman".
From Sino-Vietnamese 庵 (am) meaning "small temple, hermitage, cottage".
Feminine form of Ámr or a Greenlandic form of Amma. In Norse mythology this is the name of a giantess.

column12: East Greenlandic name related to the word amaat meaning "a woman's coat with a large hood to carry children".
Dutch form of Amatus and possibly also of Amadeus.
Elaboration of Amabel or variant of Amabilia, used by Neil Gaiman for a character (one of the ghosts) in his children's novel 'The Graveyard Book' (2010).

Variant of Amabel influenced by French (i.e., with a French feminine name suffix). Used by Haitian-born author Edwidge Danticat for a character in the historical novel 'The Farming of Bones' (1998); the book chronicles a young Haitian girl named Amabelle Desir's 1937 escape from the Dominican Republic following the Parsley Massacre and the spread of antihaitianismo.
Italian form of Amabilis and also rare French form of Amabilis. The name is unisex in Italy and strictly feminine in the francophone world. Also compare Amable.
Means "forest water" from Cherokee a ma "water" and a do hi i na ge "forest" or a da "wood".

A figure in Irish and Scottish Gaelic folklore who may assume both benevolent and malevolent roles. Amadán Mór, the Great Fool, is the Perceval-like hero of several Irish folk narratives and a sometime leader of the fairy host in narrative and poetry. Amadán na bruidhne, the fool of the fairy mounds or palaces, is greatly feared because he may administer the fairy stroke, causing paralysis, crippling, or death; he is most active in June.
One of several of Arthur's knights who embarked on a quest to learn Merlin's fate, after he had been imprisoned by the Lady of the Lake.
Coined by Sabino Arana Goiri and Koldo Elizalde as a Basque equivalent of Amadea and Amada.

Late Roman and German feminine form of Amadeus, Italian and Galician feminine form of Amadeo, Sicilian feminine form of Amadeu, Hungarian and Polish feminine form of Amadeusz and Slovene variant of Amadeja.
Languedocian and Gascon form of Amadeus.
Russian and Ukrainian form of Amadeus.
Judeo-Spanish name. Could come from Amada or be an Arabic name integrated into the language.
Is of African-Rhodesia origin and means "to be beloved".
Feminine form of Amadore (Italian) and Amador (Spanish, Galician, Portuguese).
Medieval Italian form of Amator. The modern form of the name is Amatore.
Possibly deriving in part from the Sumerian element ama ("mother"). Name borne by a Sumerian businesswoman who lived during the reign of Sargon of Akkad.

Amael is an angel of hope and a principality who resides on the third heaven. He is the ruling angel of Venus. Amael is a name likened to that of Haniel, an angel who has as many aspects as variant forms of his name.
Of uncertain etymology. A notable bearer was Amage, a queen of the Sarmatians.

column3: 天城(Japanese Kanji)|あまぎ(Japanese Hiragana)|アマギ(Japanese Katakana)
column12: from Japanese kanji “天“ (ama) meaning “sky, heaven” and “城” (gi) meaning “castle, fortress”

Of unknown origin and meaning. This was the name of the aunt of Amaya in Francisco Navarro-Villoslada's Romantic historical novel Amaya o los vascos en el siglo VIII (Amaya, or the Basques in the 8th century), published in 1879, which is set during the invasion of Visigothic Spain by the Moors.

Spanish spelling of Amagoia used in the historical novel Amaya, or the Basques in the 8th century (1879) by Francisco Navarro-Villoslada (Amagoya in the Spanish original; Amagoia in the Basque translation).
According to Inuit mythology Amaguq is a trickster and wolf god.

column12: From Japanese 天 (ama) meaning "heaven, sky" or 雨 (ama) meaning "rain" combined with 羽 (ha) meaning "feather" or 菜 (ha) meaning "vegetables, greens". Other kanji combinations are possible.
From Japanese 天 (ama) meaning "heaven, sky" combined with 日 (hi) meaning "sun, day". Other combinations of kanji characters are also possible.
From Japanese 亜 (ama) meaning "second, Asia" combined with 人 (hito) meaning "person". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: あまい(Japanese Hiragana)|遭毎, 麻妹, 愛枚, 亜米, 天移, 阿交依, 安待舞, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 亜 (a) meaning "second, Asia" combined with 舞 (mai) meaning "dance". Other kanji combinations are possible.
Feminine form of Amédée. Used in 'Amaïdée' (1889), a poem by the French author Jules Barbey d'Aurévilly.

Possibly an invented name based on the sounds found in names such as Amaya, Mayra and Leilani. (Also compare Amara, Amaira and Omayra.)This name was popularised by the Mexican actress Amairani Romero Gutiérrez (1970-), known simply as Amairani.
Means "the town loves me" in Ijaw.

From the town of Amaiur in Spain. The fortress of Amaiur was one of the last fortresses in Navarre to make a stand against the Castilian invasion of 1512. In the 20th century it was reclaimed by Basque nationalists as a symbol of resistance of the Basque, thus its usage as a name for people.

column3: あまか(Japanese Hiragana)|天芳, 亜舞馨, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 天 (ama) meaning "heavens, sky" combined with 馨 (ka) meaning "fragrance". Other kanji combinations are possible.
Means "feast for the town" in Ijaw.
Means "look upon the town" in Ijaw.
From Japanese 天 (ama) meaning "heavens, sky" combined with 子 (ko) meaning "child". Other kanji combinations are possible.
Variant spelling of Amalfrid. Through his mother Amalaberga, Amalafrid was a great-grandson of Theodemir, king of the Ostrogoths (in the 5th century AD).
Variant of Amalfrida. Amalafrida was a daughter of Theodemir, king of the Ostrogoths in the 5th century AD.
Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Amalaric.

Derived from the Germanic elements amal "work" and Gothic svinths (swind in Old High German) "strength." This name was borne by a daughter of Theodoric the Great, who became queen of the Ostrogoths after his death in 526 AD.

The first element of this name is derived from the Germanic element amal "work." The second element is derived from Gothic bairgan (bergan in Old High German) "to keep, to save, to preserve", or from Old High German burg "fortress."
Meaning unknown, possibly a masculine form of Amalia. Amaldus Nielsen (1838-1932) was a Norwegian painter.
Coined by Sabino Arana Goiri and Koldo Elizalde as a Basque equivalent of Amalia.
Hellenized form of Biblical Hebrew עֲמָלֵק (ʾĂmālēq).
Possibly based on the biblical name Amalek. This belongs to two characters in the Book of Mormon, including a Nephite record keeper who wrote 18 verses of the Book of Omni.
Esperanto form of Amalek or Amaleki.
Derived from the place name Amalfi. It is mainly used in Colombia.
Means "peaceful work", derived from the Germanic element amal "work" combined with Old High German fridu "peace."
Dutch and German form of Amalfrida.
Derived from the Old German elements *amal "vigorous, brave" and ger "spear".
Derived from the Germanic element amal "work" combined with Gothic gild "sacrifice."

The first element of this Germanic name comes from amal "work." The meaning and origin of the second element is rather uncertain: we know that it comes from gis (the original form was possibly gîs), but we don't exactly know where gis itself comes from. But there are a few possibilities. It might come from Gallo-Celtic gaiso "spear" (see Gaiseric) or it might be a short form of gisel, which means "hostage" or "pledge" (see Giselle).
Derived from the Germanic element amal "work" combined with Old High German gund "war."
Derived from the Germanic element amal "work" combined with Gothic hardus (hart in Old High German) "brave, hardy."
Derived from the Germanic element amal "work" combined with Old Norse hildr "battle."
Elaboration of Amalia with the suffix -na
Nephite traitor who becomes king of the Lamanites and wars with Nephites - killed by Teancum (c. 70 BC).
Variant of Malinalli, perhaps influenced by Amalia.
It might derive from Amal, that means "pure". Or it might derive from the name of a typical local plant, Amalaka, a sacred plant.
Derived from the Uzbek word amal meaning "influence, bewitch, charm" or the Arabic name Amal 1 combined with oy meaning "moon".
Derived from the Germanic element amal "work" combined with Old High German rât "counsel."
Catalan, Italian and Spanish form of Amalthea.
Derived from the Germanic element amal "work" combined with þruþ "strength."
Combination of Basque ama "mother" and Lur.
Derived from the Germanic element amal "work" combined with Old High German wini "friend."
Amamah is a name originate from the Qua'ranic verse 33:72 referring to the trust God placed in mankind.

column3: あまめ(Japanese Hiragana)|アマメ(Japanese Katakana)|亜豆, 甘初, 愛候海, 遇麻芽, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 愛 (a) meaning "love, affection", 候 (ma) meaning "climate, season, weather", and 海 (me) meaning "sea, ocean". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: 天美, 天海, 天実, 雨海, 雨美, 雨実, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From 雨 (ama) meaning " rain" or 天 (ama) meaning "heaven(ly)" combined with 実 (mi) meaning "fruit, reality, truth" or 海 (mi) meaning "ocean". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: 阿摩美久, 阿摩彌姑, アマミチュー(Okinawan)
column12: Amamikyu's name comes from the reading of the Chinese characters 阿摩美久 or 阿摩彌姑, which were most likely written ad hoc for the Okinawan pronunciation.
Means "peace, tranquility" in Hindi and Punjabi, ultimately from Arabic أَمْن‎ (ʾamn).

column3: 雨菜, 雨那, 雨奈, 安麻奈, 天菜, 天那, etc.(Japanese Kanji)|あまな(Japanese Hiragana)
column12: From Japanese 雨 (ama) meaning "rain" combined with 菜 (na) meaning "vegetables, greens". Other kanji combinations are possible.
Derived from Arabic أَمَان (ʾamān) meaning "security, safety, peace".

Derived from place name Amanay, itself derived from Guanche *amănay, meaning "visual". The place name refers to a port in the municipality and city of Pájara, in the island of Fuerteventura, Canary Islands.
From Arabic أمان (ʾamān) meaning "peace, safety, security" combined with Kazakh/Kyrgyz бай (bay) meaning "rich, wealthy".
From Arabic أمان (ʾamān) meaning "peace, safety, security" combined with the Turkic military title beg meaning "chieftain, master".
Derived from Kurdish amanc meaning "target, aim".
From the Quechua amánkay which is the name of a yellow lily with red streaks native to South America. By extension, the word also means "yellow".
French feminine and masculine form of Amantius.

Okinawan reading of Amamikyu, the traditional creator goddess of the Ryukyu Islands. Her name is derived from 阿 (a) meaning "a", 摩 (ma) meaning "to rub, chafe", 美 (mi) meaning "beauty" and 久 (yu) meaning "long time". These characters were probably chosen for their phonetic value in indigenous Okinawan rather than their individual meaning.
Spanish, Galician, and Jamaican Patois feminine form of Amantius.
Roman cognomen which was derived from Amandus.

A fictional character created by J.R.R. Tolkien. Amandil was the leader of the Faithful in Númenor, and came to be the eighteenth and last Lord of Andúnië. His life as Lord of Andúnië and as one of the Faithful sired the High Kings of Gondor and Arnor who preserved their ways through the Dúnedain of Middle-earth on up to Aragorn II Elessar. Elendil the Tall was his son, and Isildur his grandson.
Cognate of Amandine. Amandina of Schakkebroek is a saint in the Catholic Church. She was martyred during the Boxer Rebellion.
Alternate transcription of Punjabi Gurmukhi ਅਮਨਦੀਪ (see Amandeep).
Means "power, strength" in Xhosa and Zulu.A famous bearer is Amandla Stenberg (b. 1998) an American actress and singer.
From the Kazakh аман (aman) meaning “healthy; prosperous” and дос (dos) meaning “friend”.

column3: アマネ(Japanese Katakana)|あまね(Japanese Hiragana)|遍, 周, 吾真嶺, 彩麻音, 空満寧, 雨根, 天子, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 亜 (a, ama) meaning "second, Asia", 亜 (a, ama) meaning "love, affection", 雨 (ama) meaning "rain", 周 (amane, ama) meaning "circumference, circuit, lap", 星 (ama) meaning "star", 天 (amane, ama) meaning "heavens, sky, imperial", 普 (amane) meaning "universal, wide(ly), generally", 弥 (amane) meaning "all the more, increasingly" or 和 (amane) meaning "harmony, Japanese style, peace, soften, Japan", combined with 弥 (ne) meaning "all the more, increasingly", 峰 (ne) meaning "summit, peak", 韻 (ne) meaning "rhyme, elegance, tone", 希 (ne) meaning "hope, beg, request, pray, beseech, Greece, dilute (acid), rare, few, phenomenal", 羽 (ne) meaning "feathers", 使 (ne) meaning "use, send on a mission, order, messenger, envoy, ambassador, cause" or 望 (ne) meaning "ambition, full moon, hope, desire, aspire to, expect". Other kanji or kanji combinations can form this name as well.
Derived from Spanish amanecer "dawn (the morning period of twilight)".
Means "entrustment" via Arabic أمانات amanat. In the Quran (33:72) the word is used to describe God entrusting humans with free will. See also Emanet and Amanat.

Means "safety came", derived from Kazakh and Kyrgyz аман (aman) meaning "healthy, safe", ultimately from Arabic أمان (ʾamān), combined with Kazakh келді (keldi) or Kyrgyz келди (keldi) both meaning "came, arrived" (the past tense of Kazakh келу (kelu) or Kyrgyz кел (kel) meaning "to come").
From Kazakh аман (aman) meaning "healthy, safe" and гүл (gul) meaning "flower".
From Arabic أمان (ʾamān) meaning "peace" and gylyç meaning "sword".
May derive from the Egyptian god of the sun Amun. Name borne by a Kandake of Kush who ruled between 50 CE and 62 CE.
May derive from name of the Egyptian god Amun. Name borne by the last reigning Kandake of Kush, who ruled between 308-320 CE.

Meaning uncertain. Name borne by a reigning Kandake of Kush between 40 BCE and 10 BCE, who famously lead Kushite armies in a war against Rome from 27 BCE to 22 BCE. It is likely she was a ruling queen, as her full title was "Amnirense qore li kdwe li" ("Ameniras, qore and kandake")
From the Mao amani meaning "peaceful" and the feminine ending -ro.
Meaning uncertain. Name borne by a Kandake of Kush who ruled between 10 BCE and 1 CE. In Meroitic hieroglyphs her name is written "Amanikasheto" (Mniskhte or (Am)niskhete).
From the name of a genus of mushrooms (mostly comprised of poisonous species). The genus' name derives the Latin amanita, itself from the Ancient Greek amanítis (αμανίτης) 'fungus'

Meaning uncertain. Possibly means "begotten of Amun", deriving from the Meroitic element terike ("to beget") and Amun, the Egyptian god of the sun and air. Name borne by a Kandake of Kush, who held the title from 21 CE to 41 CE.
Meaning uncertain. Name borne by a Kandake of Kush. Amanitore is often mentioned in contemporary texts as being a co-regent with Natakamani, who was the son of Amanishakheto.
This name is a Kurdish name which means target or aim for the thing's that you want to achieve in life
From Punjabi ਅਮਨ (aman) meaning "peace" (ultimately from Arabic) combined with Sanskrit जिति (jiti) meaning "victory, conquering".
Means "one who lives a peaceful life".
Alternate transcription of Punjabi Gurmukhi ਅਮਨਜੀਤ (see Amanjeet).
Alternate transcription of Kazakh Аманжол (see Amanzhol).
From Arabic أمان (ʾamān) meaning "peace" and Sanskrit ज्योतिस् (jyotis) meaning "light".
Comes from Akan aman meaning ‘nation(s)’ + kwa meaning ‘free’.
From Japanese 雨 (ama) meaning "rain" combined with 乃 (no), a possessive particle. Other combinations of kanji characters can also form this name.
The furious and monsterous goddess born from Susanoo's pent up rage. Her name means "heaven opposing everything".
From Punjabi ਅਮਨ (aman) meaning "peace" (ultimately from Arabic) combined with Sanskrit पाल (pāla) meaning "guard, protector".

Means "peace and love" from Punjabi अमन (aman) meaning "peace" and ਪ੍ਰੀਤ (prīt) meaning "love" (ultimately from Arabic أمان (ʾamān) "peace" and Sanskrit प्रीति (prīti) "pleasure, joy, love" respectively).
Alternate transcription of Punjabi ਅਮਨਪ੍ਰੀਤ (see Amanpreet).
French variant of Amance and Occitan form of Amantius.

column4: French (Rare, Archaic)|Louisiana Creole (Rare, Archaic)|French (Quebec, Rare, Archaic)|History (Ecclesiastical)

column12: Derived from Arabic أَمَان (ʾamān) meaning "security, safety, peace".
From Arabic أَمَان (ʾamān) meaning "safety, shelter, protection" and Kazakh тай (tay) meaning "foal, colt".
Possibly a truncated from of Samantha.
Feminine form of Amant. This was the name of a French novelist, Amantine Lucile Aurore Dupin, who wrote under the pseudonym George Sand.
From Kazakh аман (aman) meaning "healthy, prosperous, safe, sound" and Kazakh тұру (turu) meaning "to rise, to stand"
Means "God knows" in Nyoro, Tooro, Nkore, and Kiga.
From Kazakh аман (aman) meaning "healthy, safe" and жан (zhan) meaning "soul".
From Kazakh аман (aman) meaning "healthy, prosperous, safe, sound" (of Arabic origin) and жол (zhol) meaning "road, way".

Amapola is the name by which plants of the genus Papaver Hroeas are known, that is the poppies. One type of poppy to Papave Sonipherum is the plant with which makes up the opium and morphine, because its elements have hallucinogenic and anesthetic power. Amapola is the title of an Argentine film 2014.
Means "spirit of the rain" in Guarani.
Means "the strong one" in Inuit. It is the name of a character in 'Atanarjuat: The Fast Runner'.
Means "rest, bliss, comfort, peace" or "simple, easy" in Mongolian.

column3: อมรา(Thai)|天笑, 天良, etc.(Japanese Kanji)|अमर(Sanskrit)|عمارہ(Shahmukhi, Urdu)|ਅਮਾਰਾ(Gurmukhi)
column12: From Thai อมร (amara) meaning "immortal, undying", ultimately from Sanskrit अमर (amara).
Means "God's grace" in Igbo. (See Amara 1 and Chukwu).

Means "marjoram (herb)" in Ancient Greek. In Greek mythology, this was the name of a prince (in some later accounts a son of king Cinyras) tasked with preparing royal or sacred perfumes. After dropping a box of perfumes and breaking many, he was transformed into a marjoram plant, which is associated with the goddess Aphrodite.
Possibly a variant of Amari with the phonetic element ray.
Transfered use of the surname Amaral. It began to be used after the Spanish rock duo Amaral, whose singer Eva Amaral also goes by the mononym Amaral.

Amarant is a Dutch girl's name. The name comes from the Greek word Amarantos which means "unfading beauty".In the 18th century it was a common name in the Netherlands. Nowadays the name still occurs sporadically in the Netherlands.
From the name of the amaranth flower, which is derived from Greek αμαραντος (amarantos) meaning "unfading".
The word amaranthine refers to "a shade of reddish-rose".

Spanish and Italian form of Amarantus. In other words, this is the masculine form of Amaranta. The 3rd-century Christian saint Amaranthus, who was martyred at Vieux near Albi in the south of France, is known by this name in Spanish.
Derived from Greek αμαραντος (amarantos) meaning "unfading" (see also Amarantha).
Latinized form of Amarantos. A known bearer was Amarantus of Alexandria, an ancient Greek writer from the 1st century BC.
From Mongolian амар (amar) meaning "rest, ease, comfort" or "simple, easy" and баян (bayan) meaning "rich, wealthy".
From Mongolian амар (amar) meaning "rest, ease, comfort" or "simple, easy" and баясгалан (bayasgalan) meaning "happiness, pleasure".
From Mongolian амар (amar) meaning "rest, ease, comfort" or "simple, easy" and билэг (bileg) meaning "gift, talent, aptitude".
From Mongolian амар (amar) meaning "rest, bliss, peace" and болд (bold) meaning "steel".
From Mongolian амар (amar) meaning "rest, ease, comfort" or "simple, easy" and буян (buyan) meaning "good deed, virtue, charity" or "fortune, blessing".
From Sanskrit अमर (amara) meaning "immortal, undying" combined with the name of the Hindu god Indra.
The meaning is bitter in Spanish

Meaning "born of poetry" relating to the modern Irish word amhrán meaning song. Was the name of ancient poet, Amargein Glúingel, who wrote the Song of Amargein and the foster of father of the hero Cú Chulainn, Amargein mac Eccit.

column3: あまり(Japanese Hiragana)|亜鞠, 亜真利, 亜真梨, 亜摩利, 亜麻梨, 亜麻莉, 亜万莉, 亜茉里, 天莉, 天里, 天梨, 天理, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: A noted bearer was a Damel of Cayor, Amari Ngoné Ndella, who ruled from 1790 AD to 1809 AD. The Kingdom of Cayor was one of the largest of most powerful kingdoms in what is now Senegal, existing from 1549 AD to 1879 AD.
Greek form of Amariah, as it first appeared in the Septuagint.
Variant of Amari, possibly influenced by Marie.
Used by J.R.R. Tolkien this is a Quenya name of unknown meaning. It possibly comes from mára meaning "good" or mar meaning "home".
English and Hungarian Latinate form of Amaryllis, in the case of the Hungarian name, derived from Hungarian amarillisz "amaryllis". This name was also used throughout the United States in the 1800s.
Alternate transcription of Greek Αμαρυλλίδα (see Amaryllida).
Hungarian form of Amaryllis; the name coincides with the Hungarian word for the flower.

column3: อมรินทร์, อัมรินทร์(Thai)
column12: From Thai อมร (amara) meaning "immortal" and อินทร์ (in) referring to the Hindu god Indra. This is a Thai epithet of Indra.
Elaboration of Marina with the prefix a-
Italian and Spanish form of Amarynceus.
Alternate transcription of Punjabi Gurmukhi ਅਮਰਿੰਦਰ (see Amrinder).
West Frisian form of Emerentia. Also compare Emerens.
Combination of the popular phonetic prefix a and Marion 2 or an elaboration of Amari.
Variant of Marisa, influenced by the name Amara.
Variant of Marise, influenced by the spelling of Amara.
Means "immortal" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit अमृत (amṛta).
Derived from Mongolian амар (amar) meaning "bliss, peace, comfort" and жаргал (jargal) meaning "happiness, blessing".
Alternate transcription of Punjabi Gurmukhi ਅਮਰਜੀਤ (see Amarjeet).
From Sanskrit अमर (amara) meaning "immortal" combined with ज्योतिस् (jyotis) meaning "light, brightness".
Derived from амар (amar) meaning "rest, ease, comfort" and хүү (khüü) meaning "son, boy".
Means "calm and peaceful" or "greetings" in Mongolian, from амар (amar) meaning "rest, ease, comfort" and мэнд (mend) meaning "health, well-being", often used as a greeting.
From Mongolian амар (amar) meaning "rest, ease, comfort" or "simple, easy" and мөнх (mönkh) meaning "forever, eternal".

The use of Amarna as a name is likely derived from the Egyptian archeological site of Amarna (also known as el-Amarna or Tell el-Amarna, لعمارنة). The city is located on the east bank of Nile River in the Egyptian province of Minya. The name Amarna comes from the Beni Amran tribe that lived in the region and founded a few settlements; the ancient Egyptian name for the city was Akhetaten.

Amarok is the name of a giant wolf in Inuit mythology. It will hunt down and devour anyone foolish enough to hunt alone at night. It is sometimes considered equivalent to the waheela of cryptozoology.
Son of Omni, Nephite record keeper.
From Sanskrit अमर (amara) meaning "undying, immortal, imperishable" and पाल (pāla) meaning "guard, protector, keeper".
From Sanskrit अमर (amara) meaning "immortal, undying" and प्रीति (prīti) meaning "pleasure, joy, love".
From Mongolian амар (amar) meaning "rest, ease, comfort" or "simple, easy" and сайхан (saikhan) meaning "nice, beautiful, handsome".
Derived from Mongolian амар (amar) meaning "bliss, peace" or "simple, easy" combined with санаа (sanaa) meaning "thought".
Means "peace, quiet; safety" in Mongolian, from амар (amar) meaning "rest, ease, comfort" and тайван (taivan) meaning "peace, tranquility".
Archaic spelling of Amaartivat (using the old Kleinschmidt orthography, used to write Greenlandic until 1973).
From Mongolian амар (amar) meaning "peace, ease, rest" and түвшин (tüvshin) meaning "level, degree".
Means "immortal, deathless", from Sanskrit अ (a) meaning "not" and मृत (mṛta) meaning "dead".

column3: 天琉, 天瑠, 天流, 天留, 彩真琉, 彩真瑠, 彩真流, 彩真留, 彩眞琉, 彩眞瑠, 彩眞流, 彩眞留, 彩麻琉, 彩麻瑠, 彩麻流, 彩麻留, 彩舞琉, 彩舞瑠, 彩舞流, 彩舞留, 愛真琉, 愛真瑠, 愛真流, 愛真留, 愛眞琉, 愛眞瑠, 愛眞流, 愛眞留, 愛麻琉, 愛麻瑠, 愛麻流, 愛麻留, 愛舞琉, 愛舞瑠, 愛舞流, 愛舞留, 空真琉, 空真瑠, 空真流, 空真留, 空眞琉, 空眞瑠, 空眞流, 空眞留, 空麻琉, 空麻瑠, 空麻流, 空麻留, 空舞琉, 空舞瑠, 空舞流, 空舞留, 亜真琉, 亜真瑠, 亜真流, 亜真留, 亜眞琉, 亜眞瑠, 亜眞流, 亜眞留, 亜麻琉, 亜麻瑠, 亜麻流, 亜麻留, 亜舞琉, 亜舞瑠, 亜舞流, 亜舞留, 吾丸(Japanese Kanji)|あまる(Japanese Hiragana)
column12: From Japanese 天 (ama) meaning "heavens; sky" combined with 琉 (ru), 瑠 (ru), both meaning "precious stone; gem, lapis lazuli", 流 (ru) meaning "flow", or 留 (ru) meaning "to detain; to fasten; to stop". It may also be from 彩 (a) meaning "coloring", 愛 (a) meaning "love", 空 (a), a form of 空く (aku) meaning "to be empty; to be open; to be free", or 亜 (a), a phonetic character combined with 真 (ma), 眞 (ma), both meaning "true", 麻 (ma) meaning "hemp", or 舞 (ma), from 舞う (mau) meaning "to dance, to twirl" combined with 琉 (ru), 瑠 (ru), 流 (ru) meaning "flow", or 留 (ru). It may also be from 吾 (a) meaning "I; me" and 丸 (maru) meaning "circle, round".Other character combinations are possible.
Greek variant of Amaryllis, from the genitive form Αμαρυλλίδος (Amaryllidos). This is also the Greek name for the amaryllis flower.

Latinized form of Greek Ἀμαρυγκεύς (Amarynkeus), though technically Amarygkeus is the correct spelling (compare Lynceus in that regard). The name is derived from Greek ἀμαρυγή (amaryge) meaning "sparkling, twinkling, glancing", which is ultimately derived from the Greek verb ἀμαρύσσω (amarysso) meaning "to sparkle, to twinkle, to glance" (see Amaryllis). Also compare Greek ἀμάρυγμα (amarygma) meaning "sparkle, twinkle". In Greek mythology, Amarynceus was a chief of the Eleans.

An epithet or title of the Greek goddess Artemis meaning "of Amarynthus", Amarynthus being a town in Euboea (according to Stephanus of Byzantium, Euboea itself). The place name may be related to the Greek personal name Amarantos (see Amarantha). Under the surname Amarysia or Amarynthia, Artemis was worshipped in Amarynthus and also in Attica.
Means "burden" in Hebrew. In the Old Testament, Amasa was a son of Haldai, and a nephew of King David who was murdered by his cousin Joab.

Amashai was the name of a minor figure in the bible who was the son of Azareel and was appointed by Nehemiah to do work in the temple at Jerusalem. He is mentioned once in Nehemiah 11:13. He is also called Amashsai, however Amashai is used in the King James version.The name allegedly means "gift of the people"
Extended form of Amasius. This name was borne by an obscure saint from the 1st century AD, who was the very first bishop of the Italian coastal city of Taranto.
Form of Amaziah used in the Greek and Latin Old Testament.
Of uncertain etymology, possibly deriving from the Lepontic element *amb-aχto ("servant") combined with the patronymic suffix -ilo.

Variant form of Άμωσις (Amosis), which is the hellenized form of the ancient Egyptian name IaH-ms or I'h-ms meaning "son of Iah". It is composed of the name of the Egyptian god Iah combined with the word mes "son" or mesu "be born". Also see Ahmose, which is the anglicized form of the aforementioned name Amosis.A well-known bearer of this name was Amasis II, an Egyptian pharaoh from the 6th century BC.

Latinized form of Ἀμασιος (Amasios), which is probably either a Greek variant form of Amasis or of Amasias. The former appears to be the more likely of the two, due to the historically close trade relations between Greece and Egypt. Alternatively, the name Amasios might possibly be derived from the name of the ancient Greek city Ἀμάσεια (Amaseia), which is nowadays known as Amasya and located in northern Turkey. The city is said to have been named after a little-known queen of the Amazons, which were a race of woman warriors from Greek mythology.A known bearer of this name was saint Amasius of Teano, who lived in the 4th century AD. He was a Greek man who was forced into exile in Italy for his opposition to the Arian heresy, where he went on to become bishop of Teano in 346 AD.

Dutch form of Amaziah. This name has always been extremely rare in the Netherlands and was also an exclusively masculine name until around the '60s of the 20th century. Around that time, the name also began to be used on females, due to the fact that the name's appearance and pronunciation is quite similar to that of Slavic feminine names like Anja, Katja, Natasja and Sonja, all of which were commonly used in the Netherlands at the time.Lastly, you might also want to compare this name with the name Amasia, which is very similar in appearance but ultimately comes from the male name Amasius.

Hellenized form of Old Persian Amāstrī, derived from *amā meaning "strength, power" and‎ *strī meaning "woman". Compare Amestris. This was the name of several historical figures, including a Persian princess and ruler of Heraclea, daughter of Oxyathres and niece of Dariush III.
Catalan, Polish, Languedocian, Provençal and Gascon form of Amatus.
Derived from Thracian *takos meaning "famous" and an unknown first element.
Variant form of Amatallah used by hispanophone muslims.
Means "maidservant of the omniscient" from Arabic أمة ال (amat al) meaning "maidservant of the" combined with عليم (alim) meaning "omniscient".
Means "maidservant of the all-provider" from Arabic أمة ال (amat al) meaning "maidservant of the" and رزاق (razzāq) "provider, sustainer".
Medieval Italian name composed of Latin amata "loved" (compare Amata) and sana "healthy".
Coined by Sabino Arana Goiri and Koldo Elizalde as an equivalent of Amata.
Means "maidservant of the merciful" from Arabic أمة ال (amat al) meaning "maidservant of the" combined with رحمن (rahman) meaning "merciful".

In Sumerian mythology she is the goddess of the ocean, possibly related to Poseidon. She was also worshipped by Sumerian immigrants in Egypt which lead to some believing her to be an Egyptian goddess. She may also be related to Ashima.

Uncertain etymology, coincides with (or perhaps derives from) Ancient Greek ἀμάθεια (amatheia) meaning "ignorance, illiteracy". Possibly related to the name of the ancient city Amathous in Cyprus, or the harbour of the same name in Laconia. This was name of one of the Nereids in Greek mythology.
A form of Amatheia. In Greek myth this was the name of one of the Nereids, the 50 daughters of the sea god Nereus.
Apparently the name of the mother of Abraham, and the mother of Haman.
An epithet of the goddess Aphrodite derived from the city of Amathus in Cyprus, one of her oldest seats of worship.
This is the name of a Frankish queen who succeeded the Anglo-Saxon Balthild and preceded Bilichild of Austrasia. Not much is known of her, though it's known that she was the wife of Chlothar III.
The name of Luke Garroway's sister in the book series "The Mortal Instruments" by Cassandra Clare (Amatis Herondale). Also means "you love" (pl) in Latin.
Means "servant of Nanaya", deriving from the Akkadian element amtu ("woman servant").
Means "the servant of Nanaya is at hand" deriving from the Akkadian elements amtu ("woman servant") and qereb ("close ,near ,at hand ,within reach").
Means "servant of Ninlil", deriving from the Akkadian element amtu ("woman servant").

column3: 天斗, 亜人, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 天 (ama) meaning "heaven, sky" combined with 斗 (to), which refers to a Chinese constellation. Other kanji combinations are possible.
Means "servant of Tashmetum", deriving from the Akkadian element amtu ("woman servant").
Means "servant of Allah", from Arabic أَمَة العَزِيْز ('amat ul-ʾazīz) meaning "servant of the mighty one".
Variant transcription of Arabic أمة العزيز (see Amat ul-'Aziz).
Means "maidservent of the bestower" from أمة (amat) meaning "maidservent" and المنان (al-mannan) meaning "the bestower".
Name of the statue of the Virgin Mary of Iurreta (in the Biscay area).Amatza's feast day is July 4.
Variant of Amora, possibly influenced by Laura and similar names.
An elderly, honorable knight who served Queen Blanche, a queen saved by Claris and Laris.
A character in The Faerie Queene by Edmund Spenser.
Possibly from the Sanskrit माया (māyā) meaning “illusion, magic”.

Meaning uncertain, possibly from Aramaic מָמוֹנָא (māmōnā) meaning "money, wealth, riches" or from a Greek root meaning "terrible violence and vehemence". This is the name of a demon who appears in numerous works on demonology, including the 17th-century grimoire The Lesser Key of Solomon (author unknown) and the Pseudomonarchia Daemonum (1563) by Dutch physician Johann Weyer. He is said to be the only being with power over the demon Asmodeus.

column3: 天世, 天代, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 天 (ama) meaning "heavens, sky" combined with 世 (yo) meaning "world, society" or 代 (yo) meaning "generation". Other kanji combinations are possible.

Meaning unknown. A mother im Brazil named Daniele Pereira Brandão Xavier registered her daughter with this name, and become viral in early 2023. This was the first time a person was given that name in Brazil. Although it might be unrelated, this name resembles a similarity with the word Abayomi, which means a type of rag doll from African Brazilian culture.
Means "greatness" in Tatar, originally taken from Arabic azamat.

From Tamazight ⴰⵎⴰⵣⵉⵖ (Amaziɣ), which is the self-designation of the Berber (Amazigh) people of North Africa. The name itself is of unknown meaning, though folk etymologies claim the meaning of "free-man", derived from Taznatit (Gurara) aze meaning "to be strong" and Tamasheq jeɣeɣ meaning "to be brave".
Unknown meaning. Possibly a combination of Amanda and Zilda.

Possibly derived from name Amazili, (first?) used in the novel of Jean-François Marmontel "Les Incas, ou la destruction de l'Empire du Pérou" (1777), where it belongs to a Peruvian maiden. Most likely this name was artificially created to imitate exotic language and has no meaning.Later it was used by Giovanni Pacini in his work "Amazilia" (1826), where it belongs to a young Indian woman, and the scene takes place in Florida. Looks like he borrowed this unsual name from the novel of Marmontel. The daughter of the composer was also named Amazilia. She is depicted on famous painting "Horsewoman" (1832) by Karl Bryullov.

From the English word amazing, which is derived from Old English āmasian meaning "to confound". This name is chiefly used in countries that has English as their secondary language, such as African countries or the Philippines.
From the large jungle in South America.
From the French name of the Amazon River (see the place name Amazon). This name was used by French actor Vincent Cassel for his daughter born 2019 in Brazil.
From the given name Amazing combined with the ending yn (see lyn).

Means "mother" in Sanskrit. This is the name of a princess of the Kashi kingdom in the Hindu epic the Mahabharata. After being rejected by her beloved, Shalva, as well by as Bhishma, she is reborn as Shikhandi in her next life.
Georgian form of Ambakoum, which is the biblical Greek form of Habakkuk.
Armenian form of Ambakoum, which is the biblical Greek form of Habakkuk.
Combination of Hebrew עַם (ʿam) meaning "people, nation" with the name Bar.
Ambara - female form; Ambar, Ambaro - male form.Sanskrit names.Meaning: the sky.
Means "upwards-exalted" in Quenya. In Tolkien's Legendarium this is the mother-name of Amrod.
Means "russet-top". In Tolkien's Legendarium this is the mother-name of Amras.
From Indonesian ambar meaning "amber", ultimately from Arabic عنبر ('anbar), or Sanskrit अम्बर (ambara) meaning "garment, sky" combined with the feminine suffix -wati.
Elaboration of Amber with the suffix -ella
Elaboration of Amber with the suffix -ine
Elaborated form of Amberly, influenced by Leah.
Variant of Amberly or a combination of Amber and Lee (See also Amberlynn and Emberlee).
Transferred use of the surname Ambers.
Languedocian and Gascon form of Amalbert.
Old Norse short form of Arnbjǫrn.
A count who joined Wigalois (Gawain's son) ill a war against King Lion of Namur
Possibly means "dear mother" in Sanskrit. Ambika is a feminine personification of the Hindu goddess Durga and also another name for Parvati.

Continental Celtic name, derived from Celtic ambio "enclosure" (or ambi "around, about" or ambitio "rich") combined with Celtic rix "king." This was the name of one of the two kings of a Gaulish tribe called the Eburones, who was famous for revolting against Julius Caesar in 54 BC (which eventually led to the extermination of the Eburones).

A medieval form of Amalhard, from the Germanic elements amal meaning "vigor, bravery" and hard meaning "strong, hard". This name was borne by Amblard, Archbishop of Lyon from c. 957 to 978, and Amblard de Vienne, a member of the Knights Templar (Master of Poitiers from 1278 to 1288.
Means "sheaf of grain" or "bouquet of flowers" in Malagasy.

Possibly derived from the older form *Ἀναϝραχία meaning "escarpment", composed of ἀνά (ana) meaning "up, upwards" and ῥάχις (rhakhis) meaning "spine, ridge". In Greek mythology Ambracia was the daughter of Melaneus, son of Apollo and Oechalia. The ancient Greek city of Ambracia in Epirus was named after her.

The history of the name "Ambransh" is none. its is the name that got deprived when two lovely parents of his decided to combine their names, Amber and Ansh, and ambransh was created. It is the only name in the world
Borne by South African racing driver Ambraüsus "Brausch" Niemann.
Variant of Ambria, or in some cases possibly a blending of Ambre and Andrea 2.
Means "amber-scented, good-scented" from the adjectival suffix -een meaning "associated with" or "related to" (as in Mehreen), or possibly a derivative of Sanskrit अम्बर (ambara) meaning "sky".
Meaning unknown, possibly a rhyming variant of Cambrie.

Allegedly means "energy of God" in Hebrew. In Jewish and Christian mythology, this is the name of an angel associated with the zodiacal sign of Gemini and the month of May. It was found engraved on a Hebrew amulet for warding off evil.
Blend of Amber and Brielle, or a feminine form of Ambriel.
Elaboration of Ambre with the suffix -etta
Feminine form of Ambrogio and Ambrogiu.
Catalan, Gascon and Cremish Lombard form of Ambrose.
German, Luxembourgish, Romansh and Cornish form of Ambrose. This name was borne by Austrian composer Ambros Rieder (1771-1855).
Corsican and Sardinian form of Ambrosius (see Ambrose).
Niçard, Provençal, Languedocian and Gascon form of Ambrose.
Elaboration of Ambrosia. May be an elaboration of French Ambrosine, a feminization of Ambrose.

This is the latinized name of Merlin in the novel "The Last Legion" written by Valerio Massimo Manfredi (b. 1943), but also in the 2007 film based on the book. In the novel, his full name is Meridius Ambrosinus (while his original Gaelic name is Myrddin Emrys), but he is usually referred to as simply Ambrosinus.
Icelandic form of Ambrosius, used to refer to historical figures.
Croatian, Lithuanian and Serbian form of Ambrosia.
Blend of Amber and Aubrey. Also compare Ambria, Amberly, Embry, Cambrie and Cambree.
Transferred use of the surname Amburo.
Variant of Amber. A known bearer of this name is the American actress Ambyr Childers (b. 1988).
Old Danish short form of Ámundi and Old Norse form of Amadeus.
Possibly means "hope" or "looking up" in Sindarin. In 'Tolkien's Legendarium' this is the name of an elf, the King of Lórien. He was also called Malgalad.
Kabardian form of Amjad.A notable bearer was Amdzhed (Amjad) Jaimoukha (1964-2017), a Circassian author who specialised in Caucasian culture.

column3: 雨, 飴(Japanese Kanji)|あめ(Japanese Hiragana)|アメ(Japanese Katakana)
column12: From Japanese 雨 "rain" or 飴 "candy".
Possibly a short form of Amadea, or a variation of Amy or Amaia.
Derived from Greek ἀμηχανία (amechania) meaning "want of means, want of resources, helplessness". Amechania was the Greek personification of helplessness and want.
Romanian and Sicilian form of Amadeus.
Alternate transcription of Arabic أمين (see Amin), as well as the Urdu and Dhivehi form.
Alternate transcription of Arabic أمينة (see Amina), as well as the Urdu and Dhivehi form.
Alternate transcription of Arabic أمينة (see Amina).
Alternate transcription of Arabic أميرة (see Amira 1), as well as the Malay form.
Amefia means 'people's king' in Ewe. Amefia is a surname that has significant transferred usage to a given name.
Latinized form of Ameinokles. This was the name of a Greek shipwright from ancient Corinth, who lived in the 8th century BC.
Derived from Ancient Greek ἄμεινον (ameinon) meaning "better" and δωρον (doron) meaning "gift".
Derived from Greek ἀμείνων (ameinon) meaning "better" and κλέος (kleos) meaning "glory".
A recent coinage, either a Livonized form of the Sanskrit Ameyaa or the Basque Amaia.

From Japanese 雨 (ame) "rain" and 子 (ko) "child".One bearer of this name is Hello! Project lyricist Ameko Kodama (児玉 雨子) (1993-), though it's not likely that Ameko is her real name since, according to namaejiten.com, no one was given the same kanji as Kodama in 1993.This name is very rarely given to girls, if given at all.

column3: 天久神乙女王御神(Japanese Kanji)
column12: An alternative name for the Okinawan creator goddess Amanchuu. Her name is derived from 天 (ame) meaning "heavens, sky", 久 (kyu) meaning "a long time", 神 (shin) meaning "spirit, deity", 乙女 (otome) meaning "daughter, maiden, virgin", 王 (ō) meaning "king", 御 (here read as 'an'), an honourific particle, and 神 (kami) meaning "spirit, deity".
Originates from the albanian word, e embel, which means sweet.
Likely a variant transcription of Amelle.
Nephite record keeper (c. 130 BC) and also a seeker of Zeniff's people (c. 121 BC).

Combination of Amelia and Anne 1. This is the name of the protagonist of a number of children's books written by Constance Heward in the early 20th century. A notable bearer of this name is Ameliaranne Ekenasio, a New Zealand netball player.
Cousin of Danain the Red. With her lover, Ernant, she was captured by the giant T rudet. She was freed when Guiron the Courteous killed Trudet.
From the word ameliorate, which means "to make something better."
Combination of Amalia and Elisabeth recorded in the 17th century.

Medieval Dutch variant of Aemilius (see Emil).However, since other medieval variants (Amilius and Emilius) are more faithful to the original, it seems more likely that this name was originally a latinized short form of masculine Germanic names that contain the element amal meaning "unceasing, vigorous, brave" (in battle). Such names often became Amel- in Dutch, e.g. Amelryck. As such, it is certainly feasible that the latinized Germanic name Amelius became increasingly conflated with Aemilius and its variant Amilius over time, to the point that its Germanic origin was eventually forced into the background.Also compare Amelia, which has regularly been confused with Aemilia and Emilia.
Gallicized feminine form of Amel 2, ultimately from the Arabic Amal 1.

Formed from the personal name Ammi (which means "my people" from Hebrew עַם (ʿam) "people, nation, kinsman" and the suffix י (i) "my") and the title מַר (mar) meaning "master". This was the name of a Babylonian rabbi of the 5th and 6th centuries.
From the English word amen, uttered at the end of a prayer or hymn, meaning "so be it".

The name of a queen helped by Sir Gawain's son Wigalois in an Arthurian romance written by German knight Wirnt von Grafenberg in the early years of the 13th century. Its origin is uncertain; some scholars argue that it might be an adoption of Arabic Amina, while others theorize a derivation from Spanish ameno "delightful" (see Amoena).

In the TV show Lucifer, there is an Archangel called Amenadiel.The name is taken from 'Theurgia Goetia' by Johannes Trithemius and the the meaning of the name is apparently defined as "treaty" in that work.

Literally translated to "the water you shall drink" in Edo, from the proverb Amen na gha won ighi le se omwan rhae, meaning "the water you shall drink will surely come to be", implying that what is destined to be, will be.
The name of the love interest of Tancrède in Voltaire's tragedy Tancrède (1760). The name itself might be an elaboration of Amena.
Alternate transcription of Arabic أمين الله (see Amin Allah).
Alternate transcription of Arabic أمين الله (see Amin Allah) chiefly used in Tunisia.
Used for girls born on Wednesday.

From Egyptian jmn-m-ḥꜣt-ꜥnḫ meaning "(king) Amenemhat lives", derived from the name of the pharaoh Amenemhat combined with ankh "life". This was the name of a son of Amenemhat II, as well as of a Middle Kingdom vizier.
Means "Wish" in Maghrebi Arabic. This name is more commonly used in Tunisia
Means "she was given by Amun" in Egyptian.

Masculine form of Amenirdis, from Egyptian jmn-jr-dj-s(w) meaning "Amun has given him" or "Amun is the one who created him", derived from the name of the god Amun combined with jrj "to do, act, make; to create, bring into being" or "with respect to", dj "to give", and sw "he, him".

From Egyptian jmn-ms or jmn-ms.s meaning "born of Amun" or "fashioned by Amun", derived from the name of the god Amun combined with msj "to give birth to; to form, create, produce". This was the name of several ancient Egyptian figures, including a pharaoh and a vizier.

column3: 天宇受売, 天鈿女(Japanese Kanji)
column12: Japanese goddess of dawn, mirth and revelry. Her name is derived from 天 (ame) meaning "sky, heavens", 宇 (u) meaning "roof, eaves, house" or "the whole world", 受 (zu) meaning "accept" and 売 (me) meaning "sell", or 鈿 meaning "ornamental hairpen" and 女 (me) meaning "woman".

Likely a diminutive derived ultimately from Amun. Ameny Qemau was an Egyptian pharaoh of the 13th Dynasty during the Second Intermediate Period. He ruled for about two years over most of Egypt, from c.1793 BCE to c.1791 BCE. His name Ameny Qemau is a filiative nomina meaning "Ameny's son Qemau", meaning that his father was likely his predecessor, the pharaoh Sekhemkare Amenemhat V.
BeninEDO language of nigeria"river water"in another word peaceful
Means "going woman, walking woman" in Cheyenne.
According to some sources means "sacred path woman" or "Milky Way woman", or from the Cheyenne ame meaning "pemmican" or meo'o meaning "path, road, way".
Alternate transcription of Arabic أميرة (see Amira 1, as well as a Maranao, Maguindanao and Malay variant.
Alternate transcription of Arabic أميرة (see Amira 1), as well as a Maranao variant.
Means "velvet (on stag antlers), bark" in Greenlandic.
In Heinrich von dem Tiirlin's Diu Crone, a lady at Arthur's court. Her lover was a giant. Both Amercile and her sister Jare failed a chastity test involving an enchanted goblet
This was the name of two poets in Irish mythology.

column3: あめり(Japanese Hiragana)|雨李, 天理, 明萌里, 愛芽梨, 杏萌麗, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 亜 (a) meaning "second, Asia", 芽 (me) meaning "bud, sprout, shoot" combined with 理 (ri) meaning "reason, logic". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: アメリア(Japanese Katakana)|あめりあ(Japanese Hiragana)|阿芽莉阿, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: Of uncertain origin and meaning. Current theories include a feminine form of Old French Amauri (see Amaury).
From the word American, meaning "an citizen of America".
Variant of America, or from the word americana meaning "things associated with America".
Late medieval variant of Ameria. It was revived in the 1800s.Its modern-day usage might in part be inspired by the masculine name Amery.
Diminutive of Amerigo, as -otto is an Italian masculine diminutive suffix.
Medieval Italian diminutive of Amerigo, as -uccio is an Italian masculine diminutive suffix.
Meaning uncertain, probably of Arabic origin.
Possibly a variant of Amaris or America.
From the Sanskrit जिति (jiti) meaning "victory, conquering".
Means "worn-out cover made of skin" in Greenlandic.
Transferred use of the surname Ames.
Amesemi was goddess of the ancient Kingdom of Kush, and wife of the god Apedemak.

Ionic Greek variant of Άμαστρις (Amāstris), the Hellenized form of an Old Persian name, perhaps from a hypothetic name like *Amāstrī- (composed of the elements *ama- "strength, strong" and *strī- "woman"). It could be connected to the biblical name Esther, both perhaps derived from the Akkadian Ummu-Ishtar "Ishtar is (my) mother" (or Ammu-Ishtar). Alternatively it could be derived from an Old Persian word meaning "friend". It was borne by the wife of Xerxes and mother of Artaxerxes.
Uncertain etymology. This was the name of one of the fifty (or fifty-one) grandsons of Thespius fathered by Heracles in Greek mythology, his mother being Eone.
Crimean Tatar and Uyghur form of Ahmad.
Means "a child born after father's death" in Ewe.
Combination of Amet and the Mongolian title хан (khan) meaning "leader, ruler, commander".
Possibly from the name of the purple-orange crystal, which is a blend of the words amethyst (see Amethyst) and citrine.
Feminine form of Ametz. This is also the name of a chapel dedicated to the Virgin Mary at Laranga.
Alternate transcription of Arabic عامر (see Aamir 1) chiefly used in North Africa.
Variant of Amorfina. A bearer of this name was Ameurfina Melencio-Herrera, a Filipino lawyer who served as an Associate Justice of the Philippine Supreme Court from 1979 to 1992.
Means "people are more valuable than material things" in Ewe.
Means "immeasurable, boundless, limitless" in Sanskrit, composed of अ (a) "not" and मेय (meya) "measurable". In Hinduism this word is used as an epithet for gods such as Ganesha.
Derived from Nahuatl ameyalli meaning "spring" and xochitl meaning "flower".
Variant of Meziane (chiefly Algerian and Moroccan).
Meaning "The one who helps" or "The helper."
Bulgarian, Russian and Ukrainian form of Amphiaraos.
Modern Greek form of Amphilochios. A notable bearer of this name is the Greek saint Amfilochios of Patmos (1889-1970), whose name is usually written as Amphilochios in non-Greek sources.
Russian and Ukrainian form of Amphilochios.
Possibly a variant of Arnfrid (f) and Arnfred (m).
Means "peaceful, calm" in Mongolian and Buryat.
Means "peaceful hero" in Mongolian, from амгалан (amgalan) meaning "peace, calm" and баатар (baatar) meaning "hero".
Means "peaceful celebration, peaceful joy" in Mongolian, from амгалан (amgalan) meaning "peace, calm" and баяр (bayar) meaning "joy".
Means "peaceful power" in Mongolian, from амгалан (amgalan) meaning "peace, calm" and төр (tör) meaning "state, government" or "power, authority".
Derived from Old Norse ámr "black, loathsome, dark" and garðr "enclosure, protection". This is the name of a giantess in Norse mythology.
Borne by an early king of Munster, and an early king of Connacht. Can be anglicized as Auley or Awley.
Amhara is the name of an Ethiopian tribe. It is also used as a female name, commonly mistaken for Amara.
Transferred use of the surname Amherst.
From Sino-Korean 雅 (a) meaning "elegant" combined with 美 (mi) meaning "beauty". This name can be formed using other hanja combinations as well.
Latinization of Amy via the variant Amya.
Either a merged form of Amy and Mariah or a variant of Amia
Spanish form of Ammiana. Also compare the masculine counterpart Amiano.
Spanish and Portuguese form of Ammianus.
Gascon and Languedocian form of Amicus as well as a direct adoption of Gascon amic "friend".
Means "friendship" in Latin. Amicitia was the Roman goddess of friendship and affection. Her Greek equivalent is Philotes.
Late Latin name meaning "friendly, welcome" from amicus meaning "friendly, amicable" and "welcome, pleasing." Compare with Amice and Ames.

column12: Padmé Amidala Naberrie is a fictional character in the Star Wars franchise.
Means "my people are righteous, my nation is just" in Hebrew.
Amidas disputes his brother Bracidas over found treasure in Book 5, Canto 4 of "The Faerie Queene" by Edmund Spenser.

A variant of Amite, the mother of Galahad according to the Vulgate Lancelot.The daughter of King Pelles, she was one of the most beautiful maidens in Britain. Although called “Amite,” her true name was Helizabel. In later stories, her name is changed to Elaine.

A variant of Amite, the mother of Galahad according to the Vulgate Lancelot.The daughter of King Pelles, she was one of the most beautiful maidens in Britain. Although called “Amite,” her true name was Helizabel. In later stories, her name is changed to Elaine.
Means "my generation of people" in Hebrew.
Derived from Old French amie "(female) friend; (female) lover", ultimately from Latin amica.
Variant of Ammiel. Occurs in the Book of Numbers 13:12: Amiel, who represented the tribe of Dan, was one of the twelve spies sent out by Moses to survey the land of Canaan.
Gascon form of Amelia as well as a feminine form of Amiel.
Malay and Indonesian form of Amir 1.
Means "my nation is my support" in Hebrew.
Means "He/she has a skinny leg" in Bandial.
Form of Ammiel used in the Latin Old Testament.
Variant of Amy popularized by American singer Amii Stewart (1956-).
Croatian, Macedonian and Serbian form of Ammianus.
Derived from Latin amicus "friend" (compare Amicus and Amic).

column3: あみか(Japanese Hiragana)|あみ加(Kanji/Hiragana)|亞魅花, 明珠歌, 安望河, 愛未可, 空弥架, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 亜 (a) meaning "second, Asia", 美 (mi) meaning "beautiful" combined with 香 (ka) meaning "fragrance". Other kanji combinations are possible.
Modern Hebrew name meaning "my people have risen up, my people rise", derived from the roots עַם (ʿam) meaning "people, nation, kinsman" and קוּם (qum) meaning "to raise".
Possibly a diminutive of Amiran and Amirindo.

From the town of Amil in Galicia, originated as a possesive form of the Germanic name Alamirus, from the elements alls "all" and mers "famous". Nowadays it is a devotional title for the virgin Mary, Nosa Señora dos Milagres de Amil.

The etymology of Amilah can be traced back to the Arabic word “amal,” which means “hope” or “expectation.” The addition of the suffix “-ah” adds a feminine touch to the name, making it a particularly fitting choice for girls.But the linguistic roots of Amilah go even deeper. It is not just a name, but a reflection of the rich Arabic language and its cultural heritage. The Arabic language is known for its poetic beauty and lyrical melodies, and Amilah captures that essence perfectly. It is a name that carries the weight of centuries of history and tradition.Furthermore, linguistically, Amilah is classified as a name with Arabic roots and is widely used in Islamic cultures. It carries a sense of spirituality and connection to the Arabic language, making it resonate deeply with those who appreciate its significance.
In Basque mythology, Amilamia is a benevolent being who helps those in need.She is known to sit by the mountain brooks combing her hair.
Old English form of Hamilcar, of historical usage, Hamilcar Barca, father of Hannibal.
A king slain by Tristan. He made frequent raids on Emperor Donisus of Saxony, who sent for Tristan (then the king of Spain) for assistance.
German feminine form of Aemilius (see Emil). Compare Emilie and Ämilia.
From Spanish 'a' + 'mi' + 'linda', directly translated as "to my pretty." It may also be a combination of Spanish 'amigo' and 'linda,' meaning "pretty friend."
From the English phrase a million.
Amilna Estêvão is an Angolan model.
Means "servant woman", deriving from the Akkadian element amtu ("woman servant").
Modern variant of Amelia. In popular culture, this is the name of a Resistance general from Star Wars: The Last Jedi.
