Contracted form of Apollodoros, Apollodotos, Apollonios and similar masculine Greek names. Also compare Apollas and the Late Greek verb ἀπόλλω (apollo) meaning "to destroy".Apollos was a 1st century Alexandrian Jewish Christian mentioned several times in the New Testament. A contemporary of Paul the Apostle, he played an important role in the early development of the churches of Ephesus and Corinth.

The Greek name for Abaddon, Hebrew for “The destroyer” or “Place of destruction”.In the Hebrew scriptures, Abaddon is a place – the realm of the unhappy dead or a place of lost souls. In Christian apocalyptic theology, Abaddon was seen as the angel of death, or even the Antichrist or Satan.
Spanish and Galician form of Apollodorus.
Form of Apollon (see Apollo) in various languages.
Coined by Sabino Arana Goiri and Koldo Elizalde as a Basque equivalent of Apolonia and Apollonie.

Form of Apolon with the Georgian nominative suffix -ი (-i). It is only used in Georgian when the name is written stand-alone.There are probably also instances where this name is the Georgian form of Apollonios.
Croatian and Serbian form of Apollonius.
Spanish and Galician form of Apollonius.
Esperanto form of Apollo via Apollon.
Serbian name for the apostle Apollos.

Origin- Iteso people of eastern Uganda and Western Kenya, from the Ateso language, a derivative of the Teso-Turkana language and eastern Nilotic culture.Opolot is the male version, with the same meaning of being a "just and fair leader, and someone who is progressive".

From Ἄποφις (Ápophis), the Greek form of Egyptian ꜥꜣpp (reconstructed as Apap) altered by Greek ὄφις (ophis) meaning "serpent, snake". The original form may be related to ꜣpp "to slither". This was the name of the Egyptian deity of chaos and darkness who attempted to swallow the sun every night, usually depicted as a massive serpent.
Apor was a Hungarian tribal chieftain, who, according to the 'Illuminated Chronicle', led a campaign against the Byzantine Empire in 959. He was the ancestor of the gens Apor.

Means "difficulty, impossibility" in Ancient Greek, from ἄπορος (aporos) meaning "impassable, without passage", i.e. "having no way in, out, or through" (itself composed of the negative prefix α (a) and πόρος (poros) "means of passing a river, ford, ferry" as well as "way or means of achieving, accomplishing, discovering"). In Greek mythology, Aporia was the personification of difficulty, perplexity and powerlessness. Her Roman name was Egestas.

column3: 吾歩路, 愛星路, 明歩, etc.(Japanese Kanji)|あぽろ(Japanese Hiragana)|アポロ(Japanese Katakana)
column12: Japanese borrowing of Apollo.It can also be written in kanji, combining an a kanji, like 吾, a phonetic kanji which can otherwise refer to the formal/literary 1st person pronoun, 愛 meaning "love, affection" or 明 meaning "bright," a po kanji (usually shifted from ho, in full or in part), such as 歩 meaning "step" or 星 meaning "star," and, usually, a ro kanji, e.g. 路 meaning "road, path; way."This name is extremely rare.

Modern Greek diminutive of Apostolis and Apostolos, as it contains the modern Greek diminutive suffix -άκης (-akis). This name is typically only used informally, meaning: it does not appear on birth certificates.
Means "water foam" in Classical Nahuatl, from the words ātl ("water") and pozōnallōtl ("foam"). This is one of the names of the Aztec goddess Chalchiuhtlicue.
Perhaps an anglicized form of Apolline; also compare Appoline.
Anatolian god which possibly means "father lion" or "father light". A Theory states that Appaliunas can be equated with Apollo

Aphian (Apphian, Apian, Appian, Amphianus, Amphian; Amfiano in Spanish and Italian) is venerated as a martyr by the Catholic Church and by the Eastern Orthodox Church. He is said to have died during the persecutions of the Emperor Galerius on April 2 in or around the year 305.
Anglicized form of Appianus, a Roman agnomen that was derived from Appius. Appian of Alexandria was a 1st- and 2nd-century Greek historian and writer in Rome.
Hellenized form of Appianus (see Appian), as well as the Armenian form.

Derivative of Appius, or possibly means "of Appia" in Latin (Appia being a town in Phrygia Major). In Roman mythology, Appias was a naiad of the Appian Well or fountain of Aqua Appia, whose waters gushed forth near the Temple of Venus Genetrix in the Forum of Iulius Caesar, Rome.

Diminutive of Albert and Albertus. A notable bearer of this name was the Dutch author Appie Baantjer (1923-2010), who was well-known for his detective fiction.In the Netherlands, the premium supermarket chain Albert Heijn (named after its late founder) is colloquially referred to as (the) Appie.
From the name of an alcoholic beverage made by freeze-distilling (or "jacking") apple cider. This is the name of a character in the series My Little Pony: Friendship is Magic.
Means "apple of Ann". Appleofann Kneebone (born Phillips) was likely named after her paternal grandmother Ann Lewis. Referring to the English phrase "apple of my eye".
Transferred use of the surname Appleton.
Perhaps form of Yevpraksiya. Used in War and Peace by Lev Tolstoy.
French form of Apraksina used in War and Peace by Lev Tolstoy.

The name of a commander of the Sasanian army against the invading Arab-Muslim forces during the reign of Yazdegerd III (632-651 CE). After the Sasanian defeat, she continued to the resistance, fighting a guerilla war until she was killed in battle.

Georgian sources state that this name is of Persian origin and means "angry, wrathful" and "ferocious, truculent". This indicates that Aprasion might be the Georgian form of افراسیاب (Afrasiyab) (see Afrasiab), probably via its archaic Georgian form აფრასიობ (Aprasiob) or აფრასიობი (Aprasiobi).A notable bearer of this name was the Georgian revolutionary Aprasion Merkviladze (1871-1907).
From Russian апрель (aprel'), meaning "April", referring to Lenin's month of birth and/or April Theses, one of Lenin's works.
Means "well done!, good job!" in Armenian.
From Persian ابریشم (abrīsham) meaning "silk". This is a cognate of Persian Abrisham.
From the name of the month of April.
From the name of the month of April, usually used as a given name for a girl born in April.
From the English word "apricity" meaning "the warmth of the sun in winter".
Georgian form of Afrīdōn (also found spelled as Afrīdūn), which is the arabized form of the Persian name Fereydūn (see Fereydoun). Also compare the Middle Persian form of Fereydūn, which is Frēdōn.

Combination of the name Aprilian and Persian شاه (shāh) meaning "king".
From the name of the month of April.
Derived from Hungarian április "(month of) April". This coinage was possibly inspired by the English name April.
Combination of April and the suffix -Lyn
From the name of the month of April, usually used as a given name for a girl born in April.
Feminine form of Apronius. In Latin this was also a name for black bryony (species Tamus communis), a medicinal plant. The 6th-century saint Apronia was a sister of Saint Aprus, Bishop of Toul.
Anglicized and English form of Apronianus.
Spanish, Italian, and Portuguese form of Apronianus.
Cognomen derived from the family name Apronius.
A Roman family name possibly derived from the cognomen aper "wild boar".
Agnomen variant of Aper. Saint Aprus was the seventh bishop of Toul. He has been considered a saint in Toul since the 10th century.
Latinized form of Greek Απρουσία (Aprousia), possibly derived from Greek α (a), a negative prefix, combined with προύση (prouse) "rain".
Latinized form of Apsandros. This name was borne by an eponymous archon of Athens, who lived in the 7th century BC.
Italian and Spanish form of Apsander.
Derived from Ancient Greek ἅπτω (apto) meaning "to join, fasten, touch, grasp" or "to kindle, set on fire" combined with ἀνδρός (andros) meaning "of a man".
Meaning unknown. Apsat was the god of birds in Svan (a subgroup of the Georgian people) mythology.

Probably derived from Ancient Greek ἀψεφής (apsephes) meaning "without care, carefree", composed of the negative prefix ἀ (a) and ψέφω (psepho) meaning "worry, care". Alternatively, the second element could be the related word ψέφας (psephas) meaning "gloom, darkness". Apsephion was the name of an eponymous archon of Athens, who lived in the 5th century BC.

Means "truthful, without deceit, sincere" in Ancient Greek, composed of the negative prefix ἀ (a) combined with ψευδής (pseudes) meaning "lying, false, untrue". In Greek mythology, Apseudes was one of the fifty Nereids, sea-nymph daughters of Nereus and the Oceanid Doris. As an Ancient Greek given name, this name was exclusively masculine.

Georgian form of Afshin. This name is mostly used in the Georgian highlands.In Georgian literature, Apshina is the name of the eponymous character of the epic poem Gogotur and Apshina (1887) written by the Georgian poet and writer Vazha-Pshavela (1861-1915).
Means "angel" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit अप्सरस् (apsaras).
Etymology uncertain, possibly from аԥсуа (apswa) meaning "Abkhaz".
Variant of Abtet recorded in the 17th and 19th centuries in East Frisia.
Chechen and Ingush form of Abu.
Possibly from the Apulia region of modern day Italy.
Spanish form of Apuleius. This is borne by Colombian writer Plinio Apuleyo Mendoza (1932-).
Etruscan form of Apollo. This is an epithet of the Etruscan fire god Śuri.
Means "the sheath of the young leaf" or "chaff, husk" in Samoan.
Rare Greenlandic name meaning "dear little snow."Combination of Aput ("snow") and -nnguaq ("sweet," "little," "dear").Related names are Aput, Aputsiaq and Aputsiannguaq.
Greenlandic name meaning "snow crystal" with the combination of Aput and suffix -tsiaq "beautiful", "fair", "fairly good", "precious", "sweet", "fair-sized", "nice", "good", "handsome".
Means "dear little snow crystal" in Greenlandic, from a combination of Aputsiaĸ and suffix -nnguaq "sweet", "dear", "little".
Derived from Chuukese a meaning "to be, to make" combined with pwete, from pwetete "soft".
From the Bashkir aҡ (aq) meaning "white, light, pure" and Persian بانو (banu)# meaning "lady".
Means "white snow leopard" in Tatar, from ак (ak) meaning "white" combined with барс (bars) meaning "snow leopard".
From the Bashkir aҡ (aq) meaning "white, light, pure" and feminine name element бикә (bikä).
Means "white neck" or "white throat" in Karachay-Balkar.
Derived from aqcha meaning "money" and gul meaning "flower, rose".
Means "holier" in Arabic, the elative form of قديس (qiddīs) meaning "holy, saintly".
Means "successor" in Arabic, from the word عَاقَبَ (aqaba) meaning "to follow".
Variant of Aĸigssiaĸ. This is the name of the main character in one of Greenland's best known myths.
Alternate transcription of Arabic عقيلة or عاقلة (see Aqila), as well as the usual Malay form.
From the name of feast given in honour of a newborn baby, alternatively from the Uzbek aqiq meaning "carnelian" or "red, crimson".
Means "little ptarmigan chick", derived from Greenlandic aqisseq "rock ptarmigan" (cf. Aqisseq) combined with a diminutive suffix.
From the Kazakh ақ (aq) meaning "white" or "pure" and жан (jan) meaning "soul".
From the Kazakh ақ (aq) meaning “white” or "pure" and күміс (kümis) meaning “silver”.
Derived from aql meaning "mind, intelligence" and "smarts, common sense, advise" and oy meaning "moon".
Younger form of Arĸaluk. A notable bearer is Aqqaluk Lynge (1947-), a Greenlandic politician, poet, and activist.
Alternate transcription of Arabic أقصى or Urdu اقصٰی (see Aqsa).
Possibly from the Kazakh ақсары (aqsarı) meaning "light yellow".
Means "white throat" in Karachay-Balkar. This was the name of a character in the love poems of Ismail Semenov.
From Bashkir аҡ (aq) meaning "white, bright, pure" and туташ (tutaš) meaning "girl".
Derived from Latin aqua meaning "water". It is also used in English in reference to a bluish-green colour.
Means "tender water". A notable bearer was the female sea serpent from the Disney Junior show 'Sofia the First'.
Middle name of singer Doda (Dorota Rabczewska).
Meaning unknown. According to legend, the name of a former Angolan princess and general, who commanded an army of 10,000 men to fight the invasion of her kingdom in the Congo.
Combination of the phonetic elements a and quan.
Combination of the phonetic elements a, qua, nee and sha. Also compare Quanisha and Acquanetta.
Combination of Latin aqua meaning "water" and French reine meaning "queen". This is the name of a mermaid queen in L. Frank Baum's novel ''The Sea Fairies'' (1911).
Means "water-carrier" or "cup-carrier" in Latin. This is a constellation in the zodiac, between Capricornus and Pisces.
One of the princesses in Disney's "The Little Mermaid." The name probably comes from aqua, water.
Spanish, Portuguese and Catalan form of Achelois.
Spanish form of Achaios via Achaeus.
Possibly derived from Nahuatl atl "water" and quetzalli "quetzal feather, something precious". Alternately, may derive from ahquetzalli, meaning "irrigation ditch" or "gruel".
Catalan and Portuguese form of Achaios via Achaeus.
Found on a list of demons.

Spanish form of Achilleus, the name of two early Christian saints, as well as a usurper of the Roman Empire (Aurelius Achilleus).Note, the legendary Greek hero from the Trojan War is known as Aquiles in Spanish.
Feminine form of Aquillius. This name was borne by Aquilia Severa, the second and fourth wife of Emperor Elagabalus.
French, German and Milanese Lombard form of Aquilinus.
Roman nomen gentile derived from Latin aquila "eagle" (see also Aquila). This name was borne by several consuls from ancient Rome.
Possibly derived from Latin aquila, meaning "eagle". Aquilo was the name of the Roman god of the north wind, equated with its Greek counterpart Boreas.
French form of Aquilo. In Roman mythology, Aquilo was the god of the north wind, equivalent to Boreas.
Derived from the surname Aquinas. Used in honor of saint Thomas Aquinas, used primarily by Catholics.

From Wampanoag Âhqunah meaning "the end of the island". This is also the name of a town on the island of Martha's Vineyard in Massachusetts. American actor Michael J. Fox gave this name to his daughter Aquinnah Kathleen born in 1995.
Transferred use of the surname Aquino. Likely in some cases it has been used as a given name in honour of the 13th-century saint Thomas Aquinas.
From ақыл (akyl) meaning "intelligance, intelect" combined with Persian زاده (zadeh) meaning "offspring"
Alternate transcription of Kazakh Ақжол (see Akzhol).
From ақ (ak) meaning "white" combined with Arabic ضياء (ḍiyāʾ) meaning "splendour, glow"
Sami name of unknown origin and meaning.
Variant of Aurora used sparingly in the 17th and 18th century.
Means "prayer, invocation" as well as "curse, imprecation, malediction" in Ancient Greek. This was the name of a goddess of vengence and destruction in Greek mythology, the personification of curses.

The name Araarsame is also rooted in Somali language and culture."Araar" – In Somali, "araar" refers to reconciliation, or making peace between people or groups. It's often used in the context of conflict resolution or bringing people together."Same" – This could come from the Somali word "samee," which means to do or make. It suggests an action or effort.Araarsame could roughly translate to "one who makes peace" or "a reconciler" — someone involved in settling disputes or fostering harmony.
Girl born on a Tuesday, in Akan. (Same as Abena)

Variant of Arabella.In medieval German literature, Arabel is the name of a character from the epic poem Willehalm (13th century) written by the German poet Wolfram von Eschenbach (died around 1220). She is the daughter of king Terramer and the wife of king Tybalt, who is wooed and won and eventually taken to wife by the protagonist Willehalm.In her case, the name might possibly be a reference to Arabia, as she and her family are all Saracens. This would also add more significance to the fact that she changed her name to Gyburc (see Gyburg) after converting to Christianity for Willehalm.
Form of Arabella in several languages.

The meaning and origin of the first element in this Germanic name is rather uncertain, and so there are various possibilities to the name's meaning. The most likely possibility is that the first element is derived from Proto-Germanic aran or arna "eagle" (ara in Gothic and arn in Old High German). However, it might also come from Old High German êra "honour, respect" (see Eraric) or from Old High German hari "army" (with reduction of the "h" - see Herbert). The second element in the name is derived from Old High German beraht "bright."

column3: 亜羅美(Japanese Kanji)|あらび(Japanese Hiragana)
column12: From Japanese 亜 (a), a phonetic character, combined with 羅 (ra), a phonetic character, combined with 美 (bi) meaning "beauty; beautiful".

Arabia (fl. 565) was the only recorded daughter of Byzantine Emperor Justin II (r. 565–578) and Empress Sophia. While mentioned in several primary sources, her name is only recorded in the Patria of Constantinople. The name is generally accepted as genuine. It appears to be a unique personal name, and Arabia seems to have been named by her great aunt, Empress Theodora, as a show of gratitude to Arab phylarch Arethas.
The son of Apollo by Babylonis.
Possibly means "to have chosen a portion ahead of another; to supplant" in Igbo.

Derived from either Tupi arasy "mother of day", itself derived from ara "day" and sy "mother; origin, source", and thus referring to the sun, or from Tupi aracê "sunrise, daybreak, morning". In some instances, however, it may also be a contracted form of Araceli.
Variant of Araci. A known bearer of this name was Aracy de Almeida (1914-1988), a Brazilian singer.

Latinized form of Greek Αρακυνθιας (Arakynthias), an epithet of the goddess Aphrodite meaning "of Arakynthos", Arakynthos or Aracynthus being a mountain upon which there was a temple dedicated to her. The place name itself is of uncertain etymology, probably of pre-Greek origin. For the second element, compare Κύνθος (Kynthos), found in other names of mountains (see Cynthia). The first element could be related to Ancient Greek ἀρά (ara) "prayer, vow, curse".
A name of an angel.-------------------------------------This name has some meanings: the first is "bronze" (written: ארד), and the second it's the name of a city in South Israel (written: ערד).
Alternate transcription of Hindi आराधना (see Aradhana).

Allegedly a Tuscan dialectical form of Erodiade. According to 'Aradia, or the Gospel of the Witches' (1899), a book composed by American folklorist Charles Leland, she was a goddess in regional Italian folklore, who gave the knowledge of witchcraft to women.
Ar-Adûnakhôr was the son of King Tar-Ardamin and the twentieth King of Númenor in .
From the name of a sacred hill in Mecca where pilgrims spend a day praying during the hajj.
MEANING - Unimpassioned, calm, a name of lord Shiva
MEANING - impassioned, calm, a name of goddess Durga

From J K Rowling's Harry Potter series, Aragog is the name of the giant spider that lives in the Forbidden Forest. He fears basilisks and is a great friend of Rubeus Hagrid, who rescued him when he was a child and cared for him. Aragog is well known for his contribution of the Chamber of Secrets in the second book.

The meaning and origin of the first element in this Germanic name is rather uncertain, and so there are various possibilities to the name's meaning. The most likely possibility is that the first element is derived from Proto-Germanic aran or arna "eagle" (ara in Gothic and arn in Old High German). However, it might also come from Old High German êra "honour, respect" (see Eraric) or from Old High German hari "army" (with reduction of the "h"). The second element in the name is derived from Old High German gund "war."

From Sanskrit अर्हत् (arhat) meaning "deserving, entitled to, worthy, venerable". This was the name of an 11th-century Burmese monk who helped to stabilize the presence of Theravada Buddhism in Southeast Asia.
Means "pathfinder", feminine word for chief, leader, one who leads the way. From ara meaning "path" and "to rise up" in Maori.
Name originally found on a Roman tombstone in Araba, Basque Country. Although the original namebearer was male, the name was revived as a unisex name at the end of the 20th century.
From the name of the valley of Araitz, located in Navarre.
Means "protection" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit आरक्ष (ārakṣa).
Means "high commander" in Quenya. In Tolkien's Legendarium, this is the original name of Argon, the youngest child of Fingolfin and Anairë. He dies shortly after arriving in Middle-earth.

Means "earth of God" or "land of God", derived from Aramaic אֲרַק (ʿăraq) meaning "earth, ground, land" and Hebrew אֵל (ʾel) meaning "God". The Book of Enoch names him as a fallen angel, one of the 200 Watchers who copulated with human women. Other sources hold him as a holy angel who guides human souls to judgment.

From the name of the Araluen Creek valley in southeastern Australia, which is said to mean "water lily" or "place of the water lilies" in the Walbunja language. It was borne by a short-lived daughter of the Australian poet Henry Kendall (1839-1882).

Variant of Aaralyn, or else a combination of the initial sound found in names such as Arabella, Ariel and Ariadne with the popular name suffix lyn (perhaps inspired by similar-sounding names Carolyn, Marilyn and Cherilyn).
Aramaneak was a legendary patriarch of Armenia. He was the son of Hayk, founder of the Armenian nation.

Used by Richard Lovelace for the titular shepherdess in Aramantha: A Pastorall, the final poem of his collection Lucasta (1649). It could be a variant of Araminta or perhaps an altered form of Amarantha.

Meaning unknown; possibly related to Persian ارمنی (Armani) "Armenian" or from Old Iranian *Rāma(n)-nī- "bringing peace" combined with the Armenian suffix -ակ (-ak). Aramanyak Haykazuni was a king of Armenia from 2026-1980 BCE. He was supposedly the son of Hayk, the legendary founder of Armenia.

column5: Air uh may uh or are uh may uh

column12: From Old Median *Rāmanīsah which meant "one who strives for peace" or "one who strives for joy" from Proto-Iranian *rāma- "joy, peace" and *ais-/*is- "to strive".
Derived from Persian آرام (ârâm) meaning "quiet, calm, tranquil"and the Turkish military title beg meaning "chieftain, master".
Diminutive of Guarani word ára meaning "sky, heavens".
Possibly derived from the Latin aramen, from aerāmen meaning "copper, bronze". As used in India, it's likely a variant of Paramita.

The King of Brittany in the time of Uther Pendragon.He was the overlord of Gannes, Benoic (Benwick), and surrounding lands, but King Claudas of Bourges refused to acknowledge him. Aramont went to war with Claudas, but Claudas drew on his allies from Gaul and managed to stalemate Aramont.Aramont then allied with Uther, and together the two kings smashed Claudas, turning his country into a wasteland. After Aramont’s death, Claudas returned and waged war on Benoic and Gannes.Aramont was also known as Hoel and might be identical with Hoel of Brittany. It is unclear whether he is identical with Faramon from the Tristan legends.

The meaning and origin of the first element in this Germanic name is rather uncertain, and so there are various possibilities to the name's meaning. The most likely possibility is that the first element is derived from Proto-Germanic aran or arna "eagle" (ara in Gothic and arn in Old High German). However, it might also come from Old High German êra "honour, respect" (see Eraric) or from Old High German hari "army" (with reduction of the "h"). The second element in the name is derived from Old High German mund "protection."

column3: 아란(Korean Hangul)|雅蘭, 娥蘭, etc.(Korean Hanja)
column12: Combination of an a hanja, like 雅 meaning "clean, pure" or 娥 meaning "pretty, lovely, beautiful," and a ran hanja, e.g. 蘭 meaning "orchid."

column3: アラン(Japanese Katakana)|あらん(Japanese Hiragana)|阿蘭, 安卵, 和蘭, 愛覧, 亜嵐, 愛藍, 愛欄, etc.(Japanese Kanji)|อรัญ(Thai)
column12: Japanese form of Alan. It can be spelled with Japanese 亜 or 亞 (a) meaning "second, Asia, sub-" or 阿 (a) meaning "nook, corner" combined with 蘭 (ran) meaning "orchid", 藍 (ran) meaning "indigo" or 卵 (ran) meaning "egg, ovum". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: 新夏, 新菜, etc.(Japanese Kanji)

column12: Avestan name that probably meant "she who speaks the injustice (to denounce it)", from arəna- "injustice" and ouuāč-ī "she who speaks". In Persian mythology this name belonged to a sister or daughter of King Jamshid. According to the 11th-century Shahnameh, she became a wife of Fereydoun and the mother of his youngest but wisest and noblest son: Iraj.
Arancia is the Italian word for orange (the fruit, not the color)
The second element is from dipa "light, lamp". The first is claimed by some to mean "forest".
This name is Christian in origin. It is derived from Serbo-Croatian arhanđel or arhanđeo "archangel", which is ultimately derived from Greek archangelos "chief angel".

Spanish origin meaning a flat discus or a washer. In Serbian origin, Arandel meaning chief angel or archangel so adding the A in Arandel to form Arandela gives it a feminine characteristic meaning Female Archangel.
"The first little light of the day, the tiny one."

In La Tavola Ritonda, a Gaulish king who, along with a king named Brandino, invaded and conquered Benoic (Benwick) – the land of Lancelot’s father Ban.Arandus and Brandino replace Claudas, named as Benoic’s destroyers in most other versions.
Variant of Arna popularized by folktales of the Basque Mountains.
Modern invented name taken from Araneus, a genus of orb-weaving spiders. Aranea is a character in Charlotte's Web.
Means "sun, mother, wood used for kindling fire by attrition, pain, being fitted or turning round".

The Quenya name Aranwë means "Kingly" or "Noble" from ara ("noble") and aran ("king"). The suffix -wë occurs in many names, though it is not exclusively masculine.Aranwë was an Elf of Gondolin and the father of Voronwë. His son stated that he was from the House of Fingolfin, suggesting that Aranwë might have been a noble elf in Gondolin.
Directly taken from Hungarian arany "gold; golden".
From Sanskrit अरण्य (araṇya) meaning "forest, wilderness". It is solely feminine in Thailand while it is unisex (typically masculine) as a Bengali name.

Aranyani (romanized: Araṇyānī, lit. 'forest') is the goddess of forests and the wild animals that dwell within them in Hinduism.Aranyani has the distinction of having one of the most descriptive hymns in the Rigveda dedicated to her. The Aranyani Suktam (Hymn 146 in the 10th mandala of the Rigveda) describes her as being elusive, fond of quiet glades in the jungle, and fearless of remote places. In the hymn, the supplicant entreats her to explain how she wanders so far from the fringe of civilisation without becoming afraid or lonely. She wears anklets with bells, and though seldom seen, she can be heard by the tinkling of her anklets. She is also described as a dancer. Her ability to feed both man and animals though she 'tills no lands' is what the supplicant finds most marvellous. The hymn is repeated in Taittiriya Brahmana and interpreted by the commentator of that work.
Originally a diminutive of Arany, now used as a given name in its own right.
Directly taken from Hungarian aranyos "sweet, lovable, cute" as well as a diminutive of Arany now used as a given name in its own right.
From Tagalog araw meaning "sun". This is the name of an ancient Tagalog god of the sun.
Means "sensor of the universe" in Guaraní.
The name of a Guanche man from La Palma who was christened in Seville.

column3: アララ(Japanese Katakana)|亜羅羅, 愛麗玲, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 亜 (a) meaning "second, Asia" or 愛 (a) meaning "love, affection", 羅 (ra) meaning "gauze, thin silk" or 麗 (ra) meaning "lovely, beautiful, graceful, resplendent" combined with 羅 (ra) meaning "gauze, thin silk" or 玲 (ra) meaning "sound of jewels". Other kanji combinations are possible.
Means "eye of the universe" in Guarani.
In Kurdish and Persian it means “equal”, “balanced”. The word Aras commonly refers to the Aras River, which flows through Turkey, Armenia, Iran and Azerbaijan.

column3: アラシ(Japanese Katakana)|あらし(Japanese Hiragana)|嵐, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 嵐 (arashi) meaning "storm". Other spellings are possible.

It means “decorated” or “adorned” in Persian/Farsi. This is how the name is pronounced in the Kabuli form of Persian/Farsi (the main standard dialect of Persian/Farsi in Afghanistan), whereas this would be pronounced as Arasteh in the Tehrani form of Persian/Farsi (the main standard dialect of Persian/Farsi in Iran).
Alternate transcription of Persian ارسطو (see Arastoo).
Means "mother of the universe" in Guaraní. The name of the wife of Tupa, the supreme god of Guaraní myth.

column3: 新仁, 新二, 新虹, 新荷(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From 新 (arata) meaning “fresh, new”, combined with 仁 (ni) meaning “benevolence, compassion”, 二 (ni) meaning “two”, 虹 (ni) meaning “rainbow”, or 荷 (ni) meaning “burden, load”.

Arathorn II is a fictional character from J. R. R. Tolkien's Middle-earth universe. He is the fifteenth of the Chieftains of the DÃºnedain, and the father of Aragorn II, one of the major characters in The Lord of the Rings.

column3: 亜羅斗, 嵐蘭人, 新人, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 亜 (a) meaning "second, Asia", 嵐 (a) meaning "storm, tempest" or 新 (ara) meaning "new", 羅 (ra) meaning "gauze, thin silk" or 蘭 (ra) meaning "orchid" combined with 斗 (to), which refers to a Chinese constellation or 人 (to) meaning "person". Other kanji combinations are possible.
Means "plowman" in Latin. This was the name of a sixth-century Christian poet from Italy.
Derived from Greek ἀρατός (aratos) meaning both "prayed for, desirable" and "prayed against, accursed".
Latinized form of Aratos. Aratus of Soli (315-240) was an Ancient Greek didactic poet known for his major extant work Phenomena.
Derived from aratz, meaning "pure", and zuri, meaning "white".It's also the name of a town in the Oltza Zendea municipality in Navarre.

Araunah was a Jebusite who was mentioned in the Second Book of Samuel who owned the threshing floor on the summit of Mount Moriah that David purchased and used as the site for assembling an altar to God. The First Book of Chronicles, a later text, renders his name as Ornan.

The name of a local water god, possibly derived from Gaulish ar-aus(i)o- meaning "temple, cheek", from Proto-Celtic *far-aws(y)o- literally meaning "in front of the ear". Very little is known about this deity, other than the town of Orange (or Auranja) being named after them.
Alternate transcription of Hindi आरव (see Aarav).

Modern Hebrew name meaning both "willow tree" and "desert" or "savanna, prairie". Traditionally the ערבה (aravah), a leafy willow branch, is used in a waving ceremony during the Jewish holiday of Sukkot. In Israel the name also refers to a geographical plain near the Jordan, appearing in Deuteronomy 3, 17 as Arabah. (Interestingly, the Hebrew word arabha "desert" may ultimately relate to English Arab.)
Malayalam and Tamil form of Aravind.
From the place name Aravis. This is the name of a main character in C.S. Lewis' 'The Horse and his Boy'.
Arawa is a variety of "flax" (Phormium tenax) native to New Zealand. Te Arawa is a historic canoe and confederation of Māori tribes.
Uncertain etymology, probably derived from an Ancient Armenian name.
From Thai อารย (araya) meaning "good, noble, righteous", ultimately from Sanskrit आर्य (ārya).
An invented name influenced by Aria 1.

From Japanese 粗 (ara) meaning "defect,flaw,roughness,coarsely" combined with and 代 (tai, dai, ka.eru, ka.waru, kawa.ru, -gawa.ri, -ga.wari, shiro, yo) meaning "age, change, generation, period, replace, substitute" or 世 (se, sei, sou, sanjuu, yo) meaning "generation, public, society, world". Other kanji or combinations of kanji can also form this name.
From the name of the mountain in the Kurdistan region.
Recorded in Lithuania on a Muslim Tatar female in the 16th-century.
Apparently means "light of God" or "moon of God" in Hebrew. This is the name of a fallen angel who was cast out of heaven by God for having relations with earthly women.
king, portmanteau of "oro anbaab" ("my father, the king")

Meaning uncertain, allegedly derived from Arabic الباز (al-Baz) meaning "the falcon" (from بَاز (bāz) "hawk, falcon" prefixed with the Arabic definite article). This name is borne by Indian actor Arbaaz Khan (1967-).
Means "lords, masters" in Arabic, the plural of رب (rabb) meaning "lord, master".
Italian form of Arbaces. It was used for the title character of Arbace (1781), an opera seria by Francesco Bianchi.
Hellenized form of Old Persian *Arbakah, derived from *arbah meaning "young, youthful" and the nominal suffix 𐎣 (-ka).
Hellenized form of Old Median *Arabazuka, meaning "having wild arms".

Medieval Basque name linked to Mariarbel.It is thought to have started as a short form of said Mariarbel and to then have developed a life of its own (including several elaborated forms).It has been recorded from the 1500s onwards.
Variant of Arbën, with adjectival suffix -or.
Gheg Albanian feminine form of Arbën by way of adding the adjectival suffix -ore.

The name represents the demonym of Albania as it used to be called in Medieval times, "Arberi/a". It ultimately goes back to the Albanian tribal name Arbër/Arbëreshë.Equivalently, the name could be the toponym of the Illyrian tribe of "Abri" who inhabited part of modern day Albania.The name is popularly held to be derived from Albanian arë "field; cropland; croft".
Tosk Albanian feminine form of Arbër by way of adding the adjectival suffix -ore.
Derived from Chechen Ӏаьрбий (arbiy) or Ingush Ӏарбий (arbiy) both meaning "Arab".
From the name of prince Arbidel, a character in folk tales from the town of Villayón, Asturias.
Meaning unknown, perhaps a diminutive of Archibald.
Bengali and Nepali variant of Aravind.
Assamese, Bengali and Nepali variant of Aravind.
Derived from the Old Norse elements ár, meaning either "year; plenty, abundance", "early", or "messenger", and bjartr meaning "bright".

Derived from Gothic 𐌰𐍂𐌱𐌹 (arbi) meaning "heritage, inheritance" combined with Old High German gast meaning "guest, stranger."Notable bearers of this name include the 4th-century Roman military officer Arbogast (of Frankish descent) and saint Arbogast of Strasbourg (7th century).

Middle English (also denoting a lawn or flower bed) from Old French erbier, from erbe ‘grass, herb’, from Latin herba. The phonetic change to ar- (common in words having er- before a consonant) was assisted by association with Latin arbor ‘tree’.

Grandson of Brutus, son of Albanact, and brother of Embrunt and Dombart.He became king of the Savage Realm and ruled Castle Sauf.He married the lady Vagés, the companion of a giant he defeated. Arbrun’s sons were Brun and Silhaut.

From the name of trailing arbutus (species Epigaea repens), a fragrant flowering plant also known as the mayflower. It is the state flower of Massachusetts in the United States, as well as the official provincial flower of Nova Scotia in Canada.

Stemming from the Old Turkic root arı- or arun- meaning "pure, clean, untainted, free from blemish". It symbolizes crystal clarity, spiritual innocence, and the essence of a soul free from burdens. It emphasizes an unblemished and noble character.
Catalan and Romanian form of Arkadios.
French form of Arcadia. It was borne by Arcadie Claret (1826-1897), a mistress of King Leopold I of Belgium.

Possibly a variant of Archana or from the English word "arcana" meaning "specialized knowledge that is mysterious to the uninitiated; mysteries or deep sercrets; elixirs". From the Latin arcanum 'secret'.
Relational name meaning cash, treasury, treasurer.

Means "Arcadian" in Ancient Greek, possibly related to ἄρκτος (arktos) meaning "bear". In Greek mythology this was the name of an eponymous king of Arcadia, a son of Zeus and Callisto. In some variants of myth, Arcas is transformed into the constellation Boötes when his mother becomes Ursa Major.
Uncertain etymology, probably a hellenised form of an Ancient Iranian name. This was the name of a Pontic prince with Persian and Macedonian Greek ancestry.
Son of the King of Saxony and the leader of Mordred’s first division, apparently the Saxon division, in the last battle.
Arcee is a character in the Transformers franchise. She is usually pink or blue in color.
Derived from Ancient Greek ἀρκέω (arkeo) meaning "to ward off, defend, assist" or "to satisfy, suffice". In Greek mythology, Arceisius was the son of either Zeus or Cephalus, and king in Ithaca.
The King of Trebes slain by Sir Laris during Arthur’s war against Thereus of Rome.
Variant of Araceli with the spelling more or less phonetical in English nature.

Possibly derived from Ancient Greek ἀρκέω (arkeo) meaning "to ward off, defend, hold out, be strong enough" or "to assist, succour, suffice". In Greek mythology, this was the name of a king of Ithaca, of varying parentage between myths; in some he is the son of Zeus and Euryodeia, in others he is the son of King Cephalus and either Procris or a bear transformed into a human woman.

From the Pokémon character Arceus, whose name comes from the combination of the Greek word αρχή (arkhé), "origin", and the Latin word deus (god). In the game lore, Arceus is the original Pokémon who created the universe. This name was given to 7 boys in 2022 in the United States coinciding with the release of the video game 'Pokemon Legends: Arceus'.
The word Armenian word for the animal, bear, is Arch.
Name of a ruler of the Bosporan Kingdom.

The first element of this name is either derived from Greek ἀρχός (archos) "master" or from Greek ἀρχή (arche) "origin, source". The second element is derived from Greek ἀγαθός (agathos) meaning "good".

The first element of this name is either derived from Greek ἀρχός (archos) "master" or from Greek ἀρχή (arche) "origin, source". The second element is derived from Greek ἀνδρός (andros) "of a man", although there is one source that claims that in this name, the second element is derived from Greek ἀνδρεία (andreia) meaning "courage" as well as "manliness". As such, there are several meanings possible for this name. These include "master of a man", "origin of a man" and "courageous master".
Latinate form of Arcangela. A known bearer was 15th-century Italian nun Archangela Girlani, whom the Catholic church has beatified.
A knight killed by Bleoberis while trying to kidnap a maiden.
Means "beginning, origin" as well as "power, authority" in Ancient Greek. Arche was the muse of origins and beginnings in Greek mythology. A moon of Jupiter was named after her.

Feminine form of Archeanax, derived from Ancient Greek ἄρχω (arkho) meaning "to rule, lead, command" (see archos) and ἄναξ (anax) meaning "master, lord". Archeanassa was a hetaera living in Athens in the late 5th century BC, with whom Plato the philosopher was deeply in love with as a young man.
Nephite soldier, one of three "choice men" (Moroni 9) slain in battle (c. AD 375).

Means "ruler of life, master of life", derived from Ancient Greek ἄρχω (archo) meaning "to begin, be first" or "to lead, rule, govern" (compare ἀρχός (archos) "master") and βίος (bios) meaning "life". Alternatively, the second element could instead be βία (bia) meaning "force, bodily strength, power".
Latinized form of Archebios. This was the name of an Indo-Greek king from the 1st century BC.
Derived from Greek ἄρχω (arkho) meaning "to lead, to rule" (see archos) and δῆμος (demos) meaning "the people".
Latinized form of Archedike. This was borne by a celebrated woman of 5th-century BC Greece, the daughter of Hippias the Peisistratid.
Derived from Greek ἄρχω (arkho) meaning "to rule, lead, command" (see archos) and δίκη (dike) meaning "justice, custom, order".

Either a variant of Archilochos or an independent name in its own right. If the latter is the case, then the first element of this name is different from that of the aforementioned name, but the second element is exactly the same: Greek λόχος (lochos) meaning "ambush". Here, the first element is in all likelihood the Greek noun ἀρχή (arche) meaning "beginning, origin, source", which you can also find in the modern English word archetype. As such, the meaning of this name is then basically "the original ambush", as in: the first ambush of its kind.
Latinized form of Archelochos. In Greek mythology, Archelochus was one of the leaders of the Dardanians, who aided the Trojans in their fight against the Achaeans.
Derived from Ancient Greek ἄρχω (arkho) meaning "to begin, lead, rule, command" (see archos) and μάχη (mache) meaning "battle".

Derived from Ancient Greek ἄρχω (arkho) meaning "to begin, lead, rule, command" (see archos) and μάχη (mache) meaning "battle". This was the name of one of the fifty (or fifty-one) grandsons of Thespius fathered by Heracles in Greek mythology, his mother being Patro. It was also the name of a son of King Priam of Troy.

In the Prophecies de Merlin, the son of Angusel, King of Scotland. He took part in the expedition to save King Richard of Jerusalem from the King of Baghdad. He succeeded his father to the throne of Scotland.
A cousin and enemy of Tristan. King Mark of Cornwall was his uncle, and the evil Andret (Andred) was his brother.Tristan killed Archeman at the Fountain of the Lion.

Means "the forerunner of death" or "the beginning of destiny" in Ancient Greek, derived from ἀρχή (arche) meaning "beginning, origin" as well as "authority, dominion" (see archos) and μόρος (moros) meaning "fate, destiny; doom, death". In Greek mythology, Archemoros was the posthumous name of Opheltes, the infant son of King Lycurgus who was prophesied to die if he touched the ground before learning to walk. He was eventually killed by a snake when his nurse left him unattended in a patch of celery.
A duke and vassal of Feirefiz, Perceval’s half-brother.
Derived from the Greek noun ἀρχός (archos) meaning "master, leader" combined with the Greek noun ἀνήρ (aner) meaning "man".In Greek mythology, Archenor is the name of one of the Niobids.
Derived from either Ancient Greek ἀρχός (archos) "master, ruler, leader" or ἀρχή (arche) "origin, source". combined with πόλεμος (polemos) meaning "war, battle".
Derived from either Greek ἀρχή (arche) meaning "beginning, origin; authority" or ἄρχω (arkho) meaning "to rule, lead, command" and τιμή (time) meaning "honour, esteem" (see timao).
Variant and feminine form of Archie.

Transferred use of the surname Archia, which is by far the most prevalent in the United States and as such might possibly be a relatively new surname. Its meaning is currently unknown, but it is possible that it is derived from the masculine given name Archie.Bearers of Archia as a given name (especially those in the African-American community) are likely to have been named after Tom Archia (1919-1977), an African-American jazz tenor saxophonist. However, it is also possible that at least in some cases, Archia is a direct feminization of Archie (i.e. people with a male relative named Archie named their daughter after said relative, but tweaked the name slightly so that it fits the gender better).

Derived from Greek ἀρχή (arche) meaning "power, rulership" (compare the related word ἀρχός (archos) meaning "master")‎ combined with the masculine name suffix -ίας (-ias). Bearer Aulus Licinius Archias was a 1st-century BC Greek poet defended by Cicero.
Variant spelling of Archibald, usually used as a surname.
Anglicised version of the Name Asibong.First Answered by King Archibong the first (Asibong Edem Ekpo Efiom Okoho)

The first element of this name is either derived from Greek ἀρχός (archos) "master" or from Greek ἀρχή (arche) "origin, source". The second element is derived from δᾶμος (damos) "the people", which is a Doric Greek variant of δῆμος (demos).
Latinized form of Archidamos. This name was borne by five kings of Sparta (Greece).
Variant form of Archedike. This was the name of a famous hetaera from Naucratis in Egypt.
Form of Archil with the Georgian nominative suffix -ი (-i). It is only used in Georgian when the name is written stand-alone.

Derived from the Greek noun ἀρχός (archos) meaning "master, leader" combined with the Greek noun λόχος (lochos) meaning "ambush", a word that later came to signify a tactical sub unit of the ancient Greek army. The word is ultimately derived from the Greek verb λοχάω (lochao) meaning "to lie in wait for, to waylay" as well as "to snare".
Latinized form of Archilochos. This was the name of a Greek lyric poet from the 7th century BC.In Greek mythology, Archilochus was a Trojan who was killed by Menelaus.

An evil magician in The Faerie Queene who represents, at various places in Spenser’s elaborate allegory, the pope and Satan.Archimago hinders the successes of the heroes Guyon, the Red Cross Knight, and Arthur through sorcery and trickery. The Red Cross Knight throws him into a dungeon, but he manages to escape.
Polish form of Archippos via its latinized form Archippus.
French form of Archippos via its latinized form Archippus.
Italian form of Archippos via its latinized form Archippus.
Derived from Sanskrit archis (अर्चिस्) "ray of light" or "luster".
Alternate transcription of Bengali অর্চিষ্মান (see Archisman).
From Sanskrit अर्चिष्मत् (arciṣmat) meaning "sun, fire, flaming, brilliant, bright".
Derived from Ancient Greek ἄρχω (arkho) meaning "to begin, lead, rule, command" (see archos) and τέλος (telos) meaning "end, result, purpose".
Variant of Archetimus (See Archetimos). This was the name of a 1st-century Ancient Greek writer.

The eponymous protagonist of 'Architrenius', a medieval allegorical and satirical poem in hexameters by Johannes de Hauvilla.According to C.S. Lewis, this poem involves "the story of the 'Arch-mourner', the youthful Architrenius, who, in mere despair at the wickedness within him and about him, sets out to seek his mother Nature and be healed. His journeys lead him through many places, including the university of Paris and the island of Thule, thus offering the author the opportunity for lavish satiric description, before the wanderer finally meets Nature.

Derived from the Greek noun ἄρχων (archon) meaning "ruler, commander".Notable bearers of this name include the Achaean statesman Archon of Aegeira (2nd century BC) and Archon of Pella, a satrap of Babylonia (4th century BC).
Means "son of Archon" in Greek, derived from the name Archon combined with the patronymic suffix ἴδης (ides).This name was borne by a tyrant of Herbita from the 5th century BC.

Means "noblewoman, lady, female ruler; rich woman" in Greek, ultimately from Ancient Greek ἄρχων (archon) meaning "leader, ruler, commander" (see Archon). This is the name of a 1939 rebetiko song by Vassilis Tsitsanis.
Variant of Archie.A notable bearer is the musician Archy Ivan Marshall (1994-), otherwise known as King Krule.
Feminine form and variant of Archie.

Possibly derived from either Ancient Greek ἄρχω (archo) meaning "to lead, rule; to begin" or ἀρχός (archos) meaning "leader, ruler, master". Archytas was an Ancient Greek philosopher, mathematician, astronomer, statesman, and strategist of 5th-century BC.

A Knight of the Round Table who killed his brother, Sanades, in combat for the love of a maiden. Arciel received a mortal wound in the fight.As soon as he was aware of it, he tried to slay the maiden to keep any other man from having her, but she fled. Galahad found Arciel in his death throes and had him buried.
It is an altered version of the Italian word "Arciro", meaning archer.
Southern variant of Arcelia and Acadian and Québécois variant of Arcélia.
Arcite is a deceitful knight in "Anelida and Arcite", a 357-line English poem by Geoffrey Chaucer. It tells the story of Anelida and her wooing by false Arcite from Thebes, Greece.

A brave knight from Flanders in the service of King Claudas.Arcois spoke up against Claudas when Claudas suggested that he might go to war with Arthur. Claudas respected Arcois’ honesty and sense of justice, and he made Arcois the constable of his court.In the Vulgate, Arcois accompanies Claudas to England and is there knighted by him.
Italian and Spanish form of Arctinus.
Latinized form of Arktinos. This was the name of a Greek epic poet, who was said to have been a pupil of Homer.

This name is often a short form of Arnoud (and other names containing the Germanic element aran or arn meaning "eagle", such as Arend) and Eduard. However, it can also be a short form of Adriaan and Adrianus, as it is in the case of the Dutch politician and minister Ard van der Steur (b. 1969) and the Dutch former speed skater Ard Schenk (b. 1944). Last but not least, in some cases, this name can also be a variant spelling of Art.

The meaning of the first element of this name is unknown to me, but the second element is probably derived from Slavic gost "guest". Also note the resemblance to the Germanic name Arbogast. This name was borne by a South Slavic chieftain from the 6th century AD.
Variant of Ardashir. This was the name of a dynast (frataraka) of Persis in the late 3rd century BC, ruling sometime after 220 to c. 205 BC.
Extremely rare variant of Ardalion, which was probably influenced by the Greek word λέων (leon) meaning "lion" (see Leon).
Form of Ardalion with the nominative suffix, used in Georgian when the name is written stand-alone.

Benedictine monk, also known as Ardanus. 13th abbot of the abbey of Saint Philibert at Tournus, diocese of Autun, France in 1028. Restored monastic buildings there, and cared for the local people during the famine of 1030 to 1033.
Variant of Hardaric, with reduction of the 'h.' Ardaric was the name of a 5th-century king of the Gepids, a Germanic tribe.
Dutch and Frisian form of Ardaric.
Tajik form of Artabānu. Also compare modern Persian Ardavan.

Meaning uncertain. In some cases it could be a transferred use of the Swedish surname Ardell. It could also possibly be variant of Ardal, or of Odell or Iredell (perhaps influenced by the initial syllable in names such as Arthur and Ardis 3).As a feminine name, it could also be a variant of Ardella or Ardelia. Also compare Ardelle.
Possibly a feminine form of Arden or a blend of Ardith and Arlene.
Middle English from Old French ardant from Latin ardens, ardent-, from ardere ‘to burn’.
Means "slate" or "slate grey", derived from a rock often used for building
Georgian form of Artabānu, likely via its modern Persian form Ardavan.

Means "lord who is half female", from Sanskrit अर्ध (ardha) meaning "half", नारी (nārī) meaning "woman, wife", and ईश्वर (īśvara) meaning "lord, ruler, god". This is the name of the Hindu diety representing the masculine and feminine energies of the universe. The right superior side of the body usually is the male Shiva and the left is the female Parvati.
From Sanskrit अर्धेन्दु (ardhendu) meaning "half moon, crescent moon".
Derived from Arabic أرض (ardh) meaning "land, earth".
Combination of the name Ardian and Persian شاه (shāh) meaning "king".
From Turkish ardıç, meaning "juniper". This is a modern invention.
Diminutive of Arden or names with the sound ard or perhaps a variant of Artie.

Short form of Ardinus. In some cases, the name can also be an elaboration of Ard, which itself is a short form of Arnoud (and other names containing the Germanic element aran or arn meaning "eagle") as well as of Eduard and Adriaan.With that said, you might also want to compare this name with Arduin, as they are quite similar in appearance.A known bearer of this name is Ardin Mourik (b. 1981), a Dutch theologian who is also active as a politician for the Dutch political party CDA (specifically, for its branch that is located in the province of Utrecht).

This name can be a contracted form of Arendina and Arnoldina as well as be a more elaborate form of Arda. Less commonly, the name is also found as a short form of names ending in -ardina, such as Bernardina and Gerardina.Known bearers of this name include the Dutch left-wing politician Ardina "Arda" Gerkens (b. 1965) and the Dutch former field hockey player Mijntje Donners (b. 1974), who carries the name as a middle name.

Variant form of Ardina, of which the spelling and pronunciation was inspired or influenced by French feminine names. However, there are also (rare) cases where it is a Dutch short form of actual French given names, such as Bernardine and Gérardine.
Means "nativity, birth" in Caló. This name is used as a Caló form of Natividad (see Molchibé).

Contracted form of Arendinus. But in other words, you could also say that this given name is a masculinization of Ardina.However, it should be noted that it is possible that there might be cases where this name is a Dutch variant of Arduinus.
From the name of the genus of flowering plants that is also called coralberry or marlberry.

Kushan goddess of wealth primarily worshipped in the early first milennium CE. She is known in the Avesta as Ashi, and parallels have also been drawn with the Greek goddess Tyche, the Persian goddess Anahita, and the Buddhist deity Hariti.
From Sanskrit आर्द्र (ārdra) meaning "wet, moist, damp". This is the name of the sixth nakshatra (lunar mansion) in Hindu astronomy, which corresponds to the star Betelgeuse.
English and French form of Hardwin via its latinized form Arduinus. Also see Arduino.A known bearer of this name was the medieval Italian king Arduin of Ivrea (955-1015).

From the Gaulish arduo- meaning "height". Arduinna was a Celtic goddess of the Ardennes Forest and region, represented as a huntress riding a boar. The name Arduenna silva for "wooded heights" was applied to several forested mountains, not just the modern Ardennes.
Latinized form of Hardwin, which would ultimately come to serve as the basis for Arduin and Arduino. This given name was borne by at least two saints.
Recorded in Iceland in 1910 (according to Guðrún Kvaran (1943-), professor of lexicography at the University of Iceland). It has been suggested that it was an Icelandic form of Welsh Aurddolen.
The name of a priestess in the computer game The Elder Scrolls.
Variant of Ardys. A notable bearer was Ardyce Bohlke (1943-2013), an American educator and politician.
Variant of Ardis, with the spelling perhaps influenced by Gladys.
Means "sand," from Old Portuguese arẽa, derived from Latin (h)arēna (making it a cognate of Arena), from an earlier version *hasēna, which may be Etruscan in origin.
Areatha is the Etruscan name for Ariadne, a character from Ancient Greek religion.
Means "noble elf" in Sindarin. This was the name of an Elf in Tolkien's book 'The Silmarillion'.
Older Latin form of Yrieix, of uncertain etymology.

column3: อารีย์, อารี(Thai)
column12: Alternate transcription of Thai อารีย์ or อารี (see Ari).
the name areeshah is a pakistan name areeshah was the first name of the baby in pakistan
it originates from the sanskrit word reet meaning rituals. areet means a person who is not bound by any rituals.
Alternate transcription of Thai อารีวรรณ (see Ariwan).
Alternate transcription of Thai อารียา (see Ariya).

The meaning and origin of the first element in this Germanic name is rather uncertain, and so there are various possibilities to the name's meaning. The most likely possibility is that the first element is derived from Proto-Germanic aran or arna "eagle" (ara in Gothic and arn in Old High German). However, it might also come from Old High German êra "honour, respect" (see Eraric) or from Old High German hari "army" (with reduction of the "h"). The second element has similar uncertainty. We know that it comes from gis (the original form was possibly gîs), but we don't exactly know where gis itself comes from. But there are a few possibilities. It might come from Gallo-Celtic gaiso "spear" (see Gaiseric) or it might be a short form of gisel, which means "hostage" or "pledge" (see Giselle).
Derived from Ancient Greek ἀρήγω (arego) meaning "to help, aid, succour" or "to ward off, prevent, avert". This was the name of a painter from Corinth in ancient Greece.
Variant spelling of Aragund. Aregund was the name of the wife of Chlothar I, a 6th-century Merovingian king of the Franks.

Derived from Greek ἀρεία (areia) meaning "warlike, martial", literally "of Ares, devoted to Ares", the feminine form of ἄρειος (areios) (see Areios). This was an epithet of the goddesses Aphrodite and Athena. In some Greek myths this name was also borne by the mother of Miletus, founder of the ancient city of Miletus.
This name was used for a character in Gail Carson Levine's 1997 book "Ella Enchanted". The book won a Newbery Medal and a movie adaptation was released in 2004 starring Anne Hathaway.

Latinized form of Greek Ἀρηΐθοος (Areithoos), which meant "warlike, swift in battle", derived from Ancient Greek ἄρειος (areios) "warlike, martial, pertaining to Ares", combined with (θοός) "swift, quick".
Etymology uncertain, perhaps from the Armenian Արեգ (arek) meaning "sun" and the Persian نازی (nazi) meaning "sweet, coy" or Armenian նազանք (nazank') meaning "affection, coquetry".
Etymology uncertain, perhaps from the Armenian Արեգ (arek) meaning "sun" and the Persian نازی (nazi) meaning "sweet, coy" or Armenian նազանք (nazank') meaning "affection, coquetry".

column3: 亜嶺公, 亜嶺功, 亜嶺紅, 亜廉久, 亜廉宮, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 亜 (a) meaning "second, Asia", 嶺 (re) meaning "peak, summit" or 廉 (re) meaning "bargain, reason, charge, suspicion, point, account, purity, honest, low price, cheap, rested, contented, peaceful" combined with 公 (ku) meaning "public, prince, official, governmental", 功 (ku) meaning "achievement, merits, success, honor, credit", 紅 (ku) meaning "crimson, deep red", 久 (ku) meaning "long time" or 宮 (ku) meaning "Shinto shrine, constellations, palace, princess". Other kanji combinations are possible.
Alternate transcription of Hebrew אראלה (see Erela).
This is a rare (American) English given name, which might possibly be derived from Aurelius.
Variant of Arely; perhaps a short form or contraction of Aracelis.
Possibly a Hispanic feminine variant of Areli (which is a masculine name in the Old Testament) or a contracted form of Araceli. Also compare Marely, Yareli and Karely.

column3: あれん(Japanese Hiragana)|亜漣, 亜廉, 亜恋, 亜零, 亜怜, 亜連, 阿蓮, 愛怜, 愛恋, 愛蓮, 愛漣, etc.(Japanese Kanji)

column12: Means "sand" in Spanish and Catalan. The word is derived from Latin arēna, harēna, from the earlier form *hasēna, which may be Etruscan in origin.

Feminine form of Arend. Also compare Arendje, which is another feminine form of the same name, but is much more common in the Netherlands.Known bearers of this name include the Dutch racing cyclist Arenda Grimberg (b. 1978) and the Dutch theologian and preacher Arenda Haasnoot (b. 1973).

This given name is a more elaborate form of Arenda, which is the feminine form of Arend. Also compare the late medieval given name Arentijn.A known bearer of this name was the Dutch composer and pianist Dina Appeldoorn (1884-1938), who carried the name as a middle name.
Variant form of Arendina, of which the spelling and pronunciation was inspired or influenced by French feminine names.

When borne by a female person, this name is a good example of how one can turn a very masculine name (Arend) into a feminine name by simply adding the diminutive suffix -je to the original name. But when borne by a male person, this name is simply a pet form because of the diminutive suffix. Also compare Arentjen, which is the medieval form of this name. Arenda is also worth a look, since it is also a feminine form of Arend (though a much less common one at that).Lastly, it might be interesting to know that arendje is also an independent word in the Dutch language and means "little eagle" in English. However, cases where Arendje as a given name was inspired by this word are likely to be few to none, due to the prevalence of Arendje as a proper given name that - via Arend - is ultimately derived from the Germanic given name Arnold.
Coined by Sabino Arana Goiri and Koldo Elizalde as a Basque equivalent of Ariadna and Ariane.
The name of a fictional character in The Keepers book series by Jackie French Koller.
Diminutive of Spanish arena meaning “sand” (see Arena). This is the name of Sandy Cheeks in the Spanish dub of SpongeBob SquarePants (1999-).

Medieval Dutch and East Frisian form of Arnold as well as a Scandinavian variant of Arend. As for the Netherlands: this given name is still in use there today, but it is not as common there as its modern form Arend is.Known bearers of this given name include the Danish-Norwegian topographical author Arent Berntsen (1610-1680), the Dutch Golden Age landscape painter Arent Arentsz (1585-1631) and Arent van Curler (1620-1667; later known as Arent van Corlaer), the Dutch founder of what is now the American city of Schenectady (located in the state of New York).
Old Hungarian name of unknown origin and meaning.
Late medieval form of Arendina (and perhaps even a corruption or variant of Arentjen in some cases), which appears to have been rather uncommon even in that era.
Italian and Spanish form of Areios via Areus.
From Cook Islands Māori are "house", and ora "life". Areora is a village in the Cook Islands.

Derived from Catalan Mare de Déu de les Ares ("Mother of God of the Ares"), which is the name of a sanctuary located on Coll d'Ares, a Catalan mountain pass in the Pyrenees. It is the site of a Marian devotion, which is why Catalan parents bestow this name upon their daughters.
Derived from Ancient Greek ἀρέσκω (aresko) meaning "to satisfy, please" as well as "to atone, make amends", combined with ἀνδρός (andros) meaning "of a man".
Possibly derived from ἀρέσκω (aresko) meaning "to please, satisfy; to make amends". Aresas of Lucania was the sixth head of the Pythagorean school in succession from Pythagoras himself.
Derived form the Greek God Ares.
Derived from Greek ἀρέσκω (aresko) meaning "to please, satisfy".
Latinized form of Aretaios. A known bearer of this name of Aretaeus of Cappadocia, a Greek physician who lived in the 1st century AD.
Derived from either Greek ἀρετάω (aretao) "to thrive, to prosper" or from Greek ἀρετή (arete) meaning "goodness, excellence" as well as "virtue, skill".

Appears to mean "she who is prayed for" from the Ancient Greek verb ἀράομαι (araomai) "to pray to", related to the noun ἀρά (ara) "prayer, vow, curse"; also compare the Ionic Greek noun ἀρητή (arete) which meant "sacred", "cursed" or "prayed". Alternatively it could be related to Ares, the name of the Greek god of war. In Greek mythology Queen Arete was the wife of Alcinous and mother of Nausicaa. A famous bearer was the 4th-century BC Greek philosopher Arete of Cyrene, daughter of Aristippus who was himself a pupil of Socrates and the founder of the Cyrenaic school of philosophy.This name should not be confused with Ancient Greek Ἀρετή (see Arete).
Italian and Spanish form of Aretaeus.
Catalan and Portuguese form of Aretaeus.
Bulgarian and Russian form of Aretaeus.
Arethas was the leader of the Christian community of Najran in the early 6th century; he was executed during the persecution of Christians by the Jewish king Dhu Nuwas in 523.

Possibly derived from the name of the god Ares. This was the name of the father of Nissus of Dulichium in the Odyssey. It’s also an ancient name of Giresun Island, a small island on the southeastern coast of Black Sea that was sacred to Ares.
Aretousa is one of the main characters in the story of Erotokritos written by Vitsentzos Kornaros.
From the first part of adjective 아름답다 (areumdapda) meaning "beautiful."On rare occasions, it can also be written with hanja, e.g. combining 雅 (a) meaning "clean, pure" with 凛 (reum) meaning "cold."
From the verbal noun of adjective 아름답다 (areumdapta) meaning "beautiful" (compare Areumdaun and the shorter, more common Areum).
From the present determiner form of adjective 아름답다 (areumdapta) meaning "beautiful" (compare Areumdaum and the shorter, more common Areum).
From Areum combined with the subject marking particle 이 (i).
Latinized form of Areios. This name was borne by two kings of Sparta, both of whom lived in the 3rd century BC.
Perhaps a feminine form of Areus, or possibly derived from Greek ἀράομαι (araomai), meaning "to pray". This is the name of one of the characters in the play La Celestina (1499) by Fernando de Rojas.
Bulgarian, Russian and Ukrainian form of Areios via Areus.
According to a user from Iraq, the name Arez is of Kurdish origin and means "Rain".
Probably derived from Arabic رِزْق (rizq) meaning "wealth, fortune" or "nourishment, sustenance".
Swedish form of Arnfastr via its later form Arnfast.
From an ancient name for the region of North West Gwynedd, derived from Welsh ar "opposite" and Môn "Anglesey". This has been used as a given name since the late 19th century.
North Frisian form of Arnfastr via the Swedish form Arfast. A known bearer of this name is German politician Arfst Wagner (b. 1954).

Means "(to be) strong as well", derived from Lithuanian ar meaning "also, too, as well (as)" combined with old Lithuanian gailas, which usually means "strong, potent" but has also been found to mean "sharp, jagged" as well as "angry, fierce, violent" and "miserable, sorrowful, remorseful". Also compare the modern Lithuanian noun galia meaning "power, might, force".

This name was used by Molière in his play, 'The Imaginary Invalid' (1673) ('Le Malade imaginaire' in French), for the main character.Most likely, it comes from the Norman surname, Argentine. Its specific etymological origin is unknown, but it probably is derived from the root of Indo-European arg, which means "clear, white, bright". Alternatively, the name may have originated from the Argan tree and would therefore be rooted in Shilha, a Berber language.
Derived from Old Breton argant "silver". This was the name of an 8th-century king of Brittany.

Derived from Old Breton argant "silver" (arc'hant in Modern Breton), and by extension "bright; shining; resplendent", and Old Breton hael "generous; prince". Argantael was the wife of Nevenoe, the first Duke of Brittany.

Name used by Italian author Torquato Tasso in his masterpiece 'Gerusalemme Liberata' (1581) and 'Gerusalemme Conquistata' (1583). Argante is a Muslim, king of Jerusalem. The name's origin is uncertain. Some hypotesis claim the tie with the Italian word argano meaning "capstan, windlass" or from Breton argant meaning "silver". Another possible origin is related with the argan tree (Sideroxylon spinosum) where argan is a Berber word (ⴰⵔⴳⴰⵏ) referred to the Northern African tree and its oil.

The first element of this name is derived from Lithuanian ar meaning "also, too, as well (as)". The second element is either derived from the Lithuanian verb gaudyti meaning "to take" as well as "to catch, to hunt" or from the Lithuanian adjective gaudus meaning "sonorous, resonant, ringing, loud, echoing".

Derived from Ancient Greek ἀργής (arges) meaning "shining, white, glancing". This was the name of several figures in Greek mythology, including a huntress turned into a doe by the god Helios after she boasted she could catch even an animal that ran as fast as the sun.
Variant and Polish form of Argia.
Feminine form of Argeios. This was the name of several characters in Greek mythology. It was also an epithet of Hera in her role as the patron goddess of the city of Argos.

Means "Argive, from Argos" in Ancient Greek. Argos is a city in the Peloponnese region of Greece and one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world. The etymology is from the Ancient Greek word αργός (argós) that means "white" or "shining" possibly for the visual impression given of the Argolic plain during harvest time.

Derived from Argelia, which is the Spanish name for the North African country Algeria. The country's name is in turn derived from the name of its capital city, namely Algiers (which is known as Argel in Spanish). The city's name is ultimately derived from Arabic الجزائر (al-Jaza'ir) meaning "the islands".

Masculine form of Argelia. Famous bearers of this name include the Cuban comedian Argelio García Rodríguez (1925–1992) and the retired Honduran soccer referee Argelio Sabillón (b. 1957), who has a stadium named after him (located in the Honduran city Santa Bárbara).

From the Spanish title of the Virgin Mary, La Virgen de Argeme, meaning "The Virgin of Argeme."She is one of the patrons of Coria in the Extremaduran province of Cáceres and the diocese of Coria-Cáceres alongside Peter of Alcántara.Its etymology is uncertain. One theory posits a derivation from Arabic حَارَة الْجَمْعِ‎‎ (ḥārat al-jamʿi), from a combination of حَارَة (ḥāra) meaning "neighbourhood, quarter; street; house" and جَمْع (jamʿ) meaning "crowd, throng, mass, legion," lining up with a traditional account that the effigy was hidden in a cave in the year 714 to avoid theft and desecration by Muslim invaders before being rediscovered in 1124. Other versions of the story of the effigy's discovery revolve around a farmer either touching the image with his ploughshare and then hearing the word arge or shouting to his cow Geme the phrase Ara, Geme! when the cow was not moving so as not to step on the holy effigy (one other version revolves around a yoke consisting of two cows named Ara and Geme).
Italian name of Greek origin (possibly related to Argentina). A famous bearer was Argene del Carlo, a second-class survivor of the Titanic disaster.

Probably the Spanish form of Argenide.The name belongs to a minor character in 100 Years of Solitude (Cien años de soledad in Spanish) by Gabriel García Márquez. Argenida is the trusted servant and confidante of Rebeca.
Likely a derivation of a family of words/names stemming from Latin argentum meaning "silver" with the -is suffix (coinciding with the word argén, referring to the argent herald).
Derived from Latin argentum, meaning "silver". Italian masculine form of Argenta.
Italian and Spanish form of Argeus.
Derived from Greek ἀργής (arges) meaning "bright, glancing" or "shining, white" (compare Argos). This was the name of a Cyclops in Greek mythology.
From the Kurdish ar-geş meaning "intense fire".
Epithet of the north-west (or east or south-west) wind, meaning "clearing, brightening" in Ancient Greek, ultimately derived from ἀργός (argos) "bright, white, shining".
Variant and Polish form of Arges. This was the name of a 3rd century saint.
Cornish, 'silver'. In 17th century Cornwall, ARGENTINE was sometimes used as a Christian name.
From the name of a type of flowering tree that produces deep pink blooms (scientific name Cercis siliquastrum).
It was the name borne by the fourth ruler of the Mongol empire's Ilkhanate division,
Latinized form of Argeia, as well as the Italian form.
Derived from the Greek adjective ἀργός (argos) meaning "bright, shining, glistening" as well as "white" (see Argus) combined with the Greek noun λέων (leon) meaning "lion".
Wife of Count Munio Nuñez (Spanish Count) who appears in the first "carta puebla" given in Spain founding the first town in the country.
Combination of either ár "year; prosperity, abundance", ár "early", or perhaps ár "messenger" with gísl "pledge, hostage". Alternatively, it can be an Icelandic form of Arngils.
Spanish form of Argimirus, which was a variant latinized form of either Ercanmar or Harimar.

Argine is the name of the Queen of Clubs on French playing cards. While the names on other cards are recognisable figures from history or mythology, Argine is more obscure, it is explained as an anagram of the Latin word regina "queen".
Means "to defend as well", derived from Lithuanian ar meaning "also, too, as well (as)" combined with Lithuanian ginti meaning "to defend, to protect".

Probably means "silver face", derived from Ancient Greek ἄργυρος (argyros) meaning "silver" and ὄψ (ops) meaning "face, eye". This is the name of several characters in Greek mythology, mostly of naiads.

Very old name used by an real king of Armenia.Was the sixth known king of the ancient country of Urartu (in eastern Anatolia) from 785 BC to 763 BC.He founded the citadel of Erebouni in 782 BC, which is the present capital of Armenia, Yerevanreference Wikipedia
The name of two kings of Urartu, an ancient kingdom in the Armenian Highlands.
Derived from Albanian argjend "silver; silver thread".

Of uncertain origin and meaning. Theories include a variant of Ardo and a derivation from Argo, the name of the ship used by Jason and the Argonauts (whose name is said to be derived from Greek άργυρος (argyros) "silver"). The name was first recorded in the early 1960s.
Probably transferred from the place name Argola in Missouri.
Unknown origin. Argolda Hill, known as Goldie Hill, was an American country music singer, born in 1933.
Transferred use of the surname Argyle.
Meaning unknown. This was the name of a IX century saint.

Feminine form of Argyros "silver". According to Pausanias, Argyra was the nymph of a well in Achaea, whose human lover Selemnos died of grief after she abandoned him. Aphrodite took pity on Selemnos and changed him into a river.
Dialect form of Argyro found in Pontus, Epirus, Silata, Cappadocia, Western Macedonia and Skiathos.
Taken from the town of Arhane (in French, Arhan) in the French part of the Basque Country. The name of the town ultimately comes from Basque haran ("valley").

Possibly derived from Old Norse Arnhildr, "eagle battle". Alternatively, could be from the Old English elements ār "honour, glory, grace" (see aizō) and hild "battle". This was the name of a saint from Oldbury-on-Severn. See Arilda.
Bosnian and Croatian form of Archimedes.
Alternate transcription of Greek Αρχόντισσα (see Archontissa).

column3: 安璃, 有里, 亜李, 明里, 亜利, 亜吏, 亜梨, etc.(Japanese Kanji)|あり(Japanese Hiragana)|아리(Korean Hangul)|雅利, 䢝里, etc.(Korean Hanja)|อารีย์, อารี(Thai)
column12: Short form of Ariadne, Ariadna, Arianna or other variants of this name.

column3: אריה(Hebrew)|アリア(Japanese Katakana)|ありあ(Japanese Hiragana)|有愛, 安莉阿, 合李亞, 明理和, etc.(Japanese Kanji)|아리아(Korean Hangul)

column12: Short form of Adriaan. In other words, this name is a more modern form of the medieval Dutch name Ariaen.

One of the sons of the Persian king Darius I. He participated in the Second Persian invasion of Greece as one of the four admirals of the fleet of his brother Xerxes I, and was killed in the Battle of Salamis in 480 BC.
Ariacus was a 4th-century Thervingian Gothic pagan ruler.
Shortened or masculine form of Ariadne.
Alternate transcription of Greek Αριάδνη (see Ariadni).
Medieval Dutch form of Ariaan. In other words: this name is a short form of Adriaen.
Likely an elaborated form of Arianny.
Possibly a variant of Ariel or influenced by the typeface Arial.
Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Arialdus.
Possibly an abbreviated form of Ariaramnes. This was the name of a satrap of Cappadocia, who lived in the 4th century BC.
Variation of Aryan, or from the English word referring to "someone whose star sign is Aries". Arian Foster (born 1986) is an American football player for the Houston Texans.
Māori form of Ariadne. Modern invented Māori name from the words āria ana meaning "tidal pool cave" in Māori.

column3: ありあな(Japanese Hiragana)|アリアナ(Japanese Katakana)|亜凛愛菜, etc.(Japanese Kanji)

column12: Derived from Welsh arian meaning "silver" (from Old Welsh argant) and Middle Welsh meaning gell "yellow" (which apparently also carried connotations of "shining", ultimately going back to Proto-Celtic *gelwo- "yellow; white"; compare Old Irish gel(o) "white; fair; shining"). According to legend, Arianell was a member of the Welsh royal family who became possessed by an evil spirit and was exorcised by Saint Dyfrig, after which she became a nun and spiritual student of Dyfrig.
Variant of Ariana in use in Latin America.
Brazilian phonetic variant of Ariane or a variant of Arianny.

Apparently a form of Arianna. This name was popularized in the early 2010s by American ring girl Arianny Celeste (1985-), born Penelope López Márquez, in whose case it is reportedly derived from a nickname she had as a child.
Italian form of Hadrian and masculine form of Arianna.
Variant transcription of Arianthi. This is borne by Arianthe Galani (1940-), an Australian actress of Greek descent.

Possibly composed of the Greek intensifying prefix ἀρι- (ari-) and ἄνθος (anthos) meaning "flower".While this does not appear to be an attested ancient Greek name, masculine equivalents - Ἀρίανθος (Arianthos) and Ἀριάνθης (Arianthes) - were recorded in the ancient Greek period.
Roman cognomen derived from Arius. Original form of https://www.behindthename.com/name/arian/submitted and Ariano
Variant of Arianwen used in the English-speaking world.
Variant of Ariana with the -ys suffix.
Hellenized form of Ariyāramna. This was the name of the paternal great-grandfather of Darius the Great.

Hellenized form of an Old Persian male name, of which the first element is derived from Old Persian aryā "Aryans". The second element is not really certain, but may have been derived from Old Persian wratha "joy". This name was borne by several kings of Cappadocia.
Ariaric was a 4th-century Thervingian Gothic pagan ruler. He lost a war to Constantine the Great in 332. His son, Aoric, was raised in Constantinople.
Of ancient Persian origin, but the meaning is unknown to me at this time. This was the name of one of the three legitimate sons of King Artexerxes II Mnemon, who lived in the 4th century BC.
Most likely a variant of Ariadna.
Means "brilliant, clever, intelligent" in Arabic and Urdu.

Germanic variant of Haribert, though there can also easily be cases where the name is a variant of Arabert and Arinbert (see Arnbert).A notable bearer of this name was the German composer Aribert Reimann (1936-2024).
Short form of Aribert.This name is often confused (as well as used interchangeably) with the Germanic names Arbeo and Arbo.
Possibly a variant of Araceli influenced by Maricel.

Latinized form of the Greek Άρικία (Arikia), probably derived from Latin aro "to plough". This is commonly thought to be the name of a consort of Hippolytos due to a verse from the Aeneid that roughly translates as "To the war also came the most fair offspring of Hippolytus, Virbius, whom, distinguished, mother Aricia sent..."; however, as Virbius is the name that Hippolytos was given after being resurrected by Athena, and Aricia was the name of the town that he was brought to after his resurrection, it’s likely that this is a misunderstanding of the text.In the literary world, Aricia was one of the main characters in Jean Racine's tragedy Phèdre (1677).
French form of Aricia. This name was used by Jean Racine in his play Phèdre (1677) which inspired Jean-Philippe Rameau to write his first opera Hippolyte et Aricie (1733).

From the name of a valley on the island of La Palma (Canary Islands, Spain). The place name is of Guanche origin, a metathesis of *adiran meaning "base, foundation; bed (of a valley)". A similar name, Aridañy, was recorded as belonging to a Guanche man from the island of Gran Canaria (late 15th century). Known bearers of this name include the Canarian-born footballers Aridane Santana (1987-) and Aridane Hernández (1989-).
Meaning uncertain; possibly a variant of Aridane.
A son of Haman in the book of Esther. Possibly related the Persian Haridata, meaning "given by Hari".

Feminine form of Aridelos. On the Greek island of Crete, the mythological Cretan princess Ariadne was also called Aridela. In other words: Aridela was an alternative name for Ariadne, which was primarily or even exclusively used on Crete.

Derived from the Greek adjective ἀρίδηλος (aridelos) meaning "clear, distinct, far seen".
