It consists of the Greek strengthening prefix ἀρι (ari) meaning "most" combined with the Greek adjective δῆλος (delos) meaning "visible, conspicuous, manifest". The latter word is ultimately derived from the Greek verb δηλόω (deloo) meaning "to make visible".

Spanish and Portuguese form of Aridius. However, in these languages, the name can also be a variant form of Arildo.A bearer of this name was Aridio Saldaña, the Dominican father of American actress Zoe Saldana (b. 1978).

This name was borne by Quintus Aridius Rufinus, a Roman consul from the early 3rd century. His name may possibly have been derived from Latin aridus meaning "dry, arid, parched". But as it is possible that he may have been a Gallo-Roman instead of a pure Roman, Aridius could also be the latinized form of a Gaulish name. Lastly, it might also be interesting to compare this name with Arrhidaeus, a Greek name that is sometimes also spelled as Arideus.
Alternate transcription of أريج (see Arij), chiefly used in Northern Africa.
Diminutive of Ariadne and other names beginning with Ari-.
Hebrew variant of Ariella, Polish feminine form of Ariel, Italian feminine form of Ariele as well as a Croatian and Albanian borrowing of the Italian name.
Creative phonetic variant of Arielle/Ariel or a Sicilian variant of Ariele.

column4: Lithuanian|Spanish (Latin American, Modern, Rare)|American (Hispanic, Modern, Rare)

column12: Variant of Arielle/Ariel, reflecting the Brazilian Portuguese pronunciation of the French form of Ariella.
Elaboration of Ariel with the popular suffix -lys (see Odalys, Marielys).

Variant form of Arian, which may possibly have been inspired by the French name Adrien in its spelling. This form ultimately led to the form Arjen, which since steadily outgrew Ariën in popularity and is nowadays by far the most common of the two. Known Dutch bearers of this name include the drummer Ariën van Weesenbeek (b. 1980) and the soccer player Ariën Pietersma (b. 1987).
Maori form of Ariel, as it appears in the original 1868 edition of Te Paipera Tapu ("The Holy Bible").
Either a diminutive of Aria 1, or from the major antagonist and God-General in Tales of the Abyss. Given after the musical term for a small song, from the Italian word "arietta."
Alternate transcription of Arabic عارفة (see Arifa), as well as the Malay and Indonesian form.
Turkish feminine form of Arif, meaning "learned, knowing, expert".
From Arabic عارفين (ʿārifīn), the plural of عارف (ʿārif) meaning "learned, knowing, expert".
Means "expert of the religion" from عارف (ʿārif) meaning "learned, knowing, expert" combined with الله (Allah)

Feminine form of Arignotos. This was the name of a female philosopher from Croton or Samos, active around the year 500 BC, who was a student of Pythagoras and Theano. Some traditions maintain she was also their daughter.

Derived from Greek ἀρίγνωτος (arignotos) meaning "well-known, far-famed" (as well as "easy to be known, recognizable" but sometimes also "infamous"), itself composed of the intensifying prefix ἀρι- (ari) and γνωτός (gnotos) "perceived, understood, known".
Variant of Arianna, the spelling influenced by Rihanna.
Māori form of Alice, which means "of noble sort, nobility".

column3: ありひこ(Japanese Hiragana)|順彦, 有彦, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From 順 (ari) meaning "order, obedience, sequence" and 彦 (hiko) meaning "prince". Other kanji combinations can be used.
Ari means "have, possess, exist" and hiro means "wide, spacious, broad".

column3: 有人, 有仁, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 有 (ari) meaning "exist, existance, belonging" and 人 (hito) meaning "man, person". Other kanji combinations can be used.
Means "peaceful king" or "king of peace" from Tahitian ariʻi meaning "noble, aristocrat, king" combined with hau "concord, peace".
From the Tahitian ari'i meaning "noble" and here meaning "beloved, favourite".
Means "powerful ruler, divine authority" in Tahitian, from arii meaning "king, chief" and mana meaning "divine power".
From the Tahitian ari'i meaning "noble" and nui, an archaic term meaning "big".
Means "respected king" in Tahitian; a combination of ari'i meaning "king" and taia meaning "respect, fear".
Means "white king"; a combination of Tahitian ari'i "king" and tea "white, light, pale".
Polynesian name, composed by "ari'i", meaning "chief", "king" and "vai", meaning "water", so the meaning is "king of the water", "king of the sea".
Old Finnish name. Possibly has Sami or Karelian origins.

column3: ありか(Japanese Hiragana)|アリカ(Japanese Katakana)|有嘉, 有佳, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From 有 (ari) meaning "to exist, to have, possess" with 嘉 (ka) meaning "praise, auspicious" or 佳 (ka) meaning "beautiful, good, lovely". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: ありかね(Japanese Hiragana)|在兼(Japanese Kanji)
column12: Meaning varies depending on the kanji used.
Means "seen and cared for" in Yoruba.

column3: アリコ(Japanese Katakana)|ありこ(Japanese Hiragana)|順子, 安李子, 愛里子, 亜李子, 亜莉子, 阿理子, 愛理子, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 有 (ari) meaning "exist" combined with 子 (ko) meaning "child". Other kanji combinations are possible.

Saint Arilda is an obscure female saint from Oldbury-on-Severn in the English county of Gloucestershire who probably lived in the 5th or 6th century. She may have been of either Anglo-Saxon or Welsh origin.

This given name is predominantly in use in Brazil. It is probably the (Brazilian) Portuguese form of Arild. Also compare Araldo and Aroldo.A known bearer of this name is the Brazilian politician Arildo Batista, who is president of the council of Jacareí, a city in southern Brazil.
Possibly a Latinized form of Arild or a variant of Árelíus.
Possibly a contracted form of Amarilla.
Variant of Agricole via the form Arigle.

column3: 存摩, 存真, 存磨, 存馬, 存麻, 有摩, 有真, 有磨, 有舞, 有馬, 有麻, etc.(Japanese Kanji)

column12: Portuguese form of the biblical place name Arimathea, given in reference to Joseph of Arimathea (José de Arimateia in Portuguese), a disciple of Jesus.

column3: 亜里美, 亜鈴実, 亜理実, 亜梨実, 阿梨実, 可望, 在実, 在心, 在美見, 在美巳, 有海, 有深, 有美, 有美巳, 有里三, 有里未, 有里巳, etc.(Japanese Kanji)|ありみ(Japanese Hiragana)
column12: From Japanese 亜 (a) meaning "second, Asia", 里 (ri) meaning "village" combined with 美 (mi) meaning "beautiful". Other kanji combinations are possible.
Means "greatly remembered" in Ancient Greek. This was the name of a sister of Aristole.
A Finnish name of unknown origin and meaning.

column3: ありん(Japanese Hiragana)|亜凜, 亜琳, 愛鈴, 杏琳, 明鈴, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: Of unknown origin and meaning, maybe related to Turkish arın meaning "purified".

column3: アリナ(Japanese Katakana)|ありな(Japanese Hiragana)|亜莉菜, 亜璃菜, 安里奈 愛李奈, 阿理菜, 有菜, etc.(Japanese Kanji)|아리나(Korean Hangul)
column12: From Japanese 亜 (a) meaning "sub-, second, Asia", 莉 (ri) meaning "white jasmine" or 璃 (ri) meaning "glassy, lapis lazuli" combined with 菜 (na) meaning "vegetables, greens". Other combinations of kanji are also possible.Usage of this name is, most likely, influenced by the name Alina.
Based on the name suffix inda, a popular suffix in the 17th century. Variant of Orinda and/or Marinda.
From Sanskrit अरिन्दम (ariṃdama) meaning "conquering, victorious, subduing enemies".
Alternate transcription of Bengali অরিন্দম (see Arindam).
Derived from the adjective arin meaning "light, airy; fast."

column3: 有音, 在根, etc.(Japanese Kanji)

column12: Hittite name meaning "lady of the forest", from Sanskrit aranya meaning "forest". This name was given to the Sun Goddess of Arinna. Also connected to the Vedic goddess Aranyani.

column3: 有乃, 有野, 亜梨乃, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 有 (ari) meaning "exist" combined with 乃 (no), a possessive particle. Other combinations of kanji characters can also form this name.

column3: 有信, etc.(Japanese Kanji)|ありのぶ(Japanese Hiragana)|アリノブ(Japanese Katakana)
column12: From Japanese 有 (ari) meaning "have, possess" combined with 信 (nobu) meaning "trust". Other kanji combinations can form this name as well.

Means "one amongst honour" or "in the midst of wealth" in Yoruba, from àárín "centre, middle" combined with either ọlá "honour, respect" or ọlà "wealth". Often given to a middle child, or one of triplets.
Derived from Thai ปริญญา (parinya) meaning "knowledge, awareness, understanding".

Hellenized form of the Old Persian name *Arya-bṛz-ana- which possibly meant "making the Aryans great", of which the first element is derived from Old Persian aryā "Aryans". The second element is not really certain, perhaps *brzi- "high". This name was, among others, the name of three kings of Cappadocia.

Meaning: "a fierce lion" or "lion-like" and "venerable".This was the name of two biblical men, Arioch was a king of Ellasar who was allied with Chedorlaomer (Gen. 14:1,9) and Captain of Nebuchadnezzar's guard (Dan. 2:14-15, 24-25).Originally appears in the Book of Genesis chap. 14 as the "King of Ellasar", part of the confederation of kings who did battle with the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah and with Abraham in the vale of Siddim.
Derived from Gaulish arios “noble” and *gaisos “spear”. Ariogaisos (flourished in 2nd century AD) was a ruler of the Quadi, a Germanic tribe, during the Marcomannic War.
Probably a variant of Arialdus. This is the name of a character from the 17th-century stage play The Swisser.

Possibly related to Ancient Greek ἀρείων (areion) meaning "better, worthier, stronger" (see aristos), or perhaps a patronymic form of the name of the god Ares (compare Areios). This was the name of a semi-legendary Ancient Greek poet and musician from Lesbos, who was supposedly rescued from pirates by a pod of dolphins. It was also the name of an immortal horse of divine origin and incredible speed in Greek mythology, in some accounts gifted with human speech and the power of prophecy.
Spanish and Portuguese form of Ariovistus.

Latinization of a Celto-Germanic given name, of which the original form and meaning are uncertain.The first known bearer of this name is Ariovistus (1st century BC), the leader of the Germanic tribe of the Suebi and other allied Germanic peoples. He and his followers were settled in Roman Gaul for some time.Later bearers of the name include the American engineer and industrialist Ariovistus "Ario" Pardee (1810-1892) and his eldest child, Ariovistus "Ario" Pardee Jr. (1839-1901).
Means "strong lion" in Hebrew, combination of the names Ari 1 and Oz 2

Ariprando Visconti is the earliest known member of the Visconti family, which ruled Milan in the Middle Ages.
From Thai อารี (ari) meaning "kind, generous" and รัตน์ (rat) meaning "jewel, gem".

column12: From Japanese 有 (ari) meaning "to possess, exist" and 沙 (sa) meaning "sand" or 紗 (sa) meaning "silk, gauze". Other kanji combinations are possible. This name is often spelled in hiragana.

column12: Alternate transcription of Thai อริสรา or อริศรา (see Aritsara).

column12: Alternate transcription of Thai อริสรา or อริศรา (see Aritsara).

Latinized form of Aristainos. A notable bearer of this name was Aristaenus of Megalopolis (2nd century BC), a strategos (military leader) of the Achaean League.
Derived from the Greek elements ἄριστος (aristos) "best, noblest" and ἀγορά (agora) "assembly, gathering place, marketplace". Compare the masculine equivalent Aristagoras.

The second element is derived from either the Greek verb ἀγορεύω (agoreuo) meaning "to orate, to speak publicly" or the Greek noun ἀγορά (agora), which can mean "assembly" as well as "market, marketplace".This name was borne by several ancient Greek tyrants, such as Aristagoras of Cyme (6th century BC) and Aristagoras of Miletus (5th century BC).
Derived from Greek ἄριστος (aristos) meaning "best" and αἰχμή (aichme) meaning "point of a spear, point of an arrow", or figuratively "war; warlike spirit".
Feminine form of Aristainetos, derived from Ancient Greek ἄριστος (aristos) meaning "best" and αἰνετός (ainetos) meaning "praiseworthy".

Derived from Ancient Greek ἄριστος (aristos) meaning "best" combined with αἰνετός (ainetos) meaning "praiseworthy". The latter word is ultimately derived from the Greek noun αἴνη (aine) meaning "praise, fame" (see Aeneas).
Derived from the Greek adjective ἄριστος (aristos) meaning "best" combined with the Greek noun αἴνη (aine) meaning "praise, fame" (see Aeneas).
Serbian name for Aristaeus, a minor Greek god of agriculture, hunting and cattle.

Possibly an Armenian form of Aristarchos, or perhaps from a Middle Persian word meaning "resurrection of the dead" (Persian رستاخیز‎ (rastâxiz)). This was borne by a 4th-century Armenian saint who was a son of Gregory the Illuminator (the religious leader traditionally credited with Christianizing Armenia). This name has been used from the 4th century CE until now.
Latinized form of Aristandros. Aristander was the name of Alexander the Great's favorite seer.

Means "(the) best of a man", derived from Greek ἄριστος (aristos) meaning "best" and ἀνδρός (andros) meaning "of a man".

Derived from the Greek adjective ἄριστος (aristos) meaning "best" combined with the Greek noun ἀνήρ (aner) meaning "man".Also compare the Greek name Aristandros, which is closely related and essentially means the same.

Russian, Ukrainian and Moldovan form of Aristarchus.
French form of Aristus. It appears in the play Les Femmes Savantes (1672) by the French playwright Molière. A known bearer was Ariste Jacques Trouvé-Chauvel (1805-1883), a French politician.
Feminine form of Aristaeus. This is the name of a character in Vivaldi's opera L'Olimpiade (1734).

Feminine form of Aristeo (Spanish). As a Greek name, it is a feminine form of names beginning with the element ἄριστος (aristos) meaning "best". Aristea is also a genus of purple/lilac flowers of African origin; the species Aristea ecklonii is known under the common names blue flies, blue stars, blue-eyed iris, or blue corn-lily.

Latinized form of Aristippos. Known bearers of this name include the ancient Greek philosopher Aristippus of Cyrene (4th century BC) and the ancient Greek tyrant Aristippus of Argos (3rd century BC).
Of uncertain origin and meaning. Theories include a feminine form of Aristide.

Possibly means "the best life" from the Greek elements ἄριστος (aristos) "best" and βίος (bios) "life" (compare Aristobios); alternatively, the second element may be Greek βία (bia) meaning "bodily strength, force; act of violence".

Sicilian form of Aristokles via it's Latinized form Aristocles.

Latinized form of the Greek name Ἀριστοκράτης (Aristokrates) meaning "the best power", from ἄριστος (aristos) "best" and κράτος (kratos) meaning "power, strength" (whence modern English aristocrat). This was the name of two Ancient Greek rulers of Orchomenus in Arcadia.
Latinized form of Aristokreon. This name was borne by a Stoic philosopher from the 2nd century BC.

Latinized form of Ἀριστόκριτος (Aristokritos), a Greek name meaning "the best judge" from the elements ἄριστος (aristos) meaning "best" and κριτής (krites) meaning "judge, critic". This was the name of several Ancient Greek people, including the father of Spartan general Lysander.

Derived from Greek ἄριστος (aristos) meaning "best" and γείτων (geiton) meaning "neighbour".
Derived from Ancient Greek ἄριστος (aristos) meaning "best" combined with γενής (genes) meaning "born" or "of a kind". This name was borne by two ancient Greek physicians from the 3rd century BC.
Derived from Ancient Greek ἄριστος (aristos) meaning "best" combined with κρέων (kreon) meaning "king, master, ruler" (also compare Kreon).

Derived from the Greek adjective ἄριστος (aristos) meaning "best" combined with the Greek noun λέων (leon) meaning "lion".

Derived from the Greek adjective ἀριστόλοχος (aristolochos) meaning "well-born", which consists of the Greek adjective ἄριστος (aristos) meaning "best" combined with the Greek noun λόχος (lochos) meaning "childbirth" as well as "ambush". Through the latter meaning, the word later came to signify a tactical sub unit of the ancient Greek army. It is the connection to combat and the military that usually made the ancient Greeks want to incorporate the word into given names (see names like Amphilochos, Astylochos and Hippolochos), but in some cases an exception was made, and this name is one of them.
Latinized form of Aristolochos. This name was borne by an Olympic victor from 344 BC.In Greek mythology, Aristolochus was one of the men who fought against Troy in the Trojan War.
Means "best battle", derived from Greek ἄριστος (aristos) "best" combined with Greek μάχη (mache) "battle."

column12: Japanese transliteration of Alice, in use among the Japanese since the 20th century, particularly in recent decades.This name can be used to combine 有 (yuu, u, a.ru, ari) meaning "exist" with 珠 (shu, tama, su) meaning "pearl, gem, jewel," 寿 (shuu, ju, su, kotobuki, kotobu.ku, kotoho.gu) meaning "congratulations, longevity" or 澄 (chou, su.mu, su.masu, -su.masu) meaning "lucidity."Examples of Arisu with 3 kanji include 亜利珠, 亜梨朱, 愛莉寿 and 愛里子 with 亜 (a, tsu.gu) meaning "come after, rank next," 愛 (ai, ito.shii, o.shimu, kana.shii, mana, me.deru, a) meaning "affection, love," 利 (ri, ki.ku) meaning "advantage, benefit, profit, gain," 梨 (ri, nashi) meaning "pear tree," 莉 (rai, ri, rei), part of 茉莉 (matsuri), which refers to the Arabian jasmine, 里 (ri, sato), referring to a unit of distance called ri, or otherwise meaning "village," 朱 (shu, ake, su) meaning "vermilion, cinnabar" and 子 (shi, su, tsu, ko, -ko, -ne) meaning "child."One fictional bearer of this name is Alice (or Arisu) Mizuki (瑞城 ありす), one of the main characters in the anime series Serial Experiments Lain.

Ariyori was the son of Saeki Ariwaka, the governor of Etchū Province (modern-day Toyama Prefecture). At the age of sixteen, he ventured into the Tateyama mountains, pursuing a white hawk. During this expedition he shot a bear who transformed into the Buddha Amitabha (Amida). This experience led Ariyori to ordain as a monk, taking the religious name Jikō, and he dedicated himself to spiritual pursuits on the mountain.Ariyori is said to have then established Tateyama as a sacred pilgrimage site embodying Buddhist concepts of hell (Jigoku) and paradise (Jōdo), represented by the mountain’s landscape. A notable legend involves his nurse, who accompanied him but couldn't complete the journey; in frustration, she cast aside her mirror, which transformed into the famous landmark known as the "Mirror Stone." His story was popularized through the Tateyama Mandalas—illustrated scrolls depicting scenes from his life and symbolizing spiritual enlightenment. Ariyori’s blending of Buddhist and Shinto beliefs reflects the religious syncretism characteristic of medieval Japan. Today, Ariyori’s legacy endures, drawing pilgrims and visitors to Tateyama, inspired by his symbolic narrative of transformation and spiritual commitment.

Georgian form of the Avestan name Arejahvant (also found written as Arejanghant, Arejanhant and Arejavan), which is derived from Avestan arej or arejah meaning "price, value, worth" combined with the Avestan suffix vant.

It is very common in India, and is commonly used as a ship name for Aryan and Sujini. It also has its origins in the Persian language, with the surname deriving from the word "Arjam," which refers to a region or locality in Iran.

At least one source lists this name as being a combination of the names Adrianus and Johannes, but it could also easily be a combination of a name starting with Ar- (such as Arend) with a name starting with Jo- (such as Jozef). It should also be noted that it is also possible that in at least some cases, Arjo is a short form of the names Arjan 1 and/or Arjen.In the Netherlands, a well-known bearer of this name is Arjo Klamer (b. 1953), a Dutch economist, professor and author.

Of uncertain origin and meaning; theories include a Hungarian form of Argus and a diminutive of Arkád.
Derived from either Greek ἀρκτικός (arktikos) "artic, northern" or from Greek ἄρκτος (arktos) "bear".
German and Russian form of Arcturus.
Of uncertain origin and meaning. It might be a direct adoption of the Scandinavian name Arla; however, it is also possible that Arla arose as an elaboration or quasi-Latinization of Arlie.
Transferred use of the surname Arland.
Probably a feminine form of Arland.

Either from the place name Arlandria or a combination of names beginning with Arl- and Andrea 2.This is the name of a 2011 song by American rock band Foo Fighters, referring to the neighbourhood where Dave Grohl lived. The song's release as the fourth single in the United Kingdom led to its rare usage there.
Possibly a quasi-Latinization of Roland via variants like Orlando.

Possibly derived from any of the Old Norse elements ár "year; plenty, abundance", ár "early", or ár "messenger" combined with laug "vowed, promised, bound in oath". It can also be an Icelandic variant of Arnlaug.
Altered form of Arlene. A known bearer of this name was Arlayne Brown (1916-1961), an American child sharpshooter.
Derived from the city of Arles in France.Fictional bearers of this name include Arle Nadja from "Puyo Puyo", and Arle Arisegawa from "The Ditzy Demons Are in Love With Me".
Contraction of армия Ленина (armiya Lenina) "army of Lenin".
English variant and Polish borrowing of Arlene.
Derived from Gaulish leno- "wood; grove, bosk".
Perhaps a blend of Arletta and Aletha.
Hungarian form of Arlette, as well as a Hispanic variant (compare Arleth).
English variant of Arlette and Polish variant of Arleta.

Most likely an adoption of the stage name of Léonie Marie Julie Bathiat (15 May 1898 – 23 July 1992), known professionally as Arletty. Arletty was a French actress, singer, and fashion model. She was found guilty of treason for an affair with a German officer during World War II, but she continued her career which included playing Blanche in the French version of A Streetcar Named Desire. Her stage name is a corruption of Arlette, which she took based on the heroine of a story by Guy de Maupassant.
Variant of Arlie. It has become specially popular in Colombia and Brazil, where it is considered a strictly masculine name.
Variant of Arley. As a feminine name, it can also influenced by the name Arelys.
Derived from Albanian ar "gold; treasure, gem; golden; precious" and lindje "east; birth" (compare lind) and thus commonly interpreted as "golden birth".
Derived from Albanian ar "gold; treasure, gem; golden; precious" and lindje "east; birth" (compare lind) and thus commonly interpreted as "golden birth".

Transferred use of the surname Arlington or from various places in America, so-called. A notable bearer of the name was American poet Edwin Arlington Robinson (1869-1935), who received the middle name when a man from Arlington, Massachusetts, was selected to pull a name out of a hat to bestow his first name, Edwin.
Transferred use of the surname Arliss.
Feminine form of the name Arlo.
Transferred use of the surname Arlotta.
Perhaps a feminine form of Arlo.
Possibly a variant of Arlen or Arline.
Variant of Arleen using the popular name suffix lynn.
Short form of Armas and Armo.
Feminine form of Armas and Armo as well as a variant of Armi.
Armaan is an arabic name also used in Pakistan. It means strong desire

Meaning & History: A modern African diasporic ancestral name meaning “one who stands rooted in strength and breathes courage.” It represents grounded bravery, inner fire, and ancestral stability.Etymology: ar – root, foundationmae – breath of courage, brave spiritUsage: African Diaspora (modern), spiritual name, legacy name.
Means "gift" in Persian. It is used as a feminine name in Iran while it is masculine in Pakistan.

Variant form of Armande, which was influenced or inspired by Latin, in that French names ending in -ce usually come from Latin names ending in -tius (for males) and -tia (for females). For example: Maxentius became Maxence in French and Constantia became Constance.With that said, you might want to take a look at the names Hermance and Hermande, which are quite similar in appearance and have the exact same etymology at the root.Also, it might be interesting to know that there is a river called Armance in France. It is one of the principal tributaries of the Armançon, a river located in the Burgundy region of France. Both their names are said to be of Celtic (or Gaulish, if you will) origin.Finally, in literature, Armance is the title of an 1827 romance novel written by Stendhal (1783-1842). The novel derives its name from Armance Zohiloff, one of the principal characters in the novel.
Italian feminine form of Armando and Slovene, Hungarian, Gascon and Provençal feminine form of Armand.
Medieval Italian diminutive of Armando, as -uccio is an Italian masculine diminutive suffix.
Feminine form of Ármann, equivalent to Hermine.

The first element of this name is derived from Lithuanian ar meaning "also, too, as well (as)". The second element is either derived from Lithuanian mantus meaning "intelligent" (see Daumantas) or from Lithuanian manta meaning "property, estate" as well as "wealth, riches, fortune".
Rare variant of French Armandine historically found in the Poitou-Charentes region.
Perhaps an invented name based on similar-sounding names such as Armani and Amari.

Possibly a Greek corruption of an Aramaic name meaning "cursed one, accursed one", likely related to Hebrew אָרַר (arar) meaning "to curse, to execrate". The Book of Enoch names him as a fallen angel, one of the 200 Watchers who copulated with human women.
A famous bearer of this name is Wayne Armartie Laryea (1952-) a British-born musician and actor with Ghanian ancestry.
Variation of Ramatha, an ancient name of Palestine.
Derived from Romanian armeancă "woman from Armenia".
Indonesian and Nigerian form of Ahmed.
Alternate transcription of Persian آرمین (see Armin 2).
Semi-Gallicized variant of Armela and French feminine form of Armel.
Feminine form of Armel. This name was borne by Armella Nicolas or La bonne Armelle (19 December 1606 – 24 October 1671), a Breton serving-maid important in French popular Catholic piety.
Derived from Albanian ar "gold" and mend "mind".

Possibly a feminine form of Arminius, the name of a 1st-century Cheruscan chief, which may be related to Herman. Also compare Arminia and Erminia. Alternatively, it could be taken from the name of the Eurasian country (see Armenia).
Spanish and Italian form of Armentarius.
Derived from Latin armentarius meaning "cow herder, cowboy, herdsman".
Derived from the Old Norse elements ár "year; plenty, abundance" and mey "maid, girl" (poetic for "daughter", an alternative form of mær), perhaps inspired by the masculine name Ármann.
Dutch and German variant form of Irmgard. This is one of the middle names of Queen Beatrix of The Netherlands (b. 1938), who was given this name in honour of her paternal grandmother.
Finnish and Estonian short form of Armida and Armilda. This name was borne by Armi Kuusela (b. 1934), Miss Universe 1952.
Possibly a variant form of Armias or Armi.

From Guanche *arəmis meaning "prey, trophy, loot", literally "arrest, seizure". This was the name of the last aboriginal king of the island of Hierro (present-day Canary Islands, Spain), who was ousted, captured and enslaved by the French conquistador Jean de Béthencourt in 1405. The Canarian-born Spanish footballer Armiche Ortega (1988-) is a known modern bearer of this name.
Diminutive of Armand. A known bearer of this name is American actor Armand "Armie" Hammer (b. 1986).
Finnish and Estonian form of Armida.
Dutch form of Armin (masculine) and Armina (feminine).

This name can be the Lithuanian form of the German name Armin as well as be an independent, authentic Lithuanian name. In the case of the latter, the name consists of Lithuanian ar meaning "also, too, as well (as)" combined with the Lithuanian verb minėti meaning "to celebrate" as well as "to remember, to commemorate".A known bearer of this name is the Lithuanian former soccer player Arminas Narbekovas (b. 1965).

Basically means "I don't want you", derived from the Georgian particle არ (ar) meaning "not, no" combined with Georgian მინდა (minda) meaning "I want".This name literally refers to the fact that the child in question was not desired by its parents.
Feminine form of Arminius. Also compare Armina and Erminia.
Italian and Spanish form of Arminius. Also compare Erminio.

The first element of this name is derived from Lithuanian ar meaning "also, too, as well (as)". The second element is derived from the Lithuanian noun mintis meaning "thought", which is related to the Lithuanian verb minti meaning "to remember, to recall".
Derived from Albanian ar "gold" and mirë "good".
Means "quiet; calm" in Persian from the word آرامش (ârâmeš) meaning "calmness; tranquillity; peace".
From the word, armistice, meaning "an agreement made by opposing sides in a war to stop fighting for a certain time; a truce." See also the name Armistice.
From the English word armistice meaning "truce, ceasefire", ultimately derived from Latin arma "arms" and -stitium "stoppage". This is the name of a character on the HBO series 'Westworld'.
Transferred use of the surname Armitage.
Altered form of Araminta. Also compare Arminta.
Means "of the palace, palatial" from Hebrew אַרְמוֹן (armon) "palace". In the Old Testament, Armoni was the son of King Saul by his concubine Rizpah.

Means "harmony" in Spanish. This name was brought to public attention by the novel 'Sembrando Flores' (1906) by Catalan anarchist Juan Montseny Carret, whose main characters are named Floreal and Armonía, and thus it came to be used by anarchist parents who were eager to reject traditional names during the Second Spanish Republic (1931-1939).
Meaning unknown. Could be a variant of Harmony or Armoni.
The name of a Gnostic angel and "aeon", identified in Sethian works.
Transferred use of the surname Armstrong.

Armulyn is a character in Andrew Peterson's Wingfeather Saga, a bard and freedom fighter. His name and character were inspired by popular singer Rich Mullins' first initial and last name (R. Mullins sounds like Armulyn).
Armynel was a popular name in 17th century Cornwall. It may be a diminutive of ARMINE, the English form of french ARMAND.
Variant of Arne 1. Arn Magnusson is a fictional character in the 'Crusades' trilogy (1998-2000) by Swedish author Jan Guillou.
Icelandic and Faroese form of Arna.
A notable bearer of this name was the American writer Arna Bontemps (1902-1973), who was born into a Louisiana Creole family. By some accounts, his birth name was Arnaud.
The spirit name of a group of Inuit from a particular region, meaning "a big woman", a spirit of the woman under the sea. Prominent in Inuit mythology.
It means "The Honored One" or "The Foremost One" or "The Highest One" in Hinduism and Buddhism
The birth name of the gluttonous beggar Irus (or Iros) from Homer's Odyssey.
From the name of a mountain in the town of Turrillas, Navarre, itself based on Basque haitz ("peak, boulder").
Means "fellow woman, girl friend, female friend" in Greenlandic.

In Inuit mythology, Arnakuagsak, meaning "old woman from the sea," was an Inuit goddess, one of the primary deities of the religion, who was responsible for ensuring the hunters were able to catch enough food and that the people remained healthy and strong.
French and Occitan variant of Arnaud.
Sicilian feminine form of Arnaldu and Gascon variant of Arnauda.
Icelandic and Faroese form of Arnaldr.
Greenlandic name of unknown meaning, possibly combination of Arnaluaĸ and suffix -nnguaq meaning "sweet, dear".
Greenlandic name of unknown meaning, maybe a combination of Arnaĸ and suffix -mineq meaning "little bit".
Greenlandic feminine name meaning "sweet little woman" (or perhaps "dear Arnaq"), derived from arnaq "woman" combined with the endearing diminutive suffix nnguaq.

Means "big bad woman". Arnapkapfaaluk was the sea goddess of the Inuit people living in Canada's Coronation Gulf area. Although occupying the equivalent position to Sedna within Inuit mythology, in that she had control of the animals of the seas, she was noticeably different as can be seen by the English translation of her name.
Greenlandic name meaning "little woman". Combination of Arnaĸ and suffix -raq meaning "young animal".

The Inuit goddess of the sea. According to most versions of the legend Arnarquagssaq, commonly known as Sedna, was once a beautiful mortal woman who became the ruler of Adlivun (the Inuit underworld at the bottom of the sea) after her father threw her out of his kayak into the ocean. Sedna's fingers, which her father had to cut off to keep her from clinging to the side of the boat, are often said to have turned into the first sea mammals. The other details of Sedna's story are told differently in different Inuit/Eskimo communities-- sometimes she provoked her father's rage by attacking him or violating cultural taboos, while other times her father was selfishly trying to save his own life by sacrificing Sedna.
Alternate transcription of Thai อาณัติ (see Anat).
The name is from the mythological concept of soul or name wandering: arnattartoq: arnattoq/arnappoq meaning "seeks a mother".
From Basque Arnatz, the name of a mountain in the town of Arbizu, Navarre.
Greenlandic name meaning "little woman". Combination of Arnaĸ and suffix -raq "young animal".
Modern Persian and Parsi form of Arənauuāčī.
Greenlandic feminine name with the combination of Arnaviaĸ and Greenlandic suffix -nnguaq "sweet, dear".
Transferred use of the surname Arnaz.
Derived from Old High German and Old Saxon arn meaning "eagle" and Old High German beraht, Old Saxon berht meaning "bright" from Proto-Germanic *berhtaz.
Derived from Old Norse ari or arn "eagle" combined with Old Norse björn "bear".
Danish, Norwegian and Faroese form of Arnbjörn.
Anglo-Scandinavian name derived from the Old Norse elements ǫrn "eagle" and brandr "fire, sword-blade".
Derived from Old Norse ari or arn "eagle" combined with Old Norse brandr "sword."
Derived from the Old Norse elements ǫrn "eagle" (genitive arnar) and dís "goddess".
Transferred use of the surname Arnell.
Variant of Arnell. This name recieved a boost in 1995, coinciding with the trial of Arnell Simpson's father, OJ Simpson.
This name is a combination of Arnel and Lyn.

Arnemetia's name contains Celtic elements are, meaning "against, beside," and nemeton, meaning "sacred grove." Her name is thus interpreted as "she who dwells in the sacred grove," suggesting Arnemetia may be a divine epithet rather than a name in its own right.
Used in Bosnia, borrowed from either German Arnold as a shoter nickname, or Norwegian Arne 1.
Silesian German variant of Ernst and Arnošt.
Transferred use of the surname Arnett.
Perhaps intended to be a feminine form of Arnold, using the Italian feminine diminutive suffix etta (compare Annetta, Netta 1).
Combination of Old Norse ǫrn "eagle" and vé meaning "holy, sanctuary".
Derived from Old Norse arn "eagle" combined with Old Norse fastr "firm, fast".

Modern Norwegian form of Arnfríðr, an Old Norse name derived from the elements arn "eagle" and fríðr "peace, love" or "beloved" (later "beautiful, fair"; compare Fríða, an Old Norse short form of Arnfríðr and other feminine names containing the element).
Combination of the Old Norse elements ǫrn "eagle" and fríðr "beautiful", originally "beloved".
Icelandic form of Arnfríðr and Faroese form of Arnfrøðr.
Derived from Old Norse ǫrn "eagle" and friðr "love, peace".
Norwegian and Icelandic form of Arngeirr.
Derived from Old Norse ari or arn "eagle" combined with Old Norse geirr "spear".
Old Swedish and Old Danish form of Arngeirr.
Derived from Old Norse arn "eagle" and gerd "enclosure".
Derived from the Old High German or Old Saxon element arn, Old Norse ǫrn meaning "eagle" and Proto-Germanic *geldą meaning "reward, gift, money".
Combination of Old Norse ǫrn "eagle" and gísl "pledge, hostage."

Anglo-Scandinavian variant of Arngrímr. This was the name of a berserker in Norse mythology; he figures in Hervarar saga, Gesta Danorum, Lay of Hyndla, a number of Faroese ballads, and Örvar-Odds saga.
Derived from Old Norse ǫrn "eagle" and grímr "person wearing a face mask".
Modern Icelandic and Faroese form of Arngrímr.
Norwegian and Faroese form of Arngunnr (see Æringunnr).
A dithematic name formed from the Germanic name elements arn "eagle" and haidu "kind, sort, type".It is borne by a female character in 'Vinland Saga', in this series the names are often Norwegian.
Derived from Old Norse ǫrn "eagle" and heiðr "honor".
Derived from the Germanic element arn meaning "eagle" combined with helm meaning "helmet, protection".
Derived from Old Norse ari or arn "eagle" combined with Old Norse hildr "battle".
Means "eagle-headed", derived from Old Norse ǫrn "eagle" and hǫfuð "head". This is a by-name for Odin.

Variant spelling of Arnika, though this name can also be directly derived from the name of the plant genus Arnica, which is ultimately of Greek origin.There might also be cases where Arnica is a combination of two existing names, such as Arnette and Monica.
Of unknown origin and meaning. Current theories include a variant of Armida and a combination of the Old Norse name elements ǫrn "eagle" and ið "industrious; work; activity".
Hungarian borrowing of Arnika. The name coincides with Hungarian árnika "arnica, leopard's bane".

Originally a Latinized diminutive form of names beginning with the element arn-, such as Arnhild, this name is used as a given name in its own right. It coincides with German Arnika "arnica, leopard's bane".

German name that first surfaced in the late 1800s. It was originally taken from the name of the town of Arnim near Berlin, later inspired by the surname of poet Bettina von Arnim and finally (mis)understood as a variant of Armin.

Derived from French arnique meaning "arnica" (as in, the plant). In other words, you could say that this name is a gallicization of Arnica.There might also be cases where Arnique is a combination of two existing names, such as Arnette and Monique.
Of uncertain origin and meaning. Theories include a feminine form of Arnis.
Old Norse name, combination of arn "bird" and ketillL "helmet."
Derived from Old Norse ari or arn "eagle" combined with Old Norse kettil "kettle, cauldron" (see also Kettil).
Derived from the Old Norse elements ǫrn "eagle" and laug "pool, hot spring" or the hypothetical word laug possibly meaning "vowed, promised, bound in oath".
Ancient Scandinavian male form of Arnlaug.

Derived from the Old Norse elements ǫrn "eagle" and lín "flax, linen". Alternatively the second element could be derived from Hlín (which occurs in many Old Norse poetic compounds meaning "woman") or Lína.
Old Swedish and modern Norwegian form of Arnljótr. This is also the feminine form, though usage nowadays appear to be exclusively masculine.
Old Norse combination of ǫrn "eagle" and ljótr "light".
Derived from the Germanic name elements ǫrn "eagle" and móðr "mind, spirit, courage".
Derived from Old Norse ǫrn "eagle" and mund "protection".
Derived from Old Norse ǫrn "eagle" and njóta "to use".
Alternate transcription of Bengali অর্ণব (see Arnab).
French form of Arnolphus. Arnolphe or 'Monsieur de la Souche' is the protagonist of the play L'école des femmes (1662) written by Molière.
From the name of a river mentioned in the Bible that most likely corresponds to the Wadi Mujib canyon stream in present-day Jordan. The name itself was possibly derived from a word meaning "noisy".
Alternate transcription of Thai อานนท์ (see Anon).
Northern and Eastern French variant of Arnaud.
Derived from the Old Norse elements ǫrn "eagle" and rós "rose".
Derived from the Old Norse elements ǫrn "eagle" and rún "secret lore, rune".
Etruscan male name of which the meaning is unknown.
Derived from the Germanic name elements ǫrn "eagle" and þjófr "thief".
Derived from the Germanic elements ǫrn "eagle" and þrúðr "strength".
Modern transcription of the Old Nose name Arnþrúðr.
Derived from the Germanic name elements ǫrn "eagle" and ulfr "wolf".
Variant of Arnulf derived from Latinized Arnolphus.
French form of Arnulf and variant of Arnoulf.
Norwegian and Swedish form of Arnold.
Relatively modern name (from 1908) created by combining the Old Norse name elements ǫrn "eagle" and veig "power, strength".
From Old English Earnwine, derived from Old English earn "eagle" and wine "friend".
Derived from Old Norse ár "year; plenty, abundance" and nýr "new", perhaps inspired by the masculine name Árni.
Variant of Arna or a combination of the Old Norse name elements ǫrn "eagle" and nýr "new".
Variant of Anya. Arnya Duchevnic was a character on the Australian 2001 situation comedy 'Flat Chat'.

column12: From Japanese 彩 (a) meaning "colour", 路 (ro) meaning "a road, a street" combined with 歩 (a) meaning "walk". Other kanji combinations are possible.
Means "warring king" or "forgotten king"; from aro meaning "face, forehead, sight; unknown, forgotten; to wage war" and ari'i meaning "king".
From Sarah J. Maas' Throne of Glass book series
A son of Gad according to Genesis 46:16 and Numbers 26:17. He was one of the 70 souls to migrate to Egypt with Jacob.

Meaning unknown.In medieval German literature, Arofel is the name of a character from the epic poem Willehalm (13th century) written by the German poet Wolfram von Eschenbach (died around 1220). He is the brother of king Terramer and the uncle of princess Arabel (who later changed her name to Gyburc).

column12: From Japanese 有 (aro) meaning "exist" combined with 葉 (ha) meaning "leaf". Other kanji combinations are possible.
The name of the goddess of mirages and shimmering heat. Her name may be related to the word ārohi meaning "to scout, reconnoitre".
Regional variant of Basque aukera "opportunity, occasion; choice".
Means "she who finally rules" in Meitei.
Occurs in the medieval Norwegian ballad 'Bendik og Årolilja', where it belongs to a princess who dies of heartache when her lover is hanged under her father's orders.
From Sino-Korean 我 (a) meaning "the self, the ego" and 論 (ron) meaning "theory".
Feminine form of Aron and masculine variant of Aruna.

A maidservant of Lady Galiene of Lothian in Guillaume le Clerc’s 'Fergus'.She set out to find a champion when Galiene’s castle, Roucebourc, was besieged, but, upon arriving at Arthur’s court, found that most of Arthur’s knights were on a quest to find the absent Sir Fergus.Arondele eventually located Fergus himself, who gladly agreed to serve as Galiene’s champion.She is called Lunette in the Dutch Ferguut.
Variant of Arona. This is also the name of a genus of deciduous shrubs, producing aronia berries, commonly known as chokeberry.
Alternate transcription of Hindi/Marathi अरुण or Thai อรุณ (see Arun).
MEANING : gentleness, calm or happy, freedom from anger. Here अ means free from + रोष means anger
Form of Harun. Possibly a name from the Kwa languages.
Low German form of Erpo.The organ builder Arp Schnittger was a known bearer of this name.
From Sanskrit अर्पण (arpaṇa) meaning "delivering, offering, dedicating".
Alternate transcription of Thai อาภาพร (see Aphaphon).
Alternate transcription of Thai อาภาพร (see Aphaphon).
Greenlandic name meaning "messenger". From Greenlandic arpappoq meaning "runs" (arpaartoq meaning "runs from house to house to give a message").
Derived from Armenian արփենի (arpʿeni) meaning "solar, bright, luminous".
Alternate transcription of Thai อาภาพร (see Aphaphon).
Alternate transcription of Thai อาภาพร (see Aphaphon).
One of the five sons of Shem, the son of Noah.
Alternate transcription of Armenian Արփինե (see Arpine 1).
From Sanskrit अर्पित (arpita) meaning "offered, delivered, entrusted".
Telugu and Kannada form of Arpita.
Catalan and Portuguese form of Archelaos (see Archelaus).
Spanish and Portuguese form of Archidamus.
Catalan, Galician and Portuguese form of Archimedes.
Catalan form of Archippos via its latinized form Archippus.
Spanish and Portuguese form of Archippos via its latinized form Archippus.
Italian and Spanish form of Arrhabaeus.
Sami combination of an unknown first element and Juoksa.

From the name of a mountain in the Spanish province of Gipuzkoa, where there is a sanctuary dedicated to the Virgin Mary. Its name is possibly derived from Basque harri "stone, rock" and ate "defile, gorge" or arte "space in between".
Variant of Aaron, possibly influenced by names like Darren.
Derived from Basque arren "request; please". Due to its meaning, it is understood as an equivalent to both Oración and Rosario.

Latinized form of the Ancient Greek given name Ἀρραβαῖος (Arrhabaios), which is probably a hellenised form of a Macedonian name of uncertain etymology. Perhaps related to the Proto-Indo-European root *wérsēn meaning "virile man" or "male animal, bull", or to Ancient Greek ἄραβος (arabos) meaning "gnashing, chattering (of teeth); ringing, rattling". This was the name of a king of Lynkestis who lived in the 5th century BC.

Latinized form of the ancient Greek given name Ἀρριδαῖoς (Arrhidaios), which might possibly be a variant form of the Greek given name Ἀρραβαῖος (Arrhabaios) (see Arrhabaeus). However, it's also possible that this is a name on its own, in which case the first element may possibly consist of the Greek prefix ar meaning "not, without" (similar to the word arrhythmia). The second element might then possibly be related to Ionic Greek rheidios meaning "easy, ready" (compare Attic Greek rhadios "easy, ready"), which is strenghtened by the fact that the spellings Arrhaidaios and Arrheidaios exist. Known bearers of this name include king Philip III Arrhidaeus of Macedon (4th century BC) and one of Alexander the Great's generals (4th century BC).
Feminine form of Arrius. Bearers of this name include Arria Major (wife of Caecina Paetus) and her daughter Arria Minor.
Italian and Spanish form of Arrhidaeus.
Catalan and Portuguese form of Arrhidaeus.
Used in the United States around the late 1800s and early 1900s. Similar to other popular names of the time ending in -ie Addie, Annie, Allie, and Abbie. Possibly influenced by Ari 1 and variants.
Possibly a variant of Harriet. This is the name of a character from 'The Borrowers' by Mary Norton.
Italian diminutive of Henry via Arrigo.
Italian diminutive of Henry via Arrigo.
Diminutive of Arrigo, as -otto is an Italian masculine diminutive suffix.
Corsican form of Henry via Arrigo.
Medieval Italian diminutive of Arrigo, as -uccio is an Italian masculine diminutive suffix.
Transferred use of the surname Arrington. The USA Social Security Administration has recorded 17 boys and 15 girls with the name Arringtion in 2001.
Italian form of Arrius.This name should not be confused with Ario, though it happens often.
Arrison is a modern, American name with no set meaning. It is a unisex variant of the masculine name, Harrison.

From the name of a sanctuary dedicated to the Virgin Mary in the Spanish province of Gipuzkoa, meaning "the place of the protruding stones". It has been used as a nom de plume by the Basque writer Julene Azpeitia (1888-1980).

Roman nomen gentile, which is ultimately derived from the Etruscan personal male name Arntni, of which the meaning is unknown. Also compare Arruns. A bearer of this name was Quintus Arrius, a Roman praetor from the 1st century BC.
A character from JRR Tolkien's works, a horse ridden by the mortal hero Húrin. The name is of uncertain etymology, but probably derived from the fictional Sindarin language.
Derived from Basque arrosa "rose", this name is considered the Basque equivalent of Rosa 1 and Rose.
Of debated origin and meaning. While the most widespread theory thinks of this name as a Basque form of Rosalie, other scholars link it to the Germanic name Rosalind.
Derived from Germanic hruod "glory" and stein "rock".
From the English word arrow, ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European *h₂érkʷo- "bow, arrow".
Means "facing the river" from ar "facing, on" and avon "waterway" in Cornish. Derived from the village of Arrowan in Cornwall.
Elaboration of Arrow using the suffix -wyn, similar to names like Bronwyn or Éowyn.
Latinized form of Arnth. Compare Arrius.
Feminine form of Arruntius. This name was borne by one of the Vestal Virgins.
Roman cognomen which was derived from Arruntius.

Roman nomen gentile, which is derived from the personal male name Arruns. This name was borne by several ancient Romans, such as the admiral and consul Lucius Arruntius the Elder and his son Lucius Arruntius the Younger, a senator.

From Greenlandic arrusaq meaning "small pelagic marine gastropod" (Latin name: "clione limicina") which is gelatinous and transparent, and shaped like little angels, having flapping "wings", hence their name in English: "sea angels".Arrusaq sometimes functioned as helping spirits for shamans in traditional society, varying in size from that of a hand to the size of a human. The name might have a connection to ataarpiaq meaning "real harp seal".
Possibly an alternate spelling of Aria 1 or Ariah.
Some uses of this name may be derivative of Aaron. It is also the name of one of the houses in 'The Song of Ice and Fire' series by George R. R. Martin.
French and Italian form of Arsaces.

From the Old Norse adjective ársæll meaning "happy in having good seasons, blessed in the year", composed of Old Norse ár "a year; plenty, abundance (esp. of crops)" and sæll "blissful, happy, blessed, fortunate".
Ancient Macedonian name of unknown meaning. In the Septuagint (Greek Old Testament), the name Arsaios appears in the Book of Esther, where it is a hellenization of Aridai (rather than Arisai).
Means "sender, messenger" from Arabic أرسل (ʾarsala) meaning "to send out, to dispatch".
Persian and Urdu form of Aslan.
Means "a hero's strength", derived from Old Persian aršan meaning "male, hero" and ama meaning "strength".
Hellenized form of Aršāma. This was the name of the paternal grandfather of Darius the Great, who possibly may briefly have been King of Persia.

Means "earthy", deriving from the Ugaritic element ‘arṣ ("earth, underworld"), combined with the feminine suffix y. Although her role is unknown, it is theorised that she was an underworld goddess. She was also possibly associated with water.
Likely an invented name based on the phonetic elements ar (cf. Arjay, Arshawn) and son.
Gascon and Picard form of Arsendis.
Coined by Sabino Arana Goiri and Koldo Elizalde as a Basque form of Arsenia.
The Moldovan form of Arsenios as well as a Russian alternate transcription of Арсений (see Arseniy).
Croatian and Serbian form of Arsenios via Arsenius.
Corsican and Sicilian form of Arsenios.

Hellenized form of Old Persian *R̥šā, derived from *(w)ŕ̥šā meaning "man, hero" or "stallion, stud" (an element used in Xerxes). This was the name of an Achaemenid Persian ruler, also known by the regnal name Artaxerxes.
Combination of Arshak and the feminine suffix ուհի (uhi).
Modern Persian and Armenian form of Aršāma.
Combination of the phonetic element ar and Shawn.
From Urdu عَرْش (ʻarś) or Hindi अर्श (arś) meaning "sky, heaven" (both of which come from Arabic عَرْش (ʕarš)) combined with Sanskrit दीप (dīpa) meaning "lamp, light".
Derived from Sanskrit ऋषि (ṛ́ṣi) denoting a singer of sacred hymns, a poet, or a sage.
Means "love for the sky" in Punjabi.
A Karelian form of Arsenios. Finnish name day March 4.
Masculine form of Arsinoe. This name occurs in Homer's Iliad belonging to the father of Hecamede, a slave or maidservant of King Nestor.
Greek form of the Old Persian name *R̥šitah, derived from *(w)r̥šā meaning "man, hero" or "stallion, stud" and‎ the hypocoristic suffix 𐎡𐎫 (-itaʰ⁠).
Older spelling of Arsyad influenced by Dutch orthography.
From Mongolian арслан (arslan) meaning "lion" and баатар (baatar) meaning "hero".

column3: Арсланбек(Kyrgyz, Kazakh, Turkmen Cyrillic, Uzbek Cyrillic)
column12: Derived from the Turkic noun arslan meaning "lion" (see Aslan) combined with the Turkish military title beg meaning "chieftain, master".Notable bearers of this name include the Turkmen boxer Arslanbek Açilow (b. 1993) and Arslanbek Sultanbekov (b. 1965), a Nogai folk musician and poet.
Derived from the Uzbek noun arslon meaning "lion", which is ultimately derived from Turkic arslan (see Aslan).
Tajik and Uzbek form of Arslanbek.
Short form of Arsenije. A known bearer of this name was the Montenegrin general Arsenije "Arso" Jovanović (1907-1948).

Possibly means "morning sun", from the Old Norse elements ár "early" and sól "sun". Alternatively, the first element may be Old Norse ár "year; plenty, abundance" (also found in the masculine name Ársæll).
Probably a spelling variant of Arsen. It coincides with the English word arson meaning "the criminal act of deliberately setting fire to property".
Meaning unknown. It maybe a diminutive of Ârssuákuluk or Ârssuatsiaĸ.
Derived from the Kyrgyz noun арстан (arstan) meaning "lion", which is ultimately derived from Turkic arslan (see Aslan).
Derived from Kyrgyz арстан (arstan) meaning "lion" combined with the Turkish military title beg meaning "chieftain, master".
Indonesian and Malay form of Arshad.

Possibly derived from the name of the city of Arta in southwestern Greece. A city with connections to Albania and Albanians. The name of the city is popularly held to be derived from Albanian artë "golden" (compare ar "gold")
Derived from Old Persian arta "truth, right, righteous" combined with Old Persian bānu "light, ray".
Latinized form of Artabānu via its Greek form Artabanos. This name was borne by at least four kings of Parthia.
Latinized variant of Artabazus or Artabrzana. It was the name of a prince and king of the Atropatene Kingdom who ruled in 221 BC or 220 BC
Latinized form of Artavazda via its Greek form Artabazos. This name was borne by two Persian satraps from Phrygia.
Greek form of an Old Persian name.
Derived from Old Persian arta "truth, right, righteous" combined with Old Persian farnah "glory, splendour, fortune".
A diminutive of the Gaelic name Artair, which is thought to mean "bear" or "stone". Also refers to the ancient Celtic word "art" which has three meanings: "a stone", "God" and "noble".

The name of an ancient goddess that was worshiped in Southern Gaul, in the region of Aquitania. She is a protector goddess that is thought to be associated with bears. The origin and meaning of her name are uncertain but appear to be of ancient Aquitanian origin and may be cognate with modern Basque arte "oak".
Irish form of Artemis, used in Irish translations of Greek myths.
Greek form of the Old Persian name *R̥tayah, derived from 𐎠𐎼𐎫 (arta) meaning "truth" and the adjectival suffix -𐎹 (⁠*-yaʰ⁠).

Derived from Old Persian arta "truth, right, righteous" combined with Old Persian kāma "desire, wish". A well-known bearer of this name was Artakama, the second wife of Ptolemy I Soter I; her husband was the founder of the Ptolemaic Kingdom in ancient Egypt.
Greek form of the Old Persian name *R̥takāma meaning "desiring Arta" or "wishing for truth", derived from 𐎠𐎼𐎫 (arta) meaning "truth" and 𐎣𐎠𐎶 (kama) meaning "wish, desire".
Catalan and Aragonese cognate of Artald.
Derived from Old High German hart "strong; hard" and Old High German walt "power, authority".
From Old Irish art meaning "bear" combined with a diminutive suffix.
Means "noble woman" in Quenya. Artanis was the given name of Galadriel, given to her by her father.
Hellenized form of Artafarnah. This was the name of a brother of King Darius I of Persia.
Shortened form of names beginning with Art-, like Artūras and Artemijus.
The name of a daughter of Cyrus the Great, meaning "pillar of Arta, the deified true".
Means "the people as well", derived from Lithuanian ar meaning "also, too, as well (as)" combined with Baltic tauta meaning "people, nation" (see Vytautas).
Means "doer of truth, justice" in Old Persian, derived from 𐎠𐎼𐎫 (arta) meaning "truth, righteousness" and *vard- "to do, work".
Meaning unknown. This name's only bearer was the wife of the crown prince Darius, who later committed adultery with Xerxes I. This name may be related to the similar masculine name Artayntes.

Meaning unknown. This name was borne by a commander of Xerxes I, who almost killed Xerxes' brother Masistes in an argument, but Masistes was saved by Xenagoras, who was given rule of Cilicia because of this. This name may be related to the Old Persian feminine name Artaynte.

Hellenized form of Old Persian *Artazauštrī meaning "who is in favor of Arta/Ṛta, the deified Truth" or "who is devoted to Arta". This name was borne by a Persian princess (5th century BC); Artazostre was the daughter of Darius the Great by his wife Artystone.
Shortened form of names beginning with Art-, like Artūra and Artemidė.

Basque name derived from arte.This word arte has several different meanings in Basque: "holm oak", "art; of art", "time; moment; span of time", "patience" as well as "difference; contrast".As a given name, Artea is most likely used in reference to the holm oak seeing as "nature names" used to be common given names in Basque culture and were rediscovered in the 20th century. In addition to this, holm oaks also had a special place in Basque folklore; they used to be planted at the entrance of farmsteads to protect the home and its inhabitants.
Means High valor/HonorAlso A Name of A Character in The Faerie Queene
Of uncertain origin and meaning; theories include a variant of Adelia, reflecting the Appalachian pronunciation.
Possibly a Latinized form of Arthur or a masculine form of Arthelais.

Presumably a short form or contraction of Artemidoros (compare Zenas, Alexas, Phileas). This name is mentioned briefly in the New Testament, in Saint Paul's letter to Titus. According to George Rippey Stewart in American Given Names (1979): 'It is chiefly remembered from General Artemas Ward, of the Revolution (born 1727). But there are other examples. In the mid-19th century the humorist C. F. Browne took Artemus (thus spelled) as his pseudonym.'
Languedocian and Gascon form of Artemios.
Italian and Spanish feminine form of Artemio, Sicilian feminine form of Artemiu and Polish feminine form of Artemiusz.

Uncertain etymology, possibly derived from the name of the goddess Artemis, or perhaps the Ancient Greek word ἀρτεμής (artemes) meaning "safe, unharmed, perfectly healthy". In Greek mythology, Artemiche was a young noblewoman whose family angered Apollo, and was turned into a bird by Artemis and Leto to save her from death.
Form of Artemis in various languages.
Georgian and Italian form of Artemis.In Georgia, Artemide is an alternative name for the Greek goddess: the standard Georgian name for her is Artemida.
German and Polish form of Artemidoros.
Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Artemidoros.
Spanish, Albanian and Galician form of Artemis.
Portuguese form of Artemisius via Artemisios.
Ukrainian form of Artemisia. Artemiziya Halytska (1912-1985) was an Ukrainian nationalist.
Italian and Latinized form of Artemon.

Likely from Artois, the name of a region in France (for which "artesian wells" are named), itself derived from Atrebates, a Belgic tribe that inhabited the region of Gaul and Britain during Julius Caesar's time; Atrebates is cognate with Irish aittrebaid meaning "inhabitant".In the Elizabethan play The Birth of Merlin, this is the name of the sister of the Saxon leader Ostorius, who used her wiles to seduce King Aurelius Ambrosius of Britain, blinding him to the gradual Saxon invasion of his kingdom. Uther Pendragon discovered her treachery, but she managed to have Aurelius banish his brother from court. In the end, Artesia and her brother betrayed and murdered Aurelius. When Uther reclaimed the kingdom, he had Artesia executed.
Variant of Arthur, used in Andrew Peterson's Wingfeather Saga. The character was inspired by the author's brother, Arthur.
The name of a character from the online game 'World of Warcraft'. It is obviously derived from the name Arthus.

In Sepnser's "The Faerie Queene", Arthegall is a brave knight who is first introduced as the lady knight Britomart’s future husband in Book III and who later goes on his own journey as the protagonist of Book V (in order to free Eirena from the clutches of Grantorto), where he represents the virtue of justice. Though Arthegall is bested by Britomart when they meet and fight due to a case of mistaken identity, he is a strong knight whose ideas about justice are strict and uncompromising. He rides with a metal man at his command named Talus who sometimes fights on his behalf, and he wields a powerful sword known as Chrysaor. Although Arthegall is ultimately a heroic character, he does occasionally go too far and has to be held back from slaying too many people. This demonstrates how justice can be tricky to carry out, even for a great knight like Arthegall.
Derived from Cornish arth "bear" (ultimately from Proto-Celtic *arto- "bear").

Saint Arthelais (544–560) is venerated as a Christian saint.Daughter of Roman imperial proconsul Lucius and Aithuesa. The emperor Justinian desired her, but she had taken vows of holy chastity and so fled to Benevento, Italy where she stayed with her uncle Narses Patricius. En route she was kidnapped by highway men, but was miraculously freed after three days.
Possibly a blend of Arthur and Othello.
Derived from Welsh arth "bear" (ultimately from Proto-Celtic *arto- "bear") and geni "to be born".

Arthi is a Balmiki ritual, similar in form to the Hindu practice of Aarti in which light from wicks soaked in ghee or camphor is offered to Bhagawan Valmiki. Arthi is a form of bhakti devotion. The word also refers to the traditional devotional song that is sung during the ritual.-------------------------------------Aarti also spelled arti, arati, arathi, aarthi (In Devanagari: आरती ārtī) - Hindu religious ritual of worship, a part of puja, in which light from wicks soaked in ghee (purified butter) or camphor is offered to one or more deities. Aarti is derived from the Sanskrit word ārātrika (आरात्रिक), which means something that removes rātrī, darkness (or light waved in darkness/night) Another word from which Aarti is thought to be derived is the Sanskrit word Aaraartikyam (Sanskrit: आरार्तिक्यं)
Alternate transcription of Thai อาทิตยา (see Athittaya).
Possibly intended as a feminization of Arthur.

In Guillaume le Clerc’s 'Fergus', the nephew of a malevolent king who besieged Lady Galiene of Lothian in the castle of Rocebourc.Galiene obtained the services of Sir Fergus, Arthur’s knight, as her champion. Fergus slew Arthofilaus and defeated his uncle.In the Dutch Ferguut, Arthofilaus becomes Macedone.

A Hindu feminine given name; it is derived from the Hindu religious ritual with the same name.
Invented name, possibly intended as a variant of Artie following the stress pattern of Mikia and Takia.

Transferred use of the surname Artigas, given in honour of political leader, military general and statesman José Gervasio Artigas (1764-1850), a national hero of Uruguay and the wider Rio de la Plata region.
Meaning unknown. Possibly influenced by Artemise.

Likely deriving from the name of the goddess Arti, with the elements paya ("pasture") and pati ("lord") (both of which stem from a common root). This was the name of a major Scythian goddess of fertility, warfare, and sovereignty. She was equated by Herodotus of Halicarnassus with Aphrodite Ourania.
Derived from the Gaulish word artos "bear".Artio was a Gaulish goddess worshipped by the Helvetii and Treveri.

Azerbaijani name of Turkic origins, derived from the name elements ar, "man", and togrul, "to justify oneself", with the intended meaning of "man who justifies himself". This was the name of an ancient Turkic leader, Artogrul bey, who was the father of Osman bey, founder of the Ottoman state.
Variant of the Russian name Artyom.
Derived from Albanian artor, an archaic term for a farmworker who works in the fields.

Variant of Artorius used for a character in the 2012 video game Dark Souls: Artorias of the Abyss.Name of one of Gwyn, the lord of Cinder's knights, fought the abyss with his beloved Dog Sif, whom he trapped to save her/him from the abyss.

From the Etruscan praenomen Arnthur, of uncertain etymology. It may have been borrowed from the Messapic name Artas/Artorres. This name eventually became the Roman gens Artoria, of which multiple members have been found in inscriptions. It has been speculated that Artorius was the origin of the Welsh name Arthur.

Of debated origin and meaning. While some scholars propose a derivation from the Etruscan praenomen Arnthur, perhaps Latinized as Artor, others have proposed a Messapic origin, identifying a nomen Artorres, said to mean "descendant of Artas". Lucius Artorius Castus (fl. 2nd century AD), a Roman military commander, has been suggested as a potential historical basis for King Arthur.

one of the Armenian dynasties Significance: Arts, which comes from the eagle, and run - blood.It symbolizes Power, courage.

The most likely possibility is that the first element is derived from Proto-Germanic aran or arna "eagle" (ara in Gothic and arn in Old High German). However, it might also come from Old High German êra "honour, respect" (see Eraric) or from Old High German hari "army" (with reduction of the "h"). The second element in the name is derived from Gothic vulfs "wolf."

From Thai อรุณ (arun) meaning "dawn, daybreak, sunrise" and รัตน์ (rat) meaning "gem, jewel".
