A traditional feminine name of Turkic origin, predominantly used within the Karakalpak and Kazakh nominal systems. The name is an authentic Kipchak-Nogay compound formed by two distinct elements:Aruv (арув): The modern Karakalpak and Nogay phonetic realization of the Common Turkic root $arïg$ (or $*arïq$), meaning "pure," "clean," "virtuous," or "physically beautiful." This specific sound shift ($-ıg/-ıq \rightarrow -uv$) distinguishes it from the Southeastern/Karluk branches (which favor ariq) and Southwestern/Oghuz branches (which favor arı).Khan (хан / қан): The historical Central Asian sovereign title khan or qan ("ruler," "monarch"). While traditionally masculine in political administration, it has a deep, documented history across Eurasian nomadic dynasties as a prestigious feminine suffix used to denote noble or high-born lineage.Modern comparative historical linguistics and Hunnolo-Turkological studies identify Aruvkhan as the direct, living linguistic continuation of the Proto-Turkic compound $*arïyqan$ ("the pure princess/ruler").This ancient compound is famously recorded in 5th-century Byzantine diplomatic manuscripts by the historian Priscus of Panium, who visited the court of Attila the Hun in 448 AD and recorded the name of Attila's chief Empress as Erekan (also transliterated as Herekan). In Western traditions and secondary Germanic heroic legends, this original name was later contracted and popularized as Kreka (or Herka/Helche).The phonetic evolution from the 5th-century Hunnic primary recording to the modern Karakalpak name follows established morphophonemic laws of the Steppe languages, proving that the modern name directly preserves the Empress's true title: Hunnic (Priscus's Greek Transcription): Erekan : Proto-Turkic *Arï(y)-qan > Middle Turkic: Arïg-khan > Modern Karakalpak: Aruvkhan
Means "pansy" in Hungarian. This was used by the Hungarian author Zsigmond Móricz for his 1940 novel of the same name.

Invented name using the popular elements ar (present in Arshawn), vay (like in Vayda and Vayla) and ya. This name was brought to attention in 2021 by American vloggers Ebonie and Byron Baxter Sr., who used it for their newborn daughter.

The first element of this name is derived from Lithuanian ar meaning "also, too, as well (as)". The second element is derived from the old Lithuanian verb vaidyti meaning "to visit, to appear", which is related to the modern Lithuanian verb vaidentis meaning "to haunt" as well as "to appear, to see". Also compare modern Lithuanian vaiduoklis meaning "ghost, apparition" and vaidytis meaning "to quarrel, to wrangle".
Means "early awake, early rising". This is the name of one of Sól's horses in Norse mythology.
Means "(to) rule as well", derived from Lithuanian ar meaning "also, too, as well (as)" combined with Baltic vald meaning "rule" (see Visvaldas).
From Old Persian *arvāh meaning "swift" and 𐎱𐎠𐎫 (pātaʰ) meaning "protected".

Arvazena Cooper was an Oregon pioneer, she traveled the Oregon Trail and settled in the Willamette Valley. She was born in North Carolina according to Wikipedia. She and her sister Melzena were the namesakes of Zena, Oregon, now a ghost town.

Basically means "I had not expected you", derived from the Georgian particle არ (ar) meaning "not, no" combined with Georgian ველოდი (velodi) meaning "I expected", which ultimately comes from the verb ლოდინი (lodini) meaning "to expect, to await".This name literally refers to the fact that the child in question was unexpected by its parents.
A short form of names containing arv, such as Arvilla
Derived from the word Ayurveda the traditional Hindu system of medicine, which is based on the idea of balance in bodily systems and uses diet, herbal treatment, and yogic breathing.
Variant of Arvel, possibly meaning "wept over".
Means "(to) hope as well", derived from Lithuanian ar meaning "also, too, as well (as)" combined with Baltic vil meaning "hope" (see Viltautas).
Unknown, possibly related to Arvel. In the 2007 film "Bonneville" Jessica Lange played Arvilla Holden, a widow on a road trip to deliver her late husband's ashes to California.
Either a Scandinavian form of Arwin (see Erwin) or a combination of the Old Norse name elements ari "eagle" and vinr "friend".
Means "abundant riches" in Mongolian, from арвин (arvin) meaning "copious, abundant" and баян (bayan) meaning "rich, wealthy".
Means "copious talent" in Mongolian, from арвин (arvin) meaning "copious, abundant" and билэг (bileg) meaning "gift, talent, aptitude".
Means "abundant virtue, copious good luck" in Mongolian, from арвин (arvin) meaning "rich, copious, abundant" and буян (buyan) meaning "good deed, virtue, charity" or "fortune, blessing".
Alternate transcription of Hindi/Marathi अरविन्द or अरविंद, Kannada ಅರವಿಂದ or Punjabi Gurmukhi ਅਰਵਿੰਦ (see Aravind).
Means "abundant light" in Mongolian, from арвин (arvin) meaning "rich, copious, abundant" and гэрэл (gerel) meaning "light".
Means "abundant flowers" in Mongolian, from арвин (arvin) meaning "rich, copious, abundant" and цэцэг (tsetseg) meaning "flower".
Means "abundant happiness" in Mongolian, from арвин (arvin) meaning "rich, copious, abundant" and жаргал (jargal) meaning "happiness, blessing".

Possibly a Latinized form of an old Celtic name, composed of the elements ard "high, paramount" and rhaig "king". This was the name of a legendary, possibly historical, British king of the 1st century AD. References to him appear in a poem by Juvenal; Geoffrey of Monmouth's Historia Regum Britanniae; William Shakespeare's Cymbeline; and Geoffrey Chaucer's Canterbury Tales.
Form of Arvīds. First recorded in 1943.
Means "increasing joy" in Mongolian, from арвижих (arvijikh) meaning "to accumulate" and баяр (bayar) meaning "joy, celebration".
Means "increased virtue" in Mongolian, from арвижих (arvijikh) meaning "to accumulate" and буян (buyan) meaning "good deed, virtue, charity" or "fortune, blessing".
Means "increased happiness" in Mongolian, from арвижих (arvijikh) meaning "to accumulate" and жаргал (jargal) meaning "happiness, blessing".

Means "to wither as well", derived from Lithuanian ar meaning "also, too, as well (as)" combined with the Lithuanian verb vysti meaning "to wither, to wilt, to fade". Also compare the similar-looking Lithuanian verb išvysti meaning "to see" (and therefore also Arvydas).

Derived from Old English ār "honour, glory" (from aizō) and weald "powerful, mighty" or "authority, leader". This was the name of the last King of the Isle of Wight and last pagan king in Anglo-Saxon England.
Alternate transcription of Thai อาวุธ (see Awut).
Variant of Arwen, unrelated to the Welsh name Arwyn.
From Sanskrit अर्य (arya) meaning "excellent, best, master, lord" and देव (deva) meaning "god". This was the name of a 2nd or 3rd-century Buddhist monk and scholar.
Sanskrit name originating from the Hindu deity Aryaman. Means 'companion' or 'close friend'.
Derived from Sanskrit आर्य (ārya) meaning "noble, honourable".
Combination of the name Aryan and Persian شاه (shāh) meaning "king".
Possibly deriving from the Sanskrit elements ārya (“noble”), and varman ("armour, protection").

In ancient Greece he was King of the Molossians in the 4th century BCE. He was the son of King Alcetas I, brother of Neoptolemus I, and grandfather of Pyrrhus.This was also the name of one of the bodyguards of Alexander the Great.
From a Lydian name that was cognate with the Hittite term 𒂖 (arawanni-) meaning "free" as in a free person, not a slave. This was the name of the wife of Astyages, the last king of the Median Empire.
Possibly derived from Amaryllis or a variant of Ariel.
Variant of Erin or Aaron (See also Aaryn and Arin).
Ukrainian variant and Belarusian form of Arina.
From the Javanese noble title arya meaning "respected, esteemed, noble", ultimately from Sanskrit आर्य (ārya).
From Javanese aryana meaning "mind, sense, reason".
Greek form of the Old Persian name *Aruša meaning "white".
Means "lion" in Kazakh, ultimately from Turkic arslan.
From Kazakh арыстан (arystan) meaning "lion" and the Turkish military title beg meaning "chieftain, master".
Polish form of Aristippos via its latinized form Aristippus.
Derived from Buryat ариун (ariun) meaning "pure, clear".

Biblical Hebrew male name given in 1 Kings 16:9, of a steward of Zimri. The name is transliterated from the Biblical Hebrew אַרְצָא (‘arza’), meaning “Earth” or “Earthy.” From אֶרֶץ (‘eretz’), meaning “earth,” “land.”
Derived from Tuvan аржаан (arzhaan) meaning "water spring, stream".
Possibly from arzi- meaning "to merit, to deserve".
Possibly derived from the Punjabi noun ਅਰਜ਼ (arz) meaning "petition, supplication, request".
Means "my wish, my desire", from Turkish and Azerbaijani arzu meaning "wish, desire" (of Persian origin) and the first person singular possessive suffix -m.
Means "desirable man", from Persian آرزو‎ (ârezu) meaning "desire, wish, hope."

column3: 朝, 麻(Japanese Kanji)|あさ(Japanese Hiragana)
column12: Derived from the Japanese kanji 朝 (asa) meaning "morning" or 麻 (asa) meaning "hemp, flax".Other kanji combinations are also possible.
Alternate transcription of Arabic أسعد (see As'ad).

Means "the land is finished" in Akan. The implication of this name is that there is no more land for the dead to be buried - so the child is encouraged to live as there will be no more space for his/her burial.
Means "one selected for birth" in Yoruba.
Means "best of the Æsir". This is a by-name for Odin and Thor in Norse mythology.

아사달(阿斯達)(Asadal) is a place name recorded in the Samguk Yusa where it is said that Tangun established and ruled the capital of Gojoseon(? ~ 108 BCE). There is a theory that Joseon(朝鮮) is a semantic transliteration of Asadal.There is also a story about a stonemason from Baekje named Asadal, who is said to have constructed the Seokgatap (Stone Pagoda) of Bulguksa Temple in Silla. He is known through the tale of Asadal and his wife Asanyeo(阿斯女).
Alternate transcription of Thai อัษฎาวุธ (see Atsadawut).
Alternate transcription of Thai อัษฎาวุธ (see Atsadawut).
From Arabic أسد (ʾasad) meaning "lion" or أسعد (ʾasʿad) meaning "happier, luckier" combined with the Turkic military title beg meaning "chieftain, master".
West African form and rare feminine form of Asad.
Masculine name in the Rotooro language, Uganda East Africa.
Alternate transcription of Bengali আসাদুজ্জামান (see Asaduzzaman).
Tajik and Uzbek form of Asadullah.
From the Arabic phrase أسد الزمان (ʾasad az-zamān) meaning "lion of the era", derived from أسد (ʾasad) meaning "lion" combined with زمان (zamān) meaning "time, age, era".
From the given name Asad meaning "lion" combined with xo'ja meaning "master".
From Japanese 亜 (a) meaning "second, Asia", 沙 (sa) meaning "sand" combined with 絵 (e) meaning "picture, painting, drawing, sketch". Other kanji combinations are possible.
Greek form of Asahel, as it first appeared in the Septuagint.
Derived from Old Norse áss "god" and alfr "elf".

column3: 朝右衛門(Japanese Kanji)|浅右エ門(Kanji/Katakana)
あさぎ(Japanese Hiragana)|アサギ(Japanese Katakana)|浅黄, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 浅黄 (asagi) meaning "light yellow". It combines 浅 (asa) meaning "light, pale" with 黄 (ki) meaning "yellow". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: 朝治, 朝春, 朝陽, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 朝 (asa) meaning "morning" combined with 治 (haru) meaning "govern, regulate, administer", 春 (haru) meaning "spring" or 陽 (haru) meaning "light, sun, male". Other kanji combinations are possible.

Means "made by God" in Hebrew.In the Bible, Asahel was the nephew of King David, as well as the younger brother of Abishai, David's General, and of Joab. Asahel is mentioned in the book of 2 Samuel in Chapters 2 and 3.

column3: 朝日子, 朝彦, 旭子, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: It comes from Japanese 朝 (asa) meaning "morning" combined with 彦 (hiko) meaning "boy, prince". Other kanji combinations are possible as well.

column3: 朝日奈, 朝比奈, etc.(Japanese Kanji)

column12: Asa can mean "morning" or "river shallow", and hiro can mean "wide, spacious, broad".

column3: 紹人, 麻人, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 紹 (asa) meaning "introduce" or 麻 (asa) meaning "flax" combined with 人 (hito) meaning "person". Other kanji combinations are possible.
Means "Yahweh has made" or "made by Yahweh" in Hebrew. This was the name of several characters in the Old Testament.

column3: 麻一, 旭一, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 麻 (asa) meaning "flax" combined with combined with 一 (ichi) meaning "one". Other kanji combinations can be used.

column3: アサカ(Japanese Katakana)|朝香, 朝霞, 阿咲佳, 亜咲花, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 阿 (a) meaning "nook, corner", 咲 (sa) meaning "blossom", and 霞 (ka) meaning "mist, cloud". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: 朝月, 朝咲, 朝姫, 朝希, 朝喜, 朝葵, 浅黄, 央実貴, 旭輝, 旭岐, 亜咲希, 歩咲, 綺々, 綺咲姫, etc.(Japanese Kanji)|あさき(Japanese Hiragana)
column12: From Japanese 朝 (asa) meaning "morning" combined with 月 (ki) meaning "moon" or 咲 (ki) meaning "blossom". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: 麻子, 朝子, etc.(Japanese Kanji)|あさ子(Kanji/Hiragana)|あさこ(Japanese Hiragana)|アサコ(Japanese Katakana)
column12: From Japanese 麻 (asa) meaning "flax" or 朝 (asa) meaning "dynasty, imperial court" combined with 子 (ko) meaning "child". This name can be formed from other combinations of kanji as well.
Derived from asal meaning "honey" and bonu meaning "lady".
Norwegian, Icelandic, and Estonian form of Azalea.
Derived from asal meaning "honey" and gul meaning "flower, rose".
Variant spelling of Azalia. A known bearer of this name is Asalia Nazario, the Puerto Rican mother of American actress Zoe Saldana (b. 1978).
Derived from asal meaning "honey" and oy meaning "moon".
From asal meaning "honey" and poshsha, an endearing epithet used for women and girls.
Means "she is still beautiful" in Nguni.
Asame means morning beauty" or "beautiful dawn".
Means "apostles" in Akan. It is also a surname. A famous bearer is Ghanaian soccer player Asamoah Gyan (1985-).
This name means "has no equal" in Sanskrit.

Kazakh, Crimean Tatar and Georgian form of Hasan. A known Georgian bearer was prince Asan-Mirza of Kakheti (died in 1750), the third son of king Davit II of Kakheti.The etymology might possibly be the same in Bulgaria. A known Bulgarian bearer is the former soccer player Asan "Asensi" Abishev (b. 1957).

column3: あさな(Japanese Hiragana)|愛紗南, 旭菜, 朝南, 麻菜, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: The name Asana is a derivative of Hassan. In Northern Ghana, it is the name given to the second born of a pair of twin girls. The first born twin is named Fuseina According to superstition, the second twin is considered to be the older twin because it is said that during the trauma of birth, the older twin send the younger twin ahead to make sure the world is safe.Male versions of the names are Alhassan and Fuseini.
Latinized form of Asandros. This was the name of a governor of Lydia, who lived in the 4th century BC.
Italian and Spanish form of Asander.

Possibly derived from Ancient Greek ἆσαι (asai), an inflected form of ἄω (ao) "to satiate" ultimately related to ἥδομαι (hedomai) "to be pleased, enjoy oneself", combined with ἀνδρός (andros) "of a man". Alternatively, the first element could instead be the related ἀσάω (asao) "to take a surfeit, to glut oneself".
From Japanese 晨 (asa) meaning "dawn; morning; daybreak" combined with 野 (no) meaning "area". Other kanji combinations are possible.
Possibly derived from Swahili asante "thank you".

아사녀(阿斯女)(Asanyeo) is a wife of Asadal, a stonemason from Baekje. They are known through the tale of Asadal and Asanyeo, which takes place during the construction of the Seokgatap (Stone Pagoda) of Bulguksa Temple in Silla.
Faroese and Icelandic form of Asher.
One of the Asaphites appointed by David to the temple service.

Derived from asar (or Aššur) meaning the god Ashur, the chief deity of the Assyrian pantheon and haddon (or Addu) meaning the brother, the benefactor. Asarhaddon (or Esarhaddon) was the king of the Neo-Assyrian Empire from 681 BCE until his death in 669 BCE.

column3: あさり(Japanese Hiragana)|アサリ(Japanese Katakana)|亜沙梨, 亜沙里, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From the Japanese kanji 亜 (a) meaning "second, Asia" combined with 沙 (sa) meaning "sand" and 梨 (ri) meaning "pear" or 里 (ri) meaning "village". Other kanji combinations are also possible.As a vocabulary word, アサリ (asari) refers to the Ruditapes philippinarum, the Japanese littleneck or Manila clam.
From Japanese 浅 (asa) meaning "shallow", 三 (sabu) meaning "three" combined with 郎 (rou) meaning "son". Other kanji combinations are possible.
From Japanese 旦 (asa) meaning "morning, dawn" combined with 咲 (saki) meaning "blossom". Other kanji combinations are possible.

From Greenlandic asassaĸ meaning "dear, loved one"-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------Derived from Greenlandic asavaa meaning "love him/her/it" with the passive participle "-saĸ"

column3: 麻太郎, 朝太郎, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 麻 (asa) meaning "hemp" or 朝 (asa) meaning "morning" combined with 太 (ta) meaning "plump, thick, big", and 郎 (ro) meaning "son". Other kanji combinations can be used.

column3: アサト(Japanese Katakana)|あさと(Japanese Hiragana)|麻人, 吾左音, 彩沙仁, 亜砂斗, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 朝 (asa) meaning "morning" combined with 人 (to) meaning "person". Other kanji combinations are possible.
The name of a raga or melody. This name belongs to a minor character in Hinduism, a lover of Karna whose father, the king, rejects their marriage out of arrogance.
Means "they still appear" in Xhosa. A famous bearer is South African actress Asavela Mngqithi.
Alternate transcription of Thai อัศวิน (see Atsawin).

column3: 朝也, 朝弥, 麻矢, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 朝 (asa) meaning "morning" or 麻 (asa) meaning "flax" combined with 也 (ya) meaning "also", 哉 (ya), an exclamation or 矢 (ya) meaning "arrow". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: あさよ(Japanese Hiragana)|アサヨ(Japanese Katakana)|あさ代(Kanji/Hiragana)|亜佐世, 亜佐代, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 亜 (a) meaning "second, Asia", 佐 (sa) meaning "aid, help" combined with 世 (yo) meaning "world". Other kanji combinations are possible.
From Japanese 朝 (asa) meaning "morning" combined with 喜 (yoshi) meaning "rejoice". Other kanji combinations are possible.
From Japanese 朝 (asa) meaning "morning" combined with 雪 (yu) meaning "snow". Other kanji combinations are possible.

Form of Ashbel used some older English translations of the Old Testament, including the Tyndale Bible, the Bishops' Bible (1568) and the Douy-Rheims Bible.Fictional bearers include Asbel from the movie Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind and Asbel Lhant, the protagonist of Tales of Graces. A known real life bearer is Asbel Kiprop, a Kenyan middle-distance runner and Olympics gold medallist.
The name Asbina is a very unique and rare name hence why it’s special. The true meaning of Asbina is The Guided One, the one who strives after guidance.
Derived from the Old Norse name elements áss "god" and bjǫrg "help, save, rescue".

Means "soot" in Ancient Greek. Asbolus was the name of a centaur prophet who read omens in the flight of birds in Greek mythology. A small planetoid (called a centaur) was named after him. It was also the name of one of Actaeon’s dogs.
Derived from Old Norse áss "god" combined with Old Norse brandr "sword."

Transferred use of the surname Asbury, commonly used in America, possibly in honour of British-American Methodist minister Francis Asbury (1745-1816). A famous bearer of the name was American serial killer Asbury Respus (1878-1932).
From a diminutive of an Old Norse name, possibly Ascall or Ásketill.

German and Danish form of Ascanius. It can also be a younger form of an ancient Germanic name that consists of the elements asc meaning "ash tree" and wini meaning "friend".Known bearers of this name include the German landscape painter Ascan Lutteroth (1842-1923) and the German author Ascan von Bargen (b. 1976).

Uncertain etymology, coincides with Ancient Greek ἄσκαρος (askaros) meaning both "castanet (musical instrument)" and "kind of shoe". Ascarus was a sculptor of ancient Thebes, who made a statue of the Greek god Zeus.
Feminine form of Ascelin. This was the name of a 12th-century French saint, a Cistercian mystic.
Late Latin for "armpit", related to the Indo-European root *aks meaning "axis". This is the name of the third brightest star in the constellation Sagittarius.
Variant of Ascensión used outside of Spanish speaking countries, among both genders.
Variant or short form of Ascher.
Besides Aschenputtel, another name for Cinderella in German.
Means "digging in the ashes" in German. This is the German name for Cinderella used by the Brothers Grimm.

Derived from the Greek noun ἀσχολία (ascholia) meaning "occupation, business, engagement". Also compare the Greek adjective ἄσχολος (ascholos) meaning "busy, engaged, without leisure".This was the name of a 4th-century bishop of Thessaloniki in northern Greece, who is venerated as a saint in the Eastern Orthodox Church.

Dutch and German form of Answin. A known bearer of this name is Prince Constantijn of the Netherlands (b. 1969), who carries the name Aschwin as a middle name, in honour of his maternal grandfather's only brother, Aschwin zur Lippe-Biesterfeld (1914-1988).
Catalan form of Asklepios via Asclepius.
French form of Asklepiades via it's Latinized form Asclepiades.
Italian form of Asklepiades via it's Latinized form Asclepiades.
Spanish, Portuguese, Catalan, and Galician form of Asklepiades via its Latinized form Asclepiades.
Latinized form of Asklepigeneia. This was the name of a 5th-century Athenian philosopher and mystic.
Galician, Italian and Spanish form of Asklepios via Asclepius.
Latinized form of Asklepiodotos it was the name of a saint martyred with Maximus and Theodore in 310.
French form of Asclepius via Asklepios. It is the name of a ninth century saint.
Combination of the Germanic name elements asc "ash tree" and walt "ruler".
Latinized form of the Old English name Æscræd, composed of the elements æsc "ash tree; spear, lance; ship" and ræd "advice, counsel, wisdom".
The name is associated with the character from the Latin work "Satyricon," written by Gaius Petronius. Ascyltos is a former gladiator and a companion of the narrator, Encolpius, in the story.
Alternate transcription of Thai อัษฎา (see Atsada).

Pen name of Albanian poet Aleksandër Stavre Drenova (1872-1947), who was known as Asdreni (literally "the Asdren"); ultimately an acronym of his full name. Among other works, Asdreni was the writer of the national anthem of Albania.
From Navajo asdzą́ą́ "woman" (especially one about 50 years of age or older). This name may be given to a sickly newborn in the hopes of her surviving to become a mature woman.
The name of a Navajo creation goddess whose name means "changing woman" or "woman who changes".
Means "steep slope" or "insurmountable, impenetrable" in Kurdish.
Ibn Yazid, a narrator of Hadith had this name.
Alternate transcription of Arabic أسيل (see Asil 2).

Derived from Haitian Creole ase "enough" and fi "daughter; girl" and therefore meaning "enough girls". Now rare, this name was traditionally given after having many daughters, in hopes that the next child would be a boy.
Means "He is close to me" in Nyakyusa.
Meaning “he laughs; he who has laughed”.
It is a name which asks a question, meaning “what does he laugh at?” or “what has made him laugh?”
Spanish form of Asella. A notable bearer of this name is the Cuban chess player Asela de Armas Pérez (b. 1954), who won the title of Woman International Master in 1978.
Variant of Åshild via the short forms Åsil and Åsel.

Derived from the Latin noun asella meaning "little she-ass". It is the feminine version of asellus, which is a diminutive of Latin asinus meaning "ass, donkey".This name is not to be confused with the Latin name Ascella, which is very similar in appearance and pronunciation.A notable bearer of this name is saint Asella of Rome, a nun and hermitess who died around 406 AD.
French form of Asella. This name is not to be confused with Axelle.

Derived from Haitian Creole ase "enough" and lòm "man" and therefore meaning "enough men". Now rare, this name was traditionally given after having many sons, in hopes that the next child would be a girl.
Means "beautiful, elegant, graceful" in Kazakh, of Arabic origin.
Kyrgyz form of Asem, meaning "beautiful". This name was popularized by the Kyrgyz movie Pure Coolness. In 2007, the year the movie was released, 20% of newborn girls in Kyrgyzstan were named Asema.
From Kazakh әсем (asem) meaning "beautiful, elegant, graceful" and гүл (gul) meaning "flower".
Greek variant transcription of Ασημίνα (see Asimina), as well as an Albanian form.
Either an adoption of Turkish Asena or a corruption of Asenath.
Form of Ashurbanipal found in the Bible.
Polish and modern German form of Asenath—older German bibles used Asenath.
From the Karachay-Balkar эсен (esen) meaning "healthy, happy, unharmed" and ай (ay) meaning "moon".
Derived from Arabic أَسَد (ʾasad) meaning "lion" (see Asad). In Kazakh it is solely masculine while in Chechen it is feminine and masculine.

A character in JRR Tolkien's works, a horse (of unknown sex) ridden by the elf Glorfindel. The name is derived from the fictional Sindarin language and means "sunlit foam", from ast meaning "light of the sun, heat of the sun" and faloth meaning "large foamy wave".

Contracted form of Middle Persian اسفندارمذ (spandarmad) meaning “holy thought” that was originally the name of the fourth Amahraspand (divine deity) in Zoroastrianism. Esfand is the twelfth month of the solar Persian calendar as well as a name for the wild rue, used in fumigation against evil eye.
Alternate transcription of Pashto اسفندیار (see Asfandyar).
Derived from the Germanic name elements áss "god" and fastr "firmly, fast".
Old Norse name derived from Old Norse áss "god" and friðr "love; peace; protection".
Derived from Old Norse áss "god" and garðr "enclosure, protection".
Means "soldier" in Azerbaijani, ultimately from Arabic عَسْكَر (ʿaskar) meaning "army, soldiers".
Combination of Old Norse ás "god" and gautr "Goth, Geat".

The name of a character from the RPG game ''Undertale''. In the game Asgore is the powerful king of the monsters, who plans to use seven human souls in order to destroy the barrier that imprisons all monsters underground.
Old Swedish and Norwegian form of Ásgrímr.
Derived from Old Norse áss "god" and grímr "person wearing a mask".
Combination of Old Norse áss "god" and gunnr "war, battle, fight".
Possibly from the Armenian աշխէն (aşxen), originally from Old Iranian axşaena “dark-skinned, having a dark complexion”.
Combination of the prefix a with Shanae.
Chuvash feminine given name derived from Aisha and Fatima.
Possibly from Arabic أشعر ('ash'ara) meaning "alarm, alert, notify" or أشار ('ashar) meaning "observe, advise".

Means "beautiful peace" in Arabic.Having beauty and tranquility equally; possessing qualities that create a calm and inviting atmosphere along with physical attributes that provide great pleasure or satisfaction to see, hear, think about, etc.
From the name of 10th-century Islamic scholar and jurist Abu Hasan al-Ash'ari, who founded the Ash'ari branch of Sunni Islam.
Derived from Erzya ашо (ašo) "white" and ава (ava) "woman".

Means "Best Truth", from Avestan 𐬀𐬴𐬀 (aṣ̌a) "truth" and 𐬬𐬀𐬵𐬌𐬱𐬙𐬀 (vahišta) "best". In Zoroastrianism, Asha, commonly referred to as Asha Vahishta, is the Amesha Spenta, the hypostasis or genius of truth or Righteousness found in the Younger Avesta.
Combination of the prefix A- and the name Shawn.
Variant of Ashante, or a combination of the phonetic element a with the name Shantae (or with the name Shawn and the phonetic element tay).
Combination of the prefix a and Shayla.

Possibly means "flowing" from a prosthetic aleph (Hebrew: א) and the Hebrew verb שבל (shobel) "to flow forth" (the source of Shobal), or possibly derived from the noun אֵשׁ (ʾesh) "fire" and the verb בעל (ba'al) "to be lord (over), to own, to control". In the Old Testament this name belonged to the second son of Benjamin. A known bearer was American pioneer physician Ashbel Smith (1805-1886), a leader in the development of Texas.
Transferred use of the surname Ashby.
Variant of Ash. In the case of American singer Ashe, it is short for Ashlyn.
Means "may he make you perfect" in Amharic.

Possibly an altered form of Acheron, the name of a god of an underworld river in Greek mythology. This was used for Asheron Realaidain, the titular character in the fantasy online role-playing game Asheron's Call.

Simply from the English word, given in reference to the biblical story of Job (see Job-rakt-out-of-the-ashes) and/or the phrase ashes to ashes, dust to dust, also considered a vernacular form of Hebrew Aphrah (a place name taken from Micah 1:10).According to the English antiquarian William Camden (1551-1623), the given names Ashes and Dust were in use during the reigns of Queen Elizabeth I and King James VI and I.

Transferred use of the surname Ashford, which itself is derived from the name of one of several places called Ashford in England. All but one of these derive the second element of their name from Old English ford meaning "ford" - for the one in North Devon, it is derived from Old English worō or worth meaning "enclosure".As for the first element of their name: for most places, it is derived from Old English æsc(e) meaning "ash tree(s)". But for Ashford in the county of Kent, it is derived from Old English æscet or æsceat meaning "clump of ash trees". And for the one in the county of Surrey (formerly Middlesex), it is derived from the medieval personal name Eccel, which itself is ultimately derived from Old English ecg or ecca meaning "sword".As such, depending on the place that the ancestor of a bearer of the surname originally came from, the meaning of the surname can be: "ford by the (clump of) ash trees", "enclosure full of ash trees" and "Eccel's ford".
Means "she is appreciated" in Bette Obudu.

Means "like Ashk" or "of the Parthian (Arsacid) Empire" in Persian, referring to an old Iranian kingdom that lasted until the 3rd century.
The name of the first son of Gomer, and a Japhetic patriarch in the Table of Nations.

From Armenian աշխարհ (ashkharh) meaning "world, universe" and the feminine suffix ուհի (uhi).Note that Ashkharhuhi corresponds to the spelling of Armenian Աշխարհուհի (Ašxarhuhi), whereas Ashkharuhi reflects the Armenian pronunciation.

Feminine Armenian given name with a number of possible meanings and etymologies - firstly, from the Ossetian ӕхсин (æxsin) meaning "lady, mistress", or otherwise from Middle Median *xšay-, meaning "to shine" or the Ossetian æхсид (æxsid) meaning "dawn".-------------------------------------Armenian form of Roxana. Ashkhen was also the name of a Queen of Armenia and a member of the Arsacid dynasty by marriage to King Tiridates III of Armenia during the early to late 3rd century AD, and is considered a Saint in the Armenian Apostolic Church.

A character in the novel "Taltos" by Anne Rice.

Possibly a combination of Ashley and the Sikh name suffix -leen, from Hindi लीन (līn) meaning "engrossed, absorbed (in truth)" (Gurmukhi ਲੀਨ; compare Lina). Alternatively the initial syllable could be taken from Ashwin.

From Sanskrit आश्लेष (āśleṣa) meaning "embrace". This is the name of the ninth nakshatra (lunar mansion) in Hindu astronomy, which corresponds to a group of five stars in the constellation Hydra.

His defeat of the Mitanni king Shuttarna II marks Assyria's independence from this kingdom, and the beginning of its emergence as a powerful empire.

From the Karachay-Balkar асыл (asıl) meaning "real, precious, noble" and the Turkic title khan meaning "king, ruler".
Derived from the Uzbek asil meaning "real, genuine", "precious", or "dear" and poshsha, an endearing name for a girl or woman.

The first element is derived from Arabic áslama "to submit, to surrender" (and is thus etymologically related to the word islam and the name Eslam). The second element of this name is derived from the Ottoman Turkish military title beg (also bey) meaning "lord, chief(tain), master", making it the Turkish equivalent of the Arabic-Persian military title amir, emir. Some experts theorize it is derived from Old Turkic bég, which itself is probably ultimately derived from Proto-Turkic bek meaning "firm, solid, stable". Others theorize it is ultimately derived from Old Iranian baga (possibly via Sogdian beĝe) meaning "God, lord, master". Also compare Uzbekistan, which is the name of a country in Central Asia.

A local heroine from Melite in Phthia whose story was apparently meant to provide an etiology for the local surname and cult of Artemis. Aspalis has been speculated to have originally been a western Semitic hunting goddess identified with Artemis.The exact story of Aspalis, known from Antoninus Liberalis, is as follows. Melite was once ruled by a tyrant so cruel that the citizens dared not pronounce his real name, dubbing him Tartarus. He would order for the most beautiful girls to be brought to him and made them his concubines against their will. When he sent for Aspalis, daughter of Argaeus, the girl hanged herself rather than be violated. Her brother Astygites swore to avenge her death before her body would be taken out of the noose.He put on his sister's clothes, hiding a sword underneath, and in this disguise got into the tyrant's palace and killed him. The citizens threw the tyrant's body into a river which from that circumstance became known as Tartarus, and crowned Astygites with a wreath to express gratitude to him. As they were going to give burial to Aspalis, they found that her body had disappeared, but a wooden statue of Artemis was discovered on the spot (It is believed that Artemis turned her body into statue out of pity). It became a cult object, and was referred to as "Aspalis Ameilete Hekaerge"; а young she-goat was sacrificed to the goddess every year via being hanged by the city maidens, this being a ritual imitation of Aspalis' suicide

Alleged Lithuanian goddess of stoves and, more specifically, stove corners.Aspelenie was first recorded by Polish historian and theologian Jan Łasicki in his treatise on idolatry De diis Samagitarum caeterorumque Sarmatarum et falsorum Christianorum, written ca. 1582 and published in 1615.Her name is clearly a Latinization, however, an original form, if there ever was one, has since been reconstructed: Užpelenė. The meaning of her name is yet unknown.There are, however, theories that link her to the "snake cult" prevalent in Baltic mythology and folklore. Snakes were considered messengers of the gods and treated accordingly. They were thought to be guardians of the home and a symbol of fertility, bringing good harvest and wealth.Snakes liked to live in the corners of the stoves or near stoves, so with stoves being the realm of Aspelenie, they might have been sacred to her.Since Łasicki was not intimately familiar with Lithuanian culture or language, the academic opinion on the value of his writings ranges from a valuable resource to a practical joke.

From the name of the flower. J. R. R. Tolkien used this name on one of his characters in The Lord of the Rings.

In Iran, this is also the name of a daily newspaper.Known bearers of this name include the Indian Urdu poets Majaz (1911-1955) and Majrooh Sultanpuri (1919-2000), whose real first name was Asrar.

The latter two are respectively the former and current official Bible of the Roman Catholic Church.In the Septuagint (Greek Old Testament) Asriel occurs only in verse 25:18 of 1 Chronicles, where it is a form of Azarel.In literature, the English author Philip Pullman (b. 1946) used the name for a character in his His Dark Materials series, first released in 1995.

Combination of the Germanic elements as "god" and run "secret"
Can be a short form of names beginning with áss "god", ask "ash tree", or aðal "nobility". In Iceland, it’s a modern name derived from the Icelandic word assa "(female) eagle".
Alternate transcription of Arabic أسعد (see As'ad).
Alternate transcription of Thai อัษฎ (see Atsada).
Alternate transcription of Thai อัษฎาวุธ (see Atsadawut).
Alternate transcription of Thai อัษฎาวุธ (see Atsadawut).
French transcription of Asadur, the Western Armenian form of Asatur.
Western African and Kazakh form of Hassan.
Form of Hassan used in parts of French-influenced western Africa, especially in Senegal.
From the proto-Norse byname *AndswaruR meaning "he who answers".
This was the name of a king of Dardania in Greek mythology, son of Tros and younger brother of Ilus.

Ivorian name of unknown meaning. This was the name adopted by American revolutionary Assata Shakur (1947-2025). According to her, the name means "she who struggles" in Arabic, however, that meaning would be closer to Jahida or Jihada.
Alternate transcription of Thai อัศวิน (see Atsawin).
Latinate form of Assel, itself a short form of Askhilt. This name was recorded in the 16th century.
Alternate transcription of Arabic عاصم (see Asim 1).
Means "you made me famous" in Amharic.
Judeo-Catalan, Judeo-Anglo-Norman and Finnish form of Asher.
The name of Assia Wevill. She was the lover of Ted Hughes, the husband of Sylvia Plath.
Name of the patron saint of Elphin, Ireland.
Alternate transcription of Arabic أسيل (see Asil).
Alternate transcription of Arabic عاصم (see Asim 1).
Meaning unknown, though it is probably related to Assingúnge.
Assir was a son of Korah of the house of Levi according to Exodus 6:24, born in Egypt. It was also the firstborn son of Jehoiachin, King of Judah.
Portuguese form of the place name Assyria.
From Assis, the Portuguese word for the town of Assisi (Italy). This was the birthplace of saint Francis of Assisi.
Variant of Assivus, using the suffix -at.
Possibly derived from Latin asservo "watch over, observe". This name was recorded in Gascony, between 1283 and 1286.
Derived from French assomption "assumption". This name is given in reference to the assumption of the Virgin Mary into heaven (compare Asunción).

Dutch form of Ahasuerus. One bearer was Willem Anne Assueer Jacob Schimmelpenninck van der Oye (1834-1889), a Dutch baron and politician who was president of the senate of the Netherlands from 1888 to his death.
Means "the nice one" or "the unselfish one" in Bandial.
Italian form of Asunción also used as a word.
Polish form of Ashur, the Assyrian (Mesopotamian) god.
From old French assurer, eaning, "a positive declaration intended to give confidence; a promise." Referencing the promises of God in the Bible.
Combination of the Old Norse name elements áss "god" and sveinn "boy".
Alternate transcription of Arabic آسيا or آسية (see Asiya) chiefly used in North Africa.
Variant of Ásta, although folk etymology likes to connect this name to Icelandic ást "love".
Slovene short form of Anastazija, used as a given name in its own right.
Feminine form of Astacus. Possibly the name of a nymph in Greek mythology.
Alternate transcription of Astafiy, which is a Russian form of Eustathius (compare Yevstafiy). This was used for a character in Fyodor Dostoyevsky's short story 'An Honest Thief' (1848).
Means "we are eight" in Old Ossetian.

In Sethian Gnosticism, Astaphaios is an archon. In 'On the Origin of the World', he is one of the three sons of Yaldabaoth, with the other two being Yao and Eloai. In the Apocryphon of John, he is the third of the seven archons.
The name of an Aksumite god.
A character in the video game 'Elder Scrolls'. The name is possibly a variant of Astraea.

Astarael is the seventh of the seven bells used by necromancers and the Abhorsen in Garth Nix's Old Kingdom trilogy. Astarael is the Weeper, the bell that throws everyone who hears her deep into Death.
Astarion Ancunín is a character from the Baldur's Gate video game series.
Diminutive of both Anastas and Astap.
Dialectal variant of Øystein or a combination of the element egg "edge of a sword" or agi "awe, terror" with steinn "stone".
English variant form or spelling of Estelle.
From Turkic āŕ meaning "few, little, small" and temür meaning "iron".
Old Judeo-Spanish form and Judeo-French variant of Esther via Greek aster, "star". It was already used in Judeo-Latin.
Coined by Sabino Arana Goiri and Koldo Elizalde as a Basque form of Asteria.
Catalan and Georgian form of Asterios.
Lithuanian and Croatian feminine form of Asterios.
Croatian and Serbian form of Asterios.
Lithuanian form of Asterios via Asterius.
Perhaps related to or a diminutive of the name Aster of Greek origins, meaning "star".
Portuguese form of Asterios via Asterius.
Italian and Spanish form of Asterius.
Gallicized form of Asterios as well as a Catalan variant of Asteri.
Russian and Ukrainian form of Asterios.

Derived from Greek άστρο (astro) or αστέρι (asteri), both meaning "star". This is the name of the title character of a 1959 Greek film (played by Aliki Viougiouklaki), a remake of a 1929 movie (itself loosely based on Helen Hunt Jackson's 1884 novel Ramona).

Possibly derived from the Greek noun ἀστήρ (aster) meaning "star" (genitive ἀστέρος; compare Asteria and Asterope) and an uncertain second element. In Greek mythology this name belonged to multiple characters, including a nymph who inhabited a Caucasian mountain stream that bore gold.
Latinized form of Asteropaios. In Greek mythology, this was the name of an important ally of Troy during the Trojan War. He was a grandson of the river god Axius.

Derived from the Greek adjective ἀστεροπαῖος (asteropaios) meaning "of lightning", which is ultimately derived from the Greek noun ἀστεροπή (asterope) meaning "lightning" (see Asterope).In Greek mythology, Asteropaios was an important ally of Troy during the Trojan War. He was a grandson of the river god Axius.
Derived from or related to Asterope, meaning "lightning". This was the name of a daughter of Pelias in Greek mythology.
Italian and Spanish form of Asteropaeus.
Form of Asteria used by Edmund Spenser in his poem 'Muiopotmus; or, the Fate of the Butterfly' (1591), where it belongs to a nymph turned into a butterfly.
Derived from Old Norse ást "love" and heiðr "bright, clear" or heiðr "honour, worth", perhaps inspired by the Old Norse name Ásheiðr.
Newly created name inspired by Astrid.
Derived from the Old Norse element áss "god" and the name of the Norse god Þórr (see Thor).
Russian and Ukrainian form of Astyanax.
name of Sanskrit origin denoting a brahmin with the gotra of atri (अत्रि). Believed to being directly originating from the septarishi atri.
Transferred use of the surname Astin, which was itself derived from a contraction of the Anglo-Norman French given name Asketin, a diminutive of Old Norse Ásketill.

Possibly derived from Ancient Greek ἄστυ (asty) meaning "city, town", or perhaps ἀστός (astos) meaning "townsman, citizen, freeman". It was borne by an obscure saint from the 3rd century AD, who was martyred at Halmyris together with saint Epictetus.
There was an early Christian saint by this name, a 2nd-century Illyrian martyr. He was a bishop of Dyrrhachium (now Durrës in Albania).
Transferred use of the surname Astley.
A dithematic name of Germanic origin formed from the name element *AST "branch (of a tree)" and *WOLF "wolf".
From the Astures, a Celtic tribe that gave name to the Spanish region of Asturias.

Derived from the Italian noun astore meaning "goshawk", which effectively makes this name an Italian cognate of Astor.A known bearer of this name was the Italian trumpeter and composer Astore Pittana (1912-2010).

Variant form of Astore. Known Italian bearers of this name include the former soccer player Astorre Cattabrini (b. 1922) and the military leaders Astorre II Baglioni (1526-1571) and Astorre I Manfredi (c. 1345-1405).
Latinized form of Astraios, the masculine form of Astraia (see Astraea).

A latinised greek word, meaning "One who reaches the stars", resembling the word astrolabe (an astronomical instrument).The unique name was borne by the son of Pierre Abélard and Héloïse d'Argenteuil.

Derived from Old Norse áss "god" and ráð "advise, counsel, decision". The first name element is sometimes associated with the Old Norse word ást meaning "love, affection", but a connection is not likely.
Combination of Astra and the feminine suffix -wati.
Catalan, Italian and Spanish form of Astraea.
French form of Astraea and Astraeus.
From Greek ἀστήρ (aster) meaning "star". This name was used by Scottish singer Donovan for his daughter born 1971.
Italian and Spanish form of Astraeus.
Possibly a Polish Medieval form of Astrid.
Catalan and Portuguese form of Astraeus.
Bulgarian, Russian and Ukrainian form of Astraios.
Czech and Slovak variant and Kashubian form of Astrid.
Latvian version of the name Astrid.
Possibly derived from Greek ἀστήρ (aster) meaning "star".

This treacherous lady tried to trick Gawaine, through her lies, into killing her husband. Gawaine fought the husband; when the husband told his side, Gawaine did not know whom to believe. He tried to take them both to find someone who could tell him which was in the right.
Means "little star" in Armenian, from Greek aster meaning "star" and the diminutive ik.

Claimed to mean "love fire" from Old Norse ást "love" and eldr "fire". Astrild was a personification of love in Scandinavian poetry (particularly during the Baroque and Rococo eras), probably introduced in the 17th century by Swedish poet Georg Stiernhielm.
Derived from Ancient Greek ἀστήρ (aster) meaning "star". This is the name of a star nymph in Greek mythology, also called Asteria, a daughter of the sun god Helios and wife of the river god Hydaspes.
This is borne by Astrith Baltsan (1956-), an Israeli concert pianist; it is uncertain if her name has the same etymological origins as Ástríðr.
From the Greek "star taker". Son of Héloïse & Abélard, born c. 1116.
Derived from the Old Norse elements áss "god" (which becomes ást when preceding a liquid r, compare Ástríður) or ást "affection, love, devotion" and rós "rose".

Derived from Provençal astruc "lucky", ultimately from Greek aster "star" and thus having the extended meaning of "born under a good star".It was generally given as an amuletic name and sometimes used as a translation of Hebrew Mazel Tov and/or Gad.
A famous bearer is Brazilian vocalist Astrud Gilberto (1940-).
Feminine form of Astruc. This name was also used as a Judeo-Spanish translation of Mazal.
Judeo-Italian and Judeo-Spanish form of Astruc.
Means "born under a good star" in Occitan.
Latinized form of Astruc via a diminutive form.
Latinized form of Haistulf and Aistulf. Used by a few saints and beatified saint astolfus of Mainz and astolfo lobo.

Hellenized form of Akkadian Ishtovigu or Ištovigu, from Old Median R̥štivaigah, ultimately derived from Ancient Iranian rishti vaiga, meaning "swinging the spear". Modified through folk etymology by Greek ἄστυ (ásty) meaning "city" and ἄγνυμι (ágnumi) meaning "break". This was the name of a Median king, who lived in the 6th century BC.
Feminine form of Astyanax. This was the name of Helen of Troy’s maid, supposedly the first author of erotic texts and poetry.

Means "city lord" or "lord of the city", derived from Greek ἄστυ (asty) meaning "city, town" and ἄναξ (anax) meaning "master, lord, chief".In Greek mythology, Astyanax was the nickname of the firstborn son of Hector and his wife Andromache, named Σκαμάνδριος (Skamandrios) at birth.
Semi-latinized form of Astykrateia, the feminine form of Astykrates. This was the name of several characters in Greek mythology.
Derived from Ancient Greek ἄστυ (asty) meaning "town, city" and δαμάζω (damazo) meaning "to tame, subdue".
Derived from Ancient Greek ἄστυ (asty) meaning "town, city" and δαμάζω (damazo) meaning "to tame, subdue".
Latinized form of Astydameia. In Greek myth this name belonged to five individual characters.
Derived from Ancient Greek ἄστυ (asty) meaning "city, town" and κράτος (kratos) meaning "power, strength".

Latinized form of Ἀστύλοχος, derived from Greek ἄστυ (asty) meaning "city, town" and λόχος (lochos) meaning "ambush", a word that later came to signify a tactical sub unit of the ancient Greek army. The word is ultimately derived from the Greek verb λοχάω (lochao) meaning "to lie in wait for, to waylay" as well as "to snare".
Latinized form of Astylochos. In Greek mythology, this is the name of one of the suitors of Penelope.

Derived from the Greek adjective ἄστυλος (astylos) meaning "without pillar, without support". It consists of the Greek negative prefix ἀ (a) combined with the Greek noun στῦλος (stylos) meaning "pillar, support".A known bearer of this name was the ancient Olympic athlete Astylos of Croton (5th century BC).
Derived from Greek ἄστυ (asty) meaning "city, town" and μέδων (medon) meaning "ruler", itself from μέδω (medo) meaning "to protect, to rule over".
Latinized form of Astymedousa, which is the feminine form of Astymedon. In some Greek myths this name belongs to a princess of Mycenae who is a later wife of Oedipus.

Feminine form of Astynomos. Alternatively, the second element could be derived from the related Greek words νομός (nomós) meaning "district", from νέμω (nemo) meaning "I divide, I distribute", or from νομή (nome) meaning "a pasture, a grazing" or "spreading, multiplication." This is the name of several women in Greek mythology, including the mother of Calydon by Ares, a woman commonly called Chryseis in the Iliad of Homer, and one of the children of Niobe (a Niobid).
Possibly derived from ἄστυ (ástu) meaning "city, town" and νόμος (nomos) meaning "law, custom".
Derived from Ancient Greek ἄστυ (asty) meaning "town, city" and νόος (noos) meaning "mind, thought". This was the name of several characters in Greek mythology, including two defenders of Troy.

Derived from the Greek adjective ἀστυόχος (astyochos) meaning "protecting the city". It consists of the Greek noun ἄστυ (asty) meaning "city, town" combined with the Greek verb ὀχέω (ocheo) meaning "to bear, to carry, to hold fast, to sustain", which is closely related to the Greek verb ἔχω (echo) meaning "to have, to hold, to possess". Also compare the Greek noun ὀχή (oche) meaning "prop, support" as well as "nourishment, food" (see Antiochus).
Latinized form of Astyochos. This was the name of a Spartan naval commander from the 5th century BC.In Greek mythology, Astyochus is the son of Aeolus and a king of Lipara.

Latinized form of Greek Ἀστυπάλαια (Astypalaia) which meant "ancient city", derived from Ancient Greek ἄστυ (asty) meaning "town, city" and παλαιός (palaios) meaning "old (in years), aged, ancient" (compare the related word πάλαι (palai) meaning "long ago, in days of yore"). This name was borne by a lover of the god Poseidon in Greek mythology.
Derived from Ancient Greek ἄστυ (asty) meaning "city, town" combined with φίλος (philos) meaning "friend, lover".
Latinized form of Astyphilos. This name was borne by an eponymous archon of Athens, who lived in the 5th century BC.
Means "gate of the city", derived from Ancient Greek ἄστυ (asty) "city, town" combined with πύλη (pyle) "gate, entrance". In Greek mythology, this was the name of a Paeonian killed by Achilles.
Latinized form of Astypylos. In Greek mythology, Astypylus was a Paeonian killed by Achilles.

column3: 明日, 安酸, 阿子, 亜澄, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 明日 (asu) meaning "tommorrow" or other kanji pronounced in the same way.
Means "turmoil of the soul", from Persian آشوب (ashub) meaning "riot, turmoil" and جان (jan) meaning "soul, being, life".
Means "tranquil, peaceful, quiet" in Turkish, ultimately from Persian آسوده (āsūda).
Possibly a variant of Asaelu, Samoan form of Asahel, or Asielu, Samoan form of Asiel.

Deriving from the Germanic elements ansu- ("god") and gīslaz ("hostage"). This name is part of an inscription in Proto-Norse on Kragehul I, a lance-shaft from Denmark that has been dated to between 200 and 475 CE.

column3: あすは(Japanese Hiragana)|アスハ(Japanese Katakana)|明日葉, 明日羽, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 明日 (asu) meaning "tomorrow" and 葉 (ha) meaning "leaf, needle, blade", or from 飛 (asu) meaning "to fly" and 羽 (ha) meaning "plume, feather". Other kanji combinations can be used.

column3: 明日妃, 明日飛, 明日陽, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 明日 (asu) meaning "tomorrow" combined with 妃 (hi) meaning "a ruler's wife; queen; empress", 飛 (hi) meaning "to fly" or 陽 (hi) meaning "light, sun, male". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: あす貴(Kanji/Hiragana)|明日喜, 明日希, 明日貴, 明日輝, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 明日 (asu) meaning "tomorrow" combined with 喜 (ki) meaning "rejoice". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: 明日子, 明寿子, 安末子, 安主子, 安寿子, etc.(Japanese Kanji)|あすこ(Japanese Hiragana)
column12: From Japanese 明日 (asu) meaning "tomorrow" combined with 子 (ko) meaning "child". Other kanji combinations are possible as well.
Old Swedish and Old Danish form of Ásulfr.
Derived from Old Norse as "god" and ulf "wolf."

column3: あすま(Japanese Hiragana)|愛洲馬, 明日真, 明日磨, 明日茉, 明日馬, 明日麻, 明馬, 未来磨, 遊馬, 飛海, 飛馬, 飛麻, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 愛 (a) meaning "love, affection", 明日 (asu) meaning "tomorrow", 明 (asu) meaning "bright, light", 未来 (asu) meaning "future", 遊 (asu) meaning "play" or 飛 (asu) meaning "fly", 洲 (su) meaning "continent, sandbar, island, country" combined with 馬 (ma) meaning "horse", 真 (ma) meaning "true, reality", 磨 (ma) meaning "grind, polish, scour, improve, brush (teeth)", 茉 (ma) meaning "jasmine", 麻 (ma) meaning "flax, linen, hemp" or 海 (ma) meaning "sea, ocean". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: あすみ(Japanese Hiragana)|アスミ(Japanese Katakana)|安純, 阿澄, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 安 (a) meaning "peace, low, cheap, relax, inexpensive" combined with 純 (sumi) meaning "innocent". Other kanji combinations are possible.
From 明日 (asu) meaning "tomorrow", 美 (mi) meaning "beauty", and 子 (ko, shi) meaning "child". Other kanji combinations are possible.A notable bearer is Asumiko Nakamura, a manga artist.

column3: アスナ(Japanese Katakana)|明日菜, 明日奈, 亜子那, 愛朱名, 勝珠七, 空寿南, 日澄楠, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From kanji 明日 (asu) meaning "tomorrow" combined with 菜 (na) meaning "greens, vegetables" or 奈 (na) meaning "Nara, what?, apple tree". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: 明日乃, 明日望, 飛乃, 愛澄, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
明日来, 波空, 空澄羅, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 明日 (asu) meaning "tomorrow" combined with 来 (ra) meaning "to come". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: 明日多, 明日大(Japanese Kanji)
column12: made with 明日(asu) meaning "tommorow" and 大(ta) meaning "large" or 多(ta) meaning " many".

column3: 亜斯登, 明日人, 明日斗, 安人, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 明日 (asu) meaning "tomorrow" combined with 人 (to) meaning "person". Other kanji combinations are possible.
Alternate transcription of Hindi आशुतोष or Bengali আশুতোষ (see Ashutosh).
From Japanese 明日 (asu) meaning "tomorrow" combined with 代 (yo) meaning "generation". Other kanji combinations are possible.
Icelandic and Faroese form of Ásvaldr.
Either derived from the Germanic name elements áss "god" and herr "army" or a variant of Ásvarðr.
Old Norse combination of áss "god" and vǫrðr "guard".
Icelandic and Faroese form of Ásvarðr.
A relatively modern Scandinavian name, it is derived from Old Norse áss "god" combined with Old Norse veig "strength".

Swedish form of the Old Norse name Ásví, which was derived from áss "god" combined with an unknown second element, possibly vé "devoted, dedicated" (from vīgja or vígja "to consecrate (in heathen sense)"; compare Véfreyja).
Old Norse combination of áss "god" and vár "spring".
Means "one who moves through darkness toward the light".
From Indonesian and Malay aswad meaning "black", ultimately derived from Arabic أسود (aswad).
Dutch and German form of Answin.

column3: Асят, Азиет(Western Circassian, Circassian, Eastern Circassian)
column12: Variant of Asya 2, meaning "Asia", not to be confused with Asiyat

column5: /á.sy.kʰis/(Attic Greek)|/ˈa.sy.kʰis/(Egyptian Greek)|/ˈa.sy.çis/(Koine Greek, Byzantine Greek)|/ˈa.si.çis/(Constantinopolitan Greek)
column12: Greek form of an Ancient Egyptian name. This was the name of an Egyptian pharaoh mentioned by Herodotos.
From Kazakh and Kyrgyz асыл (asil) meaning "precious, noble" (of Arabic origin) combined with the Turkish military title beg meaning "chieftain, master".
From Kazakh асыл (asil) meaning "precious, noble" and the Turkic title khan meaning "leader, ruler".
Derived from Arabic أَصِيل‎ (ʾaṣīl) meaning "original, authentic" combined with Murat.
From the Tatar асыл (asyl) meaning "precious, noble" and бий (biy) meaning "princess".
From Kazakh асыл (asil) meaning "precious, noble" (of Arabic origin) and жан (zhan) meaning "soul" (of Persian origin).
Latinized form of Asynkritos. This name once belonged to one of the Seventy Disciples.
Derived from Ancient Greek ἀσύγκριτος (asynkritos) meaning "incomparable, surpassing, unlike".
Polonised form of Assyrian god's name Ashur.
From Sino-Vietnamese 乙 (ất) referring to the second of the ten Heavenly Stems of the traditional Chinese calendar.
Means "one of twins" in Fante, dialect of Akan.
Alternate transcription of Arabic عطاء (see Ata 2).
Means "gift of the most merciful" in Arabic.
From Turkmen ata meaning "father, ancestor" and baý meaning "rich, wealthy".
Supreme goddess of the Taínos worshipped as a goddess of fresh water and fertility.
Alternate transcription of Thai อรรถชัย (see Atthachai).

column3: 与, 與, 与絵, etc.(Japanese Kanji)|あたえ(Japanese Hiragana)|アタエ(Japanese Katakana)
column12: From 与え/與え (atae) meaning "gift, godsend."A kanji that can be read as e can be suffixed, like 絵 meaning "picture, drawing."This name is rarely used.
Romano Iberian chthonic underworld goddess. Romans identified her with the goddess Proserpina.

The name of a goddess worshiped by the ancient Iberians, Lusitanians, and Celtiberians. Her name possibly comes from the proto-Celtic *atte- and *geno- which together mean "reborn", or else *ad-akwī- meaning "night".
Means "father came" from Turkmen ata meaning "father, ancestor" and geldi meaning "came".
The name Atahan first originated in 1930s after the Kemalist revolution. Legends speculate that people who bear this name tend to have network connection problems.
Variant transcription of Attai.This transcription is used in The Complete Jewish Bible.

Given name derived from the Ataídes surname, a noble Portuguese family whose surname derives from the Freguesia do Ataíde, currently part of Vila Meã, in Portugal. The village name probably comes from Athanagild, 6th-century king of Visigothic Hispania who may have founded it.
From Turkish ata "father, ancestor" and kan "blood".
From Azerbaijani ata meaning "ancestor" and kişi meaning "man".
The titular heroine of François-René de Chateaubriand's novella, 'Atala' and a character in 'The Hunger Games' series.
Original Greek form of Atalanta. This was borne by a sister of the 4th-century BC Macedonian general Perdiccas.
Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Athalaric.
Croatian, Swedish and Norwegian form of Athalaric. In Swedish and Norwegian, the name is not used outside of translations of historical documents about the 6th century AD king of the Ostrogoths.
Means "he whose course is set towards aataat (harps seals)" in Greenlandic.
Greenlandic name with the combination of Âtâlia and suffix nnguaq meaning "sweet, dear".
Possibly from the Hebrew meaning "God is great".
Means "rising of the moon" in Tongan.

Used as a title in both Cossacks and Turks."Ataman" derives from Gothic "father of men-warriors", or Turkic Ata-man, "father of horsemen". Cossacks kept in their speech the original meaning of the word, sometimes saying "father-ataman" ("bat'ka-ataman"). At war atamans had unlimited power, but in times of peace they were only to carry out decisions of the Cossack Circle and keep order in the community.
Means "good wind for sailing" in Tongan.
This name means "Adam". This was the name of of a Rapa Nui man on Easter Island who lived during the 1800s named Atamu Tekena (d. 1892). He was an ariki "king".
From Medieval Turkic ata meaning "father, ancestor" and the given name Myrat
Catalan and Swedish form of Athanagild.
Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Athanagild.
Italian, Portuguese and Spanish form of Athanaric.
Croatian, Swedish and Norwegian form of Athanaric.
Coined by Sabino Arana Goiri and Koldo Elizalde as a Basque equivalent of Atanasia and Athanasie.
Catalan and Provençal form of Athanasius.
Dutch, Finnish and German variant of Athanasius.
Means "created to shine" in Yoruba, from tàn "to shine, brighten" and dá "to create".
Means "water shell", from atl "water" and tapachtli "sea shell, coral".
Alternate transcription of Thai อรรถพล (see Atthaphon).
Alternate transcription of Thai อรรถพล (see Atthaphon).

column3: อรรถพงศ์, อรรถพงษ์(Thai)
column12: Alternate transcription of Thai อรรถพงศ์/อรรถพงษ์ (see Atthaphong).
Alternate transcription of Thai อรรถพล (see Atthaphon).
Alternate transcription of Thai อรรถพล (see Atthaphon).

column3: อรรถพงศ์, อรรถพงษ์(Thai)
column12: Alternate transcription of Thai อรรถพงศ์/อรรถพงษ์ (see Atthaphong).
From the Indo-European *hxehxtr- "fire". In Zoroastrianism, Atar is the Zoroastrian concept of holy fire and, in later Zoroastrianism, became the god of fire and the element itself.
Means "receive with cupped hands" in Setswana.
Derived from Avestan ātar "fire" combined with Avestan pāiti "to protect, to defend" or Avestan pāyu "protector". As such, the name either means "protected by the fire" or "protector of the fire"

Atargatis was the chief goddess of northern Syria in Classical antiquity. She was also referred to as Derketo (Ancient Greek: Δερκετὼ) or Deasura (by Romans).According to the myth, Atargatis fell in love to a mortal shepherd called Hadad and they had a daughter called Semiramis. Semiramis later on became queen of Assyria. She was most well-known for creating the famous hanging gardens of Babylonia.Atargatis accidentally caused the death of Hadad. She could not live with her guilt and drowned herself into a lake near Ascalon. Waters however could not hide her beauty and she was transformed into a mermaid. A woman with a tail of a fish. Story of Atargatis is one of the first mermaid stories ever told.The name Atargatis derives from the Aramaic form ʿAtarʿatheh, which comes in several variants. The name ʿAtarʿatheh is widely held to derive from a compound of the Aramaic form ʿAttar, which is a cognate of ʿAțtart minus its feminine suffix -t, plus ʿAttah or ʿAtā, a cognate of ʿAnat. Alternatively, the second half may be a Palmyrene divine name ʿAthe (i.e. tempus opportunum), which occurs as part of many compounds. It has also been proposed that the element -gatis may relate to the Greek gados "fish". (For example, the Greek name for "sea monster" or "whale" is the cognate term ketos). So Atar-Gatis may simply mean "the fish-goddess Atar".

From the Japanese word 当たり (atari) meaning "a hit, a good move" (specially in the game of Go). Atari is the name of an American videogame company that released the video game console Atari 2600 in the year 1977. Starting in 1979, this name has been given to at least 85 boys and 53 girls in the United States.
Means "little father" in Quenya. In Tolkien's Legendarium this is the mother-name of Curufin, the fifth son of Fëanor and Nerdanel, and the father of Celebrimbor.
The good son of Mari 3, student of Etsai.

Atarsamain ("morning star of heaven") was an astral deity of uncertain gender, worshipped in the pre-Islamic northern and central Arabian Peninsula. Worshipped widely by Arab tribes, Atarsamain is known from around 800 BC and is identified in letters of the Assyrian kings Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal. Atarsamain may be identical with Allāt, whose cult was centred on Palmyra and also with Attar.According to Dierk Lange, Atarsamain was the main deity in a trinity of gods worshipped by what he calls the Yumu'il Confederation, which he describes as a northern Arab tribal confederation of Ishmaelite ancestry headed by the "clan of Kedar" (i.e. the Qedarites).
Means "wilderness flower" in Mongolian, from атар (atar) meaning "wilderness, untouched land" and цэцэг (tsetseg) meaning "flower".

Means "folly, delusion, error" as well as "disaster, ruin, misfortune, doom" and "bane, pest" in Ancient Greek. In Greek mythology she was the goddess (daimona) of mischief, blind folly, and delusion, leading men down the path to ruin while the Litai (prayers) follow and try to mitigate damage. By later accounts, she avenges misdeeds and inflicts punishments on the wicked. In the Iliad she was called the eldest daughter of Zeus, while in Theogeny she is one of the many children of Eris.

Atea is a creator deity in several Polynesian cultures. Atea means "clear, white" in different Polynesian languages. Atea, a shapeless being, was the giver of light to the universe. This gave rise to Rangi and Papa, who's children eventually divided their parents into heaven and earth. In other creator stories Atea is the husband of Papa. Atea, as a Polynesian concept, can be considered equivalent to the Big Bang.

Atete, in Oromo mythology and religion, is a fertility goddess worshipped in the Kafa province in Ethiopia. Her worship was assimilated into the Christian cult of the Virgin Mary, but she's probably the subject of an ancient fertility rite performed by women who collect various sacred plants and throw them into the river known now as 'Astar Yo Mariam' ('The Epiphany of Mary').

In Arabic, Atheer refers to the "luster/light which reflects off a sword."A notable person with this name was the Arab scholar/historian, Ibn al-Athir (1160-1233).The word itself is not gendered -- it's a noun with a positive, poetic meaning that can be applied to either sex. That said, in contemporary naming practices, especially in Egypt, Lebanon, and parts of the Levant, Atheer is primarily considered a feminine name.In Gulf countries (Saudi Arabia, UAE, etc.) it can be unisex, though still more common for females.So, while it can be used for males, be aware that in some regions it might be perceived as a feminine name. If you're considering it for a boy, and cultural perception matters, you might want to pair it with a traditionally masculine middle name.
Late 16th century from French athéisme, from Greek atheos, from a- ‘without’ + theos ‘god’.

Short form of Athelstan, or directly from the Old English element æðele meaning "noble".A known bearer is the British biochemist Athel Cornish-Bowden (1943-), whose great-uncle was Athelstan Cornish-Bowden (1871-1942), a land surveyor in South Africa.

This name was borne by several ancient Greeks, such as statesman Athenagoras of Syracuse (5th century BC) and general Athenagoras of Macedon (2nd century BC).

As Athenogenes entered the flames, he sang the Phos Hilaron in joy. He was martyred in the reign of Emperor Diocletian.
Means "glory of Athena" from the name of the god Athena combined with Greek κλέος (kleos) meaning "glory".

Zeus knocked the mountain to the ground near Macedonia, and it became Mount Athos, or the "Holy Mountain."In "The Three Musketeers" by Père Alexandre Dumas, Athos is one of the titular characters, his name deriving from the village of Athos in the commune Athos-Aspis.
