From the name of the city in the American state of Georgia, originally a short form of Atlantica, which is ultimately from the name of the Atlantic Ocean (itself the genitive of Atlas).It may also be considered a contracted form of Atalanta.

Variant latinization of Greek Ἀτλαντείη (Atlanteie), because its proper latinized form is Atlantia. In Greek mythology Atlanteie was a Hamadryad nymph who consorted with King Danaus of Libya and was perhaps the mother of some of the Danaïdes: Hippodamia, Rhodia, Cleopatra, Asteria, Glauce, Hippomedusa, Gorge, Iphimedusa, and Rhode.
Slovak form of Atlanteia and Atlantia.

Atlantes was a powerful sorcerer featured in chansons de geste. In Boiardo's Orlando Innamorato (1482), where he is known as Atalante, the magician fears that Rugiero (Boiardo's spelling) will convert to Christianity and aid Charlemagne against the Saracens. To prevent this and forestall Rugiero's death, he constructs a magic garden ringed by glass on Mt. Carena in the Atlas Mountains, after which he is named.1 In Orlando Furioso, Atlantes' magical castle is filled with illusions, in order to divert Ruggiero (Ariosto's spelling) from what he has foretold as certain doom. Ruggiero is later set free by Bradamante and after numerous trials and quests sires a great line of heroes. He later dies betrayed fulfilling the destiny foretold by Atlantes.
Taken from the mythological place name Atlantis, from Ancient Greek Ἀτλαντὶς (νῆσος) (Atlantis (nesos)) meaning "(island) of Atlas".
Refers to a kind of brightly coloured satin material used in making traditional Uzbek women's dresses.

Possibly derived from Nahuatl atlan "water, in the water" and tonan "our mother". This was an Aztec goddess of the coast, lepers, and disease, patron of those born with physical disabilities or ailments, or who suffered from illnesses involving open sores.
Derived from Nahuatl atlatl "spear-thrower, spear-throwing lever" and the diminutive or reverential suffix -tzin.
Transferred use of the surname Atlee.
Feminine variant of Atlee and Atley.
Transferred use of the surname Atley.
Combination of the word at ("you" in a Hebrew female pronoun) and the name Li 2. Making it relative to Liat.
From Nahuatl atl "water" and popoca "to smoke, emit smoke".
Derived from Sanskrit आत्मन् (atman) meaning "soul, spirit, life".
Combination of Atma and the feminine suffix -wati.
Chuvash feminine given name possibly meaning "born on Friday".
From Spanish atocha meaning "esparto grass". This is the name of a local title of Virgin Mary, Nuestra Señora de Atocha ("Our Lady of Atocha") venerated in Madrid, Spain.
Borne by a Guanche prince from Benahoare (modern-day La Palma).
Variant of Atoya, a combination of the popular phonetic element a with the name Toya. Also compare LaToya.

column3: 彩十子, 安都子, 亜登子, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 彩 (a) meaning "colour", 十 (to) meaning "ten" combined with 子 (ko) meaning "child". Other kanji combinations are possible.

In the case of film director Atom Egoyan (1960-), it is taken from atom bomb (from Greek atomos meaning "uncut, unhewn; indivisible", derived from Greek α, a negative prefix, combined with tomos "a cutting", from temnein "to cut"), given to him by his Armenian-Egyptian parents to mark the completion of Egypt's first nuclear reactor.

column3: 愛富, 亜都夢, 亜斗夢, 亜斗武, 亜富, 亜人夢, 亜十夢, 亜登夢, 亜土夢, 阿斗夢, 阿度夢, 愛斗武(Japanese Kanji)|あとむ(Japanese Hiragana)|アトム(Japanese Katakana)
column12: Japanese derivation of the English word atom.As a unisex name, it can be used as 愛富, 亜都夢, 亜斗夢 or 亜斗武 with 愛 (ai, ito.shii, o.shimu, kana.shii, mana, me.deru, a) meaning "affection, love," 富 (fu, fuu, tomi, to.mu) meaning "abundant, enrich, wealth," 亜 (a, tsu.gu) meaning "Asia, come after, rank next," 都 (tsu, to, miyako) meaning "capital, metropolis," 斗 (to, tou) meaning "Big Dipper," 夢 (bou, mu, kura.i, yume, yume.miru) meaning "dream, illusion, vision" and 武 (bu, mu, take.shi) meaning "military, warrior."As a masculine name, it can be used as 亜富, 亜人夢, 亜十夢, 亜登夢, 亜土夢, 阿斗夢, 阿度夢 or 愛斗武 with 人 (jin, nin, -to, hito, -ri) meaning "person," 十 (ji', juu, ju', to, too) meaning "ten," 登 (shou, chou, to, tou, dou, a.garu, nobo.ru) meaning "ascend, climb up," 阿 (a, o, omone.ru, kuma) meaning "corner, flatter, nook," 度 (taku, to, do, -ta.i, tabi) meaning "degrees, time" and 土 (to, do, tsuchi) meaning "earth, ground, soil."Bearers of this name include footballers Atomu Nabeta (鍋田 亜人夢) (1991-) & Atomu Tanaka (田中 亜土夢) (1987-) and actor Atomu Shimojō (下條 アトム) (1946-).This name is rarely given to children, if given at all.
Derived from Nahuatl atl "water" and tonalli "day, warmth of the sun".
Diminutive of Renato, Fortunato, and other names ending in -ato.
Alternate transcription of Persian أتوسا (see Atousa).
Atoq Navarro is a South American archaeologist and main antagonist of Uncharted: Drake's Fortune.

column3: 花鶏, 花鳥, 亜鳥, 娃鳥, etc.(Japanese Kanji)|あとり(Japanese Hiragana)|アトリ(Japanese Katakana)
column12: From 花鶏 (atori), referring to the brambling bird.Other kanji can be used for this name, like 鳥 meaning "bird" for the second kanji, 亜 or 娃 for the first kanji, the latter meaning "beautiful."One fictional bearer of this name is Atoli (アトリ), a main character in the '.hack//G.U.' series.This name is rarely used.
Means "water bird" in Nahuatl, from atl "water" and tototl "bird". Can refer to several specific kinds of birds, including pelicans, herons, wild geese, and other water-dwelling birds.

Means "water parrot", deriving from the Nahuatl elements atl ("water, a body of water") and toztli ("yellow parrot"). Name borne by an Aztec queen that possibly ruled as tlatoani (ruler of a city-state) in her own right.
Variant of Atousa beared by a famous influencer and ADHD coach.

Created by German author Michael Ende for the hero of his fantasy novel 'Die unendliche Geschichte' (1979; English: 'The Neverending Story'). The character is a boy warrior whose name is explained as meaning "son of all" in his fictional native language, given to him because he was raised by all of the members of his village after being orphaned as a newborn.
Italian and Spanish form of Atreus.
Catalan, Portuguese and Romanian form of Atreus.
Bulgarian, Russian and Ukrainian form of Atreus.
“Wife of Atri” in Sanskrit and feminist form of Atreyu in modern times

Anglicized variant of Atréju, which was created by German author Michael Ende for the hero of his fantasy novel 'Die unendliche Geschichte' (1979; English: 'The Neverending Story'). The character is a boy warrior whose name is explained as meaning "son of all" in his fictional native language, given to him because he was raised by all of the members of his village after being orphaned as a newborn.Current usage is influenced by the name of a Californian metal-core band named after the hero in 'The neverending story'.
A star in the constellation Triangulum Australe
Means "attacker". This is a byname for Odin.
Armenian form of Adurnarseh, equivalent to ատր- (atr-) meaning "fire" combined with the given name Nerseh.
A Finnish form of Hadrianus. Finnish name day March 4.
Originally a variant of Atso, this name is now also considered a short form of Artur and used as a given name in its own right.
Derived from Thai อัษฎ (atsad) meaning "eight".
Alternate transcription of Thai อัษฎาวุธ (see Atsadawut).
Means "eight weapons" from Thai อัษฎ (atsad) meaning "eight" and อาวุธ (awut) meaning "weapon", referring to the eight weapons presented to a king during a coronation.

Means "Yahweh has reserved" or "Yahweh has set aside" in Hebrew, which some sources appear to believe indicates to a figurative meaning of "(being kept) near to God". The name is derived from Hebrew אָצַל (atsal) meaning "to reserve, to lay aside" (see Azel) combined with Hebrew יָהּ (yah) meaning "Yahweh". Also compare the Biblical Hebrew given name Esli, which appears to have the same etymological origin.This was the name of a character from the Old Testament, who appeared in 2 Kings 22:3 (also known as 4 Kings 22:3). He was a son of Meshullam and was himself the father of Shaphan the scribe.
Meaning uncertain, most likely of Alanian origin. In Caucasian mythology Atsamaz is a musician who plays a magical golden pipe. He is also a hero in the Nart sagas.
Atsani means "thunderbolt" in Thai and has been used to name 2 tropical cyclones
Means "knight, cavalier" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit अश्विन् (aśvin).

Coined by Sabino Arana Goiri as a Basque equivalent of Angustias, who based the name on the Basque word atsekabe "sorrow, anguish, suffering". Later, however, it was used as an equivalent of Consuelo.

Of debated origin and meaning. Theories include a derivation from Basque atsegin "pleasure, delight, bliss; pleasant, nice; amicable; pleased, happy, delightful; supportive, helpful, kind" and a derivation from hats egin "to breathe, to take a breath". It is occasionally considered a Basque equivalent of Consuelo.
Atsen which means"Visitor" is a male given name among the Afizere people of Nigeria. who are predominantly in Jos Plateau and Bauchi State Nigeria.
In Inuit mythology, Atshen is a cannibalistic spirit.
Finnish and Estonian form of Azzo.

column3: 纂, 敦, 厚, 暖, 淳, 阿鶴, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 纂 (atsu) meaning "gather, compile", 敦 (atsu) meaning "affinity, kindness", or 篤 (atsu) meaning "cordial, faithful, sincere". Other kanji or kanji combinations can be used.

column3: あつあき(Japanese Hiragana)|アツアキ(Japanese Katakana)|熱顕, 暖旺, 醇亮, 敦晟, 厚昭, 纂旭, 豊堯, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 篤 (atsu) meaning "honest" combined with 晃 (aki) meaning "clear". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: あつえ(Japanese Hiragana)|アツエ(Japanese Katakana)|熱映, 温栄, 豊慧, 淳重, 厚慧, 篤枝, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 熱 (atsu) meaning "passion, temperature" combined with 永 (e) meaning "eternity, long, lengthy". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: 暖理, 溌春, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From 暖 (atsu) meaning "warm" and 理 (haru) meaning "logic, reason". Other kanji combinations can be used.

column3: 渥火, 渥日, 厚妃, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 渥 (atsu) meaning "moisten, make moist" combined with 火 (hi) meaning "fire". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: 温彦, 宏彦, 純彦, 敦彦, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 温 (atsu) meaning "warm" combined with 彦 (hiko) meaning "boy, prince". Other kanji combinations are also possible.A famous bearer is Atsuhiko Ejiri, a retired Japanese footballer. He played in a midfield position for JEF United Ichihara.

column3: 貴裕, 逸裕, 厚博(Japanese Kanji)
column12: Japanese masculine name derived from either 貴裕, meaning "precious; plentiful", 逸裕 meaning "escape, break free; plentiful" or 厚博 "thick and broad, rich, plentiful".

column3: 厚人, 厚仁, 篤仁, 敦仁, 充仁, etc.(Japanese Kanji)|あつひと(Japanese Hiragana)|アツヒト(Japanese Katakana)
column12: From the stem of adjective 厚/篤い (atsui) meaning "kind, cordial, hospitable, warm" (also used as 敦 or 充, the last one meaning "full") combined with 人 (hito) meaning "person," also used as 仁 meaning "benevolence, compassion, humanity."

column3: 渥一, 厚市, 淳一, 敦一, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 渥 (atsu) meaning "moist" combined with 一 (ichi) meaning "one". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: 淳一郎, 充一郎, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 淳 (atsu) meaning "honest, simple, unsophisticated", 一 (ichi) meaning "one" combined with 郎 (rou) meaning "son". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: 淳二, 淳弐, 篤司, 篤時, 篤二, 敦, 敦時, 敦冶, 諄二, 温久, 温二, 厚, 厚至, 厚治, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 淳 (atsu) meaning "pure" combined with 二 (ji) meaning "two". Other kanji combinations are possible.A famous bearer is Atsuji Miyahara​, a Japanese wrestler and Olympic champion in Greco-Roman wrestling.

column3: 篤二郎, 篤次郎, 厚二郎, 敦次郎, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 篤 (atsu) meaning "honest", 二 (ji) meaning "two" combined with 郎 (rou) meaning "son". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: 篤花, 惇佳, 醇香, 敦歌, 敦香, 諄耶, 淳夏, 厚香, 京佳, 温香, 貴香, 扱, 亜津香, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 篤 (atsu) meaning "honest" combined with 花 (ka) meaning "flower". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: 渥幹, 渥樹, 杏槻, 温輝, 温己, 貴規, 貴樹, 厚基, 彩月季, 充己, 淳希, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 渥 (atsu) meaning "moist" combined with 幹 (ki) meaning "tree trunk". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: あつま(Japanese Hiragana)|渥真, 敦真, 厚馬, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 渥 (atsu) meaning "moist" or 敦 (atsu) meaning "kindness, affinity" combined with 真 (ma) meaning "real, genuine". Other combinations of kanji can form this name as well.

column3: 厚正, 京昌, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From 厚 (atsu) meaning "thick, heavy, kind" or 京 (atsu) meaning "capital city, Tokyo, Kyoto, ten quadrillion, ten thousand billion" combined with 雅 (masa) meaning "elegant, graceful". Other kanji combinations can be used.
From Japanese 純 (atsu) meaning "pure, innocent" combined with 瞳 (me) meaning "pupil". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: アツミ(Japanese Katakana)|渥美, 敦美, 暖己, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 渥 (atsu) meaning "glossy, moisten, moist, cordial, kind" combined with 美 (mi) meaning "beautiful". Other kanji combinations are possible as well.

column3: 温美子, 敦美子, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From 温 (atsu) meaning "warm" or 篤 (atsu) meaning "deep, true, sincere" combined with 美 (mi) meaning "beauty", and 子 (ko, shi) meaning "child". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: アツム(Japanese Katakana)|纂, 集, 侑, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From 侑 (atsumu) meaning "to help, to assist, urge to eat", 集 (atsumu) meaning "to gather, congregate" or 纂 (atsumu) meaning "editing, compiling, gather". Other spellings are possible.

column3: あつな(Japanese Hiragana)|アツナ(Japanese Katakana)|亜津奈, 渥奈, 温奈, 淳名, 篤菜, 惇菜, 敦奈, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 亜 (a) meaning "second, Asia", 津 (tsu), a place name, such as Tsu city in Mie prefecture combined with 奈 (na) meaning "apple tree". Other kanji combinations are possible.

From Japanese 篤 (atsu) meaning "deep, true, sincere" or 敦 (atsu) meaning "honest" combined with 直 (nao) meaning "straight, direct" or 尚 (shou, nao) meaning "esteem, furthermore, still, yet". Other kanji combinations can be used.

column3: 篤人, etc.(Japanese Kanji)|あつんど(Japanese Hiragana)|アツンド(Japanese Katakana)
column12: Shift from Atsuhito.This name is very rarely used.

column3: あつ乃(Kanji/Hiragana)|あつの(Japanese Hiragana)|篤乃, 惇乃, 淳野, 厚野, 渥野, 渥乃, 諄乃, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 篤 (atsu) meaning "honest" combined with 乃 (no), a possessive particle. Other combinations of kanji characters can also form this name.

column3: 厚信, 篤信, etc.(Japanese Kanji)|あつのぶ(Japanese Hiragana)|アツノブ(Japanese Katakana)
column12: From Japanese 厚 (atsu) meaning "thick, heavy" or 篤 (atsu) meaning "deep, true, sincere" combined with 信 (nobu) meaning "trust". Other kanji combinations can form this name as well.

column3: 渥訓, 温規, 温教, 温法, 厚紀, 厚, 厚範, 充文, 淳永, 淳慎, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 渥 (atsu) meaning "moist" combined with 訓 (nori) meaning "teach, instruct". Other kanji combinations are also possible.A famous bearer is Atsunori Inaba, a Japanese former professional baseball player. He was the Most Valuable Player of the 2006 Japan Series.

column3: 温男, 教生, 渥郎, 渥男, 厚於, 厚男, 厚郎, 淳央, 醇郎, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 温 (atsu) meaning "warm" combined with 男 (o) meaning "male". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: 篤郎, 篤朗, 敦良, 敦郎, 淳朗, 重郎, 郭郎, 諄郎, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 篤 (atsu) meaning "honest" combined with 郎 (rou) meaning "son". Other kanji combinations are possible.A famous bearer is Atsuro Watabe, a Japanese actor.

column3: 京茂, 厚重, 慎茂, 篤重, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From 京 (atsu) meaning "capital city, Tokyo, Kyoto, ten quadrillion, ten thousand billion" or 厚 (atsu) meaning "thick, heavy, kind" combined with 重 (shige) meaning "layers, folds". Other kanji combinations can be used.

column3: 温助, 温祐, 温輔, 厚佑, 淳祐, 敦助, 敦祐, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 温 (atsu) meaning "warm" combined with 助 (suke) meaning "help, assistance". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: あつたか(Japanese Hiragana)|アツタカ(Japanese Katakana)|京崇, 敦堯, 渥天, 惇剛, 重敬, 淳琢, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 篤 (atsu) meaning "honest" or 熱 (atsu) meaning "passion, temperature" combined with 孝 (taka) meaning "filial piety" or 堯 (taka) meaning "high, far". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: 篤威, 篤毅, 惇岳, 敦剛, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 篤 (atsu) meaning "honest" combined with 威 (take) meaning "intimidate". Other kanji combinations are possible.
From Japanese 宏 (atsu) meaning "wide, spacious, great, vast", 太 (ta) meaning "thick, big" combined with 郎 (rou) meaning "son". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: 敦斗, 敦人, 敦翔, 厚斗, 厚人, 厚翔, 篤斗, 篤人, 篤翔(Japanese Kanji)|あつと(Japanese Hiragana)|アツト(Japanese Katakana)
column12: This name combines 敦 (ton, tai, dai, chou, atsu.i) meaning "industry, kindliness", 厚 (kou, atsu.i, aka) meaning "thick, heavy, rich, kind, cordial, brazen, shameless" or 篤 (toku, atsu.i) meaning "fervent, kind, cordial, serious, deliberate" with 斗 (to, tou) meaning "Big Dipper, sake dipper", 人 (jin, nin, -to, hito, -ri) meaning "person" or 翔 (shou, kage.ru, to.bu) meaning "fly, soar."This name is rarely given to boys, if given at all.

column3: アツヤ(Japanese Katakana)|敦也, 篤也, 纂哉, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: Derived from 纂 (atsu) meaning "compile, gather" or 敦 (atsu) meaning "candid, sincere, honest" and 也 (ya) meaning "also". Other kanji combinations can spell this name.

column3: 温安, 篤康, 敦坦, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 温 (atsu) meaning "warm", 篤 (atsu) meaning "deep, true, sincere" or 敦 (atsu) meaning "honest" combined with 安 (yasu) meaning "peace, quiet", 康 (yasu) meaning "peaceful" or 坦 (yasu) meaning "flat, smooth, level".

column3: あつよ(Japanese Hiragana)|篤世, 惇代, 春代, 修代, 惇葉, 敦代, 農代, 厚代, 安都代, 渥世, 阿都世, 亜都代, 亜津世, 諄代, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 篤 (atsu) meaning "honest" combined with 代 (yo) meaning "generation" or 世 (yo) meaning "world". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: 敦成, 敦義, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From 敦 (atsu.shi) meaning "kindness, honesty" and 成 (yoshi) meaning "become". Other kanji combinations can be used.

column3: 京行, 京千, 京征, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From 京 (atsu) meaning "capital city, Tokyo, Kyoto, ten quadrillion, ten thousand billion" and 行 (yuki) meaning "line, row". Other kanji combinations can be used.
From Ossetian ацы (atsy) meaning "present, real, true" and рухс (rukhs) meaning "light". This is the name of a character in the Nart sagas, the daughter of the god Khur.
Means "twin" in Fante, an Akan language.

Attaces (died 418 A.D.) was king of the western Alans in Hispania (the Iberian Peninsula, modern Spain and Portugal).The Alans were an ancient and medieval Iranian nomadic pastoral people of the North Caucasus.
Alternate transcription of Thai อรรถชัย (see Atthachai).
From Guanche *hata-tagarest, meaning "here is the frost". This was recorded as the name of a 5-year-old Guanche girl from Tenerife who was sold at the slave market in Valencia in 1494.
Name borne by three Guanche women, aged 26, 28 and 30, who were sold at the slave market in Valencia in 1494.

The name comes from the verb ענה ('ana), which can mean one of four things: "to answer", "to be occupied with", "to afflict", or "to sing".In the Bible, there are three people named Attai. The first, in 1 Chronicles 2:35, is one of the descendants of Jerahmeel. He is the son of Jarha, grandson of Sheshan, father of Nathan, and grandfather of Zabad. The second, in 1 Chronicles 12:11, is the sixth of Gad's captains. The third, in 2 Chronicles 11:20, is the son of King Rehoboam and his second wife, Maakah; as well as the brother of Abijah, Ziza, and Shelomith.
Means "leaning wood" in Cherokee, from *ada meaning "wood", and *gulkalu, a verb that implies something long, leaning against some other object.
Derived from an Ancient Germanic word meaning "fatherly, paternal".
Variant of Atallah, a masculine Arabic name, which is borne by Attallah Shabazz (1958-), the eldest daughter of American activist Malcolm X.
Possibly derived from Greek ἀταλός (atalos) meaning "delicate, tender" or the related ἀτάλλω (atallo) meaning "to bring up a child, to foster", "to grow" or "to skip, gambol, frolic".

Latinized form of Attalos. This was borne by numerous ancient Greek historical figures, including a general of Alexander the Great and three kings of Pergamon in Asia Minor.The famous marble statue The Dying Gaul is a Roman copy of a lost bronze sculpture which was commissioned by the 3rd-century BC king Attalus I to celebrate his defeat of the Galatians, a Celtic tribe.

From Guanche *hata-tanaṭda, meaning "here is the (personified) authority". This was recorded as the name of a 35-year-old Guanche woman from Tenerife who was sold at the slave market in Valencia in 1494.
Alternate transcription of Thai อรรถพล (see Atthaphon).
Alternate transcription of Thai อรรถพล (see Atthaphon).

column12: Alternate transcription of Thai อรรถพงศ์/อรรถพงษ์ (see Atthaphong).
Alternate transcription of Thai อรรถพล (see Atthaphon).
Alternate transcription of Thai อรรถพล (see Atthaphon).

column3: อรรถพงศ์, อรรถพงษ์(Thai)
column12: Alternate transcription of Thai อรรถพงศ์/อรรถพงษ์ (see Atthaphong).
Derived from Persian آتش (ātash), meaning "fire", with the intended meaning of "fiery".

column3: อรรถสิทธิ์(Thai)
column12: Alternate transcription of Thai อรรถสิทธิ์ (see Atthasit).

column3: อรรถสิทธิ์(Thai)
column12: Alternate transcription of Thai อรรถสิทธิ์ (see Atthasit).
Alternate transcription of Thai อรรถวุฒิ (see Atthawut).
Alternate transcription of Thai อรรถวุฒิ (see Atthawut).

Guanche name meaning "here is the beautiful young woman", derived from the Guanche demonstrative *hata and *teneriht "gazelle", used here to mean "beautiful girl". This was recorded as the name of a 10-year-old Guanche girl from the island of Tenerife (present-day Canary Islands, Spain) who was sold at the slave market in Valencia in 1495. In the modern era this name has been (rarely) used in the Canary Islands since the 1970s.

The best-known (and possibly the first) bearer of this name is saint Audifax, who was of noble descent and born in the Persian Empire. Somewhere between 268 and 270 AD, he went on a pilgrimage to Rome with his parents and brother, whose names were Marius, Martha and Abachum (also known as Habakkuk). Once there, the whole family was martyred for their faith and their aid to the local Christians.Given the saint's background and the names of his immediate family, Audifax might be a latinization of his original name, which might possibly have been of Hebrew or Persian origin. If that is indeed the case, then the original form of his name appears to have been lost to time.According to one Russian source, his name is partially Hebrew and partially Latin. The first part of the name basically means "servant of God" and as such corresponds to Abdias, whereas the second part is derived from the Latin noun fax meaning "torch".Other sources claim that the name is actually fully Latin, which seems doubtful when you look at the saint's background. A Spanish source states that Audifax is a combination of the Latin verbs audio meaning "to hear, to listen" and facio meaning "to do", whilst a French source basically indicates that the name consists of the Latin adjective audax meaning "audacious, daring, bold, courageous" (see Audax) and the previously mentioned Latin verb facio meaning "to do".All in all, the meaning and origin of this name is uncertain, but the few available sources at least seem to agree that Audifax is a compound name.

From the Roman nomen gentile Aufidius, which is of uncertain origin and meaning. The first element, au, may have been derived from the Latin preverb au "away, off", but it could also have been a phonetic variant of the Latin preverb ab "from". The second element could then have been derived from Latin fides "faith", which would then roughly give the name's meaning as either "away from faith" or "from faith". Alternatively, the name could have been derived from Aufidus, a river in Apulia that is nowadays known under the name Ofanto. Aufidus was a latinization of Greek Ophidous (Ωφιδους), which was derived from Greek ophiōdēs "snaky" or opheōdēs "snake-like", both ultimately derived from Greek ophis "snake, serpent". The Greek linguistic origin is due to the fact that Apulia, although located on the Italian peninsula, had been colonized by the ancient Greeks for several centuries until it was eventually conquered by Rome in the 4th and 3rd centuries BC. Lastly, there is also a possibility that the name is etymologically related to Aufidena (sometimes given as Alfidena), the name of a city in northern Samnium which was under control of the Caraceni, the most northern tribe of the Samnites. Since the Samnites mostly spoke Oscan, it is not unreasonable to assume that the city's name is also Oscan in origin. Oscan is an extinct Italic language, just like Latin - but note that it is a cousin of Latin, not actually descended from Latin itself. I don't know what the name of the city was in Oscan, but given how the language is related to Latin, the meaning may be the same (or close to) the possible Latin meaning that I had provided earlier. In history, bearers of this name were Roman historian Aufidius Bassus and Roman magistrate Marcus Aufidius Lurco, the latter of which was also the maternal grandfather of the Roman Empress Livia Drusilla (the third wife of Emperor Augustus). In Literature, this was the name of Tullus Aufidius, a Volscian general from William Shakespeare's tragedy Coriolanus. The character was based upon a real person, namely the wealthy Volscian noble Attius Tullus Aufidius, who lived in the 5th century BC.

Name of a countess of Urgell in the 12th/13th century, probably related to Latin aurum meaning "gold". Modern usage of this name in Catalonia and Andorra stretches back to at least the 1970's.

Roman slave name, a feminine diminutive of Latin aureus "golden" (possibly the feminine form of Aureolus, a derivative of Aureus). Camden (1605) lists Aureola "pretty little golden dame".

A Roman cognomen derived from aureus "golden". It is known as the name of one of the Thirty Tyrants who rebelled against the Roman emperor Galienus and usurp the power for themselves.
Either a variant of Oretta or a transferred use of the surname Auretta.

Means "golden, gilded" in Latin, from aurum "gold" (see Aurea). An aureus was also a gold coin of ancient Rome, equivalent to 25 denarii. This was the name of a Christian saint who was martyred in the 5th century with his sister Saint Justina at the cathedral of Mainz in Germany; they were killed by invading Huns while celebrating Mass.
Combination of aur ("gravel, sand, clay") and galmr ("shouting one"). This is the name of a jǫtunn, probably another name for Ymir, the father of Þrúðgelmir and grandfather of Bergelmir.
Derived from aur "sand, clay" and grímr "person wearing a face mask or helmet" or grimmr "grim". This is the name of a jotunn in Norse mythology.
Finnish diminutive of Aura, occasionally also used in Estonia.
Derived from Latin aurum "gold" and aureus "golden, gilded". Auria was an early consort of Pamplona, and also the Roman name for the city of Ourense in Spain.

Auric Goldfinger is the antogonist of James Bond in 'Goldfinger' by Ian Flemming. The name derives from Latin #aurum "gold" and maens "golden". Also in the case of French composer Georges Auric (1899-1983), transferred from the surname Auric.

Possibly an English form of the Roman name Aureola, coined in the 19th century - revived also as Aureole, Auriol and Oriel - and used regularly since. However, Orieldis or Aurildis was a medieval name of Old German origin meaning "fire-strife", which survives in the surname Oriel. Auriel and Oriel were revived at roughly the same time, the beginning of the 20th century, and were clearly heard by parents as the same name; the Au spelling was the first to appear in official records, but one cannot be sure which name was a variant of the other. The name may also be related to Uriel.
Possibly a variant of Auriel or Ariele.
Daughter of Lord Boncenes. During the Grail Quest, Galahad visited their castle and convinced Aurience to become a nun.
Means "charioteer" in Latin. This is the name of a constellation in the northern sky, which is said to resemble a chariot and its driver.
Means "golden gem" in Neapolitan, now mostly found as a surname.

Means "born of gold", derived from Latin aurum "gold" and -gena "born from, sprung from". This was originally a poetic epithet applied to the legendary hero Perseus (whose father, the god Jupiter, came upon his mother Danaë in the form of a shower of gold). Compare the Greek adjective χρυσόπατρος (chrysopatros) meaning "sprung of a golden father"; also compare Chrysogonos.
Variation on Alaric meaning all-powerful ruler.

From the plant with the same name (Primula auricula), in German known as Aurikel.
Possibly a variant of the Spanish name Laurinda, meaning "laurel tree".
Tagalog diminutive of Aurora, Aurea and other names containing aur.

According to the 1st-century Roman historian Tacitus in his book "Germania", Aurinia was the name of an ancient Germanic prophetess, who was venerated by her people (i.e. the ancient Germans). Aurinia is most likely a latinized form of the prophetess' actual name; some sources have said that her actual name may have been Albruna, Alioruna, Aliruna or Alrynia.
Feminine form of Auriol, first recorded in Leire in 1111.

Derived from Proto-Indo-European aues meaning "brilliant, shining" (related to Proto-Italic *auzōs, from the Proto-Indo-European root *h₂éwsōs meaning "dawn" - the source also of Aurora and Auster) combined with -isma, a variant of the Latin superlative suffix -issima.

From the Latin words auris ("of gold") and stella ("star"), thus intended to mean "golden star". This name was invented by Spanish writer Miguel de Cervantes (1547-1616) as a byname for Sigismunda, one of the main characters in his novel Los trabajos de Persiles y Sigismunda. This name became popular in Venezuela and Brazil in the mid 20th century.

Lombardic cognate of Earendel. The name is attested as the name of a historical Lombardic prince.
Coined by Sabino Arana Goiri and Koldo Elizalde as a Basque form of the Spanish name Presentación. They most likely based the name on Basque aurkitu "to find; to discover".
Derived from aur "again; sand" and konungr "king". This is a by-name for the god Hœnir.
Latinization of Orflath (see Órlaith). A daughter of the 12th-century Irish chieftain Donal Og MacCarthy bore this name.
Derived from aurr ("gravel, sand, clay"). This is the name of a Jotunn in Norse mythology.

Diminutive of Aurora used primarily used in Latin America.

Possibly from Latin aurus ("gold") or a form of Aurius.
Means "produced from the thigh" in Sanskrit.

Means "beam; morning; morning star", or possibly derived from aur ("water") and vandill ("sword"). In Norse mythology one of Aurvandill's toes broke off. Thor threw it into the sky, where it became a star.
Means "one from Aurvangar". Aurvangar "the gravelly wetlands", also called Jǫruvellir "sandy plain", is the home of the dwarfs. In Norse mythology Aurvangr is the name of a dwarf.
Derived from the Longobard hansz meaning "friend, companion".
Alternate form of Osiris, notable bearer is NBA player Ausar Thompson.

Alleged Lithuanian goddess of sunbeams and sunlight.Ausca was first recorded by Polish historian and theologian Jan Łasicki in his treatise on idolatry De diis Samagitarum caeterorumque Sarmatarum et falsorum Christianorum, written ca. 1582 and published in 1615.Her name is clearly a Latinization and gives modern-day academics headaches as to what the original form, if there ever was one, might have been. Several attempts have, however, been made to reconstruct an original form. One suggestion was Aušta, in which case the name would be derived from Lithuanian aušta "it is dawning; dawn is falling; day is breaking". Another theory concludes that Ausca might have been a form of Aušra, deriving the name from Lithuanian aušra "dawn". Should that be the case, she might have been identical with the goddess Aušrinė known from Lithuanian folklore.Since Łasicki was not intimately familiar with Lithuanian culture or language, the academic opinion on the value of his writings ranges from a valuable resource to a practical joke.
From the root aus- "dawn", attached to the derivative suffix -eklis. Auseklis is a Latvian god that represents the first star to appear in the mornings on the east side of the sky.
Auset is the original form of Isis. The hieroglyphs literally translate to “woman (she) of the throne”. More generally, it means “seat”.
Catalan form of Alzeas (via the variants Auzias and Elzéar), itself an Occitan form of Eleazar.
Ausir is a child present at the Cottage of Lost Play when Ælfwine visits there, in one of J.R.R. Tolkien's tales given in The Book of Lost Tales Part One.
The name of a son of Odysseus. Taken from Ausones, the Greek form of Latin Aurunci, the name of a tribe. Aurunci is most likely derived from Latin aurum "gold".

Derivative of Auson. This is the name of a Roman poet (310-395).
Roman cognomen which was derived from the Latin noun auspex meaning "augur, interpreter of omens".
From Latin auspicius meaning "sign, omen" This name is borne by two saints from Eastern Europe who lived in the 2nd and 5th centuries AD respectively.

Derived from Aušra with the feminine adjectival suffix -inė, referring to something made from or pertaining to a noun, ultimately meaning something along the lines of "auroral; pertaining to the dawn."This name belongs to a Lithuanian goddess of the morning star and sister to Vakarinė, known as Auseklis in Latvia. Some scholars believe that she was also the goddess of youth, beauty and health and as such was referred to as "the Queen of the Stars."In Lithuanian folklore, she became the moon's love interest when the moon divorced the sun.
Spelling variant of Aušrius used by Lithuanians residing abroad.
Derived from the Old Norse elements austr "east" and the name suffix -arr, which can derive from herr "army, warrior", geirr "spear", or -varr "defender, guardian" (from warjaną).

Basque feminine name of uncertain origin and meaning. One popular theory suggests, however, that it might be derived from Agustina, while another theory links this name to Sebastiana due to Austitza's traditional prevalence in Saustitza, a town that was famous for its devotion to Sebastiana.

Queen Austregilde (548 - 580) was the third wife of Guntram, King of Orléans. She was not born into high social status and was possibly a servant of Queen Marcatrude, the second wife of Guntram; a servant of one of Guntram's courtiers; or even a slave in the household of Marcatrude's father. After Guntram's repudiation of his earlier queen in 565, she became his third wife. Objections to this marriage and to the legitimacy of Austregilde's children led to the deaths of Marcatrude's brothers and the banishment to a monastery of the Bishop of Gap, both on the orders of Guntram.Austregilde and Guntram had two sons, Clotaire and Clodomir, and two daughters, Clodoberge and Clotilde. She died in 580, possibly of smallpox. According to Gregory of Tours, she angrily blamed her doctors Nicolas and Donat, claiming their medicines were responsible for her death. She asked Guntram to kill her doctors after her death, which he did. Gregory compares her actions to those of King Herod.Modern historians have suggested skepticism about Gregory's account of Austregilde's death. E. T. Dailey notes that it "is difficult to square this passage" with Gregory's "supposedly heroic" overall portrayal of Guntram and that "marriage to lowborn women was never likely to impress Gregory". Mark A. Handley contrasts Gregory's depiction of Austregilde with that of her "glowing" epitaph, which describes her as "mother of kings, a surpassing royal wife, the light of her homeland, the world, and the court" and praises her charitable nature. Handley is critical of those that have "unnecessarily followed" Gregory's lead, saying that the "opportunity to compare and contrast... has been universally missed."
Derived from the Germanic element austra or austar, which comes from Old High German ôstan "east." The second element is derived from gisel "hostage" or "pledge."

Derived from Old Norse auðr "prosperity, riches" and *humala "hornless". In Norse mythology this was the name of the primeval cow who freed Buri, the first god, from ice.
Means "happiness, luck, prosperity, destiny" in Old Norse, used as a short form of names starting with this element.

Derived from the Old Norse elements auðr "fortune, riches" and lín "flax, linen". Alternatively the second element could be derived from Hlín (which occurs in many Old Norse poetic compounds meaning "woman") or Lína.

Authrounios is a divine or semi-divine revelatory figure in the Sethian Gnostic text Zostrianos, where he is described as a “great ruler” or high-ranking spiritual authority who instructs the protagonist during his ascent through the cosmic realms. In the narrative, Authrounios functions as a teacher of esoteric cosmology, explaining the structure of the lower worlds, the origin of the material cosmos, and the deceptive nature of creation as a reflection of higher divine realities. He appears as part of the complex hierarchy of aeons and intelligences characteristic of Sethian Gnosticism, serving a role similar to an initiatory guide who imparts salvific knowledge (gnosis) necessary for spiritual ascent. Not widely attested outside this text.
Derived from the Old Norse elements auðr meaning "wealth, fortune" (or possibly the poetic word auðr which meant "fate, destiny") and rún meaning "secret lore, rune".
Derived from the Germanic name elements auðr "prosperity, fortune, riches" and ulfr "wolf".
Old Norse variant form of Auðun.
Possibly a feminine form of Autochthon. This was the name of a mythical Mycenaean princess, a daughter of Perseus and Andromeda.

Derived from Greek αὐτόχθων (autochthon) meaning "sprung from the land itself; indigenous, native", composed of αὐτός (autos) "self" and χθών (chthon) "earth, soil". In Plato's myth of Atlantis, Autochthon was one of the ten sons of Poseidon and Cleito, twin brother to Mneseus.
Latinized form of Autokles. This name was borne by an Athenian general from the 5th century BC.
Latinized form of Autokrates. This name was borne by an ancient Athenian comic poet.

Derived from Ancient Greek αὐτός (autos) meaning "self" combined with δίκη (dike) meaning "justice, custom, order". Compare the Greek adjective αὐτόδικος (autodikos) meaning "with independent jurisdiction, with one's own law-courts".
Means "glory itself, personified glory", derived from Ancient Greek αὐτός (autos) meaning "self" combined with κλέος (kleos) meaning "glory".

Means "ruling by oneself, absolute, independent", derived from Ancient Greek αὐτός (autos) meaning "self" combined with κρατος (kratos) meaning "power, strength". Also compare the English word autocrat, which derives from the same roots.

From Ancient Greek αὐτολήκυθος (autolekythos) (composed of αὐτός (autos) meaning "self" and λήκυθος (lekythos) meaning "lekythos; oil flask or bottle") meaning "one who carries his own oil-flask", which had connotations of "shabby person, beggar" as well as the sexual euphemism of "well-hung". This was the name of an Indian slave of Favorinus, a Roman sophist and skeptic philosopher.
Spanish and Portuguese form of Autolycus.
Latinized form of Autolykos. In Greek mythology, Autolycus is a renowned thief and the maternal grandfather of Odysseus.

The first possibility is that it is derived from Greek λυκου (lykou) "of a wolf", which itself is ultimately derived from Greek λύκος (lykos) "wolf". The second possibility is that it is derived from Greek λύκη (lyke), which can mean "light" as well as "morning sunshine".
Feminine form of Ancient Greek αὐτόματος (automatos) meaning "self-willed, unbidden, spontaneous". This was the name of one of the Danaids in Greek mythology.

Derived from Greek αὐτός (autos) meaning "self" combined with the Greek noun μέδων (medon) meaning "ruler" (see Medon).This name was borne by a Greek tyrant of Eretria (4th century BC) and a Greek poet (lived somewhere between the 1st century BC and the 1st century AD).In Greek mythology, Automedon is the name of the charioteer of Achilles.
Feminine form of Autonoos (see Autonous). In Greek mythology this was the name of the daughter of Cadmus, founder of Thebes and Harmonia, one of the Bacchae in Euripides' play of the same name.
Means "self-willed" or "mind of one’s own", derived from Greek αὐτός (autos) meaning "self" and νόος (noos) meaning "mind, thought".

Hellenized form of Old Persian Vātafradātah, possibly meaning "bestowed by Vata". This was the name of a 4th-century Persian Satrap of Lydia and a dynast (frataraka) of Persis in the late 2nd-century BC, ruling sometime after 138 BC.

Derived from Greek αὔξησις (auxesis) meaning "growth, increase". This was the name of the goddess of spring growth, one of the Horai. The name also functioned as a title of the goddess Persephone, whose ascent from the underworld marked the transition from winter into spring.

Feminine form of Auxilius. In some cases, the name can also be a short form of Auxiliadora.

Derived from Latin auxiliatrix, which refers to a helper, aide or assistant of the female sex (the masculine equivalent is auxiliator). The word is ultimately derived from the Latin noun auxilium meaning "help, aid, assistance". Also see Auxilius and Auxiliadora. As a personal name, Auxiliatrix is usually bestowed on a newborn girl in honour of the Virgin Mary, since Auxiliatrix is one of her many epithets (sometimes she is even called Mary Auxiliatrix). But despite this significant religious connection, Auxiliatrix is extremely rare as a personal name. For example, in The Netherlands, there were less than 5 bearers with the name (in the entire country) in 2014.

A bearer of this name was the 5th-century saint Auxilius of Ireland, although in his case his name may possibly have been a latinized form of his original Gaelic given name.

In ancient Roman religion, Averruncus or Auruncus is a god of averting harm. Aulus Gellius says that he is one of the potentially malignant deities who must be propitiated for their power to both inflict and withhold disaster from people and the harvests.Although the etymology of the name is often connected to the Latin verb avertere, "to turn away," a more probable origin lies in averro "to sweep away," hence averrunco, "to ward off," perhaps with a reference to magical sweeping. Varro asserts that the infinitive verb averruncare shares its etymology with the god whose primary function is averting. Averruncus may be among the indigitamenta pertaining to another god such as Apollo or Mars, that is, it may be a name to be used in a prayer formulary to fix the local action of the invoked deity. Precise naming, in connection with concealing a deity's true name to monopolize his or her power, was a crucial part of prayer in antiquity, as evidenced not only in the traditional religions of Greece and Rome and syncretistic Hellenistic religion and mystery cult, but also in Judaism and ancient Egyptian religion.

The meaning of this name is uncertain at this time. Its best known bearer was American actress Avonia Jones (1839-1867), whose parents may possibly have named her after the village of Avonia (in Pennsylvania, USA), or after the genus of plants of the same name. It is uncertain what the village and the plant genus derived their name from. The village's name may be of the same etymology as the many places named Avon in the United States, while the plant genus' name may be a corruption of Greek ἀνομία (anomia) meaning "lawlessness, wickedness" (that is, if the plant genus is not named after its discoverer, about whom I can't find any information). The term 'avonia' is found several times in Biblical Greek (with the meaning of "lawlessness"), as one will see if one googles the words 'avonia' and 'lawlessness' at the same time. Finally, for the plant genus, an other possibility is that it is derived from Latin avus "grandfather", in which case it would be a reference to the plant's white, old-looking stipular scales.

Ayçelen is a modern, evocative Turkish name blending two distinct natural images: Ay (the Moon) and Çelen (a crown, a garland of flowers, or a brilliant crest).The name translates to "The Lunar Crown" or "The Garland of Moonbeams." In a modern naming context, it represents a child of striking, radiant beauty who wears the light of the moon like royalty. It carries an aura of natural elegance, suggesting a personality that is both artistic and sophisticated, bringing a crowning glory and a soft, luminous peace to her surroundings.

Ayçiçek is an authentic, highly esteemed medieval Turkic name derived from two pure Old Turkic roots: Ay (moon, symbol of beauty, light, and spiritual elevation) and Çiçek / Çeçek (flower, blossom). The name carries a dual semantic framework:1. The Literal Botanical Meaning: It refers directly to the Sunflower (Helianthus annuus), a plant that instinctively turns its face to track the light, symbolizing loyalty, warmth, radiance, and natural abundance.2. The Poetic/Cosmic Meaning: It translates to "The Moon-Flower" or "The Flower of the Moon," representing a celestial, pristine blossom that blooms in darkness, radiating a soft, mesmerizing light.Historical Figures & Regal LineageUnlike many modern botanical names, Ayçiçek carries a deeply rooted medieval aristocratic lineage across Central Asia:The 8th-Century Uyghur Empire: In historical administrative fragments and Old Uyghur civil documents dating back to the 8th century, a high-born royal princess is explicitly recorded under the archaic spelling Ay-çeçek, highlighting the name’s early elite status within the steppes.The 12th-Century Khwarazmian Empire: The name achieved immense historical gravity as the name of Ayçiçek Hatun, the mother of the legendary, unyielding ruler Jaloliddin Manguberdi (Celaleddin Harzemşah) and wife of Alaeddin Tekiş. Celebrated in Central Asian chronicles for her fierce dignity, political influence, and resilience during the catastrophic Mongol invasions, her figure transformed the name into a symbol of matriarchal fortitude.For parents, Ayçiçek is a luminous and historically grounded choice. It symbolizes a child who possesses both the delicate grace of a flower and the radiant, guiding presence of the moon. It implies a personality that naturally seeks light, exhibits deep ancestral resilience, and brings natural elegance and warmth to everyone around her.

Aydilge is an artistic and expressive modern Turkish name, fusing the celestial majesty of the moon with the poetic, soaring concept of a wish, prayer, or lyrical message. It translates directly to "the moon's wish," "the song whispered to the night sky," or "a brilliant desire born of lunar light."The morpho-semantic structure of Aydilge relies on two distinct native roots:Ay: The eternal Turkic symbol for the moon, bringing connotations of purity, emotional depth, and night-time guidance.Dilge: An evocative derivative of the Proto-Turkic verb Tile- / Dile- (to wish, to pray, to request from a higher power). Through regular Oghuz sound shifts, the initial voiceless T- stabilized into the voiced D-, and when paired with the archaic nominalizing suffix -ge, it yields dilge, signifying an articulated wish, a spoken desire, or a poetic petition.Aydilge stands out in modern Turkish onomastics due to its deeply lyrical, almost musical phrasing. It reframes the child not as a random occurrence, but as a long-awaited, cosmic answer to a beautiful prayer made under the illumination of the moon.For parents, Aydilge suggests a child deeply attuned to creativity, emotional intelligence, and communication. It evokes a personality that is inherently artistic, expressive, and highly intuitive; someone whose words carry weight, and whose dreams are structurally aligned with high, noble aspirations.

Aydolu is a majestic modern Turkish name rich in philosophical and literary history, translating to "the full moon," "the moon of complete abundance," or "a spirit filled to the brim with celestial light." It represents the zenith of lunar onomastic expressions, symbolizing absolute completion, maturity, and unblemished beauty.Linguistically, the name operates on a dual semantic axis that parents intentionally leverage. On one hand, it directly evokes the Dolunay (the astronomical full moon), capturing the visual moment when the moon achieves its ultimate luminosity and perfect spherical symmetry. On the other hand, it incorporates the literal adjective Dolu ay (a filled/abundant moon). In ancient Turkic thought, dolu (filled/replete) is a term of high spiritual blessing (kut). A "dolu" entity is one packed with wisdom, health, prosperity, and divine favor; never empty, never lacking.The name possesses a legendary pedigree within classic Turkic literature, finding its absolute historical anchor in Yusuf Has Hacib’s 11th-century Karakhanid masterpiece, the Kutadgu Bilig (The Wisdom of Royal Glory). In this highly allegorical text, one of the four chief protagonists is named Ögdülmiş, who is explicitly introduced as the son of the wise vizier Aydoldu (or Aydolun). In the narrative, the character of Aydoldu represents Kut (Fortune, Prosperity, and Statehood). By embodying the full moon, Aydoldu signifies a state and a soul that has risen to its highest peak of fullness, illuminating the world with justice and joy.For parents, Aydolu is a name of ultimate fulfillment. It symbolizes a child who is born complete, lacking nothing in character or spirit. It hints at a personality marked by immense emotional generosity, intellectual maturity, and a presence so profoundly luminous that it naturally anchors and stabilizes everyone within her sphere.

A name of pure, ancient Turkic lineage, composed of Ayım (the honorific possessive "my moon") and Bet (the archaic Turkic noun for "face," "countenance," or "aspect"). It translates to "My Moon-Faced One" or "Radiant Countenance."Linguistic Defense: It is mandatory to reject any attempt to link the component -bet to the Persian adjective bed (بد, meaning "bad" or "ugly"). The Turkic -bet is a primary noun root documented in the foundational lexicon of the Turkic world, most notably in Divanu Lugati't-Türk (11th century), where it is unequivocally defined as "face" or "visage." While phonetically convergent with the Persian term, they exist in entirely different semantic and historical universes. Any conflation between the two is an etymological error that ignores the internal evolution of the Turkic language. The name is a declaration of beauty, dignity, and heritage, a term of endearment that centers on the brightness of the bearer’s face, not a moral judgment.

Ayizan is the loa of the marketplace and commerce in Vodou, especially in Benin, Haiti and Suriname.She is a racine, or root loa, associated with Vodoun rites of initiation (called kanzo). Just as her husband Loko is the archetypal houngan (priest), Ayizan is regarded as the first, or archetypal, mambo (priestess), and as such is also associated with priestly knowledge and mysteries, particularly those of initiation and the natural world.As the spiritual parents of the priesthood, she and her husband are two of the loa involved in the kanzo rites in which the priest/ess-to-be is given the asson (sacred rattle and tool of the priesthood) and are both powerful guardians of "reglemen" or the correct and appropriate form of Vodoun service.She is syncretized with the Catholic Saint Clare. Her symbol is the palm frond, and she drinks no alcohol. Her colors are most commonly silver, blue, and white.

Meaning: "Self-sacrifice," "spiritual devotion," or "the exchange of souls." Derived from the Proto-Turkic root *aylan-, meaning "to turn," "to revolve," or "to encircle."Aylanu is a historical feminine name deeply rooted in the spiritual, mythological, and folk traditions of Central Asian and Siberian nomadic cultures.Clarification: A common modern misconception is to analyze the name as a compound of the Turkic words Ay (moon) and Nur (light) or Ayla (halo) + Nur. This is etymologically incorrect. Aylanu is an ancient, independent morphological unit derived directly from the Proto-Turkic verb root *aylan-. It does not split into a "moon-light" compound, but rather stems from the historical development of shamanic idioms.History:In the early shamanic medical and spiritual traditions of early Turkic peoples (preserved heavily in Kipchak and Oghuz variants like Kazakh/Kyrgyz and Old Anatolian Turkish), the word evolved into an idiom for ritualistic spiritual transference. To heal a dying person, a protective companion or healer would perform a ritual dance, physically turning around the patient's bed three times to absorb their affliction. This action was accompanied by the ritual phrase "Aynalayın senden!". While it literally translates to "Let me revolve around you," it functionally carries the deep spiritual weight of: "May your burdens be transferred to me" or "Let my life be sacrificed for yours." Over centuries, this ritual terminology softened into an enduring, profound term of endearment, maternal devotion, and fiercely protective love within Turkic languages.The most complete and celebrated narrative manifestation of this concept's history is found in the Book of Dede Korkut, specifically in the epic of Deli Dumrul.While the text was written down during the Islamic period (naming the angel of death as Azrael) the story preserves a much older, Pre-Islamic layer of Turkic mythology where the entity of death is originally recognized as "Aldacı" (the taker of souls/the bringer of death).When the warrior Deli Dumrul faces death at the hands of Aldacı, his aging parents refuse to trade their lives to save him. It is his devoted wife who performs the ultimate act of aylanu. Stepping forward, she challenges the cosmic order, pleading with the Creator to take her soul instead of her husband's. In the original Oghuz Turkic narrative text, she seals her vow with the definitive declaration:"Bir can değil senin için bin canım var ise yoluna feda olsun."(If I had not just one, but a thousand lives, let them all be sacrificed for yours.)Touched by this pure, unforced devotion, the Creator relents, granting the couple a shared, extended lease on life while taking the souls of the parents who chose self-preservation over loyalty.Symbolism:In a modern naming context, Aylanu is chosen to celebrate an extraordinary heritage of deep, unyielding loyalty, existential courage, and the ancestral bonds of the Eurasian steppes.For parents, the name symbolizes a child who possesses a soul capable of immense depth, profound empathy, and boundless loyalty. It suggests a personality that acts as a protective shield for others; someone whose presence brings a comforting, sheltering grace to those they love. To name a child Aylanu is to bestow upon them a legacy of luminous devotion; a character whose strength is found not in dominance, but in the fierce, protective sanctuary they offer to their loved ones.

A modern Turkish female name. It is a creative phonetic variant of the older compound name Almila (Almıla), which is derived from the Turkic elements al meaning "red, crimson" and mila / mula / milaç, early variations of alma meaning "apple". In this specific variant, the first element has been deliberately substituted with the Turkic root ay meaning "moon", shifting the poetic meaning to "Moon Apple" or "Glistening Apple of the Moon".The alternative theory proposed by some contemporary lexicographers (such as Sevan Nişanyan) suggesting that the element mila is a modern loanword borrowed from the Russian name Lyudmila (via the abbreviation Mila) is highly unsustainable due to five crucial linguistic and historical counterarguments:1. Morphological Continuity of the Variant: The phonetic shift from Almila to Aymila strictly follows traditional Turkic word-play and parallel compounding (e.g., Alsu to Aysu, Alçın to Ayçın). The structural template already existed centuries before Soviet-Turkish marriages.2. The "Apple" Polysemy in Turkic Dialects: In various Turkic dialects (such as Chuvash, Tuvan, and Khakas), the word for apple or wild plum undergoes vowel shifts and suffixations that naturally yield mila, mula, or mulaç without external Slavic influence.3. Anachronistic Phonetic Reduction: True Turkish borrowings from Russian Mila preserve the sharp Mi- sound, whereas Aymila co-exists with older variants like Aymıla and Aymula (back vowels), which are phonetically impossible to derive from the Russian soft front-vowel cluster lyud- or mi-.4. Onomastic Separation in Registration: Early 2000s civil registries in Turkey clearly distinguish between native compound names (Almila/Aymila) used by traditionalist/nationalist families and the isolated name Mila preferred by cosmopolitan or mixed-heritage families. They belong to two distinct sociological naming waves.5. Vowel Harmony Preservation: The integration of Mila as a pseudo-suffix in Aymila adheres perfectly to Turkic vowel harmony trends in female names ending in "-ila/-ilaç", serving as an indigenous organic extension rather than a structural borrowing of a foreign root.

Ayzıt (traditionally recorded in Saha/Yakut as Ajysyt or Ayıysıt) is an exceptionally beautiful, ethereal name from the oldest layers of Turkic-Siberian mythology. It translates directly to "The Bringer of Beauty," "The Bright Creator," or "The Benevolent Moon-Light Spirit."The name is a compound derived from the Proto-Turkic root Ay (meaning "moon," symbolizing pristine beauty, cycles, and celestial radiance) combined with the ancient Siberian Turkic root Ayy / Ayıı, which means "to create," "sacred deed," or "good spirit," followed by an archaic feminine agent suffix. Therefore, it embodies the essence of a celestial mother who manifests beauty, light, and new life.The Mythological Legend of AyzıtIn the rich cosmological pantheon of the Yakut and Altay Turks, Ayzıt is the Goddess of Beauty, Love, and Childbirth. She resides in the golden eastern skies, sitting upon a cloud of light, or descending to earth cloaked in the white fur of a pristine snow-fox or a graceful swan. She is the ultimate matriarch of domestic bliss, responsible for writing the fates of newborn children into the golden ledger of destiny.According to mythological accounts, when a mother is about to give birth, Ayzıt leaves her heavenly palace and brings the Kut (the divine soul-spark) from the creator deity Ülgen or Ayy Toyon, breathing it into the lips of the newborn babe. She heals the sick, comforts the grieving with her soft silver moonlight, and protects young animals in the spring. Her presence is accompanied by a gentle, fragrant breeze and the soft rustle of silver leaves, symbolizing the gentle, nurturing, and aesthetic pinnacle of the universe.Due to its short, distinct structure, Ayzıt must be strictly distinguished from several completely unrelated foreign terms:The ancient Iranian/Persian Zoroastrian city and historical record Yazd / Yezd (meaning "holy" or "place of worship" in Old Persian); the ancient Egyptian goddess Isis (Aset); the Arabic name Aisha (living/prosperous); and the various Middle Eastern variants of Aziz / Aziza. None of these share any structural, cultural, or linguistic ties with the Siberian Turkic moon-goddess.For parents, Ayzıt is a luminous, rare choice that shines with grace, creativity, and divine compassion. It symbolizes a child born to bring harmony, radiant joy, and aesthetic beauty to the world; one who possesses a healing, artistic soul that lights up the dark like the silver rays of the crescent moon.

Arabic form of Azazel. In Islamic tradition this was the original name of Iblis (Satan).
From Mongolian аз (az) meaning "fortune, luck, happiness" and баатар (baatar) meaning "hero".
Variant transcription of Ezbai.This transcription is used in the Douay-Rheims Catholic Bible.
From Mongolian аз (az) meaning "fortune, luck, happiness" and баяр (bayar) meaning "joy, happiness".
From Mongolian аз (az) meaning "fortune, luck, happiness" and билэг (bileg) meaning "gift, talent, aptitude".
Meaning uncertain, possibly a combination of Nahuatl azcatl "ant" and coatl "snake".
Means "ant-flower", from Nahuatl azcatl "ant" and xōchitl "flower". This was the name of an Aztec noblewoman.
From Mongolian аз (az) meaning "fortune, luck, happiness" and дэлгэр (delger) meaning "vast, wide" or "prosperous, abundant".
Alternate transcription of Arabic عز الدين (see Izz ad-Din) chiefly used in North Africa.
Alternate transcription of Arabic عز الدين (see Izz ad-Din) chiefly used in North Africa.
Variant of Azelia. This name is borne by American rapper Azealia Banks (1991-).
Alternate transcription of Arabic عز الدين (see Izz ad-Din) chiefly used in North Africa.
Alternate transcription of Arabic عز الدين (see Izz ad-Din) chiefly used in North Africa.
Alternate transcription of عزيزة (see Aziza), as well as the Dhivehi form.
Italian form of Agellus. The name was popularized by Massimo d'Azeglio (1798-1866) an Italian politician and writer.
This name is borne by Mexican-British actress Azela Robinson.
Victor Hugo used this name in his novel 'Les Misérables' (1862) for a daughter of the Thénardiers (a sister of Eponine and Gavroche).

From Guanche *aẓămăy-əgiwa, meaning "sutures wounds" (literally "cut-sewer"). This was recorded as the name of a 30-year-old Guanche woman from Tenerife who was sold at the slave market in Valencia in 1494.
It probably has its origins from the Arabic language. Az coming from the word عز meaning strength or might and amin coming from the word أمين meaning trustworthy.

Breton name of uncertain origin and meaning.It is sometimes linked to Breton enor "honor", a theory which goes back to the fact that Saint Azénore is occasionally rendered as Honora in Latin texts. Another theory, however, links this name to Eleanor (via Aenor, which is occasionally considered a contracted form of Azenor. Compare also Aanor), while yet another theory was put forth that Azenor might in fact represent an unknown Celtic name, possibly one containing the theonym Esus.In Breton legend it is borne by the mother of Saint Budoc, a 6th-century princess of Brest (however, the name Eleanor was not coined until the 12th century). It was used for a character in Paul Le Flem's opera Le Rossignol de Saint-Malo (1938) and also occurred briefly in the French TV series Kaamelott (as Azénor).
A feminine adaptation of Lazarus, derived from “Eleazar” as both an omission of “El” (God) and having a feminine ending (“-ah”).

Probably derived from the Jewish feast day atzeret (alternative transcription: azereth) with unclear meaning, proposed interpretations include "conclusion" and "gathering" that coincides in time with the Christian pentecost. The feast day is the last (concluding) feast day in spring.
Hellenized form of a Scythian name derived from *aza meaning "leader".
An epithet of the Greek goddesses Demeter and Persephone, likely derived from Greek ἄζη (azê) meaning "dry dirt" or ἄζω (azô) meaning "to dry up, parch" (compare Azalea).

Uncertain etymology, possibly related to ἄζα (aza) meaning "heat, dryness, drought". This was the name of a Minyan prince in Greek mythology, the youngest son of King Clymenus of Orchomenus (located in modern-day Greece).
Means "to grant victory, to make triumphant" in Arabic.
Means “strong in invasion,” “strong fortune,” or “Gad is mighty.” This was the name of a descendant of Parosh whose 1,222 descendants returned to Judah after the Babylonian exile.
Means "delight of the people" in Armenian, ultimately from ազգ (azg) meaning "people, nation" and անոյշ (anoysh) meaning "sweet; pleasant, agreeable".
Means "the breeding place" in Arabic. This is the traditional name of the star Eta Eridani in the constellation Eridanus.
From the ancient "LIVING" classical language Thamizh(Tamil). Means handsome, beautiful etc.
Derived from Arabic أزهر ('azhar) meaning "shining, bright".

Means "dragon" in Persian, likely derives from Middle Persian azdahāg, from Avestan Aži Dahāka which is associated with the demonic figure Zahhak, a tyrannical king in Persian folklore.Aži Dahāka (or Zahhāk) is one of the most infamous monsters in Zoroastrian and Persian mythology. In the Avesta, he is described as a three-headed dragon with six eyes and three mouths—a terrifying embodiment of evil. In Ferdowsi’s Shahnameh, he becomes Zahhāk, a tyrant king with serpents growing from his shoulders who must feed on human brains.
Nickname for names beginning with Az-, such as, Azariah, Azalea (English), Ayzik 2 (Yiddish), and Azadeh (Persian).
Azibo means “youth” in Nigerian. It also means “Earth” in Egyptian.
Variant of Ezilda. The town of Azilda in Ontario is named after one of the first female pioneers to settle there, Azilda Bélanger (née Brisebois), who was known for her healing abilities.
Hellenized form of the Scythian name *Azalīźa meanin "commander-in-chief", ultimately derived from *aza meaning "leader" and *rīźa meaning "desiring, commanding".
Means "magnificent, great, supreme, powerful" in Arabic, a derivative of عظم (ʿaẓuma) meaning "to be great". In Islamic tradition العظيم (al-ʿAẓīm) is one of the 99 names of Allah.
Alternate transcription of Arabic عظيمة (see Azima), as well as the Malay and Indonesian form.
From azim meaning "great, huge" and gul meaning "flower".
From the given name Azim combined with Persian جان (jān) meaning "soul, life".
Means "magnificence of Allah", from Arabic عَظِيم (ʿaẓīm) meaning "magnificence, grandiose" and الله (Allah).
Means "beauty, adornment". In ancient Persian, it meant "creed, system".

Derived from the Latin axio meaning "owl". It can also be a variant of Azzo. It is rarely used because Azio is the Italianization of Actium, the town where Octavian gained his celebrated victory over Antony and Cleopatra, on September 2, 31 BCE.
Meaning uncertain, possibly of Arabic origin.
Aziraphale is the name of a the angel in the Neil Gaiman and Terry Pratchett collaboration, Good Omens. The authors state that though the name is made up of real elements, it's made up.
Indonesian and Malay variant of Aziz.
Derived from Persian آزاد (âzâd) meaning "free, independent".
taken from the word "Azure" which means 'bight blue' or 'sky blue'. It can also be the "Azure" that means 'heaven'.
Aziyadé (1879) is a novel by French author Pierre Loti. It tells the story of the 27-year-old Loti's illicit love affair with an 18-year-old harem girl named Aziyadé.
Alternate transcription of Arabic عزيزة (see Aziza), as well as the usual Malay and Indonesian form.
From the given name Aziza and the word xon, meaning "khan".

Means "treasure, rarity, something valuable; lover" in Swahili, derived from Arabic عَزِيز‎ (ʕazīz); compare Aziz. A known (female) bearer is American model Azizi Johari (1948-), in whose case it is a pseudonym.
Combination of the name Aziz with the Kazakh word jan, meaning "dear" or "soul" (derived from Persian).
From the given name Aziz combined with jon meaning "soul, life".
Combination of the name Aziz and the Turkic title khan, meaning "king" or "ruler".
Derived frpm aziz meaning "dear, beloved", "holy, sacred" or "rare, precious" and poshsha, an endearing name for a girl or woman.
First part of compound Arabic names beginning with عزيز ال (ʿAzīz al) meaning "dear of the, beloved of the" or "excellence of the, power of the" (such as Azizullah).
Means "dear to Allah", from Arabic عَزِيز (ʿazīz) meaning "dear, darling" and الله (Allah).
Tajik and Uzbek form of Azizullah.
Means "power of women" from عزيز (ʿazīz) meaning "powerful, respected" and نساء (nisa) meaning "women"
Means "happiness, bliss" in Mongolian, from аз (az) meaning "fortune, luck" and жаргал (jargal) meaning "happiness, blessing".

Means "purer, more befitting, better" in Arabic, ultimately from the root زكا (zakā) meaning "to be good or just, to be suitable". It is sometimes used as a masculine name in Indonesia, while it is solely feminine elsewhere.

Possibly derived from the Greek name Delia 1 which means "from Delos, the island of which Artemis and Apollo, the twins gods, were born."Name of the Sorceress in the Sci Fi mini-series based of The Wizard of Oz called The Tin-Man played by actress Kathleen Robertson.

As an African name it means "powerful". As an English name, it is an alternate spelling of Azlan which is a variant of Aslan, a Turkish name meaning "lion". It is the name of the Lion in CS Lewis's book 'The Lion the Witch and the Wardrobe'.
Derived from Arabic أصلي ('aṣliyy) meaning "original, authentic, first, initial".
Derived from Arabic عزم (ʾazm) meaning "firm resolution, resolve, determination".
Means "greatness, might, importance" in Arabic, from the root عظم (ʿaẓuma) meaning "to be great".

This name is comprised of two parts: עז ('az) meaning "power, to be strong" and מוות (mavet) meaning "death". Some sources claim the combined meaning of this name is "Death is Strong".This name is used many times in the Bible. It is also the name of a town mentioned in Nehemiah 12:29.
Derived from Arabic عزم ('azm) meaning "resolution, resolve, determination".
Possibly from the Uzbek azm meaning "resolution".
Alternate transcription of Arabic عزمي (see Azmi).
From the Bashkir аҙна (azna) meaning "Friday, week" and feminine name element бикә (bikä).
Means "tender flower" in Tatar, from the Arabic-Iranian given name Asna meaning "tender" and the common name element gul.
From old Basque azenar(i), azenari ("fox", modern azeri).
Meaning ''bulky, offensive, sullen and tough person'', ultimately from Persian.
Means "honest, fair" in Armenian, ultimately from the Old Armenian Ազնիւ (azniv) meaning "good, kind, gracious, noble".
Greek form of Ezbai, as it first appeared in the Septuagint.
Possibly an elaboration of the name Azora or an English and feminine variant of the name Azaria.
From the name of the monotypic genus of flowering plants within the family Campanulaceae, whose sole species, the Azorina vidalii, is endemic to the Azores.
Meaning uncertain, possibly derived from a Breton surname meaning "healthy man" or "artisan".

Azouz is a name of Arabic origin, derived from the root ع-ز-ز (ʿ-z-z), meaning "to be powerful", "to be strong", or "to be honored." It is often interpreted as "the powerful one" or "the strong one", and is associated with traits like strength, honor, and respect.In Berber (Amazigh) culture, the name can also carry meanings related to strength and bravery, though interpretations may vary slightly depending on the region and dialect.The name is commonly used in North Africa, particularly in Algeria, Tunisia, and Morocco, where it is favored for its noble and powerful connotations. It is sometimes used as a diminutive form or affectionate nickname for individuals named Aziz, which means "dear", "beloved", or "powerful" in Arabic.
Alternate transcription of Arabic عذراء (see Azra).
Used in Morocco Tunisia and Jordan, the meaning comes from the Yassinian Arabic word Azerad which means blue. In Morocco, blue is a symbol of integrity.
Dutch and French form of Azrael.

From the Arabic surname الأذرعي (al-ʾAdhraʿī), borne by 14th-century Sunni scholar Shihab al-Din al-Adhrai. The name indicates that he came from the city of Daraa (which was known as Adhraat in ancient times) in present-day Syria.

column12: From Abul-Mahāsin Abu Bakr Zaynuddin Azraqi, an 11th-century poet who lived in Iran.
Combination of az and the name Rhiana.
From Arabic عذري (ʿadhriyy) meaning "pure, clean, chaste".
Modern English feminine form of Azriel.
Meaning uncertain, probably of Arabic origin.
From Arabic زهر (ʾazhar) "shining, bright" and دين (dīn) "religion, faith".
Possibly from Arabic عزز ('azz) meaning "strengthen, reinforce".

Believed to be inspired by the name Asherah, Azshara is the name given to one of World of Warcraft's most notable characters - Queen Azshara. In World of Warcraft Azshara is considered ruler of Naga, a fictional species that is from water - the name that Azshara is believed to derive from Asherah means "she who walks in the sea".
Derived from Nahuatl aztatl "heron, snowy egret" and mitl "arrow".
A kind of ornament made of feathers, usually a headdress, from Nahuatl aztatl "snowy egret" and tzontli "hair, crest, head; crown, headdress".

From the name of the legendary ancestral homeland of the Aztec peoples. Etymology uncertain, often said to mean "place of the herons", from Nahuatl aztatl "heron, snowy egret" and the locative suffix -tlan, though this doesn’t fit Nahuatl morphology. Other suggested meanings include "place of eagles", "place of whiteness", "place of wings", and "place near the tools".

Perhaps a contraction of Azucena and Aracely.

column12: Means "the past is greater" or "my back is greater" in Igbo.
From Spanish azul meaning "blue". This name was borne by the ninth and last wife of the Apache leader Geronimo. A known bearer is Azul Guaita (2001-), a Mexican television actress.

Fictional name meant to be derived from Portuguese, Galician, and Spanish azul meaning "blue" (of Persian origin). This is the name of a main antagonist in the television series 'Avatar: The Last Airbender'.
Possibly a blend of Azul and Azucena.
Meant to be the original masculine form of Azula, from which that name is derived. Fire Lord Azulon is a character in the American television show Avatar: The Last Airbender.

column12: From 愛 (a) meaning "love, affection", 鶴 (tsu) meaning "crane", and 美 (mi) meaning "beautiful, beauty". Other kanji combinations can be used.
Possibly a Esperanto form of Azuma.
Means "ruddy" in Guanche. It was borne by a Guanche leader from La Palma.
Bosnian male form of Azure. Number 96 in top 100 in 2012 for Bosnia and Herzegovina.
Possibly from the Hebrew word עצורה (atzurah) meaning "prisoner, stopped". Azura is the daughter of Adam and Eve and the wife (and sister) of Seth in the Book of Jubilees, chapter 4.
A name meaning "treasured one". This is used for the wife of Eber in the Book of Jubilees.
The name Azurae is derived from the Latin word "caeruleus," meaning "blue" or "sky blue," which itself traces back to the earlier Proto-Indo-European root *bleu- meaning "to be alive, to grow."
Apparently a misspelling of Azuree, the name of a perfume by the designer Estée Lauder.
Elaboration of the word azure, possibly based on Zuri.
Elaboration of Azura with the suffix -ina

column12: From Japanese 梓 (azusa) most commonly meaning "yellow catalpa tree" (scientific name Catalpa ovata), though it can also refer to several other species of plants, such as the Japanese cherry birch (Betula grossa) and the Japanese mallotus (Mallotus japonicus). The name can also be formed from 梓 (azu) combined with 沙 (sa) meaning "sand, gravel", as well as other combinations of kanji. It is often written in hiragana as well.
