column12: From Azusa combined with 子 (ko) meaning "child."This name is very rarely used.
Possibly derived from Arabic عزو ('azw) meaning "attribution".
Derived from Arabic أزور ('azwar) meaning "visit, visiting".
Means "something that cannot be told" in Tshivenda.
Possibly meaning "young female gazelle", deriving from the Arabic word azaza ("it was dear, it was expensive" referring to the difficulty in catching young gazelles).
Means "determined, resolute" as well as "lion" in Arabic, from the word عَزَمَ (azama) meaning "to determine, to decide, to be firmly resolved".
Meaning "strong." Was the father of Paltiel, a prince of the Tribe of Issachar.
From Mongolian аз (az) meaning "fortune, luck, happiness" and заяа (zayaa) meaning "future, fate, destiny".
Alternate transcription of Arabic عز الدين (see Izz ad-Din) chiefly used in North Africa.
Alternate transcription of Arabic عز الدين (see Izz ad-Din) chiefly used in North Africa.
Alternate transcription of عز الدين (see Izz ad-Din) chiefly used in North Africa.
Diminutive of Azalea and other names containing -az-.
Derived from the Germanic element athal 'noble' with the diminutive suffix -z.It is a Medieval name used by some members of the House of Este.
Maybe a diminutive of Aziz or from Abd al-Aziz

Meaning "One Offering Help".1. Father of the false prophet Hananiah from Gibeon.—Jer 28:1.2. Father of Jaazaniah, who was one of the “princes of the people” among the 25 men Ezekiel envisioned “scheming hurtfulness and advising bad counsel” against Jerusalem.—Eze 11:1, 2.3. One of “the heads of the people” whose descendant, if not he himself, attested by seal to Nehemiah’s “trustworthy arrangement.”
Diminutive of Azalea or other names beginning in -az.
From Chinese 巴 (bā) meaning "to greatly desire" or referred to a mythological snake, in addition to other hanzi that are pronounced similarly.
From Sino-Vietnamese 播 (bạ) meaning "to spread, scatter".
Form of Baadur with the nominative suffix, used in Georgian when the name is written stand-alone.
Deriving from the feminine form of the Phoenician bʿl ("Lord, master, owner"). This title was used for several goddesses of the Phoenician and Canaanite pantheons.
Yucatec Maya form of Balam. In Mayan mythology Báalam is a deity who represents jaguars.
Means "lord of the covenant", ultimately derived from Hebrew בעל (ba'al) meaning "to be lord" and ברית (berit) meaning "covenant". He is a deity that is mentioned in Judges 8:33 and Judges 9:4.
Baalham means “Jaguar” in the Classic Mayan language.

Means "lord of grace", ultimately derived from Hebrew בעל (ba'al) meaning "to be lord" and חנן (hanan) meaning "to be gracious". The name was featured by two men in the Bible (Genesis 36:38 and 1 Chronicles 27:28).

Means "lord of the wide opening", ultimately derived from Hebrew בעל (ba'al) meaning "to be lord" and פער (pa'ar) meaning "open wide". In the Bible, he was a deity that is mentioned in Numbers 25:3, Numbers 25:5, Deuteronomy 4:3, Psalms 106:28, and Hosea 9:10.

Baalshamin was a Northwest Semitic god and a title applied to different gods at different places or times in ancient Middle Eastern inscriptions, especially in Canaan/Phoenicia and Syria. The title was most often applied to Hadad, who is also often titled just Baal. Baalshamin was one of the two supreme gods and the sky god of pre-Islamic Palmyra in ancient Syria (Bel being the other supreme god). There his attributes were the eagle and the lightning bolt, and he perhaps formed a triad with the lunar god Aglibol and the sun god Malakbel. The title was also applied to Zeus.
A king of the Saxons who participated in King Aminaduc’s siege at Vambieres.He was slain by Arthur’s Sir Aglovale.
Means "son of affliction". In the Bible, this is the name of two of Solomon's purveyors, as well as the father of Zadok.
Hence, the name Baani holds a deep religious meaning in Punjabi. In Gurmukhi, Baani is written as ਬਾਣੀ, and it means 'style' or 'verge. '
Baara was one of the three wives of Shaharaim.
Means "Friday" or "Venus (planet)" in Mongolian. Cognate to Tibetan Pasang.
From Mongolian баасан (baasan) meaning "Friday" and дорж (dorj) meaning "diamond, vajra".
From Mongolian баасан (baasan) meaning "Friday" and жаргал (jargal) meaning "happiness, blessing".
From Mongolian баасан (baasan) meaning "Friday" and жав (jav) meaning "salvation, deliverance".
From Mongolian баасан (baasan) meaning "Friday" and хүү (khüü) meaning "boy, son; child".
From Mongolian баасан (baasan) meaning "Friday" combined with Tibetan ཚེ་རིང (tshe ring) meaning "long life, longevity".
Baasha of Israel is a king of Israel mentioned in Kings. Baasha of Ammon was a King of Ammon ruling in 853 BCE.
Derived from Mongolian баас (baas) meaning "excrement, manure, poo". This name was traditionally given in order to mislead bad spirits.
Means "heroic stone" in Mongolian, from баатар (baatar) meaning "hero" and чулуун (chuluun) meaning "stone".
From Mongolian баатар (baatar) meaning "hero" and жав (jav) meaning "salvation, deliverance".
From Mongolian баатар (baatar) meaning "hero" and хүү (khüü) meaning "boy, son; child".
From Mongolian баатар (baatar) meaning "hero" combined with Tibetan ཚེ་རིང (tshe ring) meaning "long life, longevity".
Means "heroic happiness" in Mongolian, from баатар (baatar) meaning "hero" and жаргал (jargal) meaning "happiness, blessing".
Kyrgyz and Yakut form of Batur.
Combination of Baatyr with the Turkish military title beg meaning "chieftain, master".
Means "hawk, falcon" in Punjabi, ultimately from Persian.
Meaning unknown. Jamamadí language is spoken in Acre and Amazonas State in Brazil.
Form of Abu Bakr used in parts of western Africa.

Allegedly from Ottoman Turkish باباجان (babacan) meaning "good-natured, pleasant, fatherly", itself from Turkish baba meaning "father" and Persian جان (jān) meaning "soul, life, darling". This given name has fallen out of use and now only survives in the patronymic surname Babajanyan.
Variant of Barbare, though it might also be descended from Barbale (in at least some cases).
Means "my father has dodged me", usually given to a son whose father died before his birth.

Babatha is the name of a Jewish woman who owned land near Petra (modern Jordan) and En-Gedi (modern Israel) in the 2nd century AD. Because her personal documents were preserved, much of her personal life is known today.
Means "the father has come back" in Yoruba, usually given to a son believed to be his reincarnated father.
Meaning unknown.Babawar is the Aboriginal local name of Shark Bay, Gascoyne, Western Australia.
Coined by Sabino Arana Goiri and Koldo Elizalde as a Basque equivalent of Amparo and Patrocinio. The name was based on Basque babes "shelter, refuge; protection" and the productive name suffix -ne.
Czech and Slovak form of Babette.

Hungarian form, German variant and Luxembourgish vernacular form of Babette. Babett Peter is a football player who had 118 appearances in the German national team winning among other titles the 2007 FIFA Wolrd Cup.
Latinate variant of Babette and Babett.
Indian unisex name also written as Babhrú (बभ्रु), masculine and sometimes feminine, or Babhrū (बभ्रू), which is purely feminine, meaning "reddish-brown, tawny".
Diminutive of Barbara (Portuguese) as well as of Babale, Babilina and Barbare (all Georgian). In the case of Babilina, however, it might actually be a short form rather than a diminutive.

A beautiful bird native to the land of Cluse (eventually ruled under Arthur by Daniel). During the day, it hovered over the ladies of Cluse, providing shade; at night, it gave off light. It was possessed of a beautiful voice. G. Rosenhagen suggests it's a derivation from papegân, German for ‘parrot’.
Of unknown meaning.Babik Reinhardt was a jazz guitarist.
Sudanese name possibly derived from the given name Bakr or from Arabic بَكَرَ (bakara) meaning "first born" or "to be early, to rise early".
Georgian and Italian form of Babylas.
Georgian feminization of Babylos, which was made by adding the Latin suffix -ina to the name.
Means "bauble" or "trinket" in French. According to the French fairytale, Babiole is the daughter of a queen. The fairy Fanfreluche tricks the queen into turning her daughter into a monkey.

Derived from the Azerbaijani noun bəbir meaning "leopard". As such, this name could be considered to be the Azerbaijani form of Babur.Known bearers of this name include the journalist Bəbir Hüseynov (b. 1932) and the poet Bəbir Məmmədzadə (1914-1942).
Azerbaijani and Kazakh form of Babur.
Arabized form of the Sahidic Coptic name Papnoute.
Variant transcription of Devanagari बाबुकाजी (see Babukaji).
Variant of Boubacar in many Western African languages.
Pakistani film actress Babra Sharif is a famous bearer.
Possibly from Persian ببر (babr) meaning "tiger, lion".
Possibly a Hellenized form of Valerius.
Latinized form of a Hellenized form of the name Valerius (see Babrios). This was the name of a 2nd-century author of a collection of Greek fables, many of which are known today as Aesop's Fables.
Short and familiar form of Barbara.
Short and familiar form of Barbara.
Short and familiar form of Barbara.
From Hindi बाबू (bābū) meaning “father, sir, mister, respected man” and भाई (bhāī) meaning “brother”.

This was the personal name of Nurhaci's eleventh son. It likely shares an element with the name of his elder brother Babutai, as it was a Manchu custom to use a consistent element when naming brothers.
From Newar बाबु (bābu) meaning "small kid" and काजी (kājī) meaning "leader".
Meaning "Leader of the Rebellion". Referring to Lord Ram.
Combination of Babur with the Turkish military title beg meaning "chieftain, master".In Uzbekistan, the local forms of this name are much more common, which are Bobirbek and Boburbek.

Babür, combined with a Perso-Turkic royal title, şah meaning "shah". As a whole, it means "shah as strong as a tiger". This was the nickname of Zahir ud-Din Muhammad, the 16th-century founder of the Mughal Empire in India.
This was the name of Nurhaci's ninth son. The meaning of his name is uncertain at this time.
Diminutive of Babale, Babilina, Barbare and their diminutive Babi, as it contains the Georgian diminutive suffix -უცა (-utsa).
From the English word baby, meaning "infant of either sex".
From the ancient place name, from the Greek form of Akkadian Bab-ilani meaning "the gate of the gods" from bab "gate" and ilani, plural of ilu "god".

Meaning uncertain. It is often confused or conflated with Babylas, but the two names are not necessarily related to each other. For example, Babylas is confirmed to ultimately be of Akkadian origin, whilst for Babylos, there is at least one source that states that the name is of Syrian (or rather Assyrian) origin and means "rebel" or "rebellion, uprising".A notable bearer of this name is saint Matrona of Perge (6th century AD), who spent some time in a monastery, disguised as a eunuch named Babylos.
Combination of Baby and the popular suffix -lyn.
From Sino-Vietnamese 博 (bác) meaning "learned, abundant, rich".
Variant of Bạch, from a non-Sino-Vietnamese reading of Chinese 白 (bạc).
From Sino-Vietnamese 匐 (bặc) meaning "to crawl, cower, silence" in Vietnamese.

A Western Armenian name derived from the Armenian word "պատասխան" (patasxan), which means "answer." This name was notably popular among Western Armenians during the 18th and 19th centuries but has since become rare.The name "Badaskhan" is pronounced as bɑdɑsˈχɑn in Western Armenian, with the "kh" sound represented by the letter "խ" (kʰ) in the Armenian alphabet. The original Armenian word "պատասխան" is pronounced as pɑtɑsˈχɑn, indicating that the name "Badaskhan" likely evolved through dialectal variations or phonetic changes over time.The use of "Badaskhan" as a personal name reflects the Armenian tradition of assigning meaningful words as names, in this case, "answer." While its popularity has waned in modern times, it remains a part of Armenia's rich onomastic heritage.

Balamir is a name of debated origins, most famously borne by the 4th-century chieftain of the Huns, often identified with Balamber. While later folk etymology attempted to link the suffix to the Slavic mir "peace" or the Gothic mēre "famous," linguistic analysis of the earliest sources suggests a purely Turkic construction.The name is composed of the root bala, meaning "child" or "young animal" (common in Old Turkic), and the archaic suffix ber. Over centuries of linguistic evolution and the influence of Persian and modern Turkish phonetics, the original ber (likely stemming from the root ber- "to give" or berk "strong/firm") shifted into its modern form, -mir. This transition is a modern Turkish take on the name, reclaiming it from historical phonetic shifts. Therefore, the -mir in Balamir is not related to the Arabic amir "commander" nor the Indo-European mir; it is a phonetic evolution of the ancient Turkic ber.For parents, the name symbolizes a child who carries the strength of an ancient lineage, as vast and enduring as the twilight over the Altai. It suggests a personality that is both resilient, like the iron-willed gallop of a nomad king, and luminous, possessing a natural gravity that anchors others in times of storm. To name a child Balamir is to bestow upon them a legacy of "bestowed vitality"; a spirit that does not merely exist, but commands its own destiny with the grace of the high steppes.

"Bound Flower," "The Flower That Binds," or fittingly within her epic context, "The Grappling Flower." The name is derived from the Proto-Turkic verb root *ban- (banmaq / bañmaq), which means "to tie," "to bind," "to fasten," or "to loop," appended to the native Turkic çiçek (flower).Clarification: The Turkic Banı vs. Persian BanuA pervasive misconception in modern onomastics is to analyze the first element of the name as the Persian loanword Bânû (بانو), which means "Lady," "Madam," or "Princess." This is etymologically incorrect. While the Islamic-era scribes who recorded the tales occasionally conflated the two due to phonetic proximity, the character’s intrinsic narrative functions reveal a purely Turkic origin.Banıçiçek is not a passive "Lady Flower"; she is structurally tied to the Proto-Turkic *ban- root. In old Turkic sports and combative terminology, this root gives rise to expressions like bağla- (to tie/secure) and bağ vurmak (to apply a bond/lock). Specifically, in traditional Turkic wrestling (güreş), "bağ vurmak" or ban- refers to the tactical grappling moves used to lock an opponent's limbs, tie up their defenses, or trip them to the ground. Banıçiçek’s name is an absolute reflection of her physical prowess; she is the literal "Grappling Flower" who binds her suitors in combat.HistoryBanıçiçek is a legendary heroine whose narrative legacy is preserved in the pre-Islamic heroic layers of Oghuz Turkic folklore. Her story represents the ancient nomadic custom of "alp kız" (heroic/warrior maiden) courtship, where Physical Prowess, Archery, Horse Racing, and Wrestling were mutual prerequisites for marriage between equals.The definitive and most celebrated manifestation of her history is found in the Book of Dede Korkut, specifically within the epic of Bamsı Beyrek, Son of Kam Büre.In the narrative, Banıçiçek is introduced not as a passive maiden awaiting rescue, but as an exceptionally skilled warrior-woman. When the hero Bamsı Beyrek seeks her hand in marriage, she refuses to accept him blindly. To prove his worth, she challenges him to 3 trials of martial equality: a Horse Race, an Archery Duel, and a hand-to-hand Wrestling Match.During the wrestling match, the text describes a fierce, unyielding physical struggle. Banıçiçek utilizes her strength and grappling maneuvers; functionally applying the bağ (wrestling locks/binds) implicit in her name's root—nearly besting Beyrek. It is only when Beyrek realizes he will lose his honor to a woman that he exerts his maximum physical effort to pin her by gripping her belt. Recognizing his strength as equal to her own, Banıçiçek honors her vow and accepts him as her betrothed.Later in the epic, when Beyrek is captured and imprisoned for sixteen years, Banıçiçek fiercely resists the political pressure of her family to marry another suitor, remaining unyielding in her loyalty until Beyrek’s dramatic return. Her narrative captures a historical era where Turkic women held high social autonomy, participated directly in warfare, and retained the agency to physically test their prospective partners.SymbolismIn a modern naming context, Banıçiçek is chosen to celebrate a magnificent heritage of athletic sovereignty, fierce autonomy, and unbreakable fidelity. It stands as an antithesis to the passive damsel archetype, offering a legacy of balanced grace and formidable strength.For parents, the name symbolizes a child who possesses a resilient spirit, an unyielding will, and the capability to stand as an equal to any challenger. It suggests a personality that balances the vibrant beauty of a flower (çiçek) with the grounding, binding tenacity (*ban-) of a protector. To name a child Banıçiçek is to bestow upon them an ancestral legacy of the Eurasian steppes; a character whose identity is defined by fierce self-reliance, martial honor, and a loyalty that cannot be broken by time or distance.

From the Chinese 葆 (bǎo) meaning "reserve, preserve" and 茜 (qiàn) meaning "madder, reeds".

column3: 宝强, 保强, etc.(Chinese)|寶強, 保強, etc.(Traditional Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 宝 (bǎo) meaning "treasure, jewel, precious, rare" or 保 (bǎo) meaning "protect, maintain" combined with 强 (qiáng) meaning "strong, powerful, energetic". Other character combinations can form this name as well.
From the Chinese 保 (bǎo) meaning "protect, defend" and 庆 (qìng) meaning "congratulate, celebrate".
From 宝 (bǎo) meaning "treasure, riches, valuables" and 仁 (rén) meaning "compassionate, humane".
From the Chinese 宝 (bǎo) meaning "treasure, jewel; precious, rare" and 绒 (róng) meaning "silk, cotton".
From the Chinese 宝 (bǎo) meaning "treasure, jewel; precious, rare" and 蕊 (ruǐ) meaning "unopened flowers, flower buds".
From the Chinese 保 (bǎo) meaning "protect, defend" and 森 (sēn) meaning "forest".

column3: 宝山, 寶珊, 宝善, etc.(Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 宝 or 寶 (bǎo) meaning "treasure, jewel, precious, rare" combined with 山 (shān) meaning "mountain, hill, peak", 珊 (shān) meaning "coral", or 善 (shàn) meaning "good, virtuous, charitable, kind". Other character combinations can form this name as well.
From the Chinese 宝 (bǎo) meaning "treasure; precious, rare" and 深 (shēn) meaning "close, dark, deep".
From the Chinese 宝 (bǎo) meaning "treasure; precious, rare" and 生 (shēng) meaning "life".
From the Chinese 宝 (bǎo) meaning "treasure; precious, rare" and 狮 (shī) meaning "lion". Other hanzi combinations are possible.
From the Chinese 葆 (bǎo) meaning "reserve, preserve" and 淑 (shū) meaning "kind and gentle".

Perhaps related to Beathan. It coincides with a Gaelic word meaning "vain, reckless, wanton, foolish". Other forms are Baothan, Baoithin/Beheen and Baolach. Baoithin was the name of a 7th-century Irish saint from Ennisboyne (originally Inis Boethine), County Wicklow.
Means "foolishly valorous", from the roots baoth "foolish, vain" and galach "valorous".
From the Chinese 保 (bǎo) meaning "protect, defend" and 天 (tiān) meaning "sky, heaven".
Vietnamese form of Baptiste, usually used in the combination Gioan Baotixita to honor Saint John the Baptist.
From Sino-Vietnamese 保衛 (bảo vệ) meaning "to defend, protect".
From the Malagasy name for the Adansonia digitata baobab tree.
From Chinese 宝 (bǎo) meaning "treasure, jewel, precious" combined with 文 (wén) meaning "literature, culture, writing". Other hanzi combinations are possible.
From the Chinese 宝 (bǎo) meaning "treasure; precious, rare" and 僖 (xī) meaning "joy, gladness, delight".
From the Chinese 葆 (bǎo) meaning "reserve, preserve" and 霞 (xiá) meaning "rosy clouds".

column3: 宝纤, 宝娴, 宝仙(Chinese)
column12: From the Chinese 宝 (bǎo) meaning "treasure, jewel, precious" and 纤 (xiān) meaning "fine, delicate, graceful", 娴 (xián) meaning "elegant, refined" or 仙 (xiān) meaning "transcendent, immortal".
From the Chinese 宝 (bǎo) meaning "treasure, jewel; precious, rare" and 香 (xiāng) meaning "fragrant, sweet smelling, incense".
From the Chinese 宝 (bǎo) meaning "treasure; precious, rare" and 心 (xīn) meaning "heart, mind, intelligence, soul".
From the Chinese 保 (bǎo) meaning "protect, defend" and 雄 (xióng) meaning "male, manly; hero; grand, imposing".
From the Chinese 宝 (bǎo) meaning "treasure, jewel; precious, rare" and 秀 (xiù) meaning "beautiful, elegant".
From the Chinese 保 (bǎo) meaning "protect, defend" and 旭 (xù) meaning "rising sun, brilliance, radiant".
From the Chinese 宝 (bǎo) meaning "treasure, jewel; precious, rare" and 嫣 (yān) meaning "charming, fascinating" or 燕 (yàn) meaning "swallow (bird)".

column3: 葆怿, 保怡, 葆怡, 宝怡, etc.(Chinese)
column12: From the Chinese 葆 (bǎo) meaning "reserve, preserve", 宝 (bǎo) meaning "treasure; precious, rare" or 保 (bǎo) meaning "protect, defend" and 怡 (yí) meaning "happy, joyful".

column3: 宝莹, 宝樱, 保莹(Chinese)
column12: From the Chinese 宝 (bǎo) meaning "treasure, jewel; precious, rare" or 保 (bǎo) meaning "protect, defend" and 莹 (yíng) meaning "luster of gems, lustrous" or 樱 (yīng) meaning "cherry, cherry blossom".
From the Chinese 葆 (bǎo) meaning "reserve, preserve" and 咏 (yǒng) meaning "sing song".

From Chinese 宝玉 (bǎoyù) meaning "precious jade". Other hanzi combinations are possible.Jia Baoyu (Chinese: 賈寶玉) is the principal character in the classic 18th century Chinese novel 红楼梦(Dream of the Red Chamber).

column3: 宝元, 宝源, 保源, 保原, etc.(Chinese)|寶元, 寶源, 保源, 保, etc.(Traditional Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 宝 (bǎo) meaning "treasure, jewel, precious, rare" or 保 (bǎo) meaning "protect, maintain" combined with 元 (yuán) meaning "first, origin", 源 (yuán) meaning "source, origin" or 原 (yuán) meaning "source, origin, beginning, meadow, field, plain". Other character combinations can form this name as well.
From the Chinese 宝 (bǎo) meaning "treasure, jewel; precious, rare" and 月 (yuè) meaning "moon" or 玥 (yuè) meaning "mythological pearl".
From Chinese 宝 (bǎo) meaning “treasure”, while 斋 (zhāi) meaning “pavilion, studio”.
From the Chinese 宝 (bǎo) meaning "treasure; precious, rare" and 长 (zhǎng) meaning "long, lasting; be good at, excel".
From the Chinese 保 (bǎo) meaning "protect, defend" and 哲 (zhé) meaning "wise, sage".
From the Chinese 宝 (bǎo) meaning "treasure; precious, rare" and 正 (zhèng) meaning "right, proper, correct".
From the Chinese 保 (bǎo) meaning "protect, defend" and 智 (zhì) meaning "wisdom, knowledge, intelligence".
From the Chinese 宝 (bǎo) meaning "treasure; precious, rare" and 柱 (zhù) meaning "pillar; support, lean on" or 祝 (zhù) meaning "pray for happiness or blessings".
From the Chinese 宝 (bǎo) meaning "treasure; precious, rare" and 壮 (zhuàng) meaning "big, large, robust".
From the Chinese 保 (bǎo) meaning "protect, defend" and 孜 (zī) means "be as diligent as possible".
Means "those who give testimony" in Setswana.

Probably from a medieval corruption of Mahomet. This appears in the Inquisition of the Knights Templar as the name of an alleged Muslim or pagan idol. In the 19th century it became associated with a Western occult symbol drawn by Eliphas Lévi, a "Sabbatic Goat" image depicting a demonic horned god.
Meaning unknown. This name was borne by Bapsi Sidhwa (1938-2024), a Pakistani American novelist.
From the English word “baptize”, meaning to “administer baptism to someone; christen”.
Polish form of Baptista used as a second name with Jan as the first name.
From бақ (baq) meaning "garden" and дәулет (daulet) meaning "country, government"
Alternate transcription of Persian باقر (see Baqir), as well as the Persian form.
From the Kazakh бақыт (baqıt) meaning "happiness, luck" and жан (jan) meaning "soul".
Means "eternity, infinate" in Uzbek, ultimately from Arabic بقاء (baqāʔ).

Means "wave, billow" in Old Norse. In Norse mythology, Bára was the daughter of the jötunn Ægir and goddess Rán, both personifications of the sea. She was sometimes referred to as Drǫfn, also meaning "wave, billow".
From Japanese 薔薇 (bara) meaning "rose". Other kanji or kanji combinations can also form this name.
Alternate transcription of Arabic براءة (see Bara'a).
Means "justification" in Azerbaijani, ultimately from Arabic براءة (barā'a).
Croatian form of Barabbas. Only used as a Biblical name.
Variant of Barabal. This name used to be Anglicized as the etymologically unrelated Annabella.
Variant of Barabbas. In literature, this is the name of the main character in Christopher Marlowe's play The Jew of Malta (ca. 1590).

Hellenized form of bar-Abbâ, which means "son of Abba" in Aramaic, derived from Aramaic bar meaning "son" combined with the Aramaic given name Abba. Since the name Abba means "father" in Aramaic, the literal meaning of the entire name would be "son of the father". In the Bible, Barabbas was a prisoner who was freed instead of Jesus Christ by Pontius Pilate during the Passover feast in Jerusalem.
Form of Barak 1 used in the Latin Old Testament.

Form of Barakel used in the Douay-Rheims Bible (1582-1610), the Clementine Vulgate (1592) and the Nova Vulgata ("Neo-Vulgate", 1979). The latter two are respectively the former and current official Bible of the Roman Catholic Church.
Greek form of Barakel, as it first appeared in the Septuagint.Barachiel is also the name of one of the seven Archangels in Judaism, as well as the Byzantine Catholic and Eastern Orthodox tradition.
From Japanese 薔薇 (bara) meaning "rose" combined with 羽 (ha) meaning "feathers". Other kanji combinations are possible.

Means "fiery lord" in Sindarin. In Tolkien's 'The Silmarillion', this was the name of the father of Beren. It was also mentioned in 'The Lord of the Rings' as the name of both a Steward of Gondor and the grandson of Eowyn and Faramir.
Etymology uncertain, possibly deriving in part from the Sumerian element bára, meaning "throne dais, ruler". Name borne by a queen of the city of Umma (fl. 2400 BCE).
Means "blessings of Allah" from Arabic بركة (baraka) meaning "blessing" combined with الله (Allah).
“blessing of God” or "God blesses", appears in the Book of Job in the Hebrew Bible

column3: 薔薇子, 茨子, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 薔薇 (bara) meaning "rose" combined with 子 (ko) meaning "child". Other kanji combinations are possible.

Tristan’s great-grandfather.The son of King Candaces of Cornwall and Cressille (Cressile), he inherited the country of Lyoness.He became king of Cornwall when his brother, Crissidés, died. His two sons were named Feriando and Felix, the latter of whom inherited his kingdoms.
Georgian form of Bahram. This name is extremely rare in Georgia today; actually, one could almost consider it to be archaic.

Etymology unknown, possibly deriving from Sumerian elements nam meaning "(area of) responsibility; destiny, fate, lot" and tar meaning "deliberate, judicious". Name borne by a queen of Lagash (circa 2384 BCE), known for her involvement in the trade of wool, silver, and bronze between Lagash, Dilmun, and Umma.
Of uncertain etymology. Name borne by an Eora woman of the Cammeraygal clan (fl. 1780s).
Etymology uncertain, perhaps from barangoló meaning "roaming".
Burmese form of Bharani, used as the name of the second lunar mansion of the Burmese zodiac.
Originally a diminutive of Ágnes, used as a given name in its own right.

Means "lightning of God" in Hebrew, derived from בָּרָק (barak) meaning "lightning" and אֵל (ʾel) meaning "God". The Book of Enoch names him as a fallen angel, one of the 200 Watchers who copulated with human women.
Spanish and Portuguese form of Barachiel.
Meaning unknown. This is the name of the Ossetian ruler of the underworld who assigns dead souls either to paradise or his realm, comparable to the Greek Hades.
Derived from Arabic براءة (bara'a) meaning "blamelessness, innocence" (see Bara'a and also Berat).Also compare the closely related names Barata and Bəraət.

Derived from Arabic براءة (bara'a) meaning "blamelessness, innocence" (see Bara'a and also Berat). According to at least one Georgian source, this is a later and more figurative meaning - the original meaning was supposedly "new moon" (in reference to the beginning of a lunar month).Also compare the closely related names Barat and Bəraət.
Combination of Barat and the Turkic military title beg meaning "chieftain, master".
Breton, Corsican, Latvian and Estonian cognate of Barbara (compare French Barbe).
Czech and Slovak form of Barbatianus.

Meaning unknown, though it is similar to the Sumerian and Akkadian epithet bibbiru meaning "shining, splendor". Barbale was the Georgian goddess of cattle, poultry fertility, the sun, women's fertility, and healing.
Catalan, Sardinian, Sicilian, Cremish Lombard and Piedmontese form of Barbara.
A combination of Barbara and Ann.
Likely influenced by the name Barbara. This is the name of the main character in the 'Barbarella' comic book.
MEANING : 'curly-haired', a species of ocimum,yellow sandal wood, gum myrrh, vermilion
Meaning "red beard" in Italian.Barbarossa is the byname of the Holy Roman Emperor Frederick I. (1122–1190).
Roman cognomen which was derived from Greek βάρβαρος (barbaros) meaning "foreign, non-Greek" (see Barbara).
English vernacular form and Manx regular form of Barbara.
Feminine form of the Latin cognomen Barbatus.
Anglicized form of Barbatianus.The 5th-century saint Barbatianus of Ravenna is sometimes called Barbatian in English.
Derived from Latin barbatus meaning "bearded" (see Barbatus) combined with the Latin suffix -ianus.A notable bearer of this name is saint Barbatianus of Ravenna (5th century AD).
Name of a Roman infantry general who died in AD 359.
Roman family name which was derived from Latin barbatus meaning "bearded" (see Barbatus).

Derived from Latin barbatus meaning "bearded". This is the name of a demon who appears in several works on demonology, including the 17th-century grimoire The Lesser Key of Solomon (author unknown), the Pseudomonarchia Daemonum (1563) by Dutch physician Johann Weyer and the Dictionnaire Infernal (1818) by French occultist Jacques Collin de Plancy.
Roman cognomen which was derived from the Latin adjective barbatus meaning "bearded".A notable bearer of this name is saint Barbatus of Benevento (c. 610-682).
Walloon form of Barbe and Barbara.
The name of an early Christian martyr from Edessa (today: Şanlıurfa, Turkey).
Double diminutive of Barbara via Bärbel.Bärbelchen is a minor character in Goethe's Faust.
Refers to the first emanation of God in Gnostic cosmogony.
Transferred use of the surname Barber.
Originally a diminutive of Barbara, occasionally used as a given name in its own right.
Originally a diminutive of Barbara, used as a given name in its own right.
Diminutive of Barbla, traditionally found in the Engadine valley.
Czech and Silesian diminutive of Barbora, not used as a given name in its own right.
Variant spelling of Barbara. It is possible that there are also cases where the name is a feminization of the surname Barbour.
Diminutive of Barbla, traditionally found in the Engadine valley and in central Grisons.
Diminutive of Barbara or other names beginning with Ba(r)-.
Czech diminutive of Barbora and Slovene diminutive of Barbara.
Derived from Galician word barca meaning "barge, small boat". This is a the name or a title of the Virgin Mary (Virxe da Barca, "Virgin of Barca") native to the town of Muxía, Galicia.
Barcelona is a city in Spain. It is the capital and largest city of Catalonia, as well as the second most populous municipality of Spain.
Possibly derived from barchin meaning "everything" and suluv meaning "beauty".
Romansh form of Bartholomew, traditionally found in the Surselva region.
Transferred use of the surname Barcroft. Barcroft Henry Thomas Boake (1866-1892) was an Australian poet.
The name of a character in J.R.R. Tolkien's The Hobbit.
From Syrian ܕܝܨܢ (bar Daiṣān) "son of the Dayṣān", referring to the Daysan River. This is the name of an Assyrian teacher and founder of the Bardaisanites.
Transferred use of the surname Barden.
Derived from Albanian bardh "to whiten; brighten" and, figuratively, "to bring honor and glory".
Feminine form of Bardh. In Albanian mythology, Bardha are pale, nebulous figures who dwell under the earth. According to old folklore, to propitiate them one strews cakes or sugar on the ground.
Derived from Albanian bardhok "fair-haired; white; white ram".
Derived from Albanian bardhosh "pallid, pale; blond or gray-haired; white bull, white steer, white ox". The name coincides with that of a village in Kosovo.
From Bardylis, the name of an ancient Illyrian king (reigned from 385 to 358 BC), which is popularly held to mean "white star" from Albanian bardhë "white" and yll "star".
Derived from Proto-Iranian *bardz- "be high", interpreted as meaning "high in status, magnificent". Bardia or Bardiya was the younger son of Cyrus II "the Great".
Probably a feminine form of Bård.
Derived from proto-Iranian *br̥jáns meaning "high, tall". This was the name of a son of Cyrus the Great, also known as Smerdis and Tanyoxarces.

Perhaps a short form of Bardolph or other Germanic names containing the element bard meaning "small axe" (in some cases "beard"). It was borne by a saint, an 11th-century archbishop of Mainz whom Pope Saint Leo IX advised to "lighten his duties and relax some of his personal austerities and mortifications".
Possibly from a Germanic name derived from the elements bard, meaning "small axe" or "beard", and wulf "wolf". Shakespeare used it for minor characters in several plays.
Spanish form of Bardomianus. This name is borne by retired Mexican soccer player Bardomiano Viveros (1951-).
Italian form and variant of Bardo.
Meaning unknown. Manga author Yana Toboso used this name for a character in her popular manga serie 'Kuroshitsuji'.
Variant of Bardot, traditionally found in the Engadine valley.

Derived from an old Iranian word that has the meaning of "tall" - compare modern Persian برز (borz) meaning "high, tall" and the Persian name Barzin.In modern Georgian, ბარძიმი (bardzimi) means "chalice, cruet".Notable bearers of this name include a 6th-century child martyr from Kola in southern Georgia, and the Georgian poet Bardzim Vachnadze (17th century).
Croatian nickname for Barbara (female) or Bariša (male).
Means "son of God", from a combination of bar and El.
From Javanese barêp meaning "first, principal, eldest".
Derived from the Uzbek barg meaning "leaf".
Derived from barg meaning "leaf" and gul meaning "flower, rose".
Name of a Christian martyr who was decapitated during the reign of Shapur II.
Derived from barr "harsh". Related to Swedish bare "magical being". In Norse mythology this is the name of a dwarf.
Alternate transcription of Pashto بريالی (see Baryalai).
Alternate transcription of Pashto بريالی (see Baryalai).
Alternate transcription of Pashto بريالی (see Baryalai).
Alternate transcription of Pashto بريالی (see Baryalai).
Variant of Brian or Brayan. Probably means "noble," "strong," or "virtuous".
From the Shipibo bari meaning "sun" and the genitive suffix -n.

A mysterious Otherwordly sea deity about whom very little is known.He does, however, make an appearance in Geoffrey of Monmouth’s Vita Merlini as the boatman who ferried the mortally wounded Arthur, in the company of Merlin and Taliesin, on his final journey to Avalon, to be cured of his deadly wound by the goddess Morgan Le Fay.Christopher W. Bruce: “Geoffrey was probably speaking figuratively.”

This name was first found in Northern Italy (Tuscany and Liguria, to be precise). Its meaning and etymological origin is unknown, though it is probably related to the name of the Italian town of Barisano, which was named Castrum Barisani (meaning "Barisan's castle") in its earliest records. A bearer of this name was Barisan of Ibelin, a knight from the 12th century AD.
The name comes from the biblical word "bara" - "ברה" - which means pure and clean (feminine).
Means "son of Jesus" in Hebrew, ultimately derived from Hebrew בר (bar) meaning "son" and ישע meaning "Jesus, to save". In the Bible, he was a false prophet that is mentioned in Acts 13:6.
Barjik (died 731) was a Khazar prince who flourished in the early 8th century.

From Aramaic 𐡁𐡓𐡉𐡅𐡍𐡄‎ (barjonah) meaning "son of Jonah". This was the patronymic of Simon Peter, appearing in the Bible in Matthew 16:17. It has had some sparse usage as a forename in English-speaking countries since the 15th century.

Barkan is a name of profound geographical and historical significance, derived from the Old Turkic bar- ("to arrive, to be present"). In the Oghuz Khan Epic, it represents a southern country of immense wealth, a land synonymous with prosperity and central power. The name evokes the image of a "guardian of the threshold" or "the one who settles." Additionally, the term barxan (often interchangeable with barkan in some dialects) denotes a "dune," symbolizing endurance and the shifting, powerful forces of nature.
Means "blessing, good fortune" in Urdu, ultimately from Arabic بركة (baraka).
Derived from Arabic Barakat "blessings" and Allah "the deity".

A modern invented name of unknown meaning.In the case of American football player Barkevious Mingo, his unusual first name was created by his mother, Barbara, by adding the first three letters of her name to a name she liked, Kevious.
Variant transcription of Mongolian Бархасбадь (see Barkhasbadi).
Means "Jupiter" in Mongolian, ultimately from Sanskrit बृहस्पति (bṛ́haspáti).
From a surname which is a variant of Barclay.
Barkos was a painter who was the father of some of the Nethinim.
Romansh variant of Barbara, traditionally found in the Surselva region.
Transferred use of the surname Barley.
Transferred use of the surname Barlow.
Old Norse byname derived from barn meaning "child".
Yugoslav form of the Hungarian name Bárnabas. Used by Hungarian diaspora across the Ex-Yugo countries, especially in Vojvodina.
Languedocian and Gascon form of Barnabas.
Medieval Italian diminutive of Barnaba, as -uccio is an Italian masculine diminutive suffix.
Means "spectrum, rainbow, series of colours" in Bengali.
Variant of Barnhard. In some instances, this name might also be a variant spelling of Bernard.
Possibly an anglicized form of Bernardino, or perhaps a diminutive of Barnard. This was used by Shakespeare for a character in his play 'Measure for Measure' (1604).
Variant of Bernardo used in Hamlet.
Transferred use of the surname Barnes.
Transferred use of the surname Barnet.
Transferred use from the surname Barnett.

Derived from Gothic barn (synonymous with Scottish bairn) "child" combined with Gothic hardus (hart in Old High German) "brave, hardy". In some instances, this name might also be a variant spelling of Bernhard.
Norwegian dialectal variant of Borgny used in Vestlandet.
Short form of names beginning with Barni- and Broni-, such as Bronimir, Barnimir, Bronisław and Barnisław. This name was borne by several dukes of Pomerania.
Derived from barno meaning "youthful, beautiful" and gul meaning "flower, rose".
Derived from Gothic barn (synonymous with Scottish bairn) "child" combined with Gothic vulfs "wolf."
Form of Bergtor via the dialectal variant Bardo. Mainly used on Trøndelag county in Norway.
Means "he blesses" in Amharic, according to Wikipedia.
Perhaps from Celtic or from Frankish *baro* "freeman, man" or another Germanic source. In England, the word merged with (probably) cognate Old English *beorn* "nobleman."
Possibly an adoption of the Italian title baronetta, the feminine form of baronetto, "baronetess; female baronet".

Derived from Old Javanese barwaṅ meaning "bear". In Balinese mythology this is the name of a lion or panther-like creature who embodies goodness, health and prosperity. Described as a benevolent guardian spirit who opposes the forces of evil, he is the archenemy of the demon queen Rangda. He is also the namesake of a form of traditional Balinese dance, which depicts his eternal battle with Rangda.
From Arabic براءة (bara'a) meaning "blamelessness, innocence". See Bara'a and Berat.
Adyghe name of Unknown Meaning. It is famous mainly as the name of the Burji dynasty’s founder.
Transferred use of the surname Barr.
Derived from barra meaning "lamb" and gul meaning "flower, rose".
This was the name of Maymunah bint al-Harith, the 11th wife of Prophet Muhammed before he changed it to Maymunah.
Means "dark headed, dark haired", from Old Irish barr meaning "top, head" and dub meaning "black".

A name that comes from the Somali word bare which means "teacher." Barre was the last name (meaning the first name of the grandfather of) Mohamed Siad Barre (Somali spelling: Maxamed Siyaad Barre). Siad Barre was the military ruler and president of Somali from 1969 until 1991.

Portuguese version of the english name Barett.Surname and first name used in Brazil and is derived from the name of several locations in Portugal(Ancient hamlets) .Used rarely on spanol language .Means ''the one that who cames from earthenware''Variation of Barett and the portuguese surname Barros
Derived from Manx barriaght "victory, conquest, win" and intended as a Manx form of Victoria.
Transferred use of the surname Barrick.

Masculine form of Barrikada. This name was used by Communist parents who were eager to reject traditional names.A known bearer of this name was the Russian physicist Barrikad Zamyshlyayev (1925-2007).

Derived from the Russian noun баррикада (barrikada) meaning "barricade". This name was used by Communist parents who were eager to reject traditional names, possibly in reference to the protests and strikes by labourers.
Transferred use of the surname Barrington.

Transferred use of the surname Barron.Known bearers of Barron as a given name include the American business magnate Barron Hilton (b. 1927), his grandson Barron Hilton II (b. 1989) and Barron Trump (b. 2006), the youngest son of the American businessman and president Donald Trump (b. 1946).
Transferred use of the surname Barrow.
Means "son of Sabas". It is the name of multiple biblical characters and saints.
Variant form of Barsanofio. Also compare Barsanofrio.

Hellenized form of the Bohairic Coptic name ⲃⲉⲣϣⲉⲛⲟⲩϥⲓ (Beršenoufi), which is ultimately derived from Ancient Egyptian wršy-nfr meaning "good guardian".This name was notably borne by an Egyptian saint from the 6th century AD.
Spanish form of Barsanuphius, and Italian variant form of Barsanofio.
Latinized form of Barsanouphios, which is a hellenization of the Bohairic Coptic name Beršenoufi.This name was notably borne by the Egyptian saint Barsanuphius the Great (6th century AD).
Derived from Mongolian барс (bars) meaning "tiger" and болд (bold) meaning "steel".
Bengali, Odia and Nepali form of Varsha.

Variant of the Old Testament place name Be'ersheba, meaning "seventh well" or "well of the oath" (Genesis 21:31). The phrase "from Dan to Be'ersheba" was the usual way of designating the Promised Land.

From Syriac ܒܪܣܡܝܐ (Barsamya), possibly meaning "son of the blind man" or "son of the divine standard". This is the name of a Christian saint and bishop of Edessa (now Şanlıurfa, Turkey).According to tradition, he was martyred in 114 AD by Roman emperor Trajan for converting many people into Christianity. It seems that his story was backdated about a century and a half in order to link the early Church of Edessa to the Apostles, so he would have actually been martyred under emperor Decius.
Means "clover" in Persian. This name was borne by a mistress of Alexander the Great (daughter of Artabazus) and also by one of his wives (Barsine-Stateira, daughter of King Darius III).
Transferred use of the surname Barsoum. St. Barsoum El Erian was a Coptic saint in the thirteenth century.
Ultimately of Turkic origin, the meaning of this name is "panther". Also compare modern Turkish pars meaning "leopard, panther".
Dutch short form of Bartholomea, though you could also say that it is the feminine form of Bart. The name is sometimes erroneously interpreted as a variant spelling of Berta.
Faroese form of Bartel and Barthold.
Akkadian form of either the Scythian name Pr̥ϑutavah ("with far-reaching strength") or the Scythian name Pṛtatavah ("mighty in battle").

An old Lithuanian masculine name composed of two elements: bart meaning "to scold", "to reprimand", or possibly from barti (verb "to chide"), and autas, a common masculine name suffix in Baltic compounds. Though the exact historical usage is uncertain, the name may have once conveyed a meaning such as "he who reprimands", possibly implying a person of authority, wisdom, or moral judgement. Like many compound names in the Baltic tradition, Bartautas reflects action or traits and may have roots in pre-Christian naming practices.
Dutch and West Frisian form of Berthold. Also compare the similar-looking name Bartel.
Medieval Low German form of Bartholomew.
Diminutive of Bartholomew. Precursor to the surname Bartlett.
Variant of Parthena. Also compare Bartina, which is similar in appearance and sound but has a different etymology.
From Old Norse barð meaning "beard, brim, verge, beak of a ship".
Short form of Bartholomeus. Notable bearers of this name include the Dutch actor Bartho Braat (b. 1950) and the South African writer Bartho Smit (1924-1986).
Dutch and English feminine form of Bartholomew.
Medieval French feminine form of Bartholomew.
Old English form of Bartholomew, derived from Latin Bartholomeus.
Icelandic and Faroese form of Bárðr.
Medieval Silesian German variant of Bartholomäus.
Latinized form of Bartimaios. In the New Testament, Bartimaeus is a blind man who was healed by Jesus.
This is a hybrid Aramaic-Greek name that means "son of Timaios", as it consists of the Aramaic noun בּר (bar) meaning "son" and the Greek personal name Timaios.
Italian and Spanish form of Bartimaeus.

Variant of Bartimaeus used in some versions of the Vulgate (Latin Bible) as well as several English Bibles: the Bishops' Bible (1568), Douay-Rheims Bible (1582-1610) and the original 1611 edition of the King James Bible.

Dutch short form of Bartholomea. The name is sometimes erroneously interpreted as a variant spelling of Bertina. In the Netherlands, a known bearer of this name is Bartina Koeman, the wife of former Dutch soccer player Ronald Koeman.
Feminine form of Bartholomew. A known bearer of this name is the late American film actress Bartine Burkett. The name is sometimes erroneously interpreted as a variant spelling of Bertine.

Possibly an archaic variant of Potira. Bartira was the name of the daughter of the chief Tibiriçá, an indigenous leader of great importance for the formation of the city of São Paulo. When she got married to the Portuguese explorer João Ramalho, she was baptized as Isabel Dias.

This name was apparently invented by the 19th-century writer Herman Melville, who perhaps intended it to mean "Bartholomew's town" from the medieval English name Bartle, a diminutive of Bartholomew, combined with the English place name suffix -by meaning "farm, settlement", from Old Norse býr. Additionally, Melville may have been inspired by the similar-sounding name Barnaby.

Transferred use of the surname Bartlett.Alternatively, one documentend usage was on the nephew of Charlemagne. He was christened by the name of Berthaelot, a diminutive of Bertha, the name of his mother and grandmother.
Transferred use of the surname Bartley.
Feminine form of Bartolo, itself a short form of Bartolomé.

Earliest form was probably Berhtwald or later Berhtoald.Bertwald (often written Berthoald or Berthold) was king of the Saxons around 600-630.Berthoald (or Bertoald) was the mayor of the palace of Burgundy from some time before 603.Bertwald, archbishop of Canterbury 692-731 (Also written Brihtwald, Beorhtweald, Bertwald, Berthwald, Beorhtwald, or Beretuald)Modern form Berthold was in southern German in Alaholfing dynasty Berthold (father of Alaholf) with Hnabi was a founder of Riechenau Abbey in 724. The name is also used by his grandson, and great-great grandson. The name was also spelled Perahtold or Perahtoldus in documents where his great-grandson Chadaloh (Duke of Friuli) is mentioned.Bertulf (or Bartholf or Barthold) was the Archbishop of Trier from 869 until his death.From 900 the name appears in Bavaria (Luitpolding dynasty). Luitpold's father-in-law was Berthold Count palatine of Swabia.The name has often been spelled Barthold or Bartold in eastern Germany and Poland since the middle ages.
Swedish, medieval Dutch and medieval Latvian form of Bartholomew.
Archaic Italian form of Bartolomeo which apparently survived in the US where it is occasionally used.Bartolommeo Bandinelli (1493 – 1560) was an Italian Renaissance sculptor.
Medieval Italian diminutive of Bartolomeo, as -uccio is an Italian masculine diminutive suffix.
Medieval Italian diminutive of Bartolo, as -uccio is an Italian masculine diminutive suffix.This name can also be a contracted form of Bartolomuccio in some cases.
Variant of Barthold or a combination of bjartr "light, shining" and ulfr "wolf" (see also Bertulf).
Transferred use of the surname Barton. In popular culture, Barton Fink is the name of a playwright in the 1991 film "Barton Fink".
Diminutive of Old Hungarian Bartalom (see Bertalan).
The name is of Turkic origin and means "wealth".
Medieval Italian diminutive of Barto, which was a rare short form of Bartolo and Bartolomeo.This name can also be a contracted form of Bartolomuccio and Bartoluccio in some cases.
Campidanese form of Bartholomew, borrowed from Catalan Bartomeu.
Diminutive of Bartholomew and other Bart- names.
Galician form and Judeo-French variant of Baruch.
Spanish spelling of Baruch. A notable bearer was Baruch Spinoza, called Baruj Espinosa in Spanish.
Means "they are in order" in Setswana.
A Saxon king killed by Aglovale at the battle of Clarence.
Name of a 6th century Scottish saint.
Means "large eyes, brilliant eyes" in Malagasy.
Alternate transcription of Pashto بريالی (see Baryalai).
Alternate transcription of Pashto بريالی (see Baryalai).
Alternate transcription of Pashto بريالی (see Baryalai).
Barzai the Wise is a character in the short story "The Other Gods" by H.P. Lovecraft.
Variant of Barzillai. In the United States it was introduced by the Puritans as a masculine name, and first (?) used for girls in the mid-18th century.
Name of one of the commanders of the Sassanian kingdom in ancient Iran and It means a nobleman sitting on a horse's saddle
From the Xitsonga basa meaning "clean, white, pure" and mbilu meaning "heart".
Emilian-Romagnol and Venetian form of Bassianus.
From Kalmyk басң (basñ) meaning "Venus (the planet)" or "Friday", ultimately from Tibetan པ་སངས (pa-sangs).
Means "be clean, be white" in Xitsonga.

Basarab I the Founder was a prince of Wallachia (c. 1310 – 1352).Basarab I's name was originally Basarabai and lost the ending -a when it was borrowed into Romanian. The name is of Cuman or Pecheneg origin and most likely meant "father ruler".
Derived from Basaraba, which is the Vlach name for the historical region of Bessarabia. It is said to be the native land of the Vlach people.

The name "Basav" is of Indian origin, particularly from the Kannada language. It is often associated with the historical figure Basavanna, who was a 12th-century philosopher, statesman, and social reformer in the Indian state of Karnataka. The name "Basav" itself doesn't have a widely recognized meaning but is often linked with reverence and admiration due to its association with Basavanna.
Short form of Baschtian, an obsolete form of Bastian.
Basciante is a knight outside Malecasta's castle in Book 3, Canto 1. of "The Faerie Queene" by Edmund Spenser.
Transferred use of the surname Bascom.
Alternate transcription of Arabic بصير (see Basir), as well as the usual Urdu form.
Alternate transcription of Arabic بصيرة (see Basira).
Romansh form of Basil 1, traditionally found in the Surselva region.
Means "king" or "royal". The name holds significant importance in the Syriac Orthodox Church. It is derived from the word "basileus"
Alternate transcription of Arabic باسم (see Basim).
Alternate transcription of Arabic باسمة (see Basima).
Alternate transcription of Arabic باسمة (see Basima).
German and Swedish form of Basemath.
Means "good news" in Urdu, ultimately from Arabic بشارة (bashāra).
A blessing rain. Can mean 'a lot of good news'.
Alternate transcription of Arabic بشيرة (see Bashira), as well as the Urdu form.
Possibly use of the surname Bashel as a given name.
Arabic and Urdu alternate transcription of Bashir as well as the Maranao form.

From Bashlam, the Chechen name for Mount Kazbek.
Name of a 12th century Coptic saint.
Means "good news, good omen" in Uzbek.
From the Awajún bashu meaning "wild turkey, curassow".
Dutch form of Basilius. A known bearer of this name was the Belgian priest and poet Basiel De Craene (1880-1956).
From the herb, unrelated to Basil 1.
Coined by Sabino Arana Goiri and Koldo Elizalde as a Basque equivalent of Basilia and Basilie.
Feminine form of Basil 1 as well as the latinized form of Basileia.

Patronymic form of Βασιλεύς (Basileus) using the suffix ἴδης (ides). Coincides with the Ancient Greek word βασιλείδης (basileides) meaning "prince", which derives from the same root word as the given name.
Means "king, chief" in Ancient Greek, used as a title as well as a given name.

Older Georgian form of Basileios (see Basil 1). This name is barely in use nowadays. Its shorter form Basil is considered more modern and is thus more in use, but even that name is rare in Georgia. It is Vasil (a shorter form of Vasili, which is the Georgian form of Vasiliy) that is most commonly used in Georgia nowadays.

Given name from the Spanish and Italian word "basilica", derived from Ancient Greek "βασιλική στοά": a large oblong building in Roman architecture used as a public forum or town hall, sometimes also a church or court building. Also the name of several towns in Greece.
French and Italian form of Basileides via its latinized form Basilides.
Spanish and Portuguese form of Basileides (see Basilides).
Latinized form of Basileides. Bearers of this name include the philosopher Basilides the Epicurean (2nd century BC) and saint Basilides (died around 205 AD).
Feminine form of Basil 1 and Basile.
French form of Basiliscus which was also used as a feminine form of this name.
Georgian and Spanish form of Basilissa.
Italian and Spanish form of Basiliscus (see Basiliskos).
Latinized form of Basiliskos. Basiliscus of Comana (died c. 310), also known as Basiliscus of Pontus, was a Greek martyr.
Ancient Greek name meaning literally "little king", a diminutive of Basileios. This was also the Greek name for Regulus, a star in the constellation Leo.
Corsican, Sardinian and Sicilian form of Basilius.
Derived from Ancient Greek βασίλεια (basileia) meaning "rule, royal power, queen" and δίκη (dike) meaning "justice".

The first element of this name is derived from the Greek noun βασιλεύς (basileus) meaning "king" (see Basil 1), though technically both βασίλεια (basileia) meaning "queen, princess" and βασίλειος (basileios) meaning "royal, kingly" are also possible.The second element consists of the Greek noun κλέος (kleos) meaning "glory". As such, the meaning of this name is "glory of the king". However, "glory of the queen" and "royal glory" are also possible.In Greek literature, Basilokles is the name of one of the characters in Plutarch's essay De Pythiae oraculis. He is better known under the latinized form of his name, which is Basilocles.
Alternate transcription of Arabic باسمة (see Basima).
Basina (c. 438 – 477) was a queen of Thuringia in the middle of the fifth century.
Alternate transcription of Arabic بصيرة (see Basira), as well as the Malay form.
Form of Bassirou used in Anglophone countries.
Means "sun" in Indonesian, ultimately from Sanskrit भास्कर (bhāskara), see Bhaskara.
Alternate transcription of Tamil பாஸ்கரன் (see Bhaskaran).
Likely transfered use of the surname Baskel.
Alternate transcription of Arabic بسمة (see Basma).

Means "venomous snake", possibly deriving from the Sumerian elements muš ("snake, reptile") and uš ("venom, poison"). Name borne by a figure from Mesopotamian mythology, a horned snake with two forelegs and wings.
Older spelling of Basuki influenced by Dutch orthography.
This name was first given to Basirullah , know as Basoor Afg
From the Uzbek bas meaning "enough, stop" and oy meaning "moon".
