column12: Means "my vision" from Arabic بصر (basar) meaning "vision, sight". It is often given in honour of Muslim theologian and writer Hasan al-Basri.
Combination of Basri and the masculine suffix -zal.
Transferred use of the surname Bass. It can also be a variant of Bas.
Possibly derived from βᾶσσα (bassa), the Doric form of Ancient Greek βῆσσα (bessa) meaning "wooded valley, glen".
Probably an Egyptian form of Pesend.
Alternate transcription of Arabic باسل (see Basil 2).
Judeo-Spanish, Judeo-French and Judeo-Anglo-Norman form of Batsheva.
(Efik and Ibibio) origin meaning little god
From Old Norse bassi meaning either "bear" or "wild boar".
The given name of a character in the 1594 Shakesperian play 'Titus Andronicus'.
Diminutive of Bass or a variant of Bessie.
Alternate transcription of Arabic باسل (see Basil 2).
Form of Basir used in parts of French-influenced West Africa.
Derived from bəsdir meaning 'that is enough'.
Diminutive of Sebastian, not commonly used as a given name in its own right.
Cremish Lombard short form of Sebastià.
Icelandic and Spanish form of Bastian.
Galician feminine form of Bastián, Corsican feminine form of Bastianu and Gascon feminine form of Bastian.
Dutch pet form of Bastiaan or short form of Sebastijn.
Adoption of French Bastille, referring to the stormed fortress in Paris during the French Revolution.
Probably use of the surname Bastille.
French variant of Bastien and Walloon variant of Bastén.
Bengali and Odia form of Vasudeva.
Means "safe, prosperous, flourishing, healthy" in Javanese, ultimately from Sanskrit वासुकि (vāsuki).
Indonesian and Malay variant of Bashir.
From Sino-Vietnamese 拔 (bạt) meaning "to pull, to extract, to choose".
From Sino-Vietnamese 弼 (bật) meaning "to aid, assist, help".
Diminutive of Bartholomew; also compare Bate. A notable bearer was American gunfighter and lawman Bartholomew 'Bat' Masterson (1853-1921), famed sheriff of Dodge City, Kansas.
Coined by Sabino Arana Goiri and Koldo Elizalde as a Basque form of Beata. The name coincides with Basque bata, absolutive plural of bat, meaning "one".
From Mongolian бат (batu) meaning "strong, firm" and the emphasis marker -аа.
Feminine form of Batalanto, which means "Warrior" in Esperanto. Batalanta, means "Female Warrior".
Derived from Mongolian бат (batu) meaning "strong, firm" and амгалан (amgalan) meaning "calm, peaceful".
It means to “hold or touch the heart”.
Batandwa was a used name reffering to followers in Christianity.
From the name of Batara Guru, one of the three trinity gods in Batak mythology. The word itself is derived from Sanskrit भट्टार (bhaṭṭāra) meaning "revered, worshipful".
From Sanskrit भट्टार (bhaṭṭāra) meaning "noble lord" and गुरु (guru) meaning "teacher, sage, guru". This is the name of the supreme deity in Javanese Hinduism.

From Indonesian batara meaning "god, deity" and sambu of uncertain meaning, possibly from Sanskrit शंभु (śambhu) meaning "sage, venerable man". In Javanese mythology, he is the god of teachers and a son of Batara Guru.

This is the name of the 12th Watcher of the 20 leaders of the 200 fallen angels that are mentioned in an ancient work called the Book of Enoch. It likely means “rain of God”, combining matar meaning "rain" and El meaning “God".
Means "strong hero" in Mongolian, from бат (batu) meaning "strong, firm" and баатар (baatar) meaning "hero".
Means "strong steel" in Mongolian, from бат (batu) meaning "strong, firm" and болд (bold) meaning "steel".
Derived from Mongolian бат (batu) meaning "strong, firm" and буян (buyan) meaning "virtue, charity" or "fortune, blessing".
This form of Bathsheba is used in the Nouvelle Français courant (NFC) translation of the Bible. Batcheba Louis is a Haitian soccer player.
Derived from a combination of the words בת means "graceful girl" or "beautiful girl" in Hebrew.
Means "strong ornament" in Mongolian, from бат (batu) meaning "strong, firm" and чимэг (chimeg) meaning "ornament".
From Mongolian бат (batu) meaning "strong, firm" and чулуун (chuluun) meaning "stone".
Middle English diminutive of Bartholomew, derived from a diminutive of Bate.
From Mongolian бат (batu) meaning "strong, firm" and дорж (dorj) meaning "diamond, vajra".
From Mongolian бат (batu) meaning "strong, firm" and Tibetan སྒྲོལ་མ (sgrol ma) meaning "saviour" (see Dolma).
From the root “بتل” (batal) used denoting from Maryam (Mary) and as a meaning of piety and purity, also means the petal of a flower.
Rare archaic form of Bótulfr, most common in Gotland, Sweden.
Transferred use of the surname Bates.
From Mongolian бат (batu) meaning "strong, firm" and гэрэл (gerel) meaning "light"

Means "god, deity" in Tagalog, derived from Sanskrit भट्टार (bhaṭṭāra) meaning "holy, honourable, venerable" (through a transmission from Malay betara). In native Tagalog mythology, Bathala is the deity who created the universe. After the arrival of the Spanish, he came to be associated with the Christian God.
Diminutive of names containing the element bǫð meaning "battle". In Norse mythology this is the name of a Jotunn.

Variant of Bathild. This was the name of a 7th-century English saint who became queen of the Franks after being sold to them as a slave. She was canonised for fighting against the slave trade, promoting monasticism and founding a convent. J.K. Rowling used this name in her final Harry Potter novel. Considering the character of Bathilda Bagshot, Rowling may have chosen the name due to its resemblance to "batty" and "old bat".

Meaning unknown. This is the name of a demon who appears in several works on demonology, including the 17th-century grimoire The Lesser Key of Solomon (author unknown) and the Pseudomonarchia Daemonum (1563) by Dutch physician Johann Weyer.
Greek form of Bethuel and Pethuel, as it first appeared in the Septuagint.
Form of the name Bathshua in the Schlachter bible translation.

Means "daughter of salvation" or "daughter of prosperity" in Hebrew. The first element is Hebrew בַּת (baṯ) meaning "daughter"; the second element could be derived from the verb יָשַׁע (yashaʿ) "to save, to deliver", which is related to the verb שוע (shawa') meaning "to cry out (for salvation)" and the nouns שוע (shua'), שוע (shoa') and שועה (shawa) all of which mean "a cry (for salvation)", or it could be derived from a noun שוע which has been interpreted as meaning "riches, wealth".According to George R. Stewart (1979): 'In the biblical text this name is sometimes only another form for Bathsheba, though at least once it is the name of another person. It occurs rarely among names in early New England. It may represent an attempt to provide a substitute for Bathsheba, without that name's evil suggestions. Bathshua, however, failed to become established.' A bearer of the variant Bathsua was the great 17th-century scholar Bathsua Makin.
Means "daughter of abundance".A notable namesake is Bathsua Makin (c. 1600 – c. 1675)
Form of Bethuel used in the English and Latin Old Testament.
Transferred use of the surname Bathurst.
Feminine form of Bathycles. In Greek mythology, Bathycleia was the mother of Halirrhothius by Poseidon, and was possibly another name for the nymph Euryte.

From the Greek name Βαθυκλῆς (Bathykles), which was derived from the Greek elements βαθύς (bathus, bathys) meaning "deep, profound" and κλέος (kleos) meaning "glory, fame". This was the name of a warrior mentioned in Homer's Iliad, one of the Myrmidons who took part in the Trojan War.
Latinized form of Ancient Greek Βάθυλλος (Bathyllos), possibly derived from the element βαθύς (bathys) "deep, profound".

Probably derived from Ancient Greek βάτος (batos) meaning "bramble bush, wild blackberry". This was the name of a naiad of the town of Sparta in Greek mythology, who married an early Spartan king, Oibalos. It was also the name of a daughter (or possibly aunt) of King Teucer.
Means "how we want it to be" in Yoruba.
Means "khan of the west" in Turkish.
Italian, Portuguese and Spanish form of Bathilda.
Coined by Sabino Arana Goiri and Koldo Elizalde as a Basque form of Beatriz and Béatrice.
Greek form of the Old Persian name *Bata meaning "wine".
Gallo form of Baptiste and older Walloon form of Batisse.
Walloon and Picard form of Baptiste.
Romansh variant of Battist and Gallo variant of Batisst.
Aragonese form of Bautista and Occitan, Sardinian, Ladin, Lombard, Venetian and Piedmontese form of Battista.
From Mongolian бат (batu) meaning "strong, firm" and жаргал (jargal) meaning "happiness, blessing".
Means "strong king, firm ruler" in Mongolian, from бат (batu) meaning "strong, firm" and хаан (kaan) meaning "khan, ruler, leader". Cognate to Batuhan.
From Mongolian бат (batu) meaning "strong, firm" and хуяг (khuyag) meaning "armour" or "warder, overseer".
Middle English diminutive of Bartholomew, from a combination of Bate and the diminutive suffix -kin.
Means "echo" (see Hed).Also a combination of Bat, means "girl, daughter", and Kol, neans "voice".According to the old sages (חז״ל) - Bat Kol is the way of connecting between God and human.
From Mongolian бат (batu) meaning "strong, firm" and мөнх (mönkh) meaning "eternal".
Derived from Mongolian бат (batu) meaning "strong, firm" and найрамдал (nairamdal) meaning "friendship".

Bato the Daesitiate (also known as Bato of the Daesitiates) was a chieftain of the Daesitiates, an Illyrian tribe which fought against the Roman Empire between 6 and 9 AD in a conflict known as Bellum Batonianum.
From Mongolian бат (batu) meaning "strong, firm" and очир (ochir) meaning "diamond" or "truncheon, staff; thunderbolt".
Alternate transcription of Arabic بتول (see Batul), as well as the usual Urdu form.
Originally it derives from a Turkish word and it means "warlord". Nowadays it is associated with Hungarian word "bride".
Means "girl of light", from a combination of Bat and Or.
Alternate transcription of Arabic بتول (see Batul).
One of the Arabic translitterations of of Patricia.
From Mongolian бат (batu) meaning "strong, firm" and сайхан (saikhan) meaning "beautiful, nice, handsome, fine".
Form of Bathshua in the Elberfelder and the Zürcher bible translations.
Means "strong axe" in Mongolian, from бат (batu) meaning "strong, firm" and сүх (sükh) meaning "axe".
Derived from Mongolian бат (batu) meaning "strong, firm" combined with Tibetan ཚེ་རིང (tshe ring) meaning "long life, longevity".
From Mongolian бат (batu) meaning "strong, firm" and суурь (suuri) meaning "base, foundation".
From the Old Norse byname Bátsveinn meaning "boatman".
Meaning, "a large, organized group of people pursuing a common aim or sharing a major undertaking." Referring to the army of God (believers).
Vernacular diminutive of Baptist and Baptiste.
From Mongolian бат (batu) meaning "strong, firm" and төгс (tögs) meaning "perfect, complete".
From Mongolian бат (batu) meaning "strong, firm" and тулга (tulga) meaning "cooking stand".
Means "strong ray of light" in Mongolian, from бат (batu) meaning "strong, firm" and туяа (tuyaa) meaning "ray, beam (of light)".
Means "prevailing, preponderant" in Turkic, though it is more frequently associated with the Turkish word batı meaning "west".
Means "firm ruler" in Mongolian, from бат (batu) meaning "strong, firm" and хаан (kaan) meaning "khan, ruler, leader".
Derived from the Turco-Mongolian honorific title ᠪᠠᠭᠠᠲᠤᠷ (baɣatur) meaning "hero" (see Bahadur).
Either a variant of Batur or derived from the Georgian adjective ბათურა (batura) meaning "plump" (in reference to a child) as well as "fat dog". For the latter meaning, compare Dzaghlika.
Derived from batu "battle" and rih "ruler, king". Cognate to Old English Beaduric and Old Norse Bǫðríkr.
From Mongolian бат (batu) meaning "strong, firm" and үүл (üül) meaning "cloud, overcast".
Combination of Bat and Yam, means “daughter of the sea; mermaid” in Hebrew, also a city near Tel Aviv.
Combination of Batyr with the Turkish military title beg meaning "chieftain, master".In Kyrgyzstan, this name is a variant of Baatyrbek.
From Kazakh батыр (batyr) meaning "hero, brave" combined with the Turkic title khan meaning "leader, ruler".
Means "daughter of Zabbai" in Aramaic. This was the native Palmyrene name of Septimia Zenobia (see Zenobia).

Derived from בַּת־צִיּוֹן meaning "daughter of Zion". This name first appears as a personification of Jerusalem or the Judean nation (mainly in a negative context). appearing in (2 Kings 19:21, Isaiah 37:22, Isaiah 1:8, and Isaiah 54:1).
Derived from Mongolian бат (batu) meaning "strong, firm, loyal" and зориг (zorig) meaning "courage, will, intention".
From Mongolian бат (batu) meaning "strong, firm" and зул (zul) meaning "light, lamp, torch".
Variant of Bảo, from a non-Sino-Vietnamese reading of Chinese 寶 (báu).
Means "gourd", especially "bottle gourd (Lagenaria siceraria)" in Vietnamese.

Derived from Ancient Greek βαυκός (baukos) meaning "delicate, soft; prudish, disdainful, affected". In Greek mythology, Baucis and Philemon were an elderly couple who showed great hospitality to the god Zeus. Baucis was also the name of a Greek poet contemporaneous with Sappho and Erinna whose work is now lost, apostrophized in Erinna's 'Distaff'.
Variant of Bauke, a diminutive form of Baue. Also possibly a variant of Auke.
Variant of Baudilio. Saint Baudilus of Nîmes is known as Baudilio or Baudelio in Spanish; see also Baudelius.
Variant of Baudilius (see Baudilio). Baudelius or Baudilius was a 3rd-century saint and martyr from Orleans.

Medieval French diminutive of masculine names that contain the Germanic element bald meaning "bold, brave" (such as Baudouin, Baudri and Thibaud), as it contains the French masculine diminutive suffix -et.
A minor Germanic goddess known from inscriptions in Northern England.
Name of a late 3rd and early 4th century missionary to the Auvergne region of Gaul.

Medieval French diminutive of masculine names that contain the Germanic element bald meaning "bold, brave" (such as Baudouin, Baudri and Thibaud), as it contains the French masculine diminutive suffix -in.
Feminine form of Baudin. In the Netherlands, this name is usually (but not always) a variant spelling of Boudine.
Languedocian and Provençal cognate of Baudoin.
From the Germanic element baud, of uncertain meaning. This is the name of the patron saint of Alessandria, who lived in the eighth century, as well as a book by Umberto Eco.
Variant of Baldram. In a medieval record this name was Latinized as Baldrannus.
An Irish knight who ruled the castle of Antiufais in Les Merveilles de Rigomer. He hosted Lancelot during the latter’s journey to Rigomer and provided him information on the road ahead.
Variant form of Baldéric via the form Baudric.

One of the most important of the less-remembered knights, Baudwin seems to have been a major figure in various pre-Malory romances. In The Avowynge of King Arthur we learn that he made three interesting vows prompted by early experiences campaigning in Spain; never to deny anyone meat and drink, never to fear death, and never to be jealous of his wife or any other woman. It is possible that Sir Baudwin should be identified with Bishop Baudwin (Baldwin).

A name of Germanic origin that has been so strongly abbreviated, that one can no longer tell with certainty what the original form and its meaning is. Some scholars think that it is derived from the name Bavo.
Transferred use of the surname Bauer.
Means "Re is his glory" in Egyptian.
Derived from the Germanic name elements baugr "ring, armlet, money" and heiðr, "heath".
Variant of Baugr. This was the name of a jotunn in Norse mythology.
Derived from Old Norse baugr "ring, money". This was the name of the sacred temple ring on which oaths were made.
Derived from Gaulish *baua, ultimately from Proto-Celtic *baṷā, "dirt, mud".
For a man, it is the diminutive form of Baue - but for a woman, it is the feminine form of Baue. However, the name is far more common on men than on women.
A Knight of the Round Table.
In older publications of the Doctrine and Covenants, and alias used by Joseph Smith was a double name, Baurak and Ale. It is identified as a Hebrew term meaning "God bless you."
Flavius Bauto (died c. 385) was a Romanised Frank who served as a magister militum of the Roman Empire and imperial advisor under Valentinian II.

Belarusian form of Bartholomaios (see Bartholomew). This form is rare and might even be archaic; Varfalamiej is the form most commonly used today.In Belarusian literature, this name is borne by Dr. Baŭtramiej Liodnik, one of the main characters of Avantury Pranciša Vyrviča ("Adventures of Pranciš Vyrvič"), a series of novels written by the Belarusian author Liudmila Rublieŭskaja (b. 1965). A film based on the novels was made in 2019 and bears the same title.
Diminutive of Baŭtramiej, which is one of the Belarusian forms of Bartholomew.
Bava or Baba is the name of various figures of the Talmud.Bava means "gate" in Aramaic
The latinised name of the German state of Bayern.Officially admitted as a name in Germany.

A name of Germanic origin that has been so strongly abbreviated, that one can no longer tell with certainty what the original form and its meaning is. Some think that it may be a short form of a name containing the Germanic element badu "battle" (like Baderic), while others think that it is derived from the Germanic element barn "child" via its Middle English form babe. This name was borne by a saint from the 7th century AD.
From the Shipibo bawa meaning "parrot" and the genitive suffix -n.
From the Kazakh бауыр (bawır) literally meaning "liver, stomach" but figuratively meaning "blood relations, siblings" and жан (jan) meaning "soul".
Alternate transcription of Thai บวร (see Bowon).
Alternate transcription of Thai บวรรัตน์ (see Bowonrat).
Alternate transcription of Thai บวรศักดิ์ (see Bowonsak).
Transferred use of the surname Baxley.
Means "part of Allah", from Uzbek baxsh meaning "lot, part, portion" (ultimately from Persian بخش (bakhsh)) and Arabic الله (Allah).
Derived from baxt meaning "happiness" and gul meaning "flower, rose".
Derived from baxt meaning "happiness" and qiz meaning "girl".
Combination of given name Baxtiyor and Uzbek jon "soul".
Transferred use of the English surname of Baxton.
Derived from the archaic Russian verb баять (bayat) meaning "to speak, to tell", which is ultimately derived from Church Slavonic bajati meaning "to speak, to talk, to tell, to narrate".
Derived from Mongolian баян (bayan) meaning "rich, wealthy" and далай (dalai) meaning "ocean, sea".
From Bashkir баян (bayan) meaning "happy" and гөл (göl) meaning "flower".
From Bashkir баян (bayan) meaning "happy" and һылыу (hiliw) meaning "beautiful, beauty".
From Mongolian баян (bayan) meaning "rich, wealthy" and мөнх (mönkh) meaning "eternal, forever".
Alternate transcription of Mongolian Баянмөнх (see Bayanmönkh).
Derived from Mongolian баян (bayan) meaning "rich, wealthy" and намар (namar) meaning "autumn".
Means "our joy" in Mongolian, from баяр (bayar) meaning "joy, celebration" and the possessive suffix -аа (-aa).
From Mongolian баяр (bayar) meaning "celebration, joy" and баатар (baatar) meaning "hero".
From Mongolian баяр (bayar) meaning "celebration, joy" and билэг (bileg) meaning "gift, talent, aptitude".
From Mongolian баяр (bayar) meaning "celebration, joy" and далай (dalai) meaning "ocean, sea".
Spanish form of Bayard used by Gabriel García Márquez for a character in his novella 'Chronicle of a Death Foretold' (1981).
From Mongolian баяр (bayar) meaning "joy, celebration" and жаргал (jargal) meaning "happiness, blessing".
Derived from Buryat баяр (bayar) meaning "joy, happiness".
Derived from Mongolian баяр (bayar) meaning "joy, happiness" and the feminine suffix маа (maa).
From Mongolian баяр (bayar) meaning "joy, celebration" and сайхан (saikhan) meaning "beautiful, nice, handsome".
From Mongolian баяр (bayar) meaning "joy" combined with Tibetan ཚེ་རིང (tshe ring) meaning "long life, longevity".
From Mongolian баяр (bayar) meaning "celebration, joy" and цэнгэл (tsengel) meaning "feast, merrymaking, gaiety".
Means "flower of joy" in Mongolian, from баяр (bayar) meaning "joy" and цэцэг (tsetseg) meaning "flower".
From Mongolian баяр (bayar) meaning "joy" and цогт (tsogt) meaning "spirited, ardent, brilliant".
From Mongolian баяр (bayar) meaning "celebration, joy" and жаргал (jargal) meaning "happiness, blessing".
Means "lord panther" in Turkish, derived from Turkish bay "rich person, noble" and pars "leopard, panther". This was the name of the fourth Mamluk Sultan of Egypt and Syria.
From Bashkir бай (bay) meaning "happy" and feminine name element бикә (bikä).
Bayek, also known as Bayek of Siwa, is a fictional character in Ubisoft's Assassin's Creed video game franchise.
French form of Paimon, found in French editions of The Grimoire of Pope Honorius.
Means "where will they go?" in Tumbuka.

column3: ဘုရင့်နောင်(Burmese)
column12: Means "king's elder brother" from Burmese ဘုရင် (bayin) meaning "king" and နောင် (naung) meaning "elder brother". This was the name of a 16th-century king of Myanmar.
Means "beys, chieftains, masters" in Azerbaijani (the plural of bəy, ultimately from Turkic beg).
Likely an invented name made to sound like names with a similar sound like Jalen or Waylon.
From Kazakh бай (bay) meaning "rich, wealthy" combined with the given name Magambet.
From Turkmen baý meaning "wealthy, prosperous" combined with Muhammet.
Possibly derived from the word baý ("wealthy") and the given name Myrat.

From the Middle English personal name "Bainard", via Norman French from ancient Germanic "Beinhard", perhaps from *bein-*, meaning "leg, bone" or a supposed element *bagin-*, meaning "dispute", and *-hard*, meaning "hard, brave."

Name of the titular main character and protagonist of the same named game and movie. It's origins aren't very touched upon. However it's said in the movie to be derived from the weapon name "bayonet" and made feminine by the suffix "-ta".
From the American English word bayou which derives from the Choctaw word bayuk meaning "small stream".
Derived from the Uzbek bayram meaning "holiday" and baxt meaning "happiness".
Derived from байрам ‎(bayram) “festivity” and бикә ‎(bikä) which is a name element.
From the Bashkir байрам ‎(bayram) meaning “festivity” and гөл (göl ) meaning "flower".
Combination of the words baýram, meaning "festival, holiday", and gözel, meaning "beautiful".
Derived from the Uzbek bayram meaning "holiday" and gul meaning "flower, rose".
From Bashkir байрам ‎(bayram) “festivity” and һылыу (hiliw) meaning "beautiful, beauty".
Given to boys born on a holiday.
Spanish form of Byron, reflecting the English pronunciation.

Derived from the Turkish military title beg meaning "chieftain, master" or Persian bai meaning "mister" combined with Persian سنگ (sang) meaning "stone, rock". Baysangur of Benoa (1794-1861) was a Chechen commander of the 19th century.
Derived from бай (bay) meaning "rich" and тимер (timer) meaning "iron".
Indonesian form of Vayu, also used as an Indonesian word meaning "wind, breeze".
Means "diamond, vajra" in Buryat, ultimately from Sanskrit वज्र (vajra).
From Persian بازار (bazar) meaning "market, marketplace" combined with Kyrgyz/Kazakh бай (bay) meaning "rich, wealthy".
Derived from Persian بازار (bâzâr) meaning "market, marketplace" and Kazakh гүл (gül) meaning "flower".
Derived from Erzya бажамс (bazhams) meaning "wish, want, dream".
Russian feminine name possibly meaning "welcome child", or else, more likely, a variant form of Bozhena.
Feminization of Basil 1 borne by Bazoline Estelle Usher who was born named Basil but later changed her name to Bazoline because she felt Basil was masculine.
Derived from the name of a Navarrese valley.
Feminine form of Bazyli. It coincides with the Polish word bazylia meaning "basil".
Polish form of Basilius. Also compare Bazyli.
Alternate transcription of بشيرة (See Bashira), chiefly used in Northern Africa.
From Vietnamese búp bê meaning "doll", borrowed from French poupée. It can also mean "calf (young cow)" in Vietnamese.
From Sino-Vietnamese 陛 (bệ) meaning "pedestal, dais, majestic".
Short form of Béatrice, hardly ever used as a given name in its own right.

Means "little bee", derived from Old Irish beach "bee" combined with a diminutive suffix. As a surname it becomes Ó Beacháin which is anglisised to Behan, as used by Irish Poet Brendan Behan. In County Clare in the west of Ireland the town Ballyvaughan also takes it's name from Beachán, Baile Uí Bheacháin, which means "Ó Beachán's townland".
Derived from the surname Beacon, or from the English word beacon meaning "prominent signal".

Beacurs is the name of Gawain’s younger brother in Wolfram von Eschenbach’s Parzival. Beacurs is implied to be a Knight of the Round Table. Beacurs takes on the part of Gawain's protect which in Chrétien de Troyes’ Perceval (romance) is assigned to Agravain. But Wolfram seems to assign more respect to Beacurs than is traditional to Agravain. The name Beacurs appears to represent French Beau-corps (‘Fair-body’). Sir Thomas Malory’s “Le Morte d'Arthur” tells a tale of Gawain's brother Gareth in which Gareth is given the nickname Beaumains (‘Fair-hands’), and Gareth uses this name while he conceals his true identity.
Derived from the Old English elements beadu "battle" and friþ "peace". Cognate to Old Norse Bárðr.
Derived from the Old English elements beadu "battle, war" and heard "hard, firm, brave".
Derived from the Old English elements beadu "battle" and noð "boldness, daring".
Derived from the Old English elements beadu "battle" and ric "power, rule".
Derived from the Old English elements beadu "battle" and wine "friend".
Derived from the Old English elements beadu "battle" and wulf "wolf". Alternative form of Beowulf, cognate to Germanic Badulf.

Means "beautiful flower" (compare Blanchefleur). This was the name of a fairy in the Middle High German romance 'Parzival' (Wolfram von Eschenbach's adaptation of 'Perceval, the Story of the Grail', a poem by Chrétien de Troyes). Beaflurs was the mother of Liahturteltart, a page to Queen Ampflise of France in the time of Uther.
Derived from Old English bēag "ring" (compare Old High German boug) and lāc "play, sport; offering, sacrifice" (from laikaz).

Comprised of the elements beag ("little") and laoch ("warrior, hero").Though having fallen out of usage as a first name, Beaglaoch is still seen in a modern context in the surname Ó Beaglaoich (anglicised as O'Begley or Begley).Historically, the Ó Beaglaoich clan were most prominent in County Donegal, later also having a strong southern presence in Counties Cork and Kerry. Notably, County Kerry members of the clan were involved in aiding the Gallowglass in the 15th century.
Derived from Old English bēag "ring" (compare Old High German boug) and mund "protection".
Derived from Old English bēag "ring" (compare Old High German boug) and noð "boldness, daring".
Derived from Old English bēag "ring" (compare Old High German boug) and wine "friend".
Derived from Old English bēag "ring" (compare Old High German boug) and wulf "wolf". Old English cognate of Baugulf.
Means "day, sun" in Sami. Its Finnish cognate is Päivä.
Possible Old English name meaning "bold battle", derived from the elements beald "bold, brave" and guð "battle".
Derived from Old English beald "bold, brave" and helm "helmet".
Derived from Old English beald "bold, brave" and here "army".
Derived from Old English beald "bold, brave" and ræd "advice, counsel, wisdom". It is a cognate to Baldred.
Derived from Old English beald "bold, brave" and wine "friend". Either an older form of or cognate to Baldwin.
Derived from Old English beald "bold, brave" and wulf "wolf". Cognate to Germanic Baldulf.
Transferred use of the surname Beale.
Transferred use of the surname Beall.
Local Aboriginal name of Myroodah Station near Looma, Western Australia.
The father of Breca in the epic Beowulf.
Scottish Gaelic and Manx form of Bernard.
Scottish Gaelic form of Berenice, this name is also considered a feminine form of Bearnard.
Bearthm Brakhage is an American director and actor. The name was likely invented by his father, Stan Brakhage.
Transferred use of the surname Beasley.
Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, and Galician form of Beatus and masculine form of Beata.
Croatian and Slovak form of Beatrice.
Hungarian form of Beatrice, reflecting the Italian pronunciation.

Dutch form of Beatrix. Notable bearers of this name include the Blessed Beatrijs of Nazareth (1200-1268), a Flemish Cistercian nun, and the eponymous character of the anonymous 14th-century religious poem 'Beatrijs'.
A blend of Beatrix and Trine.
Gascon and Franco-Provençal form of Béatrice.
Russian, Breton, Provençal, Piedmontese, medieval Spanish and medieval Occitan form of Beatrix, a Czech and Romansh variant of that name and a Brazilian Portuguese variant of Beatriz.
Georgian and Russian form of Beatrice.
Cognate as well as a Latinization of Beatrice.
English variant and Piedmontese form of Beatrice.
Provençal, Languedocian and Gascon form of Beatrix.
French and Franco-Provençal form of Beatrix.
Variant of Beatrice, or perhaps in some cases Beatriz.
West Flemish form of Beatrice and Afrikaans variant of Beatrijs.
A combination of Beau and Anna

A combination of the French masculine adjective beau meaning "beautiful, handsome" with the name Chiana. Interestingly, this given name has a strong resemblance with the French surname Beauchain and its variant Beauchaine. As such, it might be possible that in some cases, Beauchiana was inspired by the surname or even an attempted feminization of it.
A variant of Bodhi influenced by the spelling of Beau.

Gawaine’s son in Robert de Blois’ Fair Unknown romance.Born to Amie, the daughter of the King of Wales, Beaudous set out to win fame and fortune when he came of age. He called himself the Knight of Two Shields.By drawing a sword called Honoree from its sheath, he proved himself worthy to marry a princess named Biauté (Beauté), daughter of the King of the Isles. After saving Biauté from Madoines, a competing suitor, Beaudous married her.
Transferred use of the surname Beaufort.
Derived from Old French biau, bel, Middle French beau meaning "beautiful, fair; handsome, comely" combined with Old French and Middle French oncle meaning "uncle".
Joseph Broussard 1702-1765; also known as beausoleil. Leader of Acadian people of Nova Scotia.

1. A lovely maiden from the castle Landemore.She arrived at Arthur’s court at Karahes (Carhaix) during a Pentecost feast. Gawaine fell in love with her immediately, and presented her to Guenevere. Beauté rebuked Gawaine’s love, as well as that of Gliglois, Gawaine’s squire, who was equally smitten upon seeing her. Gawaine hoped to win her admiration at the Castle Orgueilleux tournament, but she refused to attend with him, going instead with the knight Aharer, who gave her a falcon to be presented to the winner of the tournament.The love-struck Gliglois, meanwhile, followed Beauté and Aharer, running behind their horses until his feet bled. Beauté finally stopped and instructed him to take a message to her sister at Landemore. The message revealed to her sister, and to Gliglois, that Beauté truly loved Gliglois but wanted to test him. Her sister knighted Gliglois, who entered the tournament and won – taking the falcon and Beauté as his prizes. Gawaine graciously relinquished his love for his former squire’s sake.2. Daughter of the King of the Isles.Her father decreed that she would be married by the knight who could pull the magnificent sword named Honoree from its sheath. Beautés’ maidservant, Clarete, carried the sword around until Beaudous, the son of Gawaine, managed to draw the sword.Meanwhile, Madoines, a jilted suitor of Beauté, invaded her lands. Beaudous arrived at the right time and defeated Madoines. Beauté and Beaudous were married.
Simply from the English word beautiful.
From the English word "beauty", ultimately derived from Latin bellus, "beautiful". See also Belle and Bella.
Derived from Middle French beau (via Old French biau, bel) "beautiful, fair; handsome, comely" and Old French viz or vit "sight, visage".

A maiden who arrived at Camelot seeking a champion to avenge the death of a knight in the Straight of Sorelois (Straits of Sorelois). She was hoping to find Lancelot, but she reluctantly accepted Arthur’s appointment of Sir Brunor the Black, or the Knight of the Ill-Fitting Coat, to the task.She is first called Maledisant (“Evil-speaking”), because throughout their journey to Sorelois, she insulted the poor knight, who proved himself lousy at jousting but superior at swordplay. Other knights witnessed her behavior toward Brunor and chastised her for being such a shrew. She later revealed that she truly loved Brunor, and that she had only scorned him in hope that he would abandon the dangerous adventure. Lancelot renamed her Bien Pensant (“Well-thinking”). Finally, after the quest, and the marriage with La Cote Male Taile, she is called Beauvivante (“Well-living”).The history of Sir La Cote Male Taile and his damsel as recorded in Malory IX parallels, or perhaps parodies, the history of Gareth and Lynette in his Book VII.With so many unnamed damsels in the tales, it seems hardly fair that a single maiden should be given three distinctive, personality-tailored names. Her story suggests, however, that anyone with some knowledge of French can coin similar names for otherwise nameless characters.
Variant of Beau, coinciding with the plural form of the French word.
From the surname Beavan, or a variant of Bevan.
Diminutive of Eva, Genoveva, and other names with a similar sound.

A diminutive of the female Biblical name Elisabeð, this name gave rise to the place name Bamburgh, its Anglo-Saxon name being "Bebbanburh". This name was used by Queen Bebba, wife of Æthelfrith, King of Northumbria in the early 7th century.
Nickname derived from bebe, a Filipino colloquialism for the English word baby.
Combination of Bebe, a Filipino colloquialism for the English word baby, and the popular suffix -lyn. This is essentially a variant of Babylyn.
Diminutive of Bebe, a Filipino colloquialism for the English word baby. This can also be a variant of Bibing.
Diminutive of any name ending in -bert.
Diminutive of any name ending in -bert, as a Gallo name, however, it is most often used as a diminutive of Albert.

Alternative diminutive of Alberto, Adalberto, Roberto and names ending with "-berto". People with this name includes famous footballer José Roberto Gama de Oliveira, known as Bebeto and volleyball player Paulo Roberto de Freitas, known as Bebeto de Freitas.
Aragonese form of Bebrycius. Not commonly used as a given name.

Latinized form of Βεβρύκη (Bebryke). In Greek legend Bebryke or Bebryce, otherwise called Βρύκη (Bryke) or Bryce, was one of the Danaids. The Bebryces, a mythical tribe of people living in Bithynia (a region of Asia Minor also known as Bebrycia), were said to be named for Bebryce (or else for a hero named Bebryx or Bebrycus).
Beburos is an angel mentioned in the Greek Apocalypse of Ezra whose name was revealed to Esdras as one of the nine angels who will govern "at the end of the world."

Allegedly an older form of Irish beag "small".In Irish mythology, Bec is one of the Tuatha Dé Danann. "She was known for having a magic well, guarded by her three daughters. When Fionn mac Cumhaill approached the well to ask for a drink, her daughters tried to prevent him from getting the water; 'one of them threw water over him to scare him away and some of it went into his mouth. From the water he gained wisdom.'"
Portuguese short form of Isabel, Rebeca, Bernardo, and other names with the "be" sound. It can also come from the word "bebé" (baby).
Means "pick-axe" in Old English. The surname Beckham derives from this name.
Transferred from the surname Bechet.A famous bearer is Bechet Dumain Allen, adopted daughter of Woody Allen, whose name was chosen to honouring jazz musician Sidney Bechet.
Variant transcription of Bechir based on French orthography.
Bechorath, son of Aphiah, of the tribe of Benjamin, was an ancestor of King Saul and of his commander Abner. According to Saul, his family was the least of the tribe of Benjamin. (1 Samuel 9)
Variant of Beckham. Beckem was given to 15 boys in 2017 per the SSA.
Transferred use of the surname Becker.
From a surname which was a variant of the surname Beckett. In some cases it might be given in honour of the English saint Thomas Becket (1118-1170).
First name of poetess Beckian Fritz Goldberg. Possibly a combination of Becki and Ann.
Referring to Ephesians 4:32, "And be ye courteous to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you."

Means "troubled lady", from Old Irish bé "woman" and a second element, perhaps chuma, meaning "grief, sorrow, wound". In Irish legend she was a woman who 'dwelt in the Land of Promise and had an affair with Gaiar, a son of Manannán mac Lir, the sea-god. Because of this she was banished to the human world where she persuaded Conn of the Hundred Battles, the High King, to take her as his wife or concubine. She grew jealous of his son Art and tried to get him banished' (Peter Berresford Ellis, 1987).
Form of Bede in various languages. Beda is a feminine name in Sweden and Finland.

One manuscript of the Prose Tristan, in departure from the others, describes Tristan’s death at the hands of a lord named Bedalis.Tristan had helped his brother-in-law, Kahedins or Ruvalen, arrange a tryst with Gargeloain, Bedalis’s wife. To avenge this disgrace, Bedalis tracked Tristan down and mortally wounded him with a poisoned lance. Afterwards, Bedalis became a pirate. He was eventually captured and executed.The romance of Palamedes alludes to the same episode. His counterpart in Eilhart von Oberge’s Tristrant is Nampetenis.
Diminutive of Obedience used in the 18th century.
From the Kurdish bedew meaning "beautiful" or bedewî meaning "beauty".
From Kurdish bedew meaning "handsome, beautiful, pretty" and can meaning "soul".
Transferred use of the surname Bedford.
Means "came to engage in wars" in Akan.
Borne by two princes from La Palma.
An Arthurian knight in Les Merveilles de Rigomer.
Lord of the Fres Marés in Ireland.He hosted Lancelot during his journey to Rigomer Castle.

Derived from Old Turkic bediz meaning "adornment, decoration, ornament" or "artistic design". In the Orkhon inscriptions and early Central Asian contexts, the term referred specifically to "statuary, carvings, or paintings."While often associated with balbal (memorial statues for fallen enemies), a bediz refers more broadly to the artistic craftsmanship of the monument itself or the "image" of the deceased. The name embodies the concept of "the one who is decorated" or "the one who creates beauty." It is related to the Old Turkic verb bediz-me-/ meaning "to decorate" or "to paint."For the parents, Bediz is a prayer for a child who carries the ancestral elegance. To carry this name is to be a bridge between the ancient craftsmanship of the past and the creative potential of the future. It is a legacy of a life well-lived; a life that is not merely seen, but is crafted with such intentionality that it becomes a monument of peace and inspiration for the entire tribe.As the master carves the silent stone to make it speak, may your life be the "Bediz" that tells a story of grace, and may your soul be the "adornment" that the world has long awaited.
Older spelling of Bejo influenced by Dutch orthography.
Turkish and Albanian form of Badri.
From Arabic بدر (badr) meaning "full moon" and فلك (falak) meaning "sky, firmament".
Possibly from the Arabic بدر (badr) meaning "full moon" and Persian ماه (mah) meaning "moon".
Meaning unknown. Bedukhæ is a character in the Nart epics and a beautiful Nart woman who falls in love with Sosruko.

The name BEDUNA is from plateau state Nigeria which means "is it bad?" It's a question name, when someone utter a word that is not good and didn't come to pass then you can ask him BEDUNA "is it bad?"
Means "will bring of happiness", from the elements będzie ("will") and ciech ("happiness").

The first element of this name is derived from Polish będzie "will be"; it is the third-person singular future tense of the verb być "to be". The second element is derived from Slavic mir "peace". As such, one could say that this name is a later (or more elaborate) form of Bytomir.
Probably from Hindi बीबी (bībī) or Urdu بی بی (bī bī) meaning "woman, lady (by Muslims)", ultimately from Classical Persian بی‌بی (bī-bī). This name is used by Mauritian Muslims.
Transferred use of the surname Beecher.
Transferred use of the surname Beechum.

Possibly a variant of Bede.Used by author J. K. Rowling in her Harry Potter series as the name of Beedle the Bard, writer of such tales as The Wizard and the Hopping Pot, Babbitty Rabbitty and Her Cackling Stump, and The Tale of the Three Brothers.
Phonetic spelling of the initials BJ.
A Low German form of Rebecca.
Transferred use of the surname Beeker.
Founder of Gushegu and Karaga. Name of one of the sons of Naa Gbewaa.
Diminutive of names ending in -bina, especially Robina.

Short form of names that contain the Germanic element bern meaning "bear", such as Berend and its rare variant Beerend.In modern Dutch, beer is also the word for "bear" (same etymological source). Recent bearers of the name (i.e. those born after 2000) are more likely to derive their name directly from the word, as a lot of modern parents are fond of so-called 'nature names'.
Variant of Bernaert, which appears to have been purely Flemish.
Feminine form of Beer. In Dutch, beertje also means "bearlet, little bear".A known bearer of this name is the Dutch television presenter Beertje van Beers (b. 1972).
Meaning "unique" and/or "one of a kind". The characters "بی" (bee) meaning "without" and "تا" (taa) meaning "alike/likeness/similar being".Commonly used in Persian culture and literature.
Transferred use of the surname Beethoven.
In the case of the character from Beverly Cleary's 'Ramona' book series, it originated as a nursery form of Beatrice (her real name), given to her by her younger sister.

Referring to Revelation 2:10, "Fear none of those things which thou shalt suffer: behold, the devil shall cast some of you into prison, that ye may be tried; and ye shall have tribulation ten days: be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life."

This name belongs to a witch from the Italian Folklore. It is said that Befana is an elderly woman in a flying broom, very similar to a witch. She visits children during the night from 5 to 6 of January, the Epiphany night. Befana gives candy, fruits or small toys to kids who behave well, and pieces of coal to bad-behaving kids. Popular beliefs say the name comes from the Epiphany, however, evidences suggest that Befana has roots in the pagan goddess Strenia.
From the Kurdish befr meaning "snow" and aw, av meaning "water".
Georgian variant of Begi. In Ossetian, most likely the name is also derived from the Ottoman Turkish title بك (beg) meaning "ruler, chief, lord".
Derived from the Uzbek beg'am meaning "carefree" and gul meaning "flower, rose".
Derived from Albanian begator "wealthy, prosperous; fertile, fruitful, abundant".
From begenç meaning "joy, happiness" and the given name Muhammet.

French form of Begga. Saint Begge (615 – 17 December 693) was the grandmother of Charles Martel, who is the grandfather of Charlemagne. She had seven churches built at Andenne on the Meuse, Belgium, where she spent the rest of her days as abbess.

Derived from the Georgian noun ბეგი (begi) meaning "bey", which is ultimately derived from the Turkish military title beg meaning "chieftain, master".This name can also be a short form of Beglar, in which case the meaning and origin remain the same.
Latinized form of Old English Béaghild.
Derived from begum, the feminine form of the Turkish military title beg meaning "chieftain, master", combined with Kyrgyz ай (ay) meaning "moon".
Derived from the Ottoman Turkish plural form of the Turkish military title beg meaning "chieftain, master".A notable bearer of this name was the Georgian poet Beglar Akhospireli (1880-1921).
Means "of the beg", from the Turkic military title beg meaning "chieftain, master".
From the name of a flowering plant, which was named for the French botanist Michel Bégon. In some cases it may be a variant of the Spanish Begoña.

A regal name derived from the Old Turkic title Beg (meaning "ruler," "lord," "noble," or "leader") and the honorific suffix oyim (denoting a lady of high status, mistress, or royalty). It translates to "The Noble Lady" or "The Lady Leader." This name is an exquisite tribute to inherent dignity, leadership potential, and aristocratic poise. It paints a picture of a person who carries herself with natural grace, commanding respect not through force, but through a calm, unshakable nobility of character that reflects her noble lineage and dignified soul.

Derived from the Ottoman Turkish gubernatorial title بكلربكی‎ (beglerbegi) meaning "bey of the beys" or "head of the beys". In turn, it is derived from the Turkish military title beg meaning "chieftain, master".The given name Begtabeg is best known for being the name of the eponymous ancestor of the Georgian noble family of Begtabegishvili, who lived in the 17th century. He was a capable scribe and calligrapher, whose best known work is his manuscript of the medieval Georgian epic The Knight in the Panther's Skin.

Begtse "Begtse the Great Coat of Mail" is the lord of war in Tibetan Buddhism, originally a pre-Buddhist war god of the Mongols, the name Begtse (Wylie: Beg tse) is a loanword from Mongolian begder, meaning "coat of mail". He is also given the name and epithet Jamsaran (Wylie: lCam sring), meaning "Great Coat of Mail", which is a translation of the Mongolian.
The name of a sister of Ibaqa Beki and Sorghaghtani Beki.
Name of a 7th century nun and saint from Hackness, Yorkshire.
Begum is a female title, denoting a daughter or wife of a Beg, title of Turko-Mongol origin meaning ''Chief'' or ''Commander''.
From Punjabi feminine singular vocative case inflection of the name Begum.
Derived from Persian به (beh) meaning "good" and آفرید (âfarid) meaning "creature".
Irish origin that derives from "bee" but means "child."
Possibly an Afrikaans variant of Beata. It is the name of Namibian fashion model Behati Prinsloo (b. 1989).
From Persian بهبود (behbūd) meaning "improvement, recovery; health, well-being".
Turkish form of Arabic بَهْجَة (bahja) meaning "joy, happiness"
Name of the king,cacique of the kingdom of Xaragua in Hispaniola. He was the older brother of Anacaona.
Derived from the Persian noun بهشت (behesht) meaning "paradise, heaven". A known bearer of this name is the Afghan news anchor Beheshta Arghand.
Translates to "joyful", it's Arabic sister name, Bahjat translates to "happiness".
Means "having good ancestry" from Persian به (beh) meaning "good" and نیا (niyā) meaning "ancestor".
Alternate transcription of Persian بهنیا (see Behnia).
Alternate transcription of Persian بهنوش (see Behnoush).
From Persian به (beh) meaning "good" and راد (rād) meaning "generous, bounteous, honest, upright".
From Persian به (beh) meaning "good" and رنگ (rang) meaning "colour".
Contracted form of Bernhard, first recorded in the 1500s and still in occasional use today.
Variant of Behrend, recorded between the 1500s and 1800s.
From Persian به (beh) meaning "good, excellent" and رخ (rokh) meaning "face, cheek".
Urdu form of Behrouz, as well as an alternate transcription of the Persian name.
Turkish form and Persian variant of Behzad
Means "good companion" from Persian به (beh) meaning "good" and تاش (tāsh) meaning "companion, partner, fellow".

Behula is a protagonist in the Manasamangal genre of Assamese and Bengali medieval epics. A number of works belonging to this genre were written between the thirteenth and eighteenth centuries. Though the religious purpose of these works is to eulogise the Hindu goddess Manasa, these works are more well known for depicting the love story of Behula and her husband Lakhindar (or Lakshindar or Lakshmindara).
Means "great friend" in Persian. From beh meaning "good" and yar meaning "friend".
From the given name Behzod and the word bek, a military title.
Combination of the name Behzod with the Persian word جان (jân) meaning "soul, life".

column3: 蓓蓓, 贝贝, etc.(Chinese)|貝貝, etc.(Traditional Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 蓓 (bèi) meaning "bud, flowerbud" or 贝 (bèi) meaning "shellfish, cowrie" combined with themselves. Other hanzi combinations can form this name as well.
Means "peaceful, peace" in Kazakh, though it can also be a combination of the Turkish military title beg meaning "chieftain, master" and Persian پولاد (pulâd) meaning "steel".
From the Chinese 蓓 (bèi) meaning "bud" and 昶 (chǎng) meaning "long day, bright, extended, clear".
Derived from Arabic al baid, meaning "the (ostrich) egg". This is the traditional name of the star Omicron 1 Eridani in the constellation Eridanus.
From the Chinese 蓓 (bèi) meaning "bud" and 德 (dé) meaning "heart, mind, morals, ethics, virtue".
From Chinese 北斗 (běidǒu) meaning "Big Dipper (constellation)". Other hanzi combinations can form this name as well.
From the Chinese 蓓 (bèi) meaning "bud" and 铎 (duó) meaning "bell".
Short form of masculine Germanic names that contain the Germanic element baug meaning "bow" as well as "bend, crook".
From 貝 (bèi) meaning "money, currency" and 兒 (ér) meaning "child".
Taken directly from the color beige.
Variant of Benjamim derived from colloquial pronunciation.
Yiddish and Judeo-French equivalent of Bella.
From the Chinese 贝 (bèi) meaning "seashell" or "money" and 灵 (líng) meaning "spirit, soul".
French-Yiddish form of Baila and/or Beila.
From the Chinese 蓓 (bèi) meaning "bud" and 霓 (ní) meaning "rainbow".
From the Chinese 蓓 (bèi) meaning "bud" and 袅 (niǎo) meaning "slender and delicate; curling upwards".
From Old Norse beinir meaning "help, benefit", ultimately from beinn meaning "straight, right" or "hospitable". In modern Icelandic, beinir means "router", derived from the same root.
Old Swedish short form of Benedikt.

Faroese feminine form of Benedict (originally a short form of Benadikta and Bænadikta, now regarded as an independent name). It was borne by Beinta Broberg (1667-1752), whom Faroese writer Jørgen-Frantz Jacobsen allegedly used as the basis for the heroine of his novel Barbara (1939).
From the Chinese 贝 (bèi) meaning "seashell" or "money" and 诺 (nuò) meaning "promise, approve".
From the Chinese 蓓 (bèi) meaning "bud" and 嫱 (qiáng) meaning "lady".

Anglicized form of Bheur or Bhuer perhaps meaning "cutting, sharp, shrill" in Scottish Gaelic, from Cailleach Bheur "sharp old wife", the name of the Scottish personification of winter, a reference to wintry winds. Alternatively her name could mean "old woman of Beara" from an Irish place name which according to legend derives from the personal name of Princess Beara of Castille, wife of King Eoghan Mór of Munster.
From the Chinese 北 (běi) meaning "north" and 蓉 (róng) meaning "hibiscus".
From Old Norse beita meaning "to pasture cattle", "to use a weapon", "to harness to a vehicle", "to steer or sail near the wind, to cruise".

column3: 北彤, 北统, 北同, 北仝, 北通(Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 北 (běi) meaning "north" combined with 彤 (tóng) meaning "red, vermillion", 统 (tǒng) meaning "command, control, unite, unify", 同 or 仝 (tóng) both meaning "same, identical, together", or 通 (tōng) meaning "pass, travel, go through". Other character combinations can form this name as well.
West Frisian diminutive of Elisabeth as well as the feminine form of Beitse.A notable bearer of this name is the Dutch racing driver Beitske Visser (b. 1995).

column3: 蓓文, 贝文, 蓓雯, 贝雯, etc.(Chinese)|貝文, 蓓雯, 貝雯, etc.(Traditional Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 蓓 (bèi) meaning "bud, flowerbud" or 贝 (bèi) meaning "shellfish, cowrie" combined with 文 (wén) meaning "literature, culture, writing" or 雯 (wén) meaning "cloud patterns". Other hanzi combinations are possible.
From the Chinese 贝 (bèi) meaning "seashell" or "money" and 曦 (xī) meaning "sunlight, sunshine, early dawn".
From the Chinese 贝 (bèi) meaning "seashell" or "money" and 雪 (xuě) meaning "snow".
From the Chinese 蓓 (bèi) meaning "bud" and 琰 (yǎn) meaning "jewel, gem, glitter of gems".
From the Chinese 蓓 (bèi) meaning "bud" and 瑶 (yáo) meaning "precious jade".
From the Chinese 蓓 (bèi) meaning "bud" and 艺 (yì) meaning "art, talent, ability".
From the Chinese 贝 (bèi) meaning "seashell" or "money" and 瑜 (yú) meaning "fine jade, virtues".
From Chinese 北 (běi) meaning "north" or 倍 (bèi) meaning "multiple times" combined with 源 (yuán) meaning "source, origin". Other hanzi combinations are possible.
Possibly from the Uzbek bejama meaning "decoration, ornament".
From the Uzbek bejama meaning "decoration" and oy meaning "moon".
It is also a Turkish name. Influenced by Ottoman Turkish culture. Shortened, it's spelled Beja, which is a type of flower.
Means "(one that) come(s) with rain" in Yoruba.
Derived from Albanian bejkush "white-haired (said of sheep); white ram".
From Javanese beja meaning "lucky, fortunate", ultimately from Sanskrit भाग्य (bhāgya).
Famously borne by American music artist Beck David Hansen (mononymously known as simply "Beck"), who was born as Bek Campbell.
Modern form of Bega, which is an old variant of Begi. Out of all the names that are descended from the latter name and still in use, Beka is the most common.
From the historical title of a wife or daughter of a bek.
Diminutive of Rebekah. A famous bearer is the American singer Bekah Liechty (2000- )
Alternate transcription of Kazakh Бекарыс (see Bekarys).

Derived from the Turkish military title beg meaning "chieftain, master" combined with Kazakh арыс (arys) meaning "foundation, support, framework" (also used as a territorial unit in the Kazakh Khanate).
From the Turkish military title beg meaning "chieftain, master" combined with Kazakh болат (bolat) meaning "steel" (of Persian origin).
From the Turkic military title beg meaning "chieftain, master" combined with Kyrgyz болот (bolot) meaning "steel".
Directly taken from Hungarian béke "peace; serenity, tranquility".
Means "America" or "American" in Khana and "English" in Ijaw.

From Egyptian bꜣkt-jtn meaning "handmaid of Aten", derived from bꜣkt meaning "female servant, handmaid" combined with the name of the god Aten. This name was borne by a 14th-century BC Egyptian princess, usually regarded as a daughter of either Amenhotep III or his son Akhenaten.
From Mongolian бэх (bekh) meaning either "ink" or "firmness" and баяр (bayar) meaning "joy, celebration".
Possibly derived from Mongolian бэх (bekh) meaning "ink" or "firm".
Tajik and Uzbek form of Behrouz.
Variant of Bakhta. Bekhta Rabah-Mazari is a well-known bearer.
From the Turkish military title beg meaning "chieftain, master" and Kazakh and Kyrgyz жан (jan) meaning "soul".
From the Turkish military title beg meaning "chieftain, master" combined with the Turkic title khan meaning "ruler, leader".
Derived from the Germanic name elements bekkr "bench" and hildr "battle, fight".
From the Turkic military title beg meaning "chieftain, master" combined with the given name Murat.
From the Turkic military title beg meaning "chieftan, master" and the given name Myrza.
From the Turkic military title beg meaning "chieftain, master" and Arabic نور (nūr) meaning "light".
Means "war time" in Akan, typically used for a child born in war.
Derived from the Turkish military title beg meaning "chieftain, master" combined with the Arabic title سُلْطَان (sulṭān) meaning "sultan, king, ruler".
From the Turkic title beg meaning "chieftain, master" and Kazakh тас (tas) meaning "stone".
Means "sturdy stone" from Turkish pek meaning "hard, firm, solid" and taş meaning "stone, rock". Alternately it may be from Old Turkish beŋdeş meaning "equal, peer".
From the Turkic military title beg meaning "chieftain, master" combined with Kyrgyz темир (temir) meaning "iron".
From Javanese bêkti meaning "devotion, veneration, respect", ultimately from Sanskrit भक्ति (bhakti).
From beg meaning "chieftan, master" combined with tosh meaning "stone, rock".
It is used by the people of the switzerlan of uganda.Kabaale
Variant of Becky mostly influenced by the name Rebekah.

Means "to swallow" in Hebrew. This is the name of several characters in the Bible. One of them, Bela ben Beor (Bela, son of Beor) was the first king of Edom.Bela is also mentioned as another name for the city Zoar in Genesis 14:2.
The mother of Feirefiz, Parsifal's half-brother, in Wolfram von Eschenbach's 'Parsifal'.

Possibly from a contraction of Bevilacqua, an Italian surname that was originally a nickname derived from the expression bevi l'acqua meaning "drinks water", probably applied ironically to a heavy drinker of alcohol. In Dante's 'Purgatorio', Belacqua was a Florentine lute-maker famed for his laziness, representing those who wait until the last opportunity before turning to God. Samuel Beckett used the name for his character Belacqua Shuah. It was also used as a surname by author Philip Pullman for the heroine of his fantasy trilogy 'His Dark Materials': Lyra Belacqua.
Means "rhetoric, eloquence" in Ottoman Turkish, ultimately from Arabic بلاغة (balāgha).
Alternate transcription of Arabic بلال (see Bilal), as well as the Bengali form.
A duke in Arthur’s service who married the Duchess of the Dark Mountain. He appears in Daniel von dem blühenden Tal, Der Stricker, 1210-1225.
Feminine form of Béla for a married woman from the given name of her husband.
Combination of Belle and Anna.B’Elanna Torres is a main character in “Star Trek: Voyager”, an American science fiction television series. She is portrayed as half-human and half-Klingon.

Spanish, Galician and Portuguese form of Bellarmino, the original Italian surname of Saint Roberto Bellarmine (1542-1621), a cardinal who is regarded as a Doctor of the Church. His surname meant "well-armed" from Italian.
Of uncertain origin and meaning. One current theory condsiders this name a diminutive of Beila.

Derived from Old French bele, the feminine form of the adjective biau, bel "graceful, elegant, courteous; noble; handsome; beautiful" and Old French assez "enough; sufficiently" (which in the context of this name would have been understood as "very").

Often translated as "fair shining one" or "fair slayer", derived in part from Celtic *bel(l)- "strong, powerful" or *belo- "bright" (cf. Belenus). This was the name of a Celtic deity often identified with Mars, sometimes referred to as Mars Belatucadrus.
A princess and wife of Lohengrin. She died of grief when Lohengrin was murdered by men sent by her parents.

It is an Amharic expression, which means "the new child is above all others". From the Amharic elements በላይ (belay) meaning "above" and ነህ (Neh) means "you".It also means "You Are On Top, you are up there" in Amharic.
Means "Bel, keep him alive", deriving from the Akkadian element balāṭu ("to revive ; to keep alive, healthy").

Possibly an elaboration of Belkis using the popular Caribbean Spanish name suffix lis (from Elizabeth or a related name). This is the real name of American rapper, songwriter and television personality Cardi B (1992-), who was born Belcalis Marlenis Almánzar to Caribbean immigrants - a Dominican father and a Trinidadian mother.
A character appearing in "Meraugis de Portlesguez" by Raoul de Houdenc, early 13th century.
Combination of Italian bel "beautiful" and colore "colour". The Italian novelist Boccaccio used this name in his work 'The Decameron' (1350).
German short form of Gabriele 2 and other names.A notable namesake is the German artist Bele Bachem.
Two characters mentioned in JRR Tolkien's works. The name possibly means "mighty eagle" in the fictional Sindarin language, from the elements beleg meaning "mighty" and thôr meaning "eagle".

Beleg, also known as Beleg Cúthalion or Beleg Strongbow for his good bowmanship, was a Sindarin Elf who served in the army of King Elu Thingol of Doriath as the chief of the Marchwardens - and was a predominant companion of Túrin Turambar.
Means "gift" in Tuvan and Kyrgyz. It is unisex among the Tuvans and solely masculine in Kyrgyzstan.
Derived from the old Slavic word белъ "white".
Means "love" in the Kalabari dialect. From the name Tamunobelema meaning "God's love".
Means mountainside, mountainous place in Turkish
Latinized feminine form of Belenus. Belena was the wife of the Gaulish solar god Belenus and the goddess of the sun and the beginning summer.
Originated from a Turkish name meaning: High in rank, or tall in general
Means "say it out loud" or "do it right" in Amharic.
Spanish, Portuguese, and Galician form of Bellerophon.
Means "lady", deriving from the Akkadian element bēltu ("lady, mistress").

Means "lady of Babylon", deriving from the Akkadian element belet (mistress, lady). This was a Babylonian name for the goddess Ishtar. Ishtar was worshipped under this name in the temple of Eturkalamma.
Means "mistress of life", deriving from the Akkadian elements bēlet ("mistress or lady") and balāṭu ("life, vigour, good health"). This was possibly an Akkadian name for the goddess Nungal.
Transferred use of the surname Belete.
An Akkadian name for the goddess Inanna, specifically in her capacity as Inanna of Uruk. Likely derives in part from the Akkadian belet ("mistress or lady").
Means "Mistress of the Palace", from Akkadian element belet ("mistress or lady"). This was the Akkadian name for the Sumerian goddess Ninegal.

Meaning unknown. This is the name of a demon who appears in several works on demonology, including the 17th-century grimoire The Lesser Key of Solomon (author unknown), the Pseudomonarchia Daemonum (1563) by Dutch physician Johann Weyer and the Dictionnaire Infernal (1818) by French occultist Jacques Collin de Plancy.
Means "lady of the gods" or "mother of the gods" in Akkadian, deriving from the elements beltu ("lady, mistress") and ilu ("god, deity"). It is another name for the mother goddess Ninhursag.

Means "Mistress of Nagar" (an ancient city in Syria), from the Akkadian element belet (meaning "mistress or lady"). Belet-Nagar was a tutelary goddess associated with kingship. She was possibly an Akkadian equivalent to the Hittite goddess Nabarbi.
Means "Lady of Nineveh", deriving from Akkadian elements belet ("lady") and ninua (likely an Akkadian form of Nineveh).

Means "mistress of the steppe". The name borne by an underworld goddess in the court of Ereshkigal who was tasked with recording information about the dead entering the afterlife. The first part of her name comes from beltu meaning "lady, mistress" and the second part derives from the Akkadian word ṣēru, meaning "steppe". This word was a euphemism for the underworld. She later became associated with the medicine goddess Gula. She remained popular into the Hellenistic period of Uruk.
Means "I trusted in the Lady of Uruk", deriving from the Akkadian element belet ("mistress, lady").

Derived from Italian bel fante meaning "fair child", which consists of the Italian adjective bello meaning "fair, beautiful" and the Italian noun fante, a medieval variant of the (now dated and rare) Italian noun infante meaning "infant, child". Using the latter word for the same overall meaning would result into bell'infante and there are variant forms of Belfante that reflect this.
Diminutive of Belfante, as -ino is an Italian masculine diminutive suffix.
Belgarath is used in David Edding's book series, the Belgariad. He is the old sorcerer that helps Garion.
Derived from the geographical name Belgium.
Name given in honor of the Argentine General Manuel Belgrano, one of the founding fathers of that country.
Transferred use of the surname Belhassen.
Derived from Latin bella "beautiful, charming, pleasant" and honor "honor".
Derived from Old Norse belja meaning "to roar". This is the name of a jotunn in Norse mythology.
Variant of Bela, Bella and Beila.
Hungarian name derived from Slavic бѣлъ (belu) "white".
Could be a combination of Bella and Ana.
Daughter of the King of Norgales (North Wales), the mother of Galihodin.Galihodin was the nephew (or natural son) of Galeholt.

Belianís of Greece is the hero of a Spanish chivalric romance novel, "The honour of chivalry", following in the footsteps of the influential Amadis de Gaula. An English abridgement of this novel was published in 1673. It is best known today because it was one of the books spared during the expurgation of Don Quixote's library in Chapter 6 of Part I of Don Quixote.
One of four miscreant brother knights killed by Gawaine in "Diu Crône" by Heinrich von dem Türlin, c. 1230
The name of a Guanche mencey (leader) from Tenerife.

A character in Arthurian legend who fell in love with Tristan while he was living and serving in Faramon’s court. When Tristan did not reciprocate, she became enraged and staged a rape scene for which Tristan was convicted and sentenced to execution.
From the Old English word geleafa, meaning "faith or trust."
Late Old English belȳfan, belēfan, alteration of gelēfan, of Germanic origin; related to Dutch geloven and German glauben, also to lief.
From the English word believer, likely referring to a believer of Christ.
The first element of this name is derived from Proto-Slavic bělъ "white, pale". Also see Běla, which is of the same etymology. The second element is derived from Slavic mir "peace".
Medieval French diminutive form of Isabel.

Gascon diminutive of Isabèl. Belina (known as Béline in French, died 1153) was a Roman Catholic virgin martyr who was canonized by Pope Innocent III in 1203. Due to the saint, this name also saw some usage in Italy. However, in Italy it is also occasionally considered a feminine form of Belenus, hiding behind a Christian guise.
Gallicized form of Belina. It was used by Molière in his play 'The Imaginary Invalid' (1673) ('Le Malade imaginaire' in French), where it belongs to the wife of Argan.

Belisama was a goddess worshipped in ancient Gaul and Britain, associated with lakes and rivers, fire, crafts and light, who was identified with Minerva in the interpretatio romana. Her name is of debated origin and meaning: theories include a derivation from Gaulish bel "strong" and the superlative suffix -isama and a derivation from the root bel "bright" and the superlative suffix -isama ( based on this she has also been speculatively claimed as companion of Belenus, whose name seems to contain the same root).
Spanish and Italian form of Belisarius.
Gallicized form of Belisa. This name was used on one of the characters in Molière's play Les Femmes savantes (1672).
English and Brazilian Portuguese adoption of Bélise.

From an Old French form of Belissendis. It is borne by a legendary daughter of Emperor Charlemagne in the poems Ami et Amile (c.1200) and Otinel or Otuel a Knight (c.1330). In the late 13th-century Arthurian tale Arthour and Merlin, Belisent is King Arthur's half-sister, the wife of Lot and mother of Gareth. Alfred Lord Tennyson also used the spelling Belicent in his Arthurian epic Idylls of the King (1859).
From old Slavic bělъ meaning "white", possibly also idiomatically "good", and slava meaning "glory".

Belisama (often spelled Belisma) is a Gaulish and British Celtic goddess of light; she is the embodiment of illumination and heat, linking the powers of the sun and moon. Her name translates to "the brightest one" or "the most powerful".The Romans equated her with Minerva due to shared domains like wisdom and craftsmanship. Like her Roman equivalent, she is a patroness of smiths, artisans, and craftsmanship.She was historically tied to specific bodies of water, most notably the River Ribble (known by the Romans as the Belisama) in northwestern England, and possibly the Mersey.
A dithematic name formed from the name elements bili "soft, tender, smooth, peaceful" and swinth "strong". The first name element may also refer to Bil, the girl in the moon in Nordic mythology.
Medieval Basque name of uncertain origin and meaning. It was first recorded in Artaxoa (in the Navarre area) in 1330.
Transferred use of the name of the country of Belize.
Diminutive of Beila and its variants.
Alternate transcription of Abu al-Qasim chiefly used in Northern Africa.
Turkish form of Bilqis.Bearers of this name include folk singer Belkıs Akkale (1956-) and judoka Belkıs Zehra Kaya (1984-).
Spanish borrowing of Bilqis. Bearers of this name include the late Cuban artist Belkis Ayón (1967-1999) and Cuban-American writer Belkis Cuza Malé (1942-).
Variant of Belkıs. Belkız Özener (1940-) is a Turkish singer.
Variant of Bela, as well as a Judeo-Spanish form.
Derived from Latin bella meaning "beautiful, charming, pleasant" and Latin bona "good, kind, right, pleasant; valid, useful, healthy".For the same elements in the reversed order, see Bonabella.
From Latin bella "beautiful" and cara "dear, beloved". See also Carabella, which is composed of the same elements in reverse order.
From Italian "bella" and "dama", meaning beautiful lady. Used in Sicily as a variant of Belladonna.
Combination of the names Bella and Dora.
Derived from Latin bella "beautiful, charming, pleasant" and a derivative of Latin flos "flower".
Combination of Bella and Maria, possibly inspired by the Virgin Mary (Bella Maria meaning "beautiful Mary").
A combination of Bella and May

Probably derived from the Latin elements bella "beautiful" and mira "wondrous" (cf. Mirabella). This name belongs to a courtesan in the play The Jew of Malta (written c. 1589 or 1590) by English dramatist Christopher Marlowe.
Bellamour is the lord of a castle and Pastorella's true father. He appears in Book 6, Canto 12. of "The Faerie Queene".

Alteration of Berengar, possibly influenced by French bel, beau meaning "fine, beautiful, great" and anger "anger" (thus "righteous anger"). This was the name of a Knight of the Round Table in Thomas Malory's 15th-century compilation of Arthurian legends 'Le Morte d'Arthur', in which Bellangere avenges the deaths of his father and grandfather by killing King Mark of Cornwall.

Perhaps derived from Latin bellare meaning "to fight". This name was used by Robert Greene for a character in his prose romance 'Pandosto: The Triumph of Time' (1588). It was also used by Henry Fielding in his play 'The Temple Beau' (1730), and by Aaron Hill (1685-1750) in his poem 'Bellaria, at her Spinnet'.
Taken from the surname Bellarmino. Bellarmino Bagatti was a 20th-century Italian archaeologist and Catholic priest of the Franciscan Order.
From Latin bella meaning "beautiful" and vita meaning "life".
Variant of Verdandi, representing an Anglicization of the name's Japanese transcription. This is the name of a major character in the manga series "Oh My Goddess!"
Italian form of Bellerophon. This was the name of an Italian composer Bellerofonte Castaldi (1580-1649).
French form of Bellerophon. It's also the name of a play.
Variant of Belly, which is a diminutive of Isabella, Isabelle, and other names containing a similar sound.
Nickname for names containing Bel- such as Isabella, Belinda, and Belle

From an Old French form of the Germanic name Belissendis, possibly composed of the elements bili "suitable, proper, fitting, decent, amiable" (cf. Biligard) and swind "strong, brave, powerful".The form Belisent belongs to a legendary daughter of Charlemagne in the poems 'Ami et Amile' (c.1200) and 'Otinel' or 'Otuel a Knight' (c.1330). In the late 13th-century Arthurian tale 'Arthour and Merlin', Belisent is Arthur's half-sister, the wife of Lot and mother of Gareth; Alfred Lord Tennyson also used the form Belicent in his Arthurian epic 'Gareth and Lynette'.
Feminine form of Bellicius. Bellicia was one of the Vestal Virgins.
Possibly a Latinized form of Belshom.
Form of Bædling found in the Phillimore translation of Domesday Book.
Transferred use of the surname Bellingham.
It can also be inspired by the Latin word bellis "daisy".
From Latin bellissima meaning "most beautiful, charming, pleasant".
From Latin bellissimus meaning "most beautiful, charming, pleasant".
Short form of Jacobello or other names ending in bello. It is also associated with the Italian word meaning "beautiful, handsome".
Derived from French belle meaning "beautiful". This is the name of Laidronette's sister in Madame d'Aulnoy's fairy tale The Green Serpent.
Gaulish name meaning “worthy of power”, name of a legendary Gallic chief.
Short form of Isabelluccia, which is a diminutive of Isabella.

From the Latin bellule (pretty, nice, well-formed), this is found in a Jewish catacomb in Rome as the name of a woman. It is possibly the precursor to such names as the Sephardic Bela and the Yiddish Shayna

Most likely a version of Elmira 1, which derives from Edelmira, stemming from Adelmar, which combines the Germanic elements adal meaning "noble" and mari meaning "famous". It is also often interpreted as meaning "beautiful sight" from Portuguese bela meaning "beautiful" and mira meaning "sight". This name was particularly popular in Portugal in the early 1900s.
Means "beautiful world", from Italian bel "beautiful, pleasant" and mondo "world". It is used as a surname in Italy.

Beloc is a classical rendering of the Semitic words bēlu and ba'al, which both mean "lord". It can be used as a theonym, personal name, or royal title. Beloc has multiple meanings, including:   A loud cry, especially to convey a command or emotion A round of drinks, especially in Britain, Australia, and New Zealand  A greeting sent to a radio station to be broadcast, especially to family or friends  An emergency service call: An occasion when the members of an emergency service are called out to duty  To yell: To utter something in a loud cry or yell  To make a loud noise: To make a loud noise  A French author: A French author (1870-1953) known for his children's verse  A surname: A surname that may come from a southern dialectal form of the French place-name Beaulieu, which means "fine place"  A commune in France: A commune in the Ariège department of southwestern France
Lithuanian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Bellona.
Ancient Greek rendering of Ba'al, ultimately derived from Ancient Semitic bʿl meaning "lord, master".
Feminine form of Beloslav. Beloslava of Bulgaria was a Bulgarian princess and Queen consort of Serbia between 1234 and 1243. She was the wife of king Stefan Vladislav I.
Russian form of Snow White, from Russian белый (belyy) "white" and снег (sneg) "snow".

From Ba'al Pe'or, the name of a Semitic god mentioned in the Hebrew Bible, meaning "Ba'al of Mount Pe'or" or "lord of the opening". In Christian demonology this is the name of a demon that represents the deadly sin of sloth.

Means "lord of the poplar", deriving from the Akkadian elements bēlu ("boss, chief, master, lord") and ṣarbat (deriving from a place name, that presumably later became associated with groves of trees. There were two cities named Ṣarbat, one in the north near Babylon, and one in the south near the Sinjar mountains). Name borne by the patron god of the city of Baz, who was thought of as part of the entourage of the underworld god Nergal. The city of Baz was known as Šapazzu in Neo-Assyrian records.
Likely a variant of Balthazar, used in the TV show Charmed.
Transferred use of the surname Belton.
Breton and Piedmontese form of Bertrand.
Diminutive of Beltramo, the Tuscan form of Bertram.
Of uncertain origin and meaning. One current theory, however, connects this name to Basque beltxo, a diminutive of beltz / baltz "black".
Derived from the Basque adjective beltz "black; dark" in combination with the feminine name suffix -ne.
Diminutive of Sabela. Not used as a given name in its own right.
Galician diminutive of Sabela and Isabel.
Apparently a feminine form of Belvedere. A notable bearer of this name was Belva Lockwood (1830-1917), one of the first female lawyers in the United States.

From an Italian word meaning "beautiful sight", from Italian bel "beautiful" and vedere "a view, sight". It was apparently coined in the early 19th century, when it first appears as a given name in United States historical records (for both Northern and Southern states), along with its feminine variant Belva.The Apollo Belvedere is a famous marble statue from classical antiquity, in which case it refers to the Belvedere Gallery of the Vatican Museum in Rome, where the sculpture once stood. The Apollo Belvedere is allegedly responsible for inspiring American painters John Trumbull and Gilbert Stuart's portrayals of George Washington. This may be the inspiration behind its use in America.It was used by American cartoonist George Webster Crenshaw in his comic strip Belvedere, which ran from 1962 to 1995, where it belongs to a male hound dog.
Variant of Belva.The name could also be interpreted as "beautiful way" reading bel as "beautiful" and via as the Latin word for "way, road".
Derived from Italian belvedere meaning "a fair sight" (compare Belvedere). This was used by English dramatist Thomas Otway for a character in his tragedy Venice Preserv'd (1682).
Maybe derived from the surname Belville.The given name of the aviation pioneer Belvin Maynard.

Apparently from the Latin word meaning "beast-like" (also written beluina), derived from bēlua "beast, monster" (Italian belva) with the adjectival suffix‎ -īnus "of, like". The author J. K. Rowling used this name in her 'Harry Potter' books for a member of the Black family.

Meaning unknown. It might possibly be derived from Belzora, the name of a port town in Texas that was abandoned in the 1870s.
From the Xhosa ba- meaning "they" or be- meaning "they (being)" and manyiwe meaning "united", ultimately "they are united, they have come united".
From a non-Sino-Vietnamese reading of Chinese 邊 (bên) meaning "side, edge, face".

column3: 勉, 弁, 便(Japanese Kanji)|べん(Japanese Hiragana)|ベン(Japanese Katakana)|בן(Hebrew)
column12: This name is used as 勉 (ben, tsuto.meru) meaning "exertion," 弁/辨 (hen, ben, araso.u, hanabira, wakima.eru, wa.keru) meaning "dialect, petal, speech" or 便 (bin, ben, tayo.ri) meaning "convenience."In the Edo Period (1603-1868), particularly in the latter part, this name was (uncommonly) given to girls and though it was mainly written in hiragana at the time, it may be related to 弁/辨. This name continued to be used in the Meiji period (1868-1912), though by then, the name gradually shifted to being a masculine-majority name. Since the second half of the 20th century, it's rarely given to boys, if given at all.
Lithuanian short form of names beginning with Ben- such as Benedikta and Slovene diminutive of Benedikta and Benjamina.

Menas "son of Abinadab" or "son of a generous father", ultimately derived from Hebrew בן (ben) meaning "son", אב ('ab) meaning "father", and נדב (nadab) meaning "to willingly give". In the Bible, he was mentioned in 1 Kings 4:11.
Short form of Gubena or Abena. This was used by early slaves in the American South - attested in the 1730s in South Carolina. It was frequently misanalyzed as Venus.
Meaning unknown. It was borne by a Guanche man from La Palma who was christened in Seville.
German form of the Biblical name Benaiah.
Probably a dialectal (värmländsk) variant of Bernhard.

Means "son of my people" in Hebrew. This is the name of several people in the Bible.
