Coined by Sabino Arana Goiri and Koldo Elizalde as a feminine form of Beñat.
Borne by a Guanche girl who was christened in Seville, Spain.
Alternate transcription of Urdu بینظیر (see Benazir).
Means valve, speech, or petal.A notable character with this name is Benben Tsukumo from Touhou Project.

column3: เบญจกัลยาณี(Thai)
column12: Means "woman of fivefold beauty" in Thai, from เบญจ (bencha) meaning "five, fivefold" and กัลยาณี (kanlayani) meaning "beautiful girl, belle". In Buddhism this term refers to a woman with five favourable attributes: beautiful hair, beautiful teeth, beautiful flesh, beautiful skin and beauty at any age.
Alternate transcription of Thai เบญจมาศ (see Benchamat).

column3: เบญจพร, เบญจพล(Thai)
column12: From Thai เบญจ (bencha) meaning "five" and พร (phon) meaning "blessing" or พล (phon) meaning "strength, power". The name เบญจพร is feminine while เบญจพล is masculine.
Alternate transcription of Thai เบญจพล (see Benchaphon).
Alternate transcription of Thai เบญจพร (see Benchaphon).
From Thai เบญจ (bencha) meaning "five" and รัตน์ (rat) meaning "gem, jewel".
Means "five colours" from Thai เบญจ (bencha) meaning "five" and วรรณ (wan) meaning "colour".
Diminutive of Bencelina and Benceline (strictly feminine) as well as transferred use of the surname Bencie (unisex).
Contracted form of Benedict. This name was also used as a secular form of Baruch.
Derived from Guanche benčom meaning "ambitious" or benchomo meaning "the greatest". It belonged to the penultimate mencey (leader) (1423-1495) of Taoro, Tenerife.
Transferred use of the surname Bendall
Means "gift of Bendis", derived from the name of the Thracian goddess Bendis (genitive Βενδῖδος) combined with Greek δῶρον (doron) meaning "gift".

The giant son of Llyr and Penardun and brother Branwen and Manawydan Fab Llyr. Some sources, however, make Bendigeid Vran and Branwen the children of Llyr by Iweriadd, while Manawydan fab Llyr was the son of Llyr by Penardun.He is more commonly referred to as Brân the Blessed, and his story is told in the Mabinogion.
Archaic Norwegian variant of Benedikt, as well as a Swedish feminine form.
Contracted form of Benedikt as well as a modern Swedish feminine form.
Posibly from Benedictus meaning "blessed" or Eudemos meaning "well people".
Thracian goddess of the moon and the hunt.
Yiddish form of Benedikt. This was generally used as a secular form of Baruch. (See also Seligmann)
North Frisian and Low German form of Benedictus (see Benedict). Also compare Bendiks.A known bearer of this name was the German painter and sculptor Bendix Passig (1864-1957).
This means is from a Liberian dialect. It means beautiful...

In the case of Dr Bendor Grosvenor, art historian, the name Bendor is derived from the Grosvenor family's medieval heraldic shield, a bend or, a golden bend (diagonal stripe), which they used until 1389 when it was claimed instead by the Scrope family, in the case Scrope v Grosvenor. The 2nd Duke of Westminster was nicknamed Bendor.
Russian transcription of Benjamin, reflecting the English pronunciation.
Short form of names that contain the element bern- "bear".
Meaning unknown, possibly invnted from the English word "beneath" and the feminine suffix "a". Beneatha Younger is character in the play "A Raisin in the Sun" by Lorraine Hansberry.
English corruption of Abena. This was used by early slaves in the American south. Attested in the 1730's in South Carolina.
Used as a pseudonym by a Taiwanese-American author that she says is based on her Chinese name, from characters meaning "benevolent" + "bell".
Benecio means blessed and is from Mexico.

Aragonese and Lombard form of Benedict.

Corsican, Sicilian and Maltese form of Benedict.
From the English word benediction, meaning "A short invocation for help".
Greek form of Benedictus (see Benedict). A bearer of this name was Benediktos Adamantiades (1875-1962), a Greek ophthalmologist after whom a disease was named.
Indonesian and Bessarabian German form of Benedictus (see Benedict).
Gascon form of Benedict and Piedmontese variant of Benedèt.
Sicilian form of Benedetta as well as a Hungarian borrowing of this name.
Medieval Italian and Neapolitan form of Benedictus.
Maltese form of Benedict and variant of Benidittu.
Derived from Latin bene meaning "well; agreeably, favorably" combined with Old High German and Old Saxon ger meaning "spear".

The name of a late 15th-century Guanche king of Anaga on the island of Tenerife (present-day Canary Islands, Spain) according to the epic poem Antigüedades de las Islas Afortunadas de la Gran Canaria (1604) by Antonio de Viana. It is possible that the name is Guanche in origin, with philologist Ignacio Reyes García suggesting a derivation from Guanche *we-n-ăwəssar meaning "old", composed of *we-n "one of the" and *wəššər "to be old"; however, Viana may have invented it for use in his poem.
Feminine form of Beneitu. Beneita de Càlaris was the judge (which equals the title of queen in medieval Sardinia) of Càlaris from 1214 to 1233.
Diminutive of Bene, in use between the 1400s and 1700s.
Transferred use of the surname Benelli.
From Latin benemeritus, a combination of bene ("good") and meritus ("worthy"), meaning "good deserving".

A knight saved from the prison of Eskalibon of Belamunt (Eskilabon) by Arthur’s Sir Garel. In return, he served Garel in the war against King Ekunaver of Kanadic, and was eventually awarded a seat at the Round Table.
Benen was the name of the first Irish Bishop of Ireland, who was a follower of St. Patrick.His name is said to be derived from Latin Benignus.
From Egyptian bnr-jb meaning "sweet of heart", derived from bnr "sweet, pleasant" and jb "heart, mind, emotions". This was the name of a queen consort of the First Dynasty in ancient Egypt.
Cornish form of Benedict, derived from Latin benedictus "blessed".
Possibly an Anglicized form of Benicia which was influenced by Vanessa. It might also be a combination of Ben and Vanessa or similar names ending in -essa.
Guernésiais and Franco-Provençal form of Benedict.
Catalan, Languedocian and Provençal form of Benedict.
Variant of Benvenida, possibly via Benvenuta.
From the English word, ultimately from Latin bene volent "well wishing".
Judeo-Anglo-Norman form of Benedict. This name was also used as a translation of Baruch.
Derived from the Germanic name elements ben "wound" and geirr "spear".
Means "steadfast, diligent, forbearing" in Toba Batak.
Means "eternal,everlasting", derived from the Old Turkic beñgü or meñgü with the exact same meaning.
From the Chinese 本 (běn) meaning "root, origin" and 光 (guāng) meaning "light, brilliant".
Hebrew boy's name meaning "son of strengths"
Hebrew boy's name meaning "Son of Grace"
From the Chinese 本 (běn) meaning "root, origin" and 浩 (hào) meaning "great, vast, numerous, abundant".
Variant of Bernhardt. Used by many Norwegian and Swedish immigrants to the Upper Midwest of the United States during the 19th century.
Means "son of Hur". The patronymic of the main character in the 1880 novel, 'Ben-Hur: A Tale of the Christ' by Lew Wallace.

Georgian short form of Beniamin as well as a Kashubian diminutive of Benedikta, Beniamina and Bernatka and Polish diminutive of Bernadeta or Bernadetta.In Georgian, this name is strictly masculine, whereas in Kashubian and Polish it is strictly feminine.
Scottish Gaelic form of Benjamin used in the Bible.
Kashubian and Lombard feminine form of Beniamin and Sicilian feminine form of Beniaminu.
Diminutive of Benedikta. The name coincides with a place name in Slovenia.
The name of the main character in the German movie Schande (1999).

column12: From Japanese 紅 (beni) meaning "crimson" combined with 羽 (ha) meaning "feathers" or 葉 (ha) meaning "leaf". Other kanji combinations are possible.
From Japanese 紅 (beni) meaning "crimson" combined with 姫 (hime) meaning "princess". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column12: From Japanese 紅 (beni) meaning "red, vermilion" and 子 (ko) meaning "child". Other kanji combinations are possible.

Spanish variant and Polish form of the Germanic name Bernhilde, which came into common usage thanks to the martyr and saint Benilde de Córdoba (known as Saint Benildis in English, died circa 853).Due to Benilda being a saint and phonetic similarities, folk etymology likes to connect her name to the same Latin source as that of Benedictus and thus giving it the meaning of "blessed". This meaning and etymology, however, are mere wishful thinking.

French form of Benilda.Originally a feminine name, Bénilde has also been used on males in France from the 1800s onwards thanks to Saint Bénilde (known as Benildus Romançon in English, 1805-1862) who chose his religious name in honor of the feminine martyr Sainte Bénilde de Cordoue (known as Saint Benildis of Cordoba in English, ~853).
Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Benilda.

Traditional Hindu name popular in eastern Uttar Pradesh and Bengal.The name of a leader who fought the British in the First Indian War of Independence in 1857 and then disappeared into the forests of Nepal.Name of ancient temple in Varanasi that was destroyed by Muslim ruler Aurangzeb. Upon the site of the old temple he built a mosque.

column12: From Japanese 紅 (beni) meaning "crimson" combined with 丸 (maru) meaning "round, circle".This name is rarely used in real life. A known bearer is Nintendo designer Benimaru Itoh.

column12: From Japanese 紅 (beni) meaning "crimson, rouge" combined with 央 (o) meaning "center, middle". Other combinations of kanji characters can also form this name.

In the Icelandic Saga af Tristram ok Ísodd, a king who managed to wrest control of Tristan’s homeland, Spain, during the chaos that followed the defeat of Biríng, Tristan’s foster-father, at the hands of King Turnes of Africa.Tristan eventually defeated Beniosus and his companions, Earls Hríngr and Siguròr, and re-conquered Spain.
Means "iron", derived from Egyptian bjꜣ n pt meaning "meteoric iron", literally "metal of the sky".
Derived from French béni soit "blessed be".
From Japanese 紅 (beni) meaning "crimson" combined with 吉 (yoshi) meaning "good luck". Other kanji combinations are possible.

Beniz is directly descended from the highly esteemed Old Turkic roots meŋiz or beŋiz, which seamlessly evolved over centuries of Turkic dialectal development into the modern Turkish word "Beniz". In its purest linguistic sense, it signifies the "face", "complexion", "facial features", or the "natural, radiant glow of one's skin".Beniz is a spectacularly profound name that transcends basic physical descriptions. Unlike generic names that mean "beautiful face", Beniz specifically celebrates the lively radiance, vibrant health, and authentic emotional expression that shines directly through a person's countenance. It is a praise of the face as a mirror to a pure, noble soul. Symbolically, it represents someone whose inner light is so powerful that it visibly illuminates their external being, signifying absolute transparency, emotional depth, and a compelling, magnetic presence. It praises an individual who is incapable of hiding their inner goodness, someone whose face reflects the serene brightness of a healthy mind, a passionate heart, and an unyielding spiritual vitality. It is a stunning tribute to the natural human form as a canvas of divine beauty and emotional truth.

column12: From the Japanese kanji 弁 (ben) meaning “valve” and 慶 (kei) meaning “be delighted”.Other kanji combinations are also possible.

Benkos Biohó (died 1621), also known as Domingo Biohó, was said to have been born in either the Democratic Republic of Congo or Angola, where he was seized by the Portuguese slaver Pedro Gomez Reynel, sold to businessman Juan Palacios, and later, after transportation to what is now Colombia in South America, sold again to the Spaniard Alonso del Campo in 1596, in Cartagena de Indias. He established the maroon community of San Basilio de Palenque some time in the 16th century. He was betrayed and hanged by the governor of Cartagena in 1621.The former African king escaped from the slave port of Cartagena with ten others and founded San Basilio de Palenque, then known as the 'village of the Maroons'. In 1713 it became the first free village in the Americas by decree from the King of Spain, when he gave up sending his troops on futile missions to attack their fortified mountain hideaway.

Beothach is a prominent figure in early Irish mythology and the Lebor Gabála Érenn (The Book of Invasions). He was the grandson of Nemed, the leader of the Nemidians who colonized Ireland.Beothach is sometimes referred to as the son of Iarbonel Fáidh (the Prophet), who was the son of Nemed. His bloodline is depicted as a direct link between the early biblical/mythical colonizers of Ireland and the ancient, magical pantheon of gods and heroes who feature prominently in the Ulster and Mythological Cycles.In some mythological accounts, Beothach is cited as one of the three great leaders (alongside his contemporaries Simeon and Briotán) who divided Ireland into three distinct parts following the collapse of the earlier Nemedian civilization.Beothach’s son, Iobáth, is recorded as the ancestor of the Tuatha Dé Danann. After the Nemidians were defeated in Ireland, Iobáth led his clan into the northern reaches of Europe. There, his descendants spent generations studying Druidism, magic, and philosophy before returning to conquer Ireland as the mystical, divine race known as the Tuatha Dé Danann

Beray is a modern Turkish female name. It is highly probable that it is a compound name formed by the combination of the Turkish verb root ber- (an archaic variant of ver-, meaning "to give") and the common noun and suffix ay meaning "moon". Under this etymology, the name conveys the meaning of "giving the moon" or "bringing light like the moon". Alternatively, if interpreted as an Old Turkic volitional/wish phrase, it can mean "may it give light like the moon".Another strong Turkic possibility is that it derived from the word beri (meaning "this side" or "towards here") combined with ay, which through phonetic dropping yields the meaning "the moon that comes closer" or "the moon that is near us".While the prefix Ber- superficially resembles the Persian preposition bar (بر) or the Arabic roots bara'a (برآء) or barat (براءة), a Semitic or Iranian origin is highly implausible. The phonological evolution of the name strictly follows Turkish vowel harmony and morphotactics. Borrowings from Arabic Bera'at or Bera traditionally preserve their distinct phonetic markers (like the glottal stop or long vowels) in Turkish orthography (e.g., Berat or Bera), whereas Beray functions purely as a native Turkic compound both in rhythm and semantic structure.

Derived from the Old Turkic verb Berki- / Berkmek ("to harden, to become strong, to fortify"). It signifies "that which is protected," traditionally referring to "enclosed gardens, fortified fields, or hardened soil." The phonetic and semantic structure is rooted in the Anatolian agricultural lexicon where hard, clay-rich earth or stone-piled borders were labeled as 'Berçin'.The attempt to link this to the Persian/Kurdish berçîn ("collection/jealous") is linguistically invalid due to the divergent phonetic evolution. The Turkish Berçin follows the internal derivation pattern of Berk (solid/hard) + -in (suffix indicating state or location). Phonologically, the Turkish term aligns with berkitmek (to solidify), whereas the loanword theories fail to account for the word's primary use in rural Anatolian topography and historical agricultural terminology.

Bergusia is a Celtic goddess, consort of the god Ucuetis, and worshipped with him at Alesia in Burgundy.The divine couple are named on inscriptions of the Romano-Celtic period, and an image of a divine couple has been found on the same site, the male figure bearing a hammer, the female appearing as a goddess of prosperity. This image, if it is indeed of the two deities, may indicate that Ucuetis was a patron god of craftsmen. This may be confirmed by the discovery of an epigraphic dedication to the couple, inscribed on a bronze vase and found in the cellar of a huge building: rubbish found in this underground room consisted entirely of scraps of bronze and iron and appears to have been part of the stock of metalsmiths. It is possible that this room was a sanctuary to the local crafts-deities of Alesia, and the superstructure itself may have a craft hall for metalworkers.

Derivative of Bernardus, though there are also cases where the name is a direct latinization of Bernardin and Bernardino. For example, the medieval Italian saint Bernardino of Siena (1380-1444) is known as Bernardinus Senensis in Latin texts of the era, and it is due to this that he is known as saint Bernardinus of Siena in (at least) Belgium and the Netherlands.
Originally a diminutive of Bernarda, used as a given name in its own right. This name is also treated as the Slovene form of Bernadette.
Sardinian and Corsican form of Bernard.
Medieval Italian diminutive of Bernardo, as -uccio is an Italian masculine diminutive suffix.
Name of an 8th century Benedictine monk of Corbie Abbey.
Judeo-French, Anglo-Norman and Friulian form of Bernard.
Transferred use of the surname Berneda.
Irish short form of Bernadette using the diminuitive suffix ín.
Derived from the Old Frankish or Old High German element bern meaning "bear" and Proto-Germanic *geldą meaning "reward, gift, money".
One of the fifteen Saxon kings who invaded Britain during Arthur’s struggle to establish power.
From the surname Bernell.In the United States, feminine usage is now archaic, while the name is still given to boys.
Either a diminutive of names beginning with the element Bern-, such as Bernadette and Bernice, combined with the French feminine ending -elle or a quasi-feminization of the surname Bernell.
Transferred use of the surname Bernett.
Variant of Bernie, which is a diminutive of Bernard.
The name is made up of the name elements bern meaning "bear" and fridu meaning "peace".
Derived from Proto-Germanic beran or bernu "bear" (bero and bern in Old High German) combined with Old High German hari "army."
Icelandic form of Bernadine from Bernharður and -ína.
Variant of the Old English name Beornheah, formed of the elements beorn "man, hero, warrior" and heah "high".
Derived from the Germanic elements bern meaning "bear" and hild meaning "battle."
Form of Beornweald found in the Phillimore translation of Domesday Book, as well as an Old High German variant form of Bernwald.
Variant of Bernadette or diminutive of names containing Bern and followed by the suffix -ita.

The first element of this name is derived from Proto-Germanic beran or bernu "bear" (bero and bern in Old High German). The second element comes from laifa, which in turn is derived from Gothic laiba (leiba in Old High German and leifr in Old Norse) "remnant, remains." By that, they actually meant the person that is left behind after one's death, so laifa is best translated (depending on the context) as "heir" or "survivor."
Variant of Bernadette. Actress Bernadette Stanislaus, profesionally known as Bern Nadette Stanis, bears this name.
Short form of names containing the element bern "bear" making it a cognate of Björn. Borne by the first abbot of Cluny venerated as a saint.
Germanic variant of Bernward and French variant of Bernouard.
Dutch and German form of Bernwald.
Derived from Proto-Germanic beran or bernu "bear" (bero and bern in Old High German) combined with Gothic vulfs "wolf."
Derived from the Proto-Germanic beran or bernu meaning "bear" (bero and bern in Old High German) combined with Gothic valdan meaning "to reign".

This name derives from the Old High German name “Bernward”, composed of two elements bern "bear" plus wart "guard".Saint Bernward (~960–1022) was the thirteenth Bishop of Hildesheim from 993 until his death in 1022.
Spanish form of Bernward and italian variant Bernoardo.
Derived from the Old German elements bern "bear" and wig "war, battle" meaning "war bear, bear of war". Cognate of Beornwig.
Variant of Berowulf. Since the 11th century, his name has appeared as Bernwelf. It may also be spelled Berowolf or Bernulf.

Uncertain etymology, possibly derived from βέρω (bero), the Macedonian form of Ancient Greek φέρω (phero) meaning "to bring, carry, bear" (compare Berenice). This was the name of multiple characters in Greek mythology, including an Oceanid, one of the fifty Nereids, a nymph daughter of Aphrodite and Adonis, and an old Epidaurian woman who nursed Semele.
The allegoric personification of the German city Berlin. Extremely rarely used as a given name.
Unaccented form of Berónica mainly used in the United States.
This name is the Italian male equivalent of Veronica, the Latinized form of Berenice. Usage is rare, though there is a Saint Beronico, martyred in Antioch and commemorated on 19th October.
Coined by Sabino Arana Goiri and Koldo Elizalde as a Basque equivalent of Verónica and Véronique.
Variant of Bernwulf, from Germanic bero "bear" and wulf "wolf."

Transferred use of the surname Berrick which was originally taken from various locational names in Kent, Shropshire, Oxfordshire, Yorkshire and Norfolk.The name itself is derived from Old English bere "barley" and wic "outlying farm".
Short form of Bersabe, the Armenian form of Bathsheba (via Ancient Greek Bersabee).
Form of Bathsheba via Greek Bersabee. Also compare Beersheba, the name of an ancient Jewish village near the boundary between Upper and Lower Galilee.
Greek form of Bathsheba, as it first appeared in the Septuagint. The modern Greek form of the name is Virsavee.
Amharic form of Bathsheba (via the ancient Greek form Bersabee), as well as an alternate transcription of Armenian Բերսաբե (see Bersabe). See also Beersheba.

Meaning unknown at this moment in time. Also compare the somewhat similar-looking names Berkant (Turkish), Berzan (Kurdish), Birzhan and Baurzhan (both Kazakh).A known bearer of this name is the Kosovar soccer player Bersant Celina (b. 1996).
Short form of Albêrt, Hubêrt and other names ending in -bêrt.
Gascon and Cremish Lombard form of Bertha als well as a Cremish Lombard short form of Albèrta.
Short form of Alberta, Roberta and other names ending in berta.
Derived from the Germanic element Old High German beraht "bright" combined with Old High German wachar "vigilant." The name might also be a form of Berthar.
Possibly derived from Old English beorht "bright".
Shortened form of names that contain the element bert (often from the Germanic element beraht meaning "bright,") like Albertas and Bertoldas.

The first element of this name is either derived from the Lithuanian noun bernas meaning "child" as well as "boy, lad" or from the Lithuanian verb berti meaning "to spread, to scatter, to strew". The second element is derived from Baltic tauta meaning "people, nation" (see Vytautas).
A duplication of the Old Frankish or Old Saxon element berht, Old High German beraht meaning "bright" (Proto-Germanic *berhtaz).
Means "knoll" in Yiddish. It is also considered the Yiddish form of the name Bertha.
Bertechildis was the fifth wife of Dagobert I, King of the Franks. Her name is a form of Berthild.
Logudorese and Nuorese diminutive of Albertu.
Derived from Old High German beraht "bright" combined with flâdi "beauty, respectability."
Variant of Bertefleda. Berteflede was a daughter of Charibert I, a 6th-century Merovingian king of Paris.

Derived from the Old Frankish or Old Saxon element berht, Old High German beraht meaning "bright" (Proto-Germanic *berhtaz) and Proto-Germanic *geldą meaning "reward, gift, money". This name was recorded ca. 823 in Latin as Bertegildis.
Derived from Old High German beraht "bright" combined with Old High German gund "war."
Danish form of Bertil. This is the name of Danish sculptor Bertel Thorvaldsen (1770-1844).
Diminutive of Berte as well as a feminine form of Bertel.
Derived from Old High German beraht "bright" combined with Old High German fridu "peace."
Old English form of Bertha, from earlier Old English Berhte meaning "bright one" (from beorht "bright"). Some forms of this name have influence of Latin (e.g. Bercta).
Berthabelle is a compound of Bertha and Belle.
Derived from Old High German beraht "bright" combined with Old High German hari "army."
Limbourgish and Luxembourgish form of Bertha, influenced by Berthe Lutgen a Luxembourgish painter, committed feminist and former secondary school teacher.
French diminutive of Berthe and Danish variant of Berteline.

Variant of Parthenia via its variant Perthenia. Also compare Barthenia.It is also possible that there are cases where this name is a combination of a feminine name that contains the Germanic element beraht meaning "bright" (such as Bertha) with a feminine name that ends in -enia (such as Bethenia and Eugenia).
Variant of Berthild. Berthilde lived in the 7th century AD and was one of the five wives of Dagobert I, king of the Franks.

Despite his advanced age, Bertholai was called "the best knight of Carmelide". Apparently this meant the best in arms, because he was not an endearing character. He was surnamed “the Red” at the beginning of his career and “the Old” at the end. Once a vassal of King Leodegrance of Carmelide (Cameliard), but was banished by Arthur and Leodegrance after the malevolent murder of another of King Leodegrance’s knights.In his exile, he met the False Guinevere, Genievre (Leodegrance’s daughter and Guenevere’s twin half-sister), who was also living in exile after the attempt by Cleodailis’ relatives to substitute her for Guenevere, Bertholai instigated a second attempt to substitute her for her more famous look-alike. They capture Arthur by luring him into the woods on a boar hunt and separating him from his companions.Then, with drugs and flattery, Genievre won his love and convinced him that she was Guenevere, the true-born. Arthur had Genievre acknowledged Queen and renounced Guenevere. Genievre wanted her rival’s death, but eventually Guenevere merely(?) condemned to lose the skin of her head (scalp?), cheeks, and palms, and be exiled forever.This split the court. Lancelot renounced allegiance to Arthur, insisting on defending Guenevere against three knights. (This caused a curious rivalry between Lancelot and Kay, who also wanted to serve as Guenevere’s champion.) Gawaine lent Excalibur to Lancelot for the battle. Thus Lancelot saved Guenevere’s skin, and Arthur gave her into Duke Galeholt’s keeping. Galeholt set her up comfortably with Lancelot in Surluse (Sorelois). At Gawaine’s urgin, Arthur tried to win back Lancelot, but failed.In his infatuation with Genievre, Arthur let his duties slip. When the Pope learned what had happened, he ordered Arthur to take back Guenevere and, when Arthur refused, interdicted Britain for twenty-one months. In the tenth month of interdiction, Genievre and Bertholai had paralytic strokes, losing the use of their limbs and all their senses except sight and hearing. They began to decay while still alive. The hermit Amustans upbraided Arthur and helped get deathbed confessions from Genievre and Bertholai, who confessed to save their souls. Gawaine took the news to Surluse, and finally Guenevere and Lancelot were persuaded to return to Arthur. By the time Guenevere arrived, after spending more than two and half years in Surluse, Bertholai and Genievere were dead.In the non-cyclical Lancelot do Lac, Lancelot championed the real Guinevere against three of Bertelay’s knights and won; Bertelay then admitted his guilt and was burned. In the Vulgate Lancelot, on the other hand, Arthur remained married to the False Guinevere for several years before both she and Bertelay contracted a mortal illness and confessed their ruse on their deathbeds.It is possible (though unlikely) that Bertholai could be identified with Malory’s Sir Bertelot, the brother of Breuse Sans Pitie.
Archaic southern French feminine form of Berthoumieu, a southern French form of Barthélémy.

Diminutive of Hubert and other names containing bert (often derived from the Germanic element beraht meaning "bright").Famous bearer of this name is Berti Vogts (born: Hans-Hubert Vogts) who is a former German footballer who played as a defender. He played for Borussia Mönchengladbach in the Bundesliga his whole professional club career and won the FIFA World Cup with West Germany in 1974. He later managed Germany (winning Euro 96 as the team's head coach), Scotland, Nigeria and Azerbaijan national team.
Diminutive of Berta, not used as a given name in its own right.
Dutch form of Bertine, with its spelling phonetical in nature.
Diminutive of Albert, not used as a given name in its own right.

Bertilak de Hautdesert is revealed to be the true name of the Green Knight, a heroic character of the Matter of Britain, originating in the 14th-century poem Sir Gawain and the Green Knight and the related medieval work The Greene Knight.The name "Bertilak" may derive from bachlach, a Celtic word meaning "churl" (i.e. rogueish, unmannerly), or from "bresalak", meaning "contentious". The Old French word bertolais is a form of "Bertilak" in the Arthurian tale Merlin from the Lancelot-Grail cycle. Notably, the 'Bert-' prefix means 'bright', and the '-lak' can mean either 'lake' or "play, sport, fun, etc".

column5: ber-TEELD(Louisiana Creole)|ber-TIL-de(Louisiana Creole, Latin American Spanish, History)|BER-TEELD(French)
column12: French variant and Spanish form of Berthilde.
Form of Berthild. Bertilia was the name of a 7th-century saint from Mareuil (France).
Form of Berthild in various languages.
In the case of Spanish singer Bertín Osborne (1954-), it is a diminutive of Norberto.
French and Provençal form of Bertinus.
Short form of Albertina as well as an elaboration of Berta.
Diminutive of Berte as well as a short form of names ending in -bertine.
Tagalog diminutive of Alberto, Roberto and other names containing berto.
Portuguese diminutive of names ending in -berto, such as Alberto and Roberto. Also compare Betinho.
Diminutive form of Bertus. In other words, one could say that this is the male equivalent of Bertina.
Derived from the Old Frankish or Old Saxon element berht, Old High German beraht meaning "bright" (compare Bertha) combined with -isma, a variant of the Latin superlative suffix -issima.
Diminutive of Bert (masculine), Berta (feminine) and other names that contain the Germanic element beraht meaning "bright".
Derived from the Old German elements beraht "bright" and lind "soft, gentle, tender".
Cremish Lombard short form of Albèrt.
Italian form of Bertulf and variant of Bertulfo.
Medieval Italian diminutive of Bertolo. In the case of the Brazilian Portuguese name, it is more likely a transferred use of the Italian surname.
Galician diminutivve of Bartolomeu, Bartomeu, Bertolameu and Bertomeu.
Variant of Bartolo; in some cases it may also have been a variant of Berto.
Means "bright counsel", derived from Old High German beraht "bright" combined with Old High German rât "counsel."

Feminine form of Bertrad.Bertrada of Prüm (7th/8th century) was the co-founder of Prüm Abbey. Bertrada of Laon (also Betrada, the younger) lived in the 8th century AD. She was the wife of Frankish king Pepin the Short and mother of Charlemagne.
French form of Bertrada. This name was borne by Bertrade of Montfort, a queen consort of France.
Spanish and Galician form of Bertrand.
Catalan, Occitan, Gascon and Medieval French form of Bertrand.
Latinized form of Bertrand. It has also been used as a latinization of Bertram, which is due to the fact that the two names have been confused with each other since early medieval times.
Medieval Gascon feminine diminutive of Bertran.
Middle French feminine form of Bertrand or Bertram.
A dithematic name formed from the German name elements berht "bright, radiant" and þruþi "strength".
Maybe derived from the surname Bertrés.
Maybe a rhotic dialect form of Beatrice. An influence of popular names beginning in Ber- like Bert is possible.
Modern form of the Old English name Beorhtric. It was the name of an 8th-century king of Wessex.
Derived from Old High German beraht "bright" combined with Anglo-Saxon ridan "to ride."

Diminutive of given names (typically of Germanic origin) that start with Bertr-, such as Bertram and Bertrude (also Bertruda).A notable bearer of this name is the Dutch actress Bertrie Wierenga (b. 1989), who is of Frisian descent.
Derived from Old High German beraht "bright" combined with þruþ "strength."
Variant of Bertrud. This was the name of a 7th-century Frankish queen consort.
Derived from Old High German beraht "bright" and run "secret lore".

Means "pincushion flower" (species Scabiosa comosa) in Mongolian, a kind of purple-blue flower in the honeysuckle genus. Ultimately derived from бэр (ber) meaning "bride, daughter-in-law, sister-in-law" and цэцэг (tsetseg) meaning "flower".
Sicilian and Sardinian form of Berto.

Medieval Italian diminutive of Berta, as -uccia is an Italian feminine diminutive suffix.In addition to that, this name was also often used as a short form of Albertuccia, Robertuccia and other pet forms that end in -bertuccia.

Medieval Italian diminutive of Berto, as -uccio is an Italian masculine diminutive suffix.In addition to that, this name was also often used as a short form of Albertuccio, Lambertuccio and other pet forms that end in -bertuccio.Known bearers of this name include the Italian diplomat Bertuccio Bagarotto (died in 1511) and Bertuccio Valier (1596-1658), a chief magistrate of the Republic of Venice.
Means "crest giver" in Turkish. From tuğ meaning "crest" and ber meaning "given".
Spanish form of Bertwin via Latinized form Bertuinus
Derived from Old High German beraht "bright" combined with Gothic vulfs "wolf."
Spanish form of Bertulf and Italian variant of Bertolfo.
East Prussian German form of Bertulis.
English form of Bertulf, also used to refer to the Mercian king Beorhtwulf.
Latinized form of Bert, as well as a short form of latinized Germanic names that contain the element beraht "bright", such as Albertus.
Derived from Old High German beraht "bright" combined with Gothic valdan "to reign" (see Berthold).
Means "bright friend", derived from Old High German beraht "bright" combined with Old High German wini "friend."

column12: From Japanese 鈴 (beru) meaning "bell". Other kanji combinations are possible.Beru (Whitesun) Lars is a character in the 'Star Wars' universe. She is the aunt and surrogate mother of hero Luke Skywalker.
Beruka is a Old Greek name and a derivative of the name Beronica.
allegedly means "pure" in Aramaic. compare Bruria
Czech and Slovak diminutive of Berenika. Also compare Beruška.
Czech and Slovak diminutive of Berenika. Also compare Beruša.

A character mentioned in JRR Tolkien's works. The name is derived from the fictional Sindarin language, and possibly means "angry queen", from a combination of bereth meaning "queen, spouse" or "supreme, sublime", ruth meaning "anger", and the feminine suffix "-iel".

The first element of this name is either derived from the Lithuanian noun bernas meaning "child" as well as "boy, lad" or from the Lithuanian verb berti meaning "to spread, to scatter, to strew". The second element is derived from the old Lithuanian noun vaina meaning "cause, reason" as well as "fault".
Derived from Old High German bero "bear" and walt "power, authority".

Perhaps an elaborated form of French béryl meaning "beryl", possibly blending it with the word lune "moon". This was used by the Belgian playwright and poet Maurice Maeterlinck for a fairy in his play 'The Blue Bird' (1908).

Derived from the Russian noun берёза (beryoza) meaning "birch tree". Also compare Bereza, which is a medieval first name of the same etymological origin.Originally predominantly a surname, Beryoza increased in popularity as a first name during the Soviet era, since a lot of Communist parents were eager to reject traditional names.

Derived from the Lithuanian noun beržas meaning "birch tree". In Lithuanian folklore and popular culture, Beržas is the name of one of the three sons of the titular character of the folk tale Eglė žalčių karalienė, which translates to English as Eglė, the Queen of Serpents.
Coined by Ervin Lázár for the title character of his novel Berzsián és Dideki.
Derived from Albanian besë meaning "pledge, word of honor; trust, faith".
From the surname Besançon. Besançon Hugues (1487-1532) was a Swiss political and religious leader who was a member of the Grand Council of Geneva.
Means "announcement (of good news)" in Turkish.Religiously this is the word for Announciation specifically known as Beşaret-i Meryem.
Form of Besarion with the nominative suffix, used in Georgian when the name is written stand-alone.
Possibly derived from Albanian besë "faith; trust; promise; oath" and artë "golden" (compare ar).
From pesaa meaning "heal, cure" and wunna/yuuna meaning "to put" in Paiute.
Variant of Passchier, probably via the archaic forms Peschier and Pesschier.
Greek form of Bezalel, as it first appeared in the Septuagint.
Form of Bezalel used in the Latin Old Testament.
Derived from Albanian besim "faith; belief" and fort "strong".

column3: በሺ(Amharic)|辺四, 邊四, 辺清, 辺詩, 辺志, 辺史, 邊清, 邊詩, 邊志, 邊史, 倍四, 倍清, 倍詩, 倍志, 倍史, 部四, 部清, 部詩, 部志, 部史, etc.(Japanese Kanji)

column12: Variant of Bisi or Bósi. This is found in the 11th-century Domesday Book.

Short form of Besarion. It began to be used as an independent name in the 18th century, thanks to the Georgian poet Besarion Gabashvili (1750-1791), who was known as Besik or Besiki. Another notable bearer of this name is the Georgian writer and poet Besik Kharanauli (b. 1939).
Form of Besik with the Georgian nominative suffix -ი (-i). It is only used in Georgian when the name is written stand-alone.This was the pen name of the Georgian poet Besarion Gabashvili (1750-1791).
Diminutive of Besarion and its short form Beso.
Of uncertain origin and meaning. It might be a diminutive of Elisabetta.
Derived from Besiana, one of the Albanian names of Podujevo, a city in north-eastern Kosovo. Allegedly, the name is ultimately derived from Albanian besë "faith; belief; trust; oath; promise".

column12: From the Turkic military title beg meaning "chieftain, master" combined with arslan meaning "lion".
Alternate transcription of Arabic بسمة (see Basma) chiefly used in North Africa.
Derived from Albanian besë "faith, trust" and mirë "good".
Besorah means news. Paired with Tova it means good news.
Manx form of Bessie and Betty.

Of Frisian origin, this name is possibly a diminutive of a shortened form of Germanic names that contain either the element bern meaning "bear" or the element beraht meaning "bright". Also compare Wessel and similar names.Known bearers of this name include the Dutch businessman Bessel Kok (b. 1941) and the Dutch author and psychiatrist Bessel van der Kolk (b. 1943).
Diminutive of Basel (via its variant Besel). It was recorded in 14th-century Frankfurt, Germany.
In the Prose Tristan, a Cornish woman who loved Tristan. When Tristan rejected her, she became the paramour of Andred, Tristan’s enemy, and conspired to reveal his affair with Isolde to King Mark.
Means "smart, well-educated" in Indonesian, ultimately from Sanskrit विस्तार (vistāra).
Referring to being steadfast in one's faith.
Bestla is a giantess in Norse Mythology. She is married to Borr and mother of Odin, Vili and Vé. One of Saturn's moons has this name.
Referencing being strong despite trials and tribulations.
Diminutive of Besarion and its short form Beso.
This is found in the Jewish catacombs of Rome as the name of a woman.
Slovak diminutive of Alžbeta (not used as a given name in its own right), Portuguese diminutive of Elisabete, Alberta ou Roberta and Romansh variant of Betta.
Derived from bɛtaŋ meaning "power" in Kenyang.

Means "wanton lady" in Irish Gaelic, from bé "woman" and téide "wantonness" (see Téide). In Irish legend she is a member of the Tuatha Dé Danann, daughter of the goddess Flidais and sister of the witch-like Bé Chuille.
Betel is a "type of plant from South and South East Asia."
Means "favourite female friend" in Bette Obudu.

From a New Testament place name, Βηθαβαρά (Bēthabará) in Greek, which is derived from Hebrew בית עברה (bēt ‛ăbārāh) meaning "house of the ford" or "place of crossing". In some versions of the New Testament, Bethabara is the city where John the Baptist met Jesus and proclaimed, 'Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world' (John 1:28-29), and where he baptized Jesus.
Referring to being thankful for God's blessings.
Variant of Bethany, influenced by Annie.
An Assyrian given name meaning “beta d alaha’ or “house of God” in English, it is an Aramaic form of the name Bethel.
Variant of Bethana. Bethena, A Concert Waltz (1905) is a composition by Scott Joplin.

From the name of a pool in Jerusalem, mentioned in the New Testament, known for its healing properties, which means "house of mercy" or "house of grace" from Aramaic בית (beth) "house, home" and חסדא (hesda) "mercy, kindness; favour, clemency". The second element could also derive from an identical word meaning "shame, dishonour".

Form of Bithiah used in some versions of the Old Testament, including the Douay-Rheims Bible. This name was popular in Scotland from the 17th century as an Anglicised form of Gaelic Beathag. It has occasionally been used as a Latinized form of Beth (a short form of Elizabeth).
The son of Perceforest, he made an unfortunate marriage to the sorceress Circe.

French form of Bethlehem, which is the name of the birthplace of Jesus Christ. It appears that the given name Bethléem has always been very rare. I came across it in the Belgian civil registry (when I was doing genealogical research), where Bethléem was the name of an 18th-century French-speaking Belgian woman who was married, had 8 children between 1729-1748 and ultimately died in 1779.
From a biblical place name meaning "house of bread" in Hebrew, the city where Jesus was born (see Bethlehem).
Variation of Bethany influenced by Daphne.
Variant of Bethany. A notable bearer is the author Bethny Ricks.

Derived from Scottish Gaelic beatha meaning "life", and therefore is related to the name Beathag. Most known bearers of this name include Bethóc Ingen mac Maíl Coluim, daughter of Malcolm II, King of Alba, as well as Bethóc, Prioress of Iona, daughter of Somerled, Lord of Argyll.
A diminutive for names containing Beth.
Dutch form of Bethuel, but less common than the main Dutch form (Betuël).

From the name of a city mentioned only in the apocryphal Book of Judith, possibly derived from the Hebrew noun בתולה (betula) meaning "virgin". The city's deliverance by Judith, when besieged by the Assyrian general Holofernes, forms the subject of the Book of Judith.
Diminutive of Bethany, Elizabeth, and other names containing beth.

Latin American variant of Betsy. This name was brought to public attention by Bethzy Zamorano, a contestant on the Mexican reality television series Bailando por un Sueño. She and her partner, actor/comedian Adrián Uribe, were runner-ups in the first season (2005), which most likely influenced the name's spike in popularity in 2006.
First made known and popularised by Argentine actress Betiana Blum (1939-), in this case being a mix of her given names Betty and Ana.

Diminutive of Beto, as it contains the Spanish masculine diminutive suffix -ico.A notable bearer of this name was the Aruban politician and activist Betico Croes (1938-1986), whose full name was Gilberto François Croes.
Derived from Turkish beti "shape, figure, build" and gül "rose". It is often interpreted to mean "as beautiful as a rose".
A Character in Rayman, a franchise of platform video games, published by Ubisoft.
Possibly from the Uzbek bet meaning "face, cheek" and qand meaning "cube sugar".
Derived from Basque beti "always", this name is now generally understood as a Basque equivalent of Perpetua.

According to the French romance Perceforest, Alexander the Great made Betis the King of England following the former’s fictional conquest of Britain. His brother, Gaddifer, was likewise made the King of Scotland. Betis was quickly accepted by the populace, being renamed Perceforest after he had killed the magician Durmart.
Diminutive of Elizabeth and other names containing a similar sound. Also compare Beta and the masculine equivalent Betito.The Chicana feminist writer Elizabeth Martínez (1925-2021) went by this name.

Medieval Basque name that was recorded from the 13th century onwards.Its origin and meaning are uncertain, however, one theory suggests that it might be a feminine form of Betri, itself an old variant of Petri, which ultimately makes Betixa a cognate of Petra.
Of uncertain origin and meaning; theories include a German-Yiddish variant of Bithiah.
Diminutive of Alžběta via the variant diminutive Běta.
Originally a diminutive of Elizabeta, occasionally used as a given name in its own right.

Meaning unknown. It is possibly of Svan origin, since Betkil is the name of a tragic protagonist from a Svan folk song.A known bearer of this name is the Georgian-born Turkish judoka Betkil Shukvani (b. 1988), who has been known under the Turkish name Bekir Özlü since 2015.
Meaning uncertain; it might perhaps be a short form of Betkil. Also compare names like Beso and Vano.
Transferred use of the surname Beton.
Tagalog diminutive of Alberto, Roberto and other names containing berto.
Means "may Bata be favorably disposed toward her" in Egyptian.
Combination of the names Bet and Riek, and a diminutive of Elisabeth-Hendrika.
Local variant of Béatrix found in the Bourgogne-Franche-Comté region of France up until the 1700s.
Short form of Elizabeth and variant or nickname of Betsy.
Spanish, Catalan and Hungarian form of Bathsheba.

Derived from Betsaida, which is the Spanish form of Bethsaida, the name of two places in the New Testament. For both places, the name is either of Aramaic or Hebrew origin and means either "house of hunting" or "house of fishing". Also compare Bethany, which is somewhat similar etymologically and also refers to a biblical place.
Means "in the shadow" in Hebrew. In the bible, this is the name of a son of Uri who was one of the architects of the tabernacle, and the name of an Israelite.
Meaning "help, aid, or give assistance", another form of the name is Etserai or Batsirai.

Apparently a pseudo-Italian elaboration of Betsy based on similar-sounding names such as Belinda and Lucinda (perhaps Betsaida; see Bethsaida). It was used by William Makepeace Thackeray in his satirical novel 'The Rose and the Ring' (1854), where it belongs to a little chambermaid.
Form of Bathshua used in some Spanish translations of the Old Testament.
Italian, Venetian and Romansh short form of Elisabetta.
Variant of Betânia, the Portuguese form of Bethania.
Transferred use of the surname Bettany. This name is borne by English historian and writer Bettany Hughes (born 1968).
Diminutive of Élîzabé and Lîzabé and thus an equivalent to English Betty.
Estonian short form of Eliisabet, Hungarian short form of Erzsébet and Swiss German short form of Elisabeth.
Possibly a diminutive of Elisabetta, or a variant of Bettina. Bettisia Gozzadini (1209–1261) was the first woman to teach at a university; specifically the University of Bologna.
Diminutive of Germanic names containing the Old Frankish or Old Saxon element berht, Old High German beraht meaning "bright" (Proto-Germanic *berhtaz).
Icelandic and Faroese form of Betty.
A combination of Betty and Anna.
Combination of Betty and Jean 2 (See also Bettyjane and Bettyjo).
A diminutive of the female given name Běta, a pet form of Alžběta. Alžběta is the Czech form of English Elizabeth. Another similar diminutive of Alžběta is Bětuška.
Diminutive of Alžběta, rarely used as a given name in its own right.
Variant of Betty, also used in Latin American countries as a short form of names containing Be- (or -be-) and -t-, like Beatriz and Alberta.
Variant of Betzabet using the -tl suffix found in Nahuatl names (e.g. Xochitl).

Variant spelling of Betsaida. This name is the most popular out of the two.A known bearer of this name is the Latin American singer Betzaida Ramírez (b. 1982), who usually performs under her given name only.
A derivation from Bethsaida, used in Venezuela.
Possibly an altered form of Betzaida, perhaps influenced by Zaira or the suffix -aira from other names (such as Yahaira or Yajaira).

Variant of the English name Betsy. Also compare Bethzy. Notable bearers include Betzy Kjelsberg (1866-1950), a Norwegian women's rights activist, suffragist and politician whose mother was from Scotland, and mathematician Mary Ann Elizabeth 'Betzy' Stephansen (1872-1961), the first Norwegian woman to be awarded a doctorate degree.

Medieval Frisian diminutive of Beuwe.Medieval Dutch bearers of the name were mostly located in what are now the provinces of North Holland, South Holland and Utrecht. For them, the name might possibly have had a different etymology, in which case a relation with modern Dutch beuk meaning "beech tree" seems to be a possibility.
Probably from Welsh bu "cow" and -no "knowing". The name of a 7th-century Welsh saint.
The name of the figure is a blend of the German word Beutel "bag" and Bartholomäus. The figure is an animated bag belonging to Father Christmas.

A word meaning “a slope from the horizontal or vertical in carpentry and stonework; a sloping surface or edge,” coming from the French for “to gape.” Flannery O'Connor used it for two characters in her 1955 short story "The River."
Probably a blend between Beverly and Evelyn.
Possibly came from the name of the fortification Beverīna (also known as Bebernīne or Bitarīna).
Transferred use of the surname Bevil.
Diminutive of Rebecca, Beckett, Beatrix and other names containing the beck sound.
Transferred use of the surname Bexley.
Likely a combination of Bex and Lynn.
Transferred use of the surname Bey.
Means "white" in Turkish, ultimately from Arabic بياض (bayāḍ).
Somali feminine name taken directly from the ordinary vocabulary word for "almond", which is perhaps ultimately from Persian بادام (bâdâm) "almond".
From Turkish bey meaning "gentleman, lord, master" combined with the Turkic title khan meaning "ruler, leader".
From the reconstructed Proto-Norse name *Baunila, possibly meaning "little bean" or "little swelling". In Norse mythology, Beyla is a servant of the god Freyr with her husband Bryggvir.

Beylan is a variant of the name Baylan. In many regions of Anatolia (including Sivas, Ankara, and Kayseri), the name carries the meanings of "graceful," "coquettish," "delicate," "well-mannered," "polite," or "mature."It is derived from the Old Turkic root bay, meaning "rich," "great," "noble," or "lord." This root is also the basis for the masculine title Bay and the feminine title Bayan. While Baylan is the more traditional spelling, Beylan reflects a common phonetic shift in various Turkish dialects where the a vowel softens toward an e.

A uniquely poetic Turkic name derived from the root Beyle- (an archaic variant of Bağla-, meaning "to tie," "to bind," or "to connect"). Etymologically, it is the direct ancestor to the modern word Bağlam ("context" or "connection"). In historical usage, a Beylem is a "corsage" or a "gathered bouquet," a collection of beautiful elements bound together into one harmonious whole. Symbolically, the name represents an individual who brings people together, a "binder" of hearts, or one who holds the threads of a narrative or community together in a state of grace. It is a name for a person who creates order out of beauty.
Variant of Bianca influenced by Beyoncé.
From the English-speaking word beyond, meaning "on the far side."
Means "born on Thursday", derived from Kazakh бейсенбі (beysenbi) meaning "Thusday" (of Persian origin).
Turkish. The name Beytullah is of Arabic origin and means "House of the God, Home of Allah, Qaba".
Turkish name meaning "very white light", combination of Beyza meaning "very white" and Nur meaning "light".
Diminutive of Bezaleel, Beryl, and other names starting with Be-.
Anglicized form of Hebrew Betsalel, meaning "in the shadow." In the bible, this is the name of a son of Uri who was one of the architects of the tabernacle, and the name of an Israelite.
Hebrew, meaning "protected by God". It occurs in the Bible as the name of a celebrated skilled craftsman. As a result, the school of arts set up in Jerusalem in the 20th century was named Bezalel.
Georgian form of Bizhan, which is an older form of Bijan.

The name of an alleged Lithuanian goddess of the evening.The form Bezlea was first recorded by Polish historian and theologian Jan Łasicki in his treatise on idolatry De diis Samagitarum caeterorumque Sarmatarum et falsorum Christianorum, written ca. 1582 and published in 1615, while Polish historian Theodor Narbutt referred to her as Bezelea in his work Dzieje starożytne narodu litewskiego, written between 1835 and 1841.Both forms are Latinizations; the original form, if there ever was one, is lost, however a Lithuanian form has since been reconstructed: Bežlėja.It has been suggested that Bežlėja might be derived from Lithuanian blista "to darken; to get dark".Since neither Łasicki nor Narbutt were intimately familiar with Lithuanian culture or language, the academic opinion on the value of their documents ranges from a valuable resource to a practical joke.

Meaning "feast of the World" in Ottoman Turkish (bezm - "feast" and âlem - "the World", taken from Persian language).Bezmiâlem Sultan (circa 1807 - 1853) was a wife of Sultan Mahmud II and mother of Sultan Abdulmejid I.

Means "one who adorns the feast", from Ottoman Turkish بزم (bezm) meaning "feast, assembly" (of Persian origin) and Persian آرا (ara), the present stem of آراستن⁩ (arastan) meaning "to decorate, adorn".
Etymology uncertain, possibly a feminine form of Bhaama.
Diminutive of Bhavana. Means “expressions” in Tamil.

Bhavānī (also known as Bhāvya, Tulajā, Turajā, Tvarita, Aṃbā, Jagadambā and Aṃbē) is an epithet associated with Durga. Bhavani translates to "giver of life" Bhavani is a name of Indian origin, deeply rooted in Hindu culture and mythology. It translates to "the Divine Mother" or "the Goddess", signifying power, fertility, and creation. Primarily used for girls, Bhavani is a name that resonates with strength and spiritual connection.
Bengali, Odia and Assamese form of Bhavani.
Bengali and Assamese form of Bhavesh.

Means "good, excellent, fortunate" or "prosperity, happiness, health" in Sanskrit. This is the name of several figures in Hinduism, including an aspect of the goddess Devi, and one of the eight queen-consorts of Krishna. It is also the name of an obscure goddess of the hunt.
Indian boy's name meaning "A wealthy person"
From Punjabi ਭਗਤ (bhagat) meaning "worshipper, devotee" (itself from Sanskrit भक्त (bhakta) meaning "devoted, loyal, faithful") and Sanskrit वीर (vīra) meaning "hero, man, brave".
From Sanskrit भाग्य (bhāgya) meaning "luck, destiny, fate, fortune" and the name of the Hindu goddess Lakshmi.
Alternate transcription of Marathi भाग्यश्री (see Bhagyashri).
From Sanskrit भाग्य (bhāgya) meaning "luck, destiny, fate, fortune" and श्री (śrī) meaning "diffusing light, radiance, splendour, beauty, holy, sacred".

Means "fearsome, terrible" in Sanskrit. This is the name of a fierce form of the Hindu god Shiva, often depicted wearing a garland of decapitated heads and accompanied by a dog. He is revered in both Hindu and Buddhist traditions, particularly in the Shaivite Hindu denomination.
Feminine form of Bhairava. In Hindu tradition she is the consort of Bhairava, the fierce form of Shiva, and the fifth of the ten Mahavidyas, the Tantric manifestations of the mother goddess Mahadevi.

Means "master of medicine" from Sanskrit भैषज्य (bhaiṣajya) meaning "curativeness, healing, remedy, medicine" and गुरु (guru) meaning "teacher, sage, master". In the Mahayana and Vajrayana Buddhist traditions this is the name of a buddha associated with medicine and healing.

Means "king of healing" from Sanskrit भैषज्य (bhaiṣajya) meaning "curativeness, healing, remedy, medicine" and राज (rāja) meaning "king". In Buddhist tradition this is the name of a bodhisattva associated with medicine and healing.

From Sanskrit भैषज्य (bhaiṣajya) meaning "curativeness, healing, remedy, medicine" and समुद्गत (samudgata) meaning "risen, come forth, appeared, begun". In Buddhist tradition this is the name of a bodhisattva associated with healing and medicine.
From Sanskrit भजन (bhajana) meaning "reverence, worship, adoration", also referring to a type of devotional song or hymn. As a Punjabi name it is sometimes feminine.
From Sanskrit भक्ति (bhakti) meaning "attachment, devotion, loyalty".
From Sanskrit भानु (bhānu) meaning "ray of light, brightness, splendour, sun".

Name- Bhanul भानुलMEANING - given by sun, gifted by sun, shining . Here भानु means sun, radiance, shining + ल from word ( ला ) means having or givenOrigin- Sanskrit, Indian, Tamil, Sikh, Buddhist, Nepali, Sinhala
Means "luminous" or "shining like the sun", from Sanskrit भानु (bhanu) "ray of light, splendour, brightness; the sun; beautiful woman" and -मत् (-mat) "as, like, having the qualities of".

Feminine form of Sanskrit भरण (bharaṇa) meaning "bearing, maintaining, supporting". This is the name of the second nakshatra (lunar mansion) in Hindu astronomy, which consists of three stars in the Aries constellation. As a given name it is used for both men and women.
Malayalam and Tamil form of Bharata.
Alternate transcription of Telugu భారతి, Kannada ಭಾರತಿ, Malayalam ഭാരതി or Tamil பாரதி (see Bharathi).
Alternate transcription of Thai ภาคภูมิ (see Phakphum).

Bharthari, also known as "Baba Bharthari" or "Jogi Sant" Bharatthari in many parts of India, is the hero of many folk stories in North India. He was the ruler of Ujjain, before renouncing the world and abdicating in the favor of his younger brother Vikramaditya.
Alternate transcription of Hindi/Marathi भारती (see Bharati).
Malayalam and Tamil form of Bhaskara.
From the Sanskrit भास्वती (bhāsvatī), meaning "shining, luminous", linked to the word भास् (bhās), meaning "light, lustre".
MEANING - a noble lady, any woman of high rank, queen (who is not crowned). Name of an enchanteressUsage- Sanskrit, Indian, Nepali, Sinhala, Hindi, Sikh, Buddhist, Tamil, Telugu

column3: ภาวัฒน์, ภวัต(Thai)
column12: Sanskritized transcription of Thai ภาวัฒน์ or ภวัต (see Phawat).

From Sanskrit भव (bhava) meaning "being, existence" combined with the feminine suffix -आनी (ānī). This is the name of a Hindu goddess of power, justice, motherhood and emotion, considered the amiable form of Durga.
From Sanskrit भव (bhava) meaning "being, existence" combined with धरणी (dharaṇī) meaning "earth".
From Sanskrit भावन (bhāvana) "producing, manifesting, thought, emotion" and दीप (dīpa) "lamp, light".
Means "lord of existence" from Sanskrit भव (bhava) meaning "being, existence" and ईश (īśa) meaning "ruler, lord".
From Sanskrit भाविन् (bhāvin) meaning "living, being, becoming, existing".

Bhawan means a house or a hall and deep means a oil lamp which provide light to us.by combining these words bhawan and deep we found that the meaning of Bhawandeep- a oil lamp which is present in a dark house or a hall provides light to the dark house or a hall and kill the darkness present in the it.It means this name has good meaning.
Combination of the names of the Hindu deities Bhawani and Shankar. In Hinduism Bhawani (or Bhavani) is a name of the goddess Parvati, who is the wife of Shankar, another name of the god Shiva.

column3: ภาวัฒน์, ภวัต(Thai)
column12: Variant transcription of Thai ภาวัฒน์ or ภวัต (see Phawat).
Alternate transcription of Hindi भावेश (see Bhavesh).
"The person that's broadminded, able to think further about future needs and wants".
Means "to be careful, cautious" in Zulu.
Means "watch the educated ones" in Zulu.
Means "look after the nations" in Zulu.
Means "look after the kingdom", from Zulu bheka "look after" and umbuso "kingdom, dominion".
Refers to a kind of bird native to the Central Highlands of Vietnam.

Means "wandering about for alms, medicancy", from Sanskrit भिक्षा (bhikṣā) meaning "begging, alms" and अटन (aṭana) meaning "wandering, roaming". This is the name of an ascpect of the Hindu god Shiva commonly depicted as a nude, four-armed ascetic associated with detachment from worldy ideas, humility, and the destruction of the ego of others.
Means "chosen, elected, appointed" in Mandaic, a derivative of ࡁࡄࡓ (bhr) meaning "to choose".

Ultimately derived from Sanskrit भुज् (bhuj) "to enjoy, consume, eat". This was the name of one of the ruler of the Kingdom of Malwa in central India, widely regarded as one of the most celebrated kings in the Indian history. After his death, he came to be featured in several legends as a righteous scholar-king.
Alternate transcription of Hindi/Marathi भूमिका (see Bhumika).
Means "black bee, black beetle" in Hindi.
Means "like a bee" from Sanskrit भ्रमर (bhramara) meaning "bee". This is the name of the Hindu goddess of bees.
From Tibetan བུ་ཆུང (bu-chung) meaning "small child, little boy".
Means "strength of the land" from Thai ภูมิ (phumi) meaning "land, earth, country, nation" and พล (phon) meaning "strength, power". It was borne by Thai king Bhumibol Adulyadej (1927-2016).
From Sanskrit भूमिका (bhūmikā) meaning "earth, ground, soil".
Alternate transcription of Hindi भूपेंद्र (see Bhupendra).
Means "lord of the earth" from Sanskrit भू (bhu) meaning "earth, land" combined with the name of the Hindu god Indra, used here to mean "lord".
From Sanskrit भू (bhu) meaning "earth, land" and ईश (īśa) meaning "ruler, lord, husband".
Variant of Bhupendra used by Sikhs.
From Sanskrit भूषण (bhūṣaṇa) meaning "embellishment, ornament, decoration".
Means "lord of the world" from Sanskrit भुवन (bhuvana) meaning "world, existence" and ईश (īśa) meaning "ruler, lord".

Means "mistress of the world, queen of the universe", from Sanskrit भुवन (bhuvana) meaning "earth, causing to exist" and ईश्वरी (īśvarī) meaning "queen, goddess, mistress". This is the name of a Hindu goddess representing the supreme energy of the universe and embodies the blueprint of existence.
Alternate transcription of Hindi भुवनेश (see Bhuvanesh).
Perhaps from Sino-Vietnamese 否 (bĩ) meaning "unlucky, unfortunate".
From Sino-Vietnamese 備 (bị) meaning "to prepare, provide, equip, complete" or 被 (bị) meaning "to cover, quilt, bedding".
Derived from Ancient Greek βία (bia) meaning "power, force, might". In Greek mythology, Bia is the personification of violence, force, anger, and raw energy.

Possibly derived from Ancient Greek βία (bia) meaning "force, power, violence" and δίκη (dike) meaning "justice, order". In Greek mythology, this was the name of a woman who accused Phrixus of assault when he spurned her advances.
Corsican diminutive of Biaghju and Sicilian diminutive of Biaggiu.

Of uncertain origin and meaning; current theories, however, include a form of Blahota or Bjegota. Biagota was possibly the wife of Boleslaus I of Bohemia, although her origins are unclear and the only evidence of her existence is in coins.
From Old Norse bjalfi meaning "fur, pelt".

column3: びあん(Japanese Hiragana)|美安, 美案, 美杏, 弥安, 弥晏, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 美 (bi) meaning "beautiful" or 弥 (bi) meaning "universally" combined with 安 (an) meaning "peace, quiet", 案 (an) meaning "plan", 杏 (an) meaning "apricot" or 晏 (an) meaning "peaceful, quiet, clear, late in the day". Other kanji combinations are possible.

Combination of Bianca and Italian bella, meaning "white-beautiful" in Italian. This is the name of the title character of the Italian fairy tale Biancabella and the Snake, written by Giovanni Francesco Straparola.
Diminutive of Bianchina. A known bearer of this name was the only sister of the famous navigator Christopher Columbus.
Hispanic variant of Vianney (see also Vianey).
From the Chinese 变 (biàn) meaning "change, transform" and 焕 (huàn) meaning "shining".

column3: 実安香, 琵杏香, 美安花, 美安香, 美杏華, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 実 (bi) meaning "seed; fruit; nut", 琵 (bi) meaning "guitar-like instrument" or 美 (bi) meaning "beautiful", 安 (an) meaning "calm, peaceful" or 杏 (an) meaning "apricot" combined with 香 (ka) meaning "fragrance" or 花 (ka) or 華 (ka) both meaning "flower". Other kanji combinations are possible.Usage of this name is, most likely, influenced by the name Bianca.
In English, this is an invented based on the popular name suffix -ianna. It is also Mexican, the meaning unknown. This is the name of a news anchor on Good Morning America, Bianna Golodryga.

Derived from either Greek βία (bia) meaning "bodily strength, force" or βίος (bios) meaning "life" combined with ἀνήρ (aner) meaning "man".This name was borne by a Greek poet from Bithynia, who lived in the 1st century AD.

column3: 彪, 标, 表, 飚, etc.(Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 彪 (biāo) meaning "tiger stripes, small tiger", 标 (biāo) meaning "mark, sign, award, prize", 表 (biǎo) meaning "surface, outside, exterior, table, form" or 飚 (biāo) meaning "whirlwind", as well as other characters that are pronounced similarly.
Means "bear-head" in Old Norse from bjǫrn "bear" and hǫfuð "head".
Old Norse and Old Danish variant of Biǫrn as well as short form of names containing the element Björn.
Derived from the Germanic name elements bjǫrn "bear" and laug possibly meaning "betrothed woman".
Form of Beatrice used in several languages.
Short form of names beginning with the element Bi-, such as Biserka and Biljana.

column3: 美波里(Japanese Kanji)|びばり(Japanese Hiragana)|ビバリ(Japanese Katakana)
column12: This name is used as 美波里 with 美 (bi, mi, utsuku.shii) meaning "beautiful, beauty," 波 (ha, nami) meaning "billow, wave, ripple" and 里 (ri, sato) meaning "parent's home, ri (unit of distance - equal to 3.927 km), village."One bearer of this name is actress Bibari "Beverly" Maeda (前田 美波里) (1948-). In her case, she got the name from her paternal grandmother (Beverly).This name is rarely given to girls, if given at all.
The given name of the artist, musician, and actress Bibbe Hansen (*1952).
Mainly a diminutive of Birgitta and its variant forms (see also Bibi).
Means "loathing, abhorring, detesting (unworthy acts in war)" in Sanskrit. This is an epithet of the hero Arjuna.
From Sanskrit विभु (vibhu) meaning "omnipresent, mighty, powerful".

column3: Биби(Bashkir)|日々, 妃々, 美々, etc.(Japanese Kanji)|ביבי(Hebrew)|비비(Korean Hangul)|雨雨(Korean Hanja)
column12: Diminutive of Birgitta and its various forms. It can also be used as a diminutive of other names beginning with or containing B, such as Bibiana and Beata. A known bearer was Swedish actress Berit Elisabet "Bibi" Andersson (1935-2019).
Derived from Persian بی‌بی‌ (bibi) meaning "madam, lady, matron" combined with the given name Aisha

column3: びびあん(Japanese Hiragana)|弥々杏, 微々鞍, 尾々案, 彌々晏, 日々安, 火々闇, 毘々庵, 未々行, etc.(Japanese Kanji)

From the Uzbek bibi meaning "mother, learned woman, authoritative woman" and Akhtar.
Form of Vivian borne by French swimmer Bienna Pélégry (1899-1989).
From the Uzbek bibi meaning "mother, learned woman, authoritative woman" and the given name Khadija.
From the Uzbek bibi meaning "mother, learned woman, authoritative woman" and hayot meaning "life".
From the Uzbek bibi meaning "mother, learned woman, authoritative woman" and jahon meaning "the world".
From the Uzbek bibi meaning "mother, learned woman, authoritative woman" and jamol meaning "beauty".
Croatian and Slovene form of Bibiana.
From the Uzbek bibi meaning "mother, learned woman, authoritative woman" and the given name Maryam.
Coined by Sabino Arana Goiri and Koldo Elizalde as a Basque equivalent of Viviana and Viviane.
Likely a diminutive of Viviana, Bibiana, Vivencia, and other names with a similar sound. This is also a diminutive of any name containing the letter B or V.
Means "I have believed or accepted" in Ijaw.
From the Uzbek bibi meaning "mother, learned woman, authoritative woman" and niyoz meaning "entreaty, alms".
From the Uzbek bibi meaning "mother, learned woman, authoritative woman" and novvot meaning "rock sugar".
From the Uzbek bibi meaning "mother, learned woman, authoritative woman" and nozik meaning "fine, delicate".
Derived from Persian بی‌بی‌ (bibi) meaning "madam, lady, matron" combined with Kazakh нұр (nur) meaning "light" (of Arabic origin).
From the Uzbek bibi meaning "mother, learned woman, authoritative woman" and oy meaning "moon".
From the Uzbek bibi meaning "mother, learned woman, authoritative woman" and qamar meaning "moon".
From the Uzbek bibi meaning "mother, learned woman, authoritative woman" and qand meaning "sugarcube".
From the Uzbek bibi meaning "mother, learned woman, authoritative woman" and qiz meaning "girl".
From the Uzbek bibi meaning "mother, learned woman, authoritative woman" and the given name Rajab.
From the Uzbek bibi meaning "mother, learned woman, authoritative woman" and rayhon meaning "basil".
