From the Chinese characters 碧 (bì) meaning "jade; green, blue" and 窈 (yǎo) meaning "obscure, secluded; refined" or 谣 (yáo) meaning "folksong, ballad".
Of uncertain meaning. This was the name of a Dharawal woman of the Gweagal clan who was knowledge holder of the Dharawal culture, entrepeneur, and tour guide.
From the Chinese 碧 (bì) meaning "jade, green, blue" and 殷 (yīn) meaning "many, great, abundant, flourishing".
From Japanese 日 (bi) meaning "sun, day" combined with 和 (yori) meaning "peace, harmony". Other kanji combinations are possible.
From the Chinese 馝 (bì) meaning "fragrance" and 幽 (yōu) meaning "quiet, secluded, tranquil, dark".
From Chinese 碧玉 (bìyù) meaning "jasper". Other hanzi combinations are possible.
From the Chinese 碧 (bì) meaning "jade, green, blue" and 圆 (yuán) meaning "circle, round" or 缘 (yuán) meaning "hem, margin" or "reason, fate".
From the Chinese 璧 (bì) meaning "piece of jade with hole" and 玥 (yuè) meaning "mysterious gem, mythological pearl" or 悦 (yuè) meaning "pleased, contented".

A nickname whose meaning is particular to the bearer. Notable namesakes include professional baseball player James Raleigh "Biz" Mackey (1897 -1965). Mackey's name was short for "business" because it was said of his opponents that he 'gave them the business'. In other words as a catcher, he kept up a running commentary to distract batters. In more recent years Biz Stone (1974-), co-founder of the social media site Twitter, bears the name based on a diminutive of his childhood pronunciation of his given name Christopher.
Derived from Kurdish zana meaning "informed, smart".
Bosnian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Byzas.

Later form of Vezhan, of which the meaning is uncertain. It may possibly be etymologically related to the New Persian verb بختن (bextan), which can mean "to sift" as well as "to sieve". The Middle Persian (i.e. older) equivalent of that verb is wēxtan meaning "to sift, to select, to choose, to separate" and is ultimately derived from Old Iranian waik- or waič- meaning "to separate". It should be noted that in Middle Persian, there is another verb wēxtan, but that one has a different meaning and slightly different etymology than the aforementioned verb whose meaning and origin I just explained. This second verb wēxtan means "to swing, to brandish, to throw" and is ultimately derived from Old Iranian waig-. Due to the fact that these verbs and their Old Iranian roots resemble each other very closely, both are an equal candidate for being the root of the given name Bizhan.
From the Chinese 馝 (bì) meaning "fragrance" and 昭 (zhāo) meaning "bright, luminous".
From the Chinese 必 (bì) meaning "surely, most certainly" and 珍 (zhēn) meaning "valuable, precious, rare" or 贞 (zhēn) meaning "faithful, loyal".
Meaning "Lynx woman", from the Anishnaabemowin words "Bizhiw" meaning "Lynx", and "Ikwe" meaning "Woman".

Possibly means "she who is pleasing". Bizilla was a love goddess considered to be the "sukkal" (vizier deity) for the goddess Ninlil. She is occasionally counted among the courtiers of Inanna, and is also closely associated with Nanaya.
Means "eunuch". In the book of Esther, the second of the seven eunuchs of King Ahasuerus' harem.
Derived from Old Norse bjǫrk "birch tree" (compare Bjarki) and herr "army, warrior".
Combination of the Old Norse name elements bjǫrk "birch tree" or bjarkan "birch tree; name of the B-rune" and ey "island; flat land along a coast" or ey "good fortune".
Derived from the Old Norse elements bjǫrk "birch tree" (genitive bjarkar) and lind "spring, fountain", which is possibly related to lind "linden tree".

Of unknown origin and meaning. Current theories include a direct adoption of Icelandic bjarmi "loom, gleam of light" and a derivation from bjarmar, the Old Norse name for a branch of Finno-Ugric peoples called Permians in English (formerly also Bjarmians). Their territory, Bjarmaland, was mentioned in Norse sagas since the Viking Age and in geographical accounts until the 16th century. It is assumed that the tribal name is related to Finnish perämaa "far-away land" and Hungarian perem "edge; verge".
Derives from a combination of Old Norse element bjǫrn "bear (animal)" and Sigrún.
Female form of Bjarni, with -sína suffix.
Sorbian form of Bernhard. Bjarnat Krawc (German: Bernhard Schneider), born 1861, was a Sorbian conductor.
Derived from the Old Norse elements bjǫrn "bear" and dís "goddess; woman, lady; sister".
Derived from the Old Norse elements bjǫrn "bear" and ey "island; flat land along a coast" or ey "good fortune".
Combination of Bjarni and Old Norse -freðr, derived from friðr meaning "love, peace". (As a name element, Old Norse friðr may mean "protection, defense".)
Derived from the Old Norse elements bjǫrn "bear" (genitive bjarnar) and fríðr "beautiful", originally "beloved".
Derived from the Old Norse elements bjǫrn meaning "bear" and garðr meaning "enclosure, yard, stronghold".
Derived from Old Norse bjǫrn "bear" and heðinn "jacket of fur or skin".
Female form of Bjarni, an Old Norse diminutive of Bjǫrn.
Derived from Old Norse bjǫrn "bear" and vǫrðr "guard".
Feminine form of Bjart and Bjartur.
Combination of Old Norse bjartr "bright" and mærr "famous".
Derived from the Old Norse elements bjartr "bright, shining" and mey, a variant form of mær "maid, girl, virgin".
Combination of Old Norse bjartr meaning "bright" (compare Bjartur) and the name of the Norse god Þórr (see Thor).
It is suggested that this name derives from Scottish Gaelic Bethóc. A notable bearer was a twelfth-century woman purported to have been the mother of Eysteinn Haraldsson, King of Norway.
Derived from the old Slavic word белъ (belu) meaning "white". Cognate of Běla.
Combination of the Old Norse name elements bjǫrn "bear" and mund "protection".
Derived from Albanian bjeshkë "mountain, alpine pasture".
Younger form of Belwar. In Norse mythology this was the name of a jǫtunn.
Short form of names starting or ending with the Old Norse name element bjǫrg meaning "help, save, rescue".
Masculine form of Bjørg or a short form of any male name beginning with the Old Norse name element bjǫrg "help, save, rescue".
Derived from the Old Norse elements bjǫrg "help, deliverance" and heiðr "bright, clear" or heiðr "honour, worth".
Derived from the Old Norse elements bjǫrg "protection, help" and ulfr "wolf".
Faroese form of Björk which was also adopted into Danish and Norwegian.
Variant of Björn or Bjørn used outside of Scandinavia and Germany.
Norwegian modern form of Bernard, from Old Norse Bjarnarðr.
Derived from the Old Norse name elements bjǫrn "bear" and hildr "battle; fight".
Female form of Björn, a variant form derived from Bjarnína.
Combination of Bjørn and Norwegian stjerne meaning "star". Bjørnstjerne Bjørnson (1832-1910) was a Norwegian writer and Nobel laureate (Literature, 1903).
Derived from Old Norse björn "bear" combined with Old Norse úlfr "wolf." Icelandic equivalent of Bernolf.
Formed from Bjørn and the Old Norse element valdr "ruler". Also compare the Germanic cognate Bernwald.
Feminine form of Bjartr. This is the name of one of Menglǫð's maids in Norse mythology.

Means "blue" in Swedish. Ultimately derived from Old Norse blár meaning "blue" but often denoting "dark, black" (compare Bláinn). A few hundred years ago sometimes used as a variant or short form of Blasius.
Derived from Manx blaa "bloom, flower" (but also "pride, heyday"), this name has been occasionally used as an equivalent of Flora.
Diminutive of Blacatz or Blacas. The Latin form is Blacacius.
Transferred use of the surname Black, or directly taken from the color.
A rabbit who escaped from a warren called Efrafa in the book Watership Down by Richard Adams.
From the name of the animal, introduced into popular culture by the 1968 song of the same name performed by The Beatles.In some cases it might also be a transferred use of the surname Blackbird.

As a nickname the meaning is particular to the bearer, perhaps referring to dark hair color or complexion. That was the case for sportswriter William Forrest "Blackie" Sherrod (1919-2016). Blackie can also be a diminutive for given names or surnames containing the element black such as Blackburn or Blackwell. The former was a given name for Virginia House of Delegates speaker Edgar Blackburn "Blackie" Moore (1897-1980).
Transferred use of the surname Blackman.
Transferred use of the surname Blackshear.
Transferred use of the surname Blackwell.
Form of Old Norse Blakkr which occurs in Domesday Book.
Name of a Frankish Dux of Aquitanien

Transferred use of the surname Blade or from the Old English blæd ‘leaf of a plant,' of Germanic origin; related to Dutch blad and German Blatt.Blade is the 'hero' name of Marvel comics half-vampire, vampire-hunter, protagonist Eric Brooks. He was portrayed by actor Wesley Snipes in the 'Blade' film trilogy and Kirk "Sticky Fingaz" Jones in the television adaptation.
Transferred use of the surname Bladen. Has resurged in modern terms because of the popular sounds found in other names such as Blade and Braden.
East Prussian German short form of Ladislaus.
Old English byname derived from blæc meaning "black, dark". This is a cognate of Old Norse Blakkr.
Derived from the Old English elements blæc "black, dark" and mære "famous".
Derived from the Old English elements blæc "black" and mann "man".
Means "black stone" in Old English, from blæc "black" and stan "stone".
Derived from the Old English elements blæc "black" and sunu "son".
Derived from the Old English elements blæc "black, dark" and wine "friend".
Derived from Old English blæc "black" and wulf "wolf". This is the source of the place name Blakesley (see Blakesley).
Derived from the Old Norse elements blær "wind gust, gentle breeze" and dís "goddess; woman, lady; seeress".
This name derives from Old English elements blǣd "splendor" and swiþ "strong, mighty".

Means "raven", literally "blue-black one", a derivative of Old Norse blár "blue, dark, livid" (the colour used to describe corpses and bruises, e.g. hel-blár "black as death"). This was originally a byname.

Coincides with and is most often used in the sense of the Icelandic noun blær "gentle breeze, gust of wind", but was possibly originally popularised by the novel Mutiny on the Bounty (1932), deriving from the Icelandic pronunciation of the character William Bligh’s surname. It was originally an exclusively masculine name, but was approved for feminine use by the Icelandic government after a court ruling in 2013.

on of the Earl of Llychlyn and one of the Three Just Knights of Arthur’s Court. He was dedicated to preserving justice through “earthly Law”, in contrast to his fellow knights, who followed the Law of the Church and the Law of Arms.He’s also said to have been among the Twenty-Four Knights of Arthur’s Court.There may be a relation between this knight and Merlin’s foster-father Blaise.

Feminine diminutive of Blaesus. Blaesilla (364–384) was a Roman widow and disciple of Jerome. Most of the knowledge about Blaesilla's life comes from the writings of Jerome, in which he described her piety and virtue. She also inspired Jerome to translate the book of Ecclesiastes. Blaesilla was widowed at the age of 18; at first, she enjoyed her freedom as a widow, but after a life-threatening fever, became "a changed woman" and a severe ascetic, practicing fasting as a spiritual discipline. Her fasts dramatically weakened her, and she died within four months, at the age of 20. Modern writers and researchers have connected Blaesilla with the eating disorder anorexia nervosa; she has been called "the first victim of anorexia nervosa, described in the literature".
Derived from the Old Norse elements blær "gentle breeze, gust of wind" and varr "aware, cautious".

Combination of the Old Norse name elements blár "blue; dark; black" and ey "island; flat land along a coast" (which is also often related to the Old Norse name element auja "(gift of) luck; fortune").
Derived from the Slavic elements blag "good, gentle, kind, blessed" and mir "peace".
A Knight of the Round Table defeated and taken prisoner by the Queen’s Knights during a tournament.
From Old Norse blár meaning "blue, dark, black".
French form of Blasia and feminine form of Blaise.
Elaboration of Blake using the popular name suffix lyn.
From Old English blæc meaning "black, dark" or blac meaning "pale" combined with Old English eg meaning "island" or hæg meaning "enclosure".
Transferred use of the surname Blakesley.An example of a bearer of this name is Blakesley Grace Sutter (b. 2009), the daughter of the American reality TV personality Ryan Sutter and his wife Trista.
Old Norse byname meaning "black". It is a cognate of Blæc.

Son of Nestor, brother of Sir Bleoberis de Ganis, cousin of Lancelot, and a Knight of the Round Table.Of the two brothers, Blamore was accounted the better man of arms. Blamore and Bleoberis once arraigned King Anguish of Ireland for the death of a cousin of theirs. Blamore was the one who fought the actual trial by combat against Anguish’s champion, Sir Tristram. Defeated, Blamore tried to insist on death rather than surrender. Bleoberis seconded his brother’s request, but Tristram and the judges refused to allow it. Later, when Lancelot and Guenevere were accused of treason, Blamore joined other knights in pledging his support to Lancelot and followed him into exile. Lancelot made him Duke of Limousin in Guienne.After Arthur’s death he became a hermit at Glastonbury and assisted in Lancelot’s burial. Once he had stabilized his own lands, he joined Bleoberis, Ector, and Bors on a crusade to Jerusalem, where they died fighting the Turks on Good Friday.

A knight who owned a white hart that Gawaine pursued on his first adventure.Gawaine chased the hart into Blamoure’s castle, where Gawaine’s hounds killed it. This induced Blamoure to slay two of Gawaine’s hounds. Enraged, Gawaine engaged Blamoure in combat, defeated him, and prepared to cut off his head.As Gawaine’s sword fell, Blamoure’s paramour threw herself across her lover’s body and was decapitated. Aghast, Gawaine granted mercy to Blamoure and sent him to Arthur’s court.
A masculine equivalent of Blanche. Also compare Demiblanc and Blanchard, other names recorded in Domesday Book.
Combination of Blanca and Nieves. This is the Spanish form of the tale character name Snow White.
Occitan form of Blanca and Blanche.

An Hungarian princess and a companion of Florete, the daughter of Emperor Filimenis.When Filimenis went to war with Arthur, Blanchandine and Florete accompanied the emperor’s army. They fell in love with Gawaine and Floriant, respectively, and defected from Filimenis’s camp to Arthur’s.Eventually, the war ended and Blanchandine married Gawaine.

Means "white flower" in French. It is borne by a number of characters, who reflect purity and idealized beauty, in literature of the High Middle Ages, notably in the romances of Floris and Blanchefleur and Tristan and Iseult.
One of Arthur’s knights in the Middle-English Sir Gawain and the Carl of Carlisle.

The fairy mistress of Gawain, by whom she had a son named Guinglain.She raised Guinglain ignorant of his true name. Upon attaining knighthood, he was forced to adopt the label ‘The Fair Unknown’.Blanchemal lived in the island of Gernemue.
Combination of Blanche and Neige, used as a French translation of Snow White.
Latinized form of Blanche, recorded in 14th-century French-speaking Switzerland.
Either a transferred use of the surname Bland or an English form of Blandus.
Variant of Blenda or taken directly from Swedish blända "to dazzle, to blind (by bright light)".
Feminine form of Blandus. Blanda is also the name of an ancient Roman city in southern Italy.
Blandamour, whose name indicates bland, or boring, love, is a knight in Book 4 of "The Faerie Queene". He and Paridell have a superficial friendship.
Fântâna Blanduziei ('Blanduzia's Fountain' in English) was a literary and political weekly magazine which was first published in 1888 and run by Romanian poet Mihai Eminescu.
From the English word blanket. A famous bearer of this is Michael Jackson's son, whose nickname is Blanket Jackson.
Variant of Blanchefleur used in Eilhart von Oberge's 12th century Middle High German romance Tristrant, the oldest surviving complete version of the Tristan and Iseult story in any language.
Means "babbling pole; staff". This is the name of a Jotunn in Norse mythology.

Knight of the Round Table and godson of King Bors of Gannes.He fought for Arthur against the rebellion at the beginning of the king’s reign, and also against the Saxons at Carmelide and against King Agrippe in the Waste Land.His name seems to possess the same root as Bleoberis, to whom Blaris may be identical. He might be identical with Plaarin.
Transferred use of the surname Blase or a variant of Blaise.
Alternate name of Elaine, half-sister of Arthur, used in the Vulgate Merlin.

This name can be a hellenized form of Blasius (see Blaise), but it can also be a genuine Greek name in its own right. In that case, it is derived from the Greek noun βλαστός (blastos) meaning "young shoot, bud, sprout", which itself is ultimately derived from the Greek verb βλαστέω (blasteo) meaning "to sprout". Also compare the Greek noun βλάστη (blaste) meaning "growth". Finally, the name Blasios is an old name - Vlasios is the modern form. It should be noted, though, that despite being different from each other, both Blasios and Vlasios are technically spelled the same in the Greek script (namely, as Βλάσιος). This is explained by the fact that the first letter of the name (the beta) was a 'b' in ancient Greek, but it is a 'v' in modern Greek.

Combination of Swedish blå "blue" and sippa "anemone". This is the Swedish name for the plant hepatica nobilis, also known as common hepatica. It is the middle name of Swedish folk singer Sofia Karlsson.
Derived from Ancient Greek βλαστός (blastos) meaning "a bud, sprout, shoot", figuratively "offspring, scion". This was the name of a nymph in Greek mythology, mother of the seer Epimenides.
Derived from the Greek noun βλαστός (blastos) meaning "sprout, shoot, bud", which ultimately comes from the Greek verb βλαστάνω (blastano) meaning "to bud, to sprout, to grow".

Latinized form of Blastos. According to the Bible, Blastus was the chamberlain of Herod Agrippa (Acts 12:20), a mediator for the Sidonians and Tyrians, and was believed to be involved in the events that led to Herod's death.
Latinized form of a Germanic name derived from the elements blad "blade, leaf" and berht "bright".
Derived from Irish blath "flower; blossom". This was the name of two virgin saints. It was usually Anglicized as Flora.
Possibly means "flower son" in Irish, from Old Irish bláth "flower" and macc "son".
Old Norse byname, combination of blár "blue", "dark", "black" and tǫnn "tooth". Means "blue-tooth".
From Catalan blau, cognate with English Blue.
From the book series Black Dagger Brotherhood by J. R. Ward
Likely an invented name made to sound like Clayton.
Croatian short form of Blaženka and Slovene variant of Blažka.
Name used in reference to St. Blaze.
Diminutive of Blagoje (also compare Blaž). A notable bearer of this name is the Montenegrin prime minister and president Blažo Jovanović (1907-1976).
Transferred usage of the surname Bleaker.

12th-century Welsh storyteller known in French as Bledhericus, Bleheris or Blihis (Blihos) Bliheris (possibly Bledri ap Cydifor, who is mentioned in several texts, including being credited by both Thomas of Britain and Wauchier de Denain as the original source of their early Arthurian poems. References to the narrative authority of one Master Blihis (Maistre Blihis) repeat throughout the Elucidation, wherein the character named Blihos Bliheris also appears as knight.
Derived from Welsh blaidd "wolf" and rhi "ruler".
Transferred use of the surname Bleecker.
Transferred use of the surname Bleeker.
Meaning "stay pious". The name is literally made up of the two German words bleibe, meaning "stay", and fromm, meaning "pious" or "devout".
Variant of Bleiddudd. Bleiddud was Bishop of St David's (then known as Menevia) in Wales from 1061 to 1071.
Welsh form of the Brythonic name *Bledjojüd- meaning "wolf lord", from Proto-Brythonic *blėð meaning "wolf" (Welsh blaidd) and *jʉð meaning "lord" (Welsh udd).

Thought to mean "Wolf-Man", from Welsh blaidd meaning "wolf".Bleiddwn is the offspring of brothers Gwydion and Gilfaethwy when they were transformed into wolves. Math took him and transformed him into a human being, baptising him Bleiddwn ("wolf-man").
In Henrich’s Diu Crône, a lady at Arthur’s court who failed in a chastity test.

Derived from Breton bleiz "wolf; gray" and thus nowadays commonly considered the Breton equivalent of French Loup, this name was in former times also used as a phonetic approximation to Blois and given in honor of the Blessed Charles of Blois, Duke of Brittany.From the early 1600s onwards, when every given name had to be linked with a Catholic saint, Bleiz was also used as a Breton bona fide equivalent of Saint Blaise due to its phonetic similarities.

From a place name which was derived from Old Swedish blædh "blade". According to Swedish tradition, the place was named after a woman named Blenda who defended the land against invading Danes in the local men's absence. It is also associated with the Swedish verb blända meaning "to dazzle, to blind".

Tristan’s mother in the Icelandic Saga af Tristram ok Ísoud. She replaces Blancheflur (Blancheflor) from the earlier German sources and is the counterpart of Blesinbil in Norse Tristan legend.The daughter of King Philippus and Queen Philippia (Philippía) of England, she revolted against her brother, Mórodd (Mark), when her parents died. The short rebellion ended in a truce.Her lover, Plegrus, was killed jousting with the Spanish knight Kalegras, with whom she fell in love. They had a son, Trostan, and she died soon after her lover.

A Knight of the Round Table from Gannes, first mentioned by Chrétien de Troyes. His name may derive from a twelfth-century storyteller named Bleheris mentioned in several texts.Son of Nestor, godson of King Bors, brother to Sir Blamore de Ganis, and cousin to Lancelot. He is father of Nestor of the Fountain, and Lord of the Castle of Gannes. He’s sometimes called “Bleoberis of the Wilderness”.
Derived from Albanian bleron "to become verdant, to sprout".
Portuguese and Spanish form of Blaesilla.
Variant of Blesila influenced by names ending in -ilda.
From the English word bless meaning "to invoke divine favor upon".
Means 'Blessed Son'. It is a Christian name.

From the English word "blessed" meaning "having divine aid, or protection, or other blessing; held in veneration; revered", ultimately from Old English blētsian, blēdsian "to consecrate (with blood)".
Blending of the English word bless and the name Jessica.
Plural form of Blessing. It is most used in Malawi.
From the English words bless and more, chiefly used in Zimbabwe.
From the given name Blessing combined with the ending yn (see lyn).

Derived from Albanian bletë "bee". According to Albanian folk belief, the bee is a sacred animal: when an animal ceases to live, Albanians predominantly use the verb ngordh while when a bee ceases to live, the verb vdes is used (which is used to refer to human death), alluding that bees are beings of a higher caste, comparable to humans.A famous bearer of this name is Bleta "Bebe" Rexha (b. 1989), an Albanian-American singer and songwriter.
From the French word for "Blue". Not typically used in France.

Of uncertain origin and meaning. Some academics consider Bleuzenn a Breton cognate of either Welsh Blodeuyn or Welsh Blodwen while others consider this name a derivation from Middle Breton bleuzuenn "flower". Due to this latter theory, Bleuzenn is occasionally claimed to be the Breton form of Flora. Either way, Saint Bleuzenn is the Breton patron saint of flowers.

The first element is derived from Old High German blich "lightning, glow" or blicchan "to flash, to shine." The second element is derived from gardan "to hedge in, to enclose, to fence in" or from Gothic gards "house, garden, (court)yard."
Derived from Old High German blich "lightning, glow" or blicchan "to flash, to shine" combined with Old High German helm "helmet, protection."
Derived from Old High German blich "lightning, glow" or blicchan "to flash, to shine" combined with Old Norse hildr "battle."
Derived from Old High German blich "lightning, glow" or blicchan "to flash, to shine" combined with þruþ "strength."
From the name elements blid meaning "cheerful, mild, joyful" and rat meaning "advisor, counsel"The name element blid is derived from the same root as the english word blithe.
From the name elements blid meaning "cheerful, mild, joyful" and hiltja meaning "battle"The name element blid is derived from the same root as the english word blithe.
Name of a 7th century Italian monk.

Used by author Suzanne Collins in her novel 'Catching Fire' for District Seven's male Quarter Quell tribute, likely given in reference to the English word for plant disease. It may ultimately come from Old English blæce/blæcðu, a skin condition, or from Old Norse blikna, meaning "to become pale".
Modern word name; Dutch for "lightning". Popular name for fast pets, such as dogs or horses.

Invented by author José Saramago for his book "Memorial do Convento", first published in 1982. In this work, Blimunda is called Seven Moons (Sete-Luas), for her ability to see in the dark and through people and objects. In the end, she marries Baltasar, who is known as Seven Suns (Sete-Sóis).
Derived from Albanian bli(n) "sturgeon" or bli(r) "linden tree, lime tree; linden flower".
Derived from Albanian bli(r) "linden tree, lime tree; linden flower" and erë "wind; scent".
Allegedly a corruption of Moninne. This name was usually anglicized as Blanche.
A phonetic rendering of the English word "blinks". Used by the eponymous feline main character of the Xbox game 'Blinx: The Time Sweeper".
One of Arthur’s knights in Arthour and Merlin, who participated in the battle against Rions’ (Ryons) Saxons at Carhaix.
Transferred use of the surname Bliss or simply from the English word "bliss".
Invented name. Means "perfect happiness" in American English.
Combination of the English-speaking word 'bliss' and the popular suffix 'tina.
Derived from Old Saxon blīthi, Old High German blīdi meaning "happy, joyous" and Proto-Germanic *geldą meaning "reward, gift, money".
Means "gentleness, friendliness" in Icelandic, ultimately derived from Old Norse blíðr "kind, gentle, friendly", making this name a cognate of Blythe.
Derived from Old English blíðe "merry; friendly" (compare Blíða and Blida).
From the name elements blid meaning "cheerful, mild, joyful" and heri meaning "army"The name element blid is derived from the same root as the english word blithe.
From the word blitz, meaning a sudden and strong military attack, which is derived from German blitzkrieg.
Short form of names containing the name element BLID "blithe, joyous, happy".
The name is composed of the elements bliz (close, near) and bor (fight; struggle). The designated nameday in Poland is January 28 and March 12.
Meaning unknown, though it might come from Old English blac "pale, shining, white" or blæc "black". The surname Bloxham derived from this name.
Blodrin was a treacherous Elf in Tolkien's legendarium, known as Blodren in some versions.

Derived from the Dutch word bloem meaning "flower".In the Netherlands, the best known example of a bearer of this name is Bloem Van Landuyt (b. 2004), who is one of the daughters of Dutch actress Angela Schijf (b. 1979) and her husband Tom Van Landuyt (b. 1967), a Belgian actor.

As a Dutch name, it is a variant of Bloem. But as a Yiddish name, it is a transcription of Blume. A known bearer of this name was Bloeme Evers-Emden (1926-2016), a Dutch Jewish teacher, child psychologist, and author who attended school with the famous diarist Anne Frank (1929-1945).

The first element of this name is derived from Dutch bloem "flower", which ultimately comes from Gothic blôma. The second element is derived from Gothic hardus (hart in Old High German) "brave, hardy".
Derived from Polish błogi "blessed, blissful" combined with Slavic slav "glory". As such, the meaning of this name is roughly "blissful glory".
Daughter of Urbin of the Mountain (Urpin) and sister of Brun, a knight killed by Gawaine.To avenge her brother, she plotted Gawaine’s murder, but she eventually fell in love with Gawaine.
Daughter of Urbin of the Mountain (Urpin) and sister of Brun, a knight killed by Gawaine. To avenge her brother, she plotted Gawaine’s murder, but she eventually fell in love with Gawaine.
Combination of the Old Norse elements blóm "bloom, blossom, flower" and either ey "island; flat land along a coast" or ey "good fortune".

German name meaning "blond".The word "blond" derives from Old French "blont" = "fair", "blond", via Medieval Latin "blundus" = "yellow", perhaps from Frankish "blund", possibly related to Old English "blonden-feax" = "gray-haired" from "blondan, blandan" = "to mix"
Possibly an extremely rare Anglicized form of Blandine influenced by Blondie and Dean.

According to legend, Blondel was a troubadour who rescued the English king Richard the Lionheart, who had been captured while returning from the Crusades and was being held for ransom. The story goes that Blondel traveled Europe looking for Richard by playing the first verse of a song only they knew. When he heard Richard playing the second verse, he knew he had found him.The name Blondel refers to someone with blond hair. The troubadour's real name was Jean de Nesle; he was nicknamed Blondel because of his blond hair.

From a diminutive of French blonde meaning "fair-haired". This is the name of two characters in Madame d'Aulnoy's fairy tales: Belle-Etoile's mother in Princess Belle-Etoile (whose sisters are named Roussette and Brunette) and a minor character in The Imp Prince. It was later used by the Comtesse de Ségur for the protagonist of her fairy tale Blondine, Bonne-Biche, and Beau-Minon; this Blondine is a girl who becomes lost in an enchanted forest.

Name of New York farmer Bloodgood Haviland Cutter (1817–1906). He was known as a 'farmer poet'. Well known author Mark Twain humorously dubbed Cutter the 'Poet Lariat' in Twain's non-fiction travelogue 'Innocents Abroad'. Cutter's first name was his paternal grandmother's maiden name.
From the English word bloom, ultimately derived from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleh₃- ("to thrive, flower, bloom").
Perhaps related to the word blosc "blast"
Means "the one with the bloody hair". The bloody hair is supposedly referring to red sea foam. In Norse mythology, Blóðughadda was the daughter of Ægir and Rán.
The name of a purported medieval Swedish queen consort, meaning "the female sacrificer" or "the maiden sacrificer".
Related to Norwegian blava "to shine". This is the name of a dwarf in Norse mythology.
Italian form of Blue and English diminutive of Bluford.
From the name of the flower, used to some extent as a first name when flower names were in vogue at the end of the 19th century.
From the name of the small, round berry.
Very rare but has been used in the US since the 1700s, particularly in Mississippi and Oklahoma.
From the English name for the bluebonnet flower.
Variant of Bluford, or transferred use of the surname Blueford.

Native American Chinook legends tell tales about of a hero named Bluejay who gets into rather sticky situations at times and other times helps out humanity.In one of the tales Bluejay is a female and another set of stories it is a different person named Bluejay and they are male.
Derived from French bluet, a variant of bleuet, "cornflower".

Diminutive of Blue, often used as a nickname for a red-head in Australia. This is the name of the titular character in the Australian children's cartoon Bluey (2018), whose name possibly comes from the Australian Cattle Dog named Bluey, who holds the world record as the oldest dog to have ever lived.
Variation of Buford, possibly transfer of the surname Bluford.
Of unknown origin and meaning. The name was usually anglicized as Blanche.
German-Yiddish form of Bluma. The name coincides with German Blume "flower".
A giant who once managed to capture Jack the Giant-Killer, but was killed, along with his brothers, when Jack managed to escape.

Bluto is the name of the main antagonist of the famous Popeye series since 1932 - partly. There was a brief change of name to Brutus (1957 - 1978) during an apparent copyright dispute, but his name was reverted back to Bluto during the 1970s where it has remained his official name (although a 1988 comic book tried to remedy this by making Bluto and Brutus twin brothers).
Transferred use of the surname Bly.
The name is used in Northern Iraq.
Arabized form of the Sahidic Coptic name Panoute.
Arabized form of the Bohairic Coptic name Phnouti. In other words, one could say that this is a cognate or a variant form of Bnouda.
Short form of Willibrord, though it can also be a simplified spelling of Beau.
From Sino-Vietnamese 蒲 (bồ) meaning "cattail, vine" or 菩 (bồ) referring to a kind of tree.
From Sino-Vietnamese 部 (bộ) meaning "part, division; ministry; classifier".
From Sino-Korean 珤 "treasure, jewel; precious, rare" and 雅 "elegant, graceful, refined". A famous bearer is South Korean singer Kwon BoA (1986-).
This archaic West Frisian given name can be a variant form of Boye as well as be a derivation of West Frisian boai meaning "boy".
Means "farmer, peasant, landowner" in Old Norse.
An epithet that Jesus gave to the apostles James and John in the Book of Mark, traditionally said to mean "sons of thunder".
Transferred use of the surname Boardman.
Scottish Gaelic form of Boaz used in the Bible.
Means "His kingdom drew near" in Setswana.

A diminutive or variation of Bob. This is the name of Boba Fett who is a bounty hunter from Star Wars. Boba Fett is a sly reference to another hotshot jockey, Bob Falfa, the drag racer played by none other than Mr. Ford in ''American Graffiti.''

column3: 보배(Korean Hangul)|寳培, 寳䔒, 甫培, 㻉培, 甫拜, etc.(Korean Hanja)
column12: From Korean 보배 (bobae) meaning "treasure," shifted from Middle Korean 보ㅂᆡ (popoy), from Sino-Korean 寶貝. Other hanja used for this naem include 寶 (bo) meaning "treasure," 甫 (bo) meaning "big; beginning," 㻉 (bo) meaning "jade," 培 (bae) meaning "culture, cultivation; education," 䔒 (bae) meaning "bud" and 拜 (bae) meaning "prostration; bending, stooping."

One might think that this name is a blend of the name Bob with Jaan, but that is not the case. In Belgium and the Netherlands, the use of this rare first name originated with the Flemish singer and musician Bobbejaan Schoepen (1925-2010). It was not his real first name, but rather, his stage name (which he adopted in 1945). He took the name from the South African war song "Bobbejaan klim die berg", which translates to "Baboon Climbs the Mountain" in English. In the Afrikaans language, bobbejaan means "baboon" and is ultimately derived from Dutch baviaan, which also means "baboon". Despite this origin and meaning of the name, some Belgian and Dutch parents have been inspired (thanks to Bobbejaan Schoepen) to bestow this name as an actual first name upon their sons. As such, in 2010, there was a total of 19 male bearers (of all ages) in all of the Netherlands. Lastly, it might be interesting to know that Bobbejaan Schoepen founded a Belgian amusement park in 1961, which he had named after himself. It is called Bobbejaanland (which basically means "land of Bobbejaan") and is located in or near the village of Lichtaart.
Either a variant of Bobette, most likely influenced by Beth, or a combination of Bob/Bobbie and Beth.
From the English-speaking word bobbin, which spools thread.
Variant of either Bobbijo or Bobbyjoe.
Combination of Bobby and Joe. Bobbijo is the feminine counterpart.
Means "grandmother" in Yiddish. This is the feminine equivalent of Zeyde.
Variant of Robert using the short form Bob.
Variant of Babette, most likely influenced by Bobbie or as a feminine diminutive of Bob.
Dutch feminine variant of Bob, or a pet form of Robina, Robine or Robien.
Tajik and Uzbek form of Babur, possibly via Babir. Also compare Bobur.A known bearer of this name is the Uzbek professional soccer player Bobir Davlatov (b. 1996).
From the given name Bobir combined with Persian جان (jān) meaning "soul, life".
Coined by Sándor Weöres who apparently based it on Hungarian bóbita "tuft" referring to the feathers on a bird's head.
This was the name of a 10th century saint.
From Tajik бобо (bobo) meaning "grandfather" combined with Persian جان (jān) meaning "soul, life".
From the surname Bobola. This name is used as a second given name with Andrzej as a first name in honor of Andrzej Bobola, a 17th-century Polish saint.
Means "nothing can be compared to my own" in Ijaw.
Means "I didn't do it on my own" in Ijaw.
A French hypochoristic form of Ratbod.
Variant of Barbara, influenced by Bob.

Short form of Robert, Robin and other names. Famous bearers of this name include the South African-Canadian painter and potter Bobs Cogill Haworth (1900-1988), and American actor Bobs Watson (1930-1999).
From the English surname Bobson meaning "son of Bob"
Bobur means Lion, Tiger, brave as Tiger, brave as Lion. This name actually was used as an adjective for lion/tiger
Tajik and Uzbek form of Baburbek.
Combination of the given name Bobur and the Persian word جان (jān), meaning "soul, life".
From Sino-Vietnamese 卜 (bốc) meaning "to divine, prophesy". This was the name of Quách Bốc, a general who revolted against Emperor Lý Cao Tông in 1209.
From the Chinese 伯 (bó) meaning "older brother" and 偲 (cāi) meaning "talented".
From the Chinese 博 (bó) meaning "rich, plentiful" or "play, gamble, win" and 沧 (cāng) meaning "dark blue, dark green".

The King of Media who served the Roman Procurator Lucius.Lucius called upon him to join Rome’s war against Arthur. He led a force of soldiers at the battle of Soissons, where he killed or badly wounded Bedivere, and was slain by Bedivere’s nephew.

Likely a corruption of the Ancient Greek name Bucephalus.American country singer-songwriter Hank Williams, Jr. occasionally goes by the name Bocephus. His father gave him the nickname after Grand Ole Opry comedian Rod Brasfield's ventriloquist dummy. Bocephus King is a Canadian indie musician.
From the Chinese 伯 (bó) meaning "older brother" and 昌 (chāng) meaning "light of sun; good, proper".
Probably from Mingrelian ბოჩი (bochi) meaning "(male) goat, sheep". In Georgian mythology this was the name of a patron god of cattle.

Derived from Mingrelian ბოში (boši) or (boshi) meaning "boy". As such, this name is the Mingrelian equivalent of Bichia.Also compare dialectal Georgian ბოვში (bovshi) and standard Georgian ბავშვი (bavshvi), which both mean "baby, child".It is possible that there is also an etymological connection to Bochi, the name of an ancient Georgian (or rather Kartvelian) deity.
The name of a god in the Muisca religion.
From the Chinese 博 (bó) meaning "rich, plentiful" or "play, gamble, win" and 崇 (chóng) meaning "esteem, honour".
From the Chinese 伯 (bó) meaning "older brother" and 川 (chuān) meaning "stream, river".

column5: /ʔɓo˨˩ kəwŋ͡m˧˧ ʔajŋ̟˧˧/|/ʔɓow˦˩ kəwŋ͡m˧˧ ʔɛɲ˧˧/|/ʔɓow˨˩ kəwŋ͡m˧˧ ʔan˧˧/
column12: From Sino-Vietnamese 蒲公英 (bồ công anh) meaning "dandelion".
Bod is a classic British children's TV and book series about a little boy named Bod.
Derived from Old English boda meaning "messenger, herald, prophet".

The name Bodan is a name of South Slavic or possibly Germanic origin, it is a shortened form of the name Slobodan which is of Serbian origin and means Freedom. Alternatively it could derive from Proto-Germanic *butmaz (ground) via Proto-Indo-European *bʰudʰmḗn (bottom)
From the Chinese 伯 (bó) meaning "older brother" and 焘 (dào) meaning "shine, illuminate; envelope".
In Irish mythology, Bodb Derg was a son of Eochaid Garb or the Dagda, and the Dagda's successor as King of the Tuatha Dé Danann.
Possibly a variant of Baði. Related to Icelandic budda "money-bag" and Norwegian boddi "newborn pet". In Norse mythology Boddi is one of the sons of Karl and Snør.

Popularized by American skier Bode Miller (1977-), born Samuel Bode Miller, in whose case it was inspired by the English word bode meaning "to indicate by signs, as future events", according to his 2005 autobiography. He claims that his name is pronounced as two syllables, unlike the vocabulary word, because 'the diminutive form stuck'.
Derived from Gothic biutan "to offer" or Old High German boto "bid, offer" combined with Gothic gasts (gast in Old High German) "guest, stranger."
Derived from Gothic biutan "to offer" or Old High German boto "bid, offer" combined with gisel "hostage" or "pledge."
For feminine uses it is a Swedish dialectal variant form of Bodil and for masculine uses it is a Swedish dialectal variant form of Botolf.
Swedish dialectal variant form of Bodil recorded in Scania and Halland.
Derived from Gothic biutan "to offer" or Old High German boto "bid, offer" combined with Old High German mâri "famous."
Transferred use of the surname Bodene; a corruption of the French Baudouin.
Derived from Gothic biutan "to offer" or Old High German boto "bid, offer" combined with Old High German rât "counsel."
From the stem of verb 보듬다 (bodeumda) meaning "to embrace, hug, clasp."

Bodhana is a Yiddish name, made from the combined elements of BOD (the Ukranian word meaning G-d) and HAN (from the Hebrew, meaning gracious).Put together, Bodhana means "G-d graced". It is also considered the Yiddish form of the Polish name Bogdana.

Means "dharma of enlightenment" in Sanskrit, from Sanskrit बोधि (bodhi) "state of enlightenment" and धर्म (dharma) "that which is established, law, duty, virtue". This was the name of a semi-legendary Buddhist monk who lived during the 5th or 6th century CE.
Variant of Bodhi, from Sanskrit बोधिन् (bodhin).

Means "enlightened being" from Sanskrit, literally "one whose essence is perfect knowledge", composed of बोधि (bodhi) "perfect knowledge, perfect wisdom" (see Bodhi; also related to Buddha) and सत्त्व (sattva) "essence, reality, being". In Buddhism, a bodhisattva is a person who is on the path towards the attainment of bodhi (perfect knowledge) or Buddhahood.

Serbian king Constantine Bodin (fl. 1072–1108) was a ruler of Duklja, the second, although titular, King of Duklja and Dalmatia from 1081 to 1101, succeeding his father, King Michael.Meaning: defender of lifeNote: Not in connection with French BAUDOUIN because it is from proto Slavic.
Means "she likes to come to the world" in Ijaw.
Derived from Gaulish Bodd "good will" and Breton mael "prince". This is the name of a 6th century saint.
An ancient form of modern Hungarian boldog "happy", but its meaning at the time was "rich".

From the Malagasy bodo meaning "childish, young" and malala meaning "beloved, esteemed, revered". The name Bodo is often given to baby girls as a placeholder before a chosen name is given, and is sometimes retained as a woman's name, or, as a here, as a prefix in the name.
Of uncertain origin and meaning; theories include a Hungarian borrowing of Budimir.
Derived from Celtic boduus or boduo(s) "crow" combined with gnato, which can mean both "knowing, intelligent" and "son."
Directly taken from Hungarian bodza "elderberry; elder (tree)".
Old Swedish and Danish younger form of Bói.
Dutch and Afrikaans form of Buddha.
Older spelling of Budi influenced by Dutch orthography.
Older spelling of Budiman based on Dutch orthography.
Older spelling of Budiono based on Dutch orthography.
Portuguese form of Bohemond via Latinized form Boemundus.
Variant transcription of Buntoro based on Dutch orthography.
The name of an ancient Delphic priestess and hymn-writer, likely derived from the location Boeotia, ultimately from the Ancient Greek word βοώτης (boṓtēs) meaning “herdsman”.

column5: /biː.ˈoʊ.təs/(English)|/boe̯.ˈoː.tus/(Classical Latin)|/be.ˈo.tus/(modern Ecclesiastical Latin)|/boi̯.ɔː.tós/(Attic Greek)|/βy.o.ˈtos/(Koine Greek)|/vy.o.ˈtos/(Byzantine Greek)|/vi.o.ˈtos/(Constantinopolitan Greek)
column12: Derived from Greek βοώτης (bootes) meaning "herdsman", itself from βοῦς (bous) meaning "ox, cow".
From the Chinese 博 (bó) meaning "rich, plentiful" or "play, gamble, win" and 儿 (ér) meaning "son, child".

Dutch form of Boso. This given name is extremely rare in the Netherlands nowadays and is more commonly found as a patronymic surname.In Dutch literature, Boes is the name of the main character of the Dutch comic strip Boes, which became so popular that it was made into an animated television series (with the same title) in the late 1980s. The television series is known as Ox Tales in the Anglosphere. With that said, it should be noted that since Boes is an ox, his name might possibly be a play on boe, which is the Dutch equivalent of moo, the characteristic sound that bulls and cows make. Alternatively, it is also possible that his creators were inspired by the ancient Greek word βοῦς (bous) meaning "bull, ox", which is pronounced the same as Boes.
Diminutive of Boudewijn, Radboud, or Bode; derived from bot/bod meaning "help, remedy; command; victory" in Old Germanic, or derived from buit meaning "brother, buddy" in Low-Saxon.

From a Roman cognomen derived from Ancient Greek βοηθός (boethos) meaning "auxiliary, assistant, helper". This was the cognomen of a Roman senator, philosopher, and martyr who was a central figure in the translation of the Greek classics into Latin (full name Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius).
Latinized form of Boethos.Early Greek translation of Ezra.
From the Chinese 博 (bó) meaning "rich, plentiful" or "play, gamble, win" and 繁 (fán) meaning "numerous, complicated, complex".

column3: 伯芳, 波方, 博方, etc.(Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 伯 (bó) meaning "father's older brother, paternal elder uncle", 波 (bō) meaning "wave" or 博 (bó) meaning "abundant, plentiful, extensive, ample" combined with 芳 (fāng) meaning "fragrant, virtuous, beautiful" or 方 (fāng) meaning "upright, honest, fair". Other character combinations can form this name as well.
Meaning unknown; possibly related to Bófi. This is the name of a dwarf in Norse mythology.

column3: 博峰, 博锋, 博芬, etc.(Chinese)
博凤, 波凤, 博枫, 波枫, 博丰, 波丰, etc.(Chinese)|博鳳, 波鳳, 博楓, 波楓, 博豐, 波豐, etc.(Traditional Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 博 (bó) meaning "wide, extensive, gamble" or 波 (bō) meaning "wave", combined with 凤 (fèng) meaning "male phoenix, male firebird" or 枫 (fēng) meaning "maple" or 丰 (fēng) meaning "luxuriant, lush, beautiful". Other hanzi combinations are possible.
From Old Norse bófi meaning "knave, rogue."
From the Chinese 博 (bó) meaning "rich, plentiful" or "play, gamble, win" and 夫 (fū) meaning "man, husband".

A character created by J.R.R. Tolkien in 'The Hobbit'. Bofur is a Dwarf in Thorin's Company who is related to Bifur and Bombur. Bofur is not one of Durin's Folk, he is one of Moria.Tolkien took the name from the Dvergatal "Catalogue of Dwarves" in the Völuspá, a part of the Poetic Edda.
as strong as a bullafter boğaç han in the book of dede korkut
Transferred use of the surname Bogart.The use of the name is likely due to legendary American screen actor Humphrey Bogart (1899 - 1957), who more popularly went by the nickname Bogie.
Old Hungarian name of possibly Slavic origin which is said to mean "rich, wealthy". In Western Hungary, this is a byname of Saint Julian.
Means "flourishing garden, flourishing orchard" in Uzbek.
Feminine form or variant of Bogdał.
Cognate of Bogdan, meaning "gift of God".
Old East Slavic form of Bogdan.
Combination of the Old Norse name elements bogi "bow" and dís "goddess; woman, lady; sister" or dis "wise woman, seeress; woman, virgin".

Derived from Old Norse bogi meaning "bow" (compare Bogi) combined with ey meaning "island" or ey meaning "good fortune". It has also been proposed that this may be an Icelandic form of Bogei, an archaic Norwegian dialectal variant of Baugheid (see Baugheiðr).
Derived from Old Norse bogi "bow" (also compare Bogi) and hildr "battle", perhaps modelled on Borghildur.
Transferred use of the surname Bøgild.
Polabian and Pomeranian form of Bogusław.
Directly taken from the archaic Hungarian word boglár "ornament".
Short form of names Bogdan, Bogoljub, Bogomil, Bogomir or Bogoslav.

Composed of the members Bog ("God") and dar ("gift, present"). The name is considered to be equivalent in meaning to the name Adeodatus, and thus Bogodar celebrates its name-day on the days of St Adeodatus' memorial.
From the Slavic elements богъ (bogu) meaning "God" and lyuby meaning "love".
Possibly from.Polish bóg "God" and Old Slavic вити (viti) "to bend, to twist".
Composed of the Slavic elements bogu "god" and chwal "to praise, to glorify". As such, the meaning of this name is "to praise God, to thank God".
From Sino-Korean 甫 (bo) meaning "begin; man, father; great" or 普 (bo) meaning "wide, large" and 劍 (geum) meaning "knife, sword". Other hanja combinations are possible.
Lower Sorbian cognate of Bohuměr. In former times, this name was usually Germanized as Gottfried.
The name originates from slavic culture. It means God + kind.
Latinized form of Bogumil, a famous bearer of this name was Bogumił Piotr who was Archbishop of Gniezno and also a hermit.
Diminutive of names beginning with Bog-, such as Bogdan, Bogumił, Bogumir and Bogusław.

The first element of this name is derived from Polish bóg "god", which is ultimately derived from Proto-Slavic bogъ "god". The second element is derived from Polish sądzić "to judge" (also compare Croatian suditi and Czech soudit, both of which mean "to judge"). As such, the meaning of this name is roughly "God judges".
Diminutive of Bogdana, Bogumiła, and Bogusława.
Short form of names beginning with the element Bògù-, such as Bògùmił and Bògùsłôw.
Polish name from Slavic bogŭ "god, deity" combined with volstĭ "power, rule, sovereignty". In Old Polish, the deuterotheme became włość "manor, estate".
Derived from the Slavic elements bogu "god" and wola "will".
From Sino-Korean 步 (bo) meaning “step, pace, walk, stroll” combined with 慊 (gyeom) meaning “pleased, satisfied”. Other hanja combinations can form this name as well.
From Sino-Korean 甫 "begin; man, father; great" or 寶 "treasure, jewel; precious, rare" (bo), and 炅 "brilliance" or 璟 "luster of gem" (gyeong).
Derived from Upper Sorbian bóh "god" and česćić "to honour; to venerate, to revere". In former times, this name was usually Germanized as Ehregott.
Derived from Upper Sorbian bóh and chwalić "to praise". In former times, this name was usually Germanized as Gottlob.
From Chinese 博 (bó) meaning "wide, extensive, gamble" combined with 豪 (háo) meaning "brave, heroic, chivalrous". Other hanzi combinations are possible.
Variant of Bohdana. Used mostly in Western Ukraine.
Latvianised form of Bohdan. See Bogdans for usual Latvian form.

From Chinese 薄荷 (bòhé) meaning "mint". One fictional bearer of this name is Bòhé Lánzé (藍澤 薄荷), who is also known as Minto Aizawa in the original Japanese or Corina Bucksworth in the English dub, from Tokyo Mew Mew/Mew Mew Power.
From the Chinese 博 (bó) meaning "rich, plentiful" or "play, gamble, win" or 伯 (bó) meaning "older brother" and 赫 (hè) meaning "bright, radiant, glowing".
French form of Bohemond via Latinized form Boemundus.

From Italian Buamundo, which is of uncertain meaning. According to the Norman historian Orderic Vitalis it was derived from Latin Buamundus, the name of a mythical Gigas (giant), originally given as a nickname to the crusader prince Bohemond I (christened Mark; c. 1058-1111) by his father because he was extremely large at birth.
Spanish form of Bohemond via Latinized form Boemundus.

column3: 博恒, etc.(Chinese)|博恆, etc.(Traditional Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 博 (bó) meaning "wide, extensive, gamble" combined with 恒 (héng) meaning "constant, persistent". Other hanzi combinations are possible.
Variant of Bahrom, which is the main Tajik and Uzbek form of Bahram.
From the Chinese 博 (bó) meaning "rich, plentiful" or "play, gamble, win" and 虎 (hǔ) meaning "tiger; brave, fierce".

From Sino-Korean 甫 (bo) meaning "begin; man, father; great" or 普 (bo) meaning "wide, large" and 姬 (hui) meaning "beauty; imperial concubine" or 熙 (hui) meaning "bright, splendid." A famous bearer is South Korean actress Lee Bo-hee (1959-).
Upper Sorbian form of Bohumír. In former times, this name was usually Germanized as Gottfried.
Diminutive of Bohumila, rarely used as a given name in its own right.
Diminutive of Bohuslav, used as a given name in its own right. Also Belarusian, usage deriving from Polish Bogusz.
Derived from Upper Sorbian bóh "god" and wěra "faith". In former times, this name was usually Germanized as Traugott.
Korean form of Puxian, from Sino-Korean 普賢 (bohyeon). This is the Korean name for the bodhisattva Samantabhadra.

From Sino-Korean 甫 (bo) meaning "begin; man, father; great" or 普 (bo) meaning "wide, large" and From Sino-Korean 亨 "smoothly, progressing, no trouble" or From Sino-Korean 賢 "virtuous, worthy, good; able" Other hanja combinations are possible
From Sino-Vietnamese 培 (bồi) meaning "to reinforce, strengthen, accumulate".

derives from the Germanic name “Boiamund”, composed of two elements: From the Frisian and Germanic elements boii, Bojen, Boje "ruler, dweller" and mundō "protector, protection, tutelage, guardianship". In turn the name means "protector of the Boii". The Boii were a Gallic tribe of the later Iron Age, attested at various times in Cisalpine Gaul (northern Italy), Pannonia (Hungary and its western neighbours), in and around Bohemia (after whom the region is named), and Transalpine Gaul. Original form of Bohemond.
Derived from Old Irish buaid meaning "victory, profit" and mál "noble, chief".

Boifinat is a newly created name from India with Hindu cultural roots. In my family, it means “young stronger protector.” It symbolizes a youthful spirit, emotional strength, and the ability to protect others even as the youngest in the family.The name was invented to reflect someone unique—someone who stands out from society, acts differently, and brings a creative or “crazy” energy in a positive way.It is used as a first name only, primarily for boys, and is currently unique to my family and community. The name is not traditional or ancient; it is a new, modern creation with deep emotional meaning.Nickname: RobinPronunciation: BOY-fi-natOrigin: India, Hindu cultureSymbolism: strength, youth, uniqueness, emotional power
Means "someone to lean on" in Setswana.

column3: 보인(Korean Hangul)|寶仁, 寶人, etc.(Korean Hanja)
column12: From Sino-Korean 寶 (bo) meaning "treasure" combined with 仁 (in) meaning "compassionate" or 人 (in) meaning "man, person, mankind, people". Other character combinations can form this name as well.
Transferred use of the surname Boise or the place name Boise.

Saint Boisil (died 661) was a monk of Melrose Abbey, an offshoot of Lindisfarne, then in the Anglo-Saxon Kingdom of Northumbria, but now in Scotland, where he must have been one of the first generation of monks.
A fictional character BoJack F. Horseman from the adult animated series "BoJack Horseman"
Diminutive of names ending with -borg, such as Valborg and Ingeborg.

From the Chinese 博 (bó) meaning "rich, plentiful" or "play, gamble, win" or 伯 (bó) meaning "older brother" and 凯 (kǎi) meaning "triumphant; triumph, victory".

Latinized form of Boleslav. Boleslaus was the brother of Duke Wenceslaus of Bohemia (the inspiration for the Christmas carol) and became notorious for his murder.
Diminutive of Bodil. Bolette Wrangel is a character in the play 'Fruen fra havet' (Engl. 'The Lady from the Sea') written by Norwegian playwright Henrik Ibsen in 1888.

From the Chinese 博 (bó) meaning "rich, plentiful" or "play, gamble, win" or 伯 (bó) meaning "older brother" and 梁 (liáng) meaning "bridge" or 亮 (liàng) meaning "bright, light, brilliant, radiant, enlightened".

column3: 愽林, 博林, 波林, 博琳, 波琳, etc.(Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 博 (bó) meaning "wide, extensive gamble" or 波 (bō) meaning "wave", combined with 林 (lín) meaning "forest" or 琳 (lín) meaning "fine jade, gem". Other hanzi combinations are possible. A character from the TV series The Legend of Korra bears this name.

Uncertain etymology. In Greek mythology, Bolina was the eponymous nymph of the ancient town Bolina in Achaea, Greece. She was made immortal by the god Apollo after she fled into the sea to escape his advances.

column3: 伯苓, 柏灵, 波玲, etc.(Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 伯 (bó) meaning "the eldest in the order of seniority among brothers" combined with 苓 (líng) meaning "Poris cocos (plant)". Other hanzi combinations are possible.
From Sino-Vietnamese 部領 (bộ lĩnh) meaning "leader". Đinh Bộ Lĩnh (924-979) was the founding emperor of the Đinh dynasty.
Variation on Bulissa, influenced by Boli.
From the name of the country in South America. The country got its name from the surname Bolívar, in honour of the revolutionary Simón Bolívar.
Derived from the Uzbek bol meaning "honey" and jahon meaning "the world".
Medieval Polish short form of Bolesława. Princess Bolka (1352 - 1427/1428) was the last representative of the Bytom-Koziel Piasts.

Derived from the Turkish elements bol meaning "abundant, plentiful" and kan meaning "blood". The name traditionally implies a brave, vigorous, or high-spirited person full of life and vitality (literally "one with abundant blood").While it bears a phonetic resemblance to the Turkish word "Balkan" ("chain of wooded mountains") and the Turkish word "Volkan" (meaning "volcano", itself a loanword from French volcan), these are etymologically unrelated.
Unknown etymology. This was the name of a Syracusan general.
From the Ancient Germanic elements bolo meaning "friend" and landa meaning "land".
Means "small bowl, drinking cup" in Icelandic and Old Norse, originally a byname for a fat or stocky man.
A historical name from Southern Alsace.
Means "crystal gem" in Mongolian, from болор (bolor) meaning "crystal" and эрдэнэ (erdene) meaning "jewel, treasure".
Means "clear crystal" in Mongolian, from болор (bolor) meaning "crystal" and тунгалаг (tungalag) meaning "transparent, clear" or "serenity".
Bolossy Kiralfy, born Balázs Königsbaum, was one of The Kiralfy Brothers, a pair of dancers and performers popular internationally in the late 19th and early 20th century.
From Kyrgyz болот (bolot) meaning "steel" and the Turkish military title beg meaning "chieftain, master".
Means "think of the future" in Ijaw.
Derived from the Uzbek bol meaning "honey" and qiz meaning "girl".
An animated dog being the title hero in the movie 'Bolt' (2008). The name comes from a lightning bolt mark on his side.
Spanish variant of Voltaire. A famous bearer is ecuadorian president Lenín Moreno.
Derived from Old Norse bǫl "bale, misfortune, evil" and þorn "thorn, spike". In Norse mythology, Bǫlþorn was a giant (jǫtunn) and the father of Bestla.
Croatian short form of Baltazar, cognate of Slovene Boltežar and Hungarian Boldizsár.
Means "wakes up with the lord" in Yoruba.
Means "as god wishes, one who follows the will of god" in Yoruba.

Old Norse name meaning "evil-doer, malefactor" with the combination of bǫl "misfortune", "evil", "bale" and verk "work, piece of work, business, deed". Bǫlverkr is another name for Óðinn who is a character in Norse Mythology.
Counselor to Earl Milon, who desired Enide, Erec’s wife. Milon and Bolvin tried to kidnap the woman, but Erec killed them both.
Contracted form of большая железная дорога, meaning "big railroad".
This is the name of a foolish and clumsy character in Vietnamese folktales.
From native Koream 봄 (bom) meaning "spring(time)."A famous bearer is singer Park Bom (1984-), who was a member of South Korean girl group 2NE1 before its disbandment in 2016.
Meaning "fort or enclosure". The word actually originates from Swahili and is traditionally known as an enclosure, a stockade or fort used to protect people's livestock (usually sheep and cattle).
Possibly transfered usage of the surname Boman.
Bomba the Jungle Boy is a series of American boys' adventure books produced by the Stratemeyer Syndicate under the pseudonym Roy Rockwood; it was published between 1926 and 1938.
The name is derived from the German word Bombarde "bombard (the weapon)".Kanonine and Bombardine were twins born during the battle of Leipzig in October 1813.
Possibly descended from Latin bombax meaning "cotton" or "indeed (interjection)" or from German Bombast meaning "pompous language".

A Dwarf in J.R.R. Tolkien's "The Hobbit." A relative of Bifur and Bofur, and the fattest of the Dwarves in Thorin's company.Tolkien took the name from the Dvergatal "Catalogue of Dwarves" in the Völuspá, a part of the Poetic Edda.
Related to bimbult ("bumpy; uneasy"). This is the name of a dwarf in Norse mythology.
From Bom suffixed with pluralising marker 들 (deul).
Combination of Bom and 결 (gyeol) meaning "layer, ply; chance, opportunity, moment."
From Sino-Korean 普 "universal, general, widespread" and 美 "beautiful, pretty; pleasing".
The middle name of Freddie Mercury, whose given name was Farrokh Bomi Bulsara.
From the Chinese 伯 (bó) meaning "the eldest in the order of seniority among brothers" and 明 (míng) meaning "bright, light, clear". Other hanzi combinations are possible.

Given in honour of AC/DC rock star "Bon" Scott, who was born Ronald Scott. His nickname was given to him at school, to differentiate him from another Ronald in his class. As he had recently emigrated from Scotland to Australia, he was named Bon, a reference to "Bonnie Scotland".
From Sino-Korean 寶 (bo) meaning "treasure, valuables" and 娜 (na) meaning "elegant, graceful".
Derived from Latin bona "good or brave woman".
Derived from Latin bona, the feminine form of the adjective bonus, "good; kind; noble" and Catalan aunir, a variant of unir "to unite".
From Latin bona meaning "good" (feminine form of bonus) and bella meaning "beautiful".
Meaning uncertain; it is likely a medieval variant of Bonaccorsa.
Derived from Latin bonus meaning "good" and Latin deus meaning "God".
Judeo-Spanish and Judeo-Catalan equivalent of Judeo-Italian Bonadonna.
Derived from Italian bona, an older form of buona, the feminine form of the adjective buono, "good; pleasant; kind" and donna "woman; lady".
Derived from Latin bona “good, kind, right” and femina “woman, female”. See also Bonafilia.
Derived from Latin bona, the feminine form of the adjective bonus, "good; kind; noble" and filia "daughter".Due to its meaning, Bonafilia was used as an amuletic name.

Older Catalan and Provençal form of Boniface.Notable people include anti-Jewish writer Bonafos Caballeria, born Jewish in the early 15th century. He converted to Christianity and won the favour of Queen Maria of Aragon and Naples, and was murdered in 1464.Astruc Bonafos Caylar is listed in the index of known Jews in late-mediaeval France in Rabbi Heinrich Gross' book, "Gallia Judaica".

Derived from the Italian adjective buono meaning "good" as well as "fair" combined with giunta, the feminine past participle of the Italian verb giungere meaning "to arrive". As such, the name is basically a reference to the safe arrival of a newborn.A notable bearer of this name was the Italian poet Bonagiunta Orbicciani (c. 1220-c. 1290). He also appears as a character in the poem Divine Comedy written by the Italian poet Dante Alighieri (c. 1265-1321).
Derived from Old French bone joie "good joy".

From Latin Bonaiuncta, in which the first element derives from Latin bonus meaning "good" and the second element means "arrival" (ultimately deriving from the Latin verb iungere). This is a Christian and Jewish cognate of Bona-aunis.
"Bonaking is a name that signifies leadership, translating to 'born to rule'. It reflects a powerful presence and an innate ability to lead others.
Derived from Latin bonus meaning "good" combined with Old German walt meaning "power, authority".
Variant of Bonamy. This name was occasionally used by medieval English Jews as a translation or secular name of Benjamin due to its phonetic similarity.
Derived from Latin bona meaning "good" and Latin amica meaning "friend"
Derived from the Italian adjective bono meaning "good" combined with the Italian noun amico meaning "friend".
Derived from Old French bone, the feminine form of the adjective bon, "good (virtuous, having positive qualities)" and Old French amie "(female) friend; (female) lover", ultimately form Latin amica.
Transferred use of the surname Bonamy. This name was borne by British literary scholar Bonamy Dobrée (1891-1974), who was given the name because it was a family surname.
Transferred use of surname Bonaparte in honour of Napoleon Bonaparte.
Transferred use of the surname Bonar.
Hybrid compound of Latin bonus "good" and Germanic hard "strong, brave, hardy".

Taken from the title of the Virgin Mary Nostra Signora di Bonaria or Madonna di Bonaria. The name literally means "gracious; kind-hearted; sweet-natured", from Italian bonaria, the feminine form of the adjective bonario or "good air; good wind" in reference to her being the patron saint of sailors and mariners. The name is mainly used in Sardinia and it is often found in the combination Maria Bonaria.
Shortened form of names beginning with Bon-, like Bonaventūras and Bonifacijus.
Combination of bono "good" and Astruc. This name was used as a translation of Gad and Mazal Tov.
Of uncertain origin and meaning. One current theory connects this name to Bonat.
From Latin bona "good, kind, right" (from bonus) combined with vera "true" (from verus).
Means "langsat" in Vietnamese, rarely used as a given name.
Possibly derives from Hungarian boncol meaning "to autopsy", itself derived from bont "to demolish" and szol a frequentative suffix.
Derived from the Italian adjective bono meaning "good" combined with the Italian noun compagno meaning "companion, friend".

Derived from the Italian adjective bono meaning "good" combined with the Italian noun conte meaning "count" or "earl" (also compare Contessa).This name can also be a short form of Bonincontro.A notable Italian bearer of this name was the Ghibelline general Bonconte da Montefeltro (c. 1250-1289). He also appears as a character in the poem Divine Comedy written by the Italian poet Dante Alighieri (c. 1265-1321).
From Japanese 凡 (bon) meaning "ordinary, common, mediocre" combined with 大 (dai) meaning "big, great". Other kanji combinations are possible.
Combination of bon (see Bono) and David.
Form of Bóandi meaning "farmer, landowner, yeoman, master".
Variant of Bóandi. This is the name of one of Karl and Snør's sons in Norse mythology.
Derived from Catalan bon "good" and Franco-Provençal bon "good; right" and Catalan and Old Occitan dia "day".

Of debated origin and meaning. Some modern-day scholars consider this name a variant of Bendit, while others connect this name to Catalan bon (compare Bono) and dit, the past participle of Catalan dir "to say", and thus giving this name the meaning of "well said".
Bonduwa was Lonkundo’s first wife in the Mongo mythology complex.
Derived from Old French bone, the feminine form of the adjective bon "good".
Derived from French bon enfant "good child".
Derived from and Old French bon "good (virtuous, having positive qualities)" and Anglo-Norman enfaunt "child". This name was also used as a secular form of Benjamin.
Aragonese and Judeo-Provençal form of Bonitus.
Possibly a combination of Bonnie and the suffix -ette.

Diminutive of Bonfante, as -ino is an Italian masculine diminutive suffix.
Latinized form of the medieval Italian name Buonfiglio (see Bonfiglio). This name was borne by an Italian saint from the 12th century AD.

Means "girl, woman", from Vietnamese bóng meaning "shadow, reflection" and Sino-Vietnamese 紅 (hồng) meaning "pink".

Hungarian and Slovak feminine form of Boniface. In Hungarian history, this name was borne by Erzsébet Bonifácia (born and died 1399), the short-lived daughter of Jadwiga I, Queen of Poland (sister of Mária/Marija I, Queen of Hungary and Croatia) and Vladislavas Jogaila, Grand Duke of Lithuania (later Władysław II Jagiełło, King of Poland); the princess was named for her godfather Pope Boniface IX.

Slovenian and Lithuanian feminine form of Bonifatius. In Lithuanian history, this name was borne by Elžbieta Bonifacija (born and died 1399), the short-lived daughter of Jadwiga I, Queen of Poland and Vladislavas Jogaila, Grand Duke of Lithuania (later Władysław II Jagiełło, King of Poland); the princess was named for her godfather Pope Boniface IX.

Feminine form of Bonifacy. This name was borne by Elżbieta Bonifacja (born and died 1399), the short-lived daughter of Jadwiga I, Queen of Poland and Vladislavas Jogaila, Grand Duke of Lithuania (later Władysław II Jagiełło, King of Poland); the princess was named for her godfather Pope Boniface IX.

Variant form of Bonifatsiy. A known bearer of this name was the Soviet philosopher Bonifaty Kedrov (1903-1985). In his case, Bonifaty is just a variant transcription of Bonifatiy: the spelling is exactly the same in Russian, so they are really the same name.
Gallurese and Sassarese form of Boniface.

Variant of Bonifacius, itself a variant of Bonifatius; the name originally meant "good fate" (from Latin bonum "good" and fatum "fate"), but folk law altered the meaning to "well-doer" or "doer of good deeds" (from Latin bonum and facere "to do"). Also compare Bonifaz. This was a middle name of Prince Johannes von Thurn und Taxis (1926-1990), a German banker, industrialist and socialite (full name Johannes Baptista de Jesus Maria Louis Miguel Friedrich Bonifazius Lamoral).

Means "good hour" or "finally", given to children whose birth was long-awaited or celebrated, or who were born early in the morning. Ultimately derived from Latin bonus "good" and hora "time, hour".

Combination of the phonetic elements bon (from Bonnie or Bonita), quee and sha. This is the name of a character in the song Xmas Blues (1996) by Big Tyme (Ricardo Spencer).
Meaning "planted in a tray".The name is unconventional and might be seen as unusual or unique by many people.

The name Bootaan is of Somali origin and carries a powerful and positive meaning. In Somali, Bootaan is often associated with characteristics like strength, courage, and dignity. It's a traditional Somali name that reflects qualities admired in Somali culture, particularly in relation to leadership, bravery, and standing firm in the face of challenges."Bootaan" may be derived from the Somali word "booto," meaning "pride" or "nobility." The name can be interpreted to symbolize someone who is noble, strong, or carries themselves with dignity.
Means "herdsman, ploughman" in Greek, derived from βοῦς (bous) "ox, cow". This is the name of a constellation in the northern sky.

Transferred use of the surname Booth, which is derived from Middle English bothe meaning "booth, bothy, hut", which itself is ultimately derived from Old Norse búð meaning "booth, dwelling, shelter". The surname originally referred to someone (often a herdsman) who lived in a small hut or bothy.Known bearers of Booth as a given name include the American novelist and dramatist Booth Tarkington (1869-1946) and the American politician Booth Gardner (1936-2013).

Transferred use of the surname Boots or a nickname whose meaning is particular to the bearer.Notable namesakes including saxophonist Homer Louis "Boots" Randolph (1927-2007), is famed for the Benny Hill theme song 'Yakety Sax' as well as featuring in recordings by Elvis Presley and Roy Orbison among other well known singers.

Short form of Børge or variant of Bjor.
Derived from Hungarian bóra "bora (northern to north-eastern katabatic wind in the Adriatic Sea)".

column3: 보람(Korean Hangul)|寳濫, 寳蘫, 寳覽, 保濫, etc.(Korean Hanja)
column12: From native Korean 보람 (boram) meaning "fruitful, useful, worthwhile."It can also be written with hanja, such as 寳 (bo) meaning "treasure" or 保 (bo) meaning "protection, defence," combining that with 濫 (ram) meaning "overflow; diffusion; float," 蘫 (ram) meaning "clear water," 覽 (ram) meaning "view; observation; prospect," and the such.Female bearers of this name include singer and actress Jeon Boram (1986-) and singer Park Bo-ram (1994-).

Means "ancient, old" in Khmer, ultimately from Sanskrit पुराण (purana).
From Kazakh боран (boran) meaning "blizzard, storm" combined with the Turkic military title beg meaning "chieftain, master".
Derived from боран (boran) meaning "hurricane" and бийке (biyke) meaning "mistress".

Meaning uncertain, possibly from Mongolian борогчин (borogchin) meaning "(female) bird" or "brown skin (of female animals)". This was the name of a 13th-century Alchi Tatar woman and the senior wife of Mongol ruler Batu Khan (c. 1205-1255), the grandson of Genghis Khan. In 1257, she served as regent of the Golden Horde, a division of the Mongol Empire.
Possibly an invented name, perhaps based on Borut. This is the name of the titular character in the film 'Borat' (2006).
Means "round girl" from Tuvan борбак (borbak) meaning "round, spherical" and кыс (kys) meaning "girl, daughter".
Means "round boy" from Tuvan борбак (borbak) meaning "round, spherical" and оол (ool) meaning "boy, son".
Derived from Albanian borë "snow" and bardhë "white".

"Sister goddess" of Embeth and Wilbeth and one of "The Three Bethen" or "Three Virgins", a group of allegedly pre-Christian goddesses who later became "unofficial" saints.Their cult is somewhat of a mystery: having been known since the Middle Ages, it is only regionally distributed, mainly in Bavaria, Baden, South Tyrol, Alsace (above all Strasbourg) and the Rhineland. If there had ever been antique records of this Triple Goddess cult, those have been lost. The oldest authentic records of Borbeth date back to the 14th century, when she was quickly linked to Embeth whose veneration had been attested since the 12th century.Either way, their cult became fairly popular when the "girls" got appointed companions of Saint Ursula in the 15th century.The origins and meanings of their names have been lost to time. Since the Romantic period, there have been speculations that their names might be corruptions of some not yet identified Ancient Germanic names - a theory which in recent times is being taken more and more seriously. Research on it is being done.
Directly taken from Hungarian borbolya "barberry, berberry".
Means "brown stone, grey stone" in Mongolian, from бор (bor) meaning "brown, grey, dark" and чулуун (chuluun) meaning "stone"
Originally a diminutive of Borbála, used as a given name in its own right.
Variant of Burdukhan. This is the name that the Alan princess and Georgian queen consort Burdukhan of Alania (12th century AD) is also known by.
Derived from Greek βορέας (boreas) "north wind". Kung Bore (King Bore) is a Swedish personification of winter.
From the Boreal Forest, which was named after the Greek god Boreas, who was a purple-winged god of the North Wind in Greek mythology.
Variant of Borbardha. This is the Albanian cognate of Schneewittchen.

Created by author George R. R. Martin for a character in his series "A Song of Ice and Fire" and the television series "House of the Dragon". In the series, Boremund Baratheon is the Lord of Storm's End and the head of House Baratheon early in the reign of King Viserys Targaryen during the middle years of the Targaryen dynasty in Westeros.

This name is best known for being the name of Borena of Alania (11th century AD), an Alan princess who went on to become queen of Georgia after marrying the widowed king Bagrat IV of Georgia. It is because of her that the Georgians became acquainted with the name Borena; she brought the name to Georgia. Considering that the Alans spoke an Eastern Iranian language that was descended from Scytho-Sarmatian, it is highly likely that the name Borena has its roots in that language as well. In fact, a prevailing theory is that the name means "chestnut-brown, maroon" in that language.
Dialectal variant of Berit found in Norrland and Västergötland.
Means "one who fights, one who struggles", refering to in revolution.

Boril of Bulgaria was the emperor of Bulgaria from 1207 to 1218.
Derived from Slavic bor "battle" combined with Slavic mir "peace". A known bearer of this name is Borimir Perković (b. 1967), a former Croatian soccer player.

A fictional character created by J.R.R. Tolkien. After his younger nephew, Frór, and brother were slain, Borin departed from the Ered Mithrin with his younger nephew, Thrór, to the Lonely Mountain in eastern Middle-earth, and lived there until his death. Thrór would someday be King of the Lonely Mountain, until the dragon Smaug assaulted it.
Means "fighter", from Vlach boriti meaning "to fight".
Form of Boris with the nominative suffix, used in Georgian when the name is written stand-alone.
Originally a diminutive of Borbála (via the variant diminutives Bori and Boris), now used as a given name in its own right.
Either derived from the Slavic element borti "battle" or from the Slavic name element бор (bor) "pine tree". This name is borne by Macedonian conductor Borjan Canev (born 1973).
Derived from Faroese børkuvísa "tormentil" (a type of flower).
This is the name of the Ossetian god of cereals and grain and the son of Khorældar. He was killed by Batraz, causing the Narts to fall to famine.
From Mongolian бор (bor) meaning "brown, grey, dark" and хүү (khüü) meaning "boy, son; child".
Old Norse name and byname meaning "bark". Alternatively, it could derive from the given name Bǫðríkr, composed of bǫð "battle" and ríkr "ruler, king, mighty" (cognate to Old English Beaduric).
Either taken directly from the Icelandic word börkur "bark" (the outermost layer of trees), or from the Old Norse name Bǫrkr.

Bormana was a Celtic goddess, the female equivalent of the god Borvo (Bormanus). Bormana was worshipped alongside Bormanus as his consort.The pair of them were, for example, worshipped at Die (Drôme) in the south of France. The goddess also occurred independently at Saint-Vulbas (Ain). Bormana was considered a goddess of water and healing. Bormana was named after the Celtic word for “to Boil”, she was associated with the 2 Hot spring baths called; Bourbon-Lancy and Bourbonne-les-Bains both named after her and her consort.

An Australian shrub with pink or red flowers which are famed for their exquisite scent. The plant is named after Francesco Borone, a talented botanical field assistant who came to a tragic end.

Transferred use of the Italian surname Borromeo, given in honour of the Italian saint Charles Borromeo (1538-1584).

Created by author George R. R. Martin for a character in his series "A Song of Ice and Fire". In the series, Borros Baratheon is the patriarch of House Baratheon and the Lord of Storm's End during Viserys Targaryen's reign in Westeros.
Derived from Hungarian bors "pepper" and borsikafű "summer savory".
Bort is an eastern Ashkenazi Jewish name for a man with a beard.

This was the name of the first wife of Temujin, better known as Genghis Khan, the founder of the Mongol Empire. Borte, or Börte, became the head of the first Court of Genghis Khan, and Grand Empress of his Empire.
Means "brown headed" or "grey headed" in Mongolian, from бор (bor) meaning "grey, brown, dark" and толгой (tolgoi) meaning "head".

She was revered by ancient tribes, particularly in Gaul (modern-day France), as the divine feminine consort to the hot-spring god Borvo (also known as Bormanus).
