Germanic given name of uncertain meaning. Some sources state that it is a short form of Germanic given names that contain the element boto meaning "bid, offer" (such as Bodegisel - also compare Bode), whilst others state that it is a short form of Germanic given names that contain the element burg meaning "protection", such as Burghard (see Burchard). Also compare somewhat similar names, such as Anso, Gero and Odo, all of which are short forms of Germanic given names that start with a certain element.Other sources derive the name from Old High German bôsi meaning "evil", which ultimately comes from Proto-Germanic *bausuz meaning "bad" as well as "inflated, swollen" and "proud, arrogant" (compare the English verb to boast). One source has even linked the name to ancient Greek φόως (phoos) meaning "(to) the light (of day)", but that seems to be a bit of a stretch.With that said, a known bearer of this name was the 6th-century Frankish duke Bodegisel (also found written as Bodogisel), who is said to have been known by the nicknames Boggis and Boso. Other bearers include the Frankish nobleman and king Boso of Provence (9th century AD) and the German bishop Boso of Merseburg (10th century AD).
French form of Boso. A known bearer of this name was Boson de Talleyrand-Périgord (1832-1910), a French nobleman and prince of Sagan.

Italian form of Boso. A known bearer of this name was Boso of Arles (10th century AD), a Frankish nobleman who spent much of his life in Italy (where he was known as Bosone) and at one point became a Margrave of Tuscany there.

The origins of the name Bouldin are from the ancient Anglo-Saxon culture of Britain. It is derived from the Old English personal name Bealding, which was originally derived from the name Beald. Bouldin Settlers in United States in the 17th CenturySound was what guided spelling in the essentially pre-literate Middle Ages, so one person's name was often recorded under several variations during a single lifetime. Also, before the advent of the printing press and the first dictionaries, the English language was not standardized. Therefore, spelling variations were common, even among the names of the most literate people.

In his case, the name was essentially a nickname, but his nephew Braccio I Baglioni (1419-1479) was named after him and so in that instance it was an actual given name.

The meaning of this medieval Italian given name is either "a lion's paw" or "he who captures the lion". In the case of the former meaning, the name is derived from Italian branca meaning "paw, claw" combined with Italian leone meaning "lion". In the case of the latter meaning, the first element of the name is derived from brancare, a dialectal form of the Italian verb abbrancare meaning "to grasp, to seize". The second element of the name is the same as with the first meaning. With that said: the first meaning given is probably the most likely one, since a lion's paw was often used as a charge in heraldry - to such a degree that brancaleone had even become part of heraldry jargon. In other words: the use of Brancaleone as a given name must have been inspired by heraldry.However, it should be noted that there are two sources that claim that the name is a combination of two given names, namely Branca (a short form of Brancazio, which is a variant form of the given name Pancrazio) and Leone 1. This is not that implausible in itself, since Italians have liked to combine given names since medieval times, as names like Giambattista and Giancarlo will prove. But it is hard to find further proof to support this claim.Known real-life bearers of this name include the Genovese nobleman Brancaleone Doria (1337-1409) and Brancaleone degli Andalò (1220-1258), a Bolognese senator of Rome. In popular culture, Brancaleone is the given name of the main character in "L'armata Brancaleone" (1966), an Italian film about a well-meaning but incompetent knight.

Medieval Dutch form of Brendan via its medieval Latin form Brandanus. The use of this name started in honor of the Irish monastic saint Brendan the Navigator (died circa 577 AD), who was quite popular in the Low Countries throughout the Middle Ages.In medieval Dutch literature, this name occurs in the 12th-century poems Boec van Sente Brandaen ("Book of Saint Brendan") and Van Sente Brandane ("Of Saint Brendan"). The latter poem was the most influential and is also known under the title De reis van Sente Brandane ("The Voyage of Saint Brendan") and the various spellings thereof. Both poems are adaptations (rather than literal translations) of the 9th-century Latin text Navigatio sancti Brendani abbatis ("The Voyage of Saint Brendan the Abbot").

The King of Estranggorre (Estrangore). He married a daughter of Adrian of Constantinople and thus became the brother-in-law of Adrians’s other daughter, the mother of Saigremor le Desree (Sagramore).Brandegoris joined the rebellious kings in their campaign against King Arthur. He pledged to bring 5,000 mounted men to the battle of Bedegraine. In that battle Brandegoris, King Idres, and King Agwisance (Anguish) unhorsed Sirs Griflet and Lucas. He was defeated by Arthur, Ban and Bors.Surviving the battle, Brandegoris seems not to have joined the second coalition of rebel kings, for he is almost certainly to be identified with King Brandegore, on whose daughter Sir Bors begat a son, Helin le Blank. Bors revisited Brandegoris when Helin was fifteen years old and, with Brandegoris’ consent, brought the boy to Arthur’s court.King Brandegoris himself, however, seems never to have officially joined Arthur’s court, though he allied with him in order to expel the Saxons from Britain, and also joined him in the war against Claudas. He married the daughter of Contantinople, and had a beautiful daughter, upon whom Sir Bors fathered Helain the White. He also fathered a son named Evadeam, also known as the Dwarf Knight. His wife had a son from a previous marriage named Sagremor (Sagramore) – later a Knight of the Round Table.It has been argued that his original name means “Bran of Gore” and that he was originally identical with the god Bran. It seems to be a reference to the Welsh Bran and the land of Gorre (Gore) invented by Chrétien de Troyes.

Brandoch Daha is a lord in the novel "The Worm Ouroboros" by Eric Rücker Eddison.

Means "black raven" in Irish. In Irish legend this was a board game played by the heroes and gods. It was also the name of a king of Leinster (whom the 'Annals of Ulster' say died in 604); he was a good friend of Mongán of the Dál nAraidi but coveted Mongán's wife, Dubh Lacha. 'He tricked Mongán into giving him Dubh Lacha although Mongán, the son of Manannán mac Lir, used his magic powers to get her back. Brandubh treacherously slew the son of the High King Aedh and Aedh made war on him. Brandubh sent a spy to kill Aedh but was later slain by Saran. A Christian embellishment has Brandubh raised from the dead by a miracle.'

The lord of La Dolorous Garde before Lancelot conquered it. When the Saxons invaded Britain at the beginning of Arthur’s reign, Brandin joined them against Arthur. Niniane, the Lady of the Lake, was briefly his paramour and taught him some enchantments that he applied to his castle.Brandus fled before Lancelot, tried to attack Arthur, and shortly thereafter, disguised as a vavasour, invited Gawaine, Ywaine, and thier companions to La Doloreuse Chartre, where they met some of their companions alive whose names they had read on false graves at Dolorous Garde. What Brandus had not told Gawaine and Ywaine was that he intended to imprison them, too, in Dolorous Chartre.Lancelot rescued them. Lancelot also forced him to release Gawaine and a number of other prisoners from the Dolorous Prison, a jail located in another of Brandin’s castles.Brandus may perhaps be identified with Malory’s Sir Brian of the Isles.

Also, compare Brandin.Known bearers of this name include the American professional football player Brandyn Dombrowski (b. 1985) and the American gridiron football player Brandyn Thompson (b. 1989).

He was the son of Ellain the Brown, the brother of Bruhalt (Bruhaut) and Hector, and the uncle of Segurant the Brown.

Alternately, could be taken directly from the English word brass, a metal alloy of copper and zinc, possibly derived from Proto-Germanic brasō "fire, pyre".Brass Crosby (1725-1793) was Lord Mayor of London in 1790, named for his mother’s maiden name. He had a famous run-in with the British Government over freedom of the press. It is said that his defiant attitude in the affair gave rise to the expression 'as bold as brass'.

Brastias originally was a knight of Duke Gorlois.Merlin diguised Sir Ulfius as Sir Brastias on the night Uther begat Arthur. Later, on his accession to the throne, Arthur made Brastias warden to wait upon the north from Trent forwards, for it was that time the most party the king's enemies.Brastias served Arthur well in the first wave of rebellion. With Ulfius, Brastias traveled across the Channel to summon Kings Ban of Benwick and Bors to Arthur’s aid. On the way, the two of them had to joust down eight of King Claudas’ knights who tried to stop them.Brastias fought in the battle of Bedegraine, but afterward seems to drop out of Malory’s account, with no mention that he remained with Arthur long enough to serve at the Round Table. Brastias must already have been at least approaching middle age by the time of Arthur’s coronation, and he may have retired early into a hermitage.He had originally been in the service of the Duke of Tintagel (possibly Gorlois).

Son of Gwawrddur Hunchback, brother of Duach, Nerthach, and the lady Gwenwledyr, and one of Arthur’s warriors.According to Culhwch and Olwen, Brathach and his brothers were sprung from the Highlands of Hell.
Derived from the Slavic element bratu "brother".

There are two possible explanations for the etymology of the first element of this name. The first explanation is that it is derived from Slavic brati "reap, gather", which would make the whole name an older form of Berimir. The second explanation is that it is derived from Slavic bratu "brother", which would then make the whole name a variant form of Bratomir. The second element of this name is derived from Slavic mir "peace".
Derived from the Slavic elements bratu "brother" and lyub "love".
Means "brother of peace", derived from Slavic bratu "brother" combined with Slavic mir "peace". Also compare Bratimir.
A mix of Bruce/Bryce and Claude.
Portuguese form of Braulio. Known bearers of this name include former Brazilian soccer player Bráulio Barbosa de Lima (b. 1948) and Bráulio Tavares (b. 1950), a Brazilian writer and poet.

Apparently derived from Germanic brahuila meaning "bright, radiant" - with one source saying that it is etymologically related to Old High German brand or brant "sword". However, I am not sure how much stock should be put into that, since it seems like its pronunciation would be akin to brilla (BREEL-lah), which makes it look suspiciously close to the Italian verb brillare "to shine, to sparkle" and ultimately comes from berillus, a latinized form of Greek beryllos. Perhaps Germanic peoples did adopt this Latinate-Greek word into their own language as brahuila? Pretty much all sources agree that the name of Bruilio originated in (Visigothic) Spain, so it could indeed be possible that in Germanic Spain of that time a foreign word from neighbouring (mostly Latinate) countries was adopted and germanized. A notable bearer was Braulio of Zaragoza, a (Visigothic-)Spanish saint from the 7th century AD.
Transferred from the surname "Braun", which means "brown."
Feminine form of "Braun", which means "brown" in German.
Late medieval Yiddish name derived from German braun "brown" and Bräune "brownness", it is a cognate of Breindel. This name was recorded in early 16th-century Frankfurt, Germany.

Probably an English variant of Bronwyn. A known bearer of this name is Braunwyn Windham-Burke (b. 1977), who stars in the American reality television series The Real Housewives of Orange County (2006-).
Among Arthur’s knights at the Round Table.He’s in the list Chrétien de Troyes begins in line 1691 of Erec and Enide.

From the French brave, from the Italian bravo, itself either from Provençal brau 'show-off', from the Gaulish *bragos 'fine', or from the Latin *bravus, from a fusion of pravus and barbarus into a root *bravus.
Variant of Brave, with the popular name suffix -en, possibly influenced by Raven.
From the English word "bravery" meaning "being Brave, a brave act".
Variant of Brawley. A known bearer of this name is American Republican politician Brawleigh Graham.
Transferred use of the surname Brawley. A known bearer of this name is American actor Brawley Nolte (b. 1986), the son of American actor Nick Nolte (b. 1941).
Either a short form of Braxton or an invented name based on Braxton and other names ending in X like Dax and Maddox.
Variant of Braxton using the popular phonetic suffix den, found in such names as Hayden and Aidan.
An invented name, based on other similar names such as Paisley and Brinley.
Invented name combining the phonetic elements brax (like in Braxton) and son.
Transferred use of the surname Bray, derived from Cornish bre meaning "hill".
Medieval Cornish name which is said to be derived from Cornish bregh "brave; fine".
Combination of the phonetic elements bray and la, possibly intended as a feminine form of Braylon.
Probably an invented name, using the same sounds found in names such as Braelyn and Gayle.
Combination of the phonetic elements bray and lee, in line with names like Braelyn and Briley.

Possibly a combination of the English surname Bray, from the Cornish bre 'hill' combined with the suffix -leen. Another possibility is that it's a feminized variant of Brayden combined with the suffix -leen.
Either a combination of the popular elements bray and son or a transferred use of the surname Brayson.
Transferred use of the surname Brayton. It began rising in popularity in the 1990s along with other names containing the elements bray and ton.
From the English word meaning "bold, shameless, obvious" or "made of brass, of brass colour".
From the name of the Latin American country.
Either transferred use of the surname Brazos or from a Spanish word meaning "arms".
Short for names beginning with Bre-, Bri-, and Bry-, most notably Brianna.
Possibly a variant of Bree, Breagh or Bria. Actress Brea Grant played Daphne Millbrook on Heroes.

Latinized form of Breage, from Cornish bregh "brave". The 5th-century Cornish saint Breage is also known as Breaca or Bray. Breage is also probably the source of the medieval Cornish name Braya.K.M. Sheard writes, "The similarity to Bridget and Brigantia may not be coincidental; bregh comes ultimately from Celtic *briga- "might, power", the same potential derivation as Bridget. It is therefore not beyond the realms of possibility that St. Bray represents a survival of the worship of the goddess in Cornwall."
Derived from Gaelic breac "speckled, spotted" combined with a diminutive suffix. This was the name of a 6th-century Irish saint who was famous as a healer.
Breadan is another spelling for Brayden.
Referring to the word of God as the only thing required for subsistence.
Transferred use of the surname Breagan.
Name of a 5th century Irish saint, venerated in Cornwall and South West England.
Allegedly derived from Scottish Gaelic brèagha, ultimately from Old Irish bregda, "fine, handsome, beautiful".
Short form of Brianna, or elaboration of Bree.
The name originated from the name Brianna
Variant of Briana possibly inspired by Hannah.
Originates from the Old English verb brǣðan (to exhale, breathe), derived from the noun brǣth (breath, odor, vapor).
Languedocian and Gascon form of Brice.
Breca (sometimes spelled Breoca) was a Bronding who, according to the Anglo-Saxon poem Beowulf, was Beowulf’s childhood friend.
Derived from Irish brecc "freckled, speckled" combined with a diminutive suffix, making it a cognate of Brychan. This was a common name in early Ireland, borne by at least 13 saints.
Likely taken from the Old Irish word brecc meaning “speckled, spotted; trout”. It probably originated as a nickname given to somebody with freckles.
Transferred use of the surname Brecken.
Either a variant of Brooklyn or an elaboration of Brecken or Brock with the popular name suffix -lyn.
From the medieval Danish word bredje, meaning "battle axe". This name is rarely used outside Norway. Brede is also a surname.
in ancient assyrian mythilogy this was the name of daughter of god of gods "il". Assyrian may refer to: Anything from Assyria, an ancient empire in Mesopotamia.
This is one of the many names of Lord Peter Wimsey, a fictional character created by Dorothy L. Sayers. It is also the name of his firstborn son.
Variant of Brianne, or a combination of Bree and Ann.
Rare combination of Bree and Lee.
Combination of Bree and the popular name suffix lyn.
A combination of Bree and Lynn.
Probably an invented name, perhaps based on Breanna. (See also Brina.)
Transferred use of the surname Brees. A notable bearer of the surname is quarterback Drew Brees
Likely a variant of Brianne or an elongation of Bryn.
From the English word "breeze" referring to "a light, gentle wind". From the Dutch bries 'breeze', from the Eastern Frisian brîse 'breeze', from brisen 'to blow fresh and strong'.
This name may be derived from the word breezy.One fictional bearer of this name is Breezie Hedgebot Robotnik, a character from the Adventures of Sonic the Hedgehog television series.
From the adjective (see Breeze). It is also used as a diminutive for names containing -bri/bre(e)-, like Brianna or Sabrina.
Variant spelling of Breffny, which is the standard anglicization of Bréifne (see Breifne).
Anglicized form of Bréifne (see Breifne).A known bearer of this name is the Irish reality television star Breffny Morgan (born circa 1987).
Variant spelling of either Bréifne (see Breifne) or its anglicization Breffny.A notable bearer of this name is the Irish actor Brefni O'Rorke (1889-1946).

A fictional character created by J.R.R. Tolkien. Bregalad, known in the common tongue as Quickbeam, was an Ent at the time of the War of the Ring. He was significantly younger than elder Ents such as Treebeard. He guarded the rowan trees and resembled a rowan himself.
Provençal and Franco-Provençal form of Bridget.
Feminine form of Brecht. See also Brechtje.
The second king of Rohan, in J.R.R. Tolkien's literary works. In Peter Jackson's film versions, Aragorn rides a horse by the name of Brego (apparently in honor of the king).

Derived from Old English bregu "ruler" (compare Breguswið) and wine "friend". This was the name of a medieval Archbishop of Canterbury, the successor of Cuthbert. After his death in 764, Bregowine was considered a saint and a vita (or hagiographical life) about him was written in the 12th century.

Derived from Old English bregu "ruler" (supposedly borrowed from Old Norse bragr "best, most splendid"; compare Bragi) and swiþ "strong". This was borne by the mother of the 7th-century English saint Hilda of Whitby.
Likely either a variant of Briana or a combination of the prefix bre and Hannah.
A traditional name with unknown etymology in the Rantzau family.

Likely derived from Bréifne (also Bréfne), the name of a medieval Irish kingdom. The meaning of its name is uncertain, as it is disputed amongst scholars. Some derive the name from Old Irish brí meaning "hill", whilst others state that it is derived from the feminine given name Bréfne.
Variant of Bree inspired by the spelling of Leigh.
Variant spelling of Bria or an elaboration of Breigh.
Likely a variant of Breelyn or Braelyn.
German-Yiddish variant of Breindel (see also Bräunle).
Means "broad; wide". This is the name of one of Karl and Snør's sons in Norse mythology.
Alternate transcription of Pashto بريښنا (see Breshna).

An alleged Lithuanian goddess.The form Breksta was first recorded by Polish historian and theologian Jan Łasicki in his treatise on idolatry De diis Samagitarum caeterorumque Sarmatarum et falsorum Christianorum, written ca. 1582 and published in 1615, while Polish historian Theodor Narbutt referred to her as Brekszta in his work Dzieje starożytne narodu litewskiego, written between 1835 and 1841.Both forms are Latinizations; the original form, if there ever was one, is lost, however a Lithuanian form has since been reconstructed: Brėkšta.Although both Łasicki and Narbutt mention this goddess by very similar names, they differ on her presumed function: Łasicki refers to Breksta as a goddess of twilight, opening the door to speculations that her name might in fact be an epithet (or a "euphemism") of the goddess Vakarė. In Narbutt's opinion on the other hand, she was a goddess of darkness and dreams.As for the meaning of her name, there is a theory that Brėkšta might be derived from Lithuanian brėkšti "it is dawning; dawn/dusk is falling" (which might corroborate Łasicki's notion of her being a goddess of twilight).Since neither Łasicki nor Narbutt were intimately familiar with Lithuanian culture or language, the academic opinion on the value of their writings ranges from a valuable resource to a practical joke.

Latinized form of Βρεμουσα (Bremousa), which allegedly meant "raging woman" from Greek βρέμω (bremo) "to roar, shout, rage". This was the name of one of the twelve Amazon warriors who followed Penthesilea into the Trojan War.
Short form of Brendan, Brenda and other names starting with Bren-.
Short form of Labrencis, used as a given name in its own right.
Combination of Brenda and Lee, popularised by singer Brenda Lee (1944-).
Variant of Brendalí using the Caribbean Spanish name suffix liz (from Elizabeth or a related name), especially popular in Puerto Rico.
Elaboration of Brenda using the popular name suffix lyn, possibly modelled on Gwendolyn.
Irish variant of Brendan as well as one of the Spanish forms of the name.
Italian and Spanish form of Brendan via its medieval Latin form Brendanus.
Meaning uncertain, could be a masculine form of Brenda, a variant of Brendan or a variant of Breno.
Probably a combination of two names, such as a name starting with B- with René or Renée.A known bearer of this name is the American research professor and author Dr. Brené Brown (b. 1965).
A diminutive of names with the element or sound of -bren-, such as Brenna or Brendan.
Transferred use of the surname Brenner.
Variant of Brenley. This name was brough to limited public attention by Brennley Brown, a contestant in the 12th season of the American TV show 'The Voice'.

Brennos, chieftain of the Senones, led an army of Cisalpine Gauls in their attack on Rome in the Battle of the Allia, in 387 BC. Another Brennos was one of the leaders of the army of Gauls who attempted to invade and settle in the Greek mainland in 278 BC. After a looting spree and after managing to pass Thermopylae by encircling the Greek army and forcing it to retreat he made his way to the rich treasury at Delphi but he was defeated by the re-assembled Greek army.It has been debated whether Brenno was an actual given name or rather a title.
Transferred use of the surname Brentley.
Transferred use of the surname Brentson.
Alternate spelling of Breca, a character from Beowulf.
Cornish form of Brioc. This name was borne by a Welsh saint who is commemorated in St. Breock.
The sister of Medea (Medeas), the lecherous female ruler of Crudele castle.Her other sisters included Lavina, Agnena, and Pulizena.
Possibly from Bresi, which is a form of the Old English name Beorhtsige.
Transferred use of the surname Breslin.
Old Irish name derived from Celtic *brestelo-s "strife, war". It was borne by Bressal mac Ailello Thassaig, an early king of the Uí Liatháin, an early kingdom of Munster in southern Ireland.
From Old Norse bresta meaning "to burst, break".
Early Anglicization and Gallicization of Brithael. In Arthurian legend, Bretel is a servant of Gorlois.
Means "snowbank; snowdrift". Is related to Breiðr.
Slovak and Slovene form of the Czech name Břetislav, which has Slavic roots. Nicknames for this name include Bret or Brett, Slávek, Slavo, and Břeťa.
In the case of Filipino-American beauty influencer and social media personality Bretman Rock (1998-) he was named after wrestlers Bret Hart and The Rock.
Transferred use of the surname Breton.
In Greek mythology, Brettia was the eponymous nymph of Abrettene, Mysia.
Scandinavian form of the Old English name Brihtgifu, a metathesis of Beorhtgifu.
Feminine variant of Brett using the popular name suffix lyn.
Variant of Brittany, possibly inspired by Brett.
Either a variant of Britton or a transferred use of the surname Bretton.
Rare Dutch form of Bruno. The form Bruin is more common and better attested.

Derived from the place name Bréval, ubicated in north-central France. Recorded as other forms, ultimately comes from the Germanic name Berher and French val "valley", albeit the first element was later reinterpreted as bref "small".
Invented name combining the sounds present in the names Brendan and Kevin.
Transferred use of the surname Brewer.
Transferred use of a surname Brewster.
Combination of the phonetic elements brex and lee or possibly intended as a variant of Bexley.
Combination of the phonetic elements brex and lyn.
Derived from the place name Brixia, the Latin name of an ancient city situated in Gallia Cisalpina, now Brescia in Lombardy, Italy.

Means "heather" in Spanish, taken from the title of the Virgin Mary Nuestra Señora del Brezo meaning "Our Lady of the Heather". She is venerated in the Spanish province of Palencia.According to folk legend, the Virgin Mary appeared to two shepherds and entrusted them with the mission of finding a carving of the Virgin located in the mountains of Liébana, a nearby city. When the shepherds arrived at the place, they found a ruined hermitage, and a new apparition revealed to them that this was the place where a sanctuary should be built.
Very rare variant of Brianna modelled on Rhianna.
Variant of Bree or a diminutive of any name containing the element -bri-, such as Brian, Briana, Gabriella, etc.

From a Brythonic name derived from the Celtic element *brigo "high, noble, mighty". As such this name can be viewed as a Breton cognate of Brian. In the case of Saint Briac, who arrived in Brittany with Saint Tugdual circa 548, this was a short form of the old Welsh name Briafael.
In Palamedes, one of two knights who murdered the Good Knight Without Fear. His companion was Ferrant.

A powerful jouster who guarded the Spring of the Two Sycamores. He was considered undefeatable; he had even knocked down Gawaine. This lasted until he was conquered by Lancelot and received a mortal wound. His brother, Belyas the Black (Belias), and father, Broadas, were also slain by Lancelot.
Feminine form of Briag, this name is occasionally also considered a Breton cognate of Cornish Breaca.
A knight who joined Nogant in an assault on Queen Fenise of Ireland. Arthur’s forces joined Nogant but Arthur soon learned that he was a coward, and the siege was lifted.
Old Welsh form of the Brythonic name *Brigomaglos, which was composed of the Proto-Celtic elements *brigos, *brigā meaning "might, power" and *maglos "chief, noble".
Scottish Gaelic equivalent of Brianna, Brianne.
Combination of the name Annette and Briana. OR Brianne.
An invented name, blending Brianna and Rhiannon.
Likely an elaboration of Briana with the suffix tay.
An invented name, using the same sounds found in names such as Briana, Kiara and Tiara.
This is the French form of the Ancient Greek name Briareus, and is used in Tome IV of Victor Hugo's novel Les Misérables.
Derived from Ancient Greek βριαρός (briaros) meaning "strong, stout". This was the name of one of the Hecatoncheires (giants with one hundred hands) in Greek mythology. He was also known as Aegaeon.
Elaboration of Brice using the popular name suffix lyn.
Feminine form of Bricio (compare Brizia). This name coincides with the name of a town in Castile and León, Spain.
Name of a 7th century Irish saint.
Spanish form of Bricius. It can also be a short form of Fabricio.
Originally a nickname from the English word brick (having the slang meaning "a good fellow" from 1840). It was used for a character in Tennessee Williams' play 'Cat on a Hot Tin Roof' (1955).
Combination of the word Brick and the popular suffix lee.
Invented by adding lyn to the end of the word Brick. Likely a variant of Brooklyn.

Bricta or Brixta was a Gaulish goddess who was a consort of Luxovius. It has, however, been suggested that if "Bricta is a title incorporating Bríg, it may actually be a title assigned to Sirona rather than a separate goddess". Either way, the Gaulish theonym is derived from the word brixtom or brixta "magic".
Latinized form of the Old English name Brihtgifu, a metathesis of Beorhtgifu.
A form of the Old English name Beorhtflæd.
Variant form of Beorhtgyth, an Old English name derived from the elements beorht "bright" and guð "battle".
Form of Beorhtmann found in the Phillimore translation of Domesday Book.
Variant form of Beorhtnoth, an Old English name derived from the elements beorht "bright" and noð "boldness, daring".
Form of Beorhtstan found in the Phillimore translation of Domesday Book.
A form of the Old English name Beorhtwulf.
Form of Beorhtwig found in the Phillimore translation of Domesday Book.
Medieval German and archaic Romansh short form of Brigitta, via the variant Brigida.
Name of seven Kings of the Picts.
Irish variant of Bridie and Manx variant of Breeshey as well as a Manx cognate of Bríd and Brìde.
Anglicized form of Brídín, which is a diminutive of Bríd.
Transferred usage of the place name Bridgemont.
Transferred use of the surname Bridges.
Variant of Bridget. A known bearer is the American actress and singer Bridgit Mendler (1992-).
Originally a short form of Alberik.

Variant of Brianne. This is the name of a character in George R. R. Martin's 'A Song of Ice and Fire' series, as well as the TV show based on the books 'Game of Thrones'. Martin did not originate this form, though, for it was in use in the United States well before the first book in the series was published in 1996.
Means "noble, privileged" in Old Breton (cf. Brian).
Transferred use of the surname Brierley.
Possibly a Latinized form of Bríd or Brígh.
Derived from Celtic *brigant- "high" or *briga- "might, power". This was the name of an important Brythonic goddess. She is almost certainly the same deity as Bridget, the Irish goddess.
Variant of Bridgette (or perhaps an Anglicized variant of Brigitte).
Transferred use of the surname Brigg.
Combination of the name Briggs with the name element ton.
Feminine form of Brigham. This name was mostly used by Mormon parents who wanted to honor Brigham Young, who was the 2nd president of the LDS Church.
Diminutive of Brighid. See also Brídín.
A unique form of spelling for the Celtic goddess, Brigid. She was the goddess of many things.
Variant of Brighton coinciding with the English word brighten meaning "to become or make bright or brighter, to become more cheerful".
From the English word brighly meaning "in a bright way", possibly inspired by names with a similar ending like Amberly and Baily.
Possibly a transferred use of the surname Brighton or from the English town of Brighton.

Related to the Celtic root brixs meaning "high, hill". According to Galician mythology, Brigo was the first person who settled in Galicia, and he was grandson of Noah and father of Artai. This character is often identified with Breogán, from the Irish legendarium 'Lebor Gabála Érenn'.
Medieval name recorded in 1219, possibly derived from the Old English name Beorhtwynn.

From Sanskrit बृहद्रथ (Bṛhadratha), meaning "the one with the great chariot", from Sanskrit बृहत् (bŕhat) "large, great" and रथ (ratha) "chariot". This was the name of the founder of the Brihadratha dynasty, the earliest ruling dynasty of Magadha.
From Sanskrit बृहस्पति (bṛhaspati) meaning "Jupiter (the planet)" or "Thursday". This is the name of a Hindu god associated with the planet Jupiter.

Means "ruler of Brij" from the place name ब्रज (Braj), also known as Brij or Brijbhumi, which is a region in Uttar Pradesh, India, considered to be the land of the Hindu god Krishna, combined with the name of the god Indra, used here to mean "lord".

Compound of the place name ब्रज (Braj), also known as Brij or Brijbhumi, a region in Uttar Pradesh, India, where the Hindu god Krishna is supposed to have lived as a child, and Lal, which is an epithet of Krishna.
A combination of the popular feminine names Brianna and Mackenzie.
Means "brilliant, shining" in Indonesian, borrowed from Dutch briljant.
Means "brilliant, sparkly, gemstone" in Spanish. A notable bearer was Brillante Mendoza (1960-), a Filipino independent film director.

Coined by Lord Conway in the early 17th century for his daughter (who would later become a well-known English letter-writer).At the time of his daughter's birth, Lord Conway was governor at Brill in the Netherlands - which is allegedly also the inspiration behind this name.
From the English word brilliance meaning "intense brightness of light".
From the English word brilliant meaning "(of light or color) very bright and radiant".
Combination of the phonetic elements bry and lyn, likely based on the sounds found in other names such as Briley and Braelyn.
Possibly derived from Old Norse brim meaning "surf, surge" (compare Brimir) combined with herr meaning "army, warrior". This is also the Icelandic name for the city of Bremen, Germany.

The name can be interpreted as a dithematic Germanic name composed of brem "famous; boasting" and sind "path, journey".Arthur’s sister in the Vulgate Merlin.The daughter of Hoel and Igerne (Igraine), she married King Urien (Uriens) and had a son named Yvain (Ywaine). Her sister was called Blasine. She encouraged her son to take service with Arthur.Her role is assumed by Morgan le Fay in the Post-Vulgate.
Derived from the Old Norse elements brim "surf, surge; surface of the sea" and hildr "battle, fight".
Variant of either Brimir or Brími.

Probably related to Old Norse brim meaning "surf, surface of the sea". Alternatively, it could mean "flickerer", from brími "fire". This is possibly another name for Ymir in Norse mythology. It is also the name of Odin’s sword, and eventually became a poetic word meaning "sword".

Means "the terrible one, the grim one, the snorting one, the angry one", derived from Ancient Greek βρίμη (brime) meaning "strength, power, threat, menace" or "bellowing, roaring". This was the name of a minor goddess worshipped in Thessaly, as well as an epithet of several Ancient Greek goddesses associated with the underworld, most notably Hecate, Demeter, and Persephone.
Derived from the Old Norse elements brim "surf, surge; surface of the sea" and rún "secret lore, rune".

Locational name, from the Brindabella mountain range on the border of New South Wales and the Australian Capital Territory. Usually said to be from a local language, meaning "two hopping mice" - hopping mice are native Australian mice. Another theory is that it is from brindy brindy, meaning "water running over rocks", with a European -bella added to suggest "beautiful".
The name Brindin is a rare variant on the names Brandon and Brendan. It is more closely related to the name Brindon.
Brij is the birth place of Lord Shri Krishan.and Indra is the lord of Gods,by Vedic.
Diminutive of Sybrina used in the 18th century.
A name coined during World War 1 with the literal meaning "bring peace".

Coined from the German phrase Bring Friede "bring peace!". The name was given to girls in Germany during and after the two world wars to express the desire for peace.A notable bearer of the name is the German politician Bringfiede Kahrs who served as Senator in Bremen.
Diminutive of Sabrina. An example is Sabrina "Brini" Maxwell, a fictional character.
Transferred use of the surname Brinker.Name of character in the novel, A Separate Peace.
Variant of Brinkley. A notable bearer is American long-distance swimmer Brinkleigh Hansen (2009-).
Transferred use of the surname Brinkley.
Variant of Brinley or transferred use of the surname Brinly.
Variant of Brinley. Also compare Brynnlee.
Transferred use of the surname Brinsley.
Transferred use of the surname Brinson.
Transferred use of the surname Brinton.

English and Guernésiais form of Briog via the Latinization Briocus. Brioc (died c. 502) was a 5th-century Welsh holy man who became the first abbot of Saint-Brieuc in Brittany. He is one of the seven founder saints of Brittany.
Meaning unknown, perhaps related to Bhreacain (see Brecan). This was the name of a saint from the 5th century AD, who brought christianity to the village Rosmuck in Ireland.

Derived from Breton and Middle Welsh bri, ultimately from Proto-Celtic *brigo "high, noble" or *brīgos "importance". Briog (died c. 502) was a 5th-century Welsh holy man who became the first abbot of Saint-Brieuc in Brittany. He is one of the seven founder saints of Brittany.
Possibly a form of Brioc combined with Celtic *maglos "noble, chief" (compare Maglocunos).
A variant spelling of Brisen the enchantress's name.
Likely a blend of Briseida, Brígida, or Bricio with Griselda.
The name of a witch in Arthurian legend. One theory connects it to Old Norse brisinga "glowing, twinkling" (a word-forming element associated with Freya's famous necklace, the brísingamen).
This given name is probably a combination of Briseida or Brigida with any name ending in -enia or -senia (depends on which name is used for the first part of the name), such as Eugenia and Yesenia.
Italian and Spanish form of Briseus.

Probably derived from Βρῖσα (Brisa) (also Βρήση), the name of a location in Lesbos, Greece. A connection to the Ancient Greek word βρίθω (britho) meaning "to be heavy, weighed down; to bear down" or "to prevail" has also been suggested, but this is likely folk etymology. This was an epithet of the god Dionysos in Smyrna. It was also the name of the father of Briseis.
Probably means "to shine, to show off", compare the Nynorsk verb brisa.
A variant spelling of Brisen the enchantress's name.
Possibly a medieval Portuguese form of Brígida.

the name brisley is of Anglo-Saxon origin and typically functions as a locational name referring to someone from a specific place. It is most prominently tied to a small village in Norfolk, England and has historical roots dating back in medieval times. the meaning of the name brisley is the Gadfly Meadow the most common etymological breakdown suggests it comes from the Old English words brīosa (meaning Gadfly) and lēah (meaning a "woodland clearing" or "meadow").
A variant spelling of Brisen the enchantress's name.
Transferred use of the surname Briston.
Variant of Brittany incorporating the name of the place Britain.
Possibly from Latin britannica meaning "of Britannia, British", as in the title of the Encyclopædia Britannica, the oldest English-language general encyclopedia.

Latin byname meaning "of Britain". This was one of the bynames of Emperor Claudius after the Roman conquest of Britain in 43 AD. Claudius also gave it to his son, Britannicus (full name Tiberius Claudius Caesar Britannicus; 41-55 AD).
Derived from either Old Breton brit "mind, spirit" or Old Breton Britto "Briton" and hael "generous; noble".
Spanish variant of Brittany. This name ranked #8 in Ecuador in 2014.
Latinized form of Brihtgifu, a variant of Beorhtgifu.
Allegedly a combination of Britney and Christina.
Taken from the English word British.
Modern name, probably a blend of Brittany and the popular phonetic suffix lee.
Combination of Brit (short for Brittney) and Lynn
Either a variant of Britton or derived from the surname Briton.
Transferred use of the surname Britt.
Transferred use of the surname Britten.
Diminutive of Brittany, Britannia, and other names starting with Brit-.
Variant of Brixhida, possibly modelled on English Bridget.
Possibly an Albanian form of French Brigitte as well as a masculine form of Brixhida.
Alternate Latinization or German form of Bricius (see Brice).
A combination of the phonetic sound brix with the popular name suffix lee.
From the name of a district in South London, England.
Variant and feminine form of Brixton.
Potential diminutive of Brixton. In the case of Pusha T’s daughter, it’s in reference to cocaine.
A variant of Brianna. In both, 2002 and 2006 there were 46 girls named Briyanna.
Italian form of Brice and diminutive of Fabrizio.

Derived from Greek βρίζω (brizo) meaning "to slumber". This was the name of an Ancient Greek goddess who was known as the protector of mariners, sailors, and fishermen, as well as being credited with sending prophetic dreams.

The name of a Serbian Princess. The etymology of her name is unclear. It may be derived from Veronica, Berenice or Bernardine, or a nickname of her mother, taken from her feudal estate Brnjak. Lastly, it may be taken from the male name Prnjak.
Transferred use of the surname Broadus.
Latinized version of the Irish name Broccán.
From the old Welsh name Brochfael, in which the second element is mael "prince". This was the name of a legendary Welsh king who gave land to Saint Melangell.
A Knight of the Round Table who embarked with the others on the Grail Quest.
Transferred use of the surname Brodén.
Modern form of Old Norse Bróðir.
Transferred use of the surname Broderick.
Variant of Brody, influenced by Bodhi.
Variant of Brody. According to the US Social Security Administration, 24 baby boys and 13 baby girls were named Brodi in 2006
Elaboration of Brodi with the same ending as Maddox and Dax.
Transferred use of the surname Brodrick. See also Broderick.
The first element is derived from Old High German prôdi "weakness, decrepitude" or Old High German brôt "bread." The second element is derived from Gothic vulfs "wolf."
Derived from Polish brodzić "to wade, to flounder" combined with Slavic slav "glory".
Anglicized form of Brogán used outside of Ireland.
Derived from the Proto-Celtic elements *brogis, *mrogis "territory, region" and *māros "great".
Anglo-Scandinavian name (originally byname) meaning "without breeches", composed of Old Norse brók "breeches, pants" and -lauss "-less".
Derived from the Georgian noun ბროლი (broli) meaning "crystal" (as in the glass, not the mineral). In some cases, this name can also be a short form of the related name Nazibrola.
Transferred use of the surname Brolin.
Means "of crystal" in Georgian. It is derived from Georgian ბროლის (brolis), which is the genitive of the noun ბროლი (broli) meaning "crystal" (see Brola).

Derived from the English word broccoli. This is the name of a fictional character from the Dragon Ball media franchise. In the series, Broly is a green-haired villain and belongs to the Saiyan race, like Goku and Vegeta.

Brom is a fictional character in Christopher Paolini's Inheritance Trilogy. He is a former Dragon Rider and good member of the Varden. He is the trilogy's main character's mentor through the first book. He also created the Varden.

Latinized form of the Ancient Greek given name Βρόμερος (Bromeros), which might have been derived from Ancient Greek βρόμος (bromos) meaning "loud noise; roaring, crackling, clanging" or figuratively "rage, fury". The modern Greek word βρομερός (bromeros) "foul, stinky, dirty" is related to it. Bromerus was the name of a king of Lynkestis, who lived in the 5th century BC.
Transferred use of the surname Bromleigh.
Transferred use of the surname Bromley.
Transferred use of the surname Bron. Otherwise, it could be a short form of LeBron or Bronson.
From the English word bronc meaning "untamed horse".
Derived from the English word bronco, which describes a wild horse.
Feminine form and masculine short form of Bronys.
Italian and Spanish form of Bronisław via Latinized form Bronislaus.
French form of Bronisław, via its Latinized form Bronislaus.
Old Polish diminutive of names starting with the Old Slavic element borna "defence, protection", such as Bronisław and Bronisąd.
Either a variant of Bronia or a short form from Brunhilde.
Derived from the Slavic element borna "protection" and the American name Jay 1. Comic character Bronjay, from Heaven Sent Gaming's Reverie, has this name.
Norwegian dialectal variant of Brynhilda used in Rogaland and Sunnhordland.
Variant of popular Bronwyn, or from the Welsh elements bron meaning "breast" and llyn meaning "lake".

Ser Bronn of the Blackwater is the name of a character from the Song of Ice and Fire books by GRR Martin and the TV show Game of Thrones based upon the former. Being a recent invention for a fictious world resembling Medieval Europe, no actual or alleged etymology is known, also it may refer to Bruno or brown.
Variant of Bräunle. It was recorded in early 16th-century Frankfurt, Germany.
Swedish dialectal form of Brynjulf (see Bryniulfr).
Variant of either Brynhildr (when used for a girl) or Bryniulfr (when used for a boy).
In Robert Mannyng’s chronicle, a Saxon lord who allied with Mordred and was slain at the final battle against Arthur.
Variant of Brynhildr (when used for a girl) or Bryniulfr (when used for a boy).
Diminutive of LeBron, Bronius, and other names containing bron.
From Ancient Greek βροντή ‎(bronte) meaning "thunder". Bronte was the personification of thunder in Greek mythology, counterpart to Astrape "lightning".
Transferred use of the place name Bronx. It began gaining popularity as a given name after singers Pete Wentz and Ashlee Simpson used it for their son in 2008.
Combination of Bronx and the popular name suffix -ton. According to the SSA, this name was given to 5 boys in 2017.
East Prussian German form of Bronius.
Bronze is a yellowish-brown alloy of copper with up to one-third tin. It is a modern first name. In the US, 5 girls and 9 boys were given this first name in 2018.
Transferred use of the surname Brooker.
Variant of Brooks.Was given to 10 girls and 17 boys in 1982.
Diminutive and feminine form of Brooks.
Transferred use of the surname Brookson.
Very rare, in reference to the plant or another use of the surnames Broom or Broome.
Transferred use of the surname Broox, which is a variant of the surname Brooks.
Medieval German diminutive of both Ambros and Ambrosia. The diminutive suffix -ke suggests that it was probably of Low German origin.
Obsolete diminutive form of both Ambros and Ambrosia.Coincidentally, "Brösel" is the modern German word for "crumb".

This was borne by Cuban actress Broselianda Hernández Boudet (1964-2020), who was the daughter of Cuban dramatist and critic Rosa Ileana Boudet (1947-). It was perhaps inspired by the mythological place name Brocéliande.
German diminutive form of Ambrosius (see Ambrosios), which is now rather archaic or at least old-fashioned.
Short form of Ambrosius (see Ambrosios). This name is now rather archaic and one is more likely to come across it in German-speaking areas as a surname, rather than a first name.

Means "mortal lord" or "lord of the mortals", derived from either the Greek adjective βρότειος (broteios) meaning "mortal, human" or the Greek noun βροτός (brotos) meaning "mortal man" combined with ἄναξ (anax) meaning "master, lord, king".

Possibly derived from Greek βροτός (brotos) meaning "mortal man, human being", though it has also been connected to βροντή (bronte) meaning "thunder". This was the name of several characters in Greek mythology, including a legendary hunter and son of Tantalus.
Indian origin Sanskrit Brat meaning vow or oath

The first element is derived from Old High German prôdi "weakness, decrepitude" or Old High German brôt "bread." The second element is derived from Old High German hari "army." It is also possible that this name comes from (or is related to) Old High German brôdar "brother", which is a possibility that cannot be ruled out.
From the English word brother meaning "male sibling".
Old Danish and Medieval English form of Bróðir.
Transferred use of the surname Brown.

Variant of Brown. Notable namesake is Henry Browne Blackwell, an English born publisher and social reformer who was one of the founders of the Republican Party in the US. Blackwell and wife Lucy Stone helped organize the American Woman Suffrage Association to lobby for the legal right to vote for American women.
Transferred use of the surname Brownell.
Transferred use of the surname Browning.
Transferred use of the surname Brownlow.
Transferred use of the surname Broxton.

From Catalan bruc meaning "tree heath", a species of flowering plant native to the Mediterranean basin. This is also the name of a town in Catalonia where, according to the legend, a young drummer in the Peninsular War (1807-1814) deceived the enemy troops into believing the Spanish troops were larger than they were merely by playing the drum.
Combination of Bruce and Lee (see also surname Lee 2), honouring the actor, director, martial artist, martial arts instructor and philosopher Bruce Lee (1940-1973).
Spanish variant of Brucelee, mainly used in Peru.
The nephew of Brian of the Isles, Arthur’s enemy. He murdered the noble Meliot of Logres, and was slain in turn by Perceval.
Brudus was a leader of the Picts.
From the Tibetan འབྲུག ('brug) meaning "dragon, thunder" and མོ (mo) meaning "female, woman".

From the Catalan title of the Virgin Mary, Mare de Déu de Bruguers, meaning "Mother of God of Bruguers." She is venerated at the hermitage in the municipality of Gavà in the comarca of Baix Llobregat, hence the high concentration of its usage in that comarca.
Name - Bruhi ब्रूहिMEANING - say, to pronounce, speak Origin - Sanskrit Usage - hindi, Marathi, Gujarati, Indian, Tamil, Telugu, Nepali, Sinhala, Sikh, Buddhist
Dutch form of Bruno. It coincides with the Dutch word for "brown". This was also the name of the bear in medieval fables of Reynard the Fox.

The name of an Irish saint, listed in the 17th-century Martyrology of Donegal under May 29: 'Bruinsech Cael (the slender), Virgin, daughter of Crimthann of Mag Trea'. She has been identified with Buriana, an Irish saint who traveled to Cornwall.
Short form of Bruisten. This name is unlikely to ever be used/revived in modern times, due to its similarity to the Dutch verb bruisen "to fizz", which may have some teasing potential.
Short form of Bruisten. This name is unlikely to ever be used/revived in modern times, due to its similarity to the Dutch verb bruisen "to fizz", which may have some teasing potential.
Usage - Hindi, Sanskrit, Indian, Tamil, Telugu, Nepali, Sinhala, Bengali, Sikh, Buddhist, Mauritian, Fijian Origin -Sanskrit MEANING - to say, pronounce, speak
Derived from Middle French brun "brown (the color)" (ultimately from Old French brun “polished, shiny, brown”), and denoting a man with brown hair.

Brunchildis is a variant of the name Brunhilde. It refers to the legendary Merovingian Queen of Austrasia, Visigothic princess who married King Sigebert I of the Franks. She was one of the most powerful, ruthless, and politically savvy women in early medieval Europe, ruling Austrasia and Burgundy for decades.The name means, 'Battle armor" or "armored battle maiden", derived from the Old Germanic words brunjo (armor) and hild (battle).
Combination of an Old Norse word brundi (related to Norwegian brund "reindeer bull") and Bialfi.
Dutch variant of Bruno and Bruna.
Respelling of Brunita, a Spanish diminutiv of Bruna.

Italian diminutive of Bruna. Derived from Middle French brune, the feminine form of the adjective brun, "brown (the color)" (ultimately from Old French brun “polished, shiny, brown”), and denoting a woman with brown hair.
Derived from Old High German brunja "breastplate, cuirass" or brûn "brown" combined with Old High German fridu "peace."
Derived from the Old English elements brun "brown" and gar "spear".
Derived from Old High German brunja "breastplate, cuirass" or brûn "brown" combined with Gothic hardus (hart in Old High German) "brave, hardy."
Derived from the Old English elements brun meaning "brown" and hyse meaning "youth warrior" (also found in Godhyse).
Variant of Brúnn. This is the name of a dwarf and another name for Odin in Norse mythology.
Old Danish form of Brúni as well as a German diminutive of the feminine names Brunhild and Brunhilde.A notable bearer of this name was the German actress Bruni Löbel (1920-2006).
Variant of Bronislava influenced by names beginning with the element Brun-, such as Brunhilde.
Medieval French form of a Germanic name, in which the second element is swind meaning "strong". The first element may be brun "armour, protection" or brunna "brown".
Late Old English name meaning "brown lock (of hair)", composed of the elements brun "brown" and locc "hair, curl" (probably originally a byname).
Derived from the Old English elements brun "brown" and mære "famous".
Derived from the Old English elements brun "brown" and mann "person, man".
Derived from the Germanic name elements brúnn "brown, shining" and maðr "man".
Means "brown; shining". Related to German Bruno.
Form of Brünhild, used by Richard Wagner in 'Der Ring des Nibelungen'.

Pseudo-German variant of Bruno used for the titular character of Sacha Baren Cohen's 2009 comedy film 'Brüno', about a flamboyantly gay Austrian fashion designer.Note that in real-life German, the name Bruno is never spelled with an umlaut.
Derived from Old High German brunja "breastplate, cuirass" or brûn "brown" combined with Old High German mund "protection."
Feminine form of Brunon found in the Bourgogne-Franche-Comté region up until the 1700s.
Allegoric personification of the city (and the fromer state) of Braunschweig (Brunswick), Germany. Very rarely used as a given name.

Likely derived from the Germanic element brunna "armour, protection" or brun "brown". This is the name of several characters in Arthurian tales, including the father of Sir Galehaut and the Knight of the Ill-Fitting Coat.
Derived from Old High German brunja "breastplate, cuirass" or brûn "brown" combined with Old High German rât "counsel."

Derived from Old High German brunja "breastplate, cuirass" or brûn "brown" combined with rîcja "powerful, strong, mighty." The second element is also closely related to Celtic rîg or rix and Gothic reiks, which all mean "king, ruler."
Transferred use of the surname Brunson.
Derived from Old High German brunja "breastplate, cuirass" or brûn "brown" combined with Old High German stain "stone."
Medieval Dutch variant form of Bruynsten and Medieval German form of Brunstein.
Late Old English name composed of the elements brun "brown" and sunu "son".
Transferred use of the surname Brunton. James Brunton Stephens (1835-1902) was a Scottish-born Australian poet, and author of 'Convict Once'.
Corsican, Sardinian and Sicilian form of Bruno.
Derived from Old High German brunja "breastplate, cuirass" or brûn "brown" combined with Gothic vulfs "wolf."
Derived from Old High German brunja "breastplate, cuirass" or brûn "brown" combined with Old High German wart "guard."
Variant of Brunwine, an Old English name composed of the elements brun meaning "brown" and wine meaning "friend".

From Aramaic בְּרוּרְיָה (bəruryā) meaning "certain is Yahweh, clarity is Yahweh", derived from the roots בָּרוּר (barúr) "clear, evident, certain" and יָהּ (yah) referring to the Hebrew God. The name is sometimes posited as a Hebraized form of the Latin name Valeria. This was the name of a 2nd-century female Talmudic sage, the wife of Rabbi Meir.
From Old Norse brúsi meaning "buck, he-goat".
Variant of Brucelee, mainly used in Nicaragua (particularly the North Caribbean Autonomous Region) and Peru.
Medieval Dutch variant form of Bruynsten.
Bulgarian, Catalan, Croatian, Russian, Serbian and Ukrainian form of Brutus.
Galician, Italian and Spanish form of Brutus.
Bruttia Crispina was Roman empress from 178 to 191 as the consort of Roman emperor Commodus. Her marriage to Commodus did not produce an heir, and her husband was instead succeeded by Pertinax.

Appears to be a diminutive form of the Latin name Brutus, which means "heavy" or "dull". Notably associated with figures such as Lucius Junius Brutus, the traditional founder of the Roman Republic, and Marcus Junius Brutus, one of Julius Caesar's assassins.
A Finnish variant spelling of Bruno.
Medieval Dutch form of Brunstein. This is not to be confused with the medieval Dutch word bruynsten (which is bruinsten in modern Dutch) meaning "(the) brownest".
Medieval Dutch variant form of Bruynsten.
Diminutive of Bryan, Bryden, Bryanna, and other names beginning in bry.

From брѧцати (bręcati) "to clank, to make metal noises" and слава (slava) "glory". Bryachislav Izyaslavovich was Prince of Polotsk between 1003-1044 and was father of Vseslav Charodey (Bryachislavovich).
Variant of Bryony or a feminine form of Brian.Bryane Heaberlin is a football player from the USA, currently playing for the German club 1. FFC Frankfurt.
Variant of Brianne and Brian (See also Bryanne and Bryanna).

Uncertain etymology, sometimes also found spelled as Βρύασσις (Bryassis). Possibly derived from – or otherwise, related to – Greek βρυασμός (bryasmos), which can mean "delight, lust" as well as "voluptuousness". Also compare Greek βρυάζω (bryazo) "to swell, to teem". Last but not least, Greek βρυάκτης (bruaktes) or (bryaktes) also seems related, as it basically means "the jolly god, the joyous god" and is used in reference to the god Pan. A known bearer of this name was Bryaxis, an ancient Greek sculptor from the 4th century BC.
Feminine form of Bryce using the popular name suffix lynn (see Lynn).
Variant of Bryson. According to the SSA, 22 boys were given the name Bryceson in 2018.
Variant of Braden, perhaps influenced by Bryan.
Diminutive of Bryce and variant of Brie.
Transferred use of the surname Bryer.
From the name of an island off the southwestern coast of Cornwall, one of the Isles of Scilly. This was adopted as a pen name by the English novelist Annie Winifred Ellerman (1894-1983).
Derived from from Old Cornish breilu "rose" (vocative) combined with the singulative suffix en. This is a modern Cornish name.
He who creates/nurtures nature. In some Indian traditions this name is also an alternate name for Lord Vishnu.
Variant of Brendan. Brynden Rivers is a character in George R. R. Martin's A Song of Ice and Fire novels.
Faroese and Norwegian form of Bryndís.

Variant of the Old Norse name Brynolf/Brynjulf which combined the two words brynja meaning "coat of mail" and ulfr meaning "wolf". This name was mostly used in the Western part of Sweden during the 17th and 18th centuries.
Derived from the Germanic name elements brynja "coat of mail, armour, protection" and garðr "enclosure", "protection".
Medieval Norwegian and Swedish variant of Brynhildr.
Derived from Old English bryne "fire, flame, burning".
Derived from Old Norse brynja "coat of mail, armor, protection" and ulfr "wolf".
Modern form of the Old Swedish name Bryniolf, itself a form of the Old Norse Bryniulfr.
Derived from Old Norse brynja "coat of mail, armour, protection" and ketill "cauldron hat, helmet".
Derived from Welsh bryn meaning "hill", and Welsh diminutive suffix -ell or Welsh suffix -lle meaning "place". Brynle Williams (1949–2011) was a Welsh Conservative politician.
Combination of Old Norse brynja meaning "coat of mail (or plate), byrnie, corselet" and the name Leifur (which is itself related to Old Norse leif meaning "inheritance, legacy").
A combination of Bryn and Lynn.
Elaborated form of Brynn (probably influenced by Brenna) as well as a variant of Bryna.
Derived from the Old Norse elements brynja meaning "coat of mail (or plate), byrnie, corselet" and steinn meaning "stone".
Pet form of names beginning with Bryn-, derived from the Old Norse word brynja "armour, protection".
Derived from Old Norse brynja meaning "coat of mail (or plate), byrnie, corselet" combined with Þór.
Variant of Brinton, influenced by the name Bryn.
From the Latin name for bryony, the wild twining plant (see Bryony).
Combination of the phonetic elements bry and sha.
Possibly derived from Ancient Greek βρύσις (brysis) meaning "bubbling up" or βρύω (bryo) meaning "to be full to bursting; to abound with, teem, gush".
Variant of Bristol, the spelling influenced by that of Crystal.
Variant of Bryson influenced by other names ending in ton or ston.
Combination of Brython and the suffix gwen meaning "white, fair, blessed".
The name of a medieval Cornish saint.
Alternate transcription of Arabic ابتهال (see Ibtihal), chiefly used in Morocco.
Alternate transcription of Arabic ابتهال (see Ibtihal), chiefly used in Morocco.
Alternate transcription of Arabic ابتسام (see Ibtisam) chiefly used in North Africa.
Alternate transcription of Arabic ابتسام (see Ibtisam) chiefly used in North Africa.
From Chinese 布 (bù) meaning "fabric, textile". Other hanzi can also form this name.
From Lao ບົວ (bua) meaning "lotus" or "fruit" and ຈັນ meaning "moon".
Derived from Irish buaidh meaning "victory" (compare Boudicca, Buddug). It is Anglicized as Victor.

column3: ບົວລອຍ(Lao)|บัวลอย(Thai)

column12: From Tagalog buwan meaning "moon, month". This is the name of a goddess of the moon in traditional Tagalog mythology.
From Persian بی‌بی‌ (bibi) meaning "madam, lady, matron", combined with ажар (azhar) meaning “beautiful complexion, attractive, charming appearance”.
Likely from the English vocabulary word for a boy or young man, bub. Also a shortened version of Bubba.
Western African form of Abu Bakr.
In the American South, the name is from a term of endearment usually thought to be based on the word brother.
A variant of Bubba, likely based on the Appalachian pronunciation.
From the word "bubble". Mainly used as a nickname.
Formed from the English word bubble and Sanskrit प्रीति (prīti) meaning "pleasure, joy, love".
Maybe from the english world Bubbles and -ette. Or from Babette.
A nickname meaning "little boy" (from the German word Bube "boy").It was borne by the German boxing champion Bubi Scholz.

In ancient Roman religion, Bubona is thought to have been a goddess of cattle, but she is named only by Saint Augustine. Georg Wissowa thought that a festival of cattle (ludi boum causa) mentioned by Pliny must have been dedicated to Bubona. Those who celebrated the rites were called Bubetii, a title which appears only in Pliny.

Means "noble lady" from Persian بی‌بی‌ (bibi) meaning "matron, lady, woman" combined with سارا (sara) meaning "noble, pure". A notable bearer was Bubusara Beyshenalieva (1926-1973), a Kyrgyz ballerina.

Means "bull-headed" in Ancient Greek, derived from βοῦς (bous) "ox" and κεφαλή (kephale) "head".Bucephalus was the horse of Alexander the Great, and one of the most famous horses of antiquity. Ancient accounts state that Bucephalus died after the Battle of the Hydaspes in 326 BC, in what is now modern Pakistan, and is buried in Jalalpur Sharif outside of Jhelum, Pakistan. Another account states that Bucephalus is buried in Phalia, a town in Pakistan's Mandi Bahauddin District, which is named after him.In author Franz Kafka's story 'The New Lawyer' (1916), Bucephalus is a bar-approved lawyer who immerses himself 'in law books ... far from the tumult of Alexander's battles'. In the 2006 novel by Katharine Roberts 'I am the Great Horse', the life of Alexander and his horse are told from the viewpoint of Bucephalus.

Possibly a diminutive of names containing the Old English element burg "fortress", as in the case of an 8th-century abbess by this name who corresponded with Saint Boniface and whose full name was Heahburg. Alternatively, it could be related to the Old English verb bugan meaning "to bow down".
From the surname Buchanan. A fictional bearer is the Marvel Comics character James Buchanan "Bucky" Barnes.
Alternate transcription of Tibetan བུ་ཆུང (see Bhuchung).
From the name of a fictional creature (hippogriff) that is featured on the movie Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban.
Transferred use of the surname Buckingham. A known bearer of this name was the American writer and politician Buckingham Smith (1810-1871).
Transferred use of the surname Buckland.
Transferred use of the surname Buckley 1.
Transferred use from the placename Buckminster in England.It is the second name of the American architect and inventor Richard Buckminster Fuller, usually known as Buckminster Fuller.
Transferred use of the surname Buckner.
Diminutive of Buck, Buckminster, or Buchanan.It is also the name of Captain America’s best friend Bucky who’s real name was James Buchanan Barnes.
Latinized form of Boukolion. This was the name of several characters in Greek mythology, one of them being a king of Arcadia.
Latinized form of Boukolos. This is the name of several characters in Greek mythology, one of them being the son of Hippocoön, a king of Sparta.

Derived from either Romanian bucur, an archaic form of the adjective bucuros "joyful", a bucura "to become joyful" or bucurie "joy". This name was borne by Bucur, the legendary Romanian shepherd who is said to have founded Bucharest (Bucureşti in Romanian), giving it his name.
Means "Mercury (planet)" in Mongolian, ultimately derived from Sanskrit बुध् (budh) meaning "awaking, intelligent, wise".
Possibly means "swelling one (of rounded shapes)", "elevated". This is the Hungarian form of Bleda, the name of the brother of Attila.
Etymology unknown, possibly from the Sanskrit 'Buddhashri' meaning "sacred as a Buddha". This was the personal name of Princess Supreme Noguk.
Short form of Buddy. In American culture Bud, Budd, and Buddy were often as a nickname for a son named for his father to avoid name confusion. It later became used as an independent name.

column3: Будда(Mongolian Cyrillic)|ᠪᠤᠳ᠋ᠳ᠋ᠾᠠ(Traditional Mongolian)|仏陀(Japanese Kanji)|ぶっだ(Japanese Hiragana)
column12: Old English name of uncertain meaning, perhaps related to Brythonic boud "victory". It coincides with an Old English word meaning "beetle" (and could be a byname derived from it).
Latinized form of Buddha, borrowed from Ancient Greek Βούδδας (Boúddas) "Buddha". This was the renaming of Terebinthus of Turbo, a purported pupil of Scythianus during the 1st to 2nd century AD.
Means "reasonable" in Sinhalese, ultimately from Sanskrit बुद्धि (buddhi).
"lord of wisdom " ; "lord of intelligence ". Here बुद्धि means wisdom + ईश means lord
A variation of Buddy and Buddie
Alternate transcription of Sinhala බුද්ධික (see Buddhika).

Derived from Welsh budd "profit, advantage". It is a cognate of Boudicca, the name of a 1st-century queen of the Iceni (a Celtic people) who is known as Buddug in Welsh, and is sometimes considered a Welsh equivalent of Victoria.

Means "oxen-yoker", derived from Ancient Greek βοῦς (bous) meaning "ox, cow" and δέω (deo) meaning "to bind, tie, fasten". Budeia, also called Βουζύγη (Bouzyge), is the name of a daughter of Lycus in Greek mythology. It is also an epithet of the goddess Athena.

Means "Mercury (planet)" or "wise, intelligent, learned" in Sanskrit. In Hindu mythology this is the name of the god of the planet Mercury who also represents intellect and wisdom. According to legend he was born out of an affair between the moon god Chandra and the astral goddess Tara, with his birth ultimately leading to a great war.
Means "virtuous" from Indonesian budi meaning "sense, mind, character".
From Sanskrit बुद्धि (buddhi) meaning "intellect, reason, mind" and अर्थ (artha) meaning "wealth, property".
Connected to the name Budi, which is ultimately derived from Sanskrit बुद्धि (buddhi) meaning "intellect."
Means "intelligent, wise" in Indonesian, ultimately from Sanskrit बुद्धिमान (buddhimāna).
Combination of Budiman and Persian شاه (shāh) meaning "king".

The first element of this name is derived from (Serbo-)Croatian buditi "to awaken, to (a)rouse". The second element is derived from Slavic mir "peace" or "world". In other words, this name is the Croatian and Serbian cognate of the Polish name Budzimir.

A multi-layered Turkish feminine name consisting of the ancient root buğ- combined with the traditional Turkic feminine diminutive/endearment suffix +çe. Depending on the historical dialect, the root carries diverse symbolic meanings, mirroring a shifting cloud that holds great power within:1. Steam/Vapor: buğ or buğu represents moist heat rising into the air, symbolizing ethereal beauty or a transformative spirit.2. Majestic Animals: Related to ancient animal roots like buğra (male camel) or buğaç/boğaç (bull), denoting innate strength.3. Nourishment: Tied to buğday (wheat), symbolizing fertility, harvest, and life-giving abundance.4. Passionate Intensity: In Old Turkic and certain Altaic dialects, buğ signifies inner heat, deep distress, or a sudden outburst of fiery emotion.5. Authority: Connected to leadership titles like başbuğ (chief, commander) or buğruk/buyruk (command), derived from the root of ultimate authority.

Possibly an elaboration of English burn. This was the stage name of American actress Burnu Acquanetta (1921-2004; real name Mildred Davenport), sometimes known simply as Acquanetta, who claimed it was an Arapaho name meaning "burning fire".

Variant of Berny (in which case the spelling is more phonetical) and Burney.This name can also be a diminutive of any English given name that contains burn, which are often surnames that are used as given names. Examples of such names are Burnell, Burnett, Milburn and Wilburn.Notable bearers of this name include the American animator Burny Mattinson (1935-2023) and the Dutch producer and children's book author Burny Bos (1944-2023).
The duke of the White Lake. He raised and educated Tybalt, the youth who became Lancelot’s first squire. He gave lodging to Lancelot one night as he traveled to Arthur’s court.
The name Buroku consists of the kanji's 武 and 禄. 武 means military or martial, and 禄 means blessing; happiness or prosperity.
Means "Christmas" in Akan. This may be given to children born around this time of year.
From Japanese 武 (bu) meaning "military, martial" combined with 郎 (rou) meaning "son". Other kanji combinations are possible.

This is a name of an adviser of Emperor Nero, But the full name was Sextus Afranius Burrus.

Diminutive of masculine given names that contain the Germanic element burg meaning "fortress", such as Burghard. However, there may be cases where the name is taken from the English surname Burry or where it is even a variant of the given name Barry or Berry 1.A known bearer of this name was the South African mountain biker Burry Stander (1987-2013).
Variant of Bartel, traditionally found in the Engadine valley.
Likely transferred from the surname, Burtis.
Cremish Lombard feminine form of Bùrtol.
Means "enough" in Kyrgyz. It was traditionally given to girls when her parents had "enough girls" in hopes of a male child.

From Kyrgyz бурул (burul) meaning "enough" and the diminutive suffix -ча (-cha). It was traditionally given to girls when her parents had wanted a boy and/or already had several girls, essentially meaning "stop being born girls", in hopes that their next child would be a boy.
From the given name Burul combined with кан (kan) meaning "blood".
Means "let her turn" in Kyrgyz. It was traditionally given to girls when her parents had wanted a boy, meaning "let her be the last girl", in hopes that their next child would be a boy.
A medieval Scottish form of Brunhild.

A sorcerer who imprisoned the maiden Amoret and tried to force her to become his lover. Britomart, the warrior maiden, learned of Amoret’s plight from Scudamore, Amoret’s lover. Britomart braved the enchantments of Busirane’s castle, defeated him, and freed Amoret.

From the name of 9th-century Persian mystic Bayazid Bistami (known in Indonesia as Abu Yazid al-Busthami), whose name came from the city of Bastam in present-day Iran.
Short form of Sebustianu. Bustianu Satta (1867 - 1914) is considered the best-known Sardinian poet.
Diminutive of Elizabeth influenced by the spelling of the English word busy. A known bearer is American actress Busy Phillips (1975-).
Malay and Indonesian form of Bushra.
From Japanese 武 (bu) meaning "military, martial", 太 (ta) meaning "thick, big" combined with 郎 (rou) meaning "son". Other kanji combinations are possible.
From Mongolian бүтэн (büten) meaning "whole, entire, full" and баяр (bayar) meaning "joy, celebration".

Diminutive of Arabic بثنة (bathna) meaning "soft, easy, fertile (as in soil or land)" as well as "beautiful, plump".
Butheric was a Roman general of Gothic descent.
Derived from boð ("bid, offer"). In Norse mythology Buðli is a Swedish king and the father of Brynhildr.
Combination of Buðli and the suffix -ungr ("son of; descendant of").

This name is composed by two archaic baltic elements: but, from the Lithuanian verb būti, meaning "to be, to exist" and geid, referring to the radical geidauti or geisti, meaning "to wish". The meaning could be something in the lines of "one who wishes to exist".
Meaning uncertain; it is said to be related to roundness and fatness (or rather, plumpness). As a result, it is said to mean "strong man" in a figurative sense.
Means "flower" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit पुष्प (puṣpa).

Means "topaz, yellow sapphire" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit पुष्पराग (puṣparāga).
Transferred use of the surname Butt.
Transferred use of the surname Butter, or from the food, which comes from Ancient Greek βούτυρον (bouturon).
From the English word butterball, used as an informal nickname. This nickname was given to an American football player Paul Scull (1907-1997). This name can also be used for pets.
From the name of the winged insect.

Transferred use of the English surname Button or directly from the word button itself. A known bearer of the name was the American Founding Father Button Gwinnett (1735-1777) named in honor after his mother's cousin, Barbara Button.

Transferred use of the surname Butts or a nickname with meaning particular to the bearer. Notable namesake, professional baseball player, Albert "Butts" Wagner was the older brother of baseball great Honus Wagner.
Variant of Bảo, from Sino-Vietnamese 寶 (bửu).
Derived from Arabic أويس (uwais) meaning "small wolf, little wolf" combined with Persian سر (sar) meaning "head, topmost, foremost" or "leader, chief".
Derived from the Uzbek buvi meaning "grandmother, mother" and anbar meaning "ambergris".

Means "moon" in Tagalog. It is not often used as a given name.
Means "a child whose feet came out first before the head during birth" in Ijaw.

column12: From Chinese 布 (bù) meaning "cloth, textiles; to declare, to announce" combined with 兴 (xīng) meaning "rise, prosper". Other hanzi combinations are possible.

Derived from Mongolian буян (buyan) meaning "good deed, virtue, charity" or "fortune, blessing" and цэцэг (tsetseg) meaning "flower".
Older form of Buyant. Buyantu Khan was the eighth Great Khan of the Mongol Empire.
From Mongolian буян (buyan) meaning "good deed, virtue, charity" or "fortune, blessing" and заяа (zayaa) meaning "future, fortune, fate".
Means "good luck and happiness" in Mongolian, from буян (buyan) meaning "good deed, virtue, charity" or "fortune, blessing" and жаргал (jargal) meaning "happiness, blessing".
Possibly from the Manchu buyen ("desire"). This was the personal name of a Noble Lady (6th rank consort) of the Kangxi emperor. She was the sister of Nalanzhu.
Name traditionally given to the fourth born daughter.
From Hebrew בוז (buz), "contempt". This name occurs only once in the Bible. The prophet Ezekiel mentions him as his father.
A name that can be formed as an onomatopoeia, a word based on sound, or a nickname for someone with a short haircut.Bearers include legendary jazz drummer Benjamin "Buzzy" Drootin (1920-2000).
Bvumai means "Admit". This may be a name given to say to adversary admit that you were wrong, you were defeated or that you committed the offence
Meaning "emperor", another form of the name is Hwami.
Female given name created by Alaskan Native Eskimo Baayin Asiksick in the early 1900s.

column3: 白虎(Japanese Kanji)|びゃっこ(Japanese Hiragana)|ビャッコ(Japanese Katakana)
column12: From 白虎 (byakko), referring to a white tiger, also one of the Four Symbols of the Chinese constellations which represents the west and the autumn season. This makes it cognate with Korean Baek-ho.This name is very rarely used.
From Japanese 白 (byaku) meaning "white" and 蓮 (ren) meaning "lotus."Byakuren Yanagiwara (柳原 白蓮, 1885-1967) was a Japanese poet and novelist.

column3: 白哉(Japanese Kanji)|びゃくや(Japanese Hiragana)|ビャクヤ(Japanese Katakana)
column12: From Japanese 白 (byaku) meaning "white" and 哉 (ya) meaning "exclamation mark". It is the name of a character in the popular Japanese manga and anime 'Bleach'.
Means "Saturday" in Mongolian, derived from Tibetan སྤེན་པ (spen pa) meaning "Saturn (planet)" or "Saturday" (see Pemba).
From Mongolian бямба (byamba) meaning "Saturday" and баатар (baatar) meaning "hero".
From Mongolian бямба (byamba) meaning "Saturday" and далай (dalai) meaning "sea, ocean".

From Mongolian бямба (byamba) meaning "Saturday" and жав (jav) meaning "salvation, deliverance".
From Mongolian бямба (byamba) meaning "Saturday" and очир (ochir) meaning "diamond" or "staff, truncheon; thunderbolt".
From Mongolian бямба (byamba) meaning "Saturday" and Tibetan ཚེ་རིང (tshe ring) meaning "long life, longevity".

In Greek mythology, Byblis was the daughter of Miletus, who fell in love with her twin brother Caunus and subsequently killed herself. In some versions of the legend, she is transformed into a spring or a hamadryad.
Byeol, which means star, combined with a.
From native Korean 별빛 (byeolbit) meaning "starlight," effectively a combination of Byeol and Bit (compare Bitbyeol).
Combination of Byeol and the first syllable of Haneul (compare Haneul-byeol).

From Korean 별 (byeol) meaning "star" combined with Sino-Korean 姬 (hui) meaning "beauty" or 嬉 (hui) meaning "enjoy, play" or 熙 (hui) meaning "bright, splendid, glorious". Other hanja combinations can form this name as well.
From Byeol combined with the subject marking particle 이 (i).
From Byeol suffixed with honorific 님 (nim).

From Sino-Korean 秉 "grasp, hold; bundle; authority" and 哲 "wise, sagacious". A famous bearer is South Korean businessman Lee Byung-chul (1910-1987), founder of the Samsung Group.

column12: From Sino-Korean 丙 (byeong) referring to the third of the ten Heavenly Stems or 炳 (byeong) meaning "bright, luminous, glorious" combined with 垠 (eun) meaning "boundary, limit, riverbank" or 彥 (eun) meaning "elegant, handsome, learned". Other hanja combinations can form this name as well.

column3: 병기(Korean Hangul)|炳基, 柄基, 秉岐, etc.(Korean Hanja)
column12: From Sino-Korean 炳 (byeong) meaning "bright, luminous, glorious", 柄 (byeong) meaning "handle, lever, authority" or 秉 (byeong) meaning "grasp, hold" combined with 基 (gi) meaning "foundation, base" or 岐 (gi) meaning "high, majestic". Other hanja combinations can form this name as well.
From Sino-Korean 兵 (byeong) meaning "soldier" and 光 (gwang) meaning "light".

column12: From Sino-Korean 炳 (byeong) meaning "bright, luminous, glorious" or 秉 (byeong) meaning "grasp, hold" combined with 憲 (heon) meaning "constitution, statute, law". Other hanja combinations can form this name as well.

From Sino-Korean 炳 "bright, luminous; glorious" and 守 "defend, protect, guard, conserve". A famous bearer is South Korean footballer Yoo Byung-soo (1988-).
