Meaning uncertain. The first element could be Old Norse bylr "squall, gust of wind". But the second element is more difficult to interpret, it could be derived from laysa "to loosen, to relieve", from leiptr "lightning", or from heistr "violent". This is the name of one of Loki's brothers in Norse mythology.
Variant of Beleth. This is the name of an avatar character in Fire Emblem: Three Houses.
Derived from Old Norse bylgja meaning "billow, wave". In Norse mythology, Bylgja was one of the nine daughters of the sea deities Ægir and Rán.
Variant spelling of Billie, or a diminutive of Sibyl.
Silesian equivalent of Polish Benon and German Benno.

Feminine form of Byron. This was borne by Byra Louise 'Puck' Whittlesey (1922-1988), the wife of Jack Hemingway, daughter-in-law of Ernest Hemingway and mother of actresses Mariel Hemingway and Margaux Hemingway.

Latinate form of Byrd and Byrdie.
From Kazakh бір (bir) meaning "one" combined with ханым (khanym) "lady, queen".
Old Swedish and Medieval Norwegian variant of Birgitta.

From the Old English name Byrhtferð, derived from Old English byrht, which is a variant of beorht "bright, clear", and an uncertain second element which may be derived from ferhð "spirit" or may be a West Saxon metathesis of Anglian friþ "peace" (making this name a cognate of Beorhtfrith).
Form of Byrhtferth. Byrhtferð (c. 970 – c. 1020) was an English priest and monk. He invented an older version of the alphabet in 1011.
Old Swedish variant of Byrghita (see Birgitta).

Seen as a first name in Southern Missouri. Also has been seen as a last name. Meaning: Resolute

Maybe a diminutive of a name containing the secondary name element BIZ, probably derived from BID "to sustain; to hope"

Means "crystal, beryl" in Armenian, ultimately from Greek βήρυλλος (beryllos).
Old Norse byname, from Old Norse byxa meaning "to jump".

Means "from Byzantium", with Byzantium being the latinized form of Greek Byzantion, which itself was ultimately derived from the personal name Byzas. This name was borne by Stephanus Byzantinus, who lived in the 6th century AD.
Latinized form of Greek Byzantios, which essentially meant "from Byzantium" (see also Byzantinus). This was the name of an archbishop of Bari (Italy) from the 11th century AD.

Derived from Thracian búzas "he-goat, buck" (similar to Indo-European bhugo "buck" and Greek bous "ox, cow"); since Thracian was not a Hellenic language, one could probably call Byzas a hellenization of sorts. According to legend, this was the name of the founder of the city Byzantion (better known under its latinized form Byzantium); the city's name is derived from his name (from byzantos, the genitive case of his name). Also, in Greek mythology, this was the name of the son of Poseidon and Keroessa.

Perhaps related to Byzas or to the Greek adverb βύζην (buzên) meaning "close pressed, closely". According to the Metamorphoses of Antoninus Liberalis, Byze was a nymph, daughter of Erasinos and sister of Melite, Anchiroe and Maera.
From non-Sino-Vietnamese reading of Chinese 茄 (cà) meaning "solanaceae plant".
Means "firstborn, eldest" in the Northern Vietnamese dialect.
Derived from caamania meaning “forest mother” in the Classical Tupi and Nheengatu languages.
Short form of Cabell. A notable bearer is jazz musician and band leader Cabell "Cab" Calloway III (1907-1994).

The good King of Cornwall in the Vulgate Lancelot; a vassal of Arthur.He assisted Arthur in the campaign against King Claudas of Gaul, and he led a division against Mordred at the battle of Salisbury. Presumably, he was slain there.
Variant of Cabiro, the latinized form of Kabeiro.
Transferred use of the surname Cabell. A notable bearer is jazz musician and bandleader Cabell "Cab" Calloway III (1907-1994).
The name of Virginia Kennedy given to her by her twin sister Grace (Poto) in their own private language.The story of Poto and Cabengo was popularised through a 1980 documentary film.

From cabeza "head", after the Marian title Virgen de la Cabeza, venerated in many points of Spain, specially in Andalusia. Legend has it that a shepherd found a statuette of Virgin Mary in La Cabeza hill in Sierra Morena.According to historians, the original name of the hill was Peña Rasa, which was interpreted to derive from Arabic رَأس "head" and translated back literally.

Perhaps a Latinized form of Greek Καβειρία (Kabeiria), an epithet of the goddess Demeter, possibly derived from the name of Mount Kabeiros in Asia Minor; see also Kabeiro. This was used by Italian author Gabriele D'Annunzio for the title heroine in the film Cabiria (1914), to which he wrote the screenplay. The name was later used by Federico Fellini for a character in his film Nights of Cabiria (1957).
From the Arabic câbiye(t) جَابِيَة meaning "pool".
Transferred use of the surname Cable.
Transferred use of the surname Cabot.
Means "earthquake" in Mayan. Cabrakan was the god of mountains and earthquakes.
From the surname of Saint Frances Xavier Cabrini (1850-1917), an Italian-American nun also known as Mother Cabrini; she was the first American citizen canonized by the Catholic Church (in 1946).
Transferred use of the surname Cabry, itself from the name of a river in Ireland.
From Sino-Vietnamese 各 (các) meaning "each, all, individually" or 閣 (các) meaning "chamber, room".
Possibly means "old frog", from Nahuatl caca "frog, toad" and huehue "elder, old man".
Means "small ear of corn" in Nahuatl.
Etymology uncertain, possibly from the Classical Nahuatl elements cacamatl "small corncobs, small ears of corn" and cihuatl "woman, wife". Name borne by a queen of Tenochtitlan.
Derived from Nahuatl cacamatl "small ear of corn, offshoot of larger ear of maize" and -tzin, a diminutive or reverential suffix. This was the name of a king of Texcoco.
Derived from Tupi ka'a asapaba meaning "stroll through the forest".
The name of a medicinal plant with yellow flowers, also called coçatli ("weasel"). Possibly derived from zacatl "grass, hay, straw" and xochitl "flower".
Name of an Italian crusader (Cacciaguida Degli Elisei), who was also the grandfather of Dante Alighieri.
The name of multiple Irish queens
Means "shoe owner, one who wears sandals" in Nahuatl, from cactli "shoe, sandal" and the possessive suffix -hua.
Cacimar directly translates to “Priest/Shaman who wanders”.This name belonged to a Cacique (Chief) of Puerto Rico.
From a variant Tatar word meaning "flower".
Vietnamese form of Karl Marx in honor of the German philosopher, rarely used as a given name, if at all.
From the Karachay-Balkar чач (çaç) meaning "hair" and ultimately meaning "one with luxurious hair".

Derived from Greek κᾰκός (kakos), meaning "bad". In Greek and Roman mythology, Cacus was a giant and the son of Vulcan. He was killed by Hercules after terrorizing the Aventine Hill before the founding of Rome.

One of Arthur’s nobles, listed in Biket’s Lai du Cor. He helped stop Arthur from killing Guenevere when a magical horn betrayed a trivial infidelity. Cadain’s wife was also found to be untrue by the horn.

Cadal is the name given in Lawman’s Brut to a treacherous Pict in the service of King Constantine 1 of Britain. The Pict is said to be one of King Constantine’s most trusted knights. He draws King Constantine 1 apart into a thicket or orchard pretending to have something to tell him privately and suddenly stabs him to death with a knife.
Derived from Welsh and Cornish cat "battle" and possibly Welsh man "place" or Welsh nant "brook, stream". This is also the name of a river in Dyfed, Wales.
From Sino-Vietnamese 歌謠 (ca dao) referring to a kind of Vietnamese folk song or poem.
Cadarius was a nobleman in the Kingdom of Hungary who served as Judge royal in 1146, during the reign of Géza II of Hungary.
Diminutive of Caroline. This name is borne by the titular character of Carol Ryrie Brink's children's historical fiction novel Caddie Woodlawn.

Variant of Caddie. Fictional bearers include Caddy Jellyby, a character in Charles Dickens' novel 'Bleak House' (1853), and Candace 'Caddy' Compson, a character in William Faulkner's novel 'The Sound and the Fury' (1929).
Variant of Cadell. A famous namesake is Australian champion cyclist Cadel Evans.
Invented by author Jonathan Swift for his 1726 poem Cadenus and Vanessa. The name is an anagram for the latin word decanus, meaning Dean, because he was the dean of St. Patricks.
An "ornamental passage near the close of a song or solo," 1780, from Italian cadenza "conclusion of a movement in music." See also Cadence.
Comes from the word for "younger/youngest" or "military student official," derived from the French cadet and Gascon capdet.
Possibly 'white warrior' or 'pure warrior'. In Welsh cade can be interpreted as warring, and wyn as white or fair
Gaelic byname meaning "barnacle goose". In Irish legend Cadhan was a hero who slayed a monster with the help of his hound.
Derived from Old Breton cat "battle" and (ho)iarn "iron".

Archaic transcription of Khadija. This form is mostly used in older English translations of the Koran, as well as early translations of the Arabian Nights. A notable bearer of this name is the titular character's wife from the Arabian Nights-inspired novel 'The History of Nourjahad' (1767) by Frances Sheridan.
From the name of the car brand, or perhaps in some cases transferred from the French surname Cadillac.
Form the Turkish name Kadın that got integrated into Judeo-Spanish.
Form of Kadmiel used in the Bishops' Bible (1568).
Form of Kadmiel used in the Nova Vulgata ("Neo-Vulgate"), which has been the official Bible of the Roman Catholic Church since 1979.
Derived from Welsh cat "battle" and -no "knowing". The modern Welsh word cadno, "fox", likely stems from the given name, similar to French Renard.
Variant of Caden influenced by the spelling of Jadon.

Probably a form of Cadeyrn, perhaps derived from its Cornish cognate. In Arthurian romance this was the name of Guinevere's guardian. According to the 12th-century chronicler Geoffrey of Monmouth, Cador was a ruler of Cornwall and the father of Constantine, King Arthur's successor.K.M. Sheard writes, 'It is not even beyond the realms of possibility that it derives ultimately from the name of the Celtic god Belactucadros.'

From Old Welsh cad "battle" and gwal "leader". This occurs in Shakespeare's play 'Cymbeline' (1609) as the name of Arviragus while in hiding in Wales. In some cases it may be a short form of the closely related name Cadwaladr.

Anglicized form of Cadwaladr. This spelling occurs in Shakespeare's 'Henry V'.In some cases it may be a transferred use of the surname Cadwallader.A famous bearer was Cadwallader Colden (1688-1776), born in Ireland to Scottish parents, and raised and educated in Scotland. He moved to America, where he became a physician, natural scientist, and lieutenant-governor for the Province of New York.

Derived from Old Welsh cat "battle" and an uncertain element, possibly gwallon "ruler" or uualaun, uualon "valorous" or guallaun "good, best". (Also compare Cadwal and Cadwaladr.)Notable bearers of this name include Cadwallon Lawhir, a 6th-century king of Gwynedd; Cadwallon ap Cadfan (died 634), a 7th-century king of Gwynedd; a 7th-century king of Wessex (also known as Cædwalla); and Cadwallon ab Ieuaf, a 10th-century king of Gwynedd.
Derived from Old Breton cat "battle" and (g)uethen "warrior, war".
Derived from Old Breton cat "battle" and uuobri "serious, important".
Derived from Old Breton cat "battle" and uuoret "shelter, protection".
From Old Welsh cad "battle" combined with the suffix wy. This was borne by the son of Geraint in Arthurian legend.

While nowadays generally considered a phonetic spelling of Katie or a diminutive of Cadence, Cady was originally derived from a surname which was either a variant of Cade or an Anglicized form of Ó Ceadaigh ("descendant of Céadach"), with Ceadach being a byname derived from Irish ceadach "talkative".A known bearer of the surname was the American feminist Elizabeth Cady Stanton (1815-1902). It was also used for the central character in the film 'Mean Girls' (2004).
This name appears in the Mabinogion, a collection of tales from Welsh myth.
Short form of Caetano and Carlos Eduardo.
Roman cognomen which was derived from Caecilius.
From the Latin name Caecilia.This is the name of the famous Danish jazz and rock singer, Cæcilie Nordby, born 1964.

Derived from the Latin adjective caecus meaning "blind" combined with the Latin masculine diminutive suffix -ulus. Also compare the related name Caecilius.In Roman mythology, Caeculus was the son of the fire god Vulcan. Meanwhile in real life, the Roman gens ("clan, family") Caecilia claimed that Caeculus was their eponymous ancestor.
Derived from the English word ‘cadence’ meaning melody, music. Caeda is a symbol of the sky, and also an expert Pegasus Knight.
In the Aeneid, Caeita is a wet-nurse who Aeneas buries on the bay of Gaeta.
Variant of Kayla, also used as a short form of Micaela.
Means "to be fine, to be slender" in Old Irish, derived from Old Irish coíl "slender, fine, delicate" and is (inflection form bad) "to be". This was the name of a High King of Ireland.

Most likely intended as an anagram of Cordelia. This name was first used as the name of a character in Fire Emblem: Fates. She resembles Cordelia, a character from the previous game, Fire Emblem: Awakening.
Most likely a variant of Kaylee, although in some cases it might be a variant of Caelia.
English form of Caelianus. The name has also been used in The Netherlands just a handful of times; the variant form Celian has been used a little bit more often there.
Roman cognomen which was derived from the Roman nomen gentile Caelius.

From a poetic Latin epithet of the Greek god Atlas which meant "supporting the heavens", from caelum "heaven" and ferre "to bear, to carry, to bring". In Greek mythology Atlas was a Titan punished by Zeus by being forced to support the heavens on his shoulders.

Cælin was an Orthodox priest in England in the seventh century, and brother of St. Cedd of Lastingham. The name Cælin is a spelling variant of the name of a West Saxon king Ceawlin, and is of Celtic rather than Anglo-Saxon derivation.
Means "sky" or "the heavens" in Latin (related to the word caelum). Caelus is the Roman god of the sky, the equivalent of the Greek god Uranus.
Irish name, from the same root of Caoimhìn, it means "gentle".
The name of a city in the book series, The Wheel of Time, by Robert Jordan. Likely a derivative of Camelot.

Latinized form of Kaineus. This was the name of several characters from Greek mythology, one of which was a hero of the legendary Lapith people of Thessaly. He was born a woman, with the name of Kainis (usually latinized to Caenis). After being raped by Poseidon, the god promised to grant her one wish. She wished to be given the body of a man and the lifestyle that came with that, and Poseidon subsequently fulfilled that wish. After the transformation, the brand new man changed his name to Kaineus (Caeneus in Latin) and joined in both the hunt of the Calydonian Boar as well as joining the other Lapiths in the Centauromachy, where some versions of his myth say is where Caeneus died.In the Centauromachy, Caeneus killed five (named) centaurs: Antimachus, Bromus, Elymus, Pyracmus and Styphelus. Caeneus also engaged in combat with a centaur named Latreus, who knew of Caeneus' birth sex and took offense to his chosen life. Caeneus' spear barely misses Latreus, who then strikes Caeneus in the face with his own, only for the spear to shatter across Caeneus' skin. He attempts again to kill Caeneus with his sword and receives the same results. At this point the story diverges, with some saying that Caeneus kills Latreus with a blow to the side. Others say Latreus was wounded by Caeneus and became enraged, so he instead tried to bury Caeneus under pine or fir trunks so heavy that even Caeneus' immense strength could not free him. Depending on the myth, this results in either Caeneus being buried alive, being pushed through the earth and straight into Tartarus or he instead shape-shifts and flies away as a golden-winged or tawny bird. In the myths where Caeneus kills Latreus, it is instead Monychus who buries Caeneus (albeit with the help of the other centaurs).

Latinized form of Kainis. In Greek mythology, Caenis was a woman who was raped by the god Poseidon. Afterwards, he promised her that he would grant her a single wish. Caenis then made the wish to become a man with the name of Caeneus, so that she would never again have to suffer rape or any other injustices that women often had to face. Poseidon made good on his promise, and she was transformed into the man she wanted to be.In real life, a notable bearer of this name was Antonia Caenis (died in 74 AD). She was a former slave, who was the long-term mistress of the Roman emperor Vespasian.
The name of a 4th-century BC Illyrian queen.
Latinized form of Kairos. In Greek mythology, Caerus was the personification of opportunity, luck and favorable moments.
Variant of Cesare, boosted in popularity in the 1980s by the movie The Idolmaker.

Feminine form of Caesarius. Caesaria of Arles (also called Caesaria the Elder, died c. 530), was a saint and abbess. She was born in a Gallo-Roman family and was trained at John Cassian's foundation in Marseilles.
Feminine form of Caesar - more specifically, it might be a diminutive of Caesaria.

Latinized form of Greek Καισαρίων (Kaisarion), which in turn was a Hellenized form of Caesar with the Greek diminutive suffix -ιων (-ion) added to it. As such, the name essentially meant "little Caesar". This name was borne (as a nickname or epithet) by the only biological son of Roman dictator Julius Caesar, whom he had with the Egyptian pharaoh Cleopatra. The boy was later put to death by his father's adopted son, Octavian (who would go on to become Roman Emperor Augustus).

Derived from the Latin adjective caesius, denoting a light blue or blue-grey colour, typically used to refer to the colour of a person's eyes. The same root may have given rise to the praenomen Caeso and perhaps also to the cognomen Caesar.
Transferred use of the surname Caffrey.

Transferred use of the surname Cafiero. From an Italian surname derived from Arabic kafir meaning "infidel". It was first used as a name in the late 19th century, in honor of Italian anarchist Carlo Cafiero (1846-1892).
Famous bearer of this name is Cafu (Born as Marcos Evangelista de Morais).
Transferred use of the surname Cage.Cage Wallace is a main antagonist in the post-apocalyptic drama TV Show, The 100.
Diminutive of Micajah used in the 18th century.
1. The sound and exuberance of flowing waters. -(adverb) 2. Contemporary, modern. -(noun)
Transferred use of the surname Cagney.
Variant of Çağrı used outside of Turkey.
Name of the cacique of the Turabo region of Puerto Rico at the time of the arrival of Columbus.
Transferred use of the surname Cahill.
Allegedly a modern coinage based on Carla.
From Nahuatl cahualli "one who is left behind; widow, widower".
Probably derived from cahualli "someone left behind; a widow, widower".
Means "abandoned one, one who was left behind" in Nahuatl.
Possibly from Nahuatl cahuani "to catch fire", figuratively "to shine" or "to make a name, leave a memory".

Son of Yvain the Bastard and one of Arthur’s squires in Perlesvaus.Arthur announced that he was going to take Cahus on a pilgrimage to the Chapel of St. Augustine in the White Forest. On the night before the scheduled journey, Cahus had a dream that he visited a shrine near the chapel, took a golden candle, and was stabbed in the side by a Black Knight.He awoke in Arthur’s castle and found to his astonishment that he was holding a golden candle, and had a dagger stuck in his side. He perished of the wound after presenting the candle to his king.A similar story is related about an unnamed attendant of Arthur’s in John of Glastonbury’s chronicle.
From Indonesian cahaya meaning "light" combined with adi meaning "first" in Indonesian or "beautiful, good, valuable" in Javanese.
From Indonesian cahaya meaning "light" (of Sanskrit origin) combined with the feminine suffix -ni.
From Javanese cahya meaning "beam, ray, light" combined with either the masculine suffix -na or the word ana meaning "being, having, holding".
From Sino-Vietnamese 改 (cải) meaning "to change, reform" or from a non-Sino-Vietnamese reading of Chinese 芥 (cải) meaning "Brassica vegetables".

Derived from the Chinese character 财 (cái) meaning "wealth; valuable; riches; money" or 彩 (cǎi) meaning "colour; literary or artistic talent" but also "applause; cheer".Other characters combinations are also possible.
From the Chinese 彩 (cǎi) meaning "colour" and 婵 (chán) meaning "beautiful, lovely".
From the Chinese 彩 (cǎi) meaning "colour" and 电 (diàn) meaning "lightning, electricity".
French form of Gaius and variant of Caïus

Variant of Caiete, which is the proper latinization of the Greek name Καιήτη (Kaiete), of which the etymology is uncertain. It could be derived from Greek καίω (kaio) meaning "to burn", but it could also come from Greek καιετός (kaietos) meaning "fissure produced by an earthquake". With the latter, the related καιάδας (kaiadas) meaning "pit, underground cavern" is also an option, since its variants include καιάτας (kaiatas) and καιέτας (kaietas).In Greek and Roman mythology, this is the name of Aeneas's wet-nurse (as mentioned in Virgil's the Aeneid).
From Chinese 彩虹 (cǎihóng) meaning "rainbow". Other hanzi combinations are possible.
From Chinese 才 (cái) meaning "talent, ability" and 厚 (hòu) meaning "thick".

column3: 彩花, 彩华, 彩画, 菜花(Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 彩 (cǎi) meaning "colour" combined with 花 (huā) meaning "flower, blossom" or 华 (huá) meaning "splendid, illustrious, Chinese", 彩画 (cǎihuà) meaning "colour painting", or 菜花 (càihuā) meaning "cauliflower; rape blossom". Other character combinations can form this name as well.
From the Chinese 财 (cái) meaning "wealth, riches" and 娟 (juān) meaning "beautiful, graceful".
Irish and Gaelic origins. Means pure, beautiful, and slender.
From the Chinese 财 (cái) meaning "wealth, valuable, riches" and 莲 (lián) meaning "lotus, water lily".
Meaning as of yet unknown. It might possibly be a variant of Caelan or Caillín.
Combination of Cailli (a variant of Kaylee) and Anne 1.

Derived from the Gaelic word caileag meaning "girl", or possibly from the related word cailleach meaning "old woman", which is also the name of a Scottish and Irish mythological figure (see Beira) and comes from Old Irish caillech "veiled (one)", from caille "veil", an early loanword from Latin pallium "a cloak" (i.e., the ecclesiastical garment worn by nuns).

Meaning uncertain. According to one source, the name means "little cowl" in Irish, in which case it should ultimately be derived from the Irish noun caille meaning "veil".With that example in mind, it might also be possible that the name is instead derived from the similar-looking Irish noun caill meaning "forest, woodland".A notable bearer of this name was the Irish saint Caillín of Fenagh (late 6th century AD).

The French word caillou means "pebble", and by extension it can also mean "bald head".Caillou is a half-hour children's television animated cartoon about a 4-year-old bald-headed boy named Caillou who lives with his 2-year-old little sister, Rosie (Mousseline in the original French version), his parents, his cat named Gilbert, and his stuffed animals.

Older form of Caoilte, possibly derived from Irish caol meaning "slender". In Irish legend Caílte was a warrior of the Fianna and their foremost poet. He killed the god Lir in battle during the war between the gods.
From the Chinese 彩 (cǎi) meaning "colour" and 鸾 (luán), a mythological bird.
From the lizard species and crocodile species known as caimans. See Cayman
Irish name, from the same root of Caoimhìn, it means "gentle".
Spanish and Gascon form of Cain.
Means "beautiful, fair" in Welsh. This was the name of a 5th-century saint.

From an alternative name for New York used in the Doctrine and Covenants. A possible origin could be that in the Bible, Cain, the son of Adam, had a son named Enoch. A derivative of that is Henoch, and a further derivative is Hanoch. It is the LDS belief that Adam and his people lived in America. So, in that sense, it could possibly be the site of the ancient City of Enoch (not to be confused with the righteous Enoch).
From Irish caoin meaning "gentle", and der meaning "daughter". This was the name of Queen Medb's daughter in the Ulster Cycle of Irish mythology. Some saints have borne this name as well.
Diminutive of Cai 2. The name coincides with Caio or Caeo, the name of a village in the county of Carmarthenshire, south-west Wales.

column3: 彩琴, 彩勤, 采芹, etc.(Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 彩 (cǎi) meaning "colour" or 采 (cǎi) meaning "collect, gather, pluck" combined with 琴 (qín) meaning "zither, lute", 勤 (qín) meaning "diligent, industrious, hardworking" or 芹 (qín) meaning "celery". Other character combinations can form this name as well.

Folk etymology likes to consider this name to be of Tupi origin and assigns it the meaning "water bird". Since no etymology or evidence of use by the Tupi people has ever been provided, it is likely that this is a faux-indigenous name. In all likelihood it is a variant of Caíque.

The meaning of this name is unknown.One bearer of this name was Caireall mac Curnain (alive in mid to late 5th century), aka Saint Kerrill, who was a Christian missionary in the kingdom called Tír Sogháin (now eastern County Galway).
From the name Caireall combined with the diminutive suffix án.

In medieval Irish legends, this name was borne by the mother of Niall of the Nine Hostages, a concubine of King Eochu (or Eochaid). She was treated harshly by his jealous wife Queen Mongfind, but later rescued by her son.
Old Irish and Scottish name, originally from Carn, which changed to Caibre, which changed to Cairney.Irish-Celtic meaning - Charioteer Literal meaning - stack of rocks marking a trail

Variant spelling of Kairon, possibly influenced by Ciarán (at least in the United Kingdom).The brief popularity of the name in the UK in 2009 can likely be attributed to the 10th season of the reality television series Big Brother (British version), as that season had a participant named Cairon Austin-Hill (b. 1990).
From the Chinese 偲 (cāi) meaning "talented" or 彩 (cǎi) meaning "colour" and 睿 (ruì) meaning "shrewd, astute, clever" or 瑞 (ruì) meaning "felicitous omen, auspicious".

From Irish caiseal meaning "great stone fort" or "castle". A notable bearer of the name is the Australian Sci-Fi and fantasy novelist, artist and musician Caiseal Mór. This is a modern Irish word name and not commonly used in Ireland or Northern Ireland.

Supposed to mean "little castle" from Irish caiseal meaning "castle" combined with the Irish diminutive of ín. It also coincides with the rare Irish word caislín meaning "chat" (a type of bird). This is a modern name, most likely invented by English speakers, with no (or hardly any) usage in Ireland or Northern Ireland.

Invented by English writer William Jones for his poem 'Caïssa' (1763) as the name of a dryad of chess. In the chess world, Caïssa is seen as a mythical personification of chess. The name is sporadically given to girls.
Diminutive of Caitlin and Catherine. It may also be considered a variant of Kate.
Borne by a guaire (adviser) from the island of Tamarán (modern-day Gran Canaria).
Aragonese and Louisiana Spanish form of Caietanus (see Gaetano).
Meaning unknown, possibly a transferred usage of the place name Caithness as a given name. He appeared in the Shakespearean play, Macbeth.
Scottish Gaelic name derived from a mis-analysis of Caitrìona as Caitir Fhiona. This name used to be Anglicized as the etymologically unrelated Clarissa.
Variant of Caitlin influenced by the spelling of Maitland.
French form of Gaius and variant of Caïe
Caiva was a goddess who was worshipped in Gerolstein in present-day Germany. It has been speculated that she might have been a mother goddess.
From the Chinese 彩 (cǎi) meaning "colour" and 雯 (wén) meaning "cloud patterns".
From the Chinese 彩 (cǎi) meaning "colour" and 喜 (xǐ) meaning "like, love, be fond of; happy event".
From Chinese 彩 (cǎi) meaning "colour" combined with 霞 (xiá) meaning "rosy clouds, mist". Other character combinations can form this name as well.
From the Chinese 财 (cái) meaning "wealth, riches" and 香 (xiāng) meaning "fragrant, sweet smelling, incense".
From Chinese 彩 (cǎi) meaning "colour" combined with 音 (yīn) meaning "sound, noise, tone". Other character combinations can form this name as well.
From the Chinese 彩 (cǎi) meaning "colour" and 荧 (yíng) meaning "shine, shimmer, shining, dazzling".
From Chinese 彩 (cǎi) meaning "colour" combined with 云 (yún) meaning "cloud" or 韵 (yùn) meaning "rhyme, vowel". Other character combinations can form this name as well.
From the Chinese 采 (cǎi) meaning "collect, gather" and 忠 (zhōng) meaning "loyalty, devotion".
Hispanicized form of Yaqui Kahe'eme meaning "one who does not stop to drink (water)". This name was borne by the Yaqui leader Cajemé (1837-1887), baptized José María Leyva.
Diminutive of Caja, which is used as a diminutive of Jelisaveta and Stanislava.
Derived from the Adyghe дэд (ded) meaning "very" and цӀыкӀу (tsIykIu) meaning "small".
From the English word, a sweet dessert food, ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European *gog "ball-shaped object".
From the Kurdish çakî meaning "goodness, favour".
One of the Mayan gods of lightning.
Variation of Calla using the Italian word, cala, meaning "cove." Also a nickname for the Greek Kalas.

Allegedly from Hebrew כַּלָּה (kallah) meaning "bride", a word sometimes used as a metaphor for the Sabbath (hence, "Shabbat bride"), though it is uncertain whether this is truly used as a Jewish name.Considering the submitted pronunciation is "cayla", this may be a variant of the Yiddish name Kaila (which was fairly popular in the 19th century among Ashkenazim Jews).
Derived from Spanish calahorrano, meaning "man from Calahorra".

Latinized form of Greek Κάλαϊς (Kalais), which meant "turquoise" or "chrysolite" (being the name of "a precious stone of a greenish blue"). In Greek myth Calais and his twin brother Zetes, together known as the Boreads (being sons of Boreas, god of the north wind), were Argonauts.

Meaning uncertain. Among anglophone bearers from outside Ireland, there might possibly be cases where the name is derived from the surname Calam, which is ultimately of Scottish origin.A known bearer of this name is the English actor Calam Lynch (b. 1994), whose parents are both Irish.
From the Latin word calamus meaning "reed, cane". This was the name of a possibly legendary Catalan saint who is the patroness of the town of Calaf (Catalonia).
Uncertain etymology, possibly derived from Ancient Greek καλάμη (kalame) meaning "reed, stalk, straw (of corn, wheat)". Calametis was one of the fifty daughters of King Thespius in Greek mythology.
From Greek κάλαμος (kalamos) meaning "reed". This was the name of two sculptors of ancient Greece.

Latinised form of the Spanish surname Calasanz borne by the Catholic saint Joseph Calasanz (1556-1648), who is also known as Joseph Calasanctius, probably influenced in part by Latin sanctus meaning "sacred, holy".

Derived from the surname Calasanz. Joseph Calasanz (known in Spanish as José de Calasanz; September 11, 1557 – August 25, 1648) was a Spanish Catholic priest, educator and the founder of the Pious Schools, providing free education to the sons of the poor, and the Religious Order that ran them, commonly known as the Piarists. He was a close friend of the renowned astronomer Galileo Galilei. He is honored as a saint by the Catholic Church.
A notable bearer Matthew C. Perry (American naval officer who opened Japan to the West) who has this as a middle name.
Probably a variant of Kelsey influenced by Chelsea.
Derived from a Greek name meaning "from Chalcedon". Chalcedon was a city in what is now the Asian part of Istanbul.

Latinized form of Greek Κάλχας (Kalchas), which is perhaps derived from Greek χαλκός (chalkos) "bronze". Calchas was a seer featured in Homer's 'Iliad', famous for correctly predicting many events of the Trojan War. Upon being bested in a contest of soothsaying by Mopsus, he killed himself in shame.

Latinized form of Greek Κάλχος (Kalkhos), possibly derived from Ancient Greek κάλχη (kalkhe) meaning "purple dye". This was the name of a king of the Daunians in Greek mythology, who unsuccessfully courted Circe and was turned into a pig.

This is the name of a fire demon in the 1986 young adult fantasy novel Howl's Moving Castle, written by Diana Wynne Jones.Perhaps derived from French calcifier "to calcify", stemming from Latin calx "lime, limestone", or from calx "lime" and ferre "to bring".
Transferred use of the surname Calder.
Possible variation of the name Caledonia.
Transferred use of the surname Caldwell.

Most likely a masculine form of Caledonia. In medieval tales about King Arthur, this is the name of a forest in southern Scotland and northern England. It is probably best known from the 1997 film Titanic, where it belonged to one of the main characters (namely Caledon Hockley, who went by Cal in daily life).

From the Latin name of Scotland, itself derived from Caledones, the Latin name of a tribe that inhabited the region during the Roman era, which is of unknown origin, though it may possibly come from Proto-Celtic *kaletos meaning "hard" and *ɸēdo- meaning "foot", alluding to standfastness or endurance.
Most likely a variant of Callum.
Derived from Provençal calendau "(of) Christmas", ultimately derived from Latin calendalis. Calendau is the name of the hero of Mistral’s poem Calendau (1867).

The scientific name for a genus of flowers, comprised of several kinds of marigolds. From the Latin diminutive of calendae, meaning "little calendar", "little clock" or possibly "little weather-glass".
Means "from Cales" (Ancient Roman city, today Calvi Risorta, Campania, Italy).It was an irregular praenomen (borne by the artist Calenus Canoleius) and a cognomen in the gens Fufia.
Latinized form of Kaleria as well as the Romanian form of this name.

From the English surname, Caley, meaning "jackdaw clearing" or from an Irish surname which is an altered form of Macauley. It was originally used for boys, charting for the first time in 1928 when it was given to 6 boys. It has since become more popular for girls and is sometimes seen as a variant of Kaylee, even though it has different origins.
Portuguese cognate of Alondra, occasionally used in Brazil.
Transferred use of the surname Calhoun.

Probably derived from Ancient Greek καλός (kalos) meaning "beautiful, good" and ἀδνός (adnos) meaning "holy, pure, chaste". In Greek mythology this was the name of a naiad of the river Nile in Egypt. She was one of the wives of king Aegyptus, and bore him twelve sons.
Variant of Kaliana. This name was given to 20 girls born in the USA in 2010.

Caliandra is the name of a flower, whose scientific name is Calliandra harrisii, and its denomination derives from the combination of the Greek elements Kallio (beautiful) and Andros (man), probably meaning "beautiful and masculine" or "beautiful and manlike".
Variant of Kaliana. This name was given to 12 girls born in the USA in 2010.
Variant of Calise, which might be based on Calista. It coincides with the French noun calice meaning "chalice". This is borne by Calice Becker, a French perfumer.

From the English word calico referring to something having a pattern of red and contrasting areas, specially the tri-coloured cat, resembling the color of calico cloth, a kind of rough cloth often printed with a bright pattern. Derived from Calicut, an Anglicized form of Kozhikode (from Malayalam കോഴിക്കോട് (kōḻikkōṭ), koyil "palace" combined with kota "fort, fortified palace"), the name of a city in southwestern India from where the cloth was originally exported.A noted bearer is John Rackham (1682 – 1720), commonly known as Calico Jack, an English pirate captain operating in the Bahamas and in Cuba during the early 18th century, his nickname derived from the calico clothing he wore.

Perhaps derived from Greek kallos "beauty" and doron "gift". It was used by Edmund Spenser in his poem 'The Faerie Queene' (1596), where Sir Calidore, the Knight of Courtesy, is the hero of Book VI who tames the Blatant Beast as requested by Queen Gloriana.
Calidorus is a character in 'Pseudolus', a play by the ancient Roman playwright Titus Maccius Plautus.

Possibly means "instrument of God" or "weapon of God", derived from Hebrew כְּלִי (kli) meaning "instrument, tool, weapon" combined with אֵל (ʾel) meaning "God". This is the name of an angel belonging to the order of the Thrones. He is one of the 72 angels bearing the explicit name of God (the Shem HaMephorash), as interpreted by some Christian Kabbalists.

From the name of the American state, whose name probably derives from the fictional Island of California ruled by Queen Calafia in the 16th century novel Las sergas de Esplandián by García Ordóñez de Montalvo.
Possibly related to the name for the genus of the "owl butterfly" or the Latin word meaning "darkness, mist." Name of a faerie in the game 'Lovestruck.'

Meaning unknown, but several theories have been proposed for its etymology. One such theory is that it is derived from Latin caligante meaning "fading, growing dim". In turn, the word is ultimately derived from the Latin verb caligo meaning "to steam, to darken". The latter word can also be a noun in Latin, in which case it means "fog, mist, vapor" as well as "darkness, gloom".Other theories suggest that the name is a composition of Italian calore logorante meaning "intense heat", or that it is a play on Caltagirone, the name of a town in Sicily. The town derives its name from Arabic qal'at al ghiran (also gharun and jirar), which has been said to mean "castle of jars", "rock of jars" and "hill of vases".Lastly, it is possible that this name has some connection to Calogero or Calogrenant.In literature, Caligorante is the name of a giant from canto XV (15) of the 16th-century epic poem Orlando furioso written by the Italian poet Ludovico Ariosto (1474-1533). He was captured and enslaved by the knight Astolfo, who promptly paraded him around in every city they came across.
Combination of prefix Ca- with the name Alijah, itself a variant of Elijah.
Spanish and Portuguese form of Callimachus.
Calimero is originally derived from the Greek Kallimeros, from Kalos meaning "Beautiful; Noble," and Meros meaning "Thigh; Leg". Turning out to be, "With Beautiful, Strong Legs".
Originally a contracted form of Carolina; in some cases this might also be a variant of Kalina.
Anglicized form of Calinichia. Doamna Calinichia is known as Lady Calinica in English.
Diminutive of Călina. Ana-Călina, mother of Mircea I of Wallachia, was known as Doamna Calinichia (Lady Calinichia).
Spanish and Portuguese form of Callinicus.
Meaning uncertain, possibly derived from a place name.
Spanish and Portuguese form of Kalliope.
Spanish form of Kallippos via its latinized form Callippus.
Catalan, Galician, Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Calypso.
Variant of Kelis, or an invented name based on the sounds found in names such as Calista, Kaliyah and Alise.
Possibly an alteration of Calista, formed using the popular name suffix issa.
Languedocian and Romansh form of Callistus.
French masculine and feminine form of Callistus as well as a Provençal masculine form of Calixte.
Modern name taken from the Latin word calix meaning "wine cup, chalice".
Gascon and Provençal form of Calixtus.
Variant of Kalla as well as an adoption of the plant name.
Anglicized form of Irish name Ceallachán
Transferred use of the surname Callandre.
Transferred use of the surname Callaway, in which itself, it is a variant of Calloway.
Meaning, "to summon." Referring to the calling to the work of God.
Alternate transcription of Κάλλια or Καλλία (see Kallia).
Variant of Kaliana. This name was given to 7 girls born in the USA in 2010.
Latinized form of Kallianassa. In Greek mythology, this is the name of one of the Nereids.
Latinized form of Kallianeira. In Greek mythology, this name belonged to one of the Nereids.

A variant form of Gawaine. The eldest son of King Lot of Orkney and Queen Morgawse (or Anna), Arthur’s sister or half-sister. Brother of Gareth, Gaheris and Agravaine, chief of the Orkney clan (which included his brothers and half brother Mordred), Arthur’s favorite nephew, and one of the most strongest and famous knights of the Round Table.
Latinized form of Kallikratidas. This was the name of a Spartan naval commander from the 5th century BC.

Probably derived from the Latin adjective calidus, which may be translated as "warm, hot, fiery," or "passionate". Callidia is Queen Veremonda's maid in an Italian opera called 'Veremonda, l'amazzone di Aragona' (with the English translation being 'Veremonda, the Amazon of Aragon' also known as 'Il Delio'). Callidia is the maid's name in the version of the opera that was performed in Naples, in the original version the maid's name is Vespina.

Latinized form of Καλλιδίκη (Kallidike), which is derived from Greek καλλος (kallos) meaning "beauty" and δικη (dike) meaning "justice, judgement" as well as "custom, usage". This was the name of several figures in Greek mythology, including a queen of Thesprotia who married Odysseus after the death of his wife Penelope, and one of the fifty Daenids.
Latinized form of Kallimachos. This name was borne by a Greek poet from the 3rd century BC.
Latinized form of Kallimedon. This was the name of an Athenian orator and politician from the 4th century BC.
Variant of Callan and Kellan. As a rare feminine name, it can be a variant of Kaylyn or Caelan.
Feminine form of Callinicus. This was the name of a Christian martyr from the 3rd century AD.
Latinized form of Kallinos. This was the name of an ancient Greek poet from the 7th century BC.
Related to (or derived from) Calliope, meaning "beautiful voice". This was the name of a Greek rhetor and official of the Roman Empire.

Derived from Ancient Greek καλός (kalos) meaning "beautiful, good" and possibly φάος (phaos) meaning "light". This was the name of one of the Ionides naiad nymphs in Greek mythology, whose spring waters were believed to cure diseases.
French form of Kallippos via its latinized form Callippus.
Latinized form of Kallippides. Bearers of this name include a Greek actor (5th century BC) and a Greek runner (1st century BC).
Italian form of Kallippos via its latinized form Callippus.
Latinized form of Kallippos. This was the name of a Greek astronomer and mathematician from the 4th century BC.
Latinized form of Greek Καλλιρόη (Kallirhoe), the Epic Greek form of Καλλιρρόη (see Kallirrhoe).
Variant of Callirrhoé used by French composer André Cardinal Destouches for his opera Callirhoé (1712).
Meaning uncertain. In some cases it is probably a variant of Calista, where the 't' was dropped because it had become silent in the local dialect. Also see Calissa and Callissa.

Latinized form of Kalliste. In Greek mythology, this was the name of a sea nymph, who was one of the daughters of the sea-god Triton. It was also a descriptive epithet of the goddess Artemis.In French, this name is unisex: it is the French form of both Callista and Callistus, the Latinate forms of respectively Kallista (sometimes also Kalliste) and Kallistos.
Transferred use of the surname Callister.
Latinized form of Kallisthenes. This name was borne by a Greek historian from the 4th century BC.
Latinized form of Kallistratos. This name was borne by a Greek grammarian from the 2nd century BC.
Sicilian and Sardinian form of Callistus.
Latinized form of Kalliteles. A known bearer of this name was the Olympic victor Calliteles of Laconia (also known as Sparta). He had won the wrestling contest during the 68th Olympiad in 508 BC.

Derived from Ancient Greek κάλλος (kallos) meaning "beautiful" combined with either θέα (thea) meaning "sight, view" or θεά (thea) meaning "goddess". In Greek mythology, this was a variant name for Callithyia.
Derived from Ancient Greek κάλλος (kallos) meaning "beauty" and θοός (thoos) meaning "quick, swift". Callithoe was a daughter of Celeus in Greek mythology.

Possibly derived from Ancient Greek κάλλος (kallos) meaning "beauty" and θύω (thyo) meaning "to offer in sacrifice, kill, burn" as well as "to celebrate". Alternatively, the second element could derive from either θυία (thyia), referring to the Juniperus foetidissima plant, or θύον (thyon) meaning "cypress-pine". Callithyia, also called Callithoe and Callithea, was an Argive princess and the first priestess of Argive Hera in Greek mythology. Callithyia was also the name of a daughter of Aeolus, keeper of the winds.
Latinized form of Kallixenos. A known bearer of this name was the Greek historian and author Callixenus of Rhodes (3rd century BC).
Transferred use of the surname Calloway.
From the genus name of common heather, a flowering shrub. It comes from the Greek verb καλλύνω (kalluno) meaning "to beautify, sweep clean", ultimately from καλός (kalos) "beautiful".
Derived from call meaning "wise, sensible" and gwen meaning "white, fair, blessed", or cellan meaning "little cell".

Derived from Manx caillagh, a cognate of Old Irish caillech "veiled one; (and by extension) nun; female servant" (ultimately from Old Irish caille "veil") and Irish Cróine with the intended meaning of "servant of Saint Cróine", an obscure female saint (since the names of saints were considered too holy for everyday use, they were usually prefixed until the 17th century).

Derived from Manx caillagh, a cognate of Old Irish caillech "veiled one; (and by extension) nun; female servant" (ultimately from Old Irish caille "veil") and the given name Moirrey with the intended meaning of "servant of the Virgin Mary" (since the names of saints were considered too holy for everyday use, they were usually prefixed until the 17th century).

Latinized form of Kalmana, the name of Cain's wife and twin sister in Judeo-Christian legend (e.g., found in the (first Greek redaction of the) 'Apocalypse of Pseudo-Methodius', written in Syriac in the late 7th century). This spelling was used in the 13th-century 'Golden Legend'.
This is the name of a character appearing in Perlesvaus, an Old French Arthurian romance who is the cousin of Perceval and son of Calobrutus.
This is the name of a character appearing in Perlesvaus, an Old French Arthurian romance who is one of Perceval’s eleven paternal uncles.
Latinized form of Kalokairos. This name was borne by a Roman usurper from the 4th century AD.
Feminine form of Calocero. Due to the similarities in appearance and pronunciation, this name is often confused with the name Calogera.
Portuguese form of Calocaerus and Calocerus, which are both latinizations of the Greek given name Kalokairos.

Italian form of Calocaerus and Calocerus, which are both latinizations of the Greek given name Kalokairos.Due to the similarities in appearance and pronunciation, this name is often confused with the name Calogero, which is derived from the Greek given name Kalogeros via its latinized form Calogerus.

Variant spelling of Calocaerus, which is the latinized form of the Greek given name Kalokairos. Due to the similarities in appearance and pronunciation, this name is often confused with the name Calogerus (see Calogero).This name was borne by a martyr and saint from the 2nd century AD.
Sicilian form of Kalogeros via its latinized form Calogerus (see Calogero).
Name of a knight of the round table, associated with the Welsh hero Cynon ap Clydno.
From Greek κάλος meaning "beautiful" combined with Maria.

The first element of this name is derived from Polish cały "whole, entire, complete", which is ultimately derived from Proto-Slavic cělъ "whole, entire". Also compare Czech celý and Croatian cijel, both of which mean "whole, entire". The second element of this name is derived from Slavic mir "peace". As such, this name roughly means "complete peace" or "peace is complete".
Italian form of Kalonymos via its latinized form Calonymus.
Latinized form of Kalonymos. A known bearer of this name was Calonymus of Alexandria, a Byzantine naval commander from the 6th century AD.
Gallo form of Caroline via a semi-Gallicization of Calorinn.
Used by André Gide in his novel "The Counterfeiters" for a minor character.

Variant of Calpurnia. A well-known bearer of this name is Calpernia Addams (b. 1971), an American author, actress, and transgender rights activist. Addams named herself after Calpurnia, wife of Julius Caesar in William Shakespeare's play 'Julius Caesar'; the spelling 'Calpernia' may have been taken from a tombstone that briefly appeared in the film 'The Addams Family' (1991).
Italian and Spanish form of Calpurnianus.

Roman cognomen which was derived from Calpurnius. Bearers of this name include Roman consul Marcus Pupius Piso Frugi Calpurnianus (1st century BC) and Roman politician Marcus Antius Crescens Calpurnianus (3rd century AD).
Italian and Spanish form of Calpurnius.
Likely derived from the Latin root "calpus", which means "pale" or "fair". It may also have been used as a variant of names that are associated with calvus, meaning "bald" in Latin.
Means "house dweller", derived from Nahuatl calli "house" and the suffix -catl "inhabitant".
Transferred use of the surname Calton.
This was the name of Vlad Dracul's noble Wallachian mistress, a boyar lady who became the mother of his son Vlad Călugărul ('Vlad the Monk').
English usage possibly derived from the surnames Callander, Callender. Swedish usage is a variant of Kalvander of uncertain meaning. It may be related to the surname Calvander.

A variant form of Gawaine. The eldest son of King Lot of Orkney and Queen Morgawse (or Anna), Arthur’s sister or half-sister. Brother of Gareth, Gaheris and Agravaine, chief of the Orkney clan (which included his brothers and half brother Mordred), Arthur’s favorite nephew, and one of the most strongest and famous knights of the Round Table.
From the name of the hill outside Jerusalem where Jesus was crucified, derived from the Latin noun calvaria meaning "a skull" (see Calvary).
Derived from the surname Calvert. From the elements Middle English calfhirde, from Old English calf and hierde "herdsman".
Roman cognomen that was a derivative of Calvus. Original Latin form of Calvin and Calvino.

Derived from Manx caillagh, a cognate of Old Irish caillech "veiled one; (and by extension) nun; female servant" (ultimately from Old Irish caille "veil") and the given name Bridey with the intended meaning of "servant of Saint Bridget" (since the names of saints were considered too holy for everyday use, they were usually prefixed until the 17th century).

In the case of Calybute Downing, D.D. (1606-1643), whose father was also named Calybute Downing, it appears to be a slight variation of his paternal grandmother's maiden name, Calybut. There was a similar name recorded in Domesday Book: Calebot.

Derived from Ancient Greek κάλυξ (kalyx) meaning "covering (of flowers or fruits); seed pod, husk, shell; calyx, cup of a flower". This was the name of several figures in Greek mythology, including one of the Nysiads (nymphs who nursed Dionysos), a daughter of king Aeolus, and the mother of Cycnus by Poseidon.

Derived from Manx caillagh, a cognate of Old Irish caillech "veiled one; (and by extension) nun; female servant" (ultimately from Old Irish caille "veil") and Manx Creest "Christ" with the intended meaning of "servant of Christ" (since the names of saints were considered too holy for everyday use, they were usually prefixed until the 17th century).

Derived from Manx caillagh, a cognate of Old Irish caillech "veiled one; (and by extension) nun; female servant" (ultimately from Old Irish caille "veil") and Manx doonagh "church" with the intended meaning of "servant of the Church" or "servant of the Lord".

Derived from Manx caillagh, a cognate of Old Irish caillech "veiled one; (and by extension) nun; female servant" (ultimately from Old Irish caille "veil") and the given name Patric with the intended meaning of "servant of Saint Patrick" (since the names of saints were considered too holy for everyday use, they were usually prefixed until the 17th century).
Variant of Calissa, the spelling influenced by Alyssa.
From the name of a flowering plant.
Means "bran" in Vietnamese. This is the name of the stepsister in the Vietnamese fairytale Tấm Cám, which is similar to Cinderella.
From Sino-Vietnamese 感 (cảm) meaning "to feel, emotion, affection".
From Sino-Vietnamese 琴 (cầm) meaning "zither, lute" or 擒 (cầm) meaning "to hold, seize".
From Sino-Vietnamese 锦 (cẩm) meaning "tapestry, brocade, embroidered".

column3: จามเทวี(Thai)|စာမ္မာဒေဝဳ(Mon)
column12: Etymology uncertain. Name borne by a queen of Hariphunchai (an ancient Mon kingdom, which is part of modern-day Thailand).

Possibly from the Hebrew name חַמּוּאֵל (Ḥammuʾel) meaning "wrath of God", derived from חֵמָה (ḥema) meaning "rage, wrath, fury" combined with אֵל (ʾel) meaning "God", or from קְמוּאֵל (Qemuʾel) meaning "raised by God" (see Kemuel). This is the name of an archangel in Christian and Jewish mythology.
Variant of Camellia see also Camala
Short form of the compound name Carlos Manuel, composed of Ca- and Mané. A known bearer is the Portuguese fado singer Camané (1966-), who was born Carlos Manuel Moutinho Paiva dos Santos Duarte.
Means "meadow flower" in Azerbaijani, ultimately from Persian چمن (chaman) meaning "meadow" and گل (gol) meaning "flower, rose".
Variant of Kamaria or simply a combination of the prefix Ca- and the name Maria.

Uncertain etymology, possibly derived from Ancient Greek καμάρα (kamara) meaning "anything with an arched cover; vault; span", ultimately from Old Iranian. This was the name of an Oceanid in Greek mythology, who supposedly gave her name to the ancient Sicilian city Kamarina.
Camaris sa-Vinitta is an original character created by fantasy Author, Tad Williams. Camaris comes from the Greek καμαρης meaning 'pride'. Camaris also means 'chamber' in Latin.
Another name for Mixcoatl, a god of the hunt.
Camazotz represented bats in Mayan mythology. Bats were considered symbols of rebirth and the underworld.
Either a variant of Campbell or a combination of Cam 2 and Belle. Cambelle was given to 17 girls in 2013 according to the SSA.
An invented name, probably based on the sounds found in names such as Amber, Cameron and Kimber.
Cambina is Triamond's sister and Cambell's wife in Book 4, Cantos 2–3 of Edmund Spenser's The Faerie Queene. She is well-versed in magic and able to soothe conflict.

Transferred use of the place name (used by a number of locations in the English-speaking world), derived from its old name Grantebrycge (referring to the original place in the east of England) meaning "bridge by the river Granta," where the name of the river (of unknown origin) was changed to Cante and then Cam (by Middle English) to match the current name of the town.Also from the city in Massachuseets outside of Boston where Harvard and MIT are located.
Combination of Cambria with the popular suffix ree.
Elaboration of Cambria influenced by Gabriella. This name was given to 5 American girls in 2016, and 5 more in 2018.
An invented name inspired by Cambry and the -elle suffix.
Derived from Tupi-Guarani cambucy meaning "pot; vase".

Uncertain etymology. In Greek mythology, Cameirus was the eponymous founder of Camirus in Rhodes. He was the son of the Rhodian king, Cercaphus, one of the Heliades, and his niece Cydippe, daughter of Ochimus, also a former king.
French form of Camelianus. This name was borne by a 6th-century saint who succeeded Loup as the bishop of Troyes.
Goddess who enables the child to sing.
It is of Italian and Middle French origin, and the meaning is "skin". From Italian cammeo which refers to a gem portrait carved in relief.

Variant of Qamariya. Sultana Cameria was the name Europeans used to refer to Mihrimah Sultan (1522 – 25 January 1578), an Ottoman princess, the daughter of Ottoman Sultan Süleyman the Magnificent and his wife, Hürrem Sultan. She was the most powerful imperial princess in Ottoman history according to historian Mustafa Selaniki who described her as the greatest and most respected princess and a prominent figure in the so-called Sultanate of Women.
Feminine form of Camerino. This was borne by Mexican poet Camerina Pavón y Oviedo (1862-1893).

Camerinus was was a cognomen the patrician family of the Sulpici which may have taken it from the town of Cameria or Camerium in Latium. The name is often associated with the word camera "chamber, room".
In the Aeneid, Camers is the name of an officer that Juturna disguises herself as.
Diminutive of Camille, Cameron, and other names beginning with Cam.

Catalan cognate of Camino, taken from the title of the Virgin Mary, Mare de Déu del Camí, meaning "Mother of God of the Way."She is the patroness of Cambrils in the Catalonian province of Tarragona. She is also venerated at the church in Granyena de Segarra in the province of Lleida as well as the one located in Santa Maria del Camí on the Balearic island of Mallorca.
Romansh, Catalan, Romanian and Occitan form of Camillus.
Turkish form of Jamila. This name was also at one point in the top 100 names of Azerbaijan.
Picard and Walloon masculine and feminine form and Gascon and Provençal masculine form of Camille.
Possibly derived from Arabic كامل (kāmil) meaning "complete, full, whole".
Variant of Camélien influenced by Camille.
Corsican, Sardinian and Sicilian form of Camillus.

Means "way, route; road; path" in Spanish, taken from the Spanish title of the Virgin Mary, La Virgen del Camino, meaning "The Virgin of the Way." She is the patroness of the region of León and the city of Pamplona in Navarra, forming part of the French Way to Santiago de Compostela.

From an archaic French word meaning "small pin". This is the name of the titular character in Mademoiselle de Lubert's fairy tale 'Princess Camion' (1743). Camion is the name of a princess transformed into a tiny doll, given to the prince Zirphil to be his wife.
Combination of the phonetic elements ka, mee and sha.

Latinized form of Kamisares (also spelled Kamissares), which is the hellenized form of an ancient Persian male name. Its meaning is currently unknown to me. This was the name of an Achaemenid satrap from the 4th century BC.
Transferred use of the surname Camlin.
Derived from the Romani word kamlo "dear; beloved; gentle; beautiful".
Combination of Cam 2 and the popular name suffix lyn, perhaps influenced by Camryn.
The name of a Galatian princess and priestess of Artemis whom Plutarch writes about in both On the Bravery of Women and the Eroticus or Amatorius.
A variation of the name Camille.
Variant of Cammie, i.e., diminutive of Cameron or Camilla.
Means "pot; vase" in Tupi and Guarani.
Transferred use of the surname Camp.
Means "where does he come from?" in Nahuatl.

From Latin campanella (a smallish suspended bell used in medieval monastic cloisters), itself deriving from campana, meaning "bell". It appears in "Night on the Galactic Railroad", a classic Japanese fantasy novel by Kenji Miyazawa.

From the name of the flower, which means "little bell" in Latin, diminutive of Late Latin campana "bell" (originally "metal vessel made in Campania", region around Naples). The flower is widespread across the whole temperate regions of Europe, but has the most species diversity in the Mediterranean region. This name has been used rarely since the late 19th century when flower names became popular.

Unknown etymology. Campaspe, also called Pancaste and Pacate, was the purported mistress or concubine of Alexander the Great, and a prominent citizen of Larissa. There are no contemporary sources recording her existence, which may be apocryphal. Her name came to be used as a poetic term for a man’s mistress in English.
Transferred use of the surname Camper.
Campino is the stage name of Andreas Frege.

This rare given name can be derived from the surname of Campion as well as from the name of the plant, both of which likely derive their name from Old French campion meaning "champion". A known bearer of this given name is the American writer and film director Campion Murphy (b. 1962).In literature, Campion is the name of one of the Efafran rabbits in Richard Adams' 1972 novel Watership Down.
Given in honour of Colonel Juan Vicente Campo Elías (1759-1814), regarded as a hero of Venezuelan Independence.It is most often used in Colombia with some usage in Venezuela.
From Sino-Vietnamese 錦葵 (cẩm quỳ) meaning "mallow".

From the name of a car model, made by Toyota, which derives from Japanese 冠 (kanmuri) meaning "crown (royal headdress)" and may be an anagram of the English phrase my car. It could also be viewed as a diminutive of Camryn.
Means "marble", from Sino-Vietnamese 錦 (cẩm) meaning "brocade" and 石 (thạch) meaning "stone".
From Sino-Vietnamese 甘草 (cam thảo) meaning "licorice", composed of 甘 (cam) meaning "sweet" and 草 (thảo) meaning "grass".
From Sino-Vietnamese 錦繡 (cẩm tú) meaning "brocaded silk, beautiful as brocade", composed of 錦 (cẩm) meaning "brocade" and 繡 (tú) meaning "to embroider".

Form of Kemuel used in the Bishops' Bible (1568), Douay-Rheims Bible (1582-1610), the Clementine Vulgate (1592) and the Nova Vulgata ("Neo-Vulgate", 1979). The latter two are respectively the former and current official Bible of the Roman Catholic Church.
Form of Kemuel used in the Latin Old Testament.
Derived from Gaulish *camulos "champion; servant". Camulos was an important god of early Great Britain and Gaul, especially among the Belgae and the Remi, who the Romans equated with Mars.
Transferred use of the surname Camus.
From Sino-Vietnamese 甘雨 (cam vũ) meaning "timely rain", composed of 甘 (cam) meaning "sweet" and 雨 (vũ) meaning "rain".
From Sino-Vietnamese 幹 (cán) meaning "main part of something, to work" or 檊 (cán) meaning "Chinese mulberry tree".
From Sino-Vietnamese 乾 (càn) meaning "sky, heaven, emperor, sun, male".
From Sino-Vietnamese 根 (căn) meaning "root, cause, source".
From Sino-Vietnamese 艮 (cấn) meaning "to obstruct". This is also the seventh of the Eight Trigrams, symbolizing mountains.
Variant of Cẩn. It can also come from Sino-Vietnamese 僅 (cận) meaning "merely, only" or 覲 (cận) meaning "to have an audience (with a leader)".
From Sino-Vietnamese 瑾 (cẩn) meaning "fine jade" or 謹 (cẩn) meaning "cautious, careful".
Means "to interrogate, to be careful, detailed" in Vietnamese.
From Teochew 橄欖 (cà na) meaning "Chinese olive (Elaeocarpus hygrophilus)".
From the name of the ancient city of Cana as mentioned in the New Testament, John 2:1-11, relating the story of Jesus's first miracle.

Possibly derived from Greek κανάκι (kanaki) meaning "caresses, endearments, praise", or perhaps from the word’s older root καναχή (kanakhe) meaning "sharp sound; ring or clang of metal, clattering". In Greek mythology, this was the name of a daughter of Aeolus and Enarete, and lover of Poseidon. In a variant tale, Canace was instead in a relationship with her own brother Macareus. This tradition made them children of a different Aeolus, the lord of the winds (or the Tyrrhenian king), and his wife Amphithea.
Canachus was a sculptor of Sicyon in Corinthia.
From the name of the North American country of Canada, which is derived from the Iroquoian word kanata meaning "village".

From the English word for the type of small birds, ultimately derived from Latin canis "dog", as these birds were first found at the Canary Islands, which were named for its large dogs kept by the inhabitants of the island.
Variant of Conall found in the Poppleton manuscript (14th century) as a name owned by only one of the Pictish kings, usually identified with Conall mac Taidg.
From the Persian جان (jan) meaning "soul" and Karachay-Balkar ай (ay) meaning "moon".
From Turkish can "soul, life" combined with aziz "respected, powerful, beloved".
From Persian جان (jān) meaning "soul" and Azerbaijani bacı meaning "sister".
Reduplication of Chinese 灿 (càn) meaning "bright, illuminating". Other hanzi combinations can form this name as well.
From the Persian جان (jan) meaning "soul" and the diminutive suffix -чыкъ (çıq).
Hypocorism of Juan José via baby talk.
Probably related to Old High German kanker "spider" with the transferred meaning "weaver".
Indian feminine name meaning "Fierce, impetuous, violent", an epithet of Parvati.
Variant of Candace, reflecting an older English pronunciation. It is mainly found in Guyana and the West Indies.

Uncertain etymology, possibly related to the Proto-Indo-European root *(s)kand- meaning "to shine, appear". In Greek mythology, Candalus was one of the Heliadae, a son of Rhodos and the sun god Helios.
Derived from Galician candea "candle", this name is occasionally given in honor of Candlemas (Festum Candelorium in Latin, which translates to festa das candeas in Galician; compare Candelaria).

Means "candle bearer", derived from Latin candela "a taper, a wax-light, a tallow-candle" (the source of the English word candle) and ferre "to bear". In Roman mythology Candelifera was a goddess supposed to assist at childbirth, for whom a symbolical candle or torch was lighted.The cyclical place of the goddess is uncertain. It is sometimes thought that Candelifera provides an artificial light for labor that occurs at night. A long labor was considered likely for first-time mothers, so at least a part of the birthing process would occur at night. According to Plutarch, light symbolizes birth, but the candle may have been thought of as less a symbol than an actual kindling of life, or a magic equivalent to the life of the infant. Candelifera may also be a personification of the nursery light kept burning against spirits of darkness that would threaten the infant in the coming week. Even in the Christian era, lamps were lit in nurseries to illuminate sacred images and drive away child-snatching demons such as the Gello.
Possibly a contracted form of Candellaria.
Diminutive of Cándida, Cándido and Candela.
A notable bearer is the actress and reality TV star Candiace Dillard Bassett.
Probably created from Candy and Anne 1.
Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Candidianus.
Roman cognomen which was derived from Candidus. A known bearer of this name was Gaius Valerius Candidianus, the illegitimate son of Roman Emperor Galerius (4th century AD).
Variant of Candace and Candida.Famous namesake: Candita Pennella, lead singer of Canadian pop band Candi & The Backbeat.
A character in "Mother Bombie" an Elizabethan era stage play, by John Lyly.
Taken from the English word candle.
Means "moon" in Indonesian, ultimately from Sanskrit चन्द्र (candra).
Combination of Indonesian candra meaning "moon" and the name Ningsih.
From Indonesian candra meaning "moon" combined with the feminine suffix -wati.
The name was the subject of a 1971 eponymous French pop song by Yves Heuzé. Since then, the name has experienced sporadic usage in France.
Derived from the Spanish noun canela meaning "cinnamon". It coincides with a Spanish surname (see Canela).

Derived from the Spanish noun canelo, which can mean "winter's bark tree" as well as "cinnamon tree". Also compare Canela.A known bearer of this name is the Mexican professional boxer Saúl "Canelo" Álvarez (b. 1990).
A Mayan name meaning roughly, 'mischievous forest spirit.' Appears in local mythology.

Etymology uncertain. Possibly related to Ancient Greek κάνη (kane) meaning "reed" and the Mycenaean suffix -thos, or perhaps to κανθός (kanthos) meaning "eyelid, corner of the eye". This was the name of several figures in Greek mythology, including one of the fifty sons of King Lycaon. It was also the name of a mountain near Chalcis.
From Turkish can meaning "soul, life" or by extension "darling, sweetheart" combined with Turkish feda meaning "sacrifice".
Possibly from Sino-Vietnamese 伉 (cáng) meaning "upright, take charge of".

From Chinese 倉 (cāng) meaning "granary, storehouse" and 頡 (jié) meaning "fly upwards, neck". In Chinese mythology, Cangjie was a retainer of the Yellow Emperor (Xuanyuan) who invented written Chinese characters. According to legend, his invention caused ghosts to cry in the night and the sky to rain millet. He was also said to have four eyes. He is the namesake of the Cangjie method for inputting Chinese characters into a computer.

column3: 仓理, etc.(Chinese)|倉理, etc.(Traditional Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 仓 (cāng) meaning "granary, storehouse" combined with 理 (lǐ) meaning "reason, logic". Other hanzi combinations are possible.
From the Persian جان (jan) meaning "soul" and Karachay-Balkar гоша (goşa) meaning "lady".

Cāng (苍) means "blue" or "green" while qióng (穹) means "arch", "dome", or "elevated". Together, it means "heavens", "sky", or "the blue dome of heaven". Cangqiong is the mascot for a voicebank of the same name for the Synthesizer V software.

Derived from the Italian noun can meaning "khan" as well as "dog" combined with the Italian adjective grande meaning "big, great".A notable bearer of this name was the Italian nobleman Cangrande I della Scala (1291-1329). In his case, the meaning of the name might be more like "Can the Great", since his full name was Can Francesco della Scala. He is featured prominently in Giovanni Boccaccio's Decameron (14th century).
From Sino-Vietnamese 景 (cảnh) meaning "scenery, view, landscape" or 耿 (cảnh) meaning "bright, shining".
From Chinese 灿 (càn) meaning "vivid, bright, lustrous" combined with 花 (hua) meaning "flower, blossom". Other hanzi combinations are possible.
From the Persian جان (jân) meaning "soul" and the Turkish military title beg meaning "chieftain, master".
Latinized form of Cainnech, the Old Irish form of Kenneth.
From the latin adjective canus, meaning "white" or "grey", to describe an older woman with white hair. Canidia is the name of a witch in Ancient Rome, appearing several times in Horace's writing.
Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Caninius.
From the Roman nomen Caninius, which is derived from Latin caninus "dog-like, of a dog" (which in turn is derived from Latin canis "dog").
Italian and Spanish form of Canius.
From the dog constellation "Canis Major", who who loyally follows its mythical master, Orion across the southern skies of winter.

Feminine form of Canisius, occasionally adopted as a monastic name. In the case of Canisia Lubrin (1984-), a Saint Lucian-born Canadian poet, it is more likely a variant of Canisha (see Kanisha, Kenisha).

Transferred use of the surname Canisius. From the Dutch surname Kanis. Kanis, “covered fish basket” in dialectal Dutch, is the name of an inn that used an upturned fish basket on its signage, it came into usage in honour of the Jesuit and saint Peter Canisius.
Derived from Latin canus "old, grey(-haired), elderly" or Latin canis "dog." This name was borne by Canius Rufus, a Roman poet.
Persian and turkish origin , the name cankut means the persons luckiness, happiness.
From the Chinese 灿 (càn) meaning "vivid, illuminating, bright" or 璨 (càn) meaning "gems, luster of gems, lustrous" and 娈 (luán) meaning "lovely, beautiful, docile" or 銮 (luán) meaning "bells".
From the Chinese 璨 (càn) meaning "gems, luster of gems, lustrous" and 淼 (miǎo) meaning "wide expanse of water".

Rare name of uncertain origin and meaning that first appeared in the 19th century.One theory derives Canna from the tropical flower of the same name, placing Canna among the many Victorian flower names. If that is true - and in some cases it certainly is -, then the roots of this name lie with Greek kanna "reed".Another theory, however, considers Canna a borrowing of the name of the Scottish island Canna (Canaigh in Gaelic). The meaning of Canaigh is unclear; some scholars argue that it might be related to an Irish Gaelic word for "wolf-pup", while another group of academics derive the name from a Scottish Gaelic word for "porpoise" and yet another theory believes that, thanks to the island's shape, Canaigh might be related to an Old Norse word for "knee".
Transferred use of the surname Cannan
Means "heaven, paradise" in Azerbaijani, ultimately from Arabic جنّة (janna).

Derived from Italian canna "reed" combined with a diminutive suffix. This name is borne by the protagonist of the Italian fairy tale 'Cannetella' by Giambattista Basile. Cannetella is a young princess who marries the evil wizard Fioravante.
Feminine form of Cannutius. Cannutia was one of the Vestal Virgins.
From the name of a village in Andorra where there is a sanctuary dedicated to the Virgin Mary. The name of the village is of unknown meaning.
More common variant and historical form of Canòlic.

From the English word "canon" meaning "a generally accepted rule or principle; works considered to be authentic; religious law; or catalog of saints". From the Old French canon, from Latin canōn, from Ancient Greek kanón (κανών) 'measuring rod, standard'. May also be considered a variant of Cannon.
A Narragansett Sachem and leader of Native American troops during the Great Swamp Fight and King Philip's War.
A Native American chief of the Narragansett people.

The name of the second-brightest star in the night sky. It is possibly derived from Greek Κάνωβος (Kanobos), of uncertain meaning, possibly related to Arabic جَنُوب (janub), meaning "south". In Greek mythology, this was the name of the pilot of King Menelaus' ship in the Iliad. Alternatively, it could be derived from Egyptian Coptic Kahi Nub, meaning "golden earth", referring to the name of a ruined ancient Egyptian port lying near the mouth of the Nile, named after the Greek mythological character.
Means "good hunter of the forest", from Lakota čhúŋwaŋča "forest", waókA "good hunter", and kté "to kill".
From the Turkish can meaning "soul" and özlem meaning "longing".
From the Chinese 灿 (càn) meaning "vivid, illuminating" and 霜 (shuāng) meaning "frost".
From the Persian جان (jan) meaning "soul" and Karachay-Balkar verb element сюер (süer) meaning "to love".
From the Persian جان (jan) meaning "soul" and Karachay-Balkar сурат (surat) meaning "picture".
Meaning uncertain. It is either a short form of Cavalcante, or derived from the Italian word canto meaning "song".

Possibly derived from κανθός (kanthos) meaning "eyelid, corner of the eye". In Greek mythology, Canthus was the name of an Argonaut, as well as of one of the fifty sons of Aegyptus who was killed by his wife, Eurydice, on their wedding night.
Feminine form of Cantianillus. This was the name of a saint from the 4th century AD, who was martyred along with her brothers Cantius and Cantianus.
Extended form of Cantius. This was the name of a saint from the 4th century AD, who was martyred along with his brother Cantius and sister Cantianilla.
Italian and Spanish form of Cantidianus.
Roman cognomen which was derived from Cantidius.
Italian and Spanish form of Cantidius.

Possibly derived from Latin cantidus, which in turn may have been derived from Latin cantus "(a) singing, song". This was the name of a saint who was martyred in Antioch (the exact year remains unknown).
Derived from Gaulish cant- "with" and smert "purveyor, carer", this name was probably understood in the sense of "all-purveyor".
Derived from Latin cantus "(a) singing, song". This was the name of a saint from the 4th century AD, who was martyred along with his brother Cantianus and sister Cantianilla.

Means "edge" in Spanish, taken from the title of the Virgin Mary Nuestra Señora del Canto, meaning "Our Lady of the Edge". She is the patron saint of the town of Toro, located in the Spanish province of Zamora.
Means "brave, resilient", from Sino-Vietnamese 肝 (can) meaning "liver" and 腸 (trường) meaning "intestines".
Canuleia was one of the Vestal Virgins, selected by Numa Pompilius, the second king of Rome.
Norman and Guernésiais form of Canute.
Spanish and Portuguese form of Knut. There are two Catholic saints by this name.
Name of a mythical Pictish king.
From the Chinese 灿 (càn) meaning "vivid, illuminating, bright" and 馨 (xīn) meaning "fragrant, aromatic, distant fragrance".
From the English word canyon, ultimately from Greek kanna "small reed", after the plants that grow in the bottom of canyons.

Originally spelled "Cansaeda" The meaning of this name is unknown, though thought to mean "huntress." Originally a family name carried down through both Creek and Cherokee Indigiounous American lines throughout North Carolina and Tennessee.
From a non-Sino-Vietnamese reading of Chinese 暠 or 杲 (cảo) meaning "bright, brilliant, shining".
From Chinese 操 (cāo) meaning "to control, manage" or 草 (cǎo) meaning "grass, herbs", as well as other characters with a similar pronunciation.
Means "blind warrior", from caoch "blind, one-eyed" and láech "hero, warrior".
Irishized form of Caden in analogy to Aodhán and Aidan. This name is not traditionally used in Irish Gaelic nor would be pronounced like English Caden.
From the Chinese 草 (cǎo) meaning "grass" and 花 (huā) meaning "flower".
Derived from Gaelic caol meaning "slender, comely".

column3: 草莓, 草梅, 草妹, etc.(Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 草莓 (cǎoméi) meaning "strawberry" or from 草 (cǎo) meaning "grass, straw" combined with 梅 (méi) meaning "plum, apricot" or 妹 (mèi) meaning "younger sister". Other character combinations can form this name as well.
From the Chinese 草 (cǎo) meaning "grass, herbs" and 朦 (méng) meaning "condition or appearance of the moon".
Scottish Gaelic form of Kevin. The name coincides with the Scottish Gaelic verb caomhainn "to reserve; to husband".
From the Chinese 草 (cǎo) meaning "grass" and 暮 (mù) meaning "evening, dusk, sunset".
Name of the king, cacique of Maguana a kingdom on the island of Hispaniola. He was married to Anacaona and was resisted Spanish rule.
From Sino-Vietnamese 高貴 (cao quý) meaning "noble, virtuous, precious", composed of 高 (cao) meaning "high" and 貴 (quý) meaning "precious, valuable".
Possibly means "he just left" in Nahuatl.
From Sino-Vietnamese 恰 (cáp) meaning "appropriate, suitable" or 祫 (cáp) meaning "triennial sacrifice to ancestors".
From Sino-Vietnamese 級 (cấp) meaning "rank, level, class".
Short form of names like Christoper, Caspian, or Casper.
From the English word, ultimately from Latin capabilis "able to take, able to understand".
Italian and Spanish form of Capaneus.
Catalan and Portuguese form of Capaneus.

Latinized form of Greek Καπανεύς (Kapaneus), which is possibly derived from Ancient Greek καπάνη (kapane) meaning "chariot". Alternatively, it could derived from σκαπάνη (skapane) meaning "digging, spadework" or "spade, mattock, digging tool", or perhaps from καπνός (kapnos) meaning "smoke". In Greek mythology, Capaneus was one of the Seven against Thebes, renowned for his great size, strength and arrogance. He was killed by a thunderbolt while attempting to scale the walls of Thebes, after shouting that not even Zeus could stop him from invading.
Means "one who makes noise", from Nahuatl capani "to make a cracking or slapping noise". This was an epithet of Xolotl, possibly associated with sleep or dreams.
Caparronia was one of the Vestal Virgins.

This is the brightest star in the constellation Auriga. Its name means "little she-goat" from Latin capra "she-goat" with a diminutive suffix. In Roman mythology the star represented the goat Amalthea.

Partial latinization of Kapheira (as its proper latinized form is Caphira). In Greek mythology, Capheira was an Oceanid as a daughter of the Titan Oceanus, possibly by his sister-wife Tethys. Along with the Telchines, Capheira was tasked by Rhea to nurse the infant Poseidon.
