Variant of Cepheus.Capheus 'Van Damme' Onyango is one of the eight sensate main characters of 2015 sisters Wachowski's science-fiction TV series 'Sense8'. He lives in Nairobi, Kenya.

Means "chapel" in Spanish, taken from the Spanish titles of the Virgin Mary La Santísima Virgen de la Capilla and Nuestra Señora de la Capilla (meaning "The Most Holy Virgin of the Chapel" and "Our Lady of the Chapel" respectively). It is venerated in the city of Jaén, hence the heavy concentration of this name in that city and province of Andalucia.
Derived from the place Capestrano in Italy used in honor of Saint John of Capistrano.

Roman cognomen which was derived from Latin capito meaning "big-headed", which itself is ultimately derived from Latin capitis, the genitive of Latin caput meaning "head".A known bearer of this name was the Roman tribune Gaius Ateius Capito (1st century BC).
A character from E.D.E.N. Southworth‘s 'The Hidden Hand' (published 1859). The name alludes to the words capital and capitalism as well as capitol.

Derived from Latin capitolium (related to Late Latin capitellum "small head, top of column", from which we derived our current word 'capital'), which is ultimately derived from Latin caput "head". It refers to Capitoline Hill, one of the seven hills of Rome, which haused a temple dedicated to the triple-deity named the Capitoline Triad. The name Capitolinus was a cognomen for at least two Romans from the 4th century BC, namely Marcus Manlius Capitolinus and his brother Aulus Manlius Capitolinus.

Anglicized form of Kapiton. Even though it is related, this name is not to be confused with Latin capitonis, which is the genitive of Latin capito meaning "big-headed" (see Capito).The best known bearer of this name is the 4th-century saint (and hieromartyr) Capiton of Chersonesus (a.k.a. Cherson) in Crimea.
Meaning uncertain, possibly derived from Nahuatl capolin "cherry-like tree" and ihuitztli "thorn, spine".
Transferred use of the surname Capone.
Diminutive of Caprice, Capitola, and other names beginning in Cap-.
Gascon and Languedocian form of Caprais.
Italian and Spanish form of Caprasius.
Possibly derived from Latin capra meaning "(she-)goat". A bearer of this name was Caprasius of Agen, a French saint from the early 4th century AD.
This name may be derived from Capricornus (see Capricorn). This is the name of a planet from the Battlestar Galactica franchise.

From Latin Capricornus meaning "horned like a goat" (from caper, genitive capri "goat" and cornu "horn"), a loan-translation of Greek Aigokheros, the name of the constellation. This is also the name of the tenth sign of the zodiac.
Means "goat" in Latin. The name of one of the constellations of the zodiac.
Possibly a blend of Capri (from Capri, Caprina or Caprice) and Gabriella.
From Latin caprotinus "of goats". An epithet of Juno.
Military and naval rank from the Latin word capit meaning "head" and conveying a sense of "leader" in modern use.
Combination of Carrie and the name suffix bel (inspired by Latin bella "beautiful").
From Latin cara meaning "dear, beloved" and bella meaning "beautiful".
Carabí was a tribe leader from Argentina whom put up resistance against the Spaniards for 15 years both in Santa Fé and Buenos Aires. He was the most respected tribe leader of his time.

Derived from Latin cara, meaning "face", and Old French bosse meaning "inflammation". This describes a bubo gotten through pox. This name was first used on the wicked fairy godmother in Madame d'Aulnoy's fairy tale The Princess Mayblossom (1697), though nowadays it is more famous as the name given to the wicked fairy godmother in Tchaikovsky's ballet The Sleeping Beauty (1890).
Derived from Italian cara, the feminine form of the adjective caro, "beloved, dear; precious" and cosa "thing".
A Breton variant of Caradog from the Brythonic Caratācos meaning "beloved".
Derived from Italian cara, the feminine form of the adjective caro, "beloved, dear; precious" and donna "woman; lady".
Caradoc is the father of King Angusel of Scotland by the fourth daughter of Ygerne, as related by Merlin to King Arthur in the Vulgate Merlin.

Possibly derived from surname Carafa (Caraffa), which belonged to the House of Carafa (Caraffa), a noble Neapolitan family known from XII century. Also it could be a contraction of names Cara and Fina. Carafina Gambarelli (mentioned in 1236) was married to Balduino della Scala (circa 1113 - circa 1166).
Galician form of Charalampos via Charalampus and Spanish variant of Caralampo.
Italian form of Charalampos via Charalampus and Spanish variant of Caralampio.
Variant of Carolee.A known bearer is American musician Caralee McElroy (1983-).
Combination of Cara and Leigh or a variant of Caralee.
Variant of Carolee, or else a blend of Cara and Coralie (or Aurélie).
Rare variant of Caroline, influenced by Cara
Combination of Cara and Lynn or a variant of Carolyn.
Feminine name derived from the word "caramel". Possibly also from the Italian surname Caramella.
Perhaps a variant of Caramia in the stlye of Rosalie and Valerie.
Anglicized form of Carannog. Saint Carantok was a 6th-century abbot, confessor, and saint in Wales and the West Country.
Derived from Gaulish carantos "loving", the word itself being the present participle of *car- "to love".
Carasynthia "Cara" Dune is a Human female Alderaanian who served in the Rebel Alliance as a shock trooper, and who later became a mercenary in the Star Wars Disney+ series The Mandalorian.
Derived from Gaulish carata "beloved", the word itself being the past participle of cara- "to love".
From the element "carbon" likely inspired by the name Corbin.
Transferred use of the surname Carbonel. This name was used in Barbara Sleigh's Carbonel series where Carbonel is a black cat who was owned by a witch.
Transferred use of the surname Carbonero.This name is given in honour of Colombian footballer Carlos Carbonero.

A fictional character created by J.R.R. Tolkien, Carcharoth, also known as the Red Maw, lived in the First Age of the Sun, and was the greatest werewolf that ever lived. He was of the line of Draugluin.
Latinized form of Karkinos. This was the name of a Greek playwright from the 4th century BC.
Probably a diminutive of names ending in -kard like Burkhard.
Transferred use of the surname Cardell.
Transferred use of the surname Carden.

A famous bearer is pop artist Cardi B (born in 1992 as Belcalis Marlenis Almánzar) who got her stage name from Bacardi, a white rum. The nickname was given to her because her sister's name is Hennessy which is a brand of cognac.
From the city of Cardiff in Wales. The name was given to a Samoan baby boy on the occasion of a rugby game Wales–Samoa in 2012 which was won by Samoa.
From the name of the (sometimes) bright red bird.-------------------------------------Possibly after the bird itself

A place name from the outskirts of Melbourne, Victoria. Corruption of the Bunurong or Wadawurrung word Kar-din-yarr, meaning "look to the sunrise", because it was to the east of the Wadawurrung peoples' land.
Means "remedy, solution to problem" in Turkish.
Derived from Old Occitan cara (a variant of chera) "dear; expensive" and causa "thing" with the intended meaning of "beloved person".
Variant of Carina 1 or an elaboration of Carreen (See also Carine and Kareen).
Variant of Carol 1. 11 girls in the USA were named CAREL in 1949.
Afrikaans feminine form of Carel and Spanish and Danish variant of Karelia.
Cognate of Carelia. The name coincides with the place name Carélie.
Variant of Carina 1, influenced by Karen 1. As a German name, it is also a variant of Karena.

Variant of Kerensa, which has been 'used since the early 1970s, but more often in its variant form Karenza' (Dunkling, 1983). However, the name also occurs in medieval France; it belonged to a woman who composed the last two stanzas of an Occitan poem that begins Na Carenza al bel cors avinen, meaning "Lady Carenza of the lovely, gracious body".

Meaning unknown, possibly a combination of the phonetic elements ka, ree and sha or an elaborated form of Cara. A notable bearer is the American rapper Caresha Brownlee (1994-) from the rap duo City Girls, who goes by the stage name 'Yung Miami'.

Directly from the English word caress meaning "an act or expression of kindness or affection", ultimately from Latin carus "beloved". A fictional bearer was Cassandra 'Caress' Morell, a prominent character on the American soap opera Dynasty, who appeared on the show in 1986. That year 69 girls born in the United States were named Caress.
Variant of Carissa influenced by the English word caress.

From the French word caresse meaning "caress", ultimately from Latin carus "dear, beloved". This name was borne by Caresse Crosby (1892-1970), original name Mary 'Polly' Phelps Jacob, an American socialite and the inventor of the modern bra. It was used by American author Frances Parkinson Keyes for a character in her novel Dinner at Antoine's (1948), a murder mystery set in New Orleans, Louisiana.
Transferred use of the surname Carew.
From the surname Cargill. A notable bearer was Scottish physicist and mathematician Cargill Gilston Knott (1856-1922).
Possibly a variant of Carrie or Cara, or from the ancient place name Caria. This is also an Italian surname, as well as the name of a place in Calabria, Italy.
Directly taken from Welsh cariad "love, affection; darling, sweetheart". This name is borne by British comedian Cariad Lloyd.
Meaning unknown, possibly an invented name derived from the word Caribbean.
Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Charibert.

Combination of Caroline and Alice. This is at least the case for Carice Irene Elgar (1890-1970), the only child of the renowned English composer Edward Elgar (1857-1934). She was named after her mother, Caroline Alice Roberts (1848-1920).In turn, the Dutch actress Carice van Houten (b. 1976) was named after Elgar's daughter. Her father Theodore van Houten (1952-2016) was a Dutch-British musicologist who had studied Elgar's work and published a famous article about it in 1976, i.e. the same year Carice was born.Last but not least, the recent rise in popularity of the name Carice in the Netherlands can be entirely attributed to Carice van Houten. Her career really began to kick off with the Dutch film Minoes (2001), in which she played the titular character. But the definite breakthrough came with the film Zwartboek (2006), which was a huge success and later voted as the best Dutch film of all time. It is therefore no coincidence that the name Carice sharply rose in popularity after 2006, ultimately reaching its peak in 2009.
Italian and Spanish form of Charidemus.
Possibly a combination of Carrie and the popular name suffix ella.
Elaborated form of Carrie. This is the full name of the title character of Stephen King's horror novel 'Carrie' (1974).
Catalan and Portuguese form of Charilaos via Charilaus.
Diminutive of Caridad, Carolina, Macaria, and other names containing car.
Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Carinus.
Extended form of Carus. This name was borne by a Roman emperor from the 3rd century AD.
Rhyming variant of Mario/Dario influenced by Cairo and the English word car.
Either a variant of Carisa or of Carice.

Means "dearest, most beloved" in Latin, the superlative form of the adjective cara/carus meaning "dear, beloved, loved". This was borne by a medieval French saint, Carissima of Albi, known as Carême or Chrême in French. As a modern name it may be inspired by the Italian vocabulary word meaning "dearest, fondest".
Variant of Cairistìona. Caristiona. Hebridean Sea Poem No. 1 is a 1920 composition by Granville Bantock.
Italian and Spanish form of Carystus.
Invented by the Danish author Carl Brosbøll (1816-1900) for use as a pen name; his pseudonym, Carit Etlar, was an anagram of Carl and Tertia (his given name and that of his muse, Tertia Fabricius).
Variant of Carita, a direct transcription from the Latin.
Catalan cognate of Caridad, this name is directly taken from Catalan caritat "charity".
Spanish and Italian form of Charitina. This name is mostly used in Mexico.
Spanish diminutive of Carolina, via its short form Caro 2.
Galician and Spanish form of Chariton.

French form of Cariulphus, which is the latinized form of both Chariulf and its variant form Cariulf.This is one of the names by which the obscure 6th-century Frankish saint Chariulf (often found written as Cariulf) is known in France. He was a disciple of the Frankish missionary and saint Marculf (better known under the French names Marcou, Marcouf and Marcoul), who died either on the same day as he did, or several days afterwards. As a result, they were buried together (along with an other disciple of Marculf's) in the same tomb in the abbey of Nanteuil, which was located in the diocese of Coutances in the Cotentin Peninsula of Normandy.
Old English form of Charles, cognate to Germanic "Carl".
In Brazil, this name could possibly be an elaboration of Carl.In the United States (and possibly Rare English), this name can be used as a variant of Carlene and Carline.
Variant of Carlyn/Carline or an elaboration of Carl.
A known bearer of this name is Carlens Arcus (1996-), a Haitian soccer player.
Transferred use of the surname Carless.
Likely a combination of Carly with a name that ends in -ethia, such as Alethia.
Elaborated form of Carla, apparently in imitation of Italian Carlotta and perhaps influenced by Scarlett. 'Form of Caroletta in modern American usage, especially among black American families.'
Derived from Old High German karl "man" and fridu "peace".
Very rare combination of Carl and Gustav. More commonly spelled with a hyphen, Carl-Gustav, or with a space between the names, Carl Gustav.
Friulian and Romansh form of Charles.
Either an elaborated form of Carlia (a double elaboration of Carly) or a combination of Carly/Carla and Liana.

Transferred use of the surname Carlin or a variant of Carline. A notable masculine bearer was an American rugby union and rugby sevens player: Carliln Isles. A feminine name bearer was an actress and singer: Carlin Glynn.
German and Dutch variant of Karlina and Sicilian, Romansh and English feminine diminutive of Carl.
Meaning uncertain, possibly a contraction of Carla and Linda.
French form of Carlina.In the English-speaking world, it has been used since at least the 19th century. It also coincides with a Lowland Scots word meaning "old woman, witch".
Transferred use of the surname Carling.
Variant of Carlinhos or an elaboration of Carlo/Carlos.
Meaning unknown. Most likely an elaboration of Carl or a variant of Carlisle, Carlise or Carlisa.
Variant of Carlisa in the style of Annelise and Elise (See also Charlize).
Feminine form of Carlos using the popular Puerto Rican name suffix liz (which is derived from Lizbeth or a related name).
Rare combination of the names Carl and Johan. More commonly spelled with a hyphen, Carl-Johan, or with a space between the names, Carl Johan.
Spanish form of Charlemagne. This is borne by Carlomagno Pedro Martínez (1965-), a Mexican ceramic artist and artisan, and Carlomagno Chacón Gómez (1985-), a Peruvian lawyer and politician.
A character in the 1987 science fiction novel 'The Smoke Ring' by Larry Niven.
Occitan and Piedmontese form of Charlotte.
Diminutive of Carlo, as -otto is an Italian masculine diminutive suffix.
Transferred use of the surname Carlson.
Transferred use of the surname Carlston.
Combination of Carl and the ending -tavious.
Medieval Italian diminutive of Carlo, as -uccio is an Italian masculine diminutive suffix.
Combination of the names Carly and Beth.
Short form of names that begin with the element Carm-, such as Carmen and Carmella.
Variant of Carmen and rarely used as masculine form of it.

Uncertain etymology, possibly of pre-Greek origin; however, some theories draw a relation to the Ancient Greek word κάρμα (karma) meaning "shorn, skimmed, cropped" (from κείρω (keiro) "to shear"). Another connects it to West Semitic krm meaning "vineyard". In Greek mythology, this was the name of a Cretan priest said to have purified the god Apollo after he killed Python. By some accounts he was the grandfather of the Cretan harvest goddess Carme, and may have been a demi-god of the harvest himself. This was also the name of a son of Dionysos.
Diminutive of Carmelita, Carmela, Carmen, and other related names.
Most likely a diminutive of Carmel, possibly influenced by Spanish Carmelita.
Variant of Carmelo. This is also a surname (see Carmello).
Diminutive of Carmelo, as -uccio is an Italian masculine diminutive suffix.
Sicilian form of Carmina or an elaboration of Carmen.
A diminutive of Carmen using the originally Italian diminutive ending -ella.

Possibly an elaborated form of Carmen using the popular phonetic suffix on. It is also an anagram of the name Cameron. A known bearer is Carmeon Hamilton, an American interior designer and television personality.
Means "garden" or "orchard" in HebrewA known bearer of this name is Carmia Marshall.
Form of Charmian used in Italian-language translations of Shakespeare's play 'Antony and Cleopatra' (1606).
Transferred use of the surname Carmicheal. It is also used as an anglicization of MacGillemicheil.

An enchantress of Saxon descent, she held the castle of La Roche and helped her people against King Arthur. At the same time she loved Arthur – which did not prevent her having a lover, Gadrasolain, in the castle, and threw his lady into her prison.
Perhaps a contraction of Carmen and Mindy. American makeup artist Carmindy Bowyer (1971-) appears on the reality television show 'What Not to Wear'.
Italian and Spanish form of Carminius.

Roman nomen gentile which was probably derived from Latin carminum "song, poem", which is a Late Latin form of carmen "song, poem" (see also Carmen). Improbable is a derivation from Latin carminus, which is the shortened form of carmesinus (a corruption of cremesinus, the latinized form of Arabic qermez "red"). That is because that particular word stems from medieval Latin, while many bearers predate medieval Latin times. Finally, the name Carminius was borne by several Roman consuls.

Diminutive of Carmine, as -uccio is an Italian masculine diminutive suffix.

Possibly means "vineyard of God" (or "God is my vineyard") from Hebrew כֶּרֶם (kérem) "vineyard of" and יָהּ (yah) "Yahweh". Alternatively it may be from the surname of Adolphe Crémieux (1796-1880), a French-Jewish statesman, or from the name of Crémieu, an historic Jewish community in France.
Variant and masculine form of Carmen.
Possibly derived from Carmo or Carmem.
Diminutive of Carmosa. This is the name of a comedy play written by Alfred de Musset and premiered in 1865 in Paris.
Campidanese masculine form of Carmel, borrowed from archaic Italian Carmo.
The goddess who makes strong muscles, and defends the internal organs from witches or strigae.

Derived from the flower of the same name; its etymology is uncertain. It has been suggested that it may ultimately come from English coronation (which in turn ultimately comes from Anglo-French coroner "to crown"). An other suggested possibility is Latin carn(e) or caro "flesh", because the original colour of the flower was said to be as red as flesh. Alternatively, it may be derived from Middle French carnation "person's color or complexion".
French and Gallo form of Carneus.
Transferred use of the surname Carnegie, given in honor of Scottish-American industrialist Andrew Carnegie (1835-1919).

Probably derived from Καρνεῖος (Karneios), an epithet of Apollo referring to the Κάρνεια (Karneia) festival and month, ultimately derived from κάρνος (karnos) meaning "ram (animal)". This was the name of an Ancient Greek philosopher of the Epicurean school. His only surviving writing is on the subject of the death of a friend.
After the brownish red mineral of the same name, of which the name is a corruption of cornelian, which in turn is derived from Latin cornelianus (see Cornelianus).
Transferred use of the surname Carnell. May also be used as a variant of Cornell.
Transferred use of the surname Carner.
Diminutive of "Carnegie" or "Carnation." Please note female American singer and television host Carnie Wilson.
Means "red-faced" in Quenya. In Tolkien's 'Legendarium' this is the mother-name of Caranthir, the fourth son of Fëanor and Nerdanel.

Means "ram (animal)" in Ancient Greek. This was the name of a seer from Acarnania in Greek mythology, in some accounts a son of Zeus and Europa. He was taught divination by the god Apollo, who took the epithet Carneus and established the Carneia festival after Carnus was killed. Carnus may have originally been an old Peloponnesian agricultural deity later identified with Apollo.
Galician, Italian, Spanish and Venetian form of Carus.
Combination of Carole and Carol 1 respectively and Anne 1.
Combination of Carol 1 and the popular phonetic suffix lee. A known bearer was the American performance artist Carolee Schneemann (1939-2019).
Variant of Caroline reflecting the French pronunciation.
Feiminization of Carolus. The USA Social Security Administration has registered 7 baby girls born with this name in 1969.
Combination of Carol 1 and popular suffix lie.
A combination of Carol 1 and Linda.
Variant of Caroline, reflecting the Brazilian Portuguese pronunciation of the French form of Carolina.
Jèrriais form and Brazilian Portuguese variant of Caroline.
Form of Caroline, refletcting their pronunciation.
A contraction of Carol 1 and Olivia.Carolivia Herron, born Carol Olivia Herron, is a children's book author.
Variant of Carroll or Carol 1A famous bearer of this name is Caroll Spinney (1933-2019), who portrayed Big Bird on the show "Sesame Street".
Variant of Carol 2 and Lotta recorded in the 18th century in East Frisia.
Likely a combination of Carolyn and Lynda.
Short form of Carola and Carolus.
Combination of Caro (derived from Latin carus "dear, beloved") and Sander.

In reference to the mountain range of Eastern Europe, from Thracian Greek Karpates oros, probably literally literally "Rocky Mountain"; related to Albanian karpe "rock." From 1630s in reference to the island of Carpathos in the Aegean. Also the name of a ship, the RMS Carpathia which saved survivors from the Titanic.

Transferred use of the surname Carpenter or in reference to the word carpenter, from Middle English from Anglo-Norman French, from Old French carpentier, charpentier, from late Latin carpentarius (artifex) ‘carriage (maker)’, from carpentum ‘wagon’, of Gaulish origin.

Latinized form of Greek Καρπώ (Karpô), which is derived from Greek καρπόω (karpoô) "to bear fruit; to reap or enjoy fruit". In Greek mythology this was the name of one of the Horae or Seasons; Carpo was the goddess of autumn and of the harvest, that is, the fruits of summer. A moon of Jupiter also bears this name.
Latinized form of Karpokrates. A known bearer of this name was Carpocrates of Alexandria, the founder of an early Gnostic sect from the 2nd century AD.
Latinized form of Karpophoros. Saint Carpophorus was martyred in Capua (Italy) in the 3rd century AD.
Transferred use of the surname Carr.

Means "holm oak" in Spanish (species Quercus ilex). It is taken from the title of the Virgin Mary Nuestra Señora de la Carrasca meaning "Our Lady of the Holm Oak". She is the patron saint of the municipality of Villahermosa, in the province of Ciudad Real, Spain.According to folk legend, a shepherd from Villahermosa saw a carving of the Virgin and took it. He was accused of theft and received a prison sentence. The shepherd was later released and upon returning to his town, the Virgin appeared to him on top of a holm oak, while he was herding his sheep. After recognizing the miracle, the inhabitants of the municipality built a hermitage in her honor in 1494.
Transferred use of the surname Carrera.
Combination of Carrie and Anne 1 (see also Carrie-Anne), perhaps inspired by the similar name Marianne.

This name might be derived from Gothic kara "worry" combined with rîcja "powerful, strong, mighty." (The second element is also closely related to Celtic rîg or rix and Gothic reiks, which all mean "king, ruler.") But it is probably a form of either Hariric or Gararic. Carriaric was the name of a 6th-century king of Galicia.
Transferred use of the surname Carrick.
Combination of Carrie and the popular suffix -lynn.

Elaborated form or diminutive of Carrie. In many movie adaptations of Stephen King's horror novel Carrie (1974) this is the full name of the title character, Carrie White, though her full name is spelled Carietta in the original novel.
From an Irish surname which was a variant of the surname Corrigan.
Combination of Carrie and the popular name suffix inda (compare Clarinda).
Transferred use of the surname Carrington. This name is chiefly used in the United States as a unisex name and in Zimbabwe as a masculine name.
Transferred use of the surname Carrión.
Swedish diminutive of Caroline and Carolina.
Combination of Carrol and the popular suffix -lyn.
Transferred use of the surname Carron.

Transferred use of the surname Carruthers. A known bearer of the name was the Scottish Vice Chancellor of the University of Cape Town, Carruthers Beattie, whose full name is Sir John Carruthers Beattie (1866-1946).
From the spanish surname means 'farm'. This name is not used in Spain and Spanish era.
This name was borne by a daughter of Radu cel Mare.
Transferred use of the surname Carston.

The name Cartan may be linked to terms or concepts in Somali language that emphasize strength or steadfastness, though its exact root is difficult to pinpoint. Many Somali names are descriptive, referring to virtues or traits that parents hope their child will embody, such as courage or leadership.
From the English word "cartel"; in turn from Occitan cartel or Catalan cartell meaning "poster", or from Italian cartello, a diminutive of carta, meaning "card" or "page".
Derived from kart "cart, wagon" and mari "famous, excellent".The name is attested in medieval Suebic Kingdom of Galicia.
French form of Karterios via its latinized form Carterius.
Italian and Spanish form of Karterios via its latinized form Carterius.
Latinized form of Karterios. This name was borne by at least two saints, namely Carterius of Caesarea (4th century AD) and Carterius of Sebaste (4th century AD).

Derived from Ancient Greek καρτερός (karteros) meaning "strong, stout, mighty, steadfast, obstinate" or "violent" (see kratos). This was the name of one of the 50 sons of King Lycaon in Greek mythology.
Carthalo was an officer in Hannibal's army during the Second Punic War.
Transferred use of the surname Carthy.

Transferred use of the surname Cartier. Use of the name has probably been influenced by the jewelry house Cartier, which was founded by Louis-François Cartier in Paris in 1847. A known bearer is retired American basketball player Cartier Martin (1984-).
Meaning unknown, most likely of Etruscan origin.

Celtic name, in which the second element is mandu "pony, colt, filly". The first element is less certain, perhaps from karti "drive out", or it may mean "clean, sleek". This was the name of a 1st-century queen of the Brigantes.
Transferred use of the surname Cartman.
Transferred use of the surname Cartwright.
Asturian, Corsican and Sicilian form of Carolina.
Corsican and Sardinian form of Charles.
Derived from Latin carus "dear, beloved." This name was borne by a Roman Emperor from the 3rd century AD.
Transferred use of the surname Carvel. A notable bearer is professional baseball player Carvel William "Bama" Rowell (1916-1993).
Transferred use of the surname Carvell.
Ultimately from the village of Carveth in Cornwall, from Cornish Karvergh meaning ("fort of horses"). Likely from the surname Carveth.
Italian and Spanish form of Carvilius.

Roman nomen gentile of unknown meaning. This name was borne by several Romans from the 3rd century BC. Please note that this name most likely has a different etymology than the identical-looking name of the Celtic king of Kent (England) from the 1st century BC, whose name was latinized.
An epithet of the goddess Artemis, derived from the Ancient Greek town Karyai (Καρύαι) in Laconia, part of the Peloponnese region of Greece.
From the given name Çary and gylyç, meaning "sword".
From çary meaning "king, tsar" and the given name Myrat
Derived from the greek word καρυόφυλλον meaning "carnation".
Latinized form of Karystios. This was the name of an ancient Greek grammarian from the 2nd century BC.

Latinized form of Karystos. In Greek mythology, Carystus is the name of a rural demi-god that is native to the Greek island of Euboia. He also lent his name to the ancient Euboian city-state of Carystus.
From çary meaning "king, tsar" and Persian یار (yār) meaning "friend, companion".
Spanish and Galician form of Cassander.
Transferred use of the surname Casanova.
Means "courage" in Azerbaijani, ultimately from Arabic جسارة (jasāra).
Roman cognomen which was derived from Oscan casca meaning "old". This was borne by one of the assassins of Julius Caesar: Servilius Casca. He features in Shakespeare's play 'Julius Caesar' (1599).
Derived from the English word for a waterfall, ultimately from Latin cadere "to fall".
Variant of Cashton using the popular phonetic suffix den, found in such names as Hayden and Aidan.
Possibly derived from cashisa meaning "conceal, hide."
Elaboration of Cash using the popular name suffix lyn.
From the English word, a type of fabric, ultimately borrowed from the Hindi कश्मीर (kaśmīr) (See Kashmir).
A variant of Cassius, unless an elaboration of Cash.
Spanish, Galician and Romanian form of Cassiana.
Spanish and Galician form of Cassian.

Casiel may be a combination of two Hebrew words - Kahsah, meaning cover and El, meaning God, thus giving the meaning "my cover is God".Casiel is also the Latinised form of the Hebrew Kafziel, the angel of solitude and tears in post-Biblical Judeo-Christian mythology.
French and Italian form of Casilda.
Variant of Casilda. This is the name of a character in the novel 'Don Quixote', by Spanish writer Miguel de Cervantes.
Corsican and Sicilian form of Casimir.
Spanish and Galician form of Cassius.
Galician and Spanish form of Cassiodorus.
Galician and Spanish form of Cassiopeia.
Shortening of Casiphia, a biblical place name.
From a place name mentioned only by the Old Testament prophet Ezra, said to be a corruption of Caspian. Otherwise it may mean "place of the treasury" from Hebrew keceph "silver, money".
Transferred use of the surname Casley.
Variant of Casimir, possibly orthographically influenced by Cashmere.

In Roman mythology, Casmilla is the mother of the legendary Volscian warrior queen, Camilla. Featured in Virgil’s Aeneid, Casmilla is a minor but pivotal figure whose name serves as the namesake for her famous daughter, the swift-footed huntress and devotee of Diana.Casmilla was the queen of the Volscian city of Privernum and married to King Metabus. While her specific fate is largely unmentioned in the epic, she is assumed to have died during the political upheaval that resulted in her husband being exiled by his own citizens. Before fleeing the city with their infant daughter, King Metabus adapted his wife's name (Casmilla) to create the name Camilla.
Possibly a variant of Casimira or Kashmira.
Modern Dutch form of Caspaer, which is the medieval Dutch form of Caspar.
Medieval Dutch form of Caspar via its latinized form Casparus.Also compare Caspaar, which is technically the modern Dutch form of this name, but yet has also pretty much fallen out of use.
Feminine form of Caspar. Also compare Caspara.
Possibly a variant of Caspian or Casper.
Feminine form of Casper. Also compare Caspera and Jasperina.
From the name of the caspia plant and feminization of Caspian.
Variant of Cassidy. This name was brought to public attention in 2013 by American singer and The Voice winner Cassadee Pope.
From an Irish surname that was a variant of Cassidy.
Combination of Cassie and the popular name suffix lyn.
Latinized form of Κασσανδάνη (Kassandanē), the Hellenized form of an uncertain Old Persian name. Cassandane was an Achaemenian Persian noblewoman and the "dearly loved" wife of Cyrus the Great.
Italian and Portuguese form of Cassander.
Of uncertain origin and meaning. It might be a variant of Cassarah or a transferred use of the Sicilian surname Cassarà.
Taken from the word casuarina, the sheoak tree
Transferred use of the surname Cassatt.
Variant of Cassidy or a transferred use of the surname Cassedy.
From the surname Cassel. Cassel Sharpe is fictional character in Holly Black's novel White Cat.
Possibly a diminutive of Cass. It also coincides with the word cassette, which refers to a kind of tape formerly used to record audio.
Feminine form of CassiusA famous bearer of this name is Cassiane Santana Santos Macnhães Guimarães, a Brazilian gospel singer.
Elaborated form of Cassie using the Italian feminine diminutive suffix -etta. This was borne by American gospel singer Cassietta George (1929-1995).
Variant of Casilda. It appears in 'The King in Yellow' (1895), a book of short stories by American writer Robert W. Chambers.
Alternate transcription of Arabic قاسم (see Qasim). It appears in 'Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves', one of the tales of The 1001 Nights, where it belongs to the greedy brother of Ali Baba.

This name was created for a character in King's Quest, a computer-based adventure game series developed by Sierra Entertainment.Princess of the Land of the Green Isles and the protagonist's (your character's) love interest, she is one of the main co-characters in the sixth installment of this series, "Heir Today Gone Tomorrow."The name Cassima more than likely originates from the masculine Arabic name Qasim, as her homeland seems to share many similarities with Arabic culture, as seen in architecture and dress, and the meaning of the name Qasim fits a description of the characters personality and values very well.Other possible origins of this name include Cosima or an alteration of some Cass- name, such as Cassandra.
The name of a family of daisy flowers.
Catalan and German form of Cassiodorus.
Latinized form of Kassiodoros. A well-known bearer of this name was Cassiodorus, a Roman statesman and writer from the 6th century AD.

Means "fratricide, brother-killer", derived from Ancient Greek κάσις (kasis) meaning "sibling, brother, sister" and φόνος (phonos) meaning "murder, slaughter". This was the name of the daughter of Circe and Odysseus in a later account of Greek mythology, where she killed her half-brother Telegonus for murdering her own mother. She likely originally had a different name, with Cassiphone being a later descriptive nickname.
Combination of Cass and the popular name suffix lyn.

Uncertain etymology, possibly related to Ancient Greek κασσύω (kassyo) meaning "to stitch, sew together; to ensnare". This was the name of a naiad nymph of Parnassus, and the eponym of a spring at the seat of the Oracle at Delphi said to give priestesses the power of prophecy. She may have been the same individual as Castalia, the nymph of a connected spring.

Casta is an Iberian word (existing in Spanish, Portuguese and other Iberian languages since the Middle Ages), meaning 'lineage'. It is documented in Spanish since 1417 and is linked to the Proto-Indo-European ger. A notable bearer is Casta Fierce (daughter of Circe), a secondary character from the Monster High franchise.

Latinized form of the Greek Κασταλία (Kastalia), which is of uncertain origin, possibly related to Greek καθαρός (katharos) meaning "clean, spotless, pure" or κασσύω (kassuô) "to stitch". This was the name of a nymph of the prophetic springs of the Delphic oracle on Mount Parnassos. She may be the same as the nymph Κασσωτίς (Kassôtis) (see Cassotis).
Possibly means "jeweled helmet" in Quenya. In Tolkien's legendarium this is the name of the evil King of Gondor who usurps the throne form Eldacar, the rightful king.

Means "chestnut grove" in Spanish. It is taken from the title of the Virgin Mary Nuestra Señora del Castañar meaning "Our Lady of the Chestnut Grove". She is the patron saint of the town of Béjar, in the province of Salamanca, Spain.

From a volume of poems titled 'Castara' first published anonymously in 1634. Later editions reveal the author, William Habington, who has invented the name for his wife. Maybe it is based on Latin castus "pure, chaste".
The name of one of the main characters in the 1980s animated cartoon series, She-ra Princess of Power
Derived From the Italian word castello meaning "castle". It could also be a diminutive of Castellana.
Directly taken from Latin castellana "a (female) castellan; a damsel" as well as "of or pertaining to a castle".
Romansh form of Christina, traditionally found in central Grisons.

Possibly derived from Ancient Greek κέκασμαι (kekasmai) meaning "to excel, surpass; to shine" and ἀνήρ (aner) meaning "man", making this name a doublet of Cassandra. This was the name of a wife or concubine of King Priam in Greek mythology, the mother by him of Gorgythion.
Possibly from Castilla, a region in Spain.
Transferred use of the surname Castille.
Means "castle" in Spanish. It is taken from the title of the Virgin Mary Nuestra Señora del Castillo meaning "Our Lady of the Castle".
Derived from Croatian čast "honour" (which is ultimately derived from Proto-Slavic čьstь "honour") combined with mir "peace".
Roman cognomen that was a derivative of Castus.
Spanish and Galician form of Castus.
Irish form of Castor (the mythological person).

Italian and Spanish feminine form of Castor. Known bearers include the Blessed Castora Gabrielli (died 1391), an Italian widow and Franciscan tertiary (i.e. member of the Third Order of Saint Francis), and Castora ('Castorina') Fe Francisco de Diego (1928-2019), a Spanish sculptor.

Italian feminine form of Castorino, or else a direct feminine diminutive of either Castoro or Castore, formed with the feminine diminutive suffix -ina (itself ultimately from the Latin feminine adjective-forming suffix -īna "of or pertaining to").

Italian diminutive of Castoro or Castore (both Italian forms of Castor), formed with the masculine diminutive suffix -ino (itself ultimately from the Latin masculine adjective-forming suffix -īnus "of or pertaining to").Alongside the word nutria, this is also an ordinary vocabulary word for "nutria, coypu" - a large, crepuscular, semiaquatic rodent variously thought to resemble either a large rat or a small beaver. Native to South America, the nutria was introduced to Europe, Asia and North America due to the value of its fur in Eastern Europe and Central Asia. However, outside these areas, the animal is considered a pest or even an invasive species.
Italian and Sardinian form of Castor. In both languages, this is also the ordinary vocabulary word for "beaver" (in Sardinian, this usage is alongside the word castorru).
Sardinian variant of Castoro. This is also an ordinary vocabulary word for "beaver", used alongside castoro.
Italian form of Castrensis. A known bearer of this name is the Italian former soccer player Castrense Campanella (b. 1962).

Derived from the Latin adjective castrensis meaning "of the camp, in the camp", which is ultimately derived from the Latin noun castra meaning "(military) camp, encampment".This was the name of a 5th-century Catholic bishop and saint from North Africa, who was exiled to Campania in southern Italy by the Vandals.
From a Roman nomen gentile, which was probably ultimately derived from Latin castrum "fortress, camp, castle" (see also Castrinus).
Derived from Latin castrum "fortress, camp, castle".
English form of Castricianus. This was the name of a saint from the 3rd century AD.
Derived from medieval Italian castro meaning "castle" combined with the masculine diminutive suffix -uccio.
Derived from Latin castus "pure, chaste, virtuous". This was the name of a Roman saint from the 3rd century AD.
Derived from Latin castus "pure, chaste, virtuous".
Middle Welsh form of Cassivellaunus. He is one of the sons of Beli the Great in the Mabinogi, Brut y Brenhinedd and the Welsh Triads.
Welsh form of Cassivellaunus. According to Welsh myth, he was a son of Beli Mawr.
Transferred use of the surname Caswell.
Likely derived from Celtic cad "battle" and kawaro "hero."
From Sino-Vietnamese 吉 (cát) meaning "auspicious, lucky, good".

Of debated origin and meaning. Some scholars argue that Cataldo might be an Italian adoption and adaption of Irish Cathal and Cathlarm via a corruption into Cathald by way of association with the Germanic element -ald "old". Others theorize a derivation from the Germanic elements hadu/hatu "battle, combat" and wald "power", while a last group of academics assume a corruption of Gaidoaldo.
Spanish and Corsican form of Katherine.
Spelling variant of Cătălin used by Romanians abroad or in informal contexts (for example on the internet). Note that this is not the standard spelling of the name.
Variant of Catalijntje found among Dutch colonists in America in the 1600s and 1700s.
it is a mayan name short Yacatan which was the capitol of the mayan world. it was also used in a books called Sirens Call by C H B-eliott
Latinized form of Katana via its Greek form Katanes.
Derived from the Italian city of Catania and the Italian word katane meaning "grater". It is used for the character of Princess Catania in the movie Barbie: Mariposa and the Fairy Princess.
Cremish Lombard variant of Caterìna and Venetian variant of Catarina.
Friulian form of Katherine, Low German, Silesian German and Brazilian Portuguese variant of Catarina, Danish and Norwegian variant of Katarina and Dutch variant of Catharina.
Milanese and Cremish Lombard variant of Caterìna.
Latinisation and masculinization of the feminine name Catharina.
Medieval Polish variant of Katarzyna as well as an archaic form found in East Prussia up until the late 1800s.
Transferred use of the surname Catcher.
Venetian vernacular short form of Caterina and Walloon short form of Caterine.

From Latin cathedra meaning "chair", referring to the Cathedra Petri or Chair of Saint Peter, also known as the Throne of Saint Peter. Its feast day is February 22 (note, until 1962, the Feast of the Chair of Saint Peter was also celebrated on January 18).
Variant of Catharina recorded in the 16th and 18th centuries in East Frisia.
Medieval French form or diminutive of Catherine.
Derived from Italian catena "chain", this name was taken from the title of the Virgin Mary Maria Santissima della Catena. The name is mainly found in Sicily.
Variant of Caterina, Catherine, Catrene and Katerine.
An invented name derived from the Latin word terra (meaning "earth").

From an English surname what is derived from a geographical location; 'of Catesby' a parish in Northamptonshire. Most famous bearers are Robert Catesby, the leader of the Gunpowder Plot and William Catesby one of the councillors of Richard III of England on whom Shakespeare based his character in Richard III.

Nickname whose origin can be particular to the bearer. The name Catfish comes from a diverse group of mostly freshwater fish so-called because of barbels growing near their mouths that bear a resemblance to cat's whiskers. Notable namesakes include James Augustus "Catfish" Hunter (1946-1999), MLB pitcher and member of five World Series championship teams.
Derived from Cornish kas "battle" and gostel "hostage".

Scottish form of Cathán. The name coincides with Scottish Gaelic cathan "barnacle goose". Saint Cathan was a 6th-century Irish monk revered as a saint in parts of the Scottish Hebrides of whom very little is known. He appears in the Aberdeen Breviary, Walter Bower's Scotichronicon, and the Acta Sanctorum, and a number of placenames in western Scotland are associated with him.

Masculine form of Catharina. In 2010, there was a total of 2153 bearers of this name in all of The Netherlands. A known bearer of this name was Catharinus P. Buckingham (1808-1888), an American soldier, author and industrialist.

Derived from the Mongolian word khitan via its variant form cat(h)ai - the meaning is uncertain, but it refers to the Khitan people. Cathay is the anglicized form of cat(h)ai, and was the archaic name for China. There is also an other possible etymology for this name, which is completely different than the aforementioned and only applies to female bearers of this name living in an English-speaking country: in their case, Cathay may be a variant of Cathy.

Allegedly means "beautiful (big) daisy" in the Guanche language. Recorded as the name of a 7-year-old Guanche girl who was sold as a slave in Valencia in 1494. Cathaysa is also the title of a song recorded by singer Pedro Guerra in the 1980s.
Means "helmet", derived from cath "battle" and barr "top, head".
Spelling variant of Käthe.Cäthe is the stage name of a German singer-songwriter (née Catharina Sieland).
Short form of Catherine or Catheryn
From the English word cathedral meaning "a church that contains the cathedra".
French variant of Cateline and Dutch variant of Katerine.
Possibly a blend of Catherine and names that end in -eryl, for example Cheryl and Beryl.
English variant of Kathleen and French contracted form of Catheline.
Gaelic name literally meaning "battle chief" from the elements cath "battle" and maol "chief".

A character in "Les Précieuses Ridicules"(The Absurd Précieuses or The Affected Ladies), a one-act satire by Molière in prose. The play takes aim at the précieuses, the ultra-witty ladies who indulged in lively conversations, word games and, in a word, préciosité (preciousness)
Scandinavian variant of Katrina, German contraction of Catharina and Romansh variant of Catrina.
Jèrriais form of English and French Catherine.
Masculine form of Catharina (Dutch) and Cathrine (Norwegian).
The name of Gaulish war goddess meaning "battle crow".
Variant of Katiana and elaboration of Catia.
Variant of Katie more often used as a diminutive of names beginning with C, such as Catherine or Caitlin.

Meaning "battle-prince", stemming from a Common Brittonic form reconstructed as *katu-tigernos, formed with the root *katu- ("combat"; cf. Gaul. catu- "combat, battle", Old Irish. cath "battle, troop") attached to tigernos ("lord, master"; c. Gaul. tigerno-, Old Irish. tigern, Old Welsh. tegyrned, Old Breton. Tigern).The name Catiherno, borne by a Breton priest c. 509—521, may also be related.Catigern (Welsh: Cadeyrn Fendigaid) is a figure of Welsh tradition, said to be a son of Vortigern, the tyrannical King of the Britons, and the brother of Vortimer.He appears briefly in Geoffrey of Monmouth's pseudohistorical chronicle Historia Regum Britanniae, in a section adapted from the Historia Brittonum account. His battle with Horsa is the subject of John Lesslie Hall's poem "The Death of Horsa", and he appears as a minor character in William Henry Ireland's play "Vortigern and Rowena", which was initially touted as a lost work by William Shakespeare.
A diminutive of Cátia, Catherine, Caterina or any name starting with Cat-.

Originally a (now archaic) French diminutive of Catherine. While in Louisiana French catin also means "doll; mannequin, dummy", in European French catin means "harlot, slattern" (which is no doubt the reason this form of the name fell out of usage in France).
Means "blonde" in the Cumanagota dialect, a Carib language most common to the native peoples of Venezuela. It is now a name and slang for a blonde-haired person in Venezuela.
Variant of Katisha, a blend of the prefix ka with the name Latisha.
God invoked for sharpening the minds of children as they develop intellectually
From Cattleya, a genus of orchids native to Central and South America named after the British horticulturist William Cattley. Another variant from the same origin is Cataleya.
Guernésiais form of Cateline and French variant of Cathline.
Jèrriais form of the old French name Cateline.
Transferred use of the surname Caton.

Diminutive of Cato 2, as it contains the Dutch diminutive suffix -tje. This name is not to be confused with the Dutch noun kadootje meaning "little present".In Dutch literature and popular culture, Catootje is the name of the youngest daughter and middle child of the Tromp family from the popular long-running cartoon Jan, Jans en de kinderen (which is known in English as Jack, Jacky and the Juniors). The cartoon was started in 1970 by the Dutch cartoonist Jan Kruis (1933-2017) and is continued to this day by his successors.

Possibly an invented name, a combination of Catherine and Victoria. Also compare Latori and Natori.Note, many baby name sites and books list this name as meaning 'spirit' in Hopi, but this is incorrect. There is no word for 'spirit' in any Native American language that corresponds to Catori. (Similarly, Kotori is commonly listed as meaning 'screech owl spirit' in Hopi, according to Native Languages of the Americas; they comment: 'Clearly some baby book author made a typo at some point and no one bothered to check it before repeating it, because the Hopi word for screech owl is tokori, not kotori.')
Variant of Catrina, traditionally found in central Grisons.

Possibly derived from Ancient Greek κατρεύς (katreus) referring to a kind of bird from India, probably the Himalayan monal pheasant. Alternatively, it could be of pre-Greek origin, perhaps related to κατά (kata) "downwards, against". In Greek mythology, this was a king of Crete who was prophesied to be killed by one of his own children, which came to pass when his son mistook him for an attacking pirate from a distance and speared him.
Very rare spelling variant of either Katriana or Catriona.
Contracted form of Ecaterina and Caterina.
Guernésiais and Walloon form of Catherine.
Elaboration of Catherine, possibly influenced by Catrina. It may also be a Gallicized form of Catrinel.
Variant of Catarina notably borne by Maria Cattarina Calegari, a 17th-century Italian composer.

Catti-brie (spelled Cattie-brie in later publications) is the name of a character in the 'Forgotten Realms', a series of fantasy novels by American author R. A. Salvatore which serves as a setting for the role-playing game 'Dungeons & Dragons'. Salvatore based it on the initial syllables of Caitlin and Brielle, the first and middle names of his daughter.
From the name of a tropical American orchid (genus Cattleya) with purple, pink or white flowers, which was named after William Cattley (1788-1835).
Surname, derives from a settlement named Catteral, located in England. May also derived from the pet form of Caterin.
From Sino-Vietnamese 吉祥 (cát tường) meaning "lucky".
Variant of Cattie. This is the name of a character in the 'Daughters of the Moon' book series by Lynne Ewing.

Catualda (flourished in the 1st century AD) was a Marcomannic exile who deposed the Marcomannic king Maroboduus in 18 AD. Catualda is mentioned in The Annals of the Roman historian Tacitus. Following the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest, while Germanicus was avenging Rome beyond the Rhine, Drusus attempted to divide and conquer the tribes within the vast realm of the Marcomannic ruler Maroboduus. Drusus established relations with Catualda, a young Marcomannic noble living in exile among the Gutones. After the weakening of Maroboduus following the previous invasion of Bohemia by Arminius, Catualda returned with a "strong force" in 18 AD, and having "corruptly won over the nobles", entered the palace and deposed Maroboduus. In an adjacent fortress, Catualda "found the long-accumulated plunder of the Suevi and camp followers and traders from our provinces who had been attracted to an enemy's land, each from their various homes, first by the freedom of commerce, next by the desire of amassing wealth, finally by forgetfulness of their fatherland."Catualda was however soon defeated by the "overwhelming strength" of Vibilius of the Hermunduri and was like Maroboduus forced to seek refuge in the Roman Empire. He was thus settled in Forum Julii (Fréjus) in Gallia Narbonensis. The Marcomanni were subsequently ruled by the Quadian client king Vannius, who was himself also deposed by Vibilius in coordination with his own nephews.
French form of Catullus. Catulle Mendès (1841-1909) was a French writer.

Derived from the Ancient Roman cognomen Catullus with uncertain meaning. Possibly it comes from the Gaulish catu meaning "battle" with the diminutive suffix -ullus. In alternative it comes from Latin catulus meaning "cub, whelp".
Means "four" in Indonesian, ultimately from Sanskrit चतुर् (catur).

Derived from Gaulish catu meaning "battle" combined with Gaulish rix meaning "king".This was the name of the war god of the Helvetii, a Gaulish tribe. He was also important for the Gaulish tribe of the Caturiges, since they named themselves after him. The god eventually became known as Mars Caturix in Gallo-Roman religion through identification with the Roman god Mars.
"The One Who mnos Leads welnā in Battle katu".

The first element of this name is derived from Celtic catu "battle." The second element is probably derived from Proto-Celtic volkio "to wash, to bathe." It might also refer to the Volcae, a continental Celtic tribe.
Latinized form of Catuvolcos. A bearer of this name was Catuvolcus, one of the two kings of a Gaulish tribe called the Eburones. In 54 BC, he committed suicide by poisoning himself.
Possibly the Breton form of Cadwallon. Catwallon was the abbot of Redon Abbey and the son of the Duke of Brittany Conan I of Rennes.
Variation of Catty or Catie and diminutive of Catalina.
From Sino-Vietnamese 求 (cầu) meaning "to ask for, to demand" or 球 (cầu) meaning "fine jade" or "ball, sphere".
A name found in Mayan mythology and representing the South.
Directly taken from Latin caudex meaning "tree trunk".
Latinized form of Kaunos. In Greek mythology, Caunus was the son of Miletus, grandson of Apollo and brother and lover of Byblis.
Pictish form of Constantinus (see Constantine 1).This name was borne by two medieval Pictish kings, namely Causantín mac Fergusa (born before 775–820) and Causantín mac Cináeda (c. 836-877).

Derived from the Italian noun cavalcante meaning "postilion", which in turn is derived from the Italian verb cavalcare meaning "to ride a horse".A notable bearer of this name was the Italian Epicurean philosopher Cavalcante de' Cavalcanti (c. 1220-c. 1280). He also appears as a character in the poem Divine Comedy written by the Italian poet Dante Alighieri (c. 1265-1321).
Transferred use of the surname Cavanagh
Transferred use of the surname Cavanaugh.
Transferred use of the surname Cave.
Transferred use of the surname Cavendish.

An enchantress of Saxon descent, she held the castle of La Roche and helped her people against King Arthur. At the same time she loved Arthur – which did not prevent her having a lover, Gadrasolain, in the castle, and threw his lady into her prison.
Italian patriotic name, after Camillo Cavour, leading figure in the movement toward Italian unification.
A name that means "replacement." A family may give the name to a male whose father or older brother has died.
A name that comes from the Somali word cawo which means "luck." Outside of Somalia, Somalis may spell it as Awo.
Possibly a variant of acaxochitl, "reed flower", an aquatic plant with red or white flowers. Alternately, it may mean "he/she is a flower", deriving from Nahuatl ca "is, to be" and xochitl "flower".
Derived from Tatar чаян (çayan) meaning "scorpion". This is also the name of a Tatar satirical magazine, which has been in circulation since 1923.
Variant of Kayce (in itself which is a variant of either Casey or Case).
Diminutive of Caydence, influenced by both Caydee and the name suffix -ie
Derived from the Somali words cay, meaning "insult," and diid, meaning "to reject," interpreted as "rejects insults".
Variant of Caden, the spelling is influenced by Haydn.
Spanish form of Cayenne. Besides the pepper, Cayena is also the Spanish name for the Chinese hibiscus (species Hibiscus × rosa-sinensis).
From Old Tupi quiínia meaning "hot pepper," referring to any of several very hot chilli peppers or a powder condiment or spice formed from these varieties.
A character in L. Frank Baum's book 'The Lost Princess of Oz' (1917). Her name is a misspelling of the English word "cake".
Variant of Caelan, Kaylyn or Caoilfhionn.
From the word for crocodile (caiman) in the language of the Arawak-Taíno people.
Transfered use of the surname Cayne.
Spanish and Aragonese form of Caius.
Nickname for names that begin with the letter C, like Carol 1, Caroline, Chris, etc.
Romanian form and Walloon variant of Casimir.
Possible African American variant of Kazmir.
Directly taken from Irish céadaoin meaning "wednesday", ultimately from old Irish céad meaning "first" and aoine meaning "fast".
Derived from Brythonic cat "battle" combined with Old English beald "brave, bold".
Céala is the Irishized form of Kayla. Derived from Old Irish céle meaning "companion", or from Old Irish cáel meaning "slender".
Diminutive of Ceallach; variant of Cellachán.
Derived from Gaelic ceall meaning "church", or a variant of Ceallachán, diminutive of Ceallach. Ceallan is a place in Scotland.
Created with the prefix ce and the feminization of Andre.
Combination of the phonetic element see and Anna.
Name of an early Irish missionary and saint.
Means "black-headed, dark-haired", from Old Irish cenn "head" and dub "black" combined with a diminutive suffix.
A byname sometimes interpreted as "the black hunting dog," "son of the badger," or a "follower of the church". The surname Carmody is derived from this byname.

Uncertain etymology, possibly derived from κεάζω (keazo) meaning "to split, cleave wood; to pound". This was the name of a Ciconian mentioned in the Iliad, father of Troezenus and grandfather of Euphemus.
Means "one water" in Nahuatl, a calendrical name.
This name is believed to be of Brittonic Celtic origin, a derivative of Proto-Welsh *Cawlīn, possibly linked to the Welsh word caw "skilled".Ceawlin (died ca. 593) was a King of Wessex.
Means "to suggest, to give advice" in Xhosa.

Uncertain etymology. In Greek mythology, Cebren was a Greek river-god of a tributary of the Skamander river located near Troy. He was the son of Oceanus and Tethys. The ancient city Cebrene may have been named for the river.

Uncertain etymology; some academia has theorised that it derives from an ancient name for a bird, perhaps the cormorant. This was the name of an illegitimate son of King Priam of Troy in Homer's Illiad, who acted as a charioteer for his half-brother Hector and was slain in battle by Patrocles. It was also the name of a giant mentioned in Aristophanes’ comic play The Birds.
Cremish Lombard feminine form of Cèco.

Ceccarella is the mother of the eponymous character of "Peruonto" an Italian literary fairy tale written by Giambattista Basile in his 1634 work, the Pentamerone.Ceccarella Minutolo was a Neapolitan noblewoman, whose family belonged to the most cultivated and refined court circle, who published a collection of her letters on loveand other topics, written around 1470 in a high-flown vernacular.
Short form or pet form of Francesco.Known bearers of this name include the Italian poet Francesco "Cecco" Angiolieri (c. 1260-1313) and the 14th-century Italian painter Cecco di Pietro.

Diminutive of Ceccolo, as -ino is an Italian masculine diminutive suffix. So, in other words, this name is a double diminutive of Francesco.This was the name of the younger brother of the Italian military leader Biordo Michelotti (1352-1398).
Diminutive of Cecco, which is a short form of Francesco.A known bearer of this name was the Italian military leader Ceccolo Broglia (1352-1400).
Meaning uncertain, possibly related to Nahuatl cecen "each one; one out of one" or cetl "ice, frost".
Diminutive of Cecelia using the French suffix -ette.
Cremish Lombard short form of Franceschì.
Name invented by José de Alencar for his novel "O Guarani". It is thought both as a short form of Cecilia and as a pun on the Guarani wordf sasy ("to hurt").

Dutch form of Caecilius for men and short form of Cecilia for women. For the latter group, this name can also be a Dutch variant spelling of the French name Cécile, which is also commonly used in the Dutch-speaking world.
Means "one woman" in Nahuatl, from ce "one" and cihuatl "woman".
Variant of Cecilia and a feminization of Cecil.
English, Dutch and Afrikaans form of Cécile.
Hungarian and Slovak form of Caecilianus.
Form of Caeciliana in several languages.
Italian and Spanish form of Caecilianus.
Cremish Lombard short form of Francèsch.
Means "one snake" in Nahuatl, a calendrical name.
Lodi Lombard short form of Francèsch.
Means "one eagle" in Nahuatl, a calendrical name.
Means "cold, to be cold" or "high mountain place" in Nahuatl.

Latinized form of Greek Κηδαλίων (Kedalion), of which the meaning is not entirely certain. It could have been derived from Greek κηδαλιζω (kedalizô) meaning "purifying, cleansing". However, it could also have been derived from Greek κηδεύω (kēdeuō) meaning "to take charge (of), to care for, to tend (to)". In Greek mythology, Cedalion was a daemon attendant of the god Hephaestus at his forge on the island of Lemnos.
Combination of the phonetic element see and the given name Darian, possibly influenced by the word cedar.
Possibly related to Old Celtic katus "battle". St. Cedd of Lastingham was Bishop of Essex in the seventh century.

Diminutive of Cedric.In English literature, this name is most notably borne by Cedric Errol, the titular character of the novel Little Lord Fauntleroy (1885) written by the English-American author Frances Hodgson Burnett (1849-1924). He is fondly called Ceddie by those closest to him, especially his mother.Between 1914 and 1980, the novel was made into a film four times, always under the same title. A Japanese animated TV series was also released in 1988, of which the original Japanese title was changed in most (if not all) countries. In the Netherlands, the series was aired under the name Ceddie.

This name is best known for being the name of Cedella Booker (1926-2008), the mother of the Jamaican reggae singer Bob Marley (1945-1981). Her full name at birth was Sidilla Editha Malcolm. Given how similar the name Sidilla is to her later name Cedella, it is possible that Cedella is a variant spelling or form of Sidilla. Sidilla itself may then possibly be a corrupted form of Sibylla (see Sibyl). Alternatively, the name Sidilla could be derived from the Spanish word cedilla meaning "small letter Z". It was then probably a misspelling, which her parents later changed to the slightly more correct spelling Cedella.Cedella's son Bob later went on to name his first biological daughter (born in 1967) after her, who would go on to become a musician in her own right, most notably as part of the reggae band Ziggy Marley and the Melody Makers.
Variant of Cedric. A famous name bearer is the Swedish guitarist Cederick Forsberg (1989-).
Diminutive of Mercedes. This can also be used as a diminutive of Merced, Praxedes, and other names with a similar sound.
Form of Kadmiel used in the Latin Old Testament.
Cedny means “a group of foxes” in welsh.
Derived from the Slavic word čedo meaning "child", also used as a nickname for Čedomir.
Derived from the Slavic elements chedo meaning "child" and milu meaning "gracious, dear".
Feminine form of Cedric. A famous namesake is the child actress in the 2018 movie Capernaüm, Cedra Izzam.
Variant of Cedric.Usage appears to be centred to the USA.
Perhaps intended to be a feminine variant of Cedric. This is the name of a minor character in J. K. Rowling's 'Harry Potter' series of books; the character is Cedrella Weasley, née Black.
Modern coinage intended as a feminine form of Cédric.
Variant of Cédric. It is also used on females, which makes this name one of the few -que names that are unisex (like Dominique).
Diminutive of Cecilia and other names beginning with ce. In some cases, it can be a diminutive of names starting with the letter "C."
Phonetic spelling of the initials CJ.
Spanish and Portuguese form of Cephalus.
Galician, Italian and Spanish form of Cepheus.
Catalan, Portuguese and Romanian form of Cepheus.

Variant of Kaylee. It has been influenced by the Irish word céilí, which refers to a traditional Gaelic social gathering involving folk music and dancing (sometimes storytelling and poetry), ultimately derived from Old Irish céle "companion".

Directly taken from Scottish Gaelic cèilidh, a traditional folk music and storytelling party.Its modern usage as a name was certainly influenced by the popularity of the homophonous Kaylee and its variants. This spelling is hardly ever used in Scotland itself, where Kayleigh is the most common spelling.
Derived from Welsh cein, the penult form of cain, "fair, fine; elegant" and teg "beautiful, fair, fine".

Possibly derived from Old Welsh element cein meaning "good, lovely" and drych meaning "mirror, image".It was born by a 5th century Welsh saint, Ceindrych verch Brychan. It is also the name of a medieval Welsh queen, Queen Ceindrych of Brycheiniog.
Derived from Welsh cein, the penult form of cain, "fair, fine; elegant" and gwydd "appearance; aspect; view".

Nomen of uncertain origin and meaning. The nomen resembles other Etruscan names, such as Cilnius, and the family does not appear in history before the first century. The historian Aelius Spartianus wrote that they came from Etruria, or perhaps from the town of Faventia, which was itself of Etruscan origin.
