column12: Derived from Old Irish cíar "dark, black" combined with a diminutive suffix. Compare Ciarán.

Ceithlion ((Cethlenn) is a powerful, monstrous queen and prophetess of the Fomorians in Irish mythology. Known by the epithet "of the Crooked Teeth" (or Ceithlion Chaisfhiaclach), she is famously recorded as the wife of the monstrous Fomorian king Balor of the Evil Eye and the mother of Ethniu.
Derived from Kurdish cejn meaning "feast, holiday".
Derived from Kurdish cejn meaning "feast, holiday".
Possibly means "the one who guards a high/elevated position".
Means "armed" in Northern Kurdish, from çek meaning "weapon" and -dar meaning "-ed".
French form of Celadon. This was the name of a character in the French pastoral novel 'L'Astrée' by Honoré d'Urfé, published between 1607 and 1627.

Latinized form of Greek Κελάδων (Keladôn), derived from κέλαδος (kelados) which meant "a noise as of rushing waters; loud noise, din, clamour". This was the name of several figures in Greek mythology, including an Ethiopian chief in the court of Cepheus, and a Lapith who fought against the centaurs. It was also the name of a stream in Elis.

Meaning unknown. The American author Sarah J. Maas used this for the central character in her 'Throne of Glass' series of fantasy novels, first released in 2012. She may have based it on the Greek mythological name Celaeno.
Transferred use of the surname Celange.
This is the main character of the novel Célanire cou-coupé by Maryse Condé.
Variant of Selavi influenced by the French phrase c'est la vie "that's life".
East Prussian German (short) form of Cäcilie.

Means "tree of silver" or "tall and silver" in Sindarin, from the elements celeb "silver" and orne "tree" or possibly a derivative of ornā meaning "tall". In J.R.R. Tolkien's 'The Lord of the Rings', Celeborn was the ruler of Lothlórien along with his wife Galadriel.
A river in J.R.R. Tolkien's works. The name means "silver lode" in the fictional Quenya language, from celeb meaning "silver" and rant meaning "river, lode".

Means "silver queen" in Sindarin, from celeb meaning "silver" and rían meaning "queen". This was the name of an Elf mentioned in Lord of the Rings. She was the daughter of Galadriel, the wife of Elrond, and the mother of Arwen.
Means "silver fist" in Sindarin. In 'The Lord of the Rings', Celebrimbor was the creator of the Rings of Power.

An alternate name of the character Idril from the works of JRR Tolkien. The name means "silver foot" in the fictional Sindarin language, from the name elements celeb meaning "silver" and tâl meaning "foot".
From the English word celebrity, meaning “famous or notable person”.

Variant form of Chelidonius, which is the proper latinized form of the Greek name Chelidonios.Celedonius (more often written as Celidonius and especially Chelidonius) was the name of a Roman legionary who was martyred with his fellow soldier Emeterius around 300 AD. They have since become saints, venerated in both the Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox Church. Both are the patron saints of the city of Calahorra in the Spanish province of La Rioja, where they are purported to have died.

This name could be connected to the former spelling and pronunciation of the town in Solvenia named “Celje”, that was formerly name Celeia during the Roman period. It could also mean “gift of god” and “heavenly”.
Meaning unknown. It occurs briefly in 'Culhwch and Olwen' belonging to a lady at King Arthur's court, the daughter of Sir Kay.
Variant of Selene, possibly influenced by Celine.

Derived from the Latin word celer, meaning "quick, swift", followed by the masculine diminutive suffix -inus. This was the name of an African martyr, revered for his suffering while imprisoned by Emperor Trajan Decius in Rome. He was freed and returned to Carthage, where St. Cyprian ordained him as a deacon.
Latinization of Celeste. In some cases it might also be considered a contracted form of Celestina.
Combination of Celeste and Lester or Ester.
Catalan form of Caelestinus. A known bearer of this name was the Catalan politician Celestí Boada i Salvador (1902-1939).
Portuguese form of Caelestia. Also compare the masculine counterpart Celéstio.
Derived from the English adjective celestial meaning "of the sky, heavenly", which is ultimately derived from the Latin adjective caelestis meaning "of the heavens" (see Caelestis).
Likely an elaboration of Celeste influenced by the word celestial.
Aragonese and Slovak form of Caelestinus.
Kashubian, Languedocian, Provençal, Gascon and Piedmontese form of Caelestinus and Walloon variant of Célèstin.
Italian and Spanish form of Caelestius.

Means "celestite" in Spanish. Also known as celestine, celestite is a colourless, orange or blue mineral with orthorhombic crystals, so named from Latin caelestis "heavenly, pertaining to the sky" (compare Caelestis) after its usual pale sky-blue shade.

Latinized form of Greek Κελεός (Keleos), which is derived from Greek κελεύω (keleuō) which can mean "to command, to order" as well as "to urge (on), to drive on". In Greek mythology, Celeus was the king of Eleusis.
Latinized form of Keleustanor. In Greek mythology, this is the name of a son of Heracles, whom he had with Iphis, the daughter of king Thespius of Thespiae in Boeotia.
Variant of Celidoine, king of Scotland, son of the first Nascien and Flegentine, and ancestor of Lancelot and Galahad.
Occitan form of Celia, also used as a contracted form of Ceselha.
Dutch form of Caelianus via its variant spelling Celianus.

English and Swedish form of Caelianus via its variant spelling Celianus. In the case of The Netherlands, Celian really is just a variant form of Celiaan, which is the actual Dutch form of Caelianus (also via Celianus).
Spanish and Portuguese feminine form of Caelianus.
Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Caelianus.
From the word "celibate", referring to one who abstains from sexual relations for a religious reason.
Derived from Latin caelicus, meaning "heavenly, celestial". It jumped in popularity after the Japanese car company Toyota used it for one of their vehicles in 1970.

King of Scotland, son of the first Nascien and Flegentine, and ancestor of Lancelot and Galahad.When Joseph of Arimathea visited Sarras and surrounding regions, Celidoine converted to Christianity with his father and became a devout believer. After King Mordrains of Sarras disappeared, Nascien and Celidoine, still a boy, were imprisoned by an infidel named Galafre. God lifted Nascien from the prison, for which Galafre tried to kill Celidoine by hurling him from a tower, but the arms of God broke Celidoine’s descent and carried him away.He had a number of adventures at sea which served to test his piety. He converted King Label of Persia, and later married Label’s daughter. Celidoine preceded his father to Britain, where he performed the first conversion of a Briton ruler: Duke Ganor of Galafort.He was crowned King of North Wales. He learned to interpret messages in the stars, and by doing so managed to save his kingdom from a famine. His son, Narpus, inherited his lands and title. Celidoine was buried at Camelot.Celidoine’s name seems to be some variation of Celidon, or the Caledonian forest in northern England and Scotland. R.S. Loomis points out that Celidoine’s power of prophecy seems reminiscent of Merlin’s, and that Merlin is called “Merlinus Celidonius” by Giraldus Cambrensis.
Variant of Celedonia, or directly from Spanish celidonia meaning "celandine". Also compare Chelidonia.

Variant form of Chelidonius, which is the proper latinized form of the Greek name Chelidonios. In Christian tradition this name is sometimes given to the unnamed 'man born blind' whose sight Jesus miraculously healed, according to the Gospel of John 9:1-12. The form Celedonius belonged to an early saint, martyred ca. 300.
Adoption of French Célie outside the francophone world. This form of the name was used in Alice Walker's 1982 epistolary novel 'The Color Purple'.
French form of Caelianus. Known bearers of this name are the Swiss singer Célien Schneider (b. 1986) and the late French general Charles-Célien Fracque (1875-1941).
Dutch form of Céline, chiefly used in Flanders.
Possibly derived from the name of the town in Kosovo.
Possibly means "communion", derived from Nahuatl celia "to receive, to accept (something)".

A character in Molière's play 'The Misanthrope'. Possibly from Latin caelum meaning "sky, heaven" and Ancient Greek μενος (menos) meaning "strength". As such, the meaning of the name would roughly be "heavenly strength".
Occitan, Galician and Hungarian form of Céline.
Variant form of Celinda as well as a variant spelling of Selinde. A known bearer of this name is the Dutch musical actress Celinde Schoenmaker (b. 1989).
Diminutive of Celia, Celeste, Marcela and names that start with or contain cel.

One of the maidens of Viviane, the French Damsel of the Lake, Celise seems to have held a high place in the Damsel’s service. her grasp of magic, while doubtless far short of Viviane’s, Nimue’s, or Morgan’s, was practical and useful.
From the name of a perfume called Celisse, which was introduced by Dana in 1982.
Derived from Albanian çel "to open up, to sprout, to begin" and jetë "life".
Diminutive of Celestýna, not generally used as a given name in its own right.
Taken from the name of the flower, whose name is derived from Greek κηλος (kelos) "burned".
Invented name based on rhyming names such as Nelson and Élson.
From the Galician word celta ("Celt"), thus meaning "land of the Celts". This is the name that Galician writer Eduardo Pondal gives to Galicia, reclaiming it as the quintessential land of the Celts.
Celtina is the heroine of a series of books written by Corinne De Vailly.

Possibly derived from Ancient Greek κηλόω (kêloô) meaning "to have an abnormal delivery" or perhaps "to burn"; it could also be a variant form of κηλέω (keleo) meaning "to charm, enchant, beguile". This was the name of a naiad or an oread who personified Mount Celusa or Celossa in Phliasia, mother of the river god Asopus by Poseidon in some accounts.
Diminutive of Celestina, not generally used as a given name in its own right.
Possibly a variant of Selvin, Calvin, or Kelvin.
Combination of Welsh celyn "holly" and gwen "white, fair, blessed".
From the Persian cemâl-nûr meaning "beautiful luminous".
From the Kurdish ç'em meaning "stream, river".

A fictional character created by J.R.R. Tolkien. Cemendur was the third child and son of the nobleman Axantur. He had two other siblings: Lindissë and Ardamir. He married an unnamed women and had two children named Írildë and Hallatan. His son married and had a son named Hallacar, his grandson who entered into the ruling line by marrying Tar-Ancalimë, the first Ruling Queen of Númenor.
From the name of a type of evergreen tree that produces fragrant flowers (scientific name Magnolia champaca), ultimately from Sanskrit चम्पक (campaka).

From cemre, a term used in Turkish folklore referring to the warming of temperature at the end of winter, thought to occur in three stages affecting air, water, then earth combined with naz meaning "coy".
Derived from Persian (Can), meaning "Soul, Life" and Arabic (Ab) "Water". Also used as a formal address akin to "Sir" or "Your Excellency"
Variant of Zenaida mainly used in South America.
Probably derived from the Old English elements cene "bold, keen" and beorht "bright".
Re-interpretation of Sandrine with the same French pronunciation influenced by the French word cendre "ash" and the name Cendrillon.
Possibly a diminutive of Alexandre. Alternatively, it could be derived from the French word cendre "ash", referencing to the Ash Wednesday.
Italian form of Cinderella, derived from Italian cenere meaning "cinder".
Variant of Cenric. Derived from Old English cene "bold" and ric "ruler, king".
Derived from Italian ceneri "ashes". This was traditionally given to girls born on Ash Wednesday (mercoledì delle ceneri or Ceneri in Italian). It is a cognate of Cendrillon.
Old English name, in which the first element is cene "bold, keen". This name was borne by a king of Wessex who ruled briefly, during 674; he was succeeded by his son Aescwine.
From the Chinese 曾 (céng) meaning "already" and 惠 (huì) meaning "benefit, favour, kindness".
From Kurdish çeng meaning "leap" or "handful, palm" and zêr meaning "gold, golden".
Spanish form of Cinderella, literally meaning "ash-colored".
Derived from the Proto-Celtic name *Kʷennowindos meaning "white head", from *kʷennom "head" and *windos "white".
Welsh cognate of Kenneth. 6th-century Saint Cennydd was allegedly the son of Gildas the Monk.
Variant of Zenobio, the Spanish form of Zenobius. This was borne by the 19th-century Mexican composer Cenobio Paniagua (1821-1882).
Derived from Old English cene "bold, keen" and ræd "counsel, advice". Old English cognate of Conrad.
Cremish Lombard feminine form of Cènso.
Feminine form of Centis. Another theory, however, considers this name a variant of Zenta.
Possibly means "the only one, unique", derived from Nahuatl centetl "one, a single one".

Derived from Nahuatl centli "dried ears of corn, dried maize on the cob" and teotl "deity, god; divine force". This was the name of an Aztec maize deity, depicted as both male and female; they may have been an aspect of Chicomecōātl.
Derived from Latvian centīgs "diligent, industrious, studious, zealous".
Means "dried maize, dried corncob" in Nahuatl.

From a frequent misspelling of the English noun centurion, which refers to a Roman army officer that commanded a century (i.e. a group of one hundred). This was recorded as a Puritan given name, presumably used in reference to the centurion who was present at the crucifixion according to the Gospels of Matthew, Mark and Luke (who is widely considered to be the first Christian), or due to other occurrences of centurions in the New Testament.
Means "four hundred" or "innumerable, uncountable, plenty" in Nahuatl.
Romanian form of Cinderella, from Romanian cenușă "ash".
Likely means "bold foreigner" or "keen Celt", derived from the Old English elements cene "bold, keen" and wealh "foreigner, Celt."
Derived from Old English cene "bold" and wealh "foreigner, Celt" meaning "bold foreigner".
Italian and Spanish form of Coeus (see Koios).
Derived from the Old English element ceol "keel (of a ship)". Ceol (also known as Ceola or Ceolric) was King of Wessex from 592 to 597.
Derived from the Old English elements ceol "keel, ship" and beald "brave, bold".
Derived from the Old English elements ceol "keel, ship" and beorht "bright".

Derived from the Old English elements ceol "keel (of a ship)" and friþ "peace". This name was borne by an Anglo-Saxon Christian abbot and saint, and also gave rise to the surnames Chilvers and Chorlton, and the place name Chorlton-cum-Hardy in Manchester.
Old English name meaning "army of ships, warrior of ships" derived from the elements ceol "keel" and here "army".
Original form of Ceolmer, derived from the elements ceol "keel (of a ship)" and mære "famous".
Variant of the Old English name Ceolmær, derived from the elements ceol "keel, ship" and mære "famous".
Derived from the Old English elements ceol "keel, ship" and noð "boldness, daring".
Original form of Ceolred, derived from the Old English elements ceol "keel (of a ship)" and ræd "counsel, advice".
From the Old English name Ceolræd, composed of the elements ceol "ship" and ræd "counsel, advice". This name was borne by a king of Mercia who reigned from 709 to 716.
Derived from the Old English elements ceol "keel" and ric "power, rule".
Derived from the Old English elements ceol "keel (of a ship)" and sige "victory".
Derived from the Old English elements ceol "keel" and stan "stone".
Derived from the Old English elements ceol "keel (of a ship)" and weald "powerful, mighty".
Derived from the Old English elements ceol "ship, keel" and weard "guard, guardian" meaning "ship guard, keel guard, guard of a ship"
Derived from the Old English elements ceol "keel" and wig "war".
Derived from the Old English elements ceol "keel, ship" and wine "friend".
Form of Ceolweald found in the Phillimore translation of Domesday Book.
Derived from the Old English elements ceol "keel (of a ship)" and wulf "wolf".
Derived from the Old English elements ceol "keel of a ship" and wynn "joy".
Portuguese and French form of Coeus (see Koios).
Latinized version of "Céfiro," Spanish version of Zephyr.
Latinized form of the Greek name Κηφισώ (Kephiso), which is the feminine form of Kephisos.In Greek mythology, Cephiso was one of the Mousai Apollonides, i.e. Muses that were daughters of Apollo.
Latinized form of Kephisodoros. This name was borne by an Athenian playwright from the 5th century BC.
Latinized form of Kephisodotos. This name was borne by an Athenian general and two Greek sculptors, all of whom lived in the 4th century BC.
Latinized form of Kephisophon. This name was borne by an eponymous archon of Athens, who lived in the 4th century BC.
Latinized form of Kephisos. This is the name of an ancient Greek river god.
Means "glare, gleam, glitter" in Hakha Chin.
Of uncertain origin and meaning, this name might be a variant of Sera. It was used in the 1988 movie The Land Before Time where it belongs to one of the main characters, a triceratops.

Diminutive of cerasa, an alternative Italian term to say ciliegia, both meaning "cherry". Cerasella is a 1959 Canzone Napoletana song performed by Gloria Christian and Wilma De Angelis. The song also inspired a comedy film with the same name, directed by Raffaello Matarazzo and starring Claudia Mori and Terence Hill.
From the Karachay-Balkar джер (cer) meaning "Earth" and аслан (aslan) meaning "lion".
Polish and Romanian form of Cerberus.
Galician and Portuguese form of Cerberus.
Italian and Spanish form of Cerberus.
Uncertain etymology. This was the name of several figures in Greek mythology, including one of the Heliadae (sons of Helios and Rhodos), personification of the island.

Means "of the weaving shuttle", derived from Greek κερκίς (kerkis) meaning "weaving shuttle, taper rod". This was the name of one of the Oceanids in Greek mythology, described as being lovely of form.
Meaning unknown at this time. A notable bearer of this name was the Albanian revolutionary and guerrilla fighter Çerçiz Topulli (1880-1915).

Means "the wily one; fox, weasel, thief" in Ancient Greek, derived from κέρδος (kerdos) meaning "profit, gain". In Greek mythology, Cerdo was the wife of King Phoroneus of Argos and mother of Apis and Niobe. It may have also been an epithet of the goddess Demeter.
North Frisian form of Severine, recorded on the islands of Sylt and Amrum.
Croatian and Lithuanian form of Ceres.

From the genus name of a type of night-blooming cacti found from California to Chile, from Latin cereus "waxen, waxy", which was also used as a substantive to mean "a wax-light, -taper" ("particularly those brought by clients to their patrons as presents at the time of the Saturnalia"), and so called because the cactus' shape "suggests a candle."

Means "stag (a large buck or male deer)" in French. Cerf sometimes appears in historical documents concerned with the Jews of Alsace and early modern France; it was a local translation of the Yiddish Hirsh, meaning "deer", the Hebrew equivalent of which is Zvi.
Provençal and Languedocian form of Cyrus.
Means "cheerful, bright, happy" or "clean, pure" in Indonesian, ultimately from Sanskrit चर्य (carya).
Dutch form of Cérile, with its spelling more or less phonetical in nature. Also compare Cyriel.A known bearer of this name is the Dutch soccer player Ceriel Oosthout (b. 1984).
Variant spelling of Cérile, which is an archaic French variant of Cyrille.
From the name of a flower, literally "wax-flower" from Greek κηρος (keros) "beeswax" combined with ανθος (anthos) "flower".
Latinized form of Kerinthos. This was the name of an early Gnostic who was prominent as a heresiarch in the view of the early Church Fathers.

From the brand of perfume called Cerissa, which was introduced by Charles Revson in 1974. The name itself might possibly be a variant of Cerise. It was also used by Barbara Cartland for the heroine of her historical romance novel The Heart Triumphant (1976).
Possibly from the Karachay-Balkar чериу (çeriu) meaning "army" and the suffix -мен (-men), ultimately meaning "warrior, warlike".
This is one of the names by which the 4th-century martyr and saint Serenus the Gardener is known in France.
Of uncertain origin and meaning. One current theory suggests, however, a derivation from Sharona.
Probably from Proto-Indo-European *kar- ‎(“hard”‎). See also Latin carina and carpinus.

Created by American author George R. R. Martin for his series of epic fantasy novels 'A Song of Ice and Fire', where it belongs to an evil queen who is one of the main antagonists. The name is popularly claimed to be a variant of Circe, but Martin has stated that the mythological character was not the inspiration: 'I know my Homer, of course, but Cersei is not based on Circe. Many names sound alike.'
Spelling variant of Kerstin. Note that it is still pronounced with an initial k.
Old Irish name, possibly meaning "humming sound". See also Kjartan.
Possibly a fifth century Italian female bishop.
From the colour cerulean meaning “sky blue”, derived from the Latin caeruleus, perhaps related to caelum which means “sky”. It is recently but rarely used as a name.
Transferred use of the surname Cerva, meaning "doe, hind (female deer)" in Italian.
Catalan and Franco-Provençal form of Caesar.
Spanish variant and Galician form of Cesario.
Sassarese and Gallurese form of Caesar.
Occitan and Provençal form of Caesarius.
Occitan and Provençal feminine form of Cesari and Catalan form of Caesaria.
Italian and Spanish form of Caesarius.
Portuguese form of Caesarus. He was a chieftain of the Lusitanians, a proto-Celtic tribe during the Roman conquest of Hispania.
Diminutive of Cesare, as -otto is an Italian masculine diminutive suffix.
Derived from Upper Sorbian česćić "to honour; to venerate, to revere" and měr "peace". In former times, this name was usually Germanized as Ehrenfried.
Gascon and Provençal variant of Cecília.
Milanese and Cremish Lombard form of Caesar.
Cremish Lombard feminine diminutive of Céser.
Yiddish and Silesian short form of Cecylia.

Of debated origin and meaning. While some scholars connect this name to masculine Cesare, others rather see a link to Cesio. It may also be a contracted form of Cesaria. Traditionally, this name was most commonly used in Lombardy.
Italian form of Czesław via Latinized form Ceslaus.
French form of Czesław via it's Latinized form Ceslaus.
East Prussian German and Silesian German form of Czesław.
Lithuanian and Latvian borrowing of Czesława and Czech feminine form of Česlav.
Means "water spring" in Azerbaijani, ultimately from Persian چشمه (cheshme).
From Persian چشم (čašm, češm) meaning "eye" and دلبر (delbar) meaning "beloved, sweetheart".
Means "black eyes" in Ottoman Turkish, ultimately from Persian چشم (chashm) meaning "eye" and سیاه (siyāh) meaning "black".

Allegedly means "affliction, sorrow". According to Irish legend Cessair was a granddaughter of Noah who died in the great flood. The name also belonged to a Gaulish princess who married the Irish high king Úgaine Mór in the 5th or 6th century BC.
Means "bold, brave" in Turkish, derived from Arabic جَسُور (jasūr).
Means "attacking hawk" in Lakota, from Lakota čhetáŋ "hawk" and wakhúwa "hunter, to hunt or chase".
Possibly an invented name based on Ethan.
A Roman cognomen of unknown meaning. One bearer of this name was Gaius Cornelius Cethegus who was a consul of the Roman Republic in 197 BC.

Possibly means "crooked tooth". In Irish myth she was the wife of Balor of the Evil Eye, king of the Fomorians and by him the mother of Ethniu (or Eithne, Ethlenn).Irish archaeologist R. A. Stewart Macalister (1870-1950) proposed that it was originally a variant of Ethlenn arising from the frequent identification of Lugh (son of Ethlenn) by the matronymic "Lugh Mac Ethlenn": thus, Mac Ethlenn → Mac Cethlenn. Also, the town of Enniskillen in Northern Ireland is named for her, from Irish Inis Cethlinn "Cethlenn's island".

Feminine equivalent of Cid, a byname derived from the Old Castilian loan word Çid, itself derived from the dialectal Arabic word sīdī (سيدي ) "my lord; my master", ultimately from Arabic as-sayyid (السيّد ) "the lord; the master".
Derived from Romanian cetină "fallen needle leaves".

Latinized form of the Greek Κητώ (Kētō), which meant "sea-monster" (supposedly the source of the word κῆτος (kētos) "any sea-monster or huge fish; sometimes the whale, but often the tunny-fish"). In Greek mythology Ceto was the personification of the dangers of the sea, a daughter of Pontos (Sea) and Gaia (Earth) and mother of the Gorgons and other ugly monsters, including Scylla and Echidna.
Means "advised" in Zulu. This was the name of a Zulu King,

English diminutive of Celeste, Celestia and Celestine. A known bearer of this name was the American abolitionist and philanthropist Laura Spelman Rockefeller (1839-1915), who was affectionately referred to as Cettie because of her middle name, which was Celestia.
From the Karachay-Balkar джетинчи (cetinçi) meaning "seventh" and улан (ulan) meaning "son".
Means "died coming" in Bandial. This is considered a 'death prevention' name.
Means "sky”, but more specifically “heaven" in Portuguese. It is more commonly used as part of the Marian name Maria do Céu.
Means "precious stone, jewel, gem" in Turkish, ultimately from Persian گوهر (gōhar).
Probably from Turkish ceylan meaning "antelope, gazelle" and Persian یار (yar) meaning "friend, lover".

From the historical name of the British crown colony (present-day Sri Lanka), borrowed from Portuguese Ceilão and ultimately derived from Sanskrit सिंहल (simhala), literally meaning "lionlike" and composed of सिंह (simha) meaning "lion" and the suffix -ल (-la).
Derived from the Azerbaijani noun ceyran meaning "gazelle, antelope", which is ultimately of Persian origin (see Jeiran). Also compare the related name Ceylan.

The name Ceysu is a modern Turkish feminine name formed by the combination of two native Turkic elements.The first element, cey, is a phonetic variant and dialectal form of the Old Turkic and Anatolian Turkish word çay, meaning "stream" or "creek" (cognate with Chagatai çay). This root should not be confused with the homophonous loanword çay (meaning "tea"), which entered Turkish from Mandarin Chinese via Persian.The second element is the native Turkic word su, meaning "water", which is a highly popular root and suffix in Turkish feminine names (such as Aysu, Bensu, or Tansu).Therefore, the combined meaning of Ceysu is "stream water" or "flowing water". It is important to note that despite the phonetic similarity, Ceysu is etymologically entirely unrelated to names of Arabic, Persian, or Mongolic origins such as Ceyda, Ceylan, or Ceyhun.

Derived from Ancient Greek κῆϋξ (keyx) referring to an uncertain kind of seabird, possibly meaning "tern, sea-swallow", "gannet", or "seagull". In Greek mythology, Ceyx was the husband of Alcyone. After he was killed in a shipwreck, his wife threw herself into the water, but the gods saved her and turned them both into birds.
Diminutive form of Cezariusz or Cezary.
Feminine form of Cezary and Cezariusz.
Bosnian, Croatian, Polish and Romanian form of Caesarion.
From the Karachay-Balkar джез (cez) meaning "copper, bronze" and сан (san) meaning "body, limb".
Variant of Chaabane influenced by French orthography.
Alternate transcription of Arabic شعبان (see Shaban) chiefly used in North Africa.

column12: Alternate transcription of Arabic شعبان (see Shaban) chiefly used in Algeria.
From the Chinese 姹 (chà) meaning "beautiful, colourful" and 宝 (bǎo) meaning "treasure, jewel; precious, rare".
Diminutive of María Isabel. A famous bearer is Chábeli Iglesias, a Spanish socialite.
Diminutive of Chabela. In other words, this is a double diminutive of Isabel.
Combination of Bettie and the common Filipino prefix -cha.

Empress Chabi (1225–1281) was a Khongirad empress consort of the Yuan dynasty in China, married to Kublai Khan. As such, she was the wife to the Mongol Khagan who had conquered all of China in the 1270s.
It is a type of French wine that sounds feminine.
Means "he who drinks ricewater" in Meitei.
Combination of two elements cha “bear” and borz “wolf”.
Diminutive of Mzechabuk, which tends to be used as an independent name. A notable bearer of this name was the Georgian novelist Mzechabuk "Chabua" Amirejibi (1921-2013).
From Guanche *tabuḍt, meaning "navel". This was recorded as the name of a 12-year-old Guanche girl from Tenerife who was sold at the slave market in Valencia in 1495.
The Mayan god of Agriculture, Fertility, and Rain. He is also associated with east and the colour yellow.

column3: 茶々, etc.(Japanese Kanji)|叉察, 义察(Chinese)
column12: From Japanese 茶 (cha) meaning "tea" combined with 々, a phonetic character indicting a duplication of the beginning kanji. Other kanji combinations are possible.
From the Tatar чэ чэк (che chek) meaning "flower" and бий (biy) meaning "princess".
Means "pure" in Caló. This name is used as the Caló form of Pura.
Derived from Belarusian хацець (chacieć) meaning "to want, to desire". This name was given to a long-desired child.
Form of Jacob used by Malayalam-speaking Syriac Christians in the Indian state of Kerala.
Thai name for the Jaṭāyu, a mythological bird in the Hindu epic Ramayana who has the form of a vulture. It is ultimately derived from Sanskrit जटायु (jaṭāyu) meaning "bearded vulture".
Diminutive of Chad / Chadwick. In the detective novel 'Cat Among the Pigeons' (1959) by Agatha Christie, there is a character named Lettice Chadwick, often called Chaddy.
Alternate transcription of Arabic شادي (see Shadi 1) influenced by French orthography.
Alternate transcription of Arabic شادية (see Shadiya) chiefly used in Northern Africa.
Transferred use of the surname Chadman.

Uncertain etymology, possibly related to Sanskrit छत्रावली (chatrāvalī), a series of overlapping discs resembling parasols that crown the top of a stupa, a dome-shaped Buddhist monument used to house religious relics.
Transferred use of the surname Chadrick or combination of the names Chad and Rick.

column3: 채아(Korean Hangul)|采雅, 彩雅, 采娥, 彩娥, etc.(Korean Hanja)
column12: From Sino-Korean 采 (chae) meaning "collect, gather, pluck" or 彩 (chae) meaning "colour" combined with 雅 (a) meaning "elegant, graceful, refined" or 娥 (a) meaning "good, beautiful". Other hanja combinations can form this name as well.

column3: 채안(Korean Hangul)|采晏, 彩晏, etc.(Korean Hanja)
column12: From Sino-Korean 采 (chae) meaning "collect, gather, pluck" or 彩 (chae) meaning "colour" combined with 晏 (an) meaning “peaceful, quiet, clear, later in the day”. Other hanja combinations can form this name as well.
采 (chae) meaning "collect, gather, pluck" or 彩 (chae) meaning "colour" combined with 範 meaning "standard, norm; example, model," 凡 meaning "all, everyone" or 犯 "invasion, violation,"

column3: 채빈(Korean Hangul)|采斌, 彩斌, etc.(Korean Hanja)
column12: From Sino-Korean 采 (chae) meaning "collect, gather, pluck" or 彩 (chae) meaning "colour" combined with 斌 (bin) meaning "refined". Other hanja combinations can form this name as well.

column3: 채은(Korean Hangul)|采垠, 彩恩, 蔡誾, etc.(Korean Hanja)
column12: From Sino-Korean 采 (chae) meaning "collect, gather, pluck", 彩 (chae) meaning "colour" or 蔡 (chae) referring to a type of tortoise used for divination combined with 垠 (eun) meaning "boundary, limit, riverbank", 恩 (eun) meaning "kindness, mercy, charity" or 誾 (eun) meaning "to speak gently, to be respectful". Other hanja combinations can form this name as well.

column3: 채경(Korean Hangul)|采京, 彩京, 采景, 彩景, 采敬, 彩敬, etc.(Korean Hanja)

Means "man who walks the Earth but who only sees the sky" in the language of the fictional Anurabi tribe. Chakotay was the name of the first officer in 'Star Trek: Voyager'.

Possibly means "he throws jade down" in Nahuatl, from chālchiuhtli "precious green or blue stone" and tepehua "to scatter or throw something onto the ground". Alternatively, it could mean "owner of jade mountains", with the second element deriving from tepetl "hill, mountain" and the possessive suffix -hua.

Means "bright precious stone" in Nahuatl, from chālchiuhtli "precious green or blue stone" and tlanextli "light, radiance", combined with the diminutive or reverential suffix -tzin. This was the name of the first ruler of the Toltecs in Tollan.

Means "shining precious stone" in Nahuatl, from chālchiuhtli "precious green or blue stone" and tlatonac "shining, prospering". This was the name of the second ruler of the Mexica, as well as an epithet of the goddess Chalchiuhtlicue.
Name of the other appearance of Acuecucyoticihuati.
Means "jade turkey" in Nahuatl, from Nahuatl chālchihuitl "jade, turquoise, precious stone" and tōtolin "turkey hen". In Aztec mythology, Chalchiuhtotolin was a god of disease and plague.

Means "jade bird" or "turquoise bird" in Nahuatl, referring to a brightly coloured species of songbird known as the red-legged honeycreeper. Ultimately derived from chālchiuhtli "precious green or blue stone" and tototl "bird".
Means "jade flower" in Nahuatl, from chālchiuhtli "precious green or blue stone; jade, turquoise, emerald" and xōchitl "flower".
Means "precious green or blue stone; greenstone, jade, turquoise, emerald" in Nahuatl.

Derived from Ancient Greek χαλκός (chalkos) meaning "copper, bronze" combined with either ὄψ (ops) meaning "face, eye" or ὄψ (ops) meaning "voice". This was the name of several women in Greek mythology, including a Colchian princess and sister of Medea.

From Ancient Greek χαλκώδων (chalkodon) meaning "with brazen or copper teeth, bronze-beaked", composed of χαλκός (chalkos) "copper, bronze, metal" and ὀδών (odon), the Ionic form of ὀδούς "tooth, tusk; anything pointed" (genitive ὀδόντος). This was the name of several figures in Greek mythology, including one of the fifty sons of King Aegyptus who was killed by his wife, Rhodia, on their wedding night.
Chalcol, meaning "maintain," was one of the exemplars of wisdom than whom Solomon was wiser. (I Kings 4:31)

Linguistically, is built from two clear Ancient Greek roots: χαλκός (chalkós) meaning copper/bronze/metal, and μήδομαι (mēdomai) meaning to plan, devise, or counsel. Combined with the verb of planning or counsel, it can be interpreted as “bronze-minded,” “she who plans with bronze,” or “strong in counsel.”
Derived from Ancient Greek χαλκός (chalkos) "copper" and μέδω (medo) "to protect, to rule over". In Greek mythology, this was the name of an Ithican queen, the mother of Laertes and wife of Arcesius.

Possibly derived from Ancient Greek Χαλδαῖος (Chaldaios) meaning "Chaldean, person from Chaldea". This was the name of a nymph also known as Caldene, Calchedonia, or Chalcea, mother of Solymus by Zeus in Greek mythology. A moon of Jupiter was named after her.

The name may derive from the Chalon people, one of eight divisions of the Ohlone (Costanoan) people of Native Americans who lived in Northern California. It may also derive from the French surname Chalon, of unknown meaning, possibly derived from the French town Châlons-sur-Marne. This town inspired the Old English word chaloun meaning "blanket", because of the blankets produced in the town.

From the surname Chaloner, a variant of Challinor, itself denoting a blanket maker, from Middle English chaloun "blanket". A famous bearer of the name was Admiral of the Fleet Sir Chaloner Ogle (1681-1750) who killed Bartholomew Roberts, who many consider the mark that ended the Golden Age of Piracy.

A variant form of Gawaine. The eldest son of King Lot of Orkney and Queen Morgawse (or Anna), Arthur’s sister or half-sister. Brother of Gareth, Gaheris and Agravaine, chief of the Orkney clan (which included his brothers and half brother Mordred), Arthur’s favorite nephew, and one of the most strongest and famous knights of the Round Table.In the medieval Italian poetry (like certain cantari) where the name "Chalvano' is used, he is often specifically celebrated as a "paragon of courtesy" for his interactions with mysterious hosts.
Means "indigo" in Vietnamese, from a non-Sino-Vietnamese reading of Chinese 藍 (chàm). This also refers to plants of genus Indigofera, used to make indigo.
From Sino-Vietnamese 箴 (châm) meaning "to admonish, warn" or a variant of Trâm.
From Sino-Vietnamese 枕 (chẩm) meaning "occipital, scruff of the neck".
Latinized form of Chamaileon. This name was borne by a Peripatetic philosopher from the 3th century BC, who was a disciple of Aristotle.
Derived from the Mao ocha meaning "wealth", omai meaning "people" and kho meaning "ask".
Derived from the Greek noun χαμαιλέων (chamaileon) meaning "chameleon", which consists of Greek χαμαί (chamai) meaning "on the ground" combined with the Greek noun λέων (leon) meaning "lion".
From Thai ชไม (chamai) meaning "both, two, together" and พร (phon) meaning "blessing".
Derived from chaman meaning "field of flowers" and murod meaning "wish, desire, aim".
Derived from Sanskrit चमर (chamara) meaning "yak" or "fly-whisk".
Means "skillful hero" in Mongolian, from чамбай (chambai) meaning "expert, skillful" and баатар (baatar) meaning "hero".
Transferred use of the surname Chamberlain.
Transferred use of the surname Chambers.
From the name of a semi-deciduous flowering tree native to Central and South America (species Samanea saman). It also means "antelope" in Thai.

column3: シャミ(Japanese Katakana)|ちゃみ(Japanese Hiragana)|茶実, 茶美, 茶味, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 茶 (cha) meaning "tea" combined with 美 (mi) meaning "beautiful" or 実 (mi) meaning "reality, truth, seed, fruit, nut". Other kanji combinations are also possible.Famous bearer of this name is Japanese singer Chami Satonaka.
From Mongolian чамин (chamin) meaning "stylish, elegant" and цэцэг (tsetseg) meaning "flower".
Means "be focused and diligent" in Shona.
Means "to duplicate, to imitate, to reproduce (an image of the Buddha)" in Thai, of Khmer origin.

column3: ชำนาญ(Thai)|ចំណាន(Khmer)
column12: Means "skilful, capable, experienced" in Thai and Khmer.
A survey of social media finds a considerable number of Sri Lankan women with this name,
Means "to be like a red parrot" or "in the manner of red parrot feathers", from Nahuatl chamolli "red parrot feather" and -mani "for things to be a certain way".
After the herb used for tea. Ultimately from Greek khamaimēlon "earth apple", because the flowers smell reminiscent of apples.
From the English word champion, meaning "winner".
Means "frangipani (both plant and flower)" in Hindi, referring to a plant belonging to the Plumeria genus.
From French champagne referring to a kind of sparkling white wine, originally from the name of the region in France. The given name may also come from the surname.
Derived from Hindi चंपिका (campika) meaning "little champa (Plumeria) flower".
Alternate transcription of Arabic شمس (see Shams) chiefly used in North Africa.
Tunisian Arabic transcription of Shams al-Din.
Possibly a Comorian form of Shams. A notable bearer is Comorian singer Chamsia Sagaf (1955-).
Short form of Chamunorwa. This is the nickname of Zimbabwean cricketer Chamu Chibhabha. His real name is Chamunorwa.

Combination of Chanda and Munda, the names of two asuras (demons) slain by Kali. This is the name of the fierce form of the Hindu goddess Chandi (herself a form of Parvati), considered the seventh of the eight Matrikas (mother goddesses). She closely associated with the goddesses Kali and Durga.
An epithet of Demeter 1, derived from Greek χαμαι (chamai) meaning "on the ground; to the earth".
From Sino-Vietnamese 真 (chân) meaning "real, genuine, true".
From Sino-Vietnamese 振 (chấn) meaning "shake, sway, vibrate" or 震 (chấn) meaning "shake, tremor, excite".
Variant of Trấn. It can also come from Sino-Vietnamese 昣 (chẩn) meaning "bright, brilliant, clear, morning".
Means "male child in the first pair of twins" in Dinka.

column3: 茶菜, 茶奈, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: Possibly a Bulgarian female form of Chano.
a great indian economist, author of arthashastra and a great mastermind.
From the Shipibo chana meaning "paucarcillo bird, yellow-rumped cacique" and the genitive suffix -n.
Hebrew form of Hananeel. A known bearer of the name was Kairouanan rabbi and Talmudist Chananel ben Chushiel (c. 980-1055).

Means “Wise person” from the compound name with Sanskrit and Pali roots from “Chana” (ชน) meaning person, people, race, being (from Sanskrit jana) and “nya” / “ñā” (ญา) which relates to knowledge or wisdom (jñāna in Sanskrit = knowledge).
From Thai ชน (chon) meaning "person, man, people" and ทิพย์ (thip) meaning "divine, celestial".
From Korean 찬빛 (chanbit) meaning "luminescence," a combination of the present determiner form of verb 차다 (chada) meaning "to fill" and Bit (compare Bitchan).
Meaning uncertain, possibly derived from Nahuatl chanca "lives, is making a home" and the suffix -l.
Perhaps from the French word chance meaning "luck".
Somewhat popular in the United States 1700's. Very rare today.
Variant spelling of Chancellor. A notable bearer of this name is Chance the Rapper (b. 1993), whose birth name is Chancelor Jonathan Bennett.
Likely from the English word chances. See also Chance.
Variant of Chauncey, maybe influenced by the word chance meaning "luck, fortune".

column3: ชาญชัย, ชาญชาย(Thai)
column12: From Thai ชาญ (chan) meaning "skilled, proficient" and ชัย (chai) meaning "victory" or ชาย (chai) meaning "man".
The name means "unsteady", or "restless". It is also apparently synonymous with the name of the Hindu goddess Lakshmi.

column3: จันทร์จิรา(Thai)
column12: From Thai จันทร์ (chan) meaning "moon" and จิร (chira) meaning "long-lasting, long time".
Possibly either a diminutive (in the case of the masculine use) or an inteded feminine form (in the case of the feminine use) of Chance or a variant of Chauncy.
From French chandelle, "candle". It is a cognate of the Spanish name Candela.
Chandi or Chandika is a Hindu goddess.
Mongolian variant of Cintamani, the name of a wish-granting precious stone in Hindu and Buddhist traditions. Ultimately from Sanskrit चिन्तामणि (cintamani) meaning "jewel of thought".
From Hindi चाँदनी (cā̃dnī) meaning "moonlight", ultimately from Sanskrit चन्द्र (candra) "moon".
Likely an invented name, perhaps blending Chandra with Pandora, or possibly a contraction of Shanna and Dora.

Means "protected by the moon, hidden by the moon" in Sanskrit, from चन्द्र (candra) meaning "moon" and गुप्त (gupta) meaning "protected, hidden". This was the name of several Indian rulers including Chandragupta Maurya, the first emperor of the Maurya Empire (reigned 322-297 BCE).
From Sanskrit चन्द्र (candrá) "moon" with मुख (múkha) "mouth, face" and वर्मन् (varman) "shield, armor". This was the name of the 9th ruler of the Varman dynasty, who ruled for 542 to 566.
Means "moon-faced". From Sanskrit चन्द्र (candra) meaning "moon" and मुख॑ (múkha) meaning "face".
Malayalam and Tamil form of Chandra.
Meaning "Handsome as a Moon" or "Beautiful as a Moon".

Means "moonlight" from Sanskrit चन्द्र (candra) meaning "moon" and प्रभा (prabhā) meaning "light, radiance". This is the name of a bodhisattva in Buddhist tradition, as well as the name of the eighth of the 24 tirthankaras (enlightened spiritual teachers) in Jain tradition.
Means "moonlight" from Sanskrit चन्द्र (candra) meaning "moon" and प्रकाश (prakāśa) meaning "light, bright, shining".
MEANING : it was the name of an ancient physician
From Sanskrit चन्द्र (candra) meaning "moon" and वती (vatī) meaning "having".
Possibly a variation of Chandelle or Chandra.
From Sanskrit चन्द्रिका (chandrika) meaning "moonlight, illumination, splendour". It is sometimes used as a masculine name in India while it is solely feminine in Sri Lanka.
Possibly an alternate transcription of Sinhala චාන්දනී (see Chandani).
Combination of the given name Nena and the popular Filipino suffix Cha-.

Variant of Lang, from a non-Sino-Vietnamese reading of Chinese 郎 (chàng).

From the Chinese 昌 (chāng) meaning "light of sun; good, proper" and 伯 (bó) meaning "older brother".
From Sino-Korean 昌 "light of sun; good, proper" and 福 "happiness, good fortune, blessing".
From the Chinese 昌 (chāng) meaning "light of sun; good, proper" and 璨 (càn) meaning "gems, lustre of gems, lustrous".

From Chinese 昌 (chāng) meaning "flourish, prosper, good, sunlight" combined with 德 (dé) meaning "ethics, morality, virtue". Other hanzi combinations are possible.

From the Chinese 昌 (chāng) meaning "light of sun; good, proper" and 辅 (fǔ) meaning "cheekbone" or "protective, assist" or 福 (fú) meaning "happiness, good fortune, blessing".
From the Chinese 昌 (chāng) meaning "light of sun; good, proper" and 高 (gāo) meaning "high, tall".
From the Chinese 昌 (chāng) meaning "light of sun; good, proper" and 哥 (gē) meaning "elder brother".
From Sino-Korean 昌 "light of sun; good, proper" and 均 "equal, even, fair; all, also".

From the Chinese 昌 (chāng) meaning "light of sun; good, proper" and 辉 (huī) meaning "brightness, lustre, brilliance".

column12: From Sino-Korean 昌 (chang) meaning "prosperous, florusihing" or 昶 (chang) meaning "long (day)" combined with 賢 (hyeon) meaning "virtuous, worthy, wise" or 顯 (hyeon) meaning "manifest, clear" or 炫 (hyeon) meaning "shine, glitter" or 鉉 (hyeon), which refers to a device used to lift a tripod cauldron. From Sino-Korean 昶 "a long day; bright; extended; clear" or 昌 "light of sun; good, proper" and 賢 "virtuous, worthy, good; able".

From 昌 (chāng) meaning "prosperous, flourishing" and 杰 (jié) meaning "oustanding, remarkable".

From the Chinese 昌 (chāng) meaning "light of sun; good, proper" and 峻 (jùn) meaning "high, steep, towering; stern".

column12: From Chinese 昌 (chāng) meaning "flourish, prosper, good, sunlight", 长 (cháng) meaning "long", or 常 (cháng) meaning "common, frequent, regular" and 龄 (líng) meaning "age, duration", 岭 (lǐng) meaning "mound, hill", or 玲 (líng) meaning "tinkling of jade". Other character combinations can form this name as well.
From the Chinese 昌 (chāng) meaning "light of sun; good, proper" and 隆 (lóng) meaning "prosperous, plentiful, abundant".
From the Chinese 昶 (chǎng) meaning "long day, bright, clear" and 娈 (luán) meaning "lovely, beautiful, docile".
From the Chinese 昶 (chǎng) meaning "long day, clear, bright" and 梅 (méi) meaning "plum".

“Chang” (常) means “often” or “always,” and “ming” (明) means “bright” or “clear.”
From the Chinese 嫦 (cháng), the name of a moon goddess, and 宁 (níng) meaning "peaceful, calm".

column12: From Sino-Korean 昌 (chang) meaning "prosperous, florusihing" or 昶 (chang) meaning "long (day)" combined with 玉 (ok) meaning "jade" or 沃 (ok) meaning "fertile, rich, lush", or 鈺 (ok) meaning "treasure". Other hanja combinations can form this name as well.
From the Chinese 昌 (chāng) meaning "light of sun; good, proper" and 霈 (pèi) meaning "torrential rains".

From Chinese 昌 (chāng) meaning "flourish, prosper, good, sunlight" or 长 (cháng) meaning "long" combined with 平 (píng) meaning "level, even, peaceful". Other character combinations can form this name as well.

column3: 菖蒲, 昌璞, 昌浦, 昌普, 昌谱, 昌蒲, 常浦, 常普, 长璞, etc.(Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 菖蒲 (chāngpú) meaning "Acorus" or "iris"; or from Chinese 昌 (chāng) meaning "flourish, prosper, good, sunlight", 常 (cháng) meaning "common, frequent, regular", or 长 (cháng) meaning "long" combined with 璞 (pú) meaning "uncut jade or stone containing jade", 浦 (pǔ) meaning "water’s edge, river mouth", or 普 (pǔ) meaning "general, universal, common". From Chinese 长 (cháng) meaning "long" and 琴 (qín) meaning "zither, lute". This is the name of a mythological figure found in the Shanhaijing (山海经), or Classic of Mountains and Seas. He is the son of the fire god Zhurong (祝融) who lives on Mount Yao, playing music while accompanied by three five-colored birds. His full name, including his title, is Taizi Changqin (太子长琴) "Prince Changqin".

column3: 长卿, 长庆, 长清, 长青, 常青, 常清, etc.(Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 长 (cháng) meaning "long" or 常 (cháng) meaning "common, frequent, regular" combined with 卿 (qīng) meaning "minister, noble, officer", 庆 (qìng) meaning "congratulate, celebrate", 清 (qīng) meaning "clear, pure, clean" or 青 (qīng) meaning "blue, green, young". From the Chinese 昌 (chāng) meaning "light of sun; good, proper" and 劭 (shào) meaning "encourage, excel; excellent".

From the Chinese 昶 (chǎng) meaning "a long day, clear, bright" and 淑 (shū) meaning "kind and gentle".

column3: 常先, 昌憲, 長賢, 昌贤, etc.(Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 常 (cháng) meaning "common, frequent, regular", 昌 (chāng) meaning "flourish, prosper, good", or 長 (cháng) meaning "long" and 先 (xiān) meaning “first”), 憲 (xiàn) meaning "law", or 贤 (xián) meaning "virtuous, worthy, wise". Other characters can also form this name.In Chinese mythology, Changxian (常先) was one of the prominent retainers serving the Yellow Emperor (Xuanyuan) along with Fenghou and Limu. According to legend, he contributed to the war against Chiyou by inventing the first war drum, using the skin of the Kui (a mythical ox-like creature with only one leg) for the drum surface and the thigh bones of the Leishou (thunder beast) as drumsticks.
From the Chinese 嫦 (cháng), the name of a moon goddess, and 相 (xiāng) meaning "mutual, each other".
From the Chinese 昌 (chāng) meaning "light of sun; good, proper" and 旭 (xù) meaning "rising sun; brilliance; radiant".
From the Chinese 阊 (chāng) meaning "gate of heaven" and 燕 (yàn) meaning "swallow (bird)".
From the Chinese 唱 (chàng) meaning "sing" or 昌 (chāng) meaning "light of sun; good, proper" and 谣 (yáo) meaning "folksong, ballad" or 幺 (yāo) meaning "one" or "youngest, small".
From the Chinese 昌 (chāng) meaning "light of sun; good, proper" and 怡 (yí) meaning "happy, joyful; harmony, joy".

column3: 长银, 长印, 昌胤, etc.(Chinese)

“Chang” (长) can mean “long” or “growing,” and “ying” (英) can mean “hero,” “outstanding,” or “flower.”
