column3: 千代女(Japanese Kanji)|ちよめ(Japanese Hiragana)
column12: Derived from the Japanese kanji 千 (chi) meaning "a thousand" combined with 代 (yo) meaning "generation; society, era" and 女 (me) meaning "woman; wife".Other characters combinations are also possible.

column3: 千世美, 千代美, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From 千 (chi) meaning "thousand" and 世 (yo) meaning "world" or 代 (yo) meaning "generation, age, replace, change, substitute" and 美 (mi) meaning "beauty". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: 千代音, 千世音, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: This name is made of 千 (chi) meaning "thousand", 世 (yo, se) meaning "world", or 代 (yo) meaning "generation, age, replace, substitute, period", with 音 (ne, non) meaning "sound, noise". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: 千代乃, 千世乃, etc.(Japanese Kanji)|チヨノ(Japanese Katakana)|ちよの(Japanese Hiragana)
column12: From Japanese 千 (chi) meaning "thousand" combined with 代 (yo) meaning "generation" or 世 (yo) meaning "world" combined with 乃 (no), a possessive particle. Other kanji combinations can form this name as well.

column3: 千代之介, 千代之助, 千代乃介, etc.(Japanese Kanji)|千代ノ介(Kanji/Katakana)|ちよのすけ(Japanese Hiragana)|チヨノスケ(Japanese Katakana)
column12: From Chiyo combined with the genitive particle の (no), written as 之, 乃 or the katakana equivalent ノ, and suke, originally denoting a kokushi (provincial governor) with the 2nd-highest level of suke (介), also written with other kanji like 助.One bearer of this name was actor and buyō dancer Chiyonosuke Azuma (東 千代之介), born Takayuki Wakawada (若和田 孝之) (1926-2000).This name is very rarely used.

column3: ちより(Japanese Hiragana)|千依, 千尚, 千頼, 千和, 知順, 千世理, 千世里, 千陽里, 智由, 智代理, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 千 (chi) meaning "thousand", 知 (chi) meaning "know, wisdom" or 智 (chi) meaning "wisdom, intellect" combined with 依 (yori) meaning "reliant, depend on, consequently, therefore, due to", 尚 (yori) meaning "esteem, furthermore, still, yet", 頼 (yori) meaning "trust, request", 和 (yori) meaning "harmony, Japanese style, peace, soften, Japan", or 順 (yori) meaning "obey, order, turn, right, docility, occasion". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: チヨシ(Japanese Katakana)|ちよし(Japanese Hiragana)|智良, 知義, 千喜, 千芳, 知代司, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 千 (chi) meaning "thousand" combined with 吉 (yoshi) meaning "good luck". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: 千代介, 千代輔, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From 千 (chi, sen) meaning "thousand", 代 (yo) meaning "generation, era", and 輔, 助, or 介 (suke) means "help, assist". Other kanji combinations can be used.

From Chinese 蚩 (chī) meaning "ignorant, worm" and 尤 (yóu) meaning "outstanding, particular". This is the name of a mythological tribal chieftain who famously opposed the Yellow Emperor. Various sources describe him as a horned humanoid with four eyes, six arms, and hoofed feet, with 81 brothers-in-arms. He was defeated and killed at the Battle of Zhuolu, but is said to have given rise to several ethnic minorities in southern China. The Hmong people in particular venerate him as their ancestor.

column3: 千代幸, 千代之, 千代有希, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From 千 (chi) meaning "thousand", 代 (yo) meaning "world, society", 幸 (yuki) meaning "happiness, good fortune, luck". Other kanji combinations can be used.

column3: 祺缘, 启元, etc.(Chinese)|祺緣, 啟元, etc.(Traditional Chinese)

column3: 知幸, 千雪, 智雪, 千幸, etc.(Japanese Kanji)

column3: 茅友子, 茅悠子, 茅結子, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 茅 (chi) meaning "miscanthus reed", 悠 (yu) meaning "permanence", and 子 (ko) meaning "child". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: 千友美, 知友美, etc.(Japanese Kanji)

column3: 知優乃(Japanese Kanji)|ちゆの(Japanese Hiragana)|チユノ(Japanese Katakana)
column12: From 千 (chi) meaning "thousand", 由 (yu) meaning "cause, reason, origin", and 乃 (no) meaning "from, therefore, accordingly." Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: ちゆり(Japanese Hiragana)|千百合, 知友莉, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 千 (chi) meaning "thousand" and 百合 (yuri) meaning "lily." Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: 千友, 知勇, 知友, 智遊, 痴遊, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 千 (chi) meaning "thousand" combined with 友 (yuu) meaning "friend". Other kanji combinations are possible.
The meaning of the name Chiyva is linked with destruction.

column3: チヅ(Japanese Katakana)|ちづ(Japanese Hiragana)|千都, 千鶴, 智珠, 智津, etc.(Japanese Kanji)

From Japanese 千 (chi) meaning "thousand" and 鶴 (tsu) meaning "crane (bird)" combined with 美 (mi) meaning "beautiful, beauty". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: 智津夫, 千津雄, etc.(Japanese Kanji)|ちづお(Japanese Hiragana)|チヅオ(Japanese Katakana)
column12: From Japanese 智 (chi) meaning "wisdom, intellect" or 千 (chi) meaning "thousand" combined with 津 (zu) meaning "harbour, port, ferry" and 夫 (o) meaning "man, husband" or 雄 (o) meaning "hero, male, manly". Other kanji combinations can form this name as well.This was the real name of Japanese religious leader Shoko Asahara (1955-2018), who was born as Chizuo Matsumoto.

column3: 千鶴子, 智奉子, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 智 (chi) meaning "intellect, knowledge, wisdom", 鶴 (tsuru) meaning "crane (bird)" or 奉 (zuru) meaning "to offer, to present" and 子 (ko) meaning "child", as well as other character combinations.
Variant of Cleo influenced by a misspelling of Chloe.

Short from of names containing the Old High German name element hlûd "famous", such as Chlothar. Chlodio lived in the 5th century AD and was a Merovingian king of the Salian Franks.
Variant of Chlodowald. Saint Chlodoald lived in the 6th century AD and was the son of Chlodomer, a Frankish king from the Merovingian dynasty.
Derived from Old High German hlûd "famous" combined with Old High German beraht "bright."

Derived from Old High German hlûd "famous" combined with rîcja "powerful, strong, mighty." The second element is also closely related to Celtic rîg or rix and Gothic reiks, which all mean "king, ruler." Chlodoric lived in the 6th century AD and was the son of Sigobert the Lame, a Frankish king of Cologne.

Derived from Old High German hlûd "famous" combined with Gothic sinths "way, path." Chlodosind lived in the 6th century AD and was a daughter of Chlothar I, a Frankish king from the Merovingian dynasty.
Chlodosinda (or Chlodosuinda) was a Frankish princess, the daughter of King Sigebert I and Queen Brunhilda.
Derived from Old High German hlûd "famous" combined with Gothic svinths (swind in Old High German) "strength."
Derived from Old High German hlûd "famous" combined with Gothic valdan "to reign."
Derived from Old High German hlut ("loud, famous") and wīg ("battle, fight").
Derived from Old High German hlûd "famous" combined with Old High German wîg "warrior." Also, see Ludwig.
Elaboration of Chloe formed using the Italian diminutive suffix -ella. Alternatively, it may be an anglicized variant of Cloelia.
Combination of Chloe and the name suffix lyn.
Maybe a blend of Chloe and Ayesha.
Rare combination of Chloe and the French diminutive suffix -ette.
Chloreus is an effeminate eunuch priest of Cybele in the Aeneid. Camilla attempts to kill him for his armor, and is in turn killed by Arruns.
Possibly a blend of Chloris and Clarice.
Elaborated form of Chloris, influenced by Clarissa.
Latinized form of the Greek word khlôros "pale green" (see also Chloris). This name was borne by a Western Roman emperor from the 3rd century AD.
Derived from Old High German hlûd "famous" combined with Old Norse hildr "battle."
Variant of Chlothild. Chlothilde was the wife of Clovis I, a Merovingian king of the Franks.
From the Frankish element hroþi, "fame, glory", and Gothic swinþs. Chlothsind was a Frankish princess who became the queen consort of the Lombard king Alboin.
Ancient Aleut personal name meaning "Sea otter"
Variant spelling of Cnodomar. Chnodomar was the name of a 4th-century king of the Alamanni, a Germanic tribe.
Alternate transcription of Burmese ချော (see Chaw).
From Sino-Korean 草 (cho) "grass, straw, thatch, herbs" and 娥 (a) "be beautiful; good".

The first element of this name is derived from Old Church Slavonic xotěti or xŭtěti "to want, to wish, to desire", which is ultimately derived from Proto-Slavic xъtěti "to want, to wish, to desire". column3: 朝城, 朝常, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 朝 (chou) meaning "morning" combined with 城 (jou) meaning "castle" or 常 (jou) meaning "always, constantly, consistently". Other kanji combinations are possible.Famous bearer of this name is Choujou Ooyama, he was the legislator of the Ryukyu Government and Okinawa, Japan.
From Japanese 蝶 (chou) meaning "butterfly" and 紀 (ki) meaning "chronicle". Other kanji combinations are possible.
Maghrebi transcription of Shukri (chiefly Moroccan and Algerian).
From Japanese 蝶 (chou) meaning "butterfly" combined with 海 (mi) meaning "sea, ocean". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: ちょうのすけ(Japanese Hiragana)|チョウノスケ(Japanese Katakana)|兆之輔, 朝之介, etc.(Japanese Kanji)|貞ノ助(Kanji/Katakana)
column12: From Japanese 長 (chou) meaning "chief, head, leader", 之 (no), a possessive marker, combined with 輔 (suke) meaning "help". Other kanji combinations are possible.A famous bearer was Chounosuke Iba (1916-2004), Japanese chairman of a business.
Alternate transcription of شروق (see Sherouk), chiefly used in Morocco.

column3: 猪助, 猪介, 猪輔, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: This is an uncommon Japanese name for males. 猪 (Chou) means "Boar". 輔、介, 助 (Suke) all nearly mean the same thing, "Aid, Help, Rescue, Save, Assist, Herald" etc. There are many possibilities regarding kanji for this name, this a short summary is all.

column3: 澄三郎, 蝶三朗, 長三郎, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 澄 (chou) meaning "clear, pure", 蝶 (chou) meaning "butterfly" or 長 (chou) meaning "leader; master; chief; head", 三 (zabu) meaning "three" combined with 郎 (rou) meaning "son" or 朗 (rou) meaning "bright, clear". Other kanji combinations are possible as well.
Means "jackdaw” in Chechen, referring to a type of crow.
Combination of Sino-Korean 草 (cho) "grass, straw, thatch, herbs" and Sino-Korean 元 "first; dollar; origin; head"
From an English spelling of the name of the cholla cactus.
Combination of Sino-Korean 草 (cho) "grass, straw, thatch, herbs" and From Sino-Korean 藝 (ye) "art; talent, ability; craft" or 乂 (ye) "govern, control, manage; nurture"

column3: 祖儀, 祖貽, 祖兒, etc.(Chinese)
column12: Cantonese romanisation of Zuyi or Zu'er.
From Tuvan чойган (choygan) meaning "fir" and оол (ool) meaning "boy, son".
Alternate transcription of Tibetan ཆོས་འཛོམས (see Choezom).
Names of the Merowingian Duke of Ultrajuranus. Derived from Chram (hram) "raven".
Variant of Charisse, notable person is Chrese Evans, originally named Olga Peters, granddaughter of Joseph Stalin, dictator of the Soviet Union.
Transferred use of a Swedish surname Chrisander.
Apparently a blend of Chrysanta or Christine and Cassandra.

Combination of Chris and Ann. In the case of Chrisann Brennan (1954-), a former partner of the late Apple co-founder Steve Jobs and the mother of his daughter Lisa Brennan-Jobs, her parents named her after the chrysanthemum flower, making it a variant of Chrysanta.
Alternate transcription of Greek Χρυσάνθη (see Chrysanthi).

Alemannic variant of Christiana recorded in medieval German-speaking Switzerland. This name was occasionally used in honor of Saint Chrischona, particularly in the Swiss city of Basel.According to legend, Saint Chrischona accompanied Saint Ursula and the bishop Saint Pantalus on a pilgrimage to Rome. One version of the legend has her fall ill and die upon her return to Switzerland; she was then buried on the hill Dinkelberg, known today as "St. Chrischona", not far from Basel.In another version, the pilgrims are attacked by the Huns on their way home. When Saint Pantalus is killed, Chrischona and her sisters Margaretha and Ottilia escape. Each of the sisters moves on one of the three hills bordering Basel and builds a chapel on the hilltop. They preach the gospel and convert the pagan townsfolk to Christianity, leading by example by living virtuous lives.
Variant of Chrishawn. A known female bearer is American television personality Chrisean Rock (2000-).
Combination of Chris and the popular suffix ella.
Elaborated form of Chris using the French feminine name suffix -elle.
Combination of Chris with the popular diminutive suffix ette.
Modern spelling of Christian. This is the middle name of American rapper Christopher Chrishan Dotson (1989-).
Possibly a blend of Christian and Rashawn.
In the case of American actress Chrishell Stause (1981-), her mother went into labor at a Shell station, and an attendant named Chris helped deliver the baby.
Variant of Michelle, influenced by Chris.
Combination of Chris with the popular name suffix -inda.
A blend of two names, the first one starting in Chris and the second one ending in -aine (e.g., Ghislaine or Elaine).
Transferred use of the surname Chrisley. First used in 2014 with 8 baby girls born with this name.

In the case of Indonesian singer Chrismansyah "Chrisye" Rahadi (1949-2007), who was born as Christian Rahadi, it is composed of the first part of his birth name, Chris- combined with the Indonesian suffix -syah derived from the Persian title شاه (šâh). Chrisye changed his name in 1982 when he formally converted from Christianity to Islam.
Variant transcription of Greek Χρυσόστομος (see Chrysostomos).

Short form of given names that contain the Greek adjective χριστός (christos) meaning "anointed", such as Christiaan, Christian, Christine and Christoffel.The name is unisex in the Dutch-speaking world (such as Flanders and the Netherlands), but much more commonly used on males than on females.
Diminutive of Christa, This name is now known as a water brand
A diminutive of Christian using the german diminutive suffix -chen.
Variant of Christian or Christine. Christean was given to 5 girls in 1992 according to the SSA.
Variant of Kristela influenced by French Christ.
Latinate variant of Christelle; in some cases, however, it can also be a contracted form of Christabella.

Combination of Christina and Crescentia as well as an obsolete French diminutive of names beginning with Christ-. A middle name bearer of the variant Christenze was Danish novelist Karen Blixen (1885-1962), who wrote under the pen name Isak Dinesen.
A name coined from the name elements Christ "Christus" and *Frid* "peace" by German pietists in the 18th century.
Meaning "May Christ help". See also Gotthelf.
Modern Greek transcription of Chreste. Also compare the masculine equivalent Christos.
Variant of Christiana. It could also be given in reference to the former name of the Norwegian capital (now called Oslo).
From the name of the religion, Christianity.
Combination of the name Christian and Persian شاه (shāh) meaning "king".

Elaboration of the name Christian with the -y ending in order to feminize the name. This name could also be a variant of the name Christine. This name is primarily used by Christian community in Indonesia.
Dutch and Afrikaans form of Christine.
Variant spelling of Christian. A notable bearer of this name is the Dutch professional racing driver Christijan Albers (b. 1979).
Dutch form of Christinus or Christine, depending on the sex of the bearer. A known bearer of this name is the Dutch speed skater Christijn Groeneveld (b. 1984).
Elaborated form of Christine ending with the suffix -ey.
Variant of Christian. According to the SSA, Christion was given to 7 boys in 2018.
Austrian German diminutive of given names that start with Christ-, such as Christian, Christoph and Christina.

Derived from the archaic German noun Christ meaning "Christ" combined with the German adjective lieb meaning "dear, sweet" (ultimately from ancient Germanic leub meaning "dear, beloved"). In other words, you could say that this name is a German calque of Christophilus.
Short form of Christopher or Christian.
Means "gift of Christ", derived from Χριστός (Christos) combined with δωρον (doron) meaning "gift".
Latinized form of Christodoros. This name was borne by a Greek epic poet from the 6th century AD.
Alternate transcription of Greek Χριστοφίλη (see Christofili), which is the modern Greek feminine form of Christophilos.
Perhaps a variant of Christoph or a shortened form of Christopher.
From the Ancient Greek Χριστός (Christos) meaning "anointed" and φάνεια (phaneia) meaning "appearing".
Late Greek feminine form of Christophilos as well as the French masculine and feminine form of Christophilus.
Means "beloved Christ" or "friend of Christ" in Greek. It is derived from the name of Christ combined with the Greek element φίλος (philos) meaning "beloved, dear" as well as "friend, lover".
The name Christraud is a modern blend of Christine and names ending in -traud (like Waltraud).
Standardized form of Cristoinus, a name found in a medieval Latin record, which was derived from Latin Christus meaning "Christ" and Old High German wini "friend".
Variant of Christiana or a combination of Christy and Anna.
Possibly a combination of names containing Christ such as Christiane and Christine and the suffix -vie. This name appears to be most common in the Democratic Republic of Congo.
Alternate transcription of Greek Χρυσούλα (see Chrysoula).
Compound name of Christine and Suzette.
Strictly Limburgish short form of Christian and Christopher.
French form of the Germanic name Hrothildis (see Rothild). This was the original name of Saint Clotilde (for whom the names Rohilde or Rotilde would be more accurate).
Form of Rotgang borne by an 8th-century Frankish saint.
Chrodobert was an Aleman dux (leader) in the early 7th century.
Possibly derived from Greek chroma meaning "color". This is the name of one of the protagonists of the video game Fire Emblem: Awakening. Variant of Chrome
Derived from the Greek noun χρῶμα (chroma) meaning "colour", which is a word that originally referred to the colour of one's skin (i.e. complexion).
Latinized form of Chromatios.A notable bearer of this name was the 5th-century saint Chromatius of Aquileia.

Probably derived from Ancient Greek χρῶμα (chroma) meaning "skin, surface; complexion, colour, pigment". In Greek mythology, Chromia was a daughter of king Itonus of Iton. In some traditions, she was married to Endymion.

Most likely derived from Ancient Greek χρόμος (chromos) meaning "crashing sound" or "neighing, whinnying (of a horse)". It coincides with χρόμιος (chromios), a kind of sea fish apparently named for the creaking or grunting noise it made. Also compare χρῶμα (chroma) meaning "colour".
Latinized form of Chromios. This is the name of several characters in Greek mythology, one of them being a son of king Priam.
A more or less latinized form of Rothild.

Chrothildis was a Frankish queen consort by marriage to king Theuderic III. She was formally the nominal regent for her son Clovis IV during his minority from his succession in 691 until her own death in 692, though in reality the de facto regent was Pepin of Herstal.
Variant of Chrothild. Chrotilda was the daughter of Clovis I (a Frankish king) and wife of Amalaric, a 6th-century king of the Visigoths.
A more or less latinized form of Rodelind.
A more or less latinized form of Rotrud.
A character in Molière's "L'école des femmes" (The School for Wives ).
Chrysale is a character in the play "Les Femmes Savantes" (The Learned Ladies), a comedy by Molière.

From the word referring to the pupa of a butterfly or moth or the cocoon where the pupa is enclosed inside, derived via Latin from Ancient Greek χρυσαλλίς (khrusallís), from χρυσός (khrusós) meaning "gold."A My Little Pony: Friendship is Magic villain bears this name.
Possibly a combination of Chrysa and Anna inspired by Chrysanthi.
Means "chrysanthemum" in French. This was used in Pierre Loti's novel 'Madame Chrysanthème' (1887), which was adapted into an opera in 1893 by André Messager.

From the name of the daisy-like flower, derived from the Latinized form of Ancient Greek χρῡσάνθεμον (khrusanthemon) meaning "gold flower", composed of χρῡσός (chrysos) "gold" and ἄνθεμον (anthemon) "flower". Compare Chrysanthos, composed of the same words and meaning, albeit worded differently.This name has been in occasional use from the 19th century onwards, making it one of the many Victorian flower names.

Feminine form of Chrysanthos.According to an Argive legend recorded by Pausanias, Chrysanthis informed Demeter of the abduction of Persephone by Hades when Demeter was visiting Pelasgus in Argos. Thus, in the Argive account Chrysanthis substitutes for Hecate of the Homeric hymn to Demeter.
Chrysanthemum is a female variant. There is also two Mongolian variants, Chrisathius and Tshissathies.

Latinized form of Chrysanthos. Saints Chrysanthus and Daria (3rd century – c. 283) are saints of the Early Christian period. Their names appear in the Martyrologium Hieronymianum, an early martyrs list, and a church was built in their honour over their reputed burial place in Rome.

Means "sword of gold" or "he who has a golden sword", from Ancient Greek χρυσός (chrysos) meaning "golden" and ἄορ (aor) meaning "sword hung in a belt, hanger; any weapon". In Greek mythology Chrysaor was a son of Poseidon and Medusa, he and his brother Pegasus springing from the severed neck of their mother. It was also an epithet of several deities.
Means "golden dawn, golden sunrise" in Greek.
Derivative of Cryseis, via the patronym Chryseis.
German form of Chrysippos via its latinized form Chrysippus.
French form of Chrysippos via its latinized form Chrysippus.
Means "horse of gold", derived from Greek χρυσός (chrysos) "gold" combined with Greek ἵππος (hippos) "horse".

Latinized form of Chrysippos. In history, this name was most notably borne by Chrysippus of Soli, a Stoic philosopher from the 3rd century BC. In Greek mythology, this was the name of a divine hero with a very tragic story.

Probably a variant of Chrysogone. This was the name of a Minyan princess as the daughter of King Almus of Orchomenus. She was the sister of Chryse and mother, by the sea-god Poseidon, of Chryses, father of the eponym Minyas.
Variant of Chrysogeneia. This was the name of a naiad daughter of the river-god Peneus in Greek mythology,

Feminine form of Chrysogonos. According to some sources, this was the name of the mother of Minyas in Greek mythology. Edmund Spenser used this name in his poem The Faerie Queene (1590; in the form Chrysogonee), where it belongs to the mother of Belphoebe and her twin sister Amoret.

Variant of Chrysogone used by Edmund Spenser in his poem 'The Faerie Queene' (1590), where it belongs to the virgin mother of Belphoebe and her twin sister Amoret. Chrysogonee hides in the forest and, becoming tired, falls asleep on a bank, where she is impregnated by sunbeams and gives birth to twins. The goddesses Venus and Diana find the newborn twin girls and take them: Venus takes Amoret and raises her in the Garden of Adonis, and Diana takes Belphoebe.

Means "born of gold, begotten of gold" or "gold-bearing" in Ancient Greek, derived from χρυσός (chrysos) "gold" and γόνος (gonos) meaning "offspring, child" as well as "begetting, procreation" and "race, stock, descent".

Latinized form of Chrysogonos. Saint Chrysogonus is a saint and martyr of ancient Rome venerated by the Catholic Church and the Eastern Orthodox Church. He was martyred at Aquileia, probably during the Diocletianic Persecution (303–311 AD).
Dutch form of Chrysogonos, which appears to only have been used in Flanders (albeit very rarely).

Means "speech of gold, golden-worded" in Ancient Greek, figuratively "eloquent", derived from χρυσός (chrysos) meaning "gold" and λόγος (logos) "(spoken) word, speech". This was the surname of the Italian bishop Peter Chrysologus, supposedly gifted to him by Roman Empress Galla Placidia after she listened to one of his homilies.
Latinized form of Chrysologos. This name was borne by Peter Chrysologus, a saint from the 5th century AD.
Dutch form of Chrysologus, which appears to only have been used in Flanders (albeit very rarely).
Roman cognomen borrowed from Ancient Greek Χρυσόνικος (Khrysonikos), derived from χρυσός (chrysos) meaning "gold" and νίκη (nike) meaning "victory".
Possibly derived from Ancient Greek χρυσός (chrysos) meaning "gold" and νόος (noos) meaning "mind, thought, intelligence". This was another name of Torone in Greek mythology.

Means "golden dove", from Greek χρυσός (chrysos) meaning "gold" and πελεία (peleia) meaning "dove", which is a common name element associated with female seers. In Greek mythology this was the name of a hamadryad (a type of nymph) who married Arkas, the eponymous king of Arkadia.

Means "streaming with gold" in Greek, from Greek χρυσός (chrysos) "gold" and ῥοάς (rhoás) "stream", derived from ῥοή (rhoé) "river, stream" (Compare river Chrysorrhoas). This was the by-name of John of Damascus, an Arab Christian monk, priest, hymnographer, and apologist.

Epithet of Hecate meaning "(goddess) of the lower world wearing golden sandals and drinking blood", from Greek χρυσός (chrysos) "gold", σάνδαλον (sandalon) "sandal", αἷμα (haima) "blood", ποτόν (poton) "that which one drinks" and χθόνιος (chthonios) "in the earth".
Derived from Greek χρυσός (chrysos) meaning "gold" and σθένος (sthenos) meaning "strength, power, vigour".
Dutch form of Chrysostomos, which appears to only have been used in Flanders (albeit very rarely).

Latinized form of Χρυσότελος (Chrysotelos), which should be a corruption of the rare name Χρυσοτέλης (Chrysoteles), which consists of the Greek elements χρυσός (chrysos) meaning "gold" and τέλος (telos) meaning "purpose, result, completion".However, it should be noted that at least one source claims that the name is actually derived from Greek χρυσότερος (chrysoteros) meaning "more golden". If that is true, then Chrysotelos is again a corruption, but then of what should originally be Χρυσότερος (Chrysoteros).This name was borne by an obscure saint from the 3rd century AD. He was a priest who was martyred in either Babylon or Persia on the orders of the Roman emperor Decius. His feast day is on 22 April (Roman Catholic), 30 July (Eastern Orthodox) and 7 October (Greek Orthodox).In the Greek Church, the saint is known as Chrysotelis, which is the modern Greek form of the previously mentioned name Chrysoteles.
From Greek χρυσός (chrysos) "golden" combined with θεός (theos) "god".

Derived from Ancient Greek χρυσός (chrysos) meaning "gold" and θέμις (themis) meaning "law of nature, divinely ordained justice, that which is laid down". This was the name of several figures in Greek mythology, including a daughter of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra, one of the fifty daughters of king Danaus, the first winner of a singing contest held at the Pythian games, and a Hesperide depicted on an ancient vase.
Masculine form of Chrysovalantou. A known bearer of this name is the Greek soccer player Chrysovalantis Kozoronis (b. 1992).

From the epithet of Irene Chrysovalantou, a 9th-century Greek Orthodox saint who is considered a patron of conception and fertility. It means "of Chrysobalanton", from the name of the ancient monastery in Constantinople where she was abbess (allegedly from the name of a region of the Byzantine empire which derives from Greek χρυσος (chrysos) "golden" and βαλαντιο (balantio) "coin").
Sorbian form and English variant of Christa.
From Greek χρυσός (chrysós) "gold" and the given name Eleni.
Contracted variant of Christina.The name is borne by the Canadian writer, journalist, and politician Chrystia Freeland.
Sorbian and English variant of Christina.
Variant of Christos. Chrystos, born Christina Smith, is an American writer and activist who self-identifies as two-spirit.
Polish form of Chrysippos via its latinized form Chrysippus.
Variant transcription of Heled.This transcription is used in the Septuagint Bible.
Derived from Ancient Greek χθών (chthon) meaning "ground, earth, soil" (genitive χθονός) and φυλή (phyle) meaning "tribe, race". This was the name of a princess of Sicyon in Greek mythology.

From a non-Sino-Vietnamese reading of Chinese 字 (chữ) meaning "letter, character, script".
From a non-Sino-Vietnamese reading of Chinese 助 (chữa) meaning "to treat, correct, repair" (compare Trợ).
From Sino-Vietnamese 準 (chuẩn) meaning "standard, fitting, correct".
From the Chinese 传 (chuán) meaning "summon, propagate, transmit" and 兵 (bīng) meaning "soldier, troops".
From the Chinese 传 (chuán) meaning "summon, propagate, transmit" and 超 (chāo) meaning "leap over, surpass".
From the Chinese 传 (chuán) meaning "summon, propagate, transmit" and 聪 (cōng) meaning "intelligent, clever, bright".
From the Chinese 传 (chuán) meaning "summon, propagate, transmit" and 德 (dé) meaning "heart, mind, morals, virtue, ethics".
From the Chinese 传 (chuán) meaning "summon, propagate, transmit" and 钢 (gāng) meaning "steel; hard, strong, tough".
From the Chinese 传 (chuán) meaning "summon, propagate, transmit" and 耿 (gěng) meaning "bright, shining".
From Chinese 传 (chuán) meaning "pass on" combined with 广 (guǎng) meaning "vast" or short for “Guangzhou”. Other character combinations are possible.

From the Chinese character 窗 (chuāng) meaning "window" combined with 霞 (xiá) meaning "rosy clouds, mist" or 夏 (xià) meaning "summer, great, grand".Other character combinations can form this name as well.
From the Chinese 传 (chuán) meaning "summon, propagate, transmit" and 皓 (hào) meaning "bright, luminous, clear".
From the Chinese 传 (chuán) meaning "summon, propagate, transmit" and 虎 (hǔ) meaning "tiger; brave, fierce".
From the Chinese 传 (chuán) meaning "summon, propagate, transmit" and 佳 (jiā) meaning "beautiful, fine, good, auspicious".
From the Chinese 传 (chuán) meaning "summon, propagate, transmit" and 建 (jiàn) meaning "build, establish".
From the Chinese 传 (chuán) meaning "summon, propagate, transmit" and 进 (jìn) meaning "advance, make progress" or 金 (jīn) meaning "gold, metal, money".
From the Chinese 传 (chuán) meaning "summon, propagate, transmit" and 俊 (jùn) meaning "talented, capable, handsome" or 军 (jūn) meaning "army, military, soldier".
From the Chinese 传 (chuán) meaning "summon, propagate, transmit" and 凯 (kǎi) meaning "triumphant; triumph, victory".
From the Chinese 传 (chuán) meaning "summon, propagate, transmit" and 昆 (kūn) meaning "elder brother".
From the Chinese 传 (chuán) meaning "summon, propagate, transmit" and 良 (liáng) meaning "good, virtuous".
From the Chinese 传 (chuán) meaning "summon, propagate, transmit" and 烈 (liè) meaning "fiery, ardent".
From the Chinese 传 (chuán) meaning "summon, propagate, transmit" and 禄 (lù) meaning "blessing, happiness, prosperity".
From the Chinese 传 (chuán) meaning "summon, propagate, transmit" and 眠 (mián) meaning "sleep".
From the Chinese 传 (chuán) meaning "summon, propagate, transmit" and 敏 (mǐn) meaning "agile, nimble, quick, clever, smart".
From the Chinese 传 (chuán) meaning "summon, propagate, transmit" and 明 (míng) meaning "bright, light, brilliant, clear".
From Thai ชวน (chuan) meaning "persuade" and พิศ (phit) meaning "stare, gaze".
From the Chinese 传 (chuán) meaning "summon, propagate, transmit" and 强 (qiáng) meaning "strong, powerful".
From the Chinese 传 (chuán) meaning "summon, propagate, transmit" and 虬 (qiú) meaning "young dragon".
From the Chinese 传 (chuán) meaning "summon, propagate, transmit" and 瑞 (ruì) meaning "felicitous omen, auspicious".
From the Chinese 传 (chuán) meaning "summon, propagate, transmit" and 嵩 (sōng) meaning "high, lofty".
From Chinese 传 (chuán) "to deliver, to teach, to pass down" and 堂 (táng) "main room (of house)". Other hanzi combinations are possible.
From the Chinese 传 (chuán) meaning "summon, propagate, transmit" and 添 (tiān) meaning "increase, add to".
From the Chinese 传 (chuán) meaning "summon, propagate, transmit" and 统 (tǒng) meaning "govern, command, unite".
From the Chinese 传 (chuán) meaning "summon, propagate, transmit" and 文 (wén) meaning "literature, culture, writing".
From the Chinese 传 (chuán) meaning "summon, propagate, transmit" and 先 (xiān) meaning "first, former".
From the Chinese 传 (chuán) meaning "summon, propagate, transmit" and 心 (xīn) meaning "heart, mind, intelligence, soul".
From the Chinese 传 (chuán) meaning "summon, propagate, transmit" and 雄 (xióng) meaning "male, manly, grand, hero".
From the Chinese 传 (chuán) meaning "summon, propagate, transmit" and 旭 (xù) meaning "rising sun; brilliance; radiant".
From the Chinese 传 (chuán) meaning "summon, propagate, transmit" and 耀 (yào) meaning "shine, sparkle, dazzle; glory".
From the Chinese 传 (chuán) meaning "summon, propagate, transmit" and 寅 (yín) meaning "respect, reverence; respectfully".
From the Chinese 传 (chuán) meaning "summon, propagate, transmit" and 友 (yǒu) meaning "friend, companion; friendly" or 优 (yōu) meaning "superior, excellent".
From the Chinese 传 (chuán) meaning "summon, propagate, transmit" and 裕 (yù) meaning "abundant, rich, plentiful" or 彧 (yù) meaning "refined, cultured".
From the Chinese 传 (chuán) meaning "summon, propagate, transmit" and 钊 (zhāo) meaning "endeavor, encourage, strive" or 召 (zhào) meaning "summon".
From the Chinese 传 (chuán) meaning "summon, propagate, transmit" and 志 (zhì) meaning "ideal; purpose, will".
From the Chinese 传 (chuán) meaning "summon, propagate, transmit" and 祝 (zhù) meaning "pray for happiness or blessings".
Chamorro name from the Spanish word chubasco meaning "downpour", itself from Latin pluvia "rain".
From the Spanish word chubasco, meaning "squall", which is from the Portuguese word chuva, meaning "rain".
From Sino-Vietnamese 職 (chức) meaning "duty, office, rank".
From the Chinese 楚 (chǔ) meaning "clear" and 璨 (càn) meaning "luster of gems, lustrous".
Means "anguishes" in Caló. This name is used as the Caló form of Angustias.
From Thai ชู (chu) meaning "raise, lift up" and ชัย (chai) meaning "victory".
Alternate transcription of Thai ชูชาติ (see Chuchat).
From Thai ชู (chu) meaning "to raise, to elevate, to lift" and ชาติ (chat) meaning "life, birth, origin, existence".
From the Aymara chuchi meaning "honey coloured, light coffee coloured" and nayra meaning "eye".

Chu meaning "Life" it can be used as both a girl or boy name. It also link to another name Chuchu or Chu-Chu meaning double life.It's a west African name commonly use in Ivory Coast and Liberia. The english version of the name is Eve for a girl and Adam for a guy.
The name of a character in 'Rikki-Tikki Tavi', a short story in 'The Jungle Book' (1894) by Rudyard Kipling about the adventures of a valiant young mongoose.
From the Chinese 楚 (chǔ) meaning "clear" and 慈 (cí) meaning "kind, loving, charitable, benevolent".

Used by American singer Diana Ross for her daughter born 1975. According to Ross, it originated as a misspelling of the word chutney, which refers to a type of condiment, and is derived from Hindi चाटना (chāṭnā) "to lick, to eat with appetite".Ross stated: 'Friends kept suggesting popular names like Courtney, but so many girl babies were getting that. I suddenly thought of something I liked very much — chutney. Only I didn’t know how to spell it — I put a ‘d’ where the ‘t’ should have been on the birth certificate. And that’s how my little girl became Chudney!'

column12: From the stem of Okinawan adjective 美/清らさん (churasan) meaning "beautiful, lovely," cognate to Japanese 清ら (kiyora), an archaic term referring to elegant and dazzling beauty, otherwise the stem of 清らか (kiyoraka) meaning "clean, pure, chaste."For the final element, any kanji that can be read as ra is used, like 楽 meaning "comfort, ease" or 良 meaning "good." When written after 美, any kanji that evokes an image can also be used, e.g. 心, normally read as kokoro meaning "heart, mind." As for the initial element, aside from 美, any single or multiple kanji whose readings can be shifted to chu can be used, such as 宙 meaning "space, air" or 千由, from 千 meaning "thousand" and 由 meaning "reason, cause."This name is rarely used.
Variant transcription of Hurai.This transcription is used in the Orthodox Jewish Bible.
From Thai จุไร (churai) meaning "hair, hairline" and พร (phon) meaning "blessing".
From Thai จุไร (churai) meaning "hairline, topknot" and รัตน์ (rat) meaning "gem, jewel".
From Thai จุไร (churai) meaning "hair, hairline" and วรรณ (wan) meaning "colour, tint".

From Thai ชู (chu) meaning "to raise, to elevate, to lift" and ศักดิ์ (sak) meaning "power".
Variant of Chusefa (via the Catalan form Jusepa).

Means "twice-evil Kushite". Chushan indicates Kushite origins, while Rishathan means "double wickedness". Name of a King of Mesopotamia and the first oppressor of Israel in the Book of Judges. This is likely not the King's real name, but rather, an insulting epithet.
From the Chinese 初 (chū) meaning "beginning" and 霜 (shuāng) meaning "frost".
Diminutive of Chus, which in turn is a diminutive of Jesús.

From Thai จุฑา (chutha) meaning "topknot, hairpin" and รัตน์ (rat) meaning "gem, jewel".
From the Sanskrit चुटीला chutila, meaning “silken braid with tassels”.

From Japanese 中 (chuu) meaning "China" combined with 也 (ya) meaning "also". Other kanji combinations are possible.
From Thai ชู (chu) meaning "raise, lift up" and วิทย์ (wit) meaning "knowledge, science".
From the Chinese 俶 (chù) meaning "start, beginning" and 曦 (xī) meaning "sunshine, sunlight, early dawn".
From the Chinese 楚 (chǔ) meaning "clear" and 姚 (yáo) meaning "handsome, elegant".
From Sino-Vietnamese 專 (chuyên) meaning "diligent, expert, to specialize".
Means "mouse, rat" probably a variant of the Hindi word चूहा chooha (or chuha) with the same meaning.Chuyia is the protagonist in Bapsi Sidhwa's 2006 novel 'Water'.
From the Chinese 楚 (chǔ) meaning "clear" and 潆 (yíng) meaning "tiny stream; swirl around" or 莺 (yīng) meaning "oriole, green finch".
Means "lung" in Aymara, conceptually seen as the 'heart' of a person or seat of sentiment and emotion in Aymara culture.
Chuza was the manager of Herod Antipas' household. His wife, Joanna, was a follower of Jesus.

Means "praises God" from the Slavic elements xvaliti "to praise" and bogŭ "God".
Means "praises peace" from the Slavic elements xvaliti "to praise" and mirŭ "peace".
Derived from the Slavic elements xvaliti "to praise" and slava "glory".
alternate spelling of Kyla or Shyla
Variant of Chyler. Chylar was given to 7 girls in 2009 according to the SSA.
Meaning unknown. Notable bearer of this name is Actress Chyler Leigh (1982-).
From Chinese 真 (pinyin: Zhen) which means "true", and other similarly pronounced names. This name is mainly used in Singapore.
From Chinese 慈 (cí) meaning "affectionate, genial", in addition to other hanzi that are pronounced similarly.
Short form of Cecía and Icía.
Short form of Cecilia and Carina 2, or a variant of Kia and Sia.
Variant of Caoimhe, or derived from ciabh meaning "lock of hair" in Irish.
From Irish ciabhar meaning "locks, head of hair". In Irish mythology Ciabhán was the mortal lover of Clíodhna. It is often anglicized as Keevan.
Variant of Cadhla meaning "beautiful", or Irishized spelling of Keela, itself an Anglicized form of Caoladhe, from Irish caol meaning "slender".
Invented name, likely influenced by names like Siena and Cian.
Derived from Old Irish cían meaning "long, distant".
From the Chinese 茈 (cí) meaning "gromwell plant" and 卬 (áng) meaning "lofty, high".
Likely an invented name. Perhaps a combination of the prefix Ci- and Anne 1 or a variant of Cyan. Also compare Cianna.
Means "jet black, sable", from Old Irish cíar "dark" and dub "black", combined with a diminutive suffix.
Means "son of Ciar" in Irish, from Ciar and mac, "son".

The name "Ciaron" is a variant of the Irish name "Ciarán," which is derived from the Gaelic word "ciar," meaning "black" or "dark," and the diminutive suffix "-án," which implies smallness or endearment. Therefore, "Ciarán" translates to "little dark one" or "little dark-haired one"This name has been popular for over 1500 years and is associated with at least 26 saints, including notable figures such as Ciarán the Elder and Ciarán the Younger, who were among the Twelve Apostles of IrelandThe name is traditionally masculine and has various anglicized forms, including Kieran, Keiran, Keiron, and others.It is also connected to Irish mythology and history, with links to the son of Fergus mac Róich, who gave his name to the Ciarraige tribe and County Kerry.The name Ciaron, while less common, shares the same origins and meaning as Ciarán.

From the place name Ciarraí, which is the Irish Gaelic form of Kerry meaning "Ciar's people" (from ciar meaning "black"). This name made the top 100 of most popular girls names in Derry City and Strabane in the 1990s.

Original Irish from of Kerry/Kerri. Denoted the people of Ciar (ciar-raighe), Ciar being the son of Fergus mac Róich, who gave his name to County Kerry. Ciarraighe was thus the name of the pre-Gaelic tribe who lived in the area of what is now County Kerry. However branches of the Ciarraighe were all over Ireland.
Means "marvel, wonder" in Caló. This name is used as the Caló form of Maravilla.
Somali form of Ibadah. The name is derived from the Arabic word عبادة ('ibādah) which means worship.Different variations of name exist in other languages such as Ibadat
From the Chinese 辞 (cí) meaning "words, speech, expression" and 白 (bái) meaning "white, bright, pure".
Variant of Czcibora and feminine form of Cibor.

From the English word for the insect, derived from Latin cicada meaning "tree-cricket". The insect lives underground, nourishing itself on tree roots, for as long as 17 years before emerging. The cicada has become a queer symbol, leading some transgender and non-binary people to adopt this as their new given name.
Means "brave in lineage" using a hybrid of Old Persian and Median variants of the same name, ultimately derived from Old Persian 𐎨𐎡𐏂 (čiça) meaning "lineage, type, form" and tahma "valiant, brave".
Short form of Francesco used chiefly in Southern Italy. It was borne by Sicilian actor Ciccio Ingrassia (1922-2003).

Possibly a Sicilian diminutive of Francesco. This name is borne by the titular character of the Sicilian fairy tale 'The Story of Ciccu'. Ciccu is a young man who obtains a magic coverlet, purse, and horn from fairies, and later enters the service of a greedy king, whom he outwits and later gains his throne after the king's death. The story was originally collected by Swiss-German folklorist Laura Gonzenbach and later used by Andrew Lang in 'The Pink Fairy Book'.
Spanish and Aragonese form of Cicero.
Italian form of Cicero, which has also seen some use in Romania.
Diminutive of Cecilia and other names beginning with or containing the sound Ci.
Sundanese diminutive of feminine names containing the sound cih (or other similar sounds), such as Suci or Kurniasih.
Probably a reduplicate form of Cihuaton.
Walloon and Picard form of Cécile. As a Picard name, it is predominantly found among Huguenots.

From El Cid, the nickname of 11th-century Spanish knight Rodrigo (or Ruy) Diaz de Vivar, meaning literally "The Lord" from the Spanish-Arabic term al-sid, itself from Andalusian Arabic سِيد (sīd) "lord, master", from Arabic سَيِّد (sayyid) (see Sayyid).
After the drink, Cider. Means, "strong drink"

Of uncertain origin and meaning. A derivation from Latvian ciedrs "cedar" has been suggested.

Welsh form of Ciaran and Kieran.
Given after Cíes Islands in Galicia (Spain), itself possibly from the Proto-Indo-European root *seikw ("to dry").

Derived from Polish cieszyć "to please someone" or cieszyć się "to enjoy" and sława "fame, greatness".

Cigfa is a minor character in Welsh mythology. Her full name was Cigfa ferch Gwyn Glohoyw.

Means "the world's fortune", ultimately from Persian جهان (jahān) meaning "world, universe" and بخت (bakht) meaning "fortune, luck, happiness".
From the Chinese 茈 (cí) meaning "gromwell plant" and 鸿 (hóng) meaning "wild swan".

Means "woman snake" in Nahuatl, either derived from the goddess Cihuacōātl, or from its use as a political title.
Probably means "sick woman", from Nahuatl cihuatl "woman" and cocoxqui "sick person, a patient; something withered".
Meaning uncertain. The first element is from Nahuatl cihuatl "woman".

Means "woman-like" in Nahuatl, from cihuatl "woman" and -mani "to be like, in the manner of".
From the Chinese 辞 (cí) meaning "words, speech, expression" and 欢 (huān) meaning "joyous, happy, pleased, glad; joy".
Derived from Nahuatl cihuatl "woman" and nemi "to dwell, to live (as)" or "to walk, to go about (like)", perhaps meaning "effeminate man" or "womaniser".

Means "she imagines she is a woman", derived from Nahuatl cihuatl "woman" and nenequi "to imagine, to feign, to pretend to be something one is not; to covet".
Derived from Nahuatl cihuatl "woman" and the locative suffix -pan, possibly meaning "on the woman", "in the place of the woman", or "in the way of women".
Meaning uncertain, possibly from Nahuatl cihuapilli "noblewoman, lady" and the honorific or diminutive suffix -tzin.

The name Çilem is deeply rooted in the imagery of growth and the gentle touch of nature. It stems from çıl, a root signifying "spot," "mottled," or "mark," often describing the beauty of a partridge's plumage. This is cognate with çal ("mottled"). Furthermore, it draws from the verb çile- ("to wet slightly"), derived from çi ("moisture," "dew"). It acts as a symbol of the morning dew or the delicate, speckled beauty of the natural world; a gentle, cooling touch upon the earth.It is entirely unrelated to the Persian çile/çihil (forty); it is a purely Turkic name denoting natural elegance.
From the name of an ancient region located in southern Asia Minor, which is of pre-Greek origin, possibly Anatolian. The capital city of Cilicia was Tarsus, where the apostle Paul came from.
Hungarian form of Zillah as well as a Hungarian borrowing of German Cilla, itself a variant of Zilla.
Means "silk" in Karachay-Balkar. It also refers to the 40 coldest days of winter, or 40 hottest days of summer.
Diminutive of Cecilia, Celia and Priscilla.

Cilmaya is a legendary name deeply rooted in Turkic and Volga-Ural mythology, particularly prominent in Bashkir and Tatar folklore. It translates to "wind-horse," "winged steed," or "the one who flies like the wind."The name is a compound derived from the Proto-Turkic root jel / yel, meaning "wind," "breeze," or "spirit," combined with an archaic suffix or a regular sound shift denoting speed and ethereal movement. In the Kipchak branch of Turkic languages (such as Tatar and Bashkir), the initial Proto-Turkic y- regularly shifts to a hard c- or j-, turning Yilmaya into Cilmaya.In mythological epics (such as the Bashkir epic Ural-Batyr), Cilmaya is a magnificent, celestial winged horse born from sea foam or mountain winds, capable of crossing horizons in the blink of an eye. It serves as the Northern and Western Turkic equivalent of the Altay Tulpar.The Mythological Legend of CilmayaIn the Ural-Volga epic tradition, most notably within the grand Bashkir national epic Ural-Batyr, Cilmaya is not a mere animal, but a divine, sapient celestial creature. According to legend, Cilmaya was born from the violent collision of sea foam and mountain winds. She possesses magnificent bird-like wings that span wide enough to eclipse the sun, and her hooves never truly touch the dirt, allowing her to glide over the steppes.In the epics, Cilmaya acts as the loyal companion and spiritual guide to the hero Ural-Batyr and his lineage (specifically his son Yaik). Unlike western dragons or monsters, Cilmaya understands human speech, possesses prophetic foresight, and can cross the boundaries between the upper celestial world (the heavens) and the earthly realm in the blink of an eye. When the hero faces insurmountable dark sorcery (Deos/Demons), Cilmaya uses her wings to create massive storms, scattering enemies with the power of the North wind. She represents the ultimate bond between the steppe nomad and the spirit of the horse.Other Origins:Because of its unique global phonetics, Cilmaya shares accidental acoustic boundaries with several completely unrelated global names and toponyms:Sundanese Origins (Indonesian): The geographical place name and river Cilamaya in West Java. In Sundanese, Ci means "water/river," and Lamaya relates to a local flora or historical marker, carrying a purely Austronesian root.Latin Origins: The feminine name Clemencya (or Clementia), derived from clemens, meaning "merciful," "mild," or "gentle."Spanish / Latin American Origins: Calamaya, a rare surname or localized toponymic reference with indigenous or specific colloquial Iberian roots.Greek Origins: Cilicia (Kilikía / Κιλικία), the ancient classical name for the southern coastal region of Anatolia, derived from mythological or ancient Semitic/Hittite roots.Sanskrit / Mayan Hybrid Origins: The speculative compound of Sanskrit Cil (or Cilam / Shila, meaning "stone," "conduct," or "virtue") joined with the Sanskrit/Mesoamerican concept of Maya ("illusion" or "magic").None of these cross-cultural connections share any historical or semantic links with the winged horse of the Turkic steppes.For parents, Cilmaya is a majestic choice that evokes boundless freedom, untamed imagination, and spiritual elevated power. It symbolizes a child with an unyielding free spirit, possessing the swiftness and grace to rise above life’s obstacles, leaving a trail of wonder and inspiration behind them.
A name that derives from the word cilmi which means "knowledge" or "learning."
Variant of Celidoine, king of Scotland, son of the first Nascien and Flegentine, and ancestor of Lancelot and Galahad.
Short form of Cécile Louise. Inspired by Milou. Popular in Belgium, made famous by model Cilou Annys.
The pseudonym of Italian artist Cenni di Pepo (1240-1302).
From the Chinese 慈 (cí) meaning "kind, loving, charitable" and 梅 (méi) meaning "plum".
Means "very white, snowy white" in Karachay-Balkar.
Latinized form of Kimon. Cimon was a 5th-century BCE Athenian statesman.
The meaning is unknown. This name is used in the book 'Dealing With Dragons', by Patricia C. Wrede.

Latinized form of Greek Κιναιδιον (Kinaidion), which meant "(Eurasian) Wryneck", a type of small grey-brown woodpecker (traditionally associated with passionate and restless love as well as witchcraft, i.e., used by witches in a charm to recover unfaithful lovers). In Greek mythology this was an epithet of the nymph Iynx.
Latinized form of Kinaithon. A notable bearer of this name was the Greek poet Cinaethon of Sparta (8th century BC).

Derived from Cynara, the name of the genus of thistle-like perennial plants, native to the Mediterranean region, the Middle East, northwestern Africa and the Canary Islands.The genus name comes from Greek kynara, which means "artichoke".

A lyrical compound of Çın ("Truth") and Ay ("Moon"). It translates to "The Resonating Moon" or "The Moon of Truth." It paints the image of a light so pure and clear that it illuminates the absolute truth. It represents someone who is both beautiful and deeply authentic, a beacon of clarity in a dark or chaotic world.
From the name of the American city of Cincinnati in Ohio, which is derived from the Latin cognomen Cincinnatus.
Italian form of Cincinnatus. A known bearer of the name was Italian sculptor Cincinnato Baruzzi (1796-1878).

From a Roman cognomen meaning "having curly hair". Lucius Quinctius Cincinnatus (519-430 BC) was a statesman of the Roman Republic who became a famous model of Roman virtue by the time of the late Republic. A known bearer of the name was American poet Cincinnatus Heine Miller, known by his pen name Joaquin Miller (1837-1913).

Possibly a Portuguese form of Chindaswinth.Cindazunda was the daughter of Hermerico, king of the Suebi, in the territory that would become Spain's Galicia and the north of Portugal. She married Attaces, king of the Alans, in the early 5th century. This Suebi princess is immortalized in history as a symbol of the city of Coimbra, in Portugal, and her image appears in the official coat of arms of the city.

Possibly a Dutch diminutive of Cynthia. Cindel Towani was a main character in the TV movies Caravan of Courage: An Ewok Adventure and Ewoks: The Battle for Endor, which are part of the Star Wars universe.

From the English word meaning "ashes, ember". Its use as a feminine given name appears to be influenced by Cinderella, which means "little cinder girl" from the word cinder combined with -ella, an Italian diminutive suffix.
Combination of Cindy and the name suffix dora, possibly based on similar-sounding names such as Cinderella or Cindra.

Meaning uncertain, probably from the Minangkabau phrase cindua mato (or Indonesian cindur mata) meaning "keepsake" or "beloved, lover". Cindua Mato (or Cindur Mata) is a character in Minangkabau folklore.

A powerful masculine compound of Çın ("Truth/Reality") and Er ("Man/Hero"). It translates to "A Man of Truth," "A Real Man," or "One who resonates with the ultimate reality." This name is a badge of integrity, signifying a person whose character is fundamentally grounded in honesty, strength, and unwavering principles. It is the antithesis of deception.
Derived from Celtic cingeto "marching men, warriors" combined with Celtic rix "king." This name was borne by one of the four kings of Kent in 54 BC.
Name of a Pictish king, who ruled from circa 616 to 631.
Variant of Cináed. Ciniod son of Uuredech was king of the Picts from 763 until 775.
Maybe a variant of Sinja.A well-known namesake is the German beach volleyball player Cinja Tillmann.

The imperative form of the ancient Turkic verb Çınlayu-, meaning "to resonate," "to echo," or "to sound clear like a bell." Rooted in Çın (the absolute truth/reality), Çınla serves as an existential call to "resonate with the truth." It describes a person who lives authentically, whose words and actions ring with clarity and honesty, and who cannot be swayed by falsehood.
Roman cognomen of uncertain meaning. This was the name of a Roman politician who was the father-in-law of Julius Caesar.

From the English word cinnamon, denoting a type of spice obtained from the bark of several tree species belonging to the genus Cinnamomum. It is derived from Latin cinnamomum "cinnamon", which was also used as a term of endearment. It began to be used in the United States after the debut of the television series Mission: Impossible (1966-1973), which featured the character Cinnamon Carter.
Short form of names ending in cino.
Possibly a variant spelling of चिंतन (see Chintan).
Croatian and Serbian form of Cinthia.
Masculine form of Cintia. In other words, this is the Spanish form of Cynthius; also see Italian Cinzio. This name was borne by Cuban poet Cintio Vitier (1921-2009).

Derived from Latin cinctus meaning "girdle, belt, zone (vestment)", itself from the verb cingo "to gird, to encompass". This was the name of a Roman goddess of conception, possibly an epithet of Juno as tutelary goddess of marriage. Cinxia functioned within the zone or belt (cingulum) that a bride wore to symbolize that her husband was 'belted and bound' (cinctus vinctusque) to her. The belt was tied with the knot of Hercules, intended to be intricate and difficult to untie. Augustine calls this goddess Virginiensis (from virgo "virgin"), indicating that the untying of the bridal zone is the symbolic loss of virginity.Cinxia may have been felt as present during a ritual meant to ease labor. The man who fathered the child removes his own belt (cinctus), binds it (cinxerit) around the laboring woman, then releases it with a prayer that the one who has bound her in labor should likewise release her: 'he should then leave.' Women who had experienced spontaneous abortions were advised to bind their bellies for the full nine months with a belt (cingulum) of wool from a lamb fed upon by a wolf.

Derived from Ancient Greek κινύρα (kinyra) meaning "harp, lyre, kinnor; musical instrument with ten strings", ultimately derived from Hebrew כינור (kinor) and influenced by κινυρός (kinyros) "wailing, lamenting". This was the name of a king of Cyprus and priest of Aphrodite in Greek mythology. Parts of his myth may have been derived from or influenced by the Ugaritic deity Kinnaru, a god of the lyre.
Possibly a variant of Kevin or Cobhan.

A famous bearer of the name was the Kenyan Meru human rights activist and female diviner Ciokaraine from Igembe, Kenya. She was a fierce supporter of women's rights and is known for having offered up her son's life in order to prevent a famine during the Mau Mau Uprising.
Meaning unknown. A known bearer of this name was the 13th-century Italian poet Ciolo de la Barba from the city of Pisa.
Derived from Old Irish cenn "head" and faol "wolf".
Diminutive of Cairistìona influenced by Danish Kirsten. It is the original Scottish form of Kirstin.

An Aztec deity, god of astrology and calendars. He and his wife, Oxomoco, were known as the first human couple. Derived from Nahuatl cipactli "crocodile, alligator, caiman; crocodilian monster, dragon", with the second element possibly being tonalli "day, sun, heat; day-sign; soul, fate".
From the English word cipher meaning "a secret code". The personal name Cipher could also be a spelling variation of names Sapphire and Zephyr.
Hungarian variant of Cippóra and Judeo-Anglo-Norman variant of Zipora.
Short form of Cipriána, occasionally used as a given name in its own right.
Languedocian and Provençal form of Cyprian.
Hungarian and Aragonese form of Cyprianus.
Corsican and Sicilian form of Cyprian.
Means "ability to create, creative force" in Indonesian, ultimately from Sanskrit चित्त (citta).
From the Chinese 瓷 (cí) meaning "porcelain" and 秋 (qiū) meaning "autumn".
Italian, Spanish, Galician and Portuguese feminine form of Cyrus.
From the English word circumcision, ultimately from Latin circumcision, derived from circumcido meaning “to cut around”.

Means "circumcision" in Spanish. This is given in reference to the circumcision of Jesus, as recorded in the Gospel of Luke. This event is traditionally viewed as the first time the blood of Christ was shed and thus the beginning of the process of the redemption of man; it is also seen as a demonstration that Christ was fully human, and of his obedience to Jewish law. The Feast of the Circumcision of Christ is celebrated on January 1. Since 2014 this name has been banned in the Mexican state of Sonora.
Means "ship-maker" in Sindarin. Círdan is the name of a Telerin Elf in the work of Tolkien.
Derived from Romanian cireșică, the diminutive of cireașă, "cherry".
Italian and Spanish form of Cyriaca.
Asturian and Sicilian form of Cyriacus.
Famous bearer is Cirie Fields, 4th and 3rd place finisher of Survivor: Panama and Survivor: Micronesia, respectively. Presumed to be invented.
Gascon and Provençal form of Ciril.
Name from Andrzej Sapkowski's books. Originate from elvish name Zireael that meaning "swallow" (as a bird)
Corsican and Sicilian form of Cyril.
Serbian and Bosnian variant of Cyril.
Diminutive of Ciru as well as a variant of Quirinu. The name coincides with Sicilian cirinu "a match (the tool for starting a fire)".

Derived from Proto-Germanic *Tīwaz, the same etymological root as Tyr, which evolved into Cyo and Ziu in Old High German.Cisa is mentioned in several medieval manuscripts dating back to the 12th to 14th centuries, among others the Codex Monac (circa 1135), the Codex Emmeran (circa 1135) and Melchior Goldast's Suevicarum rerum scriptores. All of these texts go back to the Excerptum ex Gallica historia, a first-century BCE record of a Swabian military victory over Roman forces.In said Excerptum ex Gallica historia, Cisa is identified as a goddess of the Suevi who was venerated in modern-day Augsburg, Germany. Her feast day, the so-called "dies Cize", was celebrated on the 59th day after the first day of August, meaning September 28 and involved games and merrymaking.19th-century scholar Jacob Grimm suggested that Cisa may be the same figure as Tyr's unnamed wife, mentioned by Loki in the 13th century Poetic Edda poem Lokasenna.Furthermore, Grimm proposed a connection between Cisa and the "Isis" of the Suebi attested by Tacitus in his 1st century CE work Germania based on the similarity of their names, if not their functions. He also referenced a record of a pagan Duke of Swabia named Esenerius who established a chapel in his castle in Kempten with a venerated image of Cisa. Grimm theorized that Cisara, Augsburg's former name, might be interpreted as *Cisae ara, "Cisa's altar".18th-century librarian Christian August Vulpius, however, believed Cisa (or Ciza, as he called her) to be a Sorbian fertility goddess and "a kind of Ceres for the Vindelici", who offered her grain, crops and cereals at her altar in Augsburg on her feast day.

Dutch short form of Francisca. This name is borne by Cisca Dresselhuys, a Dutch journalist and feminist.

Çisem is a name that captures the essence of a "gentle drizzle." Derived from the root çis, it describes the light, rhythmic fall of rain that brings life to the soil. As a name, it is a symbol of quiet renewal and the soft, nurturing power of the sky, representing one who brings vitality and freshness wherever they travel.
From the Chinese 慈 (cí) meaning "kind, loving" and 珊 (shān) meaning "coral".
Dutch and Limburgish short form for both Francisca and Franciska - one could also label it a variant spelling for Cisca (though out of the two, Ciska is certainly the most common).

From the Ecuadorian titles of the Virgin Mary, La Virgen de El Cisne and Nuestra Señora de El Cisne, meaning "The Virgin of El Cisne" and "Our Lady of El Cisne" respectively (coinciding with the word for "swan").She is venerated at the basilica in El Cisne in the southern province of Loja.This name is also used in Nicaragua, albeit very rarely on males.

Meaning unknown. One source theorizes that the name might possibly be derived from Old English cisse meaning "gravelly place" or from Old English cís meaning "fastidious". Even Old Norse kyssa meaning "to kiss" was suggested by this source, but this seems unlikely, given that this name is Anglo-Saxon in origin.Known bearers of this name include Cissa of Sussex (son of the 5th-century South Saxon king Ælle of Sussex) and the 8th-century saint Cissa of Crowland.
Variant of Cicely, a medieval English form of Cecilia.

Means "ivy-crowned" in Ancient Greek, derived from κισσόω (kissoô) meaning "to wreathe with ivy", ultimately from κισσός (kissos) "ivy". This is the name of several characters in Greek mythology, including one of the fifty sons of King Aegyptus who was killed by his wife, Antheleia, on their wedding night.

Cissonius was an ancient Gaulish/Celtic god. After Visucius, Cissonius was the most common name of the Gaulish/Celtic Mercury; around seventeen inscriptions dedicated to him extend from France and Southern Germany into Switzerland.Cissonius was represented either as a bearded, helmeted man riding a ram and carrying a wine cup, or else as a young man with winged helmet and herald's staffaccompanied by a rooster and goat.The name has been interpreted as meaning "courageous", "remote" or else "carriage-driver". He was probably a god of trade and protector of travellers, since Mercury exercised similar functions in the Roman pantheon.
Latinized form of Greek Κεῖσος (Keisos). This was the name of a legendary king of Argos, a son of Temenus.
Slovene form of Zita 1 and Zita 2.
Probably means "glowing star", from Nahuatl citlalin "star" and tona "to shine, to be warm". This was the name of an Aztec deity who created the stars alongside his wife, Citlallicue.
The name Citlalic means rising star.Citlalic has an Aztec origin.Which is also Mexican.

Means "star skirt" in Nahuatl, from citlalin "star" and icue "her skirt". This was the name of a creator goddess in Aztec mythology, said to have made the stars, the Earth, death, and darkness along with her husband, Citlalatonac.
Means "arrow stars (meteorites)" in Nahuatl, derived from citlalin "stars" and mina "to shoot, to stab".
Invented by Neal Shusterman for the main character in his book series 'Scythe', first released in 2016.
From Indonesian citra meaning "image" combined with the feminine suffix -wati.

From the English word for a pale yellow variety of quartz that resembles topaz. From Old French citrin, ultimately from Latin citrus, "citron tree". It may also be related to the Yiddish tsitrin, for "lemon tree."It is one of the birthstones for November.
Refers to a genus of flowering trees that produce fruits.
Alternate transcription of Georgian ციური (see Tsiuri).
Probably derived from the name of the ancient Greek city Cius. In Greek mythology, Cius was one of the Argonauts, joining the crew after Hylas was abducted by nymphs.
Means "the one who writes blossoms" from Hopi cíhu "blossom, flower" combined with bána "to figure, write, draw" and ka "the one that".
Roman cognomen meaning "civic, civil (of or pertaining to citizens)", or figuratively, "polite, courteous".

Means "city, town", taken from the Italian title of the Virgin Mary Madonna della Civita, which refers to a sacred image of the Virgin discovered on Mount Civita by a shepherd whose deaf-muteness was miraculously cured by it. From Chinese 慈 (cí) meaning "affectionate, genial" combined with 禧 (xǐ) meaning "happiness, auspiciousness". Other hanzi combinations are possible. This was the regnal name of Empress Dowager Cixi (1835–1908), a Manchu noblewoman who had de facto but periodical control of the Chinese government in the late Qing dynasty.

Cixilo (7th-century – fl. 694) was a Visigoth queen consort by marriage to king Egica (687–702). She was the daughter of Erwig and Liuvigoto. She married Egica in 670. She was repudiated in 687. She was, however, only temporarily moved to a convent and allowed to return and be reinstated as queen, attested in 691 as well as 694.

From Latin clāmor "clamor, loud cry, a shout", taken from the liturgical prayer 'Clamor meus ad te veniat' meaning "Let my cry come to thee".

Variant of Claribel. This was the name of the fictional character Clarabel from 'The Railway Series' of children's books by the Rev. W. Awdry and the related 'Thomas & Friends' television series. In the stories Annie and Clarabel were Thomas's passenger coaches.

Transferred use of the surname Claret, given after saint Anthony Mary Claret, a Spanish archbishop, missionary and founder of the Claretians. This name is usually given as the compound names Antonio María Claret and María Claret (Spanish) or Antoni Maria Claret and Maria Claret (Catalan).

A damsel rescued by Sir Gaheris, Arthur's nephew.

Perhaps a blend of Clarissa and Calista. This name appears in Robert Greene's prose work 'Planetomachia' (1585). It is borne by a sister of English actor Nicholas Hoult.

Variant of Clark. As a feminine name it came into use in the early 1990s, influenced by the character Clarke Betancourt from the 1990 film Mo' Better Blues. It was further popularized by Clarke Griffin, a character in the television series The 100 (2014-2020).

Contracted form of Claudemir. Also compare the somewhat similar-looking name Clotário.

Means "cloister" in Catalan, taken from the Catalan title of the Virgin Mary, Mare de Déu del Claustre, meaning "Mother of God of the Cloister," the patron saint of Solsona in the comarca of Solsonès.
Spanish form of Claustre. Rare masculine usage of this name is restricted to Latin America, particularly Mexico.
Probably from Spanish clavel ("carnation, pink clove").
From Spanish clavelina, a species of Dianthus flower named in English "rainbow pink" or "China pink".
Derived from the surname Claver. Used in honor of the saint Peter Claver.

From Latin clavis "key". The use as a given name is transferred from the humanist surname Clavius (originally Clau or Schlüssel) borne by Christopher Clavius, a 16th-century Jesuit, astronomer, and mathematician.

A variant of Clavio, the name is also identical to the Spanish noun for “nail.” Therefore, there is possibly a connotation of extraordinary steadfastness and solid reliability in times of trouble. This given name is rare, but for example, it is a name not unknown in Venezuela.

Latinized form of Kleandros. Known bearers of this name include the Greek tyrant Cleander of Gela (5th century BC) and the Greek general Cleander of Macedon (4th century BC).

Latinized form of Kleanthes. A known bearer of this name was Cleanthes of Assos, a Greek Stoic philosopher from the 3rd century BC.

He was named after his father, the Baptist preacher Cleavant Derricks (1910-1977).

From an English origin meaning "cliff". Diminutive of Cleavon or a variant of Cleve. As an independent name can be transferred use of the surname Cleave. Namesake is Canadian rock musician Cleave Anderson (b. 1968).
Meaning "cliff". Adaptation from names containing the element cleav with the suffix -on.

Variant of Clelland. It was borne by Minnesota entertainer Clellan Card (1903–1966), voice of Axel Torgeson on the children's show 'Axel and His Dog' (1954-1966).

Spanish and Portuguese form of Clementianus.

Creative masculine form of Clementina or an elaboration of Clemente.

Italian and Corsican form of Clementia.
