Combination of Nilson and the prefix cle likely taken from the name Cléber.
Either taken from the surname, Clenton, or used as a variant of Clinton.

Latinized form of Greek Κλεόβοια (Kleoboia), derived from Ancient Greek κλέος (kleos) meaning "glory" and βοῦς (bous) meaning "ox, cow, cattle". Alternatively, the second element could be interpreted as βοάω (boao) meaning "to shout, to proclaim" (also "to roar" and "to howl" when used of the wind). Compare Euboea, Meliboea and Periboea. This was the name of several characters in Greek mythology.

Latinized form of Greek Κλεοβουλίνη (Kleobouline), derived from the name Kleoboulos combined with the feminine adjectival suffix -ινη (-ine). This was the name of a 6th-century BC Greek poet from Lindos, a small town on the island of Rhodes. She was the daughter of Cleobulus, one of the Seven Sages of Greece. According to Plutarch, her real name was Eumetis.
Latinized form of Kleoboulos. This was the name of one of the Seven Sages of Greece.
Derived from Ancient Greek κλέος (kleos) meaning "glory" combined with either χαίρω (chairo) meaning "to be happy, full of cheer; to enjoy" or the related χάρις (charis) meaning "grace, kindness".

Latinized form of Greek Κλεοχαρεία (Kleochareia), derived from κλέος (kleos) "glory" and χάρις (charis) "grace, kindness". In Greek mythology, Cleocharia was a naiad and queen consort. She was the wife of King Lelex of Laconia and the mother of Myles and Polycaon.
Latinized form of Kleokritos. This name was borne by an eponymous archon of Athens, who lived in the 5th century BC.
The seneschal of King Leodegan of Carmelide. He assisted Leodegan, and Arthur, in battles against the Saxons at Carhaix and Aneblayse, and he led a battalion in Arthur’s war against Rome.
Allegedly derived from the Scottish surname McLeod.

Latinized form of Kleodora. In Greek mythology, Cleodora was a nymph of Mount Parnassos in Phokis. She was one of the prophetic Thriai, nymphs who divined the future by throwing stones or pebbles. She was loved by the sea god Poseidon and had a son called Parnassos by him. This name was also borne by one of the Danaids (i.e., the 50 daughters of Danaus).
Latinized form of Greek Κλεοδόξα (Kleodoxa), derived from Ancient Greek κλέος (kleos) meaning "glory" and δόξα (doxa) "notion, reputation, honour".

From the Latin Maria Cleophae, literally "Mary of Cleophas" (and popularly interpreted as "Mary, wife of Cleophas"). This is given in reference to the saint known in Italian as Maria Cleofe (alternatively Maria di Cleofa), who is mentioned in John 19:25 as one of the women present at the crucifixion of Jesus.A bearer of this name was 15th-century Italian noblewoman Cleofe Malatesta, also known as Cleofa or Cleopa.
Latinized form of Kleola. In Greek mythology, Cleola is the name of a daughter of Dias, son of Pelops. She was the first wife of Atreus, with whom she had Pleisthenes.

Latinized form of the Greek name Κλεόλαος (Kleolaos), which was derived from Ancient Greek κλέος (kleos) meaning "glory" and λαός (laos) meaning "people, folk". This was the name of one of the fifty (or fifty-one) grandsons of Thespius fathered by Heracles in Greek mythology, his mother being Argele.
A variation of Cleolinda. Name of a historical character in the epic fantasy 'Priory of the Orange Tree' by Samantha Shannon, inspired by the legend of Saint George and the Dragon.

Possibly a contracted form of Cleodolinda, which is of uncertain meaning. This is the name of the princess in some medieval Italian versions of the legend of Saint George and the dragon. (Saint George rescues Princess Cleolinda from being sacrificed to a dragon by taming the dragon and then killing it in exchange for the kingdom's conversion to Christianity.) This is also the pen name of Cleolinda Jones (1978-), an American blogger and author.
Derived from French cléome "cleome, spider flowers, bee plants". Cléoma Breaux Falcon (1906-1941) was a Cajun musician from Louisiana.
Latinized form of Kleomachos. This name was borne by an eponymous archon of Athens, who lived in the 3rd century BC.
Derived from Greek κλέος (kleos) meaning "glory" and βροτός (brotos) meaning "mortal man, human being".
Derived from the name of the flowering plants cleome, commonly known as "spider flowers, spider plants, spider weeds, bee plants".
Latinized form of Kleomedes. This name was borne by an ancient Greek astronomer from the 1st century BC.
Galician and Spanish form of Cleomenes.
Latinized form of Kleomenes. Cleomenes was the name of a king of Sparta (Greece) from the 6th century BC.
Variant of Cleome reflecting the pronunciation of the botanical name.
Italian form of Cleonicus (see Kleonikos) and masculine of Cleonice.

Latinized form of both Kleonides and its rare variant Kleoneides (see the entry of the former name).This was the name of a Greek author and music theorist, who is thought to have lived somewhere between the 3rd century BC and the 4th century AD.
Variant of Cleone reflecting the pronunciation of the mythological name.

column4: French (Rare, Archaic)|French (Caribbean, Rare, Archaic)|French (Quebec, Rare, Archaic)

column12: Latinized form of Kleonymos. Bearers of this name include the generals Cleonymus of Athens (5th century BC) and Cleonymus of Sparta (3rd century BC).
Latinized form of Kleopatros and masculine form of Cleopatra.
Variant form of Cléophas (masculine) and Cléophée (feminine). A known bearer of this name was the Canadian political figure Cléophe Cimon (1822-1888).

Feminine form of Cleophas. This was borne by the mother of Swiss-born Austrian painter An­gel­ica Kauff­man. Cleophea Holzhalb was painted by the Swiss painter Hans Asper in 1538 together with her cat and her dog.
Feminine form of Cléophas, possibly via Latin Cleophae (see Cleofe).Since the 1990s, this name is being slowly rediscovered.
Also called Kripa in Sanskrit, Cleophis was a key figure in the war between the Assacani people and Alexander the Great.
Latinized form of Kleoptolemos. This name was borne by an Olympic victor from 684 BC.
Latinized form of Kleosthenes. A known bearer of this name was Cleosthenes of Epidamnus, winner of the Tethrippon (chariot race) at the 66th Olympiad in 516 BC.
Latinized form of Kleostratos. This name was borne by an ancient Greek astronomer from the 5th century BC.
This was borne by American singer Cleotha "Cleedy" Staples (1934-2013), a member of the Staple Singers musical group.
Variant of Clotilde influenced by names beginning with the element Cleo-.
6th-century Lombard king, the father of Authari.
The hero of the 15th-century French prose romance Cleriadus et Meliadice. A known bearer was Antoine Clériadus de Choiseul-Beaupré (1707-1774), a French cardinal.
Saint Clerina of Carthage was a 3rd-century saint. She is said to have been the aunt of Saint Celerinus.
An irregular Roman praenomen borne by the priest Clesipus Geganius.
English feminine form of Cletus and Catalan short form of Anacleta.
Anglicized form of Clydog and Cleder.
Diminutive of Cleveland, Cleve, or Cleva.

In Ulrich’s Lanzalet, a beautiful woman from the enchanted island of Thyle.She committed some breach of courtly etiquette and was sentenced to take the form of a dragon until kissed by the best knight in the world. She hunkered in a British forest until Arthur’s knight Roidurant came along. Clidra begged him to kiss her, but he instead fled. Later, he related the story to Lancelot, who came to the forest, kissed the dragon, and restored her to her original form.An analog to this story is found in the Fearsome Kiss adventure of Le Bel Inconnu.
Transferred use of the surname Cliffe
Diminutive of Clifford, Clifton, Clifette, and Cliftona and also a variant of Cliffy and Cliff.
The eponymous hero of Chrétien de Troyes' poem Cligès.
Feminine form of Clinton.Clintona Jackson was a beauty queen in the 1950's and 1960's.
The name of the main protagonist in the short story 'The Unforgotten Hour' by Louis Arthur Cunningham. In biology, Clione is the name of a genus of floating maritime slugs, also known as sea angels.
Local vernacular corruption of Clothilde found in the Poitou-Charentes region.
Transferred use of the surname Clipper.
Derived from Albanian çliroj "to free; to set free; to release".
Galician, Spanish and Portuguese form of Cleisthenes.
Catalan form of Kleitos via its latinized form Clitus.
Latinized form of Kleitarchos. This name was borne by an ancient Greek tyrant of Eretria in Euboea (4th century BC).
Catalan, Spanish and Portuguese form of Clytemnestra.
Italian and Spanish form of Kleitos via its latinized form Clitus.
Latinized form of Kleitomachos. This name was borne by an ancient Greek philosopher of Carthaginian descent (2nd century BC).

Latinized form of Kleitophon. This name was borne by an Athenian oligarchic statesman and intellectual from the 5th century BC.In literature, Clitophon is the name of the protagonist of the novel Leucippe and Clitophon (also known as The Adventures of Leucippe and Clitophon) written by the Greek author Achilles Tatius (2nd century AD).

Derived from the English name of the plant (the German name for it being Klivie) which itself is a Latinization of Clive. The plant was named by botanist John Lindley (1799-1865) after Charlotte Florentina Clive (died 1866).Clivia is a 1933 operetta by Nico Dostal to a libretto by Charles Amberg. The plot concerns the adventures of a film star, Clivia Gray, in the South American republic of Boliguay and her romance with the Boliguayan president.
Most likely a diminutive of Clive. Could also be a variant of Clifton.
Derived from Latin cloaca, meaning "sewer", and combined with a feminine suffix. This was the name of the goddess who presided over the system of sewers in Rome, sometimes identified with Venus.
Could be a variant of Claudine
Dialectal short form of Nikolaus found in the state of Hesse.
Feminine form of Clodius and Clodio. This name was borne by one of the Vestal Virgins.
Galician and Italian form of Clodius.
From Clodoaldus, a latinized form of Chlodowald. This was the name of a 6th-century Frankish saint, better known as Saint Cloud. He was a grandson of King Clovis I who became a hermit and monk.
Italian, Portuguese and Spanish form of Clodoald.
French and Franco-Provençal form of Chlodomer.

Feminine form of Clodomiro, which is the Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of the ancient Germanic name Chlodomer.A notable bearer of this name is the Cuban revolutionary Clodomira Acosta Ferrales (1936-1958).
Variant of Chlodoswintha. It was the given name of two Merovingian princesses.
Italian and Spanish form of Hlodwig, via a Latinized form Clodovæus or Chlodoveus. This was borne by Clodoveo Carrión Mora (1883-1957), an Ecuadorian palaeontologist and naturalist.
Spanish form of Chlodoald. Notable bearers of this name are Clodualdo del Mundo Sr., a Filipino literary figure, and Clodualdo del Mundo Jr., a director.
Portuguese and Spanish form of Chlodulf.
As a masculine name, it might be an Americanized form of Klaus.As a feminine name, its origins are uncertain, however it could be inspired by names like Lois 1 or Chloris.

Probably derived from Ancient Greek κλονέω (kloneo) meaning "to drive (the enemy) in confusion, cause to rush wildly", ultimately from κλόνος (klonos) meaning "turmoil, confused motion, battle-rout" or "trembling, confusion, agitation". This was the name of an Amazon warrior in Greek mythology, as well as of a nymph of Hyria.

Means "stumbler" in French. This was the first name of a character from Victor Hugo's novel, 'The Hunchback of Notre Dame'. Clopin Trouillefou was considered the king of truants by the Parisian gypsies.
Transferred use of the surname Clopton.
Possibly a variant of Chloris influenced by Clarice.
Probably created by the Italian poet Torquato Tasso for a character of his poem 'Jerusalem Delivered' (1580). The name was also popular in the 19th century.
Spanish and Catalan form of Chloris.
Galician, Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Chlorus.
A dithematic Germanic name formed from the name elements hlut "fame" and swind "strong".
The Celtic goddess of the river Clyde.Attempts have been made to derive her name from Proto-Celtic *kluto- "fame; renown".
Perhaps a diminutive of Clotilde. This was used in the 1997 children's historical novel A Picture of Freedom: The Diary of Clotee, a Slave Girl.

Transferred use of the surname Cloud or directly from the word cloud, a visible mass of water suspended in the air. A famous bearer of the name is Cloud Strife, the protagonist of the video game metaseries 'Compilation of Final Fantasy VII'.
Transferred use of the surname Cloudesley. A famous bearer was British Royal Navy officer and politician Cloudesley Shovell (1650-1707).
Modern variant of Claudia, influenced by the English word "cloud".

Transferred use of the surname Cloudsley.A famous namesake is Sir Cloudsley Shovell, the 17th century admiral and English naval hero. His unusual Christian name is derived from his maternal grandmother, Lucy Cloudisley.
From the English word clove meaning either a slice of garlic or the dried flower bud of a tropical tree, used as a spice. This name was used by Suzanne Collins in her book The Hunger Games.
Possibly a Portuguese variant of Clovis.
Meaning unknown. Clovia is a character in the "Gasoline Alley" comic strips, first released in 1918, one of the longest running comic strips of all time in the US.
A character in the 'Poldark' series of historic novels by Winston Graham. The name is probably transferred from the name of an estate in Crowan , Cornwall.
Transferred use of the surname Cloyce.A notable bearer of this name is the American football player Cloyce Box (1923-1993).
A variant of Clyde, influenced by names like Lloyd and Floyd.
The name of a Welsh saint of the 5th century, the reputed foundress of a church named Clydai, in Emlyn.
Feminine form of Clyde in the image of Claudette.
Feminine form of Clyde influenced by Claudia.
Diminutive of Clyde, also used as a feminine form.
Clydog was a sixth-century Welsh king of Ergyng who became a saint.

From κλύμενος (klymenos) meaning "famous, renowned, notorious, infamous" in Ancient Greek (see klytos). This was the name of several characters in Greek mythology, as well as being an epithet of Hades.

Latinized form of Klytië. It was used by British author Joseph Hatton for the heroine of his novel Clytie (1874), and borne by Australian opera singer Clytie Hine (1887-1983); it was also the birth name of Australian ceramic artist Klytie Pate (1912-2010). American author William Faulkner used it for a minor character in his novel Absalom, Absalom! (1936), in which case it was a diminutive of Clytemnestra, and Eudora Welty for the title character of her story Clytie (1941).

Derived from Ancient Greek κλυτός (klytos) meaning "famous, noble" and ἵππος (hippos) meaning "horse". This was the name of one of the fifty daughters of King Thespius in Greek mythology, mother of Eurycapys by Heracles.
Derived from Ancient Greek κλυτός (klytos) meaning "famous, noble" and δῶρον (doron) meaning "gift". It is the name of two characters in Greek mythology.
Variant of Kamiyah. This name can also be spelled as C'Miya, with the "M" after the apostrophe capitalized.
Means "midwife", which is derived from Irish Cnámh meaning "bone".
Means "bone", probably originating as a nickname for a thin man.
Means "little bone", a diminutive of Cnámh.

Derived from Romanian cneaz (ultimately from Proto-Slavic *kъnędzь via Ukrainian and Russian князь (knjazʹ)) "prince; ruler of a state or principality in past times". This name was borne by the daughter of Alexandru cel Bun (Alexander the Good in English) who eventually married Vlad II Dracul.

Derived from either Old English cneof "knee, knoll", or an unknown Celtic element. This was the name of a King of Mercia in the 6th century, and also gave rise to the village of Knebworth in Hertfordshire.
Derived from Old English cniht meaning "youth, servant, retainer".

Cniva (fl. mid-3rd century AD) was a Gothic king who invaded the Roman Empire. He successfully captured the city of Philippopolis (Plovdiv in Bulgaria) in 250 and killed Emperor Decius and his son Herennius Etruscus at the Battle of Abritus as he was attempting to leave the Empire in 251. This was the first time a Roman Emperor had been killed in combat against barbarians. He was allowed by the new Emperor Trebonianus Gallus to leave with his spoils and was paid tribute to stay out of the empire.
Derived from Gothic knôds "kind" (as in 'race' or 'species') combined with Old High German mâri "famous."
Dutch short form of Jacob and Jacobus. A well-known bearer of this name is Co Adriaanse (b. 1947), a Dutch soccer manager and former soccer player.
From Sino-Vietnamese 基 (cơ) meaning "foundation, base", 機 (cơ) meaning "chance, opportunity, quick-witted", or 璣 (cơ) meaning "imperfect pearl".
From Sino-Vietnamese 固 (cố) meaning "firm, strong" or 故 (cố) meaning "old, past".
From a non-Sino-Vietnamese reading of Chinese 旗 (cờ) meaning "flag".
Means "serpent woman" in Nahuatl. This was also another name for the goddess Quilaztli, or Cihuacoatl.
From the Choctaw kowi meaning "puma" and homma meaning "red".
Variant of Cole coinciding with the English word coal.

Appears in the novel (1975), movie (1981) and musical (1998) Ragtime, on the character Coalhouse Walker Junior, and his son, Coalhouse Walker III. The writer of Ragtime, E. L. Doctorow, was inspired to name Coalhouse Jr. this after a character named Michael Kohlhaas, who has a very similar story to Coalhouse Walker Jr.
Possibly derived from Asturian cuaña "path" or Latin cava "cave".
Means "serpent-shaped earring" in Nahuatl, from cōātl "snake, serpent" and nacochtli "earring, ear plug, pendant".
Means "snake mother" or possibly "snake protector" in Nahuatl, from cōātl "snake, serpent" and nantli "mother", which can be used in the sense of "protector".
Meaning uncertain. Derived from Nahuatl cōātl "snake, serpent", possibly combined with nenetl "doll, idol", nen "in vain, useless, idle", or nemi "to live".
From the English word coast, ultimately derived from Latin costa "rib, side, wall".
Means "snake, serpent; twin" in Nahuatl, the fifth day-sign of the tonalpohualli.
Means "little serpent" in Nahuatl, the diminutive form of Coatl.
Means "serpent’s hair" in Nahuatl, from coatl "snake, serpent" and tzontli "hair, crest" or "headdress".
Means "serpent flower" in Nahuatl, from Nahuatl coatl, "serpent, snake" and xochitl, "flower".
Transferred use of the surname Cobain, likely given in honor of Lead singer and guitarist of Nirvana, Kurt Cobain (1967-1994).

From the metal or the shade of blue. Derived from German kobold, a type of house spirit. This in turn, has a few possible etymologies. One is that it come from Greek koba'los, meaning "rogue". Another theory is that it comes from the Old High German root chubisi, "house, building, hut" and the suffix -old meaning "to rule".
Transferred use of the surname Cobb.
Variant of Kobe 1 (Flemish) and Kobe 2/Coby (Modern English).
a gaelicisation of the word "cove", both a placename in County Cork, Ireland and a gaelicisation of the name Cove.

Diminutive of Jacob or Jacoba.A noted bearer is Canadian actress and model Cobie Smulders, born Jacoba Francisca Maria Smulders (b.1982); best known for her roles as Robin Scherbatsky on the television series 'How I Met Your Mother' and Maria Hill in the Marvel Cinematic Universe.
Presumably a short form of Jacobina.

Believed to mean "victorious sovereignty", from Old Irish cob "victory" and flaith "ruler, sovereign, princess". This name was relatively common in the early Irish period. It was also the name of a 7th century Pictish princess.
From Portuguese cobra from the latin colubra meaning "snake."
From Guanche *kăbūr, meaning "swaying" (literally "slow jog"). This was recorded as the name of a 10-year-old Guanche girl from Tenerife who was sold at the slave market in Valencia in 1495.
Transferred use of the surname Coburn.
From the English word cobweb meaning "spiderweb". In Shakespeare's comedy 'A Midsummer Night's Dream' (1595) this name is borne by a fairy attendant of Titania.

Possibly derived from Ancient Greek κόκκαλος (kokkalos) meaning "pine kernel", itself a diminutive of κόκκος (kokkos) "seed, grain, kernel". This was the name of a legendary Sician king, who sheltered Daedalus after his escape from the Labyrinth.
Derived from Old Irish cochall "cape, hood" combined with a diminutive suffix.

Perhaps from Cróchnait, which was derived from Irish cróch "saffron, red" (from Latin crocus) combined with a diminutive suffix. In the Fenian Cycle of Irish mythology Cochrann is a daughter of Cathair Mór, king of Leinster, and the mother of Diarmaid and Oscar; in ballads the character is known as Cróchnat.

Short form of both Cornelis and Cornelius (for men) and Cornelia (for women). It probably first started out as a contraction of a diminutive of these names, which might have been Corneelke, Corneliske, Correke or something similar. Also compare the related names Cox, Cocky and Cokkie.This name is predominantly masculine in the Netherlands, especially as an official name on birth certificates. For women, the name is now almost always an informal name.Known Dutch bearers of this name include the singer Cock van der Palm (1936-2004), the soccer player Cock Rijkens (1952-2018) and the former politician Cock Kerling-Simons (b. 1929).
The name of a 17th-century leader of the Pamunkey tribe (Powhatan Confederacy) in what is now the U.S. state of Virginia.
Roman cognomen derived from cocles "one-eyed, half-blind person, cyclops".

Either a variant of Coco or from the English word cocoa for the cocoa bean. The word cocoa comes from the Spanish word cacao, which is derived from the Nahuatl word cacahuatl. The confusion of this with coco is popularized by Samuel Johnson's A Dictionary of the English Language.As a human name, it is almost always feminine, but on pets it is often used for both sexes.

Meaning uncertain. Probably derived from cocolli, which can mean "quarrel, dispute, anger", "pain, illness", "plant tendril" (which would derive from colli "something bent, twisted, curling"), or "a responsibility, charge, burden".
Means "he/she is hated", derived from Nahuatl cocolia "to hate someone".
Meaning uncertain. This was the name of a ruler of Tepetlaoztoc, the husband of Azcaxochitl.
An Americanized spelling of Japanese Kokoro, meaning "heart".
Anglicized and Gallicized form of Kodjo.
Latinized form of Κοδράτος (Kodratos), which is the hellenized form of Quadratus.
Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Codrus.

Latinized form of Greek Κόδρος (Kodros), which is probably derived from Ancient Greek κυδρός (kydros) meaning "glorious, renowned, illustrious" (see kydos). In Greek mythology, this was the name of a legendary king of Athens.
Transferred use of the surname Coe.
Name of an 8th century Irish saint.
German variant and East Prussian German form of Celestine.
Feminine form of Coelius. This name was borne by a Vestal Virgin.
Latinized version of Kevin, derived directly from Old Irish Cóemgein.
Diminutive of Coenraad. This name is borne by South African rugby player Coenie Oosthuizen (1989-) and South African musician Coenie de Villiers (1956-).
Derived from the Old English elements cene "keen, brave" and wulf "wolf".
Latinized form of Greek Κοίρανος (Koiranos), meaning "king, ruler, commander, master" in Ancient Greek.
Anglicized form of Irish name Cobhthach and Akan name Kofi, or from the English word coffee.
Possibly a form of Cuff. This is borne by American country and western singer-songwriter Coffey Anderson (1978-).
Possibly from the Welsh imperative "cofia" meaning "remember."
A diminutive from a short form of Cúchogaidh.
Transferred use of the surname Cohan.

Brother of Noah and an early Jaredite king, son of Corihor¹ and brother to Noah. He joined his brother Noah, with "all his brethren and many of the people" to establish a rival kingdom to Shule’s (Ether 7:15). There are no further references, but he seems to have been influential, for his brother Noah later names a son after him (Ether 7:20) and the name is passed down to the end of the Jaredite lineage (Ether 13:17).
From Irish coigealach, meaning "like a distaff" or "scarecrow, effigy; tall and untidy person", derived from Old Irish coigeal "distaff", a stick used to hold flax or wool for spinning.

Coila was the muse of the poet Robert Burns, he created her as a poetic device for many of his poems. The name derives from the poetic name for the area of Kyle, Ayrshire, which itself is derived from the male names Coil, Coilus or Coel Hen, King of the Picts, who lived, ruled and died in the area.
a modern invented Irish name possibly derived from Cóilín, itself an Irish variant of Colin. Also the Irish word for Collie.

Latinization of Kointa, itself a Hellenized form of Quinta. Saint Cointha suffered martyrdom during the persecutions of Emperor Trajanus Decius. Cointha was martyred by having her feet tied to a horse then being dragged through the streets of Alexandria.

Latinized form of Kointos, which is the hellenized form of the Latin name Quintus. In other words, this name is basically a latinization of a name that is already latinate in origin.This name was borne by Cointus of Phrygia (who is better known as Quintus of Phrygia), a martyr and saint from the 3rd century AD.
Scottish Gaelic form of Constantinus (see Constantine 1).
Derived from Caló cujiñí, meaning "rose". This name is used as a Caló equivalent of Rosa 1.
Variant of Koke, which is a diminutive of Jorge. A known bearer is Spanish footballer Jorge 'Coke' Andújar Moreno (1987-).
Transferred use of the surname Coker.
From a title derived from Balinese cokor meaning "foot, leg" combined either with ida, a pronoun for a revered person or deity, or Sanskrit देव (deva) meaning "god".
Variant of Nicolaas recorded in the 18th century in East Frisia.

Guernésiais, Walloon and French diminutive of Nicolas which has been in use since the Middle Ages and features prominently in the old French lullaby Fais dodo, Colas, mon petit frère. The name coincides with Walloon colas "Eurasian jay (bird)".
Of debated origin and meaning. Theories include a feminine form of Colas and a corruption of Scholastique (compare Colastia).
Derived from Latin colata, meaning "cleansed, purified", with the connotation of "adamant, steadfast".
Spanish, Italian and Portuguese form of Colbert.
Feminine form of Colby. A known bearer is the American singer-songwriter Colbie Caillat (1985-).
Transferred use of the surname Colden. Its rise in recent years may be due to similar sounding names like Colten.
Coldin is a boy's name meaning "dark valley" that comes from the Old English name Colden.

This was the name of two famous Australian Aborigines, recorded in the early history of Sydney. The meaning of the name is yet unknown. Also, this particular spelling may be an anglicized form of the original Aboriginal name, since it is close in appearance to English (sur)names like Coleby and Colby.
Variant of Colby influenced by Cole.

Colel Cab is the Mayan earth goddess associated with bees and beekeeping. Modern Maya Daykeepers invoke her name in chants to ward off attacks to nests and solve problems for hive keepers with their bees.

Coleraine is a town in Northern Ireland. It's meaning is "Nook of the ferns". It was once a title held by the Hanger family of Driffield, Gloucestershire, England. It was also a given name in the Vansittart family of Shottesbrooke, Berkshire, England.
Coleridge as a boy's name is of Old English origin. Place name: possibly "Cole's ridge", or "dark ridge".
Transferred use of the surname Coleson.
Meaning unknown. Notable bearer of the name is Colestah (c. 1800s-1865), a Yakama medicine woman.
Portuguese form and English and Dutch variant of Colette.
Variant of Colton, incorporating the name Cole.
Truncated form of Nicoletta as well as a variant of Colette.
Possibly a transferred use of the surname Coley or a diminutive of names such as Nicole and Cole.
Derived from the Old English elements col "coal" (see kol) and grīma "mask" (see grimo). Cognate to Icelandic Kolgrímur.
Means "all-seeing", ultimately derived from Hebrew כל (kol) meaning "all, whole" and חזה (haza) meaning "to see, to have a vision". He was mentioned in Nehemiah 3:15 and Nehemiah 11:5.
Possibly a variant of Kalisha, the spelling influenced by that of Colleen or Colette.
Variant of Celidoine, king of Scotland, son of the first Nascien and Flegentine, and ancestor of Lancelot and Galahad.
Dutch form of Colin 2 or a short form of Nicolijn.
Of unknown origin and meaning. Possibly created as a feminine form of Colin 2.

This is said to have been the name of three warrior brothers who founded the Irish kingdom of Airgialla and whose descendents ruled the Scottish kingdom of Dal Riada.The name is of uncertain etymolgy and various unsubstantiated meanings are given, including 'high' or 'lofty' and 'strong man'. Another theory states that an ancestor of the three brothers adopted the surname after becoming a Roman citizen, forming it from the first element found in his hometown of Colchester. The problem with this theory is that Colchester at that time was known as Camulodunon or Camulodunum!
From Guanche *kuyya-ar-affaw, meaning "Venus (planet)" (literally "vertex down to dawn").
Transferred use of the surname Collard.
Feminine diminutive of Col, a short form of Nicholas.
Derived from Middle Welsh collen "hazel", ultimately from Old Welsh coll. Collen was a 7th-century monk who gave his name to Llangollen.
Either a femininzed form of the surname Collet or a variant of Colette.
Transferred use of the surname Colley.
Transferred use of the surname Collier.
Feminine form of Collin, variant of Colleen or Coline.
Transferred use of the surname Collinwood.
Transferred use of the surname Collis.
Variant of Collins. Collynns was given to 5 girls in 2018 according to the SSA.
From Saint Colm-Cille (Saint Columba in English). Middle name of American-Australian actor and film director Mel Gibson.
Catalan and Gascon feminine form of Columba.
Form of Kálmán in English and other languages.
From the name of the Latin American country.
Transferred use of the surname Colonel, or from the vocabulary word colonel.
From the name of the American state of Colorado, which means "colored, red" in Spanish.

Possibly derived from Ancient Greek κωλώτης (kolotes) meaning "gecko, spotted lizard", or perhaps from κολῳός (koloos) meaning "brawling, noisy wrangling, racket, din" combined with the noun-forming suffix -της (-tes). This was the name of an Ancient Greek philosopher of the Epicurean school, notable for opposing the philosophies of Plutarch and claiming that it is impossible to live by the ideas of other philosophers.
Transferred use of the surname Colquitt.Character in the house next door novel written by Anne Rivers Siddon.
Transferred use of the surname Colston, meaning “coal town.”
Meaning uncertain, possibly a diminutive form of another name, using -ton.

The name of both a medicinal herb (probably Dalea lagopus, "hare’s-foot dalea") and a kind of passerine bird recognised for its song and plumage, both also called coltotl. The former may derive from coltic "crooked thing" and otl "fruit", the latter from tototl "bird" and an uncertain first element.
Transferred use of the surname Coltrane.
German and Romanian form of Columbanus.
Spanish and Portuguese form of Columbanus.
Columbell is the lady of the squire captured by Argante in The Faerie Queene.

Derived from the Latin adjective columbinus meaning "of a dove, dove-like". In turn, the word is ultimately derived from the Latin noun columba meaning "dove" (see Columba).A known bearer of this name was saint Columbinus of Lure (7th century AD).
Transferred use of the surname Colvin. It may also be used as a variant of Calvin.
Early Jaredite king, son of Coriantum, and a late Jaredite king.
Derived from Ancient Greek κόμαιθος (komaithos) meaning "having fiery or bright hair; red hair, blond hair", composed of κόμη (kome) "hair" and αἶθος (aithos) "heat, fire".
Latinized form of Komaios. A known bearer of this name was the Olympic victor Comaeus of Megara, who won the boxing contest at the 32nd Olympiad in 652 BC.
Derived from Romanian coman, the archaic form of cuman "Cuman".
Means "tribe, wild-spirited, industrious" in Navajo. This is the name of a supervillain in the Marvel Comics series.

Comasia was bore by a II-IV century martyr and saint who would help during drought and dryness. A legend says that her name was unknown even in the past so she was named Santa (Saint) come sia meaning "be that as it may" in Italian and later became Comasia. Another source says that Comasia comes from an Ancient Greek term meaning "solemn translation (removal)".

Portuguese and Galician form of Columba.Numerous places in Portugal are named after a Santa Comba or Combinha (Saint Columba), although the exact identity of the saint is disputed. The name itself was in use up until the 19th century.

Uncertain etymology. Possibly derived from the Cretan word κόμβα (komba) meaning "crow" or "sea-bird, shearwater". This was the name of a daughter of the river god Asopus in Greek mythology, as well as a woman (who may or may not be the same character) in Ovid’s writing who apparently turned into a bird to escape danger.
Transferred use of the surname Combs.
Transferred from the surname Comer, an occupational name for a seller of combs or for someone who uses them to prepare wool or flax for spinning.
Derived from Kurdish camêr or merd, meaning "generous".
From the medicinal herb, derived from the Latin confervere meaning “healing”, or literally, "boil together".
From comhalta "foster brother, foster sister" combined with a diminutive suffix.

Latinized form of Greek Κομιτώ (Komitô), a name of uncertain etymology, perhaps derived from Greek κομίζω (komizô) meaning "to take care of, provide for". This was borne by an elder sister of the 6th-century Byzantine empress Theodora.

Roman cognomen, which is an extended form of Commodus. This name was borne by a Christian Latin poet from the 3rd century AD.
From the vocabulary word commodore, derived from French commandeur.

From the English word companion, meaning "friend, acquaintance".

Named after the computational device. This is the name of a Filipino man whose full given name is Computer Man "Cman" Lim. According to himself, he was named as such by his father so that, in case the Y2K bug came true, there would still be a computer left.

From Ancient Greek κῶμος (komos) meaning "festival, revel, carousal". This was the name of the Greek god of revelry, merrymaking, festivity, and nocturnal dalliances, cup-bearer to Dionysos. He is sometimes called a son of Bacchus and Circe; however, this is a Renaissance invention.
Means "to remain, to still exist" in Vietnamese.

Its meaning is uncertain though it likely relates to con ("hound, wolf"), a common element in Irish names of its time.Though having fallen out of use as a given name, Conaing is still seen in a modern context in the surname Ó Conaing (anglicised as O'Gunning, Gunning, O'Conaing, and Cunning).Historically, the name was notable in the town of Chaisleán Uí Chonaing (Castleconnell) in County Limerick, where the Ó Conaing family held chief seats as lords of Aos Gréine in medieval times. This Limerick branch is linked to Brian Ború, being descendents of Donnchuan (a brother of his).The name is also linked to Lough Reane in Fíonach (Fenagh) in County Carlow through a local tale involving Conaing II Beag Eaglach, a High King of Ireland. He is said to have once resided there, and Conaing's son, Cobhthach, drowned in the nearby lake one day while out with his nurse, Rian. The lake was named after Rian to honour her efforts in trying to save him.
Name of a 6th century Irish saint.
Meaning uncertain, possibly related to Latin conandus "which is to be attempted". Alternately, could be a variant of Conan.

Possibly a form of Conchita. A notable bearer of this name was the American actress Conchata Ferrell (1943-2020).

Condatis (Gaulish: 'confluence') was an ancient Celtic deity worshipped primarily in northern Britain but also in Gaul. He was associated with the confluences of rivers, in particular within County Durham in the North of England. Condatis is known from several inscriptions in Britain and a single inscription found at Alonnes, Sarthe, France. In each case he is equated with the Roman god Mars.
Likely from the name of the large bird.
Means "little condor" in Spanish. This is the title character of the Chilean comic strip Condorito (first published 1949).
The name of a queen who becomes Parzival’s wife in the chivalric romance ‘Parzival’ by Wolfram von Eschenbach.
Diminutive of Cornelius, as well as various names beginning with Cond-.

Meaning, "the feeling or belief that one can rely on someone or something; firm trust." From late Middle English, from Latin confidentia, from confidere ‘have full trust.' Referring to the confidence one may have in God.
Means "comforted" in Latin. This was an augurative name given to a child born after the death of another one.
Portuguese form of Confucius.A notable bearer of this name is Confúcio Moura, a Brazilian politician.
Italian and Spanish form of Confucius. This was borne by Italian politician Confucio Basaglia (1872-1944).

Connemara is an Irish place name occasionally used as a given name. It refers to the northwestern Irish-speaking region of County Galway. It comes from the tribal name Conmhaícne Mara or "Conmac's people by the sea".

Meaning:Connley is a modern Irish name, combining the Gaelic prefix "Conn-", meaning "chief," "leader," or "wisdom," with the suffix "-ley," which is derived from Old Irish and means "meadow" or "clearing." Therefore, the name Connley can be interpreted as "chief of the meadow," "leader of the clearing," or "wise leader in the field."• Conn- comes from the Irish "Con", which is short for "Conn", an ancient Gaelic name meaning "chief," "wisdom," or "intellect." In Irish myth, Conn was also the name of several important figures, such as Conn of the Hundred Battles, a legendary high king.• -ley is derived from Old Irish "leith" or "lath", meaning "meadow," referring to an open field or clearing in nature, often symbolizing fertility, peace, or territory.Origins:The name Connley has Irish Gaelic origins, though it is a modern creation combining traditional Gaelic roots with the English surname suffix -ley. This type of naming structure is often found in modern Irish names that combine elements of leadership and nature, reflecting both cultural heritage and contemporary naming trends.

He survives as a villain in Breton folklore, and is often considered the basis for the legends of Bluebeard and of King Mark of Cornwall in the tale of Tristan & Isolde.

From Late Latin constabilio meaning "to establish, to confirm, to strengthen". This was the name of an 11th-century Italian abbot and saint.

Diminutive of Contessa. Contessina de' Medici (1478-1515) was a daughter of the Florentine ruler Lorenzo "the Magnificent", named in honour of his paternal grandmother - Contessina de' Bardi (c.1390-1473).

Saint Conval (died c.630) was an Irish-born missionary who, when pondering his vocation, was carried by the stone he stood on across the Irish Sea to Inchinnan in Scotland. He was active in the Kingdom of Strathclyde in the area of East Renfrewshire, where there were “Conval wells” in Barrhead and Thornliebank.

From the Breton name Konwenn meaning "white dog" or "white warrior", derived from kon, singular (or plural? genitive?) of ki "dog, warrior" (compare Tanguy, Cunobelinus) combined with gwenn "white". This was the name of an early saint, found in the Breton place names Plougonven and Tre-gonoen.

This was the name of a figure of Aztec mythology, a son of Malinalxochitl who sought revenge for his mother’s abandonment by her people. He was killed and his heart thrown into a lake, where it grew into a nopal, or prickly pear cactus.

Latinized form of Greek Κοπρεύς (Kopreus), which is derived from Greek κόπρειος (kopreios) meaning "full of dung, filthy", from κόπρος (kopros) meaning "excrement, dung". Needless to say, this is quite an unflattering name to have, though it originally may have had a more positive connotation and been associated with the ownership of cattle, rather than just the cattle's dung. It may have also been given as an apotropaic name in families with high infant mortality, or to children left abandoned on a κοπρών (dung heap), who were often taken in and raised as slaves. In Greek mythology, Copreus was the herald of King Eurystheus.

Feminine form of Cordius. In the English-speaking world, this name can sometimes be a short form of Cordelia. A known bearer of this name is the American entrepreneur Cordia Harrington (b. 1954).

Fairly obscure Roman nomen gentile that originated with a plebeian family that was native to the city of Tusculum, which was an important center of worship for the Dioscuri. Only one member of this family is known to history, namely Manius Cordius Rufus (1st century BC). He was a moneyer (triumvir monetalis) under Julius Caesar.The etymology of this Roman family name is uncertain. It may have been derived from Latin cordus, which is a variant form of Latin chordus meaning "late-born" as well as "late in the season". An other etymological source for the name might be Latin corda, which is a variant form of Latin chorda meaning "cord, string". And last but not least, a derivation from cordis, the genitive singular of Latin cor "heart", is also a possibility. With regard to this last etymology, it is perhaps interesting to note that Manius Cordius Rufus minted coins that featured Venus Verticordia ("Venus the turner/changer of hearts").

From a Roman cognomen that was probably derived from Latin cordus, which is a variant form of Latin chordus meaning "late-born" as well as "late in the season". Another possibility is that the name was derived from Latin corda, which is a variant form of chorda, the latinized form of Greek khorda or khorde meaning "cord, string".Apparently, Roman parents tended to give this name to their son when he was born late (either past the mother's estimated due date, or late in the season). If this is true, then both of the aforementioned potential etymologies certainly do make sense. The first one literally refers to lateness, whilst the second one can be interpreted to refer to lateness in a more figurative way. You see, in this particular context, "cord" can refer to the umbilical cord, in which case it must be in the (figurative) sense of the child having been too attached to its mother for it to want to leave the womb (hence the child's late birth).In light of this apparent custom among (some) Roman parents, it is unlikely that this name is derived from Latin cordis, which is the genitive of Latin cor meaning "heart".Bearers of this name were the Roman historian Aulus Cremutius Cordus (1st century AD) and the Roman praetorian prefect Quintus Naevius Cordus Sutorius Macro (1st century AD).

Coming from the city of Corinth (Greece).The use as a given name may be inspired by the Episteles to the Corinthians, two books of the New Testament.On the BBC television comedy 'Two Pints of Lager and a Packet of Crisps' protagonist Janet Keogh had a son she named Corinthian.

Roman cognomen which was derived from Corioli, the name of an ancient but now lost Volscian city. Although derived from the Volscian language, it is not known what the meaning of the city's name was in Volscian. A known bearer of this name was Gaius Marcius Coriolanus, a Roman general from the 5th century BC. He is also featured in one of William Shakespeare's plays.

Short form of both Cornelis and Cornelius (for men) and Cornelia (for women), but the name is most often encountered on men. It is unisex in the Netherlands, but strictly masculine in Flanders, the Dutch-speaking part of Belgium.Notable bearers of this name include the Flemish soccer player Corneel De Ceulaer (b. 1947), the Flemish author Corneel van Kuyck (1919-1991) and the Flemish scientist and Nobel Prize winner Corneille "Corneel" Heymans (1892-1968).

Diminutive of Corneel as well as of the related names Cornelis and Cornelius (for men) and Cornelia (for women).This name is only used informally, meaning: so far it has not been used as an official name on birth certificates. It is also rather old-fashioned and one is more likely to encounter it in Flanders (the Dutch-speaking part of Belgium) than in the Netherlands, because the diminutive suffix -ke is used more often there than in the Netherlands, where the diminutive suffix -je is generally preferred (as such, see Corneeltje).

Diminutive of Corneel as well as of the related names Cornelis and Cornelius (for men) and Cornelia (for women).This name is predominantly feminine in the Netherlands, especially as an official name on birth certificates. For men, the name is nowadays exclusively an informal name, but this was not always the case in the past.
Catalan and Friulian form of Cornelius.

Named for the deep red gemstone which is also known as a carnelian. The word comes from the Latin cornum, meaning "cornel cherry" - a flowering dogwood tree with small, dark red fruit.-------------------------------------English form of the Latin name Cornelianus.
Roman cognomen which was derived from Cornelius. A bearer of this name was the Roman rhetorician Sulpicius Cornelianus, who lived in the 2nd century AD.
Variant of Cornelia, which was probably influenced by its French form Cornélie.
Diminutive of Cornelie, as it contains the Dutch diminutive suffix -ke.
Diminutive of Cornélie, as it contains the French feminine diminutive suffix -ine.
Variation of Cornelia and feminine version of Cornelius.

Feminine form of Cornelis, which was created by adding the Dutch and Frisian diminutive suffix -je to it. This particular way of feminizing masculine names is typically Dutch as well as Frisian, and originated in medieval times.

Feminine form of Cornelis, which was created by adding the Dutch and Frisian diminutive suffix -ke to it. This particular way of feminizing masculine names is typically Dutch as well as Frisian, and originated in medieval times.
Transferred use of the surname Corney.
Derived from Cornelius or a blend of the name Cor with Niels 2, this name is quite, quite rare in The Netherlands and had only 5 bearers in the 2006 statistics for Dutch names.
Feminine form of Cornificius. This name was borne by a Roman female poet and writer from the 1st century BC.
Italian and Spanish form of Cornificius.

From a Roman nomen gentile, which was derived from Latin cornificus "making horns", which itself was derived from Latin cornu "horn" and Latin facere "to make, to do". This name was borne by a Roman consul and a Roman poet, both of whom lived in the 1st century BC.

Roman cognomen which was derived from the Latin adjective cornutus meaning "horned", itself ultimately derived from the Latin noun cornu meaning "horn".A known bearer of this name was the Stoic philosopher Lucius Annaeus Cornutus (1st century AD).
Transferred use of the surname Cornwallis.

Means "choir" in Spanish, taken from the title of the Virgin Mary Nuestra Señora del Coro (meaning "Our Lady of the Choir"). She is the patroness of the city of Donostia/San Sebastián in the Basque province of Gipuzkoa.
Latinized form of Koroibos. A known bearer of this name was the Olympic victor Coroebus of Elis, who won the stadion race at the 1st Olympiad in 776 BC.
A middle Jaredite king, son of Levi.

Taken from the Venezuelan Spanish title of the Virgin Mary Nuestra Señora de Coromoto, meaning "Our Lady of Coromoto," the name taken from the cacique (chief) of a local Indian tribe, known as the Cosmes, who, legend says, twice witnessed the Virgin Mary.Our Lady of Coromoto is regarded as the patron saint of Venezuela, similar to Our Lady of Guadalupe in Mexico and Our Lady of Luján in Argentina. For this reason the name is most common in Venezuela but it also has some use in other Spanish-speaking countries.
Derived from Spanish coronación, meaning "coronation", referring to the idea that the Virgin Mother of God was physically crowned as Queen of Heaven after her Assumption.

Means "crowned" in Spanish, taken from the titles of the Virgin Mary Nuestra Señora de la Coronada and Virgen de la Coronada, meaning "Our Lady of the Crowned" and "The Virgin of the Crowned", respectively. Also compare Corona, Incoronata. She is the patron saint of Villafranca de los Barros in the western province of Badajoz (also declared the patroness of the vineyards in 2012 by the then archbishop of Mérida-Badajoz, Santiago García Aracil) and is also venerated at the hermitage in Calañas in the Andalusian province of Huelva. This name is also used in other Spanish-speaking countries, mostly in Central America.
Derived from Latin coronatus meaning "crowned".This name was borne by at least two saints.
Likely an invented name, possibly a combination of Corinna and Rhonda. Also compare Sharonda.
Means "crow". Corone was a young princess who was saved from Poseidon by Athena in Ovid's Metamorphoses.
Diminutive of Socorro, Dioscoro, and other names containing a similar sound.
Diminutive of Socorro, Dioscoro, and other names containing a similar sound.

Borrowed from Latin corpus meaning "body," more specifically referring, in this case, to the Body of Christ (Corpus Christi). This name, sometimes used with the full name Corpus Christi, is usually given to children born on or around the feast day of Corpus Christi.
Medieval Italian diminutive of Corrado, as -uccio is an Italian masculine diminutive suffix.
A name found on an ancient Ogham stone. Corrbrias is believed to be the son of Amalgaid mac Fiachrae, one of the kings of Connacht.
Short form of Cornelis and Cornelius (for men) and Cornelia (for women).This name is unisex in the Netherlands, but strictly masculine in Flanders, the Dutch-speaking part of Belgium.

A small Australian shrub whose leaves give off a fruity smell when crushed. Named in honour of the Portuguese botanist José Correia da Serra; Correia is a common Portuguese surname meaning “leather strap”, originally given to those who worked in the leather trade.

Diminutive of Cor and Corre as well as of the related names Cornelis and Cornelius (for men) and Cornelia (for women).This name is predominantly feminine in the Netherlands, especially as an official name on birth certificates. For men, the name is nowadays exclusively an informal name.
Meaning uncertain, possibly an elaboration of Corrie using the suffix esta (found in Celesta). This was borne by American physician Corresta Thisba Canfield (1833-1920).

Diminutive of Corrie, as it contains the Dutch diminutive suffix -ke. This essentially makes the name a double diminutive of Cornelia and other feminine names that start with Cor-.There are likely also cases where this name is a contraction of Cornelieke or a blend of a name that starts with Cor- with a name that ends in -(r)ieke, such as Marieke.
Transferred use of the surname Corrigan.
Short form of Corstiaan. This name was borne by Corstiaan 'Cors' Kleijwegt (1899-1967), a Dutch politician.

Diminutive of Accorsa, itself derived from Latin accursia "aided; helped". The name coincides with the Italian word corsa "a run; a race (the competition)" as well as with corsa, the feminine form of corso, "Corsican; woman from Corsica".
A vavasor in the service of Nascien and Flegentine.He left with Flegetine and his son Elicanor for Britain, where he joined with Joseph of Arimathea’s followers.
From the island of Corsica in the Mediterranean sea.
Of uncertain origin and meaning. This name is traditionally found in the Engadine valley.

column5: kor-SI-no(Italian, Spanish, Asturian, Filipino)|kur-SI-nu(Brazilian Portuguese, African Portuguese)
column12: Transferred use of the surname Corsino.
Has Hebrew origins, as the name is mentioned in the bible as one of the 4demon kings reigning over 72 demons.
Archaic Low German form of Cord, recorded between the 15th and the 18th centuries.

Variant of Curtana, from the Latin curtus, meaning "short", the name of the ceremonial sword used at the Coronation of British royalty. It is borne by an artificial intelligence creature in the Halo video game franchise, as well as Microsoft's virtual assistant, which was named for the character in the game.

From the titles of the Virgin Mary, Nuestra Señora de Cortes and La Virgen de Cortes, meaning "Our Lady of Cortes" and "The Virgin of Cortes" respectively (coincides with the words meaning "cut; style, type" or "courts").She is the patroness of Alcaraz in the province of Albacete in central Spain.
Transferred use of the surname Cortez.

From the Marian title Virgen del Cortijo, which gives its name to a chapel in Murillo de Río Leza (La Rioja).The name comes from cortijo, a kind of villa that is typical in rural Spain. The chapel was initially built within the estate, hence the association.
Means "short" in Italian and Spanish, from Latin curtus.
Either taken from the English word corvette meaning "a small warship" or the car Chevrolet Corvette.
English, German and Romanian form of Corvinus.
Italian and Spanish form of Corvinus.
Diminutive of Corvus. A bearer of this name was Marcus Valerius Messalla Corvinus, a Roman general from the 1st century AD.
Italian and Portuguese form of Corvus. Corvo Attano is the name of the lead protagonist in Bethesda studio's popular video game 'Dishonored'.
Derived from Latin corvus "raven." Marcus Valerius Corvus was a Roman hero of the 4th century BC.
Diminutive of Corazon, Socorro, and other names containing cor. Corazon "Cory" Aquino was the 11th president of the Philippines.
Probably related to Greek κορυδός (korydos) meaning "lark". This was a stock name for a shepherd in ancient Greek pastoral poems and fables.
Rare Australian name derived from the name of the tree.

From Greek Κόρυμβος (Korymbos) meaning "uppermost point, top; cluster of ivy berries". This was the name of the Greek demigod of the fruit of the ivy, son of Mystis and probable childhood companion of Dionysos.

Probably taken directly from the Ancient Greek word κορυφή (koryphe) meaning "top of the head, crown; top, apex; mountain peak", or figuratively "excellence". This was the name of one of the Oceanids in Greek mythology. In some versions of the myth, she was the mother of Coria by Zeus.

Derived from coryphaeus, which is the latinized form of the Greek word κορυφαῖος (koryphaios) meaning "head man, chief, leader". The word itself is ultimately derived from the Greek noun κορυφή (koruphe) meaning "head, top". In ancient Greece, koryphaios was originally a term in theatre: it was used to refer to the leader of the chorus. But over time, the term evolved into something more broad and general, in that it came to be used in reference to anyone who was in a position of power or leadership, such as prominent religious figures and influential philosophers.In modern popular culture, Corypheus is the name of a villain in the "Dragon Age" video game series.
Diminutive of Cosmo, Costello, and other names beginning with Cos-.
One of Jesus' ancestors in Luke 3:28.
Transferred use of the surname Cosby.
Transferred use of the surname Cosgrove.
Feminine form of Cosme and Galician cognate of Cosima.
Corsican and Campidanese Sardinian form of Cosmas.
Medieval Italian diminutive of Cosimo, as -uccio is an Italian masculine diminutive suffix.
Feminine form of Cosme and Cosmo.
Probably derived from Cosmo by adding the at that time popular name ending -aele (e.g., from the name Raffaele).
Provençal and Gascon form of Cosmas.
Latinized form of the Greek name Κοσμία (Kosmia), which meant "orderly, decent".
Feminine form of Cossinius. Cossinia was one of the Vestal Virgins.
Femenine form of the roman gens Cossutius. It was the name of a Roman woman who became engaged to Julius Caesar prior to his reaching adulthood.
Italian form of Constabilis. A famous bearer is Italian-American mobster Costabile Farace (1960-1989).
Variant transcription of Κωστάκης (see Kostakis) chiefly used in Cyprus.
Piedmontese and Venetian form of Costanza.
Italian form of Constans. It is also a common-used adjective in Italian with the same meaning of the name.
Ligurian and Venetian form of Constantine 1.
English contracted form of the Greek name Konstantina. It is borne by Costeen Hatzipourganis, an Australian interior designer of Greek descent who is the girlfriend of tennis player Nick Kyrgios.
Probably a feminine form of Costa.
Transferred from the originally Irish surname Costello.
Transferred use of the surname Costigan.
Possibly from the Karachay-Balkar чот (çot) meaning "light".
Diminutive of José or sometimes Josefa. A famous bearer is Chilean-American television actress Coté de Pablo (1979-), whose birth name was María José.
Corrupted form of ǀHúnntuǃattǃatte̥n, possibly coined to make it pronounceable by the non-native speakers.
Cotiso was the name of a Dacian king (approximately 30 BC) who ruled the mountains between Banat and Oltenia (modern-day Romania).
From Sino-Vietnamese 機智 (cơ trí) meaning "quick-witted, clever", composed of 機 (cơ) meaning "flexible" and 智 (trí) meaning "intelligence".
Variant of Caitrìona found on the Isle of Lewis.
The name of an Eastern Shoshone artist and son of Chief Washakie.
Transferred use of the surname Cotton.
Transferred use of the surname Cottonwood.
Possibly from the Karachay-Balkar чот (çot) meaning "light".
From late 18th century, from French couguar, abbreviation of modern Latin cuguarcarana, from Guarani guaçuarana.
Either a transferred use of the surname Coulson or a variant of Colson.
Means "the one who has the strength" in Fula.
From the English council, referring to a body of people that are formally constituted and meet regularly.

From the aristocratic title count, ultimately from Latin comitem meaning "companion", refering to a noble who fights alongside the king. This is more often found as a nickname, but it is rarely used as a given name.
Possibly derived from the surname Countee. A notable bearer of this name was the African-American writer and poet Countee Cullen (1903-1946).
Derived from Latin comitissa "countess". This word, while more commonly known as a title, was also used as a personal name occasionally.
Variant of Cooper. Couper was given to 12 boys in 2015 according to the SSA.

Borrowing from Old French corage (French courage), from Vulgar Latin coraticum, from Latin cor (“heart”). Distantly related to cardiac (“of the heart”), which is from Greek, but from the same Proto-Indo-European root.
From the French place name Courtenay (originally a derivative of the personal name Curtenus, itself derived from Latin curtus meaning "short").This is the original form of Courtney.

Transferred use of the surname Courtland.Possibly derived from Cortland, an archaic form of the Dutch surname Kortland, which in turn is possibly derived from a Dutch town of the same name (which might have served as the inspiration for the city Cortland in the American state of New York). The surname means "short land", derived from Dutch kort "short" and land "land". Since Dutch naming law has always strictly prohibited the use of surnames as first names, neither Cortland, Kortland or even Courtland have ever been used as a first name in The Netherlands. Therefore, Courtland's usage should be listed as (American-)English, since the United States of America does allow the use of surnames as first names.
Likely from the English word courtly, meaning "befitting of, or relating to a royal court".
Inspired by Courtney, with the -lyn suffix.
Archaic French-Yiddish and Judeo-French form of Kusel.
The word “cove” with the popular suffix -lyn added the the end of the name.
From the English vocabulary word covenant meaning "an agreement." In a biblical context, a covenant is an oath-bound agreement, often involving God and his people.

Coventina was a Romano-British goddess of wells and springs. She is known from multiple inscriptions at one site in Northumberland county of England, an area surrounding a wellspring near Carrawburgh on Hadrian's Wall. She personified a holy spring that had healing powers. Her name is generally derived from Proto-Celtic *kom-men- "memory" and *ti-ni "to melt; to disappear".
Transferred use of the surname Covey.
Abbreviation of "coronavirus disease" in reference to COVID-19.
From a Commedia Dell’Arte character, a traditional dumb trickster. It is a double diminutive of Giacomo. In French, Coviello is called Covielle
Variant spelling of Tsovinar. 'Cov' is most likely a loanword from Urartian ṣûǝ, meaning "(inland) sea." This spelling is used in an Armenian epic.
Transferred use of the surname Cowan.
Transferred use of the surname Coward.
Transferred use of the surname Cowell.
Short form of Cornelis (for men) and Cornelia (for women). Also compare Cokkie.A known bearer of this name was the Dutch actress Cox Habbema (1944-2016).

Meaning uncertain. It might be a combination of Cornelis or Cornelius with a name that starts with J-, such as Jan 1. At least, that appears to have been the case for the Limburgian soccer player Coy Koopal (1932-2003).
Meaning uncertain. It might possibly be derived from the surname Choyce. Alternatively, it might be a combination of Coy with names like Boyce and Royce.
Probably derived from Nahuatl coyolli "bell" and the affiliative suffix -tecatl.
Means "little bell", derived from Nahuatl coyolli "bell".
Means "red-winged blackbird" in Nahuatl, derived from coyolli "bell, jingle bell" and toltotl "bird".
From the name of the small dog-like animal. Has been used rarely as a given name since the 1800s, though its use is steadily increasing since the 2000s.
Means "little coyote" in Spanish. Most notably used in the novel 'The Pearl' (1947) by John Steinbeck.
Means "coyote" in Nahuatl, sometimes used to mean "foreigner".
This name is quite uncommon but it is found naturally in certain parts of Indonesia. Some indigenous tribes in Indonesia say that the name means (using rough translation) "Powerful Ancestors".
Coz in Hebrew allegedly means "a thorn", or perhaps "nimble." It occurs in the Old Testament (1 Chr. 4: 8) where Coz is sited as a descendant of Caleb.
Derived from Nahuatl cozamalotl "rainbow" combined with the affiliative suffix -catl.
Probably derived from Nahuatl cozauhqui, meaning "yellow, gold".
Means "king vulture" in Nahuatl, the sixteenth day sign of the tonalpohualli.
Meaning uncertain, possibly derived from Nahuatl cozcamecatl "string of beads used for counting" and michiuautli "fish-amaranth".
Means "jewel, necklace" in Nahuatl, sometimes used as a metaphor for an infant or small child.
Means "little jewel, little necklace" in Nahuatl, a diminutive form of Cozca.

The name of Cozma is of Greek origin. It can come from the name Kosmas, Eosmia, Eosmos. The meaning of the name Kosmas comes from the compound word Kosmos or Kosmein. In the old Greek Kosmos had two meanings: "order" and "ornament, ornament". The first of these is continued by the current "cosmos".The name reached Romanians through the Russian language, in the form of Cosma. It appears in documents from the fifteenth century both in the Romanian Country and in Moldova. Today it is especially encountered as a family name.
From the English word meaning "warm and comfortable", sometimes used as a diminutive of Cosima or Cosette.
Old High German kraft "strength, force, power".
Transferred use of the surname Cragg.

Feminine form of Cranaus, meaning "stony" in Ancient Greek. This was the name of an Athenian princess in Greek mythology, the daughter of King Cranaus. It is also the name of an island off the coast of Gytheio, where Paris of Troy and Helen spent their first night together in Greek mythology.

Means "rocky point", from Ancient Greek κραναός (kranaos) meaning "rocky, rugged" and αἰχμή (aichme) meaning "point of a spear, head of an arrow", or figuratively "war". In Greek mythology Cranaechme was a daughter of King Cranaus of Athens. Her sisters were Cranaë and Atthis.
Latinized form of Κραναός (Kranaos), meaning "rocky, rugged" in Ancient Greek. In Greek mythology, this was the name of the second king of Athens.
Transferred use of the surname Crandall.
Possibly a transferred usage of the surname Crane or directly from the word crane.

Bardic name of Sarah Jane Rees, who named herself after the village she came from, Llangrannog, which is named in honour of Saint Carannog, combined with the feminine -wen suffix, from gwen, meaning "white" or "blessed".

Possibly a feminine form of Crantor "sovereign, ruler; one who accompanies", ultimately from κραίνω (kraino) "to accomplish, perform, fulfil". This was the name of one of the Nereids in Greek mythology.
From Old Irish cráebach meaning “branches, branch-wood”.
Medieval Portuguese form of Clara and Sardinian form of Chiara.
The name of the Dutch reiziger (traveller) Crasa Wagner who identified the girl depicted in a film sequence from the Westerbork transit camp as Settela Steinbach.
From the word crash. This was used for video game character Crash Bandicoot, an orange bandicoot from his self-titled platform game series created by Sony.
Italian and Portuguese form of Crassus.

Roman cognomen which was derived from the Latin adjective crassus, which can mean "solid, thick, dense" as well as "fat, gross, plump". This name was borne by several ancient Romans, such as the Roman general and politician Marcus Licinius Crassus (1st century BC).
Medieval Romanian variant of Cristea. This name was borne by the brother of Ștefan cel Mare.
An irregular praenomen borne by Cratea Caecilius.
Latinized form of Krates. Known bearers of this name include the comic poet Crates (5th century BC) and the Cynic philosopher Crates of Thebes (3rd century BC).
Latinized form of Kratesikleia. This was the name of a Spartan queen from the 3rd century BC.
Latinized form of Kratesipolis. This was the name of a female tyrant from the 4th century BC, who ruled over both Corinth and Sicyon.
Spanish and Portuguese form of Cratylus.
Catalan form of Kratippos via its latinized form Cratippus.
Portuguese form of Kratippos via its latinized form Cratippus.
Spanish form of Kratippos via its latinized form Cratippus.
French form of Kratippos via its latinized form Cratippus.
Italian form of Kratippos via its latinized form Cratippus.
Latinized form of Kratippos. A known bearer of this name was Cratippus of Athens, an ancient Greek historian from the 4th century BC.
Spanish and Portuguese form of Kraft. It also coincides with the name of a Portuguese village.
Latinized form of Kratylos. This was the name of an ancient Athenian philosopher from the late 5th century BC.
Sicilian variant of Clàudiu and Sardinian form of Claudius.
Archaic name from the Bourgogne-Franche-Comté region.
Either a variant of Creighton or transferred use of the surname Crayton.

From the English word meaning "living being", ultimately deriving from Late Latin creatura. In the parish registers of 16th-century England this was used to refer to infants, both male and female, who survived birth only just long enough to be baptized. (In the case of one Creature Cheseman, she survived infancy and bore the name for the rest of her life.)
Possibly a diminutive of Credence or derived from a surname.

From the English word meaning "acceptance of a reason or belief as true". The name may have been popularized by Credence Barebone, a character in the 'Fantastic Beasts' films who was played by Ezra Miller.

Variant of Credence. This spelling is likely influenced by the American rock band Creedence Clearwater Revival, with the word Creedence being named after Tom Fogerty's friend Credence Newball, influenced by the English word creed "that which is believed".
A nature name meaning a stream smaller than a river. The word creek is originally from Old Norse kriki, a bend or crook, and from Middle English creke.
From the English word creek combined with the popular name suffix lyn, possibly inspired by Brooklynn and Lakelynn.
Derived from Manx creeney "wise, shrewed, common sense", intended as a Manx equivalent of Sophia.
Of debated origin and meaning. Theories include a derivation from Manx creen "old; worn out" and Manx creeney "wise".
Transferred use of the surname Cregan.
Creidhne was a goldsmith in Irish Mythology. He was the son of Brigid and Tuireann.
Transferred use of the surname Creig or variant of Craig.
Variant transcription of Kreine (which may be a Yiddish form of Keren).

Means "token of the egg", and in effect "mundane egg", from Welsh creir "a token, jewel, sacred object" and wy "egg". In the Mabinogion, a collection of tales from Welsh myth, she was a daughter of Ceridwen and one of the three most beautiful maids of the Isle of Britain. This was also the name of a 6th-century Breton saint from Wales.

Cremorna Garden is the former stage name of Mrs. Rosanna Wrayburn, a retired Victorian-era stage performer, in the 1930 novel Strong Poison by Dorothy L. Sayers. It is based on the name of Cremorne Gardens, which were popular pleasure gardens in London during the mid-19th century (from 1845 until the gardens closed in 1877), named for Thomas Dawson, 1st Viscount Cremorne (1725-1813; see the Irish place name Cremorne).
Derived from Romanian crenguța, the diminutive of creangă, "branch".
Transferred use of the surname Crenshaw.
Uncertain etymology. May have been one of the first king of Mercia, though his existence is disputed.
Perhaps an invented name, based on the English word Creole, or on similar-sounding names such as Leola.
French feminine and masculine form of Crescentius.
Spanish feminine form of Crescentianus (see Crescentian).

French and Romanian form and English variant of Crescens. In the English-speaking world, it is now considered a nature name referring to the phase of the moon, derived from Old French creissant, ultimately from Latin crescere "come forth, spring up, grow, thrive".As an English name, Crescent has been in use from the 17th century onwards, although increasingly rarely so; it was revived in the early 1970s. As a French name, it is now obsolescent while the Romanian name is not used outside of the biblical context.
English form of Crescentianus, a derivative of Crescentius derived from Crescens. This is the name of several saints.
Feminine form of Crescentianus (see Crescentian). This is the name of a saint whose feast day is celebrated on May 5.
Italian, Spanish, and Portuguese form of Crescentinus.
Derivative of Crescentius. This is the name of the patron saint of Urbino.
Spelling variation of Kreszenz and occasionally Crescens.
Italian feminine form of Crescentianus (see Crescentian).
Italian form of Crescentius. A known bearer of this name was Crescenzio Gambarelli, a 17th-century Italian painter from Siena.

Crescence is an uncommon feminine given name and surname of Latin origin. Derived from the word crescere, it means "to grow," "to increase," or "flourishing," sharing etymological roots with the words crescent and crescendo.
From the English-speaking word cresent, a face of the moon.
Diminutive of Cresencia, Crestina, Crestita, and other names starting with Cres-.

Creslin is a main character in the second book in the 'Magic of Recluse series. he possesed the power to call immense controlled storms and change the worldwide climate with Order magic, despite it's usual inability to cause harm. he was also a master blade and an outstanding musician.

Derived from Greek κρείσσων (kreisson) meaning "superior, better" and φόνος (phonos) meaning "murder, slaughter". This was the name of a great-great-grandson of Herakles in Greek mythology, a king of Messene.
Walloon, Langadocian, Judeo-French and Provençal form of Crispin.
Italian feminine form of Crispino and Languedocian and Provençal feminine form of Crespin.
Derived from the Catalan adjective creixent "growing", ultimately from the verb créixer “to grow”, this name is a cognate of Crescens. In medieval Occitania, it was used to translate Tzemach.
Transferred use of the surname Cress.
Short form of Cressida; previously a short form of Lucretia.
Derived from Old French cressant, the present participle of crestre "to increase; to augment", this name is a cognate of Crescens.
Derived from Anglo-Norman crestre, ultimately from Old French croistre "to increase; to augment".

The daughter of King Clodoveus of Cornwall, an ancestor of Mark and Tristan.Cressile married Candaces, the son of the murdered King of Lyonesse. She had twelve sons, including Crissidés, who inherited Cornwall.
The daughter of King Clodoveus of Cornwall, an ancestor of Mark and Tristan.
Transferred use of the surname Creswell.

A mythological name of unknown meaning, possibly deriving from the Luvian *kursatta, meaning "island of silver" or "island of cutting." The name of several characters from Greek mythology including a daughter of Hesperus, the mother of Pasiphae, the wife of Minos, and a granddaughter of Deucalion.The island of Crete likely derives its name from a Greek mythological figure named Crete who was one of the Titans.
Uncertain etymology. In Greek mythology, this was the name of an Achaean warrior who fought for the Greeks in the Trojan War alongside his twin brother Orsilochus.
'Creus, the Grand Solar Knight' is a character in the online game Roblox.
Spanish, Galician and Portuguese form of Creusa.
Anglicized form of the Irish name Criomhthann, from Old Irish crimthan meaning "fox". A variant, Crimhthain, was the original name of Saint Columba.
Transferred use of the surname Crewe.
Italian and Spanish form of Criasus.
Latinized form of Kriasos. In Greek mythology, Criasus is the name of a king of Argos.
Transferred use of the surname Crichton.
Transferred use of the surname Crick.
Originally a diminutive of Christina and Christine.
Short form of Quirijn. A bearer of this name was the Dutch 17th-century painter Crijn Hendricksz. Volmarijn.
Diminutive of Christian, Christer and Christoffer.
From the peninsula Crimea in the Black Sea. Use as a given name in the 19th century was probably influenced by news coverage of the Crimean war (1853–1856).
From Middle English cryme, crime, from Old French crime, crimne, from Latin crīmen combined with Middle English fightere, fyghtor, feghtere, feghtare, fiȝtare, fiȝtere, from Old English feohtere.
Portuguese and Spanish form of Kriemhild.
Italian and Portuguese form of Kriemhild.

From the English word for the purplish-red color, ultimately derived from Arabic قِرْمِز (qirmiz) "kermes", from Middle Persian کرمست* (*kermest) "worm, kermes", originally meant the kermes dye from crushed Kermes insects, but now used as a generic term for slightly bluish-red colors. This is the national color of Nepal.
Meaning "fox", from the Old Irish word crimthann.
Latinized form of Krino. This is the name of two characters in Greek mythology.
Italian and Portuguese form of Crius (see Kreios).
This is a modern Irish name which is directly derived from Irish críonna meaning "wise".

Variant form of Cariou, which is a short form of Carioulf, itself a variant form of Charioulf, which is the original French form of Chariulf. Alternatively, this name is a short form of Crioult, which is a variant form of the aforementioned Carioulf.This is one of the names by which the obscure 6th-century Frankish saint Chariulf (often found written as Cariulf) is known in France. He was a disciple of the Frankish missionary and saint Marculf (better known under the French names Marcou, Marcouf and Marcoul), who died either on the same day as he did, or several days afterwards. As a result, they were buried together (along with an other disciple of Marculf's) in the same tomb in the abbey of Nanteuil, which was located in the diocese of Coutances in the Cotentin Peninsula of Normandy.
From the devotional title of Mary "Our Lady of Criptana" in the town of Campo de Criptana, Spain.
Spanish and Portuguese form of Chrysalis. In Spanish-speaking Latin America, it is mainly used in Venezuela.
Catalan and Romanian form of Chrysanthos.A known bearer of this name was the Catalan soccer player Crisant Bosch i Espín (1907-1981).
Spanish and Galician form of Chrysanthe.
The wife of King Lac and mother of Erec, sister of King Pelles. She was a skilled sorceress, and she enchanted Erec in such a way that he could never be affected by magic.
Variant of Griselda, possibly influenced by Cristina.
Spanish and Portuguese form of Chryses.
Possibly a variant of Cristin or Christina.
Tagalog diminutive of Cristina, Crisanta and other similar names.
Catalan form of Chrysippos via its latinized form Chrysippus.
Spanish and Portuguese form of Chrysippos via its latinized form Chrysippus.
Italian form of Chrysippos via its latinized form Chrysippus.
Merging of the names Christen and Marike.
Derivative of Christina recorded in medieval Wales.
Variant of Cristóforo influenced by the Greek word chrysos ("gold"), present in names like Crisóstomo and Crisógono.
Portuguese and Spanish form of Chrysogonus.
Italian form of Chrysogonos( see Chrysogonus).
Means "crucible" as well as "melting pot" in Spanish. This is borne by Venezuelan actress Crisol Carabal (1971-).
Spanish and Portuguese form of Chrysologus.
Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Crispian.
Extended form of Crispus or otherwise a shorter form of Crispinianus.
Dutch form of Crispinus (see Crispin). A known bearer of this name is the Dutch speed skater Crispijn Ariëns (b. 1989).
Spanish and Galician form of Crispin.

Feminine form of Crispinus. A notable bearer was the 2nd-century Roman empress Bruttia Crispina, the wife of Emperor Commodus. This name was also borne by a 4th-century Christian martyr from North Africa.
English form of Crispinianus. This name was borne by a Roman saint from the 3rd century AD.
Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Crispinian.
Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Crispin.
Corsican and Sicilian form of Crispinus.
Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Crispus.
Spanish form of Crispulus. Known bearers of this name include the Spanish actor Críspulo Cabezas (b. 1981) and the Filipino lieutenant general Críspulo Aguinaldo (1863-1897).

Derived from the Latin adjective crispulus meaning "curled, having curled hair". Also see the related names Crispus and Crispinus.This was the name of an obscure saint from the 2nd century AD, who was martyred together with saint Gabinus.
Diminutive of Crispin, which has also occasionally been used for Christian and Christopher.This name is extremely rare, due to the easy association with the English adjective crispy.
Diminutive of Christopher, Christina, and other names beginning with Chris.
Of uncertain origin and meaning.It might be an elaboration of Cris, a variant of Cressa or a variant of Chryssa.
Son of King Candaces of Cornwall and Cressile. He became king of the country when his father died.He was an ancestor of King Mark of Cornwall.
Diminutive of Cristina, Cristine, and other names with a similar sound.
Diminutive of Cristine, Cristina, and other names with a similar sound.
Medieval English diminutive of Christopher which became the regular Manx form of this name.

A dithematic name formed from the Greek name element christos "anointed" and the Germanic name element wald "to rule".This name is known in southern Italy for a popular tale: "The legend of Cristalda and Pizzomunno", a tragic love story which inspired also a song by Max Gazzè.
From the name of a 1977 Chanel perfume, probably from French cristal meaning "crystal" (see Crystal).
Combination of Cristal and the popular name suffix lyn.
