Manx form of Christian. Historically, this name was used on both men and women.

Possibly a diminutive of Cristiana, a derivative of Latin christiana meaning "Christian (woman)". This was the name of a Spanish saint (from Talavera, Toledo) who was martyred during the persecutions of the Roman emperor Diocletian in the early 4th century.
Romansh form of Christina, traditionally found in the Surselva region.
Combination of the name Cristiano and the popular suffix -i (present in other names such as Ivani) or possibly a transferred use of the Italian surname Cristiani.
Medieval Italian diminutive of Cristiano, as -uccio is an Italian masculine diminutive suffix.
Diminutive of Cristina, Cristine, and other names with a similar sound.
Possibly a combination of Cristiane with a name that ends in -ele, such as Luciele or Mariele.
Italian, Catalan and Spanish form of Christinus.
Irish form of Christina, which was "brought into Scotland by Queen Margaret, and into Ireland by the Anglo-Normans."
Short form of Cristóbal and Crístofer.
Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Christodorus.
Tuscan medieval feminine form of Cristoforo.
Corsican and Sicilian form of Christopher.
Cremish and Milanese Lombard form of Christopher.
Spanish and Portuguese form of Christopher reflecting the English pronunciation.
Romansh form of Christopher, traditionally found in the Engadine valley.
Aragonese and Franco-Provençal form of Christopher.
Occitan, Gascon and Catalan form of Christopher.
Brazilian Portuguese form of Christopher. A famous bearer of the name is Cristovam Buarque (1944-), politician and Brazilian senator.
Diminutive of Cristina, Cristine, or other names with similar sounds.
Possibly connected with Ancient Greek κριθή (krithé) "barley". Critheïs was said to be the mother of Homer.
Spanish and Italian form of Kritolaos.
Latinized form of Kritolaos. This name was borne by a Greek philosopher from the 2nd century BC.
This was the name of a Gallic gladiator and military leader in the Third Servile War between the Roman Republic and rebel slaves (died 72 B.C.). His name means "one with curly hair" in Gaulish.
Italian form of Kritias and Krizia.
In Mario Puzo’s novels, “Croccifixio” is a fictional variant of the traditional Sicilian name Crocifìsso (also rendered “Crocefìsso” in Italian).
Means "cross" in Italian, making it a cognate of Cruz.
Variant of Crocifisso. A famous bearer of this name is Crocefisso Maggio (1962–), a five-pin billiards player.
Transferred use of the surname Crockett.
Derived from Greek κρόκος (krokos) "crocus". In Greek mythology, Crocus was a mortal youth who was changed by the gods into a saffron flower.
Meaning unknown. Croesus was the King of Lydia from 595 BCE to 546 BCE. He is best known for his immense wealth, which became legendary in both Greek and Persian histories.
Transferred use of the surname Croft as well as a diminutive of Crawford.
French cognate of Cruz, possibly taken from the name of St. Croix, the largest of the Virgin Islands (which was originally Santa Cruz, "Holy Cross" in Spanish, the name given by Columbus).
Italian and Spanish form of Chromius.
Transferred use from the surname Cromwell derived from the place name Cromwell.
Derived from a diminutive of crón "swarthy". This was the name of two seventh-century Irish saints and miracle-workers. Original Irish Gaelic form of Cronan.
From Irish Gaelic Crónán, from crón "swarthy". This was the name of two seventh-century Irish saints and miracle-workers.
Italian and Spanish form of Cronus.
Transferred use of the surname Crosley.
Transferred use of the surname Cross or simply from the word cross.

Meaning uncertain, perhaps from Middle Irish crobh bhan "white hand". This was the byname of Godred Crovan (d. 1095), an 11th-century Norse conqueror who ruled the Isle of Man. It has been interpreted as a mocking reference to Godred's supposed habit of wearing white gauntlets into battle and aversion to getting his hands dirty in combat.
Derived from the name of the crow bird.
Transferred use of the surname Crowe.
Transferred use of the surname Crowell.
Transferred use of the surname Crowley 1 or Crowley 2.
Elaborated form of Cruz using the popular Caribbean Spanish name suffix lis.

Plural form of Cruz, taken from the titles of the Virgin Mary La Virgen de las Cruces and Nuestra Señora de las Cruces, meaning "The Virgin of the Crosses" and "Our Lady of the Crosses" respectively. She is the patron saint of Daimiel (Spain).
Earliest known usage stemmed from the mid 4th century in Rome, following the rule of Constantine. The meaning of the name is "Crucifixion."

Means "of the cross" in Latin (the genitive form of Crux), referring to the cross of the crucifixion. This is used as the second part of compound religious or monastic names, such as Maria Crucis ("Mary of the (Holy) Cross") and Johannes Crucis ("John of the Cross").It is a Latin equivalent of Spanish de la Cruz and French de la Croix.
Crudor is the knight who requires a mantle of knights' and ladies' hair from his lady Briana before he is willing to marry her in Book 6, Canto 1 of "The Faerie Queene". He is reformed by Calidore.
Means "little grain" in Old Irish, from Old Irish cruithnecht "wheat, grain" combined with a diminutive suffix. This was the name of a 6th-century Irish saint known as one of the mentors of Columba.
Transferred use of the surname Crusoe.
Latin for "cross". This is the name of a constellation in the southern hemisphere, commonly known as the Southern Cross.
Extremely rare name which was likely inspired by the novel Cruzamante ou la Sainte Amante de la Croix by Marie Françoise Loquet, published in 1786.
Possibly an elaboration of Cruz, chiefly used in Colombia. It also coincides with a surname.
Variant of Chris or a short form of Crystal.
Variant of Crescencio. Crysencio Summerville is a Dutch footballer.
Variant of Christa possibly influenced by Crystal.
Variant of Crystalee or a combination of the sounds present in Crystal and Natalie.
Combination of Crystal with the suffix -line.
From the English word that refers to having the structure and form of crystals, or composed of crystals.
Combination of Crystal with the popular suffix lyn

Variant spelling of Crystal. Also compare Krystle. Notable bearers of this name include the Canadian-American actress Crystle Lightning (b. 1981) and Crystle Stewart (b. 1981), an American actress and beauty pageant titleholder who won Miss USA 2008.
A variant of Csobánka, the feminine spelling of Csaba.
Of debated origin and meaning. Theories include an elaboration of Csenge and an adoption of the Turkish place name.
From csiperke meaning "Agaricus (a type of mushroom)".
Directly taken from Hungarian csermely "brooklet, rivulet, little river".
From Csillag and Virág, ultimately intended to mean "star flower".
A pet name created by Endre Ady, for his wife Berta Boncza, from the word 'csacsi' meaning "small donkey".
Of Hungarian origin, meaning "herder". Masculine form of Csobánka.

Latinized form of Ktesias.A noted bearer is Ctesias of Cnidus (c. 5th century BCE), a Greek physician and historian from Cnidus in Caria. Ctesias, who lived in the 5th century BC, was physician to Artaxerxes Mnemon, whom he accompanied in 401 BC on his expedition against his brother Cyrus the Younger. Ctesias was the author of treatises on rivers, and on the Persian revenues, of an account of India entitled 'Indica' (which is of value as recording the beliefs of the Persians about India), and of a history of Assyria and Persia in 23 books, called 'Persica'.
Latinized form of Ktesibios. This name was borne by an ancient Greek inventor and mathematician from the 3rd century BC.
Latinized form of Ktesikles. This name was borne by several ancient Greeks, one of them being an Athenian general.
Latinized form of Ktesiphon. This name was borne by an Athenian orator from the 4th century BC.
Latinized form of Ktesios. This is the name of two characters in Greek mythology, one of them being one of the suitors of Odysseus' wife Penelope.

Latinized form of Greek Κτήσυλλα (Ktesylla), derived from Ancient Greek κτῆσις (ktesis) meaning "acquisition, possession, property", which is ultimately derived from κτάομαι (ktaomai) meaning "to acquire, to procure for oneself" as well as "to possess". In Greek mythology, Ctesylla was a maiden of Ioulis who eloped with the Athenian Hermochares. After she died in childbirth, she was worshipped as Aphrodite Ctesylla.
Latinized form of Ktimene. In Greek mythology, Ctimene was the younger sister of Odysseus, the legendary king of Ithaca.
Spanish and Italian form of Chthonia.
From Sino-Vietnamese 居 (cư) meaning "to live, to dwell".
From Sino-Vietnamese 渠魁 (cử khôi) meaning "excellent, outstanding, smart".
From Sino-Vietnamese 舉 (cử) meaning "to lift, to praise".
Means "horned", derived from Nahuatl cuacuahuitl "horns, antlers".

From the title of the Virgin Mary Nuestra Señora de Cuadros (Our Lady of Cuadros), native to the town of Bedmar y Garcíez in the province of Jaén, Spain. The name ultimately comes from the river next to its Marian sanctuary, river Cuadros (meaning "squares").
Possibly means "eagle flood", from Nahuatl cuauhtli "eagle" and atl "water".
Means "eagle serpent" or "wooden snake" in Nahuatl, derived from either cuauhtli "eagle" or cuahuitl "tree, wood" and cōātl "snake".
Possibly derived from cuauhtli "eagle" and copil, a kind of conical hat or headpiece.
Means "the eagle closes its eyes" in Nahuatl, from cuauhtli "eagle" and icopi "to close the eyes; to blink, to wink".
Possibly means either "eagle old woman" or "old woman’s head", from Nahuatl cuauhtli "eagle" or cuaitl "head" combined with ilama "old woman".
Possibly from Nahuatl cuauhtli "eagle" and cahua "to leave, abandon something" or "to be left; to remain, survive" (see Necahual).
Means "walks like an eagle" or "travelling eagle" in Nahuatl, from cuauhtli "eagle" and nenemi "to travel, to go about; to walk, to run".

Means "eagle cactus fruit" in Nahuatl, derived from cuauhtli "eagle" and nochtli "prickly-pear cactus fruit". Could be used to describe the hearts of victims sacrificed to Huitzilopochtli, or as a judicial title, often involved with execution.
Means "eagle banner" in Nahuatl, from cuauhtli "eagle" and panitl "banner, flag". Alternatively, the first element could be cuahuitl "tree, wood".
Means "smoking eagle" in Nahuatl, from cuauhtli "eagle" and popoca "to smoke".
Means "eagle garment", from Nahuatl cuauhtli "eagle" and quemitl "garments, clothing; ritual vestments".
Means "person from Cuauhquiyahuac" in Nahuatl, a location meaning "eagle door" or "eagle gate".
Means "eagle covert feathers" in Nahuatl, referring to the tough feathers found on the bird’s neck, back, and wings.
Derived from Nahuatl cuauhtli "eagle" and tecolotl "owl".
Meaning uncertain. Possibly a combination of cuauhtli "eagle" and either tecpan "palace", tecpantli "twenty", or tecpana "to put in order, to arrange in a row".
Possibly means "Guatemalan, person from Guatemala" in Nahuatl, derived from Cuahtemallan "Guatemala".
Means "hunchbacked eagle" or "crooked tree" in Nahuatl, from cuauhtli "eagle" or cahuitl "tree, wood" and tepotzotli "hunchback".

Means "eagle cape" in Nahuatl, from cuauhtli "eagle" and tilmatli "cloak, blanket, length of cloth". The cuauhtilmatli was a garment associated with warriors and nobility, often worn in mourning ceremonies.
Means "eagles" in Nahuatl, the plural form of cuauhtli. This was the name of an Aztec military faction. Alternatively, this name could be the plural form of cuahuitl "tree, wood".
Possibly means "wise eagle", derived from Nahuatl cuauhtli "eagle" and tlamati "to know something".
Meaning uncertain. Possibly derived from cuauhtli "eagle" or cuahuitl "tree, wood" combined with tlapetzolli "burnished, polished", which stems from petztli "pyrite; something smooth or shiny".

Etymology uncertain. Possibly means "wooden plow" or "eagle trap", derived from Nahuatl cuauhtli "eagle" or cuahuitl "tree, wood" combined with either tlapehua "to plow (a field, the land)" or tlapehualli "trap for catching animals; animals or land that have been brought under control".
Means "he talks like an eagle", from Nahuatl cuauhtli "eagle" and tlatoa "to speak; to issue commands".
Means "wooden door" or "eagle gate" in Nahuatl, from cuahuitl "tree, wood" or cuauhtli "eagle" combined with tlatzacuilotl "gate, entrance, bridge".
Possibly derived from Nahuatl cuauhtli "eagle" and xayacatl "face, mask".
Means "eagle; fifteenth day-sign of the tonalpohualli" in Nahuatl.
Means "eagle shield" in Nahuatl, from cuauhtli "eagle" and chimalli "shield".
Means "wooden staff" or "eagle staff" in Nahuatl, from cuahuitl "tree, wood" or cuauhtli "eagle" and topilli "rod, sceptre, staff of office".
Means "small tree" in Nahuatl, from cuahuitl "tree, wood" and tziquiton "a little bit".
From Nahuatl cuauhtli "eagle" and tzitzimatl "supernatural being; demon".
Means "eagle head" in Nahuatl, from cuauhtli "eagle" and tzontecoma "head, skull".

From Nahuatl cuauhxilotl which has two seperate meanings; the first refers to a tropical tree that bears cucumber-like fruit (also called the cuajilote), derived from cuahuitl "tree, wood" and xilotl "green ear of maize, young corncob"; the second refers to the chest and back feathers of the golden eagle, derived from cuauhtli "eagle" and xilotl.
Possibly means "green tree, tree with green leaves" or "new growth", derived from Nahuatl cuahuitl "tree, wood" and xoxoctic "green, unripe" or xoxoctia "to turn green".
Means "eagle heart" or "centre of the tree, pith" in Nahuatl, from cuauhtli "eagle" or cuahuitl "tree, wood" and yōllōtl "heart, life".

Means "eagle hair" or "wooden head" in Nahuatl, from cuauhtli "eagle" or cuahuitl "tree, wood" combined with tzontli "hair, head". It can also be derived directly from the vocabulary word cuauhtzontli, meaning either "eagle wig, crown, feathered headdress" (a kind of ornament worn by captains, tied to their backs), or "tree trunk, tree top".
Possibly derived from Nahuatl cuaitl "head" and zolin "quail".
Taken from the English word Cub, sometimes used as a pet form of names beginning with the letter C.
Goddess who helped the child transition from cradle to bed.
Transferred use of the surname Cuban.
English corruption of Kwabena. This was used by early slaves in the American south. Attested in the 1730's in South Carolina.

Derived from Latin cubitus meaning "reclined, lying down", which is ultimately derived from the Latin verb cubito meaning "to recline, to lie down (often)". Also compare the Latin noun cubitum meaning "elbow" and the Greek noun κύβιτον (kybiton) meaning "elbow".In French literature, Cubitus is the name of a corpulent talking dog, who is the main character of the Franco-Belgian comic Cubitus, which was created in 1968 by the Belgian/Walloon cartoonist Dupa (1945-2000). In the Dutch-speaking part of Belgium, namely Flanders, Cubitus is known as Dommel, which is most likely derived from the Dutch verb dommelen meaning "to doze, to snooze".
Cornish form of Cybi. Saint Cuby was a 6th-century Cornish bishop, saint and, briefly, king, who worked largely in North Wales.
Diminutive of Pilar, Refugio, Concepción and other feminine names, from the diminutive ending -uca. Cuca Gamarra is a Spanish politician.

Means "shining air". Cuchavira is the Muisca deity of the rainbow, appearing as a relief to the people after Chibchacum's devastating floods, and born from Bochica's creation of Tequendama Falls. Cuchavira is considered a protector of working women and the sick.Though traditionally identified as a male deity, in some modern interpretations Cuchavira is considered a goddess.
Borne by the Columbian football player Cucho Hernández.

From Sino-Vietnamese 菊 (cúc) meaning "chrysanthemum" and 花 (hoa) meaning "flower", referring especially to yellow chrysanthemums. This is the name of the female main character in the Vietnamese poem Phạm Công Cúc Hoa.

Means "hound of the foreign lands" in Irish, derived from Old Irish cú "dog, hound, wolf" and coicrích "foreign land, neighbouring country". This was the name of two historians who both worked on the historical chronicle 'Annals of the Four Masters'. Their names are both Latinized as Peregrine.
Means "hound of Connacht" in Irish Gaelic.

Medieval Serbian name of which the first element is of uncertain origin. It may possibly have been derived from Slavic chucha or chusha, which may signify something small. An other possibility may be Slavic chuzh "foreign, alien, strange" - compare modern Russian chuzhoy, Polish cudzy and Slovak cudzí, all of which mean "foreign, alien, strange". The second element is derived from Slavic mir "peace". A bearer of this name was Čučimir Belojević, a member of a Serbian noble family from the 10th century AD.
Means "tridax daisy (Tridax procumbens)", from Sino-Vietnamese 菊 (cúc) meaning "daisy, chrysanthemum" and 梅 (mai) meaning "plum, apricot, Ochna integerrima".

Diminutive of Cristóforo. This is also used as a strictly masculine diminutive of Refugio, as in the case of Mexican singer-songwriter José del Refugio "Cuco" Sánchez (1921-2001​). Other known bearers include Carlos "Cuco" Rojas (1954-2020), a Colombian harpist and songwriter of joropo, and Cuco Pérez (1959-), a Spanish accordionist and composer.This coincides with the Spanish word cuco meaning "cuckoo".
An indigenous alcalde of Mission San José and a member and leader of the Lakisamni tribe of the Yokut people of northern California, popularly known as Estanislao.

Phoenician origin with the meaning of "he who jokes" or "he who likes to joke". Saint Cucuphas is a is a martyr of Spain who lived from roughly 269 A.D. to 304 A.D.His feast day is July 25, but in some areas it is celebrated on July 27 to avoid conflict with the important feast day of Santiago, the patron saint of Spain.
Means "black hound" from Irish cú "hound" and dubh "black".

Anglicized form of Kojo used by early slaves in the American South. It is attested in the 1730s in South Carolina. This name was borne by Cudjoe Lewis (c. 1840-1935), the last known survivor of the Atlantic slave trade between Africa and the United States.
Derived from Old Polish cudo, czudo meaning "miracle, wonder".

Derived from Serbo-Croatian čudo "miracle, wonder" combined with Slavic mir "peace". As such, the name roughly means "miracle of peace" or "peace is a miracle". In some instances, this name is mistaken for a variant form of Čedomir and even Godemir.
Derived from Nahuatl cuēitl "skirt" and chimalli "shield".
Probably derived from Nahuatl cuecuextli, a kind of ornament worn on the leg. Alternately, it could be from cuecuexi "to shake". This was another name for the god Xocotl.
Means "poinsettia" in Nahuatl, a plant used in traditional medical infusions.
Means "lizard" in Nahuatl, derived from cuetzpalin, the fourth day-sign of the tonalpohualli.
From the Spanish word cueva meaning "cave", itself from the title of Mary Virgen de la Cueva ("Our Lady of the Cave"), belonging to the town of Esparragosa de Lares (Badajoz, Spain).

Means "holy cave" in Spanish, taken from the titles of the Virgin Mary, La Virgen de la Cueva Santa and Nuestra Señora de la Cueva Santa, meaning "The Virgin of the Holy Cave" and "Our Lady of the Holy Cave" respectively.She is venerated at the sanctuary in Altura in the Valencian province of Castelló.
Anglicized form of Kofi. According to George Rippey Stewart in American Given Names (1979): 'It was a common name for a black during the slave period, but died out in the late 19th century.'

English variant of Kofi, a masculine African day name for the last week day Friday.This was the name of South Carolina Black slaves and Black Seminoles in different cases. This was used from 1737–1871.
Derived from Nahuatl cuica "to sing" (or cuicatl "song") and nemi "to dwell, to live (as)" or "to walk, to go about (like)".
From the Chinese 翠 (cuì) meaning "kingfisher, green" and 嫦 (cháng), the name of a moon goddess.
From a repetition of Chinese 翠 (cuì) meaning "green jade, cyan kingfisher, blue-green" or 璀 (cuǐ) meaning "lustre of gems". Other hanzi combinations are possible.

Means "swallow bird" in Nahuatl. This was the son of Nezahualpilli, appointed by Hernán Cortés in Tenochtitlan after Cacamatzin's revolt. He never took power in Tetzcoco itself and was not regarded as legitimate by the city's nobility.
From the Chinese 翠 (cuì) meaning "kingfisher, green" and 娥 (é) meaning "be beautiful; good".

From Chinese 粹 (cuì) meaning "pure, unadulterated, essence" or 翠 (cuì) meaning "green jade, kingfisher, bluish green" combined with 芬 (fēn) meaning "fragrance, aroma, perfume". Other character combinations can form this name as well.
From Chinese 粹 cui meaning "pure" combined with 华 hua meaning "magnificent, splendid, Chinese". Other hanzi combinations are possible.
From the Irish word cuileann, meaning "holly".
Medieval Scottish Gaelic form of Cailean. Means "whelp, young dog". in Scottish Gaelic. Cuilén mac Ilduib was King of Scots from 967-971.
From the Chinese 翠 (cuì) meaning "green, kingfisher" and 莉 (lì) meaning "white jasmine".
From the Chinese 翠 (cuì) meaning "green, kingfisher" and 亮 (liàng) meaning "bright, brilliant, radiant, enlightened".
From the Chinese 粹 (cuì) meaning "pure, the best" and 粼 (lín) meaning "clear".
From the Chinese 翠 (cuì) meaning "kingfisher, green" and 铃 (líng) meaning "bell".
Means "painter" or "a painting, design, decoration" in Nahuatl.
From the Chinese 翠 (cuì) meaning "green, kingfisher" and 鸾 (luán), a mythological bird or 銮 (luán) meaning "bells".

Meaning uncertain. Possibly derived from Nahuatl cui "to take, fetch, grasp" combined with either maitl "hand" or the related elements ma "to hunt, capture", ma "as though, as, like", or -mani "in the manner of".
From the Chinese 翠 (cuì) meaning "kingfisher, green" and 明 (míng) meaning "bright, light, brilliant, clear".
Variant of Quinn, taken from the Irish Gaelic surname Ó Cuinn (in which it is the genitive form of Conn).

Two explanations for this name exist. The first is that this name is an authentic Etruscan male name of unknown meaning, which was latinized to Quintus by the ancient Romans. The second explanation is that this name is the Etruscan(ized) form of the Latin male name Quintus. Since the Etruscans adopted many Latin names and the Romans in turn adopted many Etruscan names, it is hard to tell which of the two explanations is the correct one. Perhaps it could even be so that both are correct, meaning that there are two etymologies: the lost Etruscan one, and the known Latin one.

From Chinese 翠 (cuì) meaning "kingfisher, bluish-green, green jade" combined with 平 (píng) meaning "level, even, peaceful" or 萍 (píng) meaning "wander, travel around". Other character combinations can form this name as well.
From Chinese 翠 (cuì) meaning "green, blue" combined with 琴 (qín) meaning "zither, lute". Other hanzi combinations are possibe.
From the Chinese 翠 (cuì) meaning "kingfisher, green" and 泉 (quán) meaning "spring, fountain; wealth".
From Old Irish cuire meaning "troop, host, company".
From the Chinese 翠 (cuì) meaning "green, kingfisher" and 生 (shēng) meaning "life, living, lifetime, birth".
From 翠 (cuì) meaning "kingfisher" and 詩 (shī) meaning "poem, verse, ode".
From the Chinese 翠 (cuì) meaning "green, kingfisher" and 桃 (táo) meaning "peach, marriage".

Etymology uncertain, often interpreted as deriving from Nahuatl cuitlatl "excrement" and the possessive suffix -hua combined with the locative suffix -c. This was the name of the 10th ruler of Tenochtitlan.

column3: 翠文, 翠雯, 萃文, 萃雯, etc.(Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 翠 (cuì) meaning "bluish-green, green jade" or 萃 (cuì) meaning "gather, collect, assemble" combined with 文 (wén) meaning "literature, culture, writing" or 雯 (wén) meaning "cloud patterns". Other character combinations can form this name as well.
From Chinese 翠 (cuì) meaning "bluish-green, green jade" combined with 霞 (xiá) meaning "rosy clouds, mist". Other character combinations can form this name as well.
From the Chinese 翠 (cuì) meaning "kingfisher, green" and 响 (xiǎng) meaning "sound, echo".
From the Chinese 翠 (cuì) meaning "kingfisher, green" and 欣 (xīn) meaning "happy, joyous" or 心 (xīn) meaning "heart, mind, soul".
From the Chinese 璀 (cuǐ) meaning "lustre of gems, glitter, shine" and 烨 (yè) meaning "bright, splendid, glorious, firelight".
From the Chinese 翠 (cuì) meaning "green, kingfisher" and 银 (yín) meaning "silver, wealth".
From the Chinese 翠 (cuì) meaning "kingfisher, green" and 莺 (yīng) meaning "oriole, green finch".
From the Chinese 翠 (cuì) meaning "green, kingfisher" and 媛 (yuàn) meaning "beauty, beautiful woman".
From the Chinese 翠 (cuì) meaning "green, kingfisher" and 玥 (yuè) meaning "mythological pearl".

column3: 翠云, 翠雲, 璀云, 璀芸, etc.(Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 翠 (cuì) meaning "kingfisher, blue-green, green jade" or 璀 (cuǐ) meaning "luster of gems" and 云 (yún) meaning "cloud" or 芸 (yún) meaning "art" or a kind of vegetable. Other characters can form this name as well.
From the Chinese 翠 (cuì) meaning "kingfisher, green" and 钊 (zhāo) meaning "endeavor, encourage".
This name was used in the book "Cujo" by Steven King, which later got adapted into a movie.
Romansh form of Scholastica, traditionally found in the Surselva region.
Possibly a Judeo-Spanish and Moorish form of Solomon.
Transferred use of the surname Cully.
From the English word culture. Also see Kulture.
Transferred use of the surname Culver.
Probably a form of Juliana spelled according to Turkish orthography.
Azerbaijani form of Juliet, used in translations of Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet (1596).
Meaning: "Friday" The word comes fron the Ottoman Turkish word جمعة
Transferred use of the surname Cumberland.
Derived from Old Breton cum meaning "gentle, beloved" and Old Breton delu meaning "appearance" (Middle Welsh delw "form, image"; compare second element in Cynddelw).
Means "hound of the plain" from Old Irish cú "dog, hound".

Cumhaill mac Trénmhoir was a powerful warrior and chieftain of the Fianna, an elite, roving band of hunter-warriors who protected Ireland. His name derives from the Old Irish Cumall, which translates roughly to "slave" or "bond-servant," though in tales, he was far from it. He was renowned for his strength, and was deeply tied to the land and the magical legacy of the Fianna.Cumhaill was the father of Ireland’s most famous hero, Fionn mac Cumhaill (Finn McCool). Primarily known as a tragic catalyst for the Fenian Cycle, his legacy sets into motion the adventures of his illustrious son.
Old Irish name derived from cú "wolf, hound" in combination with a second element of unknown meaning (possibly the place name Meadha).

Means "arise; stand up" in Aramaic.While not originally a name, it's use as a name is likely due to the Biblical passage in which it's found: 'Taking her by the hand he said to her, 'Talitha cumi,' which means, "Little girl, I say to you, arise."'(Mark 5:41). This passage is also the origin of the use of Talitha as a given name.
Variant of Cumi. This was borne by Cumie Talitha Walker (1874-1942), the mother of American outlaw Clyde Barrow.
Transferred use of the surname Cumming.
Transferred use of the surname Cummins.
Diminutive of Cumming, Cummins, and other names starting with Cum-.
Derived from the English-speaking word cumulus, a type of cloud. Cumulus stems from the Latin word "cumulo", which means "pile, heap, or accumulate".
Medieval Silesian German variant of Conrad via the variant Cunrad.
Corsican and Sicilian form of Concetta.
The name of two women in the 'Parzifal' by Wolfram von Eschenbach.
Latinized form of Cunedda. This was the name of a legendary king of the Britons, as told by Geoffrey of Monmouth in 'The History of the Kings of Britain'.

From Old Welsh Cunedag, from a Brythonic name *Cuno-dagos meaning "good hound, having good hounds", derived from Celtic *kū "dog, hound" and *dagos "good" (whence Welsh da). This was the name of several early Welsh rulers, notably Cunedda ap Edern, a 5th-century king of Gwynedd and the progenitor of the royal dynasty of Gwynedd.
Dutch variant and Italian, Corsican, Gascon and Provençal form of Kunigunde.

Some sources state that this name was derived from Gothic kuni "family, kin, race, kind." However, since the first known bearer of this name (a saint from the 4th century AD) originated from Scotland, we cannot exclude the possibility that it is actually Gaelic or Anglo-Saxon in origin. If Anglo-Saxon, the name might be derived from cyn "family, kin, race, kind" or cêne, cŷne "audacious." If Gaelic, the name might be derived from the Old Celtic element koun "hound."
From Sino-Vietnamese 窮 (cùng) meaning "end" or a non-Sino-Vietnamese reading of Chinese 共 (cùng) meaning "together with, same".
From a non-Sino-Vietnamese reading of Chinese 共 (cũng) meaning "also".
From Sino-Vietnamese 拱 (củng) meaning "to surround, encircle".
Variant of Cương or from Sino-Vietnamese 恭 (cung) meaning "respectful, polite".
Birth name of St. Peter the Aleut.
Of uncertain meaning, this was the name of a Jurchen chieftain who lived during the Ming dynasty. He was a fifth generation ancestor of Nurhaci.
English and French form and German variant of Kunibert.
Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Kunibert.
Derived from Gothic kuni "kin, family" and Old High German hiltia "battle".
English form of Kunimund. Cunimund was a 6th-century king of the Gepids, a Germanic tribe.
Derived from Latin cunae meaning "a cradle". In ancient Roman religion, Cunina was the goddess who protected children in the cradle.
Variant spelling of Kunibert. Cunipert was the name of a 7th-century king of the Lombards.
Latinized form of Cunipert via Kunibert and variant of Cunibertus.

Medieval Italian form of Chuniza.A notable bearer of this name was the Italian noblewoman Cunizza da Romano (13th century), who also appears as a character in the poem Divine Comedy written by the Italian poet Dante Alighieri (c. 1265-1321).
Medieval Silesian German diminutive of Kunegunde.
Transferred use of the surname Cunningham 1 or Cunningham 2.
Derived from Old Celtic koun "hound" combined with Celtic rix "king." The name might also be a form of Cyneric (see Kendrick).
Sicilian form of Konon via it's Latinized form Conon.
From Sino-Vietnamese 腳 (cước) meaning "foot, base, foundation".
Possibly related to Cội. This is the name of a man who sits under a tree on the Moon, who can be seen on the night of a full moon.
From Sino-Vietnamese 剛 (cương) meaning "hard, rigid, strong".
Means "peafowl" in the North-Central Vietnamese dialect.
Means "petiole, stem of a leaf" in Vietnamese.
The Italian language word for "heart". It's the name of the last surviving Maenad in ''Final Fantasy IV: The After Years''.
From the English word cupcake "a small cake baked in a paper container shaped like a cup, often with icing on top".
French form of Cupid. It was mentioned in Marquis de Sade's novel 'The 120 Days of Sodom' (1785) as belonging to one of the male victims.
Diminutive of Cupidon.One of the main protagonists in 'L'Anti-Justine; ou, Les Delices de l'amour' by Restif de La Bretonne.

The fertility and underworld goddess of the ancient pre-Roman population of the Piceni and the Umbri. The etymology of her name is unknown, but it could derive from Kupria, a epithet of Aphrodite, or be related to the name Cupid. Cupra is also the Latin word for "copper".
Diminutive of Cuca. In other words, this is a (strictly feminine) double diminutive of Refugio.

Cura or Aera Cura is the name of a Roman goddess who created the first human. In Latin. Hyginus seems to have created both the personification and story for his Fabulae, poem 220. The name itself is derived from Latin cura "care, concern, thought".
Used by Shakespeare in his tragedy King Lear (1606).
Contracted form of Cundrau, traditionally found in the Surselva region.
Derived from Romanian curcă "turkey-hen". This name seems to have been predominantly used by members of the Romani people.

Old Prussian god first mentioned in the peace treaty of 1249 between the Teutonic Knights and the Old Prussians. He is also mentioned in Simon Grunau's Preussische Chronik (1517-1521) and Matthäus Prätorius' Deliciae Prussicae (1635-1704).
The eponymous character in 'Curculio', also called The Weevil, a Latin comedic play for the early Roman theatre by Titus Maccius Plautus.
Variant of Kurt. This name was borne by Curd Jürgens (13 December 1915 – 18 June 1982), a German-Austrian stage and film actor. He was usually billed in English-speaking films as Curt Jurgens.
This was the name of the miner boy in The Princess and the Goblin (1872) and The Princess and Curdie (1883) by George MacDonald.
Variant of Curadin, traditionally found in the Engadine valley.
Derived from the Roman gentile name Curius.
Transferred use of the surname Curie. Likely given in honour of French chemist and physicist Marie Curie.
Possibly a feminisation of Curig using the suffix gwen meaning "white, fair, blessed".
The name of a Roman gens.A known member of the gens is the consul Manius Curius Dentatus (died 270 BC).

Transferred use of the surname Curley or else from an English surname of Norman origin, which may have been from a French place name or perhaps from a nickname meaning "curlew (a bird)" (see also Curly). It was used by John Steinbeck for a character in his novella 'Of Mice and Men' (1937).
From the English word, used by Jerome Lester Horwitz, a member of the Three Stooges comedy team, as a stage name.
Transferred use of the surname Curren.
Transferred use of the surname Currer.
Transferred use of the surname Currie.
Transferred use of the surname Currier.
Transferred use from the surname Curry.
Means "chair" or "footstool", from Arabic Al Kursiyy al Jauzah meaning "the chair of the central one". This is the traditional name of the star Beta Eridani in the constellation Eridanus.
From the Latin word curtus, meaning short.
Means "skillful (son of) Finwë" in Quenya. In Tolkien's Legendarium this is the father-name of both Fëanor and his son Curufin.
Irish Hero in the Ulster cycle

The eldest son of Ham, who was a son of Noah. He was the brother of Mizraim (Egypt), Canaan (land of Canaan), and Phut, and the father of the Biblical character Nimrod mentioned in the "Table of Nations" in the Genesis 10:6 and I Chronicles 1:8.
Meaning unknown, but possibly derived from the Hebrew name Cush (כוש) and the verb רשע (rsh') meaning "to be wicked". He was mentioned in Judges 3:8.

Derived form Irish Gaelic cuisle "pulse". This name was created in the early 1800s from the Irish term of endearment cuisle mo cridhe (usually anglicized as Cushla Macree, in former times also Cushlamachree) which translates to "pulse of my heart"; it is popularly interpreted to mean "beat of my heart".This name has hardly ever been used in Ireland itself.

From a Ashkenazi Jewish or German surname that probably derived from a Germanized form of the Ancient Greek given name Kosmas (see Cosmo). A famous bearer of the name is American Republican politician Cushman Kellogg Davis (1838–1900).

From Quechua kusi meaning "joy, happiness". A known bearer was Cusi Huarcay, a 16th-century princess and queen consort of the Inca Empire. In modern times, it is borne by American playwright Cusi Cram (1967-; born to a Bolivian father and a Scottish mother).
Diminutive of Custaunce, the medieval English vernacular form of Constance. This name was recorded in the Hundred Rolls.
Medieval English diminutive of Constance, via the vernacular form Custance.
Dialectal form of Cristal. The name used to be Anglicized as Christopher.
Medieval English vernacular form of Constance.
Sicilian and Sardinian form of Constantinus (see Constantine 1).
Corsican form of Constantia and Romansh variant of Constanzia.
Transferred use of the surname Custard.
A diminutive of Custodio and Custodia or directly transferred from the Italian surname Custodi.
From a hereditary title for Acehnese women of noble or aristocratic descent, typically placed before the given name.
Spanish form of Cuthbert. This name is mostly used in Mexico.

A monothematic Old English name deriving from the Old English element cuþ "known, familiar". This name is attested as a given name, but can be a diminutive of any name beginning with Cuth-. One notable bearer was a recorded son of Ceawlin of Wessex.
Means "famously bold", derived from Old English cuþ "known, familiar" and beald "bold, brave".
Derived from the Old English elements cuþ "known, familiar" and beorht "bright". Variant of Cuthberht.
Means "famous fortress", derived from Old English cuþ "known, familiar" and burg "fortress".
Latinized form of Cuthburg. Also compare Cuthburh.
Variant of Cuthburg. Also compare Wilburg versus Wilburh. This name was borne by the wife of the early 8th-century king Aldfrith of Northumbria.
Means "famously brave", derived from Old English cuþ "known, familiar" and heard "brave, hardy".A known bearer of this name was the 10th-century bishop Cutheard of Lindisfarne.
Means "famous beauty", derived from Old English cuþ "known, familiar" and flæd, possibly meaning "beauty".
Means "famous peace", derived from Old English cuþ "known, familiar" and friþ "peace".
Derived from the Old English elements cuþ meaning "known, familiar" and gar meaning "spear".
Means "famous army", derived from Old English cuþ "known, familiar" and here "army".
Means "famous man", derived from Old English cuþ "known, familiar" and mann "person, man".
Means "famous counsel", derived from Old English cuþ "known, familiar" and ræd "counsel, advice". Variant of Cuthred.

Means "famous counsel", derived from Old English cuþ "known, familiar" and ræd "counsel, advice".Known bearers of this name include king Cuthred of Wessex (8th century AD) and king Cuthred of Kent (early 9th century AD).
Means "famous power", derived from the Old English elements cuþ "known, familiar" and ric "ruler, king".
Means "famously strong", derived from Old English cuþ "known, familiar" and swiþ "strong".This name was borne by a 7th-century abbess of Inkberrow (near Worcester) in England.
Means "famous friend", derived from Old English cuþ "known, familiar" and wine "friend".
Means "famous wolf", derived from Old English cuþ "known, familiar" and wulf meaning "wolf".This name was borne by two 9th-century bishops from England.
Transferred use of the surname Cutler.

Transferred use of the surname Cutter.In the American television cartoon 'G.I. Joe', Cutter is the nickname of Skip A. Stone, the G.I. Joe team's hovercraft pilot. He first appeared in the cartoon in 1984 and has since made numerous appearances in the cartoon series and comic books and has been released as an action figure in the G.I. Joe toy line.

Means "moon" in Purépecha. In pre-Hispanic Purépecha mythology, the moon goddess Nana Cutzi (often translated as "the curved mother" or "mother encorvada") forms a fundamental cosmic pair with Tata Jurhiata, the sun god, and their union is believed to have brought light to the cosmos.
From Sino-Vietnamese 究 (cửu) meaning "to search, examine".
From Sino-Vietnamese 久 (cửu) meaning "eternal, enduring" or 玖 (cửu) meaning "black gemstone".
Transferred use of the surname Cuyler.
Cognate of Cvitana and Bulgarian variant transcription of Tsvetana.
Hungarian and Serbo-Croatian transcription of Tsvi.
Derived from Croatian cvijet meaning "blossom, flower" and slava "glory".
Derived from the Old English elements cwen "woman, wife" and burg "fortress".
Derived from the Old English elements cwen "woman, wife, queen" and giefu "gift".
Derived from the Old English elements cwen meaning "woman, wife" and guð "battle".
Derived from the Old English elements cwen meaning "woman, wife; queen" and hild meaning "battle".
Derived from the Old English elements cwen "woman, wife; queen" and leof "dear, beloved".
From the Old English elements cwen "woman, wife" and þryþ "strength".
Derived from the Old English elements cwic "alive" and helm "helmet, protection". This was the name of a 7th-century Anglo-Saxon King.

was a Christian holy woman who was active in Anglesey, Wales, in the early 6th century. The daughter, sister and niece of saints, she is said to have founded St Cwyllog's Church, Llangwyllog, in the middle of Anglesey, where a church is still dedicated to her.
Apparently an invented name based on similar-sounding names such as Cyan, Lysandra and Andrea 2.

Latinized form of Greek Κυανη (Kyane) which was derived from κυανος (kyanos) "cyan, azure-blue" (compare Cyan). In Greek myth she was the Naiad nymph of a spring in the Sicilian town of Syracuse, who dissolved away into the spring from grief after witnessing Hades' abduction of her playmate Persephone.

Derived from Ancient Greek κυάνεος (kyaneos) meaning "dark blue, dark colour" (compare Cyan). This was the name of a Naiad-nymph in Greek mythology, a daughter of the river god Meander and the wife of Miletus.
From the name of a fictional character in a French comic book called The Cycle of Cyann.
Historically similar to the name Chrysanth. Derived from the word 'cyan', it means "the combination of blue and green". This generally refers to a child of parents with blue and green eyes.

Latinized form of Greek Κυαξάρης (Kyaxares), which is the hellenized form of either the Old Persian name Uvaxštra or its Old Median form Huvaxšarah. This was the name of a Median king from the 6th century BC.
Possibly derived from Celtic *kob(o)- "victory". This was the name of a 6th-century Welsh saint who founded Caergybi (the Welsh name for Holyhead).
Name of the mother of Judas Iscariot in apocryphal Christian scriptures, most notably in "The Golden Legend".
Possibly a variant of Cyril influenced by Cicero
Latinized form of Kydippe. This is the name of several characters from Greek mythology, one of which is a Nereid.
Derived from Ancient Greek κυδώνιον (kydonion) meaning "quince (fruit)".

From the former name of Chania, a city on the island of Crete, Greece. It is also a poetic term for the island. In addition, it can be derived from Greek κυδωνιά (kydonia) meaning "quince tree" (itself from κυδώνι (kudoni), "quince"), ultimately from the name of the city.
Derived from the Anglo-French term, a diminutive of the Old French, cigne or "swan", which in turn came from the Latin cygnus, ultimately from the Greek, kyknos.
Cygnus is a northern constellation lying on the plane of the Milky Way, deriving its name from the Latinized Greek word for swan.
An unrecorded Old English name, the meaning of which is uncertain. It was perhaps a nickname derived from Proto-Germanic *kokh- "cough".

Unclear etymology, thought to mean "death; wraith". The first element could be from the noun cyhyr "muscle, tendon; flesh", or from cyoer, from oer "cold", with the last element being the noun aeth meaning "pain", "woe", "grief", "fear." It could also simply be the suffix -aeth (roughly equivalent to English -ness or -ity).In Welsh mythology, the Cyhyraeth (also known as the Hag of the Mist, or the Gwrach-y-Rhibyn) is a ghostly spirit (comparable with the Irish Banshee) in Welsh folklore.
Short form of Félicyin and Lucyin.
Diminutive of Cecyliô, Celestina and Celina.
Possibly a variant of Caelan or Kylen.
Variant of Celinda, perhaps influenced by the name Cyndy or the English word cylinder referring to the shape or the barrel of a gun.
Latinized form of Kyllene. This is the name of a moon of Jupiter.
Cyllin ab Caradog, legendary British king of the 1st Century AD, last pendragon of Great Britain.
Latinized form of Kylon. A known bearer of this name was the Athenian nobleman Cylon of Athens, who was one of the Olympic victors of the 35th Olympiad in 640 BC.
Variant of Sylvia. A known bearer is an American consultant and a 'de facto' First Lady of Oregon, Cylvia Hayes.
Allegedly derived from Greek σιμός (simos), meaning "bent upwards". Alternatively, it may be a variant of Sima 1.

From the name of the eponymous band consisting of Caribbean musicians living in London.The band name was derived from the chorus line of the calypso song 'dove and pigeon' coo-coo-coo-coo-fan-cy-mandy.

Means "wave-stiller, calmer of waves", derived from Ancient Greek κῦμα (kyma) meaning "wave, billow" and λήγω (lego) meaning "to stay, abate, cease". This was the name of a Nereid, a sea-nymph daughter of Nereus. Alternatively, it may have been another name of Cymopolea.
Polish form of Cyneburg. Cymbarka was the daughter of Mazovian prince Siemowit IV.

Cymburgis of Masovia was a Polish princess and a Duchess of Austria through her marriage with the Habsburg duke Ernst der Eiserne (Ernest the iron-willed). Her father was duke Siemowit IV and her mother was Aleksandra, the youngest daughter of Algirdas, Grand Duke of Lithuania.
Variant of Symir, possibly influenced by Cy.
Means "wavy", from Ancient Greek κῦμα (kyma) meaning "swell, wave, flood; sprout, fetus". This was the name of one of the Nereids in Greek mythology.

From the Greek elements κῦμα (kyma) meaning "swell of the sea, wave, billow" and κλέος (kleos) meaning "glory". In Edmund Spenser's poem The Faerie Queene (1590) this is the name of a knight characterized by indecision and fluctuations of the will. He and his fiery brother Pyrochles symbolize emotional maladies that threaten temperance. The two brothers are both slain by Prince Arthur in Canto VIII.

Derived from Ancient Greek κῦμα (kyma) meaning "wave" and δοχή (dokhe) meaning "receptacle, container", ultimately from δέχομαι (dekhomai) meaning "to accept, receive".In Greek mythology, Cymodoce was a sea nymph and one of the fifty Nereids.

Latinized form of Greek Κυμοπόλεια (Kymopoleia) meaning "wave walker", derived from κῦμα (kyma) "wave, billow" and the verb πολέω (poleô) "to go about, range over". According to Hesiod she was a daughter of Poseidon and wife of Briareus. She may have also been known as Cymatolege.
Derived from Ancient Greek κῦμα (kyma) meaning "wave, billow" and θοός (thoos) meaning "swift, quick". Cymothoe was a sea nymph and one of the fifty Nereids in Greek mythology.
Variant of Symphony using the suffix -ique (e.g., from Monique). Cymphonique Miller is a famous bearer.

Possibly derived from Ancient Greek κύων (kyon) meaning "dog" (genitive κυνός). A famous bearer was Cynane (4th century BC), half-sister to Alexander the Great. She was the daughter of Philip by Audata, an Illyrian woman, and the mother of Adea Eurydice.

A Greek "plant" name, from a genus of thistles, of which a leading member is the purple flowered artichoke.Probably originated from Zinara, in the Aegean, hence it is also considered a "place" name. The poet Horace sang of Cynara. Ernest Dowson revived the ancient Greek favourite with the poem, "I have been faithful to thee, Cynara..."
Welsh name of uncertain origin, perhaps from an Old Celtic element meaning "high, exalted" combined with Welsh or Old Celtic delw "image, effigy".
Diminutive of Cynthia. Also compare Cyndi.
Short form of names containing the Old English element cyne meaning "royal, kingly". The surname Kinsley is derived from the name. Cognate of Kuno.
Derived from the Old English elements cyne "royal" and beorht "bright".
Alternate spelling of Cyneburg, or Cyneburga.
Character that appears in Culhwch and Olwen.
Derived from the Old English elements cynn "rank, family, kin", or possibly the related cyne "royal", and gar "spear".
Derived from the Old English elements cyne "royal" and giefu "gift".
From Old English cyne meaning "royal" and gisl meaning "pledge, hostage".An alternative Celtic origin has been suggested, with the given meaning of "grey dog".

Derived from Old English cyne "royal" and guð "battle", making it a cognate of Cunigund. This name was borne by a wife of King Wihtred of Kent (c. 670-725) as well as a wife of King Coenwulf of Mercia (died 821).
Derived from the elements cyne "kingly, royal" and‎ helm "helmet". Used an Anglo-Saxon saint who was a king.
Derived from Old English cynn meaning "family" (or possibly cyne "kingly, royal") and hild meaning "battle".
Derived from the Old English elements cyne meaning "royal" and lāf meaning "legacy" (from Proto-Germanic *laibō).
Derived from the Old English elements cyne "royal" (related to cynn "rank, family, kin") and mund "protector, guardian", making it a cognate of Cunimund.
Form of Cynesige found in the Phillimore edition of Domesday Book.
Derived from Old English cyne "royal" and stan "stone".
An Anglo Saxon name meaning royal servant/ warrior.
Derived from Old English cyne "royal" and weald "powerful, mighty".
Derived from Old English cyne "royal" and wig "war, battle".
Derived from the Old English elements cyne "royal" and wine "friend".
Derived from Old English cyne "royal" and wīs "wise". A notable bearer of this name was the wife of King Penda of Mercia, also referred to as Kyneswitha (see Cyneswiþ).
Means "royal wolf", from Old English cyne "royal" and wulf "wolf". This name was borne by an 8th-century Anglo-Saxon poet as well as a king of Wessex.
Derived from the Old English name element cyne meaning "royal" and wynn meaning "joy, bliss".
Derived from the Old Welsh elements cynt meaning "first, before" and mael meaning "prince, chieftain, lord".
Derived from Welsh cynt "chief, first" and farch "horse".
Derived from Welsh cyn "chief" and bran "crow, raven". This was the name of an obscure 5th-century Welsh saint. He was one of the sons of Saint Brychan.
The name of two 5th-century Welsh saints.
Cyngen Glodrydd was a semi-legendary early sixth-century King of Powys. He was a descendant of Cadell Ddyrnllwyd, likely his son.
Derived from the Old English elements cyne "royal" and mund "protection".

Latinized form of Kyniska. Cynisca was born c. 440 BC and was a Greek princess of Sparta. She became the first woman in history to win at the ancient Olympic Games. Said Cynisca was named after her grandfather Zeuxidamus, who was called Cyniscos, a byname meaning "puppy; puppy-dog" in Ancient Greek which gave Cynisca's name the meaning of "female puppy". It is possible that this name related to a specific kind of dog in Sparta, the female bloodhounds which were famous for their ability to find their quarries by their scent.
One of Arthur’s three Counselor Knights, found in the Welsh Triads and other Welsh texts. He was the son of Clydno.

Latinized form of Greek Κυνόσουρα (Kynosoura) which meant "dog's tail", a derivative of κύων (kyôn) "dog" (genitive κυνός (kynos)) and οὐρά (oura) "tail". This was the ancient Greek name of the constellation Ursa Minor, used because it appeared to be the tail of the adjacent star-group Canis Major. In Greek myth this name belonged to a nymph of Mount Ida on the island of Crete; she was one of the nurses of the infant Zeus, who placed her among the stars.
From the Ancient Greek elements κυνός (kunós) “dog's” and οὐρά (ourá) meaning “tail”. This is an alternate name for Ursa Minor.
Old English younger form of Cyneric and Ceneric.
Likely a blend of Cynthia and Stephanie.
Either an elaboration of Cynthia or a combination of Cynthia and Ana.
Latin Cynthius "of Mount Cynthus", an epithet of Apollo.
Possible combination of Cynthia and Toya.
Derived from Proto-Celtic *kū meaning "dog" and *walos meaning "prince, chief".
Form of Cynewig found in the Phillimore edition of Domesday Book.
Latinized form of Kyparissos. In Greek mythology, he was a boy beloved by Apollo.
Variant of Zipporah, recorded in England between the 11th and 13th centuries.
From the English word cypress, a group of coniferous trees. Ultimately from Greek kuparissos.
Feminine form of Cyprian and Cyprianus.
Derived from the plant Cyperus (Κύπερος).The name day is July 4 because of Saint Cyprilla.
Possibly a contracted form of Cypriane.

Variant of Cypress influenced by the name of the country between Europe and Asia that's named Cyprus. The origin of the place name is from Greek Κυπρος (Kypros), which may get its name from the cypress tree (Greek κυπαρισσος).
Latinized form of Kypselos. This was the name of a tyrant of Corinth from the 7th century BC.
French form of Cyrus or Cyriacus. Cyr had always been in rare but steady use in France up until the 1960s, when it virtually disappeared.
Possibly derived from the name of the ancient Greek city of Cyrene, which was located in North Africa
A feminine form or diminutive of Cyrus.
Perhaps a variant of Cyril influenced by -elle.
Archaic North Frisian form of Severine, recorded on the isle of Sylt in the 1600s.
Feminine form of Cyrenius. This was the name of a saint from the Roman province of Cilicia in southern Anatolia, who was martyred by burning in 306 at Tarsus, in persecutions of Galerius.
From the Greek Κυρήνιος (Kyrenios) which is of unknown meaning, perhaps from the Greek place name Cyrene.The name is also a hellenised form of Quirinius.
Czech, Polish and Slovak form of Cyriacus.

Latinized form of the Late Greek given name Kerykos (see Kirykos) via a corruption that was caused by the name's similarity to names like Kyriakos and Kyrikos.This name is best known for being the name of a 4th-century child martyr and saint from Asia Minor, who was murdered together with his mother Julitta.
A feminine form of Cyril and potential variant of Cyrielle
Feminine form of Cyrien and variant of Cyria.
Rare French feminine form of Cyrus.
Latinized form of Kyrion. This name was borne by at least two saints.
Of unknown origin, maybe a hypochoristic form of names containing sigu "victory".

Latinized form of Greek Κύθηρα (Kythera), the name of an island of Greece, as well as an ancient town on the island. In Greek mythology, Cythera was the birthplace of the goddess Aphrodite, being the island to which she first arrived after emerging from the sea, and the source of her epithet Kythereia (Latin: Cytherea). L'Embarquement pour Cythère (1717) is the title of a painting by Jean-Antoine Watteau, also known in English as The Embarkation for Cythera, Voyage to Cythera and Pilgrimage to the Isle of Cythera.
Derived from cywair meaning “proper order, fit state or condition”.
Polish version of Zivia. A notable bearer was Cywia Lubetkin who was a Warsaw Ghetto underground leader.

From the English word czar, an alternate spelling of tsar meaning "Russian emperor, Slavic monarch", itself derived from Russian царь (carʹ), ultimately derived from Latin cognomen Caesar, used to metaphorically mean "emperor, ruler, dictator". The American rapper Meek Mill and his wife Milan Harris gave this name to their son in 2020.
The older form of Czarna (See Charna)
Means "to fight often", derived from Slavic częs(to) "often" combined with Slavic bor "battle" or borit "to fight". Also compare Chestibor.
Derived from Polish często "often" and bronić "to protect someone" or bronić się "to defend oneself".
Derived from Slavic częs(to) "often" combined with Slavic mir "peace".
Derived from często "often" and Old Polish woj, wojownik in modern Polish, "warrior".
Diminutive of Cäcilie, recorded in Silesia in the 14th century.
Medieval Silesian German diminutive of Christine.
Means "banyan" in Vietnamese, or from Sino-Vietnamese 多 (đa) meaning "many".
From Sino-Vietnamese 打 (đả) meaning "to hit, strike, stop".

column3: 다애(Korean Hangul)|多愛, 茶愛, etc.(Korean Hanja)
column12: From Sino-Korean 多 (da) meaning "many, a lot of" or 茶 (da) meaning "tea" and 愛 (ae) meaning "love". Other hanja combinations are possible.
From Sino-Korean 多 (da) meaning "much, many; more than, over" and 娥 (ah) means "Beautiful".
Of uncertain meaning. This was the name of the wife of Keish.
Athabaskan (southern Indigenous Alaskan) name meaning sandhill crane.

Derived from Arabic ضامن (daamin) meaning "guarantor, guarantee", which itself is ultimately derived from Arabic أمن (amn) meaning "security, peace". Also compare Arabic تأمين (ta'min) meaning "insurance".
Alternate transcription of Urdu دانش (see Danish).

DaanisyPronunciation: de-NEE-shhIPA Pronounciation: dɛnɪʃUsage: Modern namePossible Origin:Likely a modern invented name influenced by names such as “Daanish,” “Danish,” “Daania,” or “Daisy.”The element “Daan” may connect to Persian/Urdu dānesh meaning “knowledge” or “wisdom,” while the ending “-isy” resembles modern decorative endings found in contemporary names.Meaning (interpretive):“Wise and unique” or “knowledge with brightness.”
Form of Daniel used by Pakistanis living in the United Kingdom.

Daario Naharis is the name of a sellsword character from the Song of Ice and Fire books by GRR Martin and the TV show Game of Thrones based upon the former. The name is obviously an alternative spelling of South European forms of Darius.
Variant of Darren influenced by the spelling of Aaron.
Cantonese Chinese form of 達 (see Da).Other characters combinations are also possible.
Dabareh is a not entirely incorrect mode of Anglicizing (Jos 21:28) the name Daberath
Name of a 5th century Irish saint.
Medieval Galician variant and Aragonese form of David.

column3: 다빈(Korean Hangul)|多彬, 多嬪, etc.(Korean Hanja)
column12: From Sino-Korean 多 (da) meaning "much, many" combined with 彬 (bin) meaning "cultivated, well-bred, bright" or 嬪 (bin) meaning "court lady, palace maid". Other hanja combinations can form this name as well.
St. Dabius, or Davius, Confessor, was an Irish missionary to Scotland. He was part of the great monastic missionary effort in the British Isles, and then in Europe.
Transferred use of the surname Dabney.
Nickname of American football coach Dabo Swinney, real name William Christopher Swinney. Swinney's brother would refer to him as "that boy" as an infant, but mispronouncing it as "Dabo."
Polish form of Doubravka. This name was borne by the wife of Mieszko I of Poland.
Recorded in Montenegro in the early 1600s.
From Sino-Vietnamese 得 (đắc) meaning "get, obtain, acquire".
Combination of the popular phonetic prefix da and Cara.
Possibly from the Irish word Déiseach, translating to “from the south". A famous bearer of this name is Dacey Cash
From the Chinese 大 (dà) meaning "big, great" and 倡 (chàng) meaning "guide, leader; lead".
From the Chinese 大 (dà) meaning "big, great" and 焯 (chāo) meaning "clear and thorough".
French-influenced transcription of the Russian name Dashka. It became popular in Haiti in the 1960s and 1970s, along with other Russian names such as Nadège, Natacha and Manoucheka.
Probably a Romanic diminutive of Germanic names such as Dagobert that begin with the element tac meaning "day".
An invented name, blending the popular phonetic prefix da and Michelle.

column3: 大成, 大程, 大澂, etc.(Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 大 (dà) meaning "big, great, vast" combined with 成 (chéng) meaning "completed, finished, succeeded", 程 (chéng) meaning "rule, order, regulations" or 澂 (chéng) meaning "clear, limpid". Other character combinations can form this name as well.
Transferred use of the surname Dacher.
From Chinese 大 (dà) meaning "big, great, vast, high" combined with 川 (chuān) meaning "river, stream". Other character combinations can form this name as well.
The name of a medieval saint venerated in Cornwall, who was probably a Celtic Briton.
Feminine form of Dacius and Dacio.
Italian and Galician form of Dacian.

Derived from Guanche *dasil, meaning "footprint, step". It was borne by a Guanche princess of Tenerife who lived during the 15th century. She is best known for her marriage to a Spanish conqueror of the island.
Italian and Galician form of Dacius.
Derived from the Roman name Dacia, which is a region now serving as Moldova and Romania.
Transferred use of the surname Dacke, the name of a Swedish leader of a peasant revolt in the 16th century.
Variant of Dakota (See also Dacota and Dakoda)
From the Chinese 大 (dà) meaning "big, great" and 聪 (cōng) meaning "intelligent, clever".
Variant transcription of Ahlai, as used in 1 Chronicles 2:31.This transcription is used in English translations of the Septuagint Bible.
Sundanese diminutive of masculine names containing the sound dan (or other similar sounds), such as Ramadan, Wildan or Wardana.
From Sundanese juragan, a respectful term of address meaning "sir, master, owner, boss".
Means "the brave one", from a reduplication of Old Persian darš "to dare".
From Turkish dadaş meaning "brother, young man".

Apparently means "of the mother" in archaic Georgian. Compare modern Georgian დედა (deda) meaning "mother".This name is most common in the Georgian region of Svaneti, which is primarily inhabited by the Svans, an ethnic subgroup of Georgians. Their native language is called Svan, and the modern Svan word for "mother" is დედე (dede).A notable bearer of this name was the 17th-century Georgian prince Dadash Gelovani (also called Dadesh). He was the founder of the House of Dadeshkeliani (a Georgian aristocratic family).
Diminutive of Candida, Leonarda and other names ending in da.

Transferred use of the surname Dade.It is also an English word which refers to a kind of wading bird, according to Halliwell and Wright's edition of 'Nare's Glossary'; it is also used as an interjection, expressing excitement, distaste or fright.This was the name of a character in the film 'Hackers' (1995), and also appears in a song by The Spill Canvas, 'The Tide'.

Possibly deriving from the Sanskrit elements दधि (dadhi), meaning "thickened milk, curd" and kri, meaning "to scatter". This possibly refers to the effect of the morning sun on dew. Name borne by a warhorse from the Rigveda renowned for his swiftness.
Diminutive of Diosdado, Alejandro, Conrado, and other names containing a similar sound.
Created from the name Adrian by adding an initial D.

Of uncertain etymology, although the second element of the name (hepa) likely derives from the Hurrian sun goddess Ḫepat. Name borne by a Hittite queen who was possibly the wife of Tudhaliya I. She is known to have occupied the role of Tawananna (ruling queen) during the reign of Šuppiluliuma I, who is thought to have been her son.
Means "justice of Allah", from Persian داد (dād) meaning "justice, equity" and الله (Allah).
Derived from the Kurdish dadwer meaning "just, fair".
Altered form of Adrian, perhaps influenced by the sound of Dedrick or Deidre.

column3: 대은(Korean Hangul)|大銀, 大恩(Korean Hanja)
column12: From Sino-Korean 大 (dae) meaning "large, great" and 銀 (eun) meaning "silver" or 恩 (eun) meaning "favour, grace, mercy".
Old English cognate of Dagobert, derived from the elements dæg "day" and beorht "bright".
Derived from the Old English elements dæg "day" and helm meaning "helmet".
Derived from the Old English elements dæg "day" and the name suffix -ing.
Derived from the Old English elements dæg "day" and lāf "legacy, remainder" (from laibō).
Derived from the Old English elements dæg "day" and mund "protection".
Derived from the Old English elements dæg "day" and wine "friend". Old English cognate of Dagvin.
Derived from 대한민국(Daehanminguk) which is the current official name of South Korea.
From Sino-Korean 大 "big, great, vast, large, high" and 熙 (hee) meaning "shine". Other combinations are possible.
From Sino-Korean 大 (dae) meaning "big, great, vast, large, high" combined with 號 (ho) meaning "number, issue, edition". Other Hanja combinations are possible.
From Sino-Korean 大 "big, great, vast, large, high" and 弘 "enlarge, expand; liberal, great", 洪 "vast, immense; flood, deluge" or 泓 meaning "clear, deep pool of water" (hong).
From Sino-Korean 大 "big, great, vast, large, high" and 煥 "shining, brilliant, lustrous".

column3: 대현(Korean Hangul)|大炫, 大鉉, 大賢, 大現, 岱炫, etc.(Korean Hanja)
column12: Combination of a dae hanja, like 大 or 岱, both meaning "big, large, great," and a hyeon hanja, such as 炫 meaning "bright, brilliant; light, clear," 鉉 meaning "bowstring," 賢 meaning "benevolent; wise, sensible" or 現 meaning "appear, present; show, reveal."

column3: 대현(Korean Hangul)|大炫, 大鉉, 大賢, 大現, 岱炫, etc.(Korean Hanja)

column12: From the Awajún daék meaning "vine, rope".
Variant of Daelyn.A notable bearer is Daelin Hayes (1998-), a professional linebacker.
May be a variant of Daley.
Combination of Dale and the popular name suffix lyn, probably based on similar-sounding names such as Kaylyn, Raelyn and Shaelyn.
Short form of Adamus and its medieval Dutch form Adaem. To a lesser extent, it was also used to abbreviate Damianus / Damiaen and Damasus / Damaes.
Diminutive of Adam via the variant form Adaem.
From Sino-Korean 大 (dae) meaning "big, great, large" and 明 (myeong) meaning "bright, light, clear" or 名 (myeong) meaning "name, fame, reputation." Other hanja combinations are possible.

The name of a Zoroastrian divinity, taken from the Gathic Avestan daēnā or Sanskrit dhénā and is variously translated as "conscience", "religion", "understanding" or "that which is observed". It may be linked to the Sanskrit Dharma.
The name Danny was borrowed into Korean.

Means "three worlds" or "three realms" from Thai แดน (daen) meaning "land, realm, world" and ไตร (trai) meaning "three". More specifically the term refers to the three main realms of existence in Buddhist tradition: kāma-loka ("the world of feeling"), rūpa-loka ("the world of form") and arūpa-loka ("the world of immaterial form").

Derived from Ancient Greek δαΐφρων (daiphron), meaning both "warlike, fiery" and "wise, prudent", the former derived from δάϊς (dais) meaning "battle" and φρήν (phren) meaning "mind, heart, emotions", the latter from ἐδάην (edaen) meaning "to learn, teach, know" and φρήν (phren). This was the name of a son of Aegyptus in Greek mythology.
Derived from Sindarin daer "great". This was the name of a Sindarin Elf in 'The Silmarillion'. Daeron was the greatest of the Elven minstrels.
Korean form of Dashizhi, from Sino-Korean 大勢至 (daeseji). This is the Korean name for the bodhisattva Mahasthamaprapta.
Latinized form of Daisenor. In Greek mythology, this is the name of one of the suitors of Penelope.
From Sino-Korean 大 (dae) meaning "big, great, vast, high" combined with 植 (sik) meaning "plant, tree, to plant, to grow". Other hanja combinations can form this name as well.

Possibly means "divider, distributor; one who hosts a feast", derived from Ancient Greek δαίω (daio) meaning "to divide, share, tear" or "to host a feast". In Greek mythology, Daetor was one of the Trojan warriors who attacked the Greek fleet during the tenth year of the Trojan War.
Originates from 大 (dae) meaning "big" and 元 (won) meaning "origin". Other hanja combinations are possible as well.
Derived from Arabic ضفة (daffa) meaning "bank, shore".
Diminutive of David. A popular bearer was the cartoon Daffy Duck.
Old Norse byname meaning "silent one" or "lazy one".
Sicilian form of Dafne and Hungarian variant of Dafné.
Hungarian and Provençal form of Daphne.
Nickname for David. Dafo Trendafilov, a famous Bulgarian bagpipe (gaida) player.
Meaning uncertain. According to legend, Saint Dafrosa was the mother of Saint Bibiana.
Combination of Chinese Characters "大" meaning "Great" and "福" meaning "Good God".
Feminine form of Dag as well as a short form of names beginning with Dag-.

Flavius Dagalaifus or Dagalaiphus was a politician of the Eastern Roman Empire.The Son of Areobindus, Dagalaifus married Godisthea, the daughter of Ardabur and granddaughter of Aspar. They had a son, the consul of 506, Areobindus Dagalaifus Areobindus, who married the daughter of the Western Roman Emperor Olybrius.
Derived from the Germanic element daga "day" combined with Old High German mund "protection."
Meaning uncertain, possibly derived from the Old Irish prefix dag- "good" combined with a diminutive suffix.

Derived from the Germanic element daga "day" combined with rîcja "powerful, strong, mighty." The second element is also closely related to Celtic rîg or rix and Gothic reiks, which all mean "king, ruler."
Relatively modern name (late 19th century) created by combining Old Norse dagr "day" with bjarga "to help, save, rescue".
Derived from the Old Norse elements dagr "day" and bjǫrn "bear".
Means "bright day", derived from the Old Norse elements dagr "day" and bjǫrt "bright, shining" (from bjartr).
From the Chinese 大 (dà) meaning "big, great" and 耿 (gěng) meaning "bright, shining".
Variant of Dag via it's Old Swedish form Dagher.
Derived from Old Norse dagr "day" and -fari "farer", from the verb fara "to go, to travel" (compare Náttfari and Sæfari).
Icelandic and Faroese form of Dagfinnr.
Means "beautiful day", derived from the Old Norse elements dagr "day" and fríðr "beautiful" (originally "beloved").
Derived from the Old Norse elements dagr "day" and geirr "spear".
Possibly transferred use of the surname Dagger, or from the word dagger meaning “a short pointed weapon with sharp edges”.
Combination of the Old Norse name elements dǫgg "dew; wetness" and rós "rose".
Derived from the Germanic name elements dagr "day" and heiðr meaning "bright, clear", or possibly "heath" or "honor".
Old Swedish form of Dagr, which means "day."
Derived from Old Norse dagr "day" combined with Old Norse hildr "battle".
It's from Amharic language and Geez which is ancient ethiopian language which is dated 3000 years with Hebrew origins, it means Twice or repeated . Usually given when you look like your parents
Derived from the Old Norse elements dagr meaning "day" and maðr meaning "person, man" (genitive manns).
Old Danish form of Dagmar, derived from Old Norse Dagmær.
Derived from the Old Norse elements dagr "day" and mundr "protection".
Dagne means "judge" and is of Amharic origin.
Derived from the Amharic verb “ዳኘ” (dagna), meaning “to mediate,” combined with the suffix “-ቸው” (-chew), indicating a third person plural or honorific object (e.g., “him” or “them”).
Derived from the Germanic element daga "day" combined with Old High German bald "bold, brave."
Languedocian and Gascon form of Dagobert.
Derived from Gaulish dagos "good" and dubnos "world".
Original Gaulish form of the Latinized Dagodurnus.
Derived from Gaulish dagos "good" and durnos "fist".
Means "peaceful day," derived from the Germanic element daga "day" combined with Old High German fridu "peace."
Derived from Gaulish dagos "good" and litu- "festival, celebration, feast".
Means "famous day", derived from the Germanic element daga "day" combined with Old High German mâri "famous."
Derived from Gaulish dagos "good" and maros "great".

The name given to Mieszko I, the first historically known Piast duke of the Polans, in Dagome iudex, a document relating to Poland and placing the Polish state under the protection of the Apostolic See. Dagome is a melding of two names: the Christian Dago, for "Dagobert" (Mieszko's baptismal name), and the Slavic Me, for "Mieszko."

Meaning unknown, possibly from Old English dæg "day". Dagonet or Daguenet was a witless Knight of the Round Table in Arthurian legend, usually described as the king's fool. Introduced in the Prose Lancelot, he becomes Arthur's beloved court jester in Malory's Le Morte D'Arthur and Tennyson's Idylls of the King.
Means "good king", derived from Celtic dago "good, kind" combined with Celtic rix "king."
Derived from the Germanic element daga "day" combined with Old High German wini "friend."
Derived from Old Norse dagr "day" combined with the name of the Norse god Þórr.
Combination of the Old Norse name elements dagr "day" and ulfr "wolf".
From the Chinese 大 (dà) meaning "big, great" and 国 (guó) meaning "nation, country".
Means "majestic thunderbolt" or "splendid diamond" in Mongolian, ultimately derived from Tibetan དག་པ (dag-pa) meaning "pure, genuine, clean" and རྡོ་རྗེ (rdo-rje) meaning "diamond" or "thunderbolt."
Combination of the Old Norse name elements dagr "day" and varðr "guardian".
Relatively modern name (late 19th century) created by combining Old Norse dagr "day" and veig "power, strength".
Combination of the Old Norse name elements dagr "day" and vinr "friend".
Derived from Old Norse dagr "day" combined with Old Norse viðr "tree".
Derived from Old Norse dagr "day" and vǫr "vigilant, cautious".

column3: 다경(Korean Hangul)|多京, 多景, 多敬, etc.(Korean Hanja)
column12: From Sino-Korean 多 (da) meaning "many" combined with 京 (gyeong) meaning "capital city" or 景 (gyeong) meaning "scenery, view" or 敬 (gyeong) meaning "respect, honour". Other hanja combinations can form this name as well.
From Sino-Korean 多 (da) meaning "much, many; more than, over" and 海 (hae) meaning "sea, ocean".
A knight killed by Gawaine in a tournament at the city of Baldac (Baghdad) in Babylonia. Dahamorth’s brother, Angaras of Karamphi, tried to slay Gawaine for the incident, but was himself defeated.
From the Chinese 大 (dà) meaning "big, great" and 皓 (hào) meaning "bright, luminous, clear".
Possibly from Arabic ذهبية (ḏahabiyy) meaning "golden, gold" (also compare Dahab). This name is primarily used in Algeria.
From the Chinese 大 (dà) meaning "big, great" and 贺 (hè) meaning "congratulate, send present".
Derived from Arabic دخل (dakhala) meaning "to enter, to come in".
Transferred use of the surname Dahl with popular suffix -een.
This name means a sprout that is young and grows into a mature plant.
Variant of Dante. A notable bearer is the basketball player Dahntay Jones.
Alternate transcription of Korean Hangul 다훈 (see Da-hun).

Possibly derived from Breton da meaning "good" and hud "magic". In Breton legend this was the name of a princess, the daughter of the king of the mythical sunken city of Ys. She was portrayed as a wicked sorceress in some versions of the legends.
From Sino-Korean 多 "much, many; more than, over" and 熙 "bright, splendid, glorious".
From the Chinese 大 (dà) meaning "big, great" and 辉 (huī) meaning "brightness, lustre, brilliance".
Of uncertain meaning, this was the name of a concubine of Shilu.
From Sino-Korean 多 (da) meaning "much, many" and 勛 (hun) meaning "meritorious deed, rank". Other hanja combinations are possible.
From Sino-Korean(Hanja) 多(da) meaning "Excellent, Better, Good" and 惠(hye) meaning "Love, Grace, Beautiful, Intelligent" or 慧(hye) meaning "Wise, Intelligent, Wisdom".
From Sino-Korean 多 "much, many; more than, over" and 賢 "virtuous, worthy, good".
Derived from Old Persian dahyu meaning "land", possibly a hypocoristic form of another name containing the element.
From Sino-Vietnamese 台 or 臺 (đài) meaning "noble, pedestal, stand".
From Sino-Vietnamese 大 (đại) meaning "big, great, vast, high".

column3: 提婆達多(Japanese Kanji)|だいばだった(Japanese Hiragana)

column12: From a non-Sino-Vietnamese reading of Chinese 大鵬 (đại bàng) meaning "eagle".

column3: だいちろう(Japanese Hiragana)|ダイチロウ(Japanese Katakana)|大智郎, 大地郎, 大治朗, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: Japanese masculine name derived from 大 (dai) meaning "large, big", 智 (chi) meaning "wisdom, intelligence" and 郎 (ro) meaning "son". Other kanji combinations are possible.
From Chinese 代 (dài) meaning "generation, era" combined with 川 (chuān) meaning "river, stream". Other hanzi combinations are possible.

Possibly derived from Guanche *dăyda meaning "newborn lamb that is still being suckled by its mother". This name was listed in a baptismal register from Seville dating to the 15th century; the sex and age of the bearer were not recorded. Since the 1970s it has been used as a feminine name in the Canary Islands.
Means "skill, knowledge" in Sami. Its Finnish cognate is Taito.
Xianbei name of Husi Chun, a general of the Xianbei-led Northern and Western Wei dynasties.
Means "guest of Allah" in Arabic, from ضيف (dayf) meaning "guest" combined with الله (Allah)
Daifilo is a character in the 17th-century play "Granida" by Dutch playwright Pieter Cornelisz.

column3: 大八, etc.(Japanese Kanji)|だいはち(Japanese Hiragana)|ダイハチ(Japanese Katakana)
column12: From Japanese 大 (dai) meaning "big, great" combined with 八 (hachi) meaning "eight". Other kanji combinations can form this name as well.

column3: 大一, 大壱, 台一, 第一, 唯一, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 大 (dai) meaning "big, large" combined with 一 (ichi) meaning "one". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: だいいちろ(Japanese Hiragana)|ダイイチロ(Japanese Katakana)|大一郎, 代一郎, 大市郎, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
だいいちろう(Japanese Hiragana)|ダイイチロウ(Japanese Katakana)|大一郎, 代一郎, 大市郎, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 大 (dai) meaning "big, great", 一 (ichi) meaning "one" combined with 郎 (rou) meaning "son". Other combinations of kanji characters are also possible.

column3: 太治, 代司, 代次, 代治, 代二, 台爾, 大司, 大士, 大志, 大慈, 大次, 大治, 大爾, 大自, 大仁, 大二, 大路, 悌治, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 太 (dai) meaning "thick, big", 代 (dai) meaning "generation", 台 (dai) meaning "pedestal, a stand, counter for machines and vehicles", 大 (dai) meaning "big, great" or 悌 (dai) meaning "serving our elders" combined with 治 (ji) meaning "reign, be at peace, calm down, subdue, quell, govt, cure, heal, rule, conserve", 司 (ji) meaning "director, official, govt office, rule, administer", 次 (ji) meaning "next, order, sequence", 二 (ji) meaning "two", 爾 (ji) meaning "you, thou, second person", 士 (ji) meaning "gentleman, scholar, samurai", 志 (ji) meaning "intention, plan, resolve, aspire, motive, hopes, shilling", 慈 (ji) meaning "mercy", 自 (ji) meaning "oneself", 仁 (ji) meaning "humanity, virtue, benevolence, charity, man, kernel" or 路 (ji) meaning "path, route, road, distance". Other kanji combinations are possible.Famous bearers are Daiji Takahashi, a Japanese mixed martial artist and Daiji Yamada, a Japanese professional basketball player.
Dajin is cat character in the Japanese animation film Suzumi.

column3: 大二郎, 大二朗, 大次郎, 大治郎, etc.(Japanese Kanji)|だいじろう(Japanese Hiragana)
column12: From Japanese 大 (dai) meaning "big, great, vast, high" combined with 二 (ji) meaning "two", 次 (ji) meaning "order, sequence, next" or 治 (ji) meaning "govern, administer" and 郎 (rō) meaning "son" or 朗 (rō) meaning "bright, sonorant, clear". Other kanji combinations can form this name as well.

column3: 大二郎, 大二朗, 大次郎, 大治郎, etc.(Japanese Kanji)|だいじろう(Japanese Hiragana)
column12: Alternate transcription of Japanese Kanji 大二郎 or 大二朗 or 大次郎 or 大治郎 (see Daijirō).

column3: 大樹, etc.(Japanese Kanji)|だいじゅ(Japanese Hiragana)|ダイジュ(Japanese Katakana)
column12: From Japanese 大 (dai) meaning "big, great" combined with 樹 (ju) meaning "tree". Other kanji combinations can form this name as well.

column3: 大吉, etc.(Japanese Kanji)|だいきち(Japanese Hiragana)|ダイキチ(Japanese Katakana)
column12: From Japanese 大 (dai) meaning "big, great" combined with 吉 (kichi) meaning "good luck". Other kanji combinations are also possible.

column3: 大吉郎, etc.(Japanese Kanji)|だいきちろう(Japanese Hiragana)|ダイキチロウ(Japanese Katakana)
column12: From Japanese 大 (dai) meaning "big, great" combined with 吉 (kichi) meaning "good luck" and 郎 (rō) meaning "son". Other kanji combinations are also possible.

column3: 大子, 乃子, 台子, 代子, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 大 (dai) meaning "big, great" combined with 子 (ko) meaning "child". Other kanji combinations are possible.
The Japanese form of the goddess Mahakali or a feminine form of Daikokuten, the god of great blackness or darkness. Her name means "She of the Great Blackness of the Heavens".

column3: 黛岚, 岱岚, 黛兰, 代兰(Chinese)

column12: Recorded in the Latgale region of modern-day Latvia in the late Middle Ages. The origin and meaning of this name are uncertain; theories include, however, a derivation from Latvian daile "beauty" or daiļš "beautiful, beauteous" (compare Daila) and a derivation from Lithuanian dailidė "carpenter".
The name of an indigene from La Palma who was christened in Seville.
From Sino-Vietnamese 大量 (đại lượng) meaning "generous", composed of 大 (đại) meaning "great" and 量 (lượng) meaning "quantity".
Possibly derived from Ancient Greek δαίμων (daimon) meaning "spirit, demon, minor deity, departed soul". This was the name of one of the suitors of Penelope in Greek mythology.
From Japanese 大 (dai) meaning "big, great" combined with 夢 (mu) meaning "dream". Other kanji combinations are possible.
From Sino-Korean 多 "much, many; more than, over" and 仁 "humaneness, benevolence, kindness".
