Among the Tuatha Dé Danann, multiple Delbáeths appear across generations in the Lebor Gabála Érenn (Book of Invasions), a 11th-century pseudo-historical compilation.One of the most notable Delbáeths is a Fomorian king, father of Elatha (also Elotha or Ealadha), who himself sired Bres, the half-Fomorian king of the Tuatha Dé Danann during the Second Battle of Mag Tuired. This Delbáeth is depicted as a ruler whose lineage bridges the rival supernatural factions through intermarriages, such as Elatha's union with Ériu of the Tuatha Dé Danann.Another Delbáeth, son of Elada (a Tuatha Dé Danann figure with Fomorian ties), married Ernmas (daughter of Etarlam and granddaughter of Nuadu Airgetlám) and fathered Fiacha, whose daughters—Ériu, Banba, and Fódla—personify Ireland and feature prominently in the Milesian invasion narrative, where they name the island.Yet another is Delbáeth mac Ogma, son of Ogma (the god of learning) and Étan (daughter of Dian Cecht, the healer), who succeeded the Dagda as High King of Ireland and ruled for ten years before dying in the Second Battle of Mag Tuired against the Fomorians. He is the father of the triplets Brian, Iuchar, and Iucharba (also known as sons of Tuirenn in some traditions), as well as Fiacha and Ollam, and is sometimes linked to the mother-goddess Danand; his descendants include the war-furies such as Badb, Macha, and the Morrígan in certain genealogies.

Meaning "he is so, he does so".Delsin can be found as a word in the Walam Olum, a book loosely based on Lenape/Delaware mythology dating from the 1800s. The book however was written by a man with no Native American background from information he patched together. In the book's glossary delsin is listed as meaning 'is there', with w'dellsin meaning 'he is so' or 'he does so', which has been extrapolated into the meaning of Delsin as a given name. Though the authenticity of the word is uncertain, older authentic Lenape dictionaries list the word wdellsowagan, meaning 'behavior', which suggests that delsin and w'dellsin may be genuine Lenape words.A noted bearer of the name is one of the main characters of the popular inFamous video game series, Delsin Rowe of inFamous: Second Son. Delsin is Okomish Native American, a fictional tribe created by game developers Sucker Punch specifically for the game. He is a street artist who discovers he is a conduit (super-powered being) and is forced to go on the run as all conduits are being rounded up by the government; this leads him to Seattle where he discovers just what he is capable of and forces him to decide whether to use his powers for good or evil.

It consists of the Greek noun δῆμος (demos) meaning "people" as well as "country, land" combined with either the Greek noun χαρά (chara) meaning "joy, delight, happiness" or the Greek noun χάρις (charis) meaning "grace, kindness" (see Chares).
Latinized form of Demokoon. In Greek mythology, this is the name of an illegitimate son of king Priam of Troy, who was killed by Odysseus during the Trojan War.
From the English word democracy, from French démocratie, via late Latin from Greek dēmokratia, from dēmos ‘the people’ + -kratia ‘power, rule’.
Spanish and Portuguese form of Democritus.

Latinized form of Δημοδίκη (Demodike), derived from Ancient Greek δῆμος (demos) meaning "the people" and δίκη (dike) meaning "justice, custom, order". This name was borne by multiple characters in Greek mythology.
Latinized form of Demodokos. A notable bearer of this name was the ancient Greek poet Demodocus of Leros (6th century BC).In Greek mythology, Demodocus is a character from Homer's Odyssey.

Derived from the Greek noun δῆμος (demos) meaning "the people" combined with the Greek noun δόκος (dokos) meaning "opinion, belief". Also compare the related Greek verb δοκέω (dokeo) meaning "to expect" as well as "to think, to imagine, to suppose" (see Eudocia).
Croatian, Macedonian and Russian form of Demophilos.
Spanish and Portuguese form of Demophilos via Demophilus.
Derived from Greek δῆμος (demos) meaning "the people" and κλειτός (kleitos) meaning "splendid, famous".

Derived from the Greek noun δῆμος (demos) meaning "people" as well as "country, land" combined with κοῶ (koo), which is a contracted form of the Greek verb κοέω (koeo) meaning "to know, to be aware" as well as "to mark, to perceive, to hear". As such, the meaning of this name must be something along the lines of "to know the country" or "to hear/listen to the people".Also compare the partially related names Hippokoon and Laokoon.
Derived from Greek δῆμος (demos) meaning "the people" and κράτος (kratos) meaning "power, strength".
Latinization of the German word "Demokrat" meaning democrat.
Bosnian and Croatian form of Democritus.

Means "lion of the people", derived from Greek δῆμος (demos) meaning "the people" and λέων (leon) meaning "lion". This is the name of several figures in Greek mythology, including both a Trojan and a Greek warrior, and a centaur who fought in the battle against the Lapiths.

Uncertain etymology, possibly an altered form of Demoleon. This was the name of an Achaean warrior who participated in the Trojan War according to the Aeneid. During the siege of Troy, he was slain by the hero Aeneas, and his armour used as a prize in a later competition.
Derived from Greek peep (demos) meaning "the people" and either μέλος (melos) meaning "song" or μέλω (melo) meaning "to care, be interest in; to be cared for".
Feminine form of Demonax. This was the name of several characters in Greek mythology, one of whom was a princess.
Derived from Greek δῆμος (demos) meaning "the people" and ἄναξ (anax) meaning "master, lord, king".This name was borne by a Greek Cynic philosopher from the 2nd century AD.

Combination of the popular name prefix de and Monica. It can be spelled DeMonica or Demonica. A known bearer is American musician DeMonica Santiago, a member of the late 1980s/early 1990s R&B group The Good Girls.
Latinized form of Demonike. In Greek mythology, this is the name of two characters, one of which is an Aetolian princess.
Latinized form of Demonikos. A known bearer of this name was Demonicus of Pella (4th century BC), a trierarch who is thought to have been part of the companion cavalry of Alexander the Great.
Derived from the Greek noun δῆμος (demos) meaning "the people" combined with the Greek noun νίκη (nike) meaning "victory".
Perhaps a short form of Desdemona or combination of popular prefix de and Mona 1.
Combination of the phonetic elements da, mon and tay (cf. Lamonte, Jamonte). This also coincides with an Italian surname (see Demonte).
Derived from Greek δῆμος (demos) meaning "the people" and φανής (phanes) meaning "appearing, shining".
French form of Demophilos via Demophilus.
Means "friend of the people", derived from Greek δημος (demos) "the people" combined with Greek φιλος (philos) "friend, lover".
Derived from Greek δῆμος (demos) meaning "the people" and Epic Greek πτόλεμος (ptolemos) meaning "war" (see polemos).
Latinized form of Demoptolemos. In Greek mythology, this is the name of one of the suitors of Penelope.

This is the name of Hikaru Sulu's daughter, Helmsman of the USS Enterprise-B in the 1994 film 'Star Trek: Generations'. Perhaps by coincidence, the word demora means "delay" in both Spanish and Portuguese.
Combination of popular prefix de and Maury.
Combination of the popular name prefix De- and Morris.
Derived from Greek δῆμος (demos) meaning "the people", usually used as a short form of names containing the element.
Spanish and Portuguese form of Demosthenes.
Latinized form of Demostratos. This name was borne by five eponymous archons of Athens, the earliest of which lived in the 4th century BC.
Transferred use of the surname Dempsey.
Transferred use of the surname Dempster.
A notable bearer of the name was Demri Parrott (1969 - 1996), who was the girlfriend and ex-fiancee of Alice In Chains lead singer Layne Staley.
Diminutive of Demetre, Demna and Demur.
Variant of Temur. A known bearer of this name is the Georgian rugby union player Demur Tapladze (b. 2000).
Possibly derived from Japanese 伝 (den), meaning "legend, tradition".
From the Chinese 德 (dé) meaning "heart, mind, morals, ethics, virtue" and 娜 (nà) meaning "elegant, graceful".
English variant of Danaë, or perhaps a blend of Denise and Renee.
A character from the film Brother Bear.
Possibly a variant of Donalda. A bearer of this name is Canadian actress Denalda Williams.

From the indigenous Koyukon name of a mountain in Alaska, allegedly meaning "great one". Commonly known as Mount McKinley in the English-speaking world, Denali is the tallest peak in North America. It is also the name of a car brand (made by General Motors).
Denarie Kyla Bautista Taylor is the real name of Bella Poarch, a Filipina American TikToker. She was adopted so it might not be a Filipino name after all.
Either an elaboration of Narius with the popular name element de or taken from the name of a Roman coin, the denarius.
Means "from the danish settlement." It is also the middle name of one of the cartoon creators and founders of Hanna-Barbera Productions, William Denby "Bill" Hanna (1910-2001).
Coined by Sabino Arana Goiri and Koldo Elizalde as a Basque equivalent of Anunciación (compare Deiñe).
Perhaps a blend of Denise and Jeannine.
Most likely a variant of Denean.
From Old English elements Dene "Dane" and beald "bold, brave"
From Old English Dene "Dane" and beorht "bright". This was the name of a 9th century Bishop of Worcester.
Variant of Denae; perhaps a blend of Denise and Renee.
Originally transferred from the surname Deneen.The name was popularised in the USA by an Ivory Soap commercial and later by the pop duo August & Deneen.
From Old English Dene "Dane" and friþ "peace". This was the name of a 8th century Bishop of Sherborne.
From Old English Dene "Dane" and gisl "hostage" (from gīslaz).
Origin: Modern invented nameMeaning: Resilience; inner strength; the ability to recover and riseCreated by a mother who wanted a name that symbolized perseverance.
Derived from the Old English elements Dene "Dane" and mōd "mind, heart, spirit" (from mōdaz).
Probably a contracted form of Denver.
Denethor II is a fictional character in J.R.R. Tolkien's The Return of the King. In the novel, he is the 26th and last ruling steward of Gondor.
From Old English elements Dene "Dane" and weald "powerful, mighty" or "authority, leader".
Derived from the Old English elements Dene "Dane" and wulf "wolf". This was the name of a 9th century Bishop of Winchester.
Means "top of a sail" in Palauan.
From the Chinese 灯 (dēng) meaning "lantern, lamp" and 骊 (lí) meaning "pure black horse".
Transferred use of the surname Denham.
Possibly a short form of Denica.
Elaboration of Denice in the style of Alicia or else a variant of Denisha.
Transferred use of the surname Denilson.Famous bearers of this name are Brazilian retired footballer Denílson de Oliveira Araújo and Brazilian footballer Denílson Pereira Neves.
From the English word denim, a type of fabric, derived from the French phrase serge de Nimes, indicating that the serge (fabric) was from the town of Nîmes.
Possibly a combination of the popular name prefix De and Nina 1.
Transferred use of the surname De Niro.
Galician, Spanish and Gascon form of Denis. In Spanish it is sometimes used for women too as variant of Denise, reflecting the French pronunciation.
Possibly a variant of Denise, blending it with Tanisha.
Elaboration of Denise or Denisa in the style of Theresia.

The first element of this name is derived from Bulgarian den "day", which is ultimately derived from Proto-Slavic dьnь "day". The second element is derived from Slavic slav "glory". In other words, this name is the Bulgarian cognate of Danislav.
Transferred use of the surname Denison.
Old French diminutive of Denis, found in records from 1413 and 1421.
Variant of Dénes, the Hungarian form of Denis.
Meaning: one who has electromagnetic powers, Bequest From Ancestors.

column3: เด่นเก้าแสน(Thai)

column12: Transferred use of the surname Denley.

Derived from the name of the country of Denmark. This was borne by Denmark Vesey (c. 1767-1822), a freed slave. In Vesey's case, he was named for the state that ruled his birthplace, the Caribbean island of St. Thomas, in the 19th century.
The name of a character from the book series 'The Sword of Truth' written by Terry Goodkind.

This name could be a variant spelling of Tenne, but it could also be derived from Daniel (for men) or Danielle (for women). Another possibility is that this is just a recently invented name, since names with a double consonant followed by the ə-sound have been gaining popularity in The Netherlands (like Fenne, Jelle, Sterre, etc.) in this decade.
Possibly a variant of Danette, or a combination of Denise with the diminutive suffix -ette.
Diminutive of Denise and a variant of Denny.
Variant and feminine form of Denny.
Transferred use of the surname Denning.
Medieval English vernacular form of Dionysia.
Transferred use of the surname Dennon.

column3: 佃之介, 伝之介, 電之介, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: It could be from 佃⁠ (tsukuda, ten, den) meaning “cultivated rice field” or 伝 (den) meaning "ttansmission, conveyance, communication", 電 (den) meaning "electricity, electric, lightning" combined with means 之 (no) meaning "of, this, that" and 介 (suke) meaning "hel, assist, mediate". Other kanji combinations are possible.
Variant of Dennis. This was the name of one of the twin boys in the "Time Quintet" by Madeleine L'Engle.
Derived from the Svan noun დინოლ (dinol) meaning "little girl" (also see the Svan name Dina).
Most likely a combination of any name that starts with Den- (such as Dennis and Denzil) with any name that contains -ray-, such as Ray, Raynard and Murray.Also compare Denroy.

In most cases, this name is a combination of any name that starts with Den- (such as Dennis and Denzil) with any name that contains -roy-, such as Roy, Royston and Leroy. Also compare Denray. However, there can also be cases where this name is derived from the obscure surname Denroy, which occurs exclusively in the United States and is therefore most likely a corruption of the original surname. The original surname may have been Denoroy, which is a rare French locational surname that means "from Norroy". Norroy is the name of several villages in France, all of which are located in the Grand Est region in northeastern France. They derive their name from French noyer meaning "walnut tree" (which ultimately comes from Latin nucarium or nucarius), which thus means that their name is a reference to the fact that the villages were built in the vicinity of a lot of walnut trees.Known bearers of this name include the Jamaican reggae artist Denroy Morgan (b. 1946) and the Vincentian former cricketer Kenroy Martin (b. 1979), who carries the name as a middle name.

column3: 伝助, 伝輔, 伝亮, 伝佑, 伝甫(Japanese Kanji)|でんすけ(Japanese Hiragana)|デンスケ(Japanese Katakana)
column12: This name combines 伝 (ten, den, tsuta.u, tsuta.eru, tsuda.u, tsute, -dzuta.i) meaning "communicate, legend, tradition, transmit" with 助 (jo, suke, su.keru, tasu.karu, tasu.keru) meaning "assist, help, save, rescue," 輔 (fu, ho, tasu.keru, suke) meaning "help," 亮 (ryou, akiraka, suke) meaning "clear, help," 佑 (u, yuu, tasu.keru, suke) meaning "assist, help" or 甫 (fu, ho, haji.mete, suke) meaning "beginning, for the first time."This name was occasionally used from the Edo Period (1603-1868) to the first half of the 20th century but nowadays, it is very rarely given to boys, if given at all.

Dentatus is a Latin word meaning "toothed". It was given as a cognomen (byname) to a boy born with teeth in his mouth.A known bearer of this cognomen is the Roman consul Manius Curius Dentatus (died 270 BC)
From Latin Deocarus meaning "loved by God". This was borne by a 9th-century saint.

English, Languedocian and Gascon form of Deodatus. This name was borne by Reverend Deodat Lawson, a minister in Salem Village from 1684 to 1688 who is famous for a 10-page pamphlet describing the witchcraft accusations in the early spring of 1692.
Variant of Teodoro influenced by deus, Portuguese word for "god".
Spanish and Galician form of Deogratias.
Means "thanks to God" or "grace of God", derived from Latin deus "god" combined with Latin gratia "thanks, grace". A bearer of this name was saint Deogratias of Carthage (5th century AD).
Means "grace of God" or "gratitude, thanks to God", from Latin Deus "God" and gratia "grace".
From Sino-Korean 德 "ethics, morality, virtue" and 河 meaning "water; river, creek" or 夏 meaning "summer."
From Sino-Korean 德 (deok) meaning "ethics, morality, virtue" combined with 浩 (ho) meaning "great, numerous, vast". Other hanja combinations can form this name as well.
From Sino-Korean 德 "ethics, morality, virtue" and 惠 "favor, benefit, confer kindness". A famous bearer is Princess Deok-hye of Korea (1912-1989), the last princess of Korea.
From Sino-Korean 賢"virtuous,worthy,good" and 只 "just,simple"

column3: 덕수(Korean Hangul)|德守, 德秀, 德銖, 德壽, 德洙, 悳洙, etc.(Korean Hanja)
column12: Alternate transcription of Korean Hangul 덕수 (see Deok-su).

column3: 덕수(Korean Hangul)|德守, 德秀, 德銖, 德壽, 德洙, 悳洙, etc.(Korean Hanja)
column12: From Sino-Korean 德/悳 (deok) meaning "ethics, morality, virtue" combined with 守 (su) meaning "defend, protect, guard", 秀 (su) meaning "luxuriant, beautiful, elegant, outstanding", 銖 (su) referring to an ancient unit of currency, 壽 (su) meaning "long life, lifespan" or 洙 (su) referring to a river in Shandong province, China. Other hanja combinations can form this name as well.
Feminine or variant form of Deon, possibly influenced by DeAndre or Kendra.
Variant of Deandrea, likely influenced by Deon.
Variant of Deonne or Deanna, or possibly a variant of Diana reflecting the Spanish pronunciation.

Monothematic name from Old English element dēor "wild animal, deer". This was the name of a late-10th-century poet who created the The Lament of Deor, a poem consisting of a reflection on his misfortune.
Apparently derived from the Old English adjective deorc meaning "dark".

Probably derived from Old English dēor meaning "brave, bold, fierce" combined with the name-forming suffix ing. Alternatively the first element could be derived from Old English deore meaning "dear, beloved".
Derived from the Old English elements deore "dear" and lāf "legacy, remainder" (from laibō). This was the name of a 9th century Bishop of Hereford.
Old English name derived from the elements deore "dear, beloved" and mann "man, person"; alternatively it could mean "fierce-spirited man" from Old English dēor "wild animal, beast" and mann.
Derived from the Old English elements deore "dear" and mōd "mind, spirit" (from mōdaz).
Derived from the Old English elements deore "dear" and noð "boldness, daring".
From the Old English name Deorsige, composed of the elements deore "dear" and sige "victory".
Derived from the Old English elements deore "dear" and stan "stone".
Derived from the Old English elements dēor "dear" and swiþ "strong, mighty".
Derived from the Old English elements deore "dear" and wulf "wolf". Alternatively, the first element may derive from deor "wild animal, beast; deer".
Derived from the Old English elements deore "dear" and wynn "joy".
Polish form of Diotima. It was used as a pseudonym by the novelist and poet Jadwiga Łuszczewska (1834-1908).
Meaning, "to rely on." Referring to our dependence on God.
Referring to one's dependance on God.
Borne by DePrise Brescia (1965-), an American swimsuit model who cohosted the ESPN television workout show BodyShaping during the early to mid-1990s.
From the Chinese 德 (dé) meaning "heart, mind, morals, ethics, virtue" and 倩 (qiàn) meaning "beautiful, lovely".
From the Chinese 德 (dé) meaning "heart, mind, morals, ethics, virtue" and 巧 (qiǎo) meaning "artful, clever, skillful, ingenious".
Elaboration of Dequan with the phonetic element vion.
Invented name, probably based on Dequan and Octavius.
Combinaiton of the prefix de- with the given name Quincy, and may also be transferred use of the surname DeQuincy.

This given name originated in the United States, where it is a combination of a name starting with Der- (such as Derek and Derryl) with a name ending in -ald (such as Gerald, Reginald and Ronald). Also compare the name Darold, of which Derald can be a variant form in some cases.A known bearer of this name was the American agricultural geneticist and sesame researcher Derald Langham (1913-1991).

The meaning of this name is not wholly certain; it may be a combination of two existing, separate names. What name the first part of Deraldo could have come from, I don't know - but the second part could be either from the name Aldo or it could come from a Germanic name with the element wald "rule". A bearer of this name was Deraldo Barreto Piton (1945-2012), a Brazilian politician.
Malay short form of Abd ar-Rahman.
From Kurdish der meaning "tree, wood" and av meaning "water".
Combination of the popular name prefix da and Ray.

From Gaelic Der bForgaill, which apparently meant "daughter of Forgall". It may be an earlier form of Dearbháil or Deirbhile. This was the name of a legendary princess of Lochlann (Norway) who had been left for the Fomorii in lieu of tribute on a deserted beach. Cúchulainn happened by and slew the Fomorii and she fell in love with him. She turned herself into a swan, with a handmaiden, and followed Cúchulainn back to Ireland. Cúchulainn was hunting with a companion, Lóegaire, and he cast a stone with his slingshot bringing down one of the swans that flew over. It was Derbhorgill. He sucked out the slingshot and healed her but, being now united to him by blood, Derbhorgill was forbidden to wed him. Cúchulainn gave her to Lóegaire to wed (Peter Berresford Ellis, 1987). This was also borne by a 12th-century princess of Meath who was abducted by the king of Leinster in 1152.
Possibly a variant of Darcy or a diminutive of Dolores. A famous bearer was Brazilian actress Dercy Gonçalves (1907-2008), whose given name was Dolores.
Latinized form of Derkylidas. This was the name of a Spartan commander from the 4th century BC.
from the surname Dereef, could also be seen as a combination of the popular name prefix de and Reef.
Means "to develop, to organise" in Amharic.
Possibly a corruption of the Irish surname Derach, itself derived from the Gaelic dearg meaning "red".
Possibly an elaboration of Dereth to create a strictly feminine form of this name.
Derived from either Welsh derw "oak" or the obsolete Welsh element der(w) "true" and mael "prince, leader".
Derived from either Old Breton daeru / deru "oak" or Old Breton der, an intensifying prefix, and Old Breton gen, derived from Proto-Celtic *genos- "family, clan, descendants".

Means "tear of the sun", composed of Old Irish dér "tear" and grían "the sun" (genitive gréine; compare Aoibhgréine). In Irish legend Dér Gréine was the daughter of Fiachna Mac Retach, who married Laoghaire Mac Crimthann of Connacht.
French form of Derek, but it can also be a short form of Frédéric.
Variant of Derek perhaps blending it with Jericho.
Usually a latinized form of Dirk, but it can also be a short form of Didericus and Fredericus.
Means "laughter can never end" in Ijaw.
Borne by American former college football quarterback D'Eriq King (1997-).
Malay short form of Idris 1 إدريس.
Dutch variant form of Dirk, as well as the Frisian form of Dirk.
Hellenized form of Aramaic 𐡕𐡓𐡏𐡕 (Tarʿatta), the apocope form of 𐡏𐡕𐡓𐡏𐡕𐡄 (ʿAttarʿattā), another name of the Syrian goddess Atargatis.

When borne by a female person, this name is a good example of how one can turn a very masculine name (Derk) into a feminine name by simply adding the diminutive suffix je to the original name. But when borne by a male person, this name is simply a pet form because of the diminutive suffix.

Means "son of Derkylos" in Greek, derived from the name Derkylos combined with ίδας (idas), which is the Aeolic and Doric Greek form of the patronymic suffix ἴδης (ides).This name was borne by a Spartan commander from the 4th century BC. He is better known under the latinized form of his name, which is Dercylidas.
Possibly derived from Greek δερκύλλειν (derkyllein) meaning "to scratch the skin" or "to tear off the skin".
Meaning unknown, possibly created to sound like names such as Merl and Burl.

Invented name, possibly derived from the word dearly and the element -lis present in names such as Odalis and Herlis. Some websites claim it to mean "one who is desired", but that is likely a spurious fact.
For a man named Dean that has become a mermaid!
1. Strenght,power, energy2. Cure, remedy, aid, solution
French variant of Dermid. This was borne by a short-lived nephew of the French emperor Napoleon Bonaparte, who was named for a character in Scottish poet James Macpherson's Ossian poems.
Manx form of Diarmait. This name used to be Anglicized as both Dermot and Jerry (the latter Anglicization arose due to the variant Germot).
Possibly derived from Ancient Greek δηρός (deros) meaning "long, too long". This was the name of one of the Nereids in Greek mythology.

This is regarded as a combination of the popular name prefix de and Rhonda, and can be spelled DeRonda or Deronda. Also compare Laronda, Sharonda. In literature, it was used as a surname in Daniel Deronda (1876), the last novel George Eliot completed.

column3: 德荣, 德容, etc.(Chinese)|德榮, 德容, etc.(Traditional Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 德 (dé) meaning "ethics, morality, virtue" combined with 荣 (róng) meaning "glory, honour, flourish, prosper" or 容 (róng) meaning "appearance, form". This name can be formed from other combinations of characters as well.
Means "oak" in Cornish. This is a modern Cornish name.
Combination of the prefix De and the name Royce.
A Yiddish name taken from the Slavic, meaning 'my dear little one'.

From the English word derp. This is the name of a character in the TV series 'My Little Pony: Friendship Is Magic'. Despite being a secondary character of the series, her high popularity among adult fans has earned her the title of mascot of the brony fandom.

From Guanche *derk meaning "strength". This was recorded as the name of a nephew of a Guanche mencey (leader) of Adeje, a menceyato or kingdom on the island of Tenerife (present-day Canary Islands, Spain).
Variant of Derrell, itself a variant of Darrell.
A variation of Derren with the -ence suffix.
Possibly derived from Darryl.Most known for being the name of a character on the TV show firefly.
Feminine form of Derrick, influenced by Erica.
The name of a character in Victor Hugo's 1866 novel Les Travailleurs de la mer (Toilers of the Sea in English) set on the island of Guernsey. Déruchette is the love interest of the main character.
From the Chinese 德 (dé) meaning "heart, mind, morals, ethics, virtue" and 蕊 (ruǐ) meaning "unopened flowers, flower buds".
A Dervish is a Sufi Muslim ascetic.
Old Irish name meaning "purely fair daughter"
Latinization of the Gaelic name Derbforgaill. A notable bearer of this name is Dervorguilla of Galloway, mother of John I of Scotland.

Likely derived from Cornish derow "oak trees" (ultimately from Proto-Celtic *daru "tree"). Saint Derwa is the patron saint of Menadarva (Merther Derwa in Cornish, translating to grave of St Derwa in English) in the parish of Camborne, Cornwall. Nothing is now known about this saint, not even their gender. There have been speculations that Saint Derwa might have been and a man and in fact none other than Saint Dyfan. In modern times, however, this name has been resurrected as a feminine name.

Derwan was an early duke of the Sorbs (fl. 615–636). He is mentioned by Fredegar in his Latin chronicle as dux gente Surbiorum que ex genere Sclavinorum: "ruler of the people of the Surbi". He is the first ruler of the tribe mentioned by name.
From Welsh derw meaning "oak" and gwyn meaning "fair, white, blessed."

From the name of multiple rivers in England, which comes from Celtic dwr-gent "clear water", or else a transferred use of the surname (see Derwent). This name was used by English poet Samuel Taylor Coleridge for his son born 1800.
Transferred usage of the surname Derwood.
Of debated origin and meaning. Theories include a derivation from Welsh derw "oak" or the obsolete Welsh element der(w) "true" and gwyn "white; fair; blessed".
From the given name Derýa and geldi meaning "came, arrived".
Either a short form of Desanka or derived from Slavic des meaning ''to happen, to occur''.
Means "he stands people on their feet" in Mohawk.
From a noble title for females belonging to the Ksatria caste, placed at the beginning of the given name.
Means "forsaken, helpless" in Spanish, in effect an altered form of Desamparados. The compound name María Desamparada was used for a character on the Mexican telenovela Triunfo del amor (2010-2011).
Catalan form of Desamparados, taken from the title of the Virgin Mary, Mare de Déu dels Desamparats, meaning "Mother of God of the Forsaken."
Means "of the angels", taken from the French title of the Virgin Mary Notre Dame des Anges, meaning "Our Lady of the Angels". It is most often found in French-speaking African countries.
This name is usually a combination of Désirée with Anne 1.A known bearer of this name is the Dutch writer and philosopher Désanne van Brederode (b. 1970).
Possibly an English phonetic respelling of Désirée.
Variant of Desiree. This is the birth name of actress Scout Taylor-Compton.
Derived from French des douleurs, meaning "the sorrows" and used as the Louisiana Creole equivalent of Dolores.
Combination of the popular name prefix de and Sean, making it a variant of Deshawn. It can be spelled DeSean or Desean.

This is a word from the Book of Mormon meaning "honeybee" in the language of the Jaredites. It was used as a name for the Utah territory before it became an American state (now officially nicknamed the Beehive State as a symbol of cooperation and industry). It is occasionally used as a feminine given name, perhaps due to its similarity to Desiree.
German translation of Offred used in the series 'Die Geschichte der Magd' 'The Handmaid's Tale'.

Rao Deshalji I was the Rao of Cutch belonging to Jadeja Rajput dynasty, who ruled Princely State of Cutch as a regent from 1718 1752. His son Lakhpatji confined him in 1741 and ruled as a regent until death of Deshalji in 1752.
Combination of the popular name prefix De and Shanae, possibly based on Deshawn, Dejanae or Deja.

Derived from ancient Greek δεσπότης (despotes) meaning "lord, master", which was synonymous with κύριος (kyrios) meaning "lord, master" (see Kyrios). This was initially a form of address that indicated respect, which after the advent of Christianity became intertwined with the Christian religion, as it became a way to refer to God and to church officials (especially bishops and patriarchs). In the High Middle Ages, δεσπότης (despotes) also became a Byzantine court title, which was bestowed upon the sons or sons-in-law of reigning Byzantine emperors.A notable bearer of this name was Despot Badžović (1850-1930), an ethnic Serb teacher and political activist who was born and raised in what is now North Macedonia.

In medieval French literature, Desramé is the name of a Saracen king from several epic poems that revolve around the Frankish nobleman William of Gellone/Orange (c. 755-c. 812), such as Aliscans and Prise d'Orange (both written in the 12th century).The meaning of his name is uncertain. It is often said to be derived from Abdérame, a gallicization of Arabic Abd al-Rahman or Abd ar-Rahman. However, some scholars dispute this and suggest that it is instead derived from Spanish desramar or desramare (also desramaré) meaning "to debranch, to prune, to trim (off)" as well as "to shed (off)". According to them, this is a reference to the king's loss of his children, which results in a thinning (and ultimately death) of his family tree.Also compare Old French desramer meaning "to tear, to rip up".

Derived from Latin deus meaning "god, deity". Latin deus and dīvus "divine" are descended from Proto-Indo-European deiwos, from the same root as Dyēus, the reconstructed chief god of the Proto-Indo-European pantheon. Compare Greek Zeus (Ζεύς, pronounced zdeús), in Aeolic Greek Δεύς (deús).In Classical Latin, Deus was a general noun referring to any divine figure. In Late Latin, it came to be used mostly of the Christian God. It is inherited directly in the Romance languages, as French dieu, Spanish dios, Portuguese deus, Italian dio, and so forth.

Queen Deuteria of the Franks was a consort of King Theudebert I. She came from an aristocratic Gallo-Roman family from Auvergne. She was related to Sidonius Apollinaris, Saint Avitus, and Emperor Avitus. In Septimania, she was married with a daughter, Adia. The area was attacked by Theudebert I, who fell in love with her. He called her to court, and she brought her daughter with her. However, Deuteria's husband was still alive, and Theudebert was engaged to marry a Lombard princess, Wisigard. It's unknown whether Deuteria and Theudebert were ever married.According to Gregory of Tours, Deuteria had her daughter drowned in 536, in fear of her becoming a rival over Theudebert. Afterward, the aristocracy forced Theudebert to expel Deuteria and marry Wisigard. It is said that he wished to recall Deuteria after Wisigard's death in 540, but did not dare to.

By some accounts he was originally a disciple of the Buddha but is cast out after growing jealous of his cousin. He attempts to murder the Buddha numerous times and eventually forms a group of breakaway monks to try to divide the Buddhist community (which ultimately fails). Before dying of illness, he realises the error of his ways and attempts to apologise to the Buddha, only to be sucked into the ground and sent to naraka (hell).

Dharmakar or Dharmakara is a name of Asian origin coming from the Sanskrit धर्म ("Dharma", virtue, moral law, that which sustains creation, order of the world) + कर ("kāra", hand, part of the body held in the forearm by the wrist). The name Dharmakara carries with it the message of justice and righteousness. A just and disciplined man. This name is mentioned in the Puranas (पुराण, purāṇas) and is the birth name of Amitabha Buddha.According to Nepalese tradition, the first ruler of Nepal was Dharmakar. This mythical figure related to the Nepalese genesis was said to have been a Chinese king and accompanied a wise bodhisattva to the Kathmandu Valley, then a lake. The bodhisattva stopped the flow of water and made the region habitable. The bodhisattva established a city in the valley, Manjupattan, and, after making Dharmakara ruler of Manjupattan, returned to China.Thus, Dharmakar is a name associated with Buddhism and Sanskrit tradition, as well as referring to royalty and Nepalese history. It's a strong, noble, and ancient name.

Means "king of dharma" from Sanskrit धर्म (dharma) meaning "that which is established, law, duty, virtue" and राज (rāja) meaning "king". This is an epithet of the Hindu god Yama, as well as a title of the Buddha.

From Chinese 貂 (diāo) meaning "sable" and 蝉 (chán) meaning "cicada". This is the name of one of the Four Beauties of ancient China, whose name may be derived from the sable tails and jade decorations in the shape of cicadas which adorned the hats of high-ranking officials in the Eastern Han dynasty. Although Diaochan is based on a minor historical personage, she is mostly a fictional character. She is best known for her role in the 14th-century historical novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms, which romanticises the events in the late Eastern Han dynasty and the Three Kingdoms period.Diaochan is said to have been so luminously beautiful that the Moon itself would shy away in embarrassment when compared to her face. This description serves as the meaning behind the third pair of characters of the Chinese idiom 沉魚落雁, 閉月羞花 (chényú luòyàn, bìyuè xiūhuā), referring to the Four Beauties, which is used to compliment a woman's beauty, meaning one is so beautiful she sinks fish and entices birds to fall, eclipses the moon and shames flowers, (literally "fish dive/goose fall, moon hide/flower shame").

In Roman mythology Dies ("day") was the personification of day, and the Roman counterpart of the Greek goddess Hemera, the daughter of Nox (Night) and Scotus (Darkness).She is the goddess of the daytime, and according to Hesiod, the daughter of Erebus and Nyx (the goddess of night). Hemera is remarked upon in Cicero's De Natura Deorum, where it is logically determined that Dies (Hemera) must be a god, if Uranus is a god. The poet Bacchylides states that Nyx and Chronos are the parents, but Hyginus in his preface to the Fabulae mentions Chaos as the mother/father and Nyx as her sister.She was the female counterpart of her brother and consort, Aether (Light), but neither of them figured actively in myth or cult. Hyginus lists their children as Uranus, Gaia, and Thalassa (the primordial sea goddess), while Hesiod only lists Thalassa as their child.

Dilem is a poetic and highly expressive Turkish name rooted in the structural mechanics of the Oghuz language family. It translates directly to "my wish," "my deepest desire," "the object of my prayers," "the longed-for one," or "the answer to my prayers."The name is a direct morphological derivation of the Proto-Turkic verb tile- / dile-, meaning "to wish," "to request from a higher power," or "to yearn for." It is formed by attaching the first-person singular possessive suffix -m to the nominalized stem (Examples: Özlem, İzlem, Gizem, Eylem, Balım). This nominalization framework aligns perfectly with traditional Turkic naming customs, where children born after long years of longing, prayers, or family hardships were given names marking them as a divine gift or a granted wish.Linguistically, it bypasses any external nominal roots to maintain a completely action-oriented, sentimental Turkic profile, prioritizing the familial bond and the realization of hope.Other Origins:Because of its linguistic structure, Dilem shares a profound cross-cultural homophony with Indo-Iranian (Persian and Kurdish) terms centered around the heart, though built on completely different grammatical foundations:Persian: It echoes the word Dil (دل), which signifies the "heart," "mind," or "soul."Kurdish: It directly mirrors the affectionate Kurdish phrases Dilêm or Dilê min (دڵم / دڵێ من), which translate literally to "my heart" or "my soul."For parents, Dilem offers a beautifully tender and intimate tone. It encapsulates the immense love and expectation surrounding a child’s arrival, symbolizing a soul who is deeply cherished, profoundly wanted, and destined to be a source of fulfilled dreams and answered aspirations for their family.

Sir Dinadan is one of King Arthur's knights of the round table in Arthurian legend. He is the son of Sir Brunor Senior, the 'Good Knight without Fear,' and brother of Sirs Breunor le Noir and Daniel, and is also known as a good friend of Tristan's. As with the characters Palamedes and Lamorak, Dinadan was first named in Prose Tristan, only then to appear later in the Post-Vulgate Cycle and Sir Thomas Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur. Sir Dinadan is known as one of the wittiest and most social of King Arthur's knights.

In Georgia, the usage of this name started in honour of the Georgian princess and queen Dinara of Hereti (10th century), who belonged to the Bagrationi dynasty and is venerated as a saint in the Georgian Orthodox Church.The meaning and origin of her name is uncertain. It could possibly be of Persian origin, since her father's name was Adarnase. One Georgian source states that the name is of Kartvelian origin and means "girl" or "daughter", which makes the name related to the Svan name Dina. Another Georgian source states that the name is a Russian modification of Tamar, which originated from the 16th-century Russian story The Tale of Tsaritsa Dinara, which is thought to reflect the memory of queen Tamar of Georgia (1160-1213).Lastly, an English source dedicated to medieval Russian names states that Dinara means "breath" but neglects to mention the language of origin, even though it lists the Georgian queen as the source (or prime example) of the name.

Dutch form of an ancient Germanic given name of which the first element is derived from Anglo-Saxon thing, which can have several meanings, namely: "thing," "cause," "gathering" or "council." As such, thing is related to Old High German dingôn meaning "to judge, to condemn" and dingjan meaning "to hope." Also compare other ancient Germanic given names that start with Thing-, such as Thingulf.The second element in the name comes from Old High German man meaning "man". As such, you could say that the name as a whole basically means "man of the council". With that in mind, it is interesting to note that in English there is the noun thingman, which has the same etymological origins and more or less the same meaning as well.A known Dutch bearer of this given name was the publisher and children's author Dingeman van der Stoep (1906-1997).

Latinized form of Deinophilos. This name was borne by an eponymous archon of Athens, who lived in the 1st century AD.

Possibly derived from Aramaic dinur (also denur) meaning "of fire", derived from di "of" and nur "fire, light". Because of the similarity with the Hebrew word din "trial, judgement", this name is sometimes seen as a more elaborate form of the name Dinah. A known bearer of this name is retired Brazilian actress Dinorah Marzullo (b. 1919). In Popular Culture, this is also the name of a 1859 French opera, so named after a character in that opera.
Latinized form of Deinostratos. This name was borne by a Greek mathematician from the 4th century BC.
Possibly means "early morning, sunrise" in Sinhala.
Diminutive form of Dina 1 or Dina 2.

Latinized form of Dion. In modern-day Italy, this name is also a short form of Diodato, Dionisio and other names starting with Dio-.Known bearers of this name include the 1st-century Greek orator and philosopher Dio Chrysostom and the 3rd-century Roman historian Cassius Dio (also called Dio Cassius).
An unfortunate knight who was cuckholded by Galehaut the Brown. Having lost his lovely wife, Diocenar died from heartbreak.
Spanish and Portuguese form of Diocletian.
Derived from the Greek name Diocles (see Diokles).

Possibly derived from Ancient Greek Διός (Dios) meaning "of Zeus" and κορυστής (korystes) meaning "helmed warrior, armed warrior", itself from κόρυς (korys) "helmet". This was the name of one of the fifty sons of king Aegyptus in Greek mythology, who was married to the Daenid Hippodamia and killed by her on their wedding night.
Derived from Ancient Greek Διός (Dios) meaning "of Zeus" combined with δῆμος (demos) meaning "the people".
Latinized form of Diodemos. A known bearer of this name was the American lawyer Diodemus Socrates Dorn (1860–1913), the father of the American textile designer Marion Dorn (1896-1964).
Languedocian and Gascon form of Diodorus.
Greek feminine form of Diodoros, Spanish and Neapolitan feminine form of Diodoro, Sicilian feminine form of Diodoru and Polish feminine form of Diodor.
Spanish and Portuguese form of Diodorus.
Italian and Galician form of Diodoros.
Spanish and Portuguese form of Diophantus.
Bosnian and Croatian form of Diogenes.
Italian and Romanian form of Diogenes.
Hellenized form of Diogenianus. This was the name of a Greek grammarian from Heraclea, who lived in the 2nd century AD.

Roman cognomen which was derived from the Greek given name Diogenes.This was the name of a Greek grammarian from Heraclea, who lived in the 2nd century AD. He was known as Diogenianos in his native language.
The seneschal of King Maglory the Saxon. In the early days of Arthur’s reign, he invaded northern Britain with other Saxons. He was killed at the battle of Clarence by Sir Eliezer, King Pelles’ son.

Derived from Greek Διός (Dios) meaning "of Zeus" combined with the Greek adjective γνητός (gnetos) meaning "born". The latter word is ultimately derived from the Greek verb γίγνομαι (gignomai) meaning "to come into being, to be born". Also compare the related names Diogenes and Diognis.This name was borne by two Olympic victors; one lived in the 6th century BC and the other in the 5th century BC.
Latinized form of Diognetos. A known bearer of this name was Diognetus of Croton, who won the stadion race during the 58th Olympiad in 548 BC.
Variant of Diogenes. Also compare the related name Theognis.
Croatian and Bosnian form of Diocletian.
German, Russian and Ukrainian form of Diocletian.
Combination of dio (from Dionisio and Dionisia) and the suffix -mar, present in names such as Leomar and Gladimar. It is often conflated with Dietmar or interpreted as a variant of it.
Possibly means "honourable" in Serer. A notable bearer of this name is Bassirou Diomaye Faye (b. 1980), the current president of Senegal. He is commonly known mononymously as Diomaye.
Bosnian and Croatian form of Diomedes.
Latinized form of the Greek name Διομήδη (Diomede), the feminine form of Diomedes.
Derived from Greek Διός (Dios) meaning "of Zeus" and μέδων (medon) meaning "ruler", itself from μήδομαι (medomai) "to be mindful of, provide for, think on".
Latinization of Dione 1 as well as the Albanian form of the name.
Derived from Greek Διός (Dios) meaning "of Zeus" and ἄνασσα (anassa) meaning "queen, lady" (feminine form of ἄναξ (anax) "master, lord").
The actress Dionéa Daboville is a one notable bearer of this name.
Portuguese form of Dionysius primarily used in Brazil.

The name of two persons mentioned in the fourteenth-century fragmentary Welsh text known as The Birth of Arthur.The first is a daughter of Gorlois and Igraine, half-sister to Arthur. The second is a daughter of Gwyar and Lleu (Lot), sister to Mordred and Gwalchmai.
Variant of Dion or Dionne mainly used in Brazil.

Named in La Tavola Ritonda as the Pope during Arthur’s reign.When he heard of Tristan’s death, he offered indulgences to anyone who would pray for Tristan and his country. The text notes that he was succeeded by Pope Agabito. No known Popes correspond with these names, except perhaps Pope Donus and Pope Agatho, who ascended to the papacy in 676 and 678, respectively.
Albanian variant of Dionisi and Romansh variant of Dionys.
Medieval Catalan feminine form of Dionís and Albanian feminine form of Dionis.
Albanian, Catalan and Sardinian form of Dionysius.
Indonesian and Bessarabian German form of Dionysius.
Italian and Spanish form of Dionysos.
Spanish, Portuguese, and Italian form of Dionysodoros.
Variant of Deonte; blend of Dion and Dante.
Upper German and Romansh form of Dionysios.
Modern Greek diminutive of Dionysios, as it contains the modern Greek diminutive suffix -άκης (-akis). This name is typically only used informally, meaning: it does not appear on birth certificates.
Means "glory of Dionysos", from the name of the god Dionysos combined with Greek κλέος (kleos) meaning "glory".
Means "horse of Dionysos" from the name of the god Dionysos combined with Ancient Greek ἵππος (hippos) meaning "horse".
Latinized form of Dionysodoros. This name was borne by Dionysodorus of Caunus, an ancient Greek mathematician from the 2nd century BC.
Means "glory of Dionysos" from the name of the god Dionysos combined with Greek κλέος (kleos) meaning "glory".
Means "manifestation of Dionysos" from the name of the god Dionysos combined with Greek φανής (phanes) meaning "appearing".
Presumably a feminine form of Dionysos. This was used by Shakespeare for a character in his comedy 'Pericles, Prince of Tyre' (1607).
Lithuanian form of Dionysos via its latinized form Dionysus.
Latinized form of Diopatre. This was the name of a nymph in Greek mythology.

Derived from Ancient Greek δῖον (dion) meaning "divine, noble" and πατήρ (pater) meaning "father". This was the name of a nymph of Mount Othrys in Greek mythology; when the youth Cerambus spread rumours that she and her sisters were actually daughters of the river Spercheus and Deino, as opposed to Zeus, and that the god Poseidon transformed the nymphs into poplar trees in order to seduce Diopatre without interference, they turned him into a beetle in outrage.

Uncertain etymology. Perhaps derived from Ancient Greek διόπη (diope) meaning "ear ring" (from διά "through, between" and ὀπή "opening, hole"), from Διός (Dios) "of Zeus" and ὄψ (ops) "face, eye", or from δίοπος (diopos) "ruler, commander, captain of a ship". In Greek mythology, Diope was a daughter of Triptolemos and mother of Eumolpos.

Derived from Greek Διός (Dios) meaning "of Zeus" combined with the Greek verb πείθω (peitho) meaning "to persuade, to convince" as well as "to obey, to yield to" and "to believe, to trust (in)".This name was borne by an Athenian general from the 4th century BC, who is thought to have been the father of the poet Menander.
Derived from Greek Διός (Dios) meaning "of Zeus" and φανης (phanes) meaning "appearing".

Derived from Greek Διος (Dios) meaning "of Zeus" combined with φαντός (phantos) meaning "visible". The latter element is ultimately derived from φαίνω (phaino) meaning "to appear, reveal; to shine, give light".
Latinized form of Diophantos. This name was borne by a Greek mathematician from the 3rd century AD.
Means "friend of Zeus", derived from Greek Διος (Dios) "of Zeus" combined with Greek φιλος (philos) "friend, lover".
Feminine form of Dior. A known bearer of this name is American actress Diora Baird.
Scottish cognate of Dearbháil. This name used to be Anglicized as the etymologically unrelated Dorothy.
Catalan form of Dioscorus via Dioskoros.
Italian and French form of Dioskorides via it's Latinized form Dioscorides.
Latinized form of Dioskorides. This was the name of a Stoic philosopher from the 3rd century BC.
Latinized form of Dioskourides. Bearers of this name include a Greek general from the 4th century BC and a Greco-Roman gem cutter from the 1st century AD.
Diminutive of Diosdado, Diosdada, Gaudioso, or Gaudiosa.
Russian and Serbian form of Dioskoros.
Means "son of Dioskoros" in Greek, derived from the name Dioskoros combined with the patronymic suffix ἴδης (ides).
Means "son of Dioskouros" in Greek, derived from the name Dioskouros combined with the patronymic suffix ἴδης (ides).
Epic and Ionic Greek form of Dioskoros, because it contains κοῦρος (kouros), which is the Epic and Ionic Greek form of κόρος (koros) meaning "son, boy, lad."
Combination of dios ("god") with the popular suffix mar (cf. Edmar, Diomar) or possibly a variant of Diomar or Osmar.
Variant of Josmary apparently influenced by Spanish Dios "God". It was used for a character in the Venezuelan telenovela 'Toda una dama' (2007-2008).
Medieval name given to foundlings or infants with precarious health, probably at the basis of the Italian surname Diotallevi, in turn given to foundlings.

Medieval name given to foundlings or infants with precarious health, probably at the basis of the Italian surname Diotallevi, in turn given to foundlings. It was borne from the nobleman Diotalevo Diotalevi.

Medieval name given to foundlings or infants with precarious health, probably at the basis of the Italian surname Diotallevi, in turn given to foundlings.

Feminine form of Diotimos. Greek seer and philosopher Diotima of Mantinea was Socrates' teacher in Plato's 'Symposium'. The name also belonged to characters in Robert Musil's 'The Man without Qualities' and Hölderlin's novel 'Hyperion', the latter of which inspired a score by Italian composer Luigi Nono: 'Fragmente-Stille, an Diotima' (1980).
Derived from Greek Διός (Dios) meaning "of Zeus" combined with the Greek verb τιμάω (timao) meaning "to honour, to esteem, to revere".
Latinized form of Diotimos. This name was borne by a Stoic philosopher from the 1st century BC.

Derived from Greek Διος (Dios) "of Zeus" combined with Greek τρέφω (trepho) "to nourish, to feed" (also see Trophimus). This was the name of a minor character from the bible, who was mentioned in 3 John, verses 9–11.
Dio means godthe vanni part comes from the name Giovanni meaning gift from god!therefore Diovanni means God gift from god
Means "lamp of knowledge" from Sanskrit दीप (dīpa) meaning "lamp, light" and अञ्जन (añjana) meaning "anointing, manifesting, making clear".

Means "light maker" from Sanskrit दीप (dīpa) meaning "lamp, light" and कर (kara) meaning "maker". In Buddhist tradition this is the name of the fourth of the 27 buddhas preceding Siddhartha Gautama, known in Pali as Dīpaṃkara. According to legend he confirmed that Sumedha, a previous incarnation of Siddhartha, would become a buddha in a future life.
Alternate transcription of Bengali দীপান্বিতা (see Dipanwita).
From Sanskrit दीपान्विता (dīpānvitā) meaning "possessing lamps", derived from दीप (dīpa) meaning "lamp, light" and अन्वित (anvita) meaning "endowed with, possessing, having".
Means "lord of light" from Sanskrit दीप (dīpa) meaning "lamp, light" combined with the name of the Hindu god Indra, used here to mean "lord".
Possibly means "lord of light" from Sanskrit दीप (dīpa) meaning "lamp, light" and ईश (īśa) meaning "ruler, lord".
From Arabic ضِفْدَع‎ (ḍifda') "frog", taken from the phrase ضفدع الثاني (aḍ-ḍifdaʿ aṯ-ṯānī) meaning "the second frog". This is the name of a star in the constellation Cetus.
Means "lantern, lamp" in Javanese, ultimately from Sanskrit दीप (dīpa).

The Dipper mansion (斗) is one of the Twenty-eight mansions of the Chinese constellations. It is one of the northern mansions of the Black Tortoise. It corresponds to Sagittarius and is shaped like the Big Dipper, also refers temple in the sky or the snake-shaped basalt. The Big Dipper is an asterism of seven stars that has been recognized as a distinct grouping in many cultures from time immemorial. The component stars are the seven brightest of the formal constellation Ursa Major. The North Star (Polaris), the current northern pole star on Earth, can be located by imagining a line from Merak (β) to Dubhe (α) and then extending it. Polaris is part of the "Little Dipper", Ursa Minor.
The name of one of the Teletubbies who are green.
From Sanskrit दीप्तिमत् (dīptimat) meaning "splendid, brilliant, bright, shining".

Likely derived from Old Norse Dyr. Askold and Dir (died in 882) were princes of Kiev and founders of the first Vikings' state in the Dnieper. According to the Primary Chronicle, they were of Rurik's Varangian clan.
Means "prosperous, plentiful, abundant" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit अतिरेक (atireka).
Means "long live, long life" in Indonesian, ultimately from Sanskrit दिर्घायु (dirghāyu).
A name that comes from the Somali word diric which means "bold; fearless or daring." The name connotes courage or heroism. Outside of Somalia, a Somali person may spell the name as DIRI.
Shortned form of Dietrich, compare also Dirk.
Simplified form of Diarmaid.The name was borne by the Canadian linguist Dirmid R. F. Collis.
In Latin the adjective dirus as applied to an omen meant "dire, awful."
Lithuanian goddess whose name and function are a complete mystery. She was recorded in documents written by Jesuit monks between 1580 and 1620.

The only feminine dwarf named in the work of J.R.R. Tolkien.She was daughter of Thráin II, sister of Thorin Oakenshield, and the mother of Fíli and Kíli.Her name is identical to the Germanic name element dís "goddess".

From a medieval Swedish form of the Old Norse name Dísa, a short form of other feminine names containing the element dís "goddess". This is the name of a genus of South African orchids, which honours a heroine in Swedish legend. Disa has also been used as a Swedish short form of Desideria.
Means "you deserve saying it" in Akan.

Meaning unknown. The 6th-century Frankish saint Disciole (or Disciola), a niece of Saint Salvius of Albi and a favourite companion of Queen Radegund, "was noted for her saintly death, which is described in detail by Gregory of Tours".
Derived from Latin disciplina, meaning "instruction; discipline". In Roman mythology, Disciplina was a minor deity and the personification of discipline.
Middle English (in the sense ‘mortification by scourging oneself’) via Old French from Latin disciplina ‘instruction, knowledge’, from discipulus. Referring to Hebrews 12:11.

From the French word discothèque (French for "library of phonograph records", but it was subsequently used as a term for nightclubs in Paris), on the pattern of bibliothèque ‘library. Borne by Disco Norris, the son of surfer Justin Norris, of which the name was chosen by his siblings.
Used in reference to Proverbs 2:11, "Discretion shall preserve thee, understanding shall keep thee."
Possibly a combination of the Old Norse name element dís "goddess; woman, lady; seeress" and Ella 2.
Meaning "ibex," he was the youngest son of Seir the Horite. (Genesis 36:21)

From Chinese 帝 (dì) meaning "god, emperor", 释 (shì) taken from Sanskrit शक्र (śakra) and 天 (tiān) meaning "sky, heaven". This is the Chinese name for the deity Shakra.
The name of a few minor characters in the Hebrew Bible. It means “Antelope” in Hebrew.
From the Chinese 迪 (dí) meaning "enlighten, progress" and 爽 (shuǎng) meaning "bright, clear, happy, cheerful, refreshing".
The name is formed of the Germanic name elements dís "goddess" and bot "messenger".
Contraction of дитя, смело иди за революцией (ditya, smelo idi za revolyutsiyey) meaning "child, follow the Revolution boldly".

In the case of Disko Troop, a character in Rudyard Kipling's novel 'Captains Courageous' (1897), it was taken from the name of Disko Island, off the west coast of Greenland, given "because he was born on board his father's ship when it was iced near the island".

Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Dysnomia.

Variant of Dis Pater, derived from Latin dives, meaning "wealthy", itself probably derived from divus, meaning "godlike, divine". The occurrence of the name Dis together with the title Pater (meaning "father") may be due to association with Jupiter. In Roman mythology, this name belonged to a god of soil fertility and mineral wealth, later associated with the underworld. He was equated with Pluto, Hades and Orcus.
Derived from Georgian დიდ სტალინს გოუმარჯოს! (did Stalins goumarjos!) meaning "cheers to the great Stalin!".This name was created by Communist parents who were eager to reject traditional names.
Short form of Dauvit, used in northeast Scotland.
From Sanskrit डित्थ (ḍittha) meaning "wooden elephant, good-looking, dark-coloured young man proficient in every science".
Kashubian short form of Editka and Slovene diminutive of Dita.
Swedish and Norwegian form of Detlef.
Scandinavian variant and Silesian form of Dietmar.
Contraction of дитя новой эры (ditya novoy ery), meaning "child of new era".
Means "leave it for God" in Ijaw.
Truncated form of Editta as well as a Hungarian short form of Edit and Judit, used as a given name in its own right.
From the Dittany plant native to Crete, ultimately from Ancient Greek δίκταμνον (díktamnon).
Variant form of Diede. This name can also be a Dutch pet form of Edith via Ditje and Dittje. Also compare Didi, Ditty and Dietje.

From a Tuscan dialect, meaning "in the same month or year". From Italian detto, past participle of dire "to say," from Latin dicere "speak, tell, say", from root deik. Became popularized from meaning in English "same coloured clothes" or "the same thing".
Diminutive of Diede (Dutch) and Edith (Dutch and English). Also compare Didi, Ditte and Dietje.
Means "to entwine, to entangle" in Vietnamese.
Sicilian form of Diodoros via it's Latinized form Diodorus.

Corsican and Sicilian form of Dionisio.
Combination of dýr 'deer, wild animal' and geirr 'spear'.

From Italian diva (“diva, goddess”), from Latin dīva (“goddess”), female of dīvus (“divine, divine one; notably a deified mortal”).
Possibly a variation of Devan or Devin. Alternatively it may have come from the word 'Divine' or the word 'Divan' referring to a historical legislative body/ council in the Middle East.
Possibly from Sanskrit दिव्य (divyá) meaning "divine, heavenly" (see Divya).

Latinized form of Dietwara (possibly via its variant Thiwara), which is a younger and strictly feminine form of the unisex name Theodoar. Also compare Divera, which is very closely related.The best known bearer of this name is Divara van Haarlem (1511-1535), a Dutch Anabaptist who was Queen of the Anabaptist regime in the German city of Münster from 1534 until her death by execution. During her short life, she was also known as Dieuwertje Brouwersdochter (usually abbreviated to Brouwersdr. and literally means "brewer's daughter").In theatre, the name appears in the German-language opera Divara - Wasser und Blut (1993), which was based on the life of the aforementioned Divara van Haarlem.
The president of Nauru's name is Baron Divavesi Waqa.

Latinized form of the unisex name Dieuwer. This particular latinization is solely intended for women; the masculine equivalent is Diverus and its variant spellings.Also compare Divara, which is very closely related.

derived from the authority of God, referring to the Scripture. Popular with Puritans
Elaboration of the English word divine, or a variant of Davinia.
Middle English from Old French divinite, from Latin divinitas, from divinus ‘belonging to a deity.’

French form of Divitianus. Saint Divitien was a 4th-century bishop of Soissons.

Divonne les Bains is a popular spa town in France. I have read that Divonne derives from the original Celtic, meaning "divine water". The only famous holder of the name is Divonne Holmes a Court, the New York-born wife of Australian billionaire businessman Peter Homes a Court.
Corsican form of Devota. Saint Devota (Santa Divota in Corsican) is the patron saint of Corsica and Monaco.

Means "divine moon, celestial moon", from Sanskrit दिव्य (divya) meaning "celestial, heavenly" and इन्दु (indu) meaning "moon, night".
Means "thought, consciousness, spirit, essence" in Tagalog, ultimately from Sanskrit जीव (jīva).
Elaborated form of Dixie. It was used for the title character, a circus performer, in Dixiana (1930), a film set in the southern United States in the antebellum period.

Means "goddess" in Tagalog, borrowed from Spanish diosa.
From the Chinese 迪 (dí) meaning "enlighten, progress" and 园 (yuán) meaning "garden, park, orchard".

From Chinese 地 (dì) meaning "earth, soil, ground" and 藏 (zàng) meaning "storage, treasury, depository", a calque of Sanskrit क्षितिगर्भ (kṣitigarbha). This is the Chinese name for the bodhisattva Kshitigarbha.

Possibly a Persian form of Jamila.
Djanira da Motta e Silva (1914-1979) was a Brazilian painter, illustrator and engraver, known for her naïve depictions of Brazilian common life.
Modern transcription of Old Norse Diarfʀ, itself derived from Norse djarfr "brave, bold, daring". The name appears on several runestones and some other runic inscriptions as tiarfʀ and tiarfr.

Meaning "roots of the paperbark tree that still burn and throw off heat after a fire has died down". Famous bearer is Mandawuy Djarrtjuntjun Yunupingu, an Aboriginal Australian musician and educator.
