From Egyptian ḏd-ḥr meaning "Horus says", derived from ḏd "to say, to speak" combined with the name of the god Horus. Possibly a shortened form of the name ḏd-ḥr-jw.f-ꜥnḫ meaning "Horus says 'he will live'".
Means "(she) whom Amon gives" in Egyptian.
Means "enduring is the soul of Re" in Egyptian.

The first element of this name is probably derived from Serbo-Croatian djed "grandfather". The second element is derived from Slavic mir "peace". In other words, one could say that this name is the Croatian and Serbian form of Dedomir.

The first element of this name is probably derived from Serbo-Croatian djed "grandfather". The second element is derived from Slavic slav "glory". In other words, one could say that this name is the Croatian and Serbian form of Dedoslav.
Means "(my) food are the Two Ladies" in Egyptian.
From Egyptian ḏḥwtj-ḥtp meaning "Thoth is satisfied", derived from the name of the god Thoth (Djehuty in the original Egyptian) combined with ḥtp meaning "peace, satisfaction".
From Egyptian ḏḥwtj meaning "he who is like the ibis", the original form of Thoth.

"Thoth has given him," from ḏḥwtj (the original form of Thoth), possibly jri̯ "to do, to make, to create" or jrj "with respect to," probably rḏi̯ "to give," and sw "him." One bearer of the name was Djehutyirdis, High Priest of Thoth at Hermopolis during the 30th Dynasty in the 4th century BCE.
Western African name derived from Arabic Zeynab (see also Zeinabou).
A variant form of Zeinebou (chiefly Malian).
Diminutive of Djihene and cognate of Jeanneton.
From Egyptian ḏr, which can mean "limit, end" or "hinder, obstruct", perhaps in the context of "to hinder enemies". This was the name of the third pharaoh of the First Dynasty of ancient Egypt.
Walloon form of Gérard. The name coincides with Walloon djeråd, a variant of djuråd, "Eurasian jay (bird)".

Possibly derived from ḏsr.t-nbtj meaning "the holy one of the Two Ladies", derived from ḏsr "holy, sacred" combined with the feminine suffix t and the dual form of nbt "lady, mistress", referring to the dual goddesses Wadjet and Nekhbet. Alternatively, it could be a truncated form of ḏsr.t-ꜥnḫ-nbtj, adding the element ankh "life, to live" to make "the holy one who lives for the Two Ladies". Djeseretnebti was possibly the wife of pharaoh Sekhemkhet, although her existence is contested, as she is known primarily from clay seals and ivory cloth labels.
From Egyptian ḏt meaning "cobra" or "static, unchanging eternity". This was the fourth pharaoh of the First Dynasty, the successor of Djer.
Older form of Josèp used in Savoy.
Alternate transcription of Jibril, mainly used in Dutch-influenced regions of the continent.
Means “one who lives peacefully” from the Ewe elements "Dji" which relates to “life,” “to live,” or “spirit” and "Dula" which relates “calm,” “peace,” or “patience”.
A Haitian Creole variant of Gina reflecting an echo of W. and central African phonetic patterns and French linguistic influences.
Older spelling of Jiwo influenced by Dutch orthography.

Dutch form of Dieuwke, completely phonetical in its spelling. This "dutchized" form of a Frisian name has also been adopted by the Frisians themselves, though it is nowhere as popular in Friesland as the original form (Dieuwke).
Older spelling of Johar influenced by Dutch orthography.
Possibly a cognate of Gaya. Alternatively, it could be derived from the Spanish word joya, meaning "jewel".
Older spelling of Joyo influenced by Dutch orthography.
Alternate transcription of Serbian Ђока (see Đoka).
Older spelling of Joko based on Dutch orthography.
Version of Jônatas, based on the English form Jonathan
Older spelling of Joni 2 influenced by Dutch orthography.
Alternate transcription of Serbian Ђорђина (see Đorđina).
Transferred use of the surname Djorkaeff, named in honour of former footballer Youri Djorkaeff (1968-).
Alternate transcription of جمانة (see Jumana), chiefly used in Algeria.
Older form of Jouan used in the Arpitan Valleys of Piedmont.
Walloon form of Joachim and Joassin.
Older spelling of Jufri influenced by Dutch orthography.
Alternate transcription of Georgian ჯუმბერ (see Jumber).
Walloon form of Gérard. The name coincides with Walloon djuråd "Eurasian jay (bird)".
Older spelling of Juwita influenced by Dutch orthography.

it's a Kurdish name, mainly use as given name for male, the name includes two fraces, the first is /DL/ or /dil/ which means 'heart', and the second part is an adjective 'shad' meaning 'happy', both together means 'happy heart'.The letter /L/ in the name DLshad pronounced stronglly by the Kurdish speakers who live in the east of the Lower Zab river in both Iraqi and Iranian Kurdistan, whilt the same letter /L/ is pronounced in the rest of Kurdistan to the west of the Lower Zab in Iraqi Kurdistan, as well in Kurdistan Syria and Turkey. As well the name has the same meaning in Persian and its pronounce with slight /L/.

The first element of this name is derived from Polish długi or długo "long", which is ultimately derived from Proto-Slavic dьlgъ "long". Also compare Croatian dug "long". The second element of this name is derived from Slavic mil "gracious, dear".

The first element of this name is derived from Polish długi or długo "long", which is ultimately derived from Proto-Slavic dьlgъ "long". Also compare Croatian dug "long". The second element of this name is derived from Slavic mir "peace".

The first element of this name is derived from Polish długi or długo "long", which is ultimately derived from Proto-Slavic dьlgъ "long". Also compare Croatian dug "long". The second element of this name is derived from Slavic slav "glory".
Possibly a spelling variation of Delilah.
Combination of popular prefix D' and Maury.
Russian, Bulgarian, Ukrainian, and Belarusian form of Demetria, making it the feminine form of Dmitriy, as well as a diminutive of Dmitriy.

Means "image of life", from the Mandaic ࡃࡌࡅࡕࡀ (dmuta) meaning "image, mirror image", in Mandaeism this also refers to a concept of a heavenly counterpart of an earthly entity, and ࡄࡉࡉࡀ (hayyi, hiia) meaning "life".
Variant of Dmytro influenced by Dmitriy.
Variant of Denae, or a combination of the phonetic elements da and nay (perhaps modelled on Renee, Janae, etc).
Alternative name of Sant Dnyaneshwar (see Dnyaneshwar).
Marathi form of Jnaneshvara. It was borne by a 13th-century Marathi Hindu saint.
From Sino-Vietnamese 都 (đô) meaning "metropolis, capital city".
Possibly from Sino-Vietnamese 圖 (đồ) meaning "diagram, chart".
From Sino-Vietnamese 度 (độ) meaning "size, extent, limit".
From Sino-Vietnamese 杜 (đỗ) meaning "to stop, prevent, block".
From Sino-Vietnamese 堵 (đổ) meaning "wall, to block, to encounter".
Meaning unknown. This was the personal name of Sejong the Great (1397-1450), fourth king of the Joseon dynasty.

column3: 도아(Korean Hangul)|道雅, 度雅, 道娥, 度娥, etc.(Korean Hanja)
column12: From Sino-Korean 道 (do) meaning "path, road, way" or 度 (do) meaning "size, extent, limit" combined with 雅 (a) meaning "elegant, graceful, refined" or 娥 (a) meaning "good, beautiful". Other hanja combinations can form this name as well.
Diminutive of David used in the Charles Dickens novel 'David Copperfield'.

column3: 도아(Korean Hangul)|道雅, 度雅, 道娥, 度娥, etc.(Korean Hanja)
column12: Alternate transcription of Korean Hangeul 도아 (see Do-a).
Means "hope, faith" in Northern Sami, making it a cognate of Finnish Toivo.
Transferred use of the surname Doak.
From Sino-Vietnamese 斷 (đoán) meaning "to guess, to predict, to divine".
From Sino-Vietnamese 團 (đoàn) meaning "group" or 摶 (đoàn) meaning "model, to rely on".
From Sino-Vietnamese 端 (đoan) meaning "decent, proper, honest".
From Sino-Vietnamese 允 (doãn) meaning "allow, consent" or 尹 (doãn) meaning "govern, oversee".
Likely a transferred use of the surname Doane.
From Sino-Vietnamese 營 (doanh) meaning "encampment, barracks, to manage, operate", 楹 (doanh) meaning "column, pillar", or 瀛 (doanh) meaning "sea, ocean".
Probably a Yiddish short form of Dvorah influenced by Slavic dobro, "good".-------------------------------------Variant of Dova
Diminutive of Robert used in the 18th century.
The name of a House-Elf in the Harry Potter series of books.

From the English word "dobie". The name of a character called Dobie Gillis from the TV series "The Many Loves of Dobie Gillis". Also known bearers of this name were the American singer-songwriter Dobie Gray (1940-2011), and American baseball player Dobie Moore (1895-1947).
Derived from Slavic dob "brave, courageous" combined with Polish gniew "anger" (which is derived from Slavic gnev "anger").

Dobiel, also Dubbiel ("bear-god"), was the guardian angel of Ancient Persia. According to the Talmud, Dobiel was also one of the special accusers of Israel, and once officiated in Heaven for 21 days as a proxy for Gabriel when the latter (over whom Dobiel scored a victory) was in temporary disgrace for taking pity on the Israelites when God was angry with them and convincing the Babylonians to drive them from Babylon rather than kill them.
Derived from Slavic dobie meaning "suitable" or "courageous, valiant" and lut meaning "harsh, cruel, fierce".
Derived from the elements dobie "brave, worthy" and mir "world, peace".
Derived from Slavic dob "brave, courageous" combined with Slavic slav "glory".
Derived from the Lithuanian noun dobilas meaning "clover".
From Sino-Korean 道 (do) meaning “path, road, way” combined with 斌 (bin) meaning “refined”. Other hanja combinations can form this name as well.
Medieval English diminutive of Robert, as it is a double diminutive of Dob. This was used by Nicholas Udall for a character in his comedy Ralph Roister Doister (written ca. 1552).

Derived from the Slavic element dobru "good".It was used in Medieval Poland among Christians, then by the beginning of the 20th-century was mainly used by Polish Jews. In Poland, it may also occur as a hypochoristic form of any name beginning with the dobr- element. Among Eastern-European Jews, this was used as a vernacular Slavic form of the Latin Bona and the Germanic Gittel.
Derived from the Slavic element dobru "good".
Diminutive of Dobroslav, Dobrivoj and other names containing the Slavic element dobru meaning "good". Famous bearer is Croatian poet Dobriša Cesarić (1902 - 1980).
Derived from the Slavic elements dobru "good" and voji "soldier".
Originally a medieval Polish diminutive of Dobrosława, the name was later used as a given name in its own right.
Dobrodeia of Kiev (died 16 November 1131), was a Rus' princess, spouse of the Byzantine co-emperor Alexios Komnenos, and author on medicine. Original Ukrainian form is Dobrodiya.
Likely from Old East Slavic добръ (dobrŭ) "good" and дѣло (dělo) "act, deed, action" roughly translating to "doing of good deeds".

The name Dobrogey is a constructed or reconstructed name with roots in Slavic and potentially Indo-European languages. It is primarily associated with modern Rodnovery (Slavic Neopaganism), and as such, lacks concrete historical documentation in ancient texts. Its meaning and proposed origins are drawn from etymological analysis and contemporary Rodnover interpretations.
From Polish dobry "good, kind" and gniew "anger".
Derived from the Slavic name elements dobru "good" and lyuby "love".
Derived from Slavic dobro "good, kind" combined with Slavic mir "peace".
Means "good thought", derived from Slavic dobro "good, kind" combined with Polish myśl "thought" (which is ultimately derived from Proto-Slavic mysliti "to think").
Derived from the Slavic name elements dobro "good" and niega "delight". This name was borne by Dobroniega Ludgarda of Poland and Maria Dobroniega of Kiev.
Essentially means "good man", derived from Vlach dobro meaning "good".

Polish name from Slavic dobrŭ "good" combined with věstĭ "message, news" or vesti "to lead, conduct". In Old Polish, both deuterothemes became wieść, making it difficult to discern which element was intended.
Derived from the Old Slavonic elements dobro "good" and wit "lord, ruler".
Derived from the Slavic name elements dobro "good" and woj "warrior".
Derived from the Slavic name elements dobro "good" and żyźń "fecundity, prolificacy".
Diminutive of Dobroslava, not used as a given name in its own right.
Means "good virtues", from the old Slavic root *добръ (dobrŭ), meaning "good, kind" and Greek ἀρετή (áretí) meaning "virtue". This is the name of the bogatyr Dobrynya Nikitich.
Transferred use of the surname Dobson.
Sorbian cognate of Dobiesława and Dobroslava.
From a non-Sino-Vietnamese reading of Chinese 讀 (đọc) meaning "to read".
From Sino-Vietnamese 督 (đốc) meaning "to supervise, oversee, direct".
From Sino-Vietnamese 獨 (độc) meaning "single, solitary, independent".
Medieval Gascon and Provençal cognate of Dolça.
Derived from Galician doce "sweet" and thus a cognate of Dulce.
Diminutive of Doça and cognate of Douceline.
Diminutive of vernacular form of Docia.
Means "harmful, destructive", "unlucky", or possibly "difficult, obstructive", derived from Old Irish dochor "disadvantage; hurt, injury; loss, misery".
Short form of Odochia. In Romanian mythology, Dochia was a very beautiful shepherdess whom Emperor Trajan loved. Dochia refused him and she became a stone.
Possibly a variant of Eudocia or Theodocia or a short form of Eudocie. This name was used in America up until the 1930s.
Either from the surname Dock, or taken directly from the English vocabulary word referring to a structure attached to shore at which a ship can be secured, or the act of harbouring at one.
Transferred use of the surname Dockery.
Means "independence", from Sino-Vietnamese 獨 (độc) meaning "single, solitary, independent" and 立 (lập) meaning "set up, establish".
Middle English (in the senses "learned person" and "Doctor of the Church") via Old French from Latin doctor "teacher" (from docere "teach").
Short form of Jodocus and Judocus.
A Saxon king who participated in the Saxon invasion of northern Britain in the early days of Arthur’s reign. He was killed by Agravain at the battle of Cambenic.
Possibly meaning "firm and ripe" or "growing well".
Variant of Dodavahu used in the King James Version of the Old Testament.

From the Hebrew name Dodhawahu meaning "loved of God", which may be an extended form of David. It occurs briefly in 2 Chronicles in the Old Testament belonging to the father of a prophet called Eliezer.

The first element of of this name is uncertain origin. It may possibly be either from Old High German toto meaning "sponsor, godparent" or Old High German *dodh meaning "judgement" together with Old High German beraht and Old Saxon berht from Proto-Germanic *berhtaz meaning "bright".Dutberta is the feminine form.
Transferred from the English surname Dodd.
Scottish diminutive of George. Possibly originating from the Gaelic form of George, Deòrsa.

From the English word dodger meaning "one who dodges; one who avoids, evades, or sidesteps". Traditionally a nickname, it is occasionally used as a given name. Fictional bearers include Jack Dawkins, better known as the Artful Dodger, a character from Charles Dickens' novel Oliver Twist (1838) who befriends Oliver and entreats him to join Fagin's team of young pickpockets, as well as the title character in Terry Pratchett's 2012 novel Dodger (loosely based on Dickens' Dodger) and Mark 'Dodger' Savage, a character from the British soap opera Hollyoaks (introduced 2011). Use of the name in the United States may also be due to the popular Major League Baseball team, the Los Angeles Dodgers (formerly the Brooklyn Dodgers), particularly after World Series wins.
As a feminine name, it's a variant of Dodie. A notable masculine bearer is Dodi Al Fayed
Old English name of uncertain derivation, featuring the name-forming suffix ing.
Variant of Dodie, a diminutive of Dorothy. It is also sometimes used as a diminutive of Dolores and other names beginning with Do.

Probably of pre-Greek origin. This was the name of an Oceanid nymph in Greek mythology, by some accounts the namesake of the ancient city Dodona, though others trace it to either Dodon, a son of Zeus and Europa, or to a river of the same name.
Diminutive of Diosdado, Leonardo and other names ending in do.
Diminutive of Dolores. Could also probably be a variant of Dodie.
Frisian and northern Dutch form of Ludolf and similar Germanic names. It originated in nursery speech, as such names were (and are) too difficult for toddlers to pronounce correctly.

Contracted form of Doedeke, which is a diminutive of Doede, as it contains the Dutch and Frisian diminutive suffix -ke.This name is not to be confused with the Dutch word doek meaning "cloth, linen, fabric".
Could be a variant transcription of Dunja, of Dunya 1/Dunya 2 or a variant of Donja
From Sino-Korean 都 "elegant, refined" and 彦(eon) meaning "Noble, Great, Talented"

Possibly derived from the Old Norse toponym Dofrar, which itself is probably related to Proto-Slavic *dьbrь (dubri) "valley, ravine" and Proto-Celtic dubros "water; dark" (see dwfr), both deriving from Proto-Indo-European *dʰubʰrós "deep". Alternatively, it could be from Old Norse dofi "numbness, torpor", perhaps with the meaning "lazy one", or from daufr "deaf". In Norse mythology this is the name of a giant who lived in the Dofrafjall (Dovrefjell) mountain range.
Means "rising moon" in Turkish, from doğan meaning "rising" and ay meaning "moon".
Coined by Sabino Arana Goiri and Koldo Elizalde as a Basque equivalent of Deogracias.
Dogberry is a character created by William Shakespeare for his play Much Ado About Nothing. The name probably comes from "dogberry", another name for mountain ash, also called rowan.
The name of Dilbert's dog in the comic strip DILBERT.
Means "dew" in Icelandic, from Old Norse dǫgg.
Taken from first part of Dognat-Peregnat. Usually used to twin of Peregnat. Means "catch up" in Russian.
From Soviet propaganda slogan догнать и перегнать (dognat' i peregnat'), meaning "catch up and overtake (capitalist countries)".
Transferred use of the surname Dogo.

In the case of Uruguayan boxer Dogomar Martínez (1929-2016), it is said to be a corruption of the title Don and Omar 1, which was supposed to be his registered birth name (and still called that by his old relatives and neighbours) that his Spanish father wanted to put on the civil register.
An exhortatory puritanical name, hence it is very rarely seen.

column3: 도겸(Korean Hangul)|度慊, 島慊, etc.(Korean Hanja)
column12: From Sino-Korean 度 (do) meaning "size, extent, limit" or 島 (do) meaning “island” combined with 慊 (gyeom) meaning “pleased, satisfied”. Other hanja combinations can form this name as well.

column3: 도경(Korean Hangul)|度敬, 度景, etc.(Korean Hanja)
column12: Feom Sino-Korean 度 (do) meaning "size, extent, limit" combined with 敬 (gyeong) meaning "respect, honour" or 景 (gyeong) meaning "scenery, view". Other hanja combinations can form this name as well.

column3: 도훈(Korean Hangul)|度勲, 刀勲, 度訓, 刀訓, etc.(Korean Hanja)

column12: From Sino-Korean 都 "elegant, refined" and 熙 "bright, splendid, glorious".

column3: 도훈(Korean Hangul)|度勲, 刀勲, 度訓, 刀訓, etc.(Korean Hanja)
column12: From Sino-Korean 度 (do) meaning "size, extent, limit" or 刀 (do) meaning "sword, knife" and 勲 (hun) meaning "merits" or 訓 (hun) meaning "teaching". Other hanja combinations can form this name as well.
Alternate transcription of Korean Hangul 도현 (see Do-hyeon).
From a non-Sino-Vietnamese reading of Chinese 帶 (đới) meaning "belt, zone, joined".
From a non-Sino-Vietnamese reading of Chinese 代 (đời) meaning "lifetime, generation, living world".
From a non-Sino-Vietnamese reading of Chinese 待 (đợi) meaning "to await".

column3: 도이(Korean Hangul)|道怡, 桃怡, etc.(Korean Hanja)
column12: From Sino-Korean 道 (do) meaning "path, road, way" or 桃 (do) meaning "peach" combined with 怡 (i) meaning "cheerful, happy, joyus". Other hanja combinations can form this name as well.
Means "to follow closely, pursue" in Vietnamese.
Means "thrown up continuously (e.g. of waves)" or "to stuff, to fill" in Vietnamese.
Possibly derived from the term dobhail "unlucky".
From 都(do) meaning "captial", 道(do) meaning "road", 度(do) meaning "law" combined with 一(il) meaning "one", 日(il) meaning "day, sun". Other hanja combinations can also form this name.
Feminine form and diminutive of Dòmhnall
From Sino-Korean 桃 (do) meaning "peach" combined with 子 (ja) meaning "child". This name can be formed using other hanja combinations as well.
Comes from the name Dojen and its meaning is "chaste".

column3: 도진(Korean Hangul)|島鎭, 島辰, etc.(Korean Hanja)
column12: From Sino-Korean 島 (do) meaning “island” combined with 鎭 (jin) meaning "town, marketplace” or 辰 (jin) meaning “early morning" and also referring to the fifth Earthly Branch (7 AM to 9 AM), which is itself associated with the dragon of the Chinese zodiac. Other hanja combinations can form this name as well.

column3: 도준(Korean Hangul)|度濬, 度俊, etc.(Korean Hanja)
column12: From Sino-Korean 度 (do) meaning "size, extent, limit" combined with 濬 (jun) meaning "deep, profound" or 俊 (jun) meaning "talented, handsome”. Other hanja combinations can form this name as well.
The name of an angel who appears in the Testament of Abraham, one of the two angels (along with Puriel) charged with the task of examining the soul of each person brought to heaven after death.
Short form of Yevdokiya. Dokiya Humenna (1904-1996) was an Ukrainian writer.
From Sino-Korean 讀者 (dokja) meaning "reader". It is the name of the protagonist of the Korean webnovel Omniscient Reader's Viewpoint.
Old Hungarian diminutive of Dávid and Domonkos.

column3: 도겸(Korean Hangul)|度慊, 島慊, etc.(Korean Hanja)
column12: Alternate transcription of Korean 도겸 (see Do-gyeom).

column3: 도경(Korean Hangul)|度敬, 度景, etc.(Korean Hanja)
column12: Alternate transcription of Korean Hangul 도경 (see Do-gyeong).
Derived from Mongolian дулаан (dulaan) meaning "warm, kind".

Roman cognomen which was derived from the Latin noun dolabella meaning "small hatchet, small pick-axe".This name was borne by several Roman consuls. One of them was Publius Cornelius Dolabella (1st century BC), the son-in-law of the Roman statesman Cicero.
Feminine form and diminutive of Dòmhnall
Transferred use of the surname Dolan.
A Scottish knight in the service of lord Galehaut. Galehaut left him a viceroy of the Giant’s Isle after Tristan conquered it and slew Galehaut’s parents.
Italian form of Douceline via its latinized form Dulcelina.
Italian form of Doucelin via its latinized form Dulcelinus.
Variant of Dulcie. Popular in the UK.
Italian form of Latin name Dulcissima, meaning "sweetest", "very sweet" (superlative adjective from dulcis - "sweet"). Saint Dolcissima is a virgin and martyr, a patron saint of Sutri.

Possibly meant "the wife of Dol(a)", from the genitive of Dol(a) (an Old English masculine name or byname, itself perhaps derived from Old English dol "foolish, erring") combined with Old English wif "woman, wife".
Most likely from Persian دولت (dowlat) meaning "state, government, country" (of Arabic origin) combined with the Turkish military title beg meaning "chieftain, master".
Short form of names that end in -dolf, such as Adolf, Ludolf and Rudolf.

For men, this name is a diminutive of Dolf. For women, it is a diminutive of feminine names that contain -dolf- and -dolph-, such as Adolphine and Rudolfina.Dolfi is typically only used informally, i.e. not on birth certificates. Also, at least for women, it is rather old-fashioned and therefore rarely used now.

Dutch form of Adolf via Adolfinus. However, due to the exact similarity with the Dutch word dolfijn meaning "dolphin", there are probably cases where the parents intended to name their son after the marine mammal.
Derived from the Latin name Delphinus, which meant "of Delphi". Delphi was a city in ancient Greece, the name of which is possibly related to Greek δελφύς (delphys) "womb".

Dutch diminutive of Dolf, as it contains the Dutch diminutive suffix -je. This name is extremely rare as an official name on birth certificates: it is predominantly used informally, most often on young children.In Dutch children's literature, this is the name of the eponymous character of the popular book series Dolfje Weerwolfje ("Dolfje the Little Werewolf") written by Paul van Loon (b. 1955). A film based on the books was released in 2011 under the same name.
Asturian form and Italian variant of Adolfo.-------------------------------------Short form of Adolfo or Rodolfo.
This is the name of one of the sons of the Welsh nobleman Llywelyn Aurdorchog.
Old Norse name (perhaps originally a byname) derived from the elements dólgr meaning "enemy, fiend, battle" (cognate with Old English dolg "a wound, scar") and finnr "Sámi, Laplander".
Mongolian and Buryat form of Dolkar.
Combination of the name Dolgor and Mongolian жав (jav) meaning "salvation, deliverance".
Combination of the name Dolgor and the Mongolian feminine suffix маа (maa).

Means "White Tara's protection" in Mongolian, ultimately from Tibetan སྒྲོལ་དཀར་ (sgrol-dkar) referring to the White Tara in Buddhism, symbolizing compassion, healing, and longevity, and སྲུང་འཁོར (srung-khor) meaning "amulet, talisman, protective charm."
Derived from dolg ("hostility, battle") and þrasa ("to snort, to boast"). This is the name of a dwarf (also called Dolgþvari) in Norse mythology.
Derived from dolg ("battle") and þvari ("staff, sword, spear"). This is the name of a dwarf (also called Dolgþrasi) in Norse mythology.
Contracted form of Donaldina as well as a Latinate formation based on Gaelic Dolag, itself a feminine diminutive of Donald.

Archaic French vernacular form of Adelinde found in the Poitou-Charentes region. Today, the name is occasionally found in the Netherlands and in Afrikaans-speaking South Africa. In this case, however, the origin of the name is uncertain; it might be an adoption of the French name, but it is equally possible that it is a modern coinage, perhaps based on Dolly and names that end in -linde.

Derived from Ancient Greek δόλιος (dolios) meaning "crafty, deceitful, treacherous" (see Dolios). In Greek mythology, Dolion was the son of the god Silenus and nymph Melia, and was the eponymous founder of the Doliones tribe.

Derived from Ancient Greek δόλιος (dolios) meaning "crafty, deceitful, treacherous", which is ultimately derived from δόλος (dolos), meaning "bait, trick; deceit, guile, treachery, trickery". This was the name of a gardener slave of Penelope in the Odyssey.
Latinized form of Dolios. In Greek mythology, Dolius is one of Penelope's slaves.

From Tibetan སྒྲོལ་དཀར (sgrol-dkar) derived from སྒྲོལ (sgrol) meaning "to liberate, to save" (referring to the bodhisattva Tara 2) and དཀར (dkar) meaning "white". This is the Tibetan name for the White Tara, one of the manifestations of Tara.
Transferred use of the surname Doll.

From the English word for the US currency.From early Flemish or Low German daler, from German T(h)aler, short for Joachimsthaler, a coin from the silver mine of Joachimsthal (‘Joachim's valley’), now Jáchymov in the Czech Republic. The term was later applied to a coin used in the Spanish-American colonies, which was also widely used in the British North American colonies at the time of the American War of Independence, hence adopted as the name of the US monetary unit in the late 18th century.

This name was most notably borne by Domald of Sidraga (c. 1160-1243), a powerful Dalmatian nobleman and feudal lord who for several years was Prince of the city of Split, which was (and is) located in what is nowadays Croatia. Since not much is known about his personal life (such as the family that he was born into, which thus casts some doubt on his ethnicity), we cannot say anything for certain about the meaning and origin of his given name.If we assume that he was an ethnic Slav (the chances of which are high), then his given name is most likely of Slavic origin also. Its first element is then almost certainly derived from Slavic domu meaning "home, house" (see Domagoj). The second element of his name is much less certain, but it seems that there is a chance that through metathesis, it might be derived from Slavic vladeti meaning "to rule" (see Vsevolod) or even Slavic mladu meaning "young" (see Mladen).But if Domald was not an ethnic Slav, he might have been a Dalmatian Italian instead, in which case it seems likely that his name is of Germanic origin. After all, in his day, Italians were well familiar with Germanic given names, thanks to the influence of the Ostrogoths, the Lombards and the Franks a few centuries prior. His name should then be a variant of Domuald, which is the ancient Germanic cognate of the Old Norse name Dómaldr. It could even be a hybrid Latin-Germanic name, as these existed in Italy as early as the 8th century AD. The name should then consist of Latin dominus meaning "master, ruler, lord" (ultimately from either Latin domus "house" or Latin domo "to tame") and of Germanic wald meaning "power, rule".All in all, it is clear that at least in the case of the aforementioned Dalmatian nobleman, there are multiple possibilities for the etymology of the name Domald. But until we find out more about his personal life, none of them can ever truly be ruled out and should thus be kept in mind.

Variant of Dómaldr. Dómaldi was a legendary Swedish king who appears in the epic works 'Heimskringla' and 'Ynglinga saga' written in the 13th century by Snorri Sturluson.

Anglicized form of Domhanghart.This name is best known for being the name of saint Domangard of Maghera, an Irish saint from the late 5th century who was (and still is) also known under the name Donard (see Donard). He lived and died on a mountain that is part of the Mourne Mountains (which are located in what is nowadays county Down in Northern Ireland), which has resulted in said mountain eventually becoming named after him: it is now known as Sliabh Dónairt in Irish (and by its anglicization Slieve Donard in English), which translates to "mountain of Donard" in English.

Derived from "domun" (world) and "gart" (favor, protection, or possibly "spear"). A personal name used in early Irish and Scottish Gaelic royal lineages.Domangart Réti was king of Dál Riata in the early 6th century, following his father's death, Fergus Mór.

Modern Scandinavian form of both Dómari and Dómarr. However, when used in the context of Norse mythology, it strictly refers to the latter name.In Norse mythology, this was the name of a Swedish king who had inherited the throne after his father was sacrificed to the gods by his people, in the hope that his death would bring about a period of prosperity.
Derived from Slavic dom "house" combined with Slavic rad "care".

Derived from Gothic dôms (which is cognate with Old High German tuom) meaning "judgement" combined with Gothic hardus (hart in Old High German) meaning "brave, hardy".This name was borne by an obscure 6th-century Frankish saint, who was one of the disciples of the Frankish missionary and saint Marculf (better known under the French names Marcou, Marcouf and Marcoul). He died either on the same day as Marculf did, or several days afterwards. As a result, they were buried together (along with an other disciple of Marculf's) in the same tomb in the abbey of Nanteuil, which was located in the diocese of Coutances in the Cotentin Peninsula of Normandy.

Derived from the Old Norse noun dómari meaning "judge". The modern Swedish form of this word is domare, whilst dommer is the modern Danish and Norwegian form. All of the aforementioned words ultimately come from the Old Norse noun dómr meaning "judgement".Also compare the related ancient Scandinavian name Dómarr, which is so similar to Dómari that they are often confused with each other.

Derived from Old Norse dómr meaning "judgement" combined with either Old Norse herr meaning "army" or Old Norse arr meaning "warrior" (both ultimately come from Proto-Norse harja meaning "army" as well as "warrior").Also compare the related ancient Scandinavian name Dómari, which is so similar to Dómarr that they are often confused with each other.
Of debated origin and meaning. Theories include a variant of Tomaš and a short form of names like Domarad, Domasław and Domawit.

His filmography includes such films as Beauty and the Bastard (Tyttö sinä olet tähti, 2005), Lapland Odyssey (Napapiirin sankarit, 2010), Heart of a Lion (Leijonasydän, 2013), Tom of Finland (2017) and Tolkien (2019).

Diminutive of Domenico. Domenico Zampieri (1581-1641), known by his diminutive, Domenichino after his shortness, was an Italian Baroque painter of the Bolognese School of painters.

Anglicized form of Dometianus. In other words, one could say that this name is a variant form of Domitian. A known bearer of this name was saint Dometian, who was bishop of Melitene (now Malatya in Turkey) in the 6th century AD.
Variant form of Domitianus (see Domitian). Also compare Dometius.

This name is perhaps best known for being the name of saint Dometius of Persia (4rd century AD), who is also frequently mentioned as Domitius in relevant sources. Since most sources claim that the name Dometius is of Latin origin and virtually means "to tame", it is most likely a variant form of the name Domitius. However, there are a few sources that state that Dometius is of Greek origin. That is quite doubtful, but not necessarily impossible. The original Greek form of the name would then be Δομέτιος (Dometios), and it might be derived from Greek δόμεναι (domenai) meaning "to give". Alternatively, derivation or relation to Greek δομάω (domaō) meaning "to build" - ultimately from Greek δομή (domē) "building" - is also possible. But again, derivation from Greek is unlikely for the name Dometius - derivation from Latin is the most plausible option.

Contracted form of the early medieval Irish given name Domhan-Gabh-Art, which is said to mean "I take Art from the world (to serve his Heavenly Master)" in Irish, which refers to the legend of High King of Ireland Art mac Cuinn. The name consists of Irish domhan meaning "the world", Irish gabh meaning "I take" and the given name Art.
Derived from Old English dom "judgement, law" and here "army". Cognate to Old Norse Dómarr.
Derived from Old Norse dómr "judgement", "legal sentence", "fate", "doom" and hildr "battle", "fight".
Short form of Dominik, Dominic and other names used in various countries, as well as a Croatian short form of Domagoj.

Derived from medieval Latin domicella, which is the feminine form of domicellus, which literally means "little master" and was a term used to denote a young nobleman and/or junker. The term is a contraction of dominicellus, which is a diminutive of the Latin noun dominus meaning "master (of the house), lord".With that said, you might also want to take a look at the name Domitilla for comparison, as not only is it etymologically related, but it has occasionally also been found spelled as Domicilla and even Domicella.Lastly, a known Lithuanian bearer of this name was the graphic artist and book illustrator Domicelė Tarabildienė (1912-1985).
Variant of Domicella influenced by names ending in -etta.
Languedocian and Gascon form of Domitian.

Feminine form of Domiducus. In Roman mythology, the goddess Domiduca protected children on the way back to their parents' home. She and her male counterpart Domiducus were also deities of marriage who accompanied the bridal procession as the newlywed couple arrived to their new home together on the wedding night. The names occur as epithets of Jupiter and Juno. When the bride has been led home, 'the god Domitius is employed to install her in her house.'

Means "guiding home" or "bringing home", derived from Latin domus "house, home" and the verb ducere "to lead, to guide". Domiducus and Domiduca were epithets of the Roman gods Jupiter and Juno respectively, as marriage deities who brought or conducted the bride to her husband's home.

Short form of Dominicus. Known bearers of this name include Dutch radio DJ Domien Verschuuren (b. 1988), Belgian journalist and author Domien Sleeckx (1818-1901) and Belgian actor and director Domien De Gruyter (1921-2007).

A known bearer was English bounty hunter Domino Harvey (1969-2005), whose mother named her for the French model Dominique "Domino" Sanda (1951-).

From the Latin word dominus meaning "lord, master".

Probably derived from Ancient Greek δόναξ (donax) meaning "reed; anything made of a reed". This is the name of one of seven Hesperides (nymphs of the evening) depicted on a Late Classical period vase, along with Aiopis, Antheia, Calypso, Mermesa, Nelisa and Tara.

Anglicized form of Gaelic Domnall Bán meaning "Domnall the Fair", a nickname of Donald III, King of Scots, the second known son of Duncan I. Contraction of Russian дочь народа (doč naroda) meaning "daughter of the people". This name was created by Communist parents who were eager to reject traditional names.

From Sino-Korean 東 (dong) meaning "east" and 文 (mun) meaning "writing".

column12: From Chinese 东 (dōng) meaning "east" combined with 平 (píng) meaning "level, even, peaceful" or 萍 (píng) meaning "to wander, to travel around". Other character combinations can form this name as well.

column3: 东泉, 冬泉, 栋泉, 东权, 栋权, etc.(Chinese)|東泉, 冬泉, 棟泉, 東權, 棟權, etc.(Traditional Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 东 (dōng) meaning "east", 冬 (dōng) meaning "winter" or 栋 (dòng) meaning "pillar, beam" combined with 泉 (quán) meaning "spring, fountain" or 权 (quán) meaning "power, right, authority". Other character combinations can form this name as well.
From the Chinese 冬 (dōng) meaning "winter" and 娆 (ráo) meaning "graceful, charming, fascinating".
From Sino-Korean 東 (dong) "east, eastern" and 林 (rim) "forest, grove".

column3: 东荣, 东荣, 冬荣, 东融, etc.(Chinese)|東榮, 東榮, 冬榮, 東融, etc.(Traditional Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 东 (dōng) meaning "east" or 冬 (dōng) meaning "winter" combined with 荣 (róng) meaning "glory, honour, flourish, prosper" or 融 (róng) meaning "fuse, harmonize". Other character combinations can form this name as well.

column3: 东升, 东生, 东昇, 冬升, 冬生, etc.(Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 东 (dōng) meaning "east" or 冬 (dōng) meaning "winter" combined with 升 or 昇 (shēng) meaning "rise, ascent" or 生 (shēng) meaning "living, fresh". Other character combinations can form this name as well.

column3: 동수(Korean Hangul)|東秀, 東洙, 東脩, etc.(Korean Hanja)
column12: Alternate transcription of Korean Hangul 동수 (see Dong-su).

column3: 동수(Korean Hangul)|東秀, 東洙, 東脩, etc.(Korean Hanja)
column12: From Sino-Korean 東 (dong) meaning "east" combined with 秀 (su) meaning "luxuriant, beautiful, elegant, outstanding", 洙 (su) referring to a river in China or 脩 (su) referring to a type of dried meat given to teachers as a form of payment. Other hanja combinations can form this name as well.

From Sino-Korean 東 (dong) meaning "east" or 桐 (dong), referring to the paulownia coreana tree, and 雨 (u) meaning "rain," 佑 (u) meaning "help, assist" or 宇 (u) meaning "house," among other hanja combinations.
From Sino-Korean 棟 "the main beams supporting a house" or 東 "east, eastern" (dong), and 旭 "rising sun; brilliance; radiant" (uk).
From Sino-Korean 東 "east, eastern" and 雲 "clouds".
From Sino-Korean 烔 "heat" and 完 "complete, finish, settle; whole".

From Chinese 东 (dōng) meaning "eastern", 王 (wáng) meaning "king", and 公 (gōng) meaning "duke, lord". Dongwanggong was the male counterpart of Xiwangmu. He ruled in the east and was associated with Yang energy (as opposed to Xiwangmu’s Yin). One Han Dynasty source describes him as a humanoid with a tiger’s tail and bird’s face, riding on a black bear. He was later absorbed into Daoist religion along with his female counterpart, though his cult was never as prominent as hers.
From Sino-Korean 東 (dong) meaning "east" and 原 (won) meaning "source, origin, beginning".
From Chinese 东 (dōng) meaning "east" combined with 香 (xiāng) meaning "fragrant". Other character combinations can form this name as well.

column3: 东晓, 冬晓, etc.(Chinese)|東曉, 冬曉, etc.(Traditional Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 东 (dōng) meaning "east" or 冬 (dōng) meaning "winter" combined with 晓 (xiǎo) meaning "dawn, morning". Other hanzi combinations are possible.

column3: 东亚, etc.(Chinese)|東亞, etc.(Traditional Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 东亚 (dōngyà) meaning "East Asia". Other hanzi combinations are possible.

column3: 东岩, 冬艳, 冬炎, etc.(Chinese)|東岩, 冬艷, etc.(Traditional Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 东 (dōng) meaning "east" or 冬 (dōng) meaning "winter" combined with 岩 (yán) meaning "cliff, rocks" or 艳 (yàn) meaning "beautiful, gorgeous". Other hanzi combinations are possible.

column3: 东阳, etc.(Chinese)|東陽, etc.(Traditional Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 东 (dōng) meaning "east" combined with 阳 (yáng) meaning "light, sun, male". Other hanzi combinations are possible.

column3: 동연(Korean Hangul)|東延, 冬延, etc.(Korean Hanja)
column12: From Sino-Korean 東 (dong) meaning "east" or 冬 (dong) meaning "winter" combined with 延 (yeon) meaning "stretch, prolong". Other hanja combinations can form this name as well.
From Sino-Korean 東 (dong) "east and 榮 "glory, honor; flourish, prosper".
From the Chinese 冬 (dōng) meaning "winter" and 樱 (yīng) meaning "cherry, cherry blossom" or 瑛 (yīng) meaning "luster of gems, crystal".
From Chinese 冬 (dōng) meaning "winter" combined with 雨 (yǔ) meaning "rain" or 玉 (yù) meaning "jade, precious stone, gem". Other character combinations are possible.
From Sino-Korean 東 "east, eastern" and 潤 "soft; sleek".
Short form of names ending in -donia, such as Aldonia, Fredonia, and Caledonia.
Variant of Donnie or a diminutive of Donna.
Elaboration of Don in the form of Daniel.
Unisex variant of Donal, Donald, Donnell, Donelle and other names containing the same sound.
Most likely given in reference to any of a few American towns, or the character Tom Doniphon of the 1962 film "The Man Who Shot Liberty Vance".
Asturian and Aragonese form of Dionysius.

Spanish diminutive of Donata. As an English name, Donita may perhaps have been derived from Spanish doñita meaning "little lady", which is comparable to how Donna was derived from Italian donna meaning "lady".Known bearers of this name include the American Christian novelist Donita K. Paul (b. 1950), the American singer-songwriter Donita Sparks (b. 1963) and the Filipino-American actress Donita Rose (b. 1974).
Tajik and Uzbek form of Daniyar.
Hungarian phonetic rendering of French Denise.

From the surname of an Italian composer Donizetti, which means "descended from Donizo" in Italian, Donizo being an Italian Christian monk.A notable bearer of the name is Donizetti Tavares de Lima, a Brazilian Catholic priest.

Alternate transcription of Russian Доня (see Donya). In languages other than Russian, the name Donja can also be derived from the Spanish word doña meaning "lady", in which case it is a more phonetical spelling of the word.Also compare the South Slavic name Dunja, which is very similar in appearance and can also be etymologically related.
Derived from Albanian don "will; desire" and jetë "life".
Diminutive of Aldona via Aldónka and Donata.
From English word "donkey". This name is borne by Donkey Kong from the Super Mario games, and Donkey from the Shrek movie series.
Transferred from the Irish surname, Donley.

Meaning uncertain. It might possibly be a feminization of Donnie, or a combination of Donna with a feminine name ending in -ae. Lastly, when spelled with diacritics, this name might be a creative variant of Danaë (or otherwise inspired by it).
Manx form of Donnchadh. This name has traditionally been Anglicized as Dennis.
A combination of Donna and Lee.
Transferred use of the surname Donnally.
Combination of Donna and the popular suffix -lyn.

Combination of Donna and Mira. This is the name of a hobbit mentioned in Tolkien's legendarium. Donnamira is one of the daughters of Gerontius Took, who married into the Boffin family. Her name is meant to be similar to the names of her sisters, Belladonna and Mirabella.
Name of a Gaelic priest and early saint. He is the patron saint of Eigg.
